# Front Cover of the Volume

->[Half-leather binding with marbled paper]<-

This volume is protected by a traditional **half-leather binding** <term>half-leather: a binding style where the spine and corners are reinforced with leather, while the sides are covered in paper or cloth</term>. The decorative boards feature **marbled paper** <term>marbling: a decorative technique where colors are floated on a liquid surface and then transferred to paper to create stone-like patterns</term> in a striking pattern of dark green and black.

The spine and corner pieces are crafted from a tan-colored material, likely calfskin or goatskin, which was a common choice for durable library bindings in the 18th and 19th centuries.

# **Of Leon Battista** Alberti, **a most distinguished**
## **Florentine man, Ten Books On the Subject of Building.** <note>original Latin: "De re ædificatoria". This is the first great modern treatise on architecture, written by the "Renaissance Man" Alberti in the 1400s.</note> **A work**
## complete and finished: and diligently revised.

**However, this entire work**, which previously was read as a continuous discourse <note>the translator/editor is explaining that earlier editions were just long blocks of text without breaks</note>, **has recently been divided into chapters**, with several noteworthy subjects taken from the text and noted in the margin. **Also, a not-inelegant table** of these chapters has been made: **with a very clear index** of the words and of the things themselves worthy of knowing which are in the margin.

---

->**For sale in Paris** at the Golden Sun <note>original: "Sole aureo". This was the famous printing shop of Berthold Rembolt on the Rue Saint-Jacques.</note> on St. James Street.<-
->And at the sign of the **Three Crowns** opposite St. Benedict's.<-

<meta>This page follows the title page of Leon Battista Alberti's 'De re aedificatoria' (1512 edition). It contains a commendatory poem by Baptista Siculus, a common feature in Renaissance books where a contemporary scholar praises the author and the printer to encourage potential buyers.</meta>

### Baptista Siculus, in the persona of the author, to the Reader.

Your noble work would still survive now, Daedalus <note>The mythical master craftsman and architect of the Labyrinth.</note>, if you
had read me: you would have seen the trembling arms of your young son
flying through the air on strong wings <note>A reference to Icarus; the poet suggests Alberti’s technical knowledge is so great it could have perfected even mythical inventions.</note>.
And Archimedes could have rejoiced in finding the base from which
he might move the whole world <note>Refers to Archimedes' famous saying: "Give me a place to stand, and I will move the Earth."</note>; and freed from care,
if anyone burns to split the northern mountains:
let him surpass Babylon <note>Refers to the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, one of the Wonders of the Ancient World.</note> with constant labor:
and build hanging peaks on high Olympus.
Mount Athos is said to have been sailed through <note>A reference to the canal cut through the Mount Athos peninsula by the Persian King Xerxes.</note>; human skill taught
how to join lands with bridges: but we wish
that these things which this page marks should please you no less:
this machine <note>Here, "machina" refers to the book itself or the architectural methods it contains.</note> of ours will fight against armed walls
more cautiously: by this, an enemy can protect himself from an enemy:
and the bolts of the Thunderer <note>Jupiter, the god of lightning.</note> would have harmed the earth-born <note>The Giants of Greek mythology who rebelled against the gods.</note> less:
and the arms of the Sicilian smiths <note>The Cyclopes, who worked in the forge of Vulcan under Mount Etna.</note> would have sweated in vain:
nor would Enceladus <note>A Giant buried under Mount Etna; his stirrings were said to cause earthquakes.</note> now be crushed by Sicilian sand.
In what order a private house or royal roofs are built;
how you may adorn the sacred places of the gods or profane ones,
you will be certain: how you may cultivate the fields; how the fertile 
field may rise from there, so that the joyful granaries can scarcely hold the harvests:
from there you may correct the faults of works by what rule; or what 
limit each person should finally set for things to be done. 
Added to these things is the grace of the Roman tongue <note>The Latin language.</note>:
if by chance it pleases you to speak from the mouth without turning pale 
from any fault: here is eloquence: and you will have something to imitate.
And things which no monuments of the ancients gave to you:
here you will learn: if it does not weary you to turn over my pages 
for reading: if you learn to spare your stingy, greedy purses: 
if the bookseller fills his wide hands with ringing bronze <note>Coins.</note>.
May you not regret having read our labors: 
which the clever printer has produced with swift art 
and the strength of a learned right hand.

->**THE END.**<-

<note>Below the text is the printer's mark of Franciscus de Silva. It depicts a tree with a bird perched atop its branches. To the left of the trunk is the letter 'F' and to the right is the letter 'S', representing the printer's initials.</note>

<meta>This page continues the front matter of Leon Battista Alberti's 'De re aedificatoria', printed in Paris in 1512. Following the introductory poem on the previous page, this is the formal dedication letter written by the editor and printer Geoffroy Tory to his patrons from his hometown of Bourges.</meta>

# Geoffroy Tory of Bourges to Philibert Babou and Jean Aleman the Younger, most distinguished men.
->Sends heartiest greetings.<-

<margin>M</margin>y most virtuous and accomplished friends, there is no one who does not know that our ancestors, content with their own integrity, once practiced their method of building with little art and elegance. Content indeed with mere simplicity, they constructed and lived in houses and dwellings without great luxury or splendor. It has finally come to this: that with minds now somewhat awakened, buildings are being constructed and added to everywhere that are quite distinguished. Truly, from that time when that high-spirited King, the terror of all Italy, **Charles VIII**, returned from Naples as a victor with great glory, the art of building—certainly quite beautiful, in the Doric and Ionic styles <note>The "orders" of classical Greek architecture, rediscovered during the Renaissance.</note>, and also in the modern Italian style—began to be practiced most excellently here in France. At Amboise, Gaillon, Tours, Blois, Paris, and a hundred other noble places, one can now see conspicuous buildings in the ancient style, both public and private. One can, I say, perceive many things so polished and sculpted to perfection <note>original: "ad unguem", literally 'to the fingernail,' a phrase used by ancient stonemasons to describe a perfect, smooth joint.</note> that the French themselves seem to clearly surpass and outdo not only the Italians but even the Dorians and Ionians, the original teachers of the Italians. 

With these matters and talents flourishing so excellently, I thought it best to offer a very useful work, and to add my own diligence to it. **Leon Battista Alberti**, a familiar and brilliant author on architecture, was hiding with me, as if asleep. He seemed most worthy to be given to the press in France at this timely moment for the delight and assistance of famous and superior minds. He seemed most worthy to me, I say, and especially so because the ten books themselves, of which the whole work consists, are divided by chapters. These very chapters were accurately and diligently organized by **Robert Duré Fortunatus**, a man learned in good literature and formerly a principal at his College of Plessis in Paris during the four years I was teaching there. He gave them to me for copying, not grudgingly, but as a gift. I copied them, and furthermore I polished the entire work, cleansed it of very many errors, and transcribed the essence of the text in the margin. I have now given it to the printer to be published. I pray, most celebrated men of Bourges, allow this excellent work to go forth happily under your names—which I must always honor—into the hands of all talented people and students. 

Farewell, you pillars and most beautiful ornaments of our homeland.

At Paris, in the district of the College of Coqueret. August 18, 1512. <note>original: "xv. kal. septembres," the 15th day before the Kalends of September.</note>
->CITIZEN.<-

<summary>This is a dedicatory letter by the famous scholar-printer Geoffroy Tory, introducing Leon Battista Alberti's architectural treatise to a French audience and praising the recent arrival of Renaissance style in France following Charles VIII's Italian campaigns.</summary>
<keywords>Geoffroy Tory, Leon Battista Alberti, architecture, Bourges, Charles VIII, Robert Duré, French Renaissance, printing history</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from the contemporary (1512) preface by the editor Geoffroy Tory to the original 1485 dedication written by the famous humanist scholar Angelo Poliziano. It serves as a bridge between the publication's French context and its prestigious Florentine origins.</meta>

# A Recommendation of the Author by Angelo Poliziano to Lorenzo de' Medici.

**B**aptista Leo <note>Leon Battista Alberti (1404–1472), the quintessential "Renaissance Man"—architect, linguist, philosopher, and cryptographer.</note> the Florentine, of the most noble family of the Alberti, a man of elegant wit, the sharpest judgment, and exquisite learning, after leaving many other outstanding monuments to posterity, labored over ten books on architecture. Just as he was about to publish them—revised, polished, and dedicated to your name—he passed away. His brother Bernardo, a prudent man and one of your foremost admirers, wishing both to honor the memory and will of such a great man and to show gratitude for your favors toward him, presents these books to you, Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent," the de facto ruler of the Florentine Republic and one of the most powerful patrons of the Italian Renaissance.</note>, transcribed from the original manuscripts <note>original: "archetypis"</note> and bound into a volume. 

He indeed desired that I should adorn the gift itself and the author, Baptista, with rhythmic words. This I decided I should by no means do, lest I diminish the praise of so perfect a work and so excellent a man through the fault of my own talent. For far greater acclaim will come to the work itself from being read than anything I could achieve with words. Moreover, the praises of the author dread not only the narrowness of a letter but the poverty of my speech entirely. Indeed, no literature, however remote, and no discipline, however hidden, escaped this man. You might doubt whether he was more naturally suited for oratory or poetry; whether his speech was more serious or more witty. He so thoroughly examined the remains of antiquity that he both grasped the entire method of ancient building and restored it as a model. Thus, he devised not only machines, scaffolding <note>original: "pegmata"</note>, and many automatons <note>original: "automata," referring to self-moving mechanical devices which were a fascination of the era.</note>, but also admirable forms for buildings. Furthermore, he was considered an excellent painter and sculptor. Yet, in the meantime, he mastered all these things so precisely <note>original: "ex amussim," literally 'according to the carpenter's rule.'</note> that few could master even one. 

Therefore, concerning him, I think it better—as Sallust said of Carthage <note>A reference to the Roman historian Sallust, who wrote in *The Jugurthine War* that it is "better to be silent than to say too little" about such a great city.</note>—to remain silent than to say too little. Now, Lorenzo, I wish for you not only to grant this book a primary place in your library but also to read it diligently yourself and take care that it is read by the public and published. For it is worthy of flying through the mouths of learned men, and the patronage of literature <note>original: "patrocinium literarum"</note>, deserted by others, now rests almost entirely on you alone. Farewell.

<summary>This page contains a celebratory dedication by Angelo Poliziano to Lorenzo de' Medici, praising the late Leon Battista Alberti's genius and presenting his seminal ten-volume work on architecture.</summary>
<keywords>Angelo Poliziano, Lorenzo de' Medici, Leon Battista Alberti, architecture, Renaissance humanism, patronage, Sallust, classical antiquity</keywords>

# Index of books & chapters.
## Leon Battista Alberti the Florentine’s Index to the Ten Books on the Art of Building.

The Author’s preface, containing the necessity of the art of building, the utility of the undertaken work, its causes, and its order.

### ¶ Book One: On Lineaments <note>Alberti uses the term "lineaments" to describe the conceptual design or "lines" conceived in the mind, distinct from the physical materials of the building.</note>.

The power and reasoning of lineaments; and what a lineament is. Folio 4, front. Chapter 1.

The six primary parts of dwellings or buildings: Region, Site <note>original: "Area"</note>, Partitioning, Wall, Roof, and Opening. Three qualities contributing to each of these parts: Healthfulness, Firmness, and Amenity <note>original: "Amenitas," often translated as "delight" or "beauty."</note>. Folio 4, back. Chapter 2.

Concerning the region: the sky, or air, the sun, and the winds that cause the air itself to vary. Folio 4, front <note>The folio numbers in this index appear to refer to the printed leaves of the 1512 edition.</note>. Chapter 3.

Which region is best and most convenient from among those things which are plainly visible and under observation. Folio 5, back. Chapter 4.

Subtler signs for selecting a region: from the abundance of fruits, the multitude of elderly people, the beauty of the youth, and the integrity of births without deformities <note>original: "monstris," referring to birth defects as an indicator of environmental health.</note>. The size of limbs. The rarity of thunder, lightning, floods, and earthquakes. Proved by long observation and similarity to other places. Folio 7, back. Chapter 5.

Other more hidden benefits and disadvantages of a region, whether endowed by divine nature or by chance upon places, which a wise and well-considered person should inspect. Folio 8, back. Chapter 6.

On the site; and on the types of lines. Folio 9, front. Chapter 7.

The types of forms and figures for sites, and which of them are more useful and firm. Folio 10, front. Chapter 8.

On partitioning; and on the congruence of the parts or members to the whole and among themselves: modesty and a compact variety. Folio 11, back. Chapter 9.

On the forms of walls and columns: length, thickness, dimension, shapes, and adjacent elements. Folio 12, back. Chapter 10.

❦ How useful roofs may be: both for the inhabitants themselves and for the other parts of the buildings; and their diverse types and forms. Folio 14, front. Chapter 11.

On openings: namely windows, doors, and other things that do not pass through the entire thickness of the wall: what kind, how many, and how large. Folio 14, back. Chapter 12.

On stairs and their types. On the odd number of steps, their quantity, the intervening landings, the exit for smoke and water, the placement and opening of hearths, the mouths of wells, and sewers. Folio 16, back. Chapter 13.

### ¶ Book Two: Which is Titled "On Materials."

That which must be turned over often and much in the soul and mind beforehand, and using a small board or tablet... <note>This entry is cut off as the page ends, referring to Alberti's advice to use scale models and drawings before building.</note> Chapter 1.

## Index of books & chapters.

...or by any other thing, the whole work and its individual parts are to be prefigured by scale models <note>original: "modulis." Alberti championed the use of physical models to catch design errors before construction began.</note>, adding or subtracting without penalty, to determine what kind of building it will be, and of what quality and size; lest you repent of the deed once the work is done, and have to say: "I would not have wanted this. I would have preferred that." Folio 17, side 2.

<margin>Chapter II</margin> That nothing be beyond one's strength or against nature; but who you are, what you are doing, and in what place. Folio 18, side 2.

<margin>Chapter III</margin> Ensure first by the advice and example of experts from where the funds <note>original: "sumptus"</note> for all things necessary to complete the work itself have been prepared. Folio 19, side 2.

<margin>Chapter IV</margin> Which material for buildings should be prepared, which for the craftsman, and what are the origins of habitations or dwellings; the opinions of the ancients and those of the past regarding the felling of trees. Folio 20, side 1.

<margin>Chapter V</margin> How the wood <note>original: "materies," referring here specifically to timber for building</note> itself is to be guarded once trees are felled; where it is best preserved and most suitably placed to last longer. Folio 21, side 2.

<margin>Chapter VI</margin> Which trees are most suitable for buildings, for what use, and in which locations they are more eternal, firmer, and of the greatest duration. Folio 22, side 1.

<margin>Chapter VII</margin> Once more concerning trees, summarily and in general. Folio 24, side 1.

<margin>Chapter VIII</margin> Concerning stones: when they should be quarried and placed into the work; which are easier to work, more resistant, better, and more durable. Folio 25, side 1.

<margin>Chapter IX</margin> I have recorded several things about stones worthy of note which the ancients remembered. Folio 26, side 1.

<margin>Chapter X</margin> Concerning bricks: from where, when, and how they are to be formed, and their advantages. Folio 27, side 1.

<margin>Chapter XI</margin> The various species and natures of lime and gypsum, their similarities and differences; and several things about these not unworthy of knowing. Folio 28, side 1.

<margin>Chapter XII</margin> The three kinds of sands; also the diverse materials for building in various places. Folio 29, side 2.

<margin>Chapter XIII</margin> Whether observing the proper time for starting buildings is beneficial, and with what prayers, auguries <note>Alberti often blends his Christian worldview with the "auguries" or omens of classical Roman architects.</note>, or veneration the beginning should be undertaken. Folio 30, side 2.

## Index of books & chapters.

...stakes and piles are to be driven into the ground not with heavy mallets but with frequent blows until they are flush with the surface. Folio 33, side 2.

<margin>Chapter 4</margin> On the nature, shape, and condition of stones, the binding quality of lime and mortar, and a brief recollection of the ties and fastenings that pertain to the matter. Folio 34, side 2.

<margin>Chapter 5</margin> Certain doctrines on filling the substructures <term>substructures: pedamenta, referring here to the foundation fillings or the structural supports prepared up to ground level</term> up to the level of the open area, drawn from the monuments and examples of the ancients. Folio 35, side 1.

<margin>Chapter 6</margin> Ventilation channels or air-holes to be left in thicker walls from the bottom to the top; what the difference is between the foundation filling and the wall, and the primary parts of the wall. Types of masonry; the material and openings of the base <note>original: "podium," referring to the lower part of a wall or a continuous pedestal</note>. Folio 36, side 1.

<margin>Chapter 7</margin> On the weaving and connection of stones, and which types are made stronger or weaker by their composition or origin; and on the corners of walls and floor-planks. Folio 37, side 1.

<margin>Chapter 8</margin> On the parts of the filling <note>the 'infill' material used between the two faces of a wall</note>, the outer casings, and the types of framework <note>original: "infascinamentis," referring to bundles of sticks or wattle-work used as reinforcement</note>. Folio 37, side 2.

<margin>Chapter 9</margin> On the binding of stones, their connection, and also on the support of cornices, so that many stones may be gathered into the solidity of the wall. Folio 39, side 2.

<margin>Chapter 10</margin> On the proper method of building a wall, by which it is raised with stone and made hardened with lime. Folio 39, side 2.

<margin>Chapter 11</margin> On plastering the wall and also on covering it with casings or thin veneers, a very ancient law of architects to be observed like an oracle, with some things added (perhaps) for the warding off of lightning. Folio 40, side 2.

<margin>Chapter 12</margin> On roofs, beams, and rafters; whether they be of wood or stone, "bones must never be separated from bones" <note>An Albertian principle: the structural framework, which he calls the 'bones,' must remain integrated and connected</note>. Folio 41, side 2.

<margin>Chapter 13</margin> On curved roofs and arches, their types and construction. Folio 43, side 1.

<margin>Chapter 14</margin> The types of vaults <term>vaults: testudines, literally "tortoises," a common architectural term for arched ceilings</term>, how many and what kind they are, and how they may be completed more correctly and usefully. Folio 44, side 1.

<margin>Chapter 15</margin> On the outer layers of roofs and their utility; the types, shapes, and material of roof-tiles, gutter-tiles <note>original: "imbricibus," the overlapping curved tiles used to cover the joints of flat tiles</note>, and eaves. Folio 46, side 1.

<margin>Chapter 16</margin> On pavements, from a diligent collection of Pliny, Vitruvius, and the ancients; and a record of the various times of the year, place, air, manner, and appearance for beginning and finishing works. Folio 46, side 2.

->¶Index of the contents of Book Five (which is entitled "On the Works of Individuals").<-

<margin>Chapter 5</margin> The stations for sentries in the citadel and the marketplace; beams, roofs, water, soldiers, arms, grain, feathers <note>original: "penna," used here for bedding material or fletching for arrows</note>, vinegar, wood, cisterns, small compartments, entrances, tunnels, sewers, hidden places, along with other requirements of a monarchy. Folio 64, side 2.

**Chapter 2.** Regarding the dignity, grace, pleasantness, beauty, and ornament of buildings. What these things are and how they differ from one another through a certain rational method of building; and finally, the parts of the art itself. Folio 81, face 1.

Folio I.
-> Leon Battista on the Art of Building. <-
a

# THE BEGINNING OF THE WORK BY LEON BAPTISTA ALBERTI ON THE ART OF BUILDING.
## READ WITH GOOD FORTUNE.

The Author’s Preface containing the necessity and utility of the art of building, and the reasons and order of the work undertaken.

**O**ur ancestors handed down to us many and varied arts, sought out with the greatest industry and diligence, for the purpose of leading a good and happy life. Although all these arts seem to strive, as if in competition, to be of the greatest use to the human race, we nevertheless understand that there is something innate and inherent in them whereby each seems to promise specific and different fruits above the others. For indeed we pursue some arts out of necessity; we approve others for their utility. Others are held in high esteem because they are concerned only with things most pleasing to know. It is not for me to list what these arts are, for they are readily apparent. But if you look back through the entire number of the greatest arts, you will find none at all that does not seek and contemplate its own <term>specific</term> <note>original: "proprios"; refers to the unique domain or boundary of a specific craft</note> and particular goals, setting aside the rest. Or if you finally find one which, while being of such a nature that you cannot do without it in any way, at the same time offers utility joined with pleasure and dignity, then in my judgment you will not think that architecture should be excluded from their number. For if you consider the matter more carefully, it is both publicly and privately most convenient and intensely pleasing to the human race; and in dignity, it is not last among the first. 

But before I go any further, I think I must explain whom I wish to be considered an <term>architect</term> <note>original: "architectus"; Alberti’s definition marks a pivotal shift in history, moving the architect from a manual laborer to a conceptual intellectual</note>. For I will not bring forward a carpenter <note>original: "tignarium fabrum"; literally a "timber-worker"</note>, whom you might compare to men of the highest skill in other disciplines. For the hand of the carpenter is like an instrument for the architect. 

<margin>Who is an architect.</margin> I shall define the architect as one who, by a certain and admirable method and way, has learned both to define in mind and soul, and to complete in work, whatever—through the movement of weights and the joining and accumulation of bodies—may be most beautifully suited to the most worthy uses of mankind. To be able to do this, there is need for an understanding and knowledge of the best and most worthy things. And so, such shall be the architect. 

I return to the subject. There have been those who said that water or fire provided the principles by which it came about that gatherings of men were established. But to us, looking at the utility and necessity of a roof and a wall for hu... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence: "ad ho[mines]"</note>

<summary>This is the opening page of Alberti's foundational architectural treatise, where he defines the architect not as a manual builder but as an intellectual designer and sets out the social importance of building.</summary>
<keywords>Leon Battista Alberti, architecture, definition of an architect, social utility, building necessity, Renaissance architectural theory</keywords>

--- Page 33 ---
<meta>This page continues the Preface of Alberti’s "De Re Aedificatoria." On the previous page, Alberti began discussing the dignity and necessity of architecture. Here, he shifts his focus to the "utility" of the architect, expanding the definition of the craft from simple house-building to large-scale civil and military engineering.</meta>

-> Leon Battista Alberti’s [Work] <-

<margin>
The utility of architecture.
</margin>
...men will surely be persuaded that architecture has been of great value in bringing them together and keeping them joined in society. But we do not owe the Architect only for this: that he provided safe and desired shelters against the heat of the sun and the frosts and freezes of winter—although this is by no means a small benefit—but even more because he has devised many things, both private and public, which are beyond doubt far more useful, and repeatedly most adapted to the needs of life. How many most honorable families would our cities, and others throughout the world, have utterly lost due to the ravages of time, had not their ancestral hearths <note>original: "patrij lares"; the Lares were Roman protective spirits of the household, here symbolizing the family home</note> comforted them as if they had been received back into the lap of their ancestors?

<margin>
Daedalus approved among the people of Selinus.
</margin>
His own times approved of Daedalus <note>The mythical first architect and inventor</note>, most especially because he built a grotto <note>likely referring to a vapor bath or sudatorium</note> at Selinus <note>A Greek colony in Sicily</note> from which a warm and gentle vapor breathed out and collected in such a way that it drew out heavy sweats and cured bodies with the greatest pleasure. What of others who have devised many things of this kind which contribute to good health: places for exercise <note>original: "gestationes"; specific areas designed for walking or being carried for the sake of health</note>, for swimming, baths, and the like? Or why should I mention vehicles, mills, clocks <note>original: "horaria"; devices for telling time, such as sundials</note>, and these small things, which nevertheless are of the greatest importance in conducting one's life? 

What of the supplies of water brought from deep and hidden places, and made available for such various and convenient uses? What of the trophies, shrines, sanctuaries, temples, and the like, which he invented for the practice of religion and the benefit of posterity? 

<margin>
Praise of architecture.
</margin>
What, finally, of the fact that by cutting through rocks, tunneling through mountains, filling in valleys, restraining lakes and the sea, draining marshes, building ships, straightening rivers, clearing river mouths, and constructing bridges and harbors, the architect has provided not only for the temporary convenience of men? Indeed, he has opened up access to all the provinces of the world. As a result, men have communicated to one another through mutual services their crops, spices, gems, and the skills and knowledge of things, and whatever else contributes to health and the way of life. 

Add to these the siege engines, machines, fortresses, and those things which serve to defend and increase the homeland, liberty, property, and the honor of the city, and to propagate and stabilize the empire. Indeed, I believe this: as many cities as have come under the rule of others by siege in the memory of man, if they were asked by whom they were conquered and subdued, they would not deny it was by the architect. For they easily despised an armed enemy; but they were unable to endure any longer the force of genius, the mass of works, and the power of the engines with which the architect urged, overwhelmed, and pressed them. And conversely, it never happens that those under siege consider themselves safe enough by any other means than the help and skills of the architect. Then, if you review the expeditions undertaken, you will perhaps find more victories gained by his arts and virtue than by those of the general.

<summary>Alberti argues that architecture is essential for social cohesion, public health, and global trade. He highlights its role in civil engineering—such as bridges and water systems—and its decisive impact on military victory and defense.</summary>
<keywords>utility of architecture, Daedalus, Selinus, engineering, military technology, urbanism, civil infrastructure</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the Preface of Alberti’s "De Re Aedificatoria." On the previous page, Alberti discussed the architect's role in civil and medical contexts, specifically mentioning the healing baths of Daedalus. Here, he moves to the military and civic importance of the craft, then explores the innate human desire to build and the architect's role in preserving historical glory.</meta>

## On the art of building Folio II.
### a ii

...won under his leadership and auspices; and that the enemy more often succumbed through the architect's genius without the soldier's arms, than through the soldier's sword without the architect's counsel. And what is most excellent: the architect conquers with a small force and with the soldiers kept safe. So much for utility. 

¶ Truly, how pleasing and how deeply the care and logic of building <term>logic of building (ratio): Alberti uses "ratio" to mean the underlying intellectual principles or design theory</term> resides in our minds is apparent from many things, but especially from this: that you will find no one, provided he has the means, who is not entirely devoted to building something. And if he has thought of something pertaining to the art of building, he would not fail to bring it forward willingly and gladly, publishing it for the use of men as if nature herself commanded it. 

¶ And how often it happens: that even when occupied with other matters, we cannot help but devise some buildings in our mind and spirit. And when we look at the building of others, we immediately examine and weigh the individual dimensions; according to the strength of our intellect, we investigate what might be taken away, added, or changed, so that the work might be rendered more elegant, and we even offer advice unbidden. If something is indeed well-defined and correctly finished, who would not look upon it with the highest pleasure and delight? 

Now indeed, how much architecture has not only helped and delighted citizens at home and abroad, but has even greatly honored them—why should I mention it? Who does not claim praise for himself for having built? Is it not a glory even for private individuals that we live in houses constructed with a bit more care? Good men congratulate you for having built a wall or a most elegant portico. Because you have added ornaments to the doorposts, columns, and roof, they approve and congratulate you on your own behalf and theirs. Particularly for this reason: they understand that by this fruit of your riches, you have added much beauty and dignity to yourself, your family, your descendants, and the city. 

¶ The island of Crete was made noble primarily by the <margin>The tomb of Jove in Crete.</margin> tomb of Jove <note>original: "sepulcrum iouis"; ancient authors often cited a legendary tomb of Zeus in Crete as proof of the island's antiquity</note>; nor was Delos noble only for the oracle of Apollo, which was <margin>The temple of Apollo on the island of Delos.</margin> revered for the form and appearance of the city and the majesty of the temple. As for how much building has contributed to the authority of the empire and the Latin name, I say nothing more than this: that from these ruins <note>original: "bustis"; literally funeral pyres or tombs, here referring to the physical remains of Roman antiquity</note> and remains of ancient magnificence which we see everywhere, we have learned to believe many things from the historians which might otherwise have seemed less credible. 

The prudence of the ancients is excellently confirmed in Thucydides <note>Alberti refers to Thucydides’ "History of the Peloponnesian War," where the historian notes that if Sparta were deserted, its power would be underestimated due to its lack of grand buildings, whereas Athens' ruins would make its power seem double what it was</note>: they had prepared their city with every kind of building so that they might appear far more powerful than they actually were. And who among the greatest and wisest princes did not hold the art of building among their primary cares for spreading their name and for posterity? But so much for these things. 

¶ Finally, let it be said that the stability, dignity, and beauty of the republic owe a great deal to the architect. For he ensures that in leisure we live with pleasantness, cheerfulness, and health; in business, with profit and the increase of things; and in both, without danger and with dignity. This man, therefore...

<summary>Alberti argues that architecture is an innate human drive that provides civic dignity, military advantage, and historical credibility. He concludes that the architect is essential to the republic's stability and the quality of both public and private life.</summary>
<keywords>military engineering, civic pride, Crete, Delos, Thucydides, ruins, architect's role, utility of building</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the Preface of Leon Battista Alberti’s "De Re Aedificatoria." The previous page concluded by discussing how architecture benefits both private citizens and the state, and how we instinctively judge and mentally "rebuild" the structures we see. This page transitions into Alberti's systematic study of the art and outlines the structure of the ten books to follow.</meta>

# Leon Battista On the Art of Building.

...delight and the wonderful grace of wealth; from necessity; from the assistance and protection of inventions; and from the fruit of posterity <note>original: "fructu posteritatis"; referring to the legacy left for future generations</note>, we shall not deny that [architecture] is to be approved and cultivated; and that among the leading men who have earned honors and rewards from the human race, the architect must be held. And indeed, as we understood these things to be so, we began for the sake of our own mind to investigate its art and matters more accurately: from what principles they were derived, in what parts they were contained, and how they were defined. When I found these things to be varied in kind, almost infinite in number, wonderful in substance, and incredible in utility—so much so that it was sometimes not clear which condition of men, or what part of the republic, or what state of the city owes more to the architect, or rather the inventor of all comforts: public or private; sacred or profane; leisure or business; individuals or the entire human race—I determined for many reasons, which would be long to pursue here, to collect these same things which have been committed to writing in these ten books. Here shall be the order in treating these matters. 

¶ For we notice that a building is a certain body, which, like other bodies, consists of <term>lines (lineamenta): the precise, correct, and uniform layout of the building conceived in the mind and expressed through lines and angles</term> and matter. Of these, one is produced by the intellect, the other is taken from nature. To the former, mind and thought must be applied; to the other, preparation and selection. But we understood that neither of the two is sufficient on its own for the task, unless the hand of the skilled craftsman, which conforms the matter to the lines, is also added. 

¶ And as there were various uses for buildings, it had to be investigated whether the same definition of lines suited every work. For that reason, we distinguished the types of buildings, in which we saw that the cohesion and measure of the lines among themselves held the greatest weight; from this, the primary effect of beauty emanates. Concerning beauty, we therefore began to inquire what it might be, and what kind was owed to each thing. And as errors are sometimes encountered in all these things, we investigated in what way they might be corrected and restored.

<margin>
Note what titles are treated in this entire work throughout the individual books.
</margin>
Therefore, to each book, according to the variety of matters, its own title is inscribed in this manner. For the title of the first is: **One, Lines.** **Two, Matter.** **Three, The Work.** **Four, The Work of the Community.** **Five, The Work of Individuals.** **Six, Ornament.** **Seven, Ornament of Sacred Buildings.** **Eight, Ornament of Public Secular Buildings.** **Nine, Private Ornament.** **Ten, Restoration of Works;** with additions on ships, the history of copper-working <note>original: "æraria historia"; likely referring to bronze casting and metallurgy</note>, and of numbers and lines. What the architect contributes to the business of living.

# LEON BATTISTA ALBERTI ON
## LINEAMENTS. BOOK ONE.

### ¶ The power and nature of lineaments, and what a lineament is. Chapter I.

**D**EALING with the <term>lineaments (lineamenta): the precise, linear layout of a building conceived in the mind and expressed through lines and angles</term> of buildings, we shall collect the best and most elegant principles handed down in writing by our most skilled ancestors. We shall also include those things we have observed to be skillfully practiced in their eloquent works, and we shall transfer them into this work of ours. To these we shall also add whatever we have discovered by our own talent, investigation, care, and labor, which we believe will be of use. But since I desire to be as clear as possible, and as far as possible easy and expeditious, in writing about matters of this kind—which are otherwise difficult, rough, and for the most part very obscure—we shall explain in our own manner what it is that I am undertaking. For from here, the essential sources of our subject will be revealed, allowing the rest to be discussed in a more balanced discourse. We shall therefore begin the matter thus.

¶ The whole craft of building is composed of lineaments and structure. The entire power and logic of lineaments is consumed in this: that a right, absolute, and certain <margin>ta.</margin> path be found for fitting and joining the lines and angles by which the face of the building is contained and enclosed. And indeed, it is the function and duty of the lineament to prescribe for buildings and their parts a suitable place, a certain number, a worthy proportion <note>original: "modum"; often referring to the mathematical relationship between parts</note>, and a pleasing order, so that the whole form and figure of the building already resides within the lineaments themselves. Nor does the lineament, in its essence, require material <note>original: "materiam"; the physical wood, stone, or mortar</note> to follow it. Rather, it is of such a kind that we perceive the same lineaments in many different buildings where one and the same form is seen in them—that is, where their parts, and the positions and orders of individual parts, agree among themselves in all their angles and all their lines. It is possible to prescribe entire forms in the mind and intellect, setting aside all matter. We achieve this by noting and predefining angles and lines in a certain direction and connection. Since these things are so, a lineament will therefore be a certain and constant prescription conceived in the mind, expressed through lines and angles, and perfected by a learned mind and talent. But if we wish to investigate what the building itself and the whole structure is in its own right, it will perhaps serve the matter if we consider from what beginnings and by what progress the dwellings—which are called buildings—first began and grew. If I judge correctly, we can decide thus concerning this whole matter.

<summary>Alberti introduces the first book by defining "lineaments" as the intellectual and geometric foundation of architecture, distinct from physical materials. ## ¶ The origins of habitations or buildings. Six parts: Region, Site, Partitioning, Wall, Roof, Opening. Three qualities contributing to each: Healthfulness, Firmness, Amenity.

### Chapter II.

<margin>
The first origins of buildings to be founded.
</margin>
**I**n the beginning, the human race sought for itself spaces for resting in some safe region; and having found there a site convenient and pleasant for use, they established it and occupied the location itself. They did not wish for all domestic and private affairs to occur in the same place, but rather to recline in one area, to have a hearth in another, and to arrange other things for use elsewhere. At this point, they began to contemplate placing roofs so that they might be covered from the sun and the rains. To accomplish this, they then added the sides of walls upon which the roofs might be placed. For they understood that in this way they would be safer from cold storms and frosty winds. Finally, they opened ways and windows in the walls from the ground to the heights, through which access and social gathering were provided, and through which light and breezes might be received in fair weather, and perhaps any water or vapors caught within the home might be cleared out.

Thraso.

Eventually, I judge that this matter grew through use and art. Various kinds of buildings were invented, until the subject was expanded into nearly infinite variety. For some are public, others private, some sacred, others profane; some are established for use and necessity, others for the ornament of the city, and others for the pleasure of temples. But no one will deny that all of these have flowed from the principles we have just reviewed.

Therefore, we shall define them thus: The **Region** shall be for us the extensive width and character of the whole surrounding ground where one must build, of which the site is a part. The **Site** (<note>original: "Area"</note>) will be a certain prescribed space of ground which is enclosed by a wall for use and utility. ### Chapter III.

<margin>Pure air</margin>
**T**he ancients <note>Alberti frequently refers to "the ancients," meaning Roman and Greek authorities like Vitruvius or Pliny the Elder.</note> worked very hard to inhabit a region that was as free from every harm and as full of conveniences as possible. And indeed, the breath of spirit—by which alone we sense that life is most nourished and preserved—will contribute wonderfully to health if it be as pure as possible. Then, who is there whom it escapes how much power the sky has in generating, producing, nourishing, and preserving things? Alberti follows a common Renaissance tradition of allegorizing mythological figures as physical elements; here, Pallas represents the clear, intellectual clarity of pure air.</note>: and Homer says she is a goddess and called **Glaucopis** <note>original: "Glaucopis". <margin>Pure air; what pestilential air is.</margin>
Then, on the contrary, we shall determine that the air there is **pestilential** <note>In the medical theory of Alberti's time, disease was thought to be spread by "miasma" or "pestilential air"—foul-smelling, thick vapors arising from swamps or stagnant places.</note>: where it stands thickened and foul with a certain density of either clouds or vapors. Nor shall we recount here those physical theories: by what means the vapors are drawn out from the innermost bowels of the earth by the power of the sun and lifted into the **ether** <note>The clear upper atmosphere or the "pure" air above the clouds.</note>. In which vast space of the globe they are gathered into a great heap: either they vanish by their own immense mass, or by receiving the rays of the sun, they fall to that side where they have been dried out: and by their fall they drive the air and stir up the winds. From there, driven within the ocean, they immerse themselves; finally, poured into the sea and pregnant with moisture, wandering again in the air they are restrained by the winds: and, as if squeezed like a **sponge**, they drip and rain down the moisture expressed drop by drop: which also creates new vapors from the earth. Whether these things we have recounted be true: or whether wind is a dry smoke of the earth. Or a hot evaporation moved by a driving cold: or a blast of air: or pure air moved by the motion of the world or the course and radiation of the stars: or a generative spirit of things, by its own nature restless. Or if something occurs that does not consist in itself but rather in the air, drawn from the hot force of the highest ether and a burning directed toward the liquid air. Whether some other reason and opinion of others in this inquiry is firmer and more ancient, I think it should be passed over, because perhaps it might seem irrelevant. But here, if I am not mistaken, it will allow us to interpret why it is that we see some regions of the world to be of such a kind that they enjoy the most joyful air: while others contiguous to them and placed nearby languish in a gloomier atmosphere and, so to speak, a mournful day. For I conjecture that this happens for no other reason than that they do not agree well with the sun and the winds.

# On Lineaments. Folio V.

...region from which the force of clouds and all thickness of descending vapor is far removed. Those who study these things have found that the rays and heat of the sun act more sharply where they encounter density than when they encounter rarity. In oil more than in water; in iron more than in wool. From this they argue that the air—which seethes more vehemently in such a spot than in the surrounding area—is heavy and thick. <margin>Egyptians</margin> The **Egyptians**, contending for nobility with the other nations of the world, used to boast that they were the foremost people, and that the human race was created among them in the beginning; nor should humans have been created anywhere else than where they were to live most healthily. <margin>They boasted of their glory.</margin> For they claimed that they, above all others, were miraculously gifted by the benevolence of the gods with a sort of **perpetual spring** and a constant temperature of the air. Furthermore, **Herodotus** <note>A 5th-century BCE Greek historian known as the "Father of History."</note> writes that among the Egyptians, especially those who look toward Libya—because the breezes there never vary—people are endowed with the most sound health of all. 

And indeed, I seem to see certain cities, both in Italy and among other nations, which become sickly and pestilential for no other reason than the sudden intemperance of the air, now freezing, now boiling. Therefore, it is not without reason that one must observe how much sun and what kind of sun a region receives. Let there be nothing of either sun or shade that is more than sufficient. <margin>Garamantes.</margin> The **Garamantes** <note>A powerful Saharan tribe of antiquity, often cited by classical authors like Herodotus and Pliny to illustrate the extremes of the desert heat.</note> curse the sun as it rises and sets, because it burns them with its excessive persistence of rays. Others grow pale in what is like a perpetual night. 

That things are this way is caused not only by whether they have the axis of the globe more inclined or slanted—though that indeed does much—but also by the very layout of the places: whether they are exposed to receive the suns and winds, or whether they are obstructed. I would rather bear bad breezes than winds—yet who would not bear sharp and immoderate winds more temperately than a stagnant and therefore heavy sky? "Waters," says **Ovid** <note>Ovid, *Ex Ponto*, I.v.7-8: "Stagnant waters are corrupted unless they are moved." Alberti uses this poetic authority to support a physical theory of air.</note>, "take on corruption unless they are moved." <margin>Ovid.</margin> What of the air? Surely by motion it becomes (so to speak) remarkably cheerful. For I believe it happens through motion that vapors rising from the earth are either dissipated or are "cooked" <note>original: "concoquantur". In ancient and Renaissance physics, heat was thought to "cook" or refine raw, damp vapors into healthier air.</note> and neutralized by growing warm through movement. 

But I would wish for these winds to arrive broken by opposing mountains and forests, or weary from a long journey. I would also wish that they do not blow through places from which they might carry some snatched-up evil to us. <margin>Neighborhoods with foul odors to be avoided.</margin> Therefore, I advise avoiding the proximity of anything from which something noxious might flow. In this category are foul odors and all impure vapors of marshes and especially of filthy waters and excavations. It is well known among **natural philosophers** <term>phisicos</term> <note>original: "phisicos". Referring to those who studied "physics" or the laws of the natural world, often including physicians.</note> that every river which swells from snow carries cold and thick air. But among waters, none will be more foul than that which, stirred by no motion, wastes away; and the contagion of such a neighborhood will be more sickly than the winds one might substitute for it. For they say that by their own nature, not all winds are such as to be healthy or unhealthy. But **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the massive Roman *Natural History*.</note> says that **Theophrastus** and **Hippocrates**...

<margin>The North Wind restores and preserves health.</margin>
Following the North Wind [Aquilo], all agree it is most suitable for restoring and maintaining good health. <margin>The South Wind is harmful.</margin> All natural philosophers affirm that the South Wind [Auster] is more harmful to the human race than others: for they judge that even cattle are not without danger in the pastures when the South Wind blows. Nor have they observed storks <margin>Stork.</margin> rashly committing themselves to the South Winds anywhere. <margin>Dolphins.</margin> Dolphins are said to hear voices more clearly when they are carried by the North Wind. When the North Wind blows, an eel can survive six days without water; with the South Wind, it cannot survive, such is the thickness and diseased quality inherent in this wind. Thus, just as people fall ill and become quite phlegmatic <note>Refers to the ancient medical theory of the four humors; an excess of phlegm (pituita) was thought to cause sluggishness or respiratory issues.</note> with the South Wind: so too they report the same of the "corocussuri" <note>original: "corocuſſuri"; likely a reference to the 'coracinus', a type of fish mentioned in classical natural histories like Pliny's.</note>. <margin>Those living by the Southern Sea suffer two burnings of the sun.</margin> They also disapprove of the Southern Sea for one reason especially: that because of the reflection of the rays, they judge the region to be subjected to two suns—one from the sky, the other burning from the waters. And they understand that the greatest variation in the air occurs there when the sun sets, when the freezing shadows of night arrive. And there are those who think the evening approaches and reflections of the rays—whether reflected from the waters and the sea, or from the mountains—are more troublesome than the others, because they make the place, already heated by the sun of the whole day, more than sufficiently hot, with the heat brought on and doubled by the reflections. But if it happens that along with these suns, even heavier winds have free access to you, what could be more troublesome or less bearable? Not without reason will they also greatly disapprove of morning breezes, which offer up raw, rising vapors. We have spoken of the sun and winds, by which we clearly perceive the air is varied and made healthy or unhealthy; and we have spoken as briefly as seemed necessary here: and we shall examine these things more distinctly in their proper place.

## Which region is best and most suitable among those that are visible and in the open. Chapter IV.

Folio VI.
# On Lineaments. Book I. #

<note>original: "lycratis"; refers to Dinocrates, the architect who famously proposed carving Mount Athos into a statue of Alexander the Great.</note> ...the admirable plan of Dinocrates the architect; specifically, because the inhabitants would not have an abundance of resources due to the location. Perhaps such a region could have pleased Aristotle, especially for establishing cities that would have difficult access <note>Aristotle discussed the defensive advantages of difficult terrain in his "Politics."</note>. And I find there were nations who intended their borders to be most deserted and destitute far and wide for the sake of inconveniencing enemies. Whether it is appropriate to approve of their reasoning or not, we shall discuss elsewhere. But if these things are helpful in public matters of this kind, there is no reason for me to disapprove of their custom. 

But for placing other buildings, I shall certainly prefer a region that has many and varied approaches, by which necessities can be most conveniently transported by ship, pack-animal, and wagon, both in summer and in winter. And the region itself should be neither soaked with an excess of water nor harsh with dryness, but manageable and well-tempered. Or if that cannot be had as desired, we shall choose a place that is a little cold and dry rather than one that is less hot and more than enough moist. For cold is conquered by a roof, a wall, clothing, fire, and movement. Indeed, it is not much thought that dryness has anything in itself to severely harm the bodies or minds of men. Moreover, they think that in dry places men grow hardy, and in cold ones perhaps they become robust <note>original: "horrescere"; literally "to bristle" or "shiver," here implying a rugged or vigorous physical state.</note>. But they affirm that in moist places all bodies waste away, and in hot ones they are dissolved <note>In ancient medicine, heat and moisture were thought to "soften" or "loosen" the body's integrity, leading to weakness.</note>. And one may see that both in cold seasons and among those living in a cold place, people stand with strong bodies and remain free from diseases. Yet, although minds may excel in hot places, bodies are superior in cold ones. This too I have understood from the historian Appian.

<margin>The Numidians.</margin>
That the Numidians are especially long-lived for the reason that they have no winter that is at all cold. The best region of all, then, will be one that is slightly moist and 

<margin>The best region is lukewarm.</margin>
lukewarm. For it will produce tall and graceful men, and also those who are least gloomy. In the second place, a very convenient region will be one that, in snowy provinces, has more sun than others, and in a province parched by the sun, has more moisture and shade. But a building shall be placed in no location—no matter what kind it is—more inconveniently or unbecomingly than when it is hidden within a valley. For to omit other things that are obvious: such buildings lurk without any dignity, and, with the pleasantness of the view cut off, they possess no grace. 

<margin>Take note.</margin>
What of this: that in a short time it may be overwhelmed by the ruins of rains, and flooded by surrounding waters, and once a little moisture is absorbed, it immediately 

<margin>The inconveniences of those hidden in a valley.</margin>
becomes damp; and it continually exhales earthly vapor, which is vehemently harmful to the health of men. Minds will not flourish there, as their spirits are dulled. Bodies will not endure there. With the bindings soaked, books will rot; weapons and whatever is in the storehouses will decay; finally, they will be spoiled by the excess of dampness. Then if the sun enters there, [reflected] from all sides...

...they will be scorched by reflected rays. If they do not receive the sun, the shade will grow cold and raw, and the inhabitants will become sluggish. Add to this that if the wind penetrates there, squeezed as if through narrow channels, it will be harsher and more troublesome than is proper. If the wind does not enter at all, it happens that the stagnant air there—if I may put it this way—becomes "muddy" or foul. For we might not inappropriately consider a valley of this sort to be a pool or a swamp of air. Therefore, the site’s form should be both worthy and pleasant: by no means low and as if submerged, but rather elevated and commanding a wide view <note>original: "speculatrix"; suggesting a site that acts as a lookout or watchtower</note>, where the most cheerful air is kept in motion by a constant breeze. 

Furthermore, the site should have an abundance of those things which serve both use and pleasure: water, fuel for fire <note>original: "ignem"; referring to the availability of wood or combustible material</note>, and food. But in these matters, care must be taken that nothing hinders the health and affairs of the people. Springs must be opened and tasted. Waters must also be examined by fire <note>referring to the practice of boiling water to check for residue or observing how it reacts to heat</note> to see if they have anything viscous, moldy, or "raw" <note>original: "crudulentive"; a medical term for water that is difficult for the body to process or "cook" during digestion</note> mixed within them, which might cause the inhabitants to fall into disease. 

<margin>
Note: many troubles arise from drinking unpurified water.
</margin>

I shall pass over those common effects of bad water, such as how people are made goitrous <note>original: "gutturosi"; characterized by swellings in the throat</note> or prone to stones <note>original: "calculosi"; kidney or bladder stones</note>. I also pass over those rarer wonders of waters which the architect Vitruvius <note>Vitruvius was a Roman architect whose work "De Architectura" was the primary model for Alberti</note> has collected so learnedly and elegantly. 

There exists the opinion of the physician Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine"</note> that whoever drinks water that is not purified, but is heavy and of an unseemly taste, will suffer from a burning and swollen belly. The other members of the body—the elbows, shoulder blades, and the face—will be rendered thoroughly emaciated and wonderfully thin. Add to this that, due to a defect of the spleen and badly "congealed" blood, they will fall into various and pestilential diseases. In summer, they will waste away from a purging of the belly, with flowing bile and dissolved humors <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were the bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—that determined health</note>. Then they will also labor under more serious and long-lasting diseases for a whole year: they will be pressed by <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: "aqua intercus"; literally "water under the skin," an accumulation of fluid in the body</note>, tightness of the diaphragm, and pains in the sides. 

Younger people will go mad from black bile; the elderly will burn with the fire of inflamed humors. Women will conceive with difficulty and give birth through very difficult labors. Finally, every age and sex will fall to premature death, driven and consumed by these diseases. Truly, no day of their lives will be spent that is not sad, polluted by bad humors, and vexed by every kind of disturbance; furthermore, they will always be agitated in mind, living in sorrow and mourning. 

Much more could be said about waters which ancient historians have noted—various and wonderful things, and most powerful for the well-being or illness of the human race. But those instances are rare and perhaps better suited for showing off one's expertise than for explaining the matter at hand; moreover, we shall speak more fully of waters in their own place <note>Alberti discusses water systems in detail in Book X</note>. This point, however, must not be neglected: it is evident that all things that grow are nourished by water—plants, seeds, and everything possessing that part of life that flourishes through movement—and by their fruit and abundance, men are refreshed and nourished. If this is so, we must surely scrutinize most diligently what qualities <note>original: "succos"; literally "juices" or "essences"</note> the waters have in the region where we intend to live.

Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note> says that for the most part, men are tall and strong, and endowed with a sharp wit, because they breathe pure air and drink the healthiest waters. And we shall say that water is best in taste <margin>The best water</margin> which has no taste at all; and most suitable in color which is entirely devoid of and free from any color. Then they also report that water is best which is clear, transparent, and light; which, when poured onto a white linen cloth, does not stain it; which, when boiled, leaves no dregs. Which does not make the channel through which it flows mossy, and especially does not leave the stones stained. They add that water is very useful in which legumes <note>Referring to beans, peas, or lentils</note>, when boiled, soften well; and it is good if it makes good bread.

¶ It must likewise be investigated with equal reason that the region produces nothing pestilential or poisonous, whereby those living in that place are in danger. What of this age in Apulia <margin>Poisonous spiders in Apulia.</margin> in Italy, what incredible force of poison has increased? From certain ground spiders <note>original: "araneolis"; the "tarantula"</note>, by whose bite men are incited to various delusions of madness, and are found driven as if by a frenzy. Strange to say: there is no heavy swelling, no bruise remains that appears anywhere on the body made by the bite or sting of the poisonous little beast. These they cure with the remedies of Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle, known for his work on plants</note>. Who indeed <insert>☜</insert> asserted that he healed the bites of vipers by employing a flute-player. Therefore, musicians soothe those so dazed with various sounds of musical modes. When indeed they reach their own mode of singing, they immediately rise up as if awakened: and with alacrity, out of the desire of the soul, they perform everything with a strain of nerves and strength. And yet you will see some who have been bitten dancing, others singing, others exercising and attempting other things as their desire and madness carries them even to ultimate exhaustion: nor do they stop their work for several days until they are soaked in sweat, and they recover by nothing else except the satisfaction of the madness they have conceived and begun.

### Chapter V

**M**oreover, in choosing a region, it is not enough to have looked only at those things which are exposed to view and in the open. Rather, it is necessary to have considered the whole matter in one's mind by noting more obscure signs. Indeed, the signs of the best air and healthy waters will be if that region produces an abundance of good fruit; if it supports many elderly people of great age; if it abounds with strong and beautiful youth, and with healthy and frequent births. Add to this if it produces pure offspring, defiled by no deformities. For I have indeed seen cities—which I shall not name out of respect for the times <note>Alberti likely refers to contemporary Italian cities known for poor health, but avoids offending his patrons or specific locales.</note>—in which no woman gives birth to a child that looks like a human being, but rather every mother becomes the producer of some monster. I also saw another city in Italy where goiters <term>strumæ</term> <note>Swelling of the neck, often associated with poor water quality or iodine deficiency</note>, squinting eyes, lameness, and twisted limbs were so common that almost no family grew up there that did not have someone maimed or diminished. And they certainly advise correctly: where you see frequent and extreme dissimilarities between body and body, or limb and limb, this is caused by the force and defect of the sky and air, or by some other more hidden cause of corrupted nature. And it may pertain to the matter what they say: that in thick air we feel less hungry, while in thin air they thirst more.

<margin>
Conjecture regarding future physical constitution.
</margin>
¶ Nor is it unbecoming to have conjectured the future physical constitutions of men from the form and appearance of other living creatures. For if they see that the draft animals and livestock there are very sturdy, large-limbed, and powerful, they may hope with good reason that their children will have the same. Nor will it be irrelevant if we take signs of the air and winds from other bodies in which the vigor of life is extinguished. For we can learn these things from the nearby structures of buildings; if they have become rough and decayed <note>original: "cariosa" — referring to stone rot or "cancer" of the stone</note>, it will be a sign that harmful elements are flowing in from the outside. Also, trees leaning in one direction as if by common consent, or broken, show that they have yielded to the hostile movements of the winds. And even the native stones born in those places, or placed there, if they have become excessively rotten on the surface, attest to the varying intemperance of the place—of air that is now burning, now sluggish. And without doubt, a region of this kind in which violent movements of seasons and storms rage must be avoided above all. For if the bodies of mortals...

### ¶ Other more hidden advantages and disadvantages of a region, whether endowed by nature with riches or by chance in places, which the wise man should look into with good consideration.

## Chapter VI.

**O**ne must also investigate whether that region has been accustomed to being troubled by any more hidden disadvantages. Plato used to think that in some places a certain divine power sometimes inspires and thrives, and a boundary of spirits <term>daemonum</term> <note>Alberti refers here to the Platonic "daimons," intermediary spirits that occupy specific locales, which could be benevolent or malevolent</note> is either favorable or, on the other hand, hostile to the inhabitants. Indeed, there are places where men easily go mad; where they easily give themselves over to destruction; where they easily end their lives by hanging, or by throwing themselves from a height, or by the sword and poison. Add to these that once the more secret signs of nature have been scrutinized, it is necessary to have weighed whatever pertains to the matter. 

<margin>The practice of Demetrius.</margin>
¶ An old practice derived from the time of Demetrius <note>Likely Demetrius Poliorcetes, known for his siegecraft and military organization</note> has been maintained, not only for founding cities and towns, but even for setting up daily military camps. <margin>☞</margin> This practice is that we should inspect the livers of the cattle grazed there, to see what condition and color they might be. If these should happen to appear infected with some defect, they signal that the unhealthiness of the place should be avoided. 

¶ Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, an ancient Roman scholar</note> used to say he had discovered that in certain places very tiny creatures, like atoms, fly in the air; and, taken into the lungs by breathing, they cling to the vitals. And by gnawing, they bring on a dark and rabid disease, and thus bring about plague and destruction. Nor should it be overlooked that you will find some places which, by their own nature, are void of almost all disadvantages and free from dangers. <margin>☞</margin> But they are so exposed that foreign and arriving peoples not infrequently bring plague and calamity there. And they carry this out not only with arms and injury, such as those things which might be attributed to barbarians and savages. But they also cause great harm through friendship and hospitality. Some, because they had neighbors eager for new things <note>A Latin idiom, "rerum novarum," usually referring to political revolution or social upheaval</note>, were put in danger by their ruin and loss. 

<margin>Pera.</margin>
The plague constantly vexes Pera <note>The Genoese commercial colony in Constantinople, modern-day Galata</note> on the Black Sea <note>original: ponto</note>, a colony of the Genoese <note>original: ianuenfiū</note>, because every day slaves brought there are received who are wasting away and diseased, both from sickness of the soul and from filth and squalor.

<margin>Plot.</margin>
...[space] is that which is indeed occupied for the purpose of containing a building. For this reason, the plot has nearly everything in common with the broader region that might lead to praise or blame. However, even if this is so, this investigation and observation still involve certain principles that seem to pertain uniquely and specifically to the plot itself. There are also some that do not only serve the outline of the plot, but rather, in large part, the reasoning also pertains to the region; they are of this kind: for it is necessary to consider what we are undertaking—whether it is a public work or a private one, sacred or profane, and other things of the same kind, which we shall discuss more distinctly in their proper place. For one amount of space and location is owed to a forum, another to a theater, another to a gymnasium <note>original: *palestra*, a place for exercise and wrestling</note>, and another to a temple. Therefore, the site and measure of the plot must be determined according to the purpose and use of each. But let us proceed here with these matters in general terms, as we have begun; we shall touch only upon those things we judge to be necessary, provided I first report some things concerning lines that may serve to express the matter clearly. For it is fitting for those treating the description of a plot that we settle those elements by which the outline itself is defined. All outlining, therefore, is composed of lines and angles.

<margin>Outline.</margin>
Lines are indeed the outermost part of the outline, by which the space of the plot is entirely enclosed. However, in this outline, that part of the surface positioned where two lines intersect one another is called an angle.

<margin>Angle.</margin>
Furthermore, from the mutual intersection of two lines, four angles are drawn. If each of these is equal to any of the three remaining, they shall be called **right** angles. Those which are smaller than a right angle shall be called **acute**, just as those which are larger than a right angle shall be called **obtuse**.

<margin>Line.</margin>
Likewise, of lines, one kind is straight and another is curved; there is no need here for me to mention spiral or winding lines. A straight line is an elongated drawing from point to point, drawn such that no shorter path can be made. A curved line is a part of a circle. A circle is that drawing made by one of two points: which is so rotated on the same surface that, throughout the entire path of the drawing, it is always neither more nor less distant from the unmoving center point—around which it moves—than when it first began to be drawn. But to these it must be added that the curved line, which we said was a part of a circle, is called an **Arch** <note>original: *Arcus*, which also means a bow</note> among us architects for the sake of its resemblance.

<margin>Arch.</margin>
And the line which is drawn straight between the two endpoints of a curved line shall, by a similar comparison, be called a **Chord** <note>original: *Corda*, literally the string of a bow</note>.

<margin>Chord.</margin>
And the line which extends from the center point of the chord to the arch, forming equal angles on both sides, shall be called the **Arrow** <note>original: *Sagitta*, known in geometry as the sagitta or the height of an arc</note>. And the line which, from the unmoving point...

<margin>Arrow.</margin>

any line drawn from within the circle to that same curved and outermost line of the circle shall be called the <term>Radius</term> <note>literally "a spoke" or "ray"</note>. And the name for that immovable point <margin>The Radius.</margin> which sits in the middle of the circle shall be the <term>Center</term>. And the straight line <margin>The Center.</margin> passing through the center, which cuts the curved line of the circle in two places, shall be called the <term>Diameter</term>. Among arcs, there is likewise a difference: for <margin>The Diameter.</margin> one is whole, another is diminished, and another is composite. The whole arc is that which occupies half of the circle—that is, the arc whose chord is the diameter of the whole circle. The diminished arc is one whose chord is less than the diameter; likewise, this diminished arc is a part of a semicircle. The composite arc <note>original: *compositus*, likely referring to a pointed or ogival arch</note> consists of two diminished arcs; for that reason, it forms an angle at the top where the arcs intersect each other—a thing which happens in neither the whole nor the diminished arc. Having learned these things, we shall proceed as follows.

### The types, forms, and figures of building plots, and which of them are more useful and firm. Chapter VIII.

Some plots <note>original: *arearum*, the ground space or floor plan of a building</note> are angular, others circular. Of the angular ones, some are enclosed entirely by straight lines; others by a mixture of straight and curved lines. Indeed, as for an angular plot formed by several curved lines with no straight lines interspersed, I do not recall finding such a thing among ancient buildings. But in these matters, one must observe those things which are severely criticized if missing from the parts of a building, and which are held with grace and convenience if present: that is, that a certain variety be present in the angles, the lines, and every part. Let it not be too frequent, nor entirely rare, but so placed for use and grace that whole corresponds to whole, and like to like. They use right angles <note>90-degree angles</note> very conveniently. No one has used acute angles <note>sharp angles less than 90 degrees</note>, even in the smallest and most neglected plots, unless forced by necessity; and they considered obtuse angles <note>blunt angles greater than 90 degrees</note> to be quite decent if the logic of the site or the importance of the plot compelled it, but they maintained this rule: that they should never be unequal in number <note>meaning the angles should be balanced or symmetrical</note>. They affirm that the most spacious plot of all—and the one in which less expense is required for the enclosure, whether by bank or wall—is the round one. Next to this, they consider the one that has many projecting angles. But it is necessary that the angles be entirely comparable, mutually corresponding, and equal in every plot. And yet, they especially approve of those plots which they understand allow walls to be raised conveniently to a properly determined height for the work: such as those with six or eight angles. We have also seen a plot of ten angles that was most suitable and very beautiful. It is also true that one may correctly place...
