# Leon Battista Alberti.

...plots can have twelve or even sixteen angles. We have indeed seen a plot with twenty-four angles, but such things are rare. It is necessary that the lines of the sides be equal to those directly opposite them, and nowhere in the entire work should the longest lines be driven together with the shortest ones in a single stroke. Instead, there shall be a just and fitting proportion between them, determined by the requirements of the project.

<margin>
The placement of angles.
</margin>
He <note>likely referring to Vitruvius or an idealized ancient authority</note> commands that angles be positioned facing the direction from which an onslaught or heavy weight might threaten—whether from a cliff, or the force and impetus of water or winds—so that the angle may cleave and dissipate the approaching injury or mass. The walls should struggle against these nuisances with a strong front, rather than with the weakness of their sides.

But if the other outlines of the building prevent you from using an angle as you intended, a curve must be used; for a curved line is part of a circle, and the circle itself, in the opinion of philosophers, is one entire angle. Furthermore, a plot will be situated either on a level place, on a slope, or on the very summit of a mountain. If it is placed on level ground, one must heap up the earth and build up a <term>podium</term> <note>a raised platform or pedestal that serves as a foundation</note> as a substructure. For while this contributes greatly to the building’s dignity, if it is not done, it will cause the greatest inconvenience. In level places, the flooding of rivers and rains tends to bring in silt, which causes the ground itself to swell up gradually. Additionally, due to human negligence, the rubble and refuse that are cast out daily are not carried away, and thus the ground level easily grows up around the building. Frontinus the architect <note>Sextus Julius Frontinus, a 1st-century AD Roman civil engineer and author</note> used to say that in his time, Rome had "grown" into hills because of the frequency of fires <note>the debris from collapsed buildings raised the street levels</note>. And in this present age, we see the city itself entirely overwhelmed by ruins and filth.

<margin>
A wonderful stone vessel at Ravenna placed as a roof.
</margin>
☛ I myself have seen in Umbria an ancient chapel situated in a level place, yet it was submerged for the most part because of the increase in the soil, since that plain extends beneath the mountains. But why should I mention those things beneath the mountains when there are examples at Ravenna? Near the <term>pomerium</term> <note>the sacred boundary or open space just outside a city wall</note> stands that noble temple <note>The Mausoleum of Theodoric, famous for its monolithic dome</note> whose roof is a single, solid stone vessel; even though it sits near the sea and far from the mountains, more than a fourth of its height is now immersed within the ground by the force of time. Exactly how high the elevation of any given plot ought to be will be discussed in its proper place, when we speak of these matters not briefly as we do here, but more distinctly.

Every plot, whether made by nature or art, must be extremely firm. Regarding this, I believe we should primarily listen to those who advise that we should investigate the soil's density, rarity, or softness to see if it is capable of supporting the weight of the structure by digging pits at intervals of one or two spaces. Indeed, if the building is placed on a slope, one must foresee that the higher parts do not push down with burdensome pressure, or that the lower parts, if they should move, do not pull the rest into ruin. A very firm...

# On Outlines. Book 1. Folio XI.

...and I would wish this part of the building to be fortified from every side, as it is to be the foundation for the entire work. If the plot is on a mountain peak, it must either be built up in some part or leveled by cutting away the protruding summit of the mountain. Here we must see to it that we approach the task such that, while maintaining dignity, it is done with moderate and modest expense and labor. Perhaps it will be profitable to cut away a part from the height and build up the sloping part. That architect at Alatri <note>An ancient city in Lazio famous for its exceptionally well-preserved "Cyclopean" or polygonal masonry walls</note>, a city of the Hernici located on a rocky mountain, acted very wisely in this matter. For he saw to it that the base—whether of a citadel or a temple (which alone is seen now that the other structural additions have been destroyed)—would stand supported and underpinned by the fragments cut from the highest peak. And in that work, there is something I approve of exceedingly. For he set an angle of the plot facing the direction where the mountain slope descends steeply, and he consolidated that angle with a mass of huge fragments and very large pieces of stone. And he took care in arranging the stones so that, while practicing economy, the structure would possess beauty. And I also liked the plan of that architect who, in a place where he did not have such a great supply of stone, built a mound to sustain the weight of the mountain using frequent semicircles, with the back of the curved lines turned inward toward the mountain. This structure is not only pleasing to the eye, but it is also very strong, and it accounts for the cost efficiently. For it creates a wall that is not solid, yet has as much strength as if it were entirely solid, with a width as great as the depth of the curves <term>sagittae</term> <note>Literally "arrows"; in geometry, this refers to the distance between the midpoint of an arc and the midpoint of its chord, here describing the depth of the recessed arches used to reinforce the wall</note> there. The method of Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman author of the only surviving major ancient treatise on architecture</note> also pleases me, which I see observed everywhere in Rome by ancient architects, and especially in the Mound of Tarquin <note>The *Agger Tarquinii*, a massive defensive earthwork part of the early walls of Rome</note>, namely that <term>anterides</term> <note>A technical term for buttresses or counterforts—piers built against a wall to strengthen it</note> should be substituted as supports. But they did not observe in all places the rule that the buttresses should always be as far apart from each other as the substructure itself was high. Instead, according to the firmness or (so to speak) the instability of the mountain, they placed them sometimes closer together, sometimes further apart. I have also noticed that the ancient architects were not content with just one substructure close to the plot, but wanted the entire rock face to be secured by several tiers, like steps, down to the very base of the mountain. I think their advice should by no means be neglected.

# Leon Battista Alberti.

Those [structures] placed against the mountain wall of a basilica provide a great deal of support and convenience; for they sustain the mass of the heavy mountain and intercept the moisture flowing down the slope, preventing it from entering the building. Thus, the primary parts of the basilica are rendered drier and firmer. As for the chapels situated on the other side at the bottom of the slope, they can easily bear the weight by supporting the entire upper leveled area with arched work and by checking all the downward slips of the earth. I have also observed that the architect who built the temple to Latona <note>Likely referring to the Temple of Apollo and Latona in Rome, or a similar structure known in the Renaissance as such; Alberti often used classical examples to illustrate structural engineering.</note> in Rome provided for the work and the substructure quite correctly. For he extended an angle of the site into the overhanging mountain so that two straight walls would tolerate the force of the pressing weight, and by the placement of the angle, they would divide and dissipate the opposing burden. 

Furthermore, since we have begun to speak of the praises of the ancients who built with prudent counsel, I would not wish to overlook what comes to mind and is excellently suited to the matter. There exists a very useful practice by the architect of St. Mark’s in Venice. <note>St. Mark's Basilica, a masterpiece of Italo-Byzantine architecture. Alberti is interested in how it handles its watery, unstable foundation.</note> For when he was consolidating the site of the entire temple very densely, he left it riddled with several pits; so that if any vapors of the earth were perhaps conceived underneath, they might claim a ready exit for themselves. 

<margin>The leveling of plots.</margin> Finally, it is fitting that you make all the floor areas covered by a roof level. However, those left in the open air should be depressed from the level just enough to carry away the flow of rainwater. But enough of these matters; perhaps more has been said than this place required. For most of these things we have discussed pertain to the work of walls. But it happens that because these things are so naturally connected to one another, we do not separate them in our discussion. 

->It follows that we must speak of partition.<-

## ¶ On partition; and on the congruence, modesty, and compact variety of parts or members to the whole and among themselves. Chapter IX.

The entire force of intellect, and all the art and skill of building, is consumed in partition alone. <note>“Partition” (partitio) is a central concept for Alberti, referring to the way a building is divided into rooms and spaces that relate to one another.</note> For this single act of partition measures out the parts of the whole building and the complete relationships (so to speak) of the individual parts, and finally the consensus and cohesion of all lines and angles into a single work, taking into account utility, dignity, and grace. 

<margin>A philosophical definition of the city and the house.</margin> For if, in the opinion of philosophers, a city is like a very large house, and conversely a house is like a very small city, why should the members of these very things not be called tiny dwellings—such as the atrium, the walkway <term>xystus</term> <note>original: "xistus"; a Greek term for a covered portico or a garden walk lined with trees.</note>, the dining room, the portico, and the like? And in any of these, what could be omitted through carelesness or negligence that would not detract from the dignity and praise...

<meta>This page continues Alberti’s transition from the physical preparation of the site to the conceptual "lineaments" or design of the building. Having previously discussed foundations and environmental challenges like moisture and vapor, he now focuses on the harmonious proportion of a building’s parts, comparing an edifice to a living body.</meta>

-># Book I. On Lineaments.<-

<page-num>XII</page-num>

...hinder the work? Therefore, the greatest care and diligence must be applied in considering these matters which contribute to the work as a whole. Efforts must be made so that even the smallest parts appear to have been crafted in conformity with both talent and art. To achieve this end aptly and conveniently, all the previous points regarding the region and the site <term>area: the specific plot or footprint of the building</term> come together beautifully. It is fitting that, just as in a living creature limb responds to limb, so in a building the parts should correspond to one another. From this arises that common saying: **The greatest buildings must have the greatest members.** <note>Alberti uses the term "members" (membra) to refer to the distinct parts of a building—rooms, wings, or columns—treating the building as a biological organism.</note> The ancients observed this principle so strictly that, among other things, they even used larger bricks for public and very grand buildings than for private ones.

Thus, each part should be assigned an appropriate region and a suitable placement. They should be allocated in a way that is no larger than use requires, and no smaller than dignity demands; not in a foreign or impertinent location, but in its own proper place, so that it could nowhere have been more conveniently situated. For the part that is to be the most honorable section of the house should not be cast into a rejected corner. That which is most public should not be placed in a hidden spot. Likewise, that which is private should not be set in an open or exposed area. Add to this that consideration must also be given to the seasons, so that some areas are assigned to summer locations and others to winter ones. <margin>What the dwelling should be like.</margin> For different sites and sizes are due to different seasons: it is appropriate for summer rooms to be more spacious, while winter rooms will not be disapproved of if they are more compact. <margin>For consideration must be given.</margin> Furthermore, shade and breezes are due to summer rooms, while sun is due to those for winter. And in these things, caution must be taken lest the inhabitants, in moving from a cold place to a hot one, experience a sudden change without the air being tempered. Or, moving from a warm place into another infested by winter winds. For that would, above all else, harm the health of their bodies.

It is also necessary that these members yield to one another for the sake of establishing or composing the common praise and grace of the entire work. One should not let some parts be completely neglected while all the effort for beauty is occupied by others. Instead, they should agree among themselves in such a way that they appear to be one integrated and rightly constituted body, rather than separate and scattered limbs. Moreover, in shaping the members, one ought to imitate the modesty of nature. Just as in all other things, so too in this matter we do not praise sobriety more than we blame an unrestrained lust for building. The members ought to be moderate and necessary for the purpose at hand. For the entire method of building, <margin>The method of building.</margin> if you look at it rightly, had its origin in necessity. Convenience nourished it, use adorned it, and finally, pleasure was considered—though pleasure itself has never failed to shrink from all things immoderate. Therefore, the building shall be such that there is nothing more in its members than...

<summary>Alberti argues that a building must be proportioned like a living body, with each part ("member") sized and placed according to its function, the seasons, and its relationship to the whole. He traces the evolution of architecture from basic necessity to the pursuit of pleasure, emphasizing moderation and health.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Alberti’s discussion on the "lineaments" or design principles of architecture. Having established that a building should function like a living organism where parts correspond to the whole, he now moves into the importance of variety, the musical nature of proportion, and the transition into specific structural elements like walls and columns.</meta>

-># By Leon Battista Alberti<-

...that nothing be missing that should be present, and nothing present be disapproved of in any part. Nor would I want everything to be prescribed with only one single drawing and termination of lines, so that they do not differ from each other. Rather, some things will please if they are larger; others will be useful if they are smaller. Others will obtain praise from a **middle ground** <term>mediocritate: here meaning the "Golden Mean" or a balanced middle state, rather than poor quality</term>. Therefore, lines established as straight will please; others established with curves, and finally others defined by both ways of drawing lines will be approved—provided you observe what I often warn, lest you fall into this vice: that you seem to have made a **monster** with unequal shoulders or sides. <note>Alberti frequently uses the "monster" (monstrum) as a metaphor for architectural designs that lack symmetry or biological proportion.</note> 

Indeed, **variety** is the seasoning of grace in every thing, if it is compact and confirmed by a mutual equality between distant things; but if these same things are dissolved among themselves and differ by some inconvenient disparity, it will indeed be most absurd. For just as in a **lyre** <note>The lyre was a standard Renaissance metaphor for architectural harmony; Alberti believed that the same ratios that created beautiful music also created beautiful buildings.</note>, when deep voices correspond to high ones, and the middle voices between both resonate tuned to the song, there arises from the variety of voices a certain sonorous and wonderful equality of proportions, which delights and holds the minds in a greater way. So it happens in all other things which are made to move and hold minds. 

Moreover, these things must be carried out as use, convenience, and also the praised custom of experts may suggest. For in most things, either to resist custom takes away grace, or to agree with it is an advantage and is exceptionally conducive. Since all other most approved architects have seemed to testify by their deeds that this division—whether **Doric, Ionic, Corinthian, or Tuscan** <note>These are the four classical "Orders" of architecture, defined by the style and proportion of their columns.</note>—is the most convenient of all; not so that we may stick to their descriptions as if bound by laws when transferring them into our work, but that being advised by them, we may strive to bring forth new inventions, attaining equal or, if possible, greater fruit of praise. But we shall follow these things more distinctly in their own place, when we investigate in what way the city and the parts of the city, and what things are necessary for the use of each, should be placed.

### ¶ On the forms of walls and columns, their length, thickness, dimension, shapes, and adjacent parts. Chapter X.

But do not let it pass here, what I noted among the ancients, that they took the greatest care not to draw any outer line of the **area** <term>area: the building's footprint or ground plan</term> as a straight line, so that it would be very long and not intercepted in any places, both with the connection of curved lines and the intersection of angles. And it is clear that the most skilled men did this because they wanted the wall, as if by aids...

-># On Outlines. Book 1. Folio 13.<-

...[parts] by which it may cohere and become firmer. In reviewing the method of walls, one must begin with the most noble elements. This point in our discussion, therefore, advises that we must speak of **columns** and those things that pertain to columns; for the rows of columns themselves are nothing other than a wall that has been pierced and opened in many places. Indeed, as it is helpful to define the column itself, perhaps it would not be inept to call it a certain firm and continuous part of the wall, raised perpendicularly from the ground all the way to the top for the sake of supporting the roof. Furthermore, in the whole matter of building, you will find nothing that you would prefer to columns for the sake of labor, expense, and grace. But columns themselves have certain features among them in which they are dissimilar; here we will not omit the similarity, especially that which pertains to the **genus** <term>genus: the general category or "order" of the column</term>. Their dissimilarity, however—since that looks toward the **species** <term>species: the specific variations or subtypes of columns</term>—we shall pursue elsewhere in its proper place.

But let us begin from the very roots, so to speak, of those things placed under columns as foundations. Once the foundations have been leveled to the surface of the floor, they were accustomed to place a **small wall** 

<margin>Small wall</margin>
upon them: which we might call a "little altar" <note>original: *arula*</note>, and others perhaps a "cushion" <note>original: *pulvinar*</note>. Above this small wall they set the **base**; on the base they stood the **column**; and above the column they placed the **capital**. And this was the rule for these: that every column should swell below the middle <note>This refers to *entasis*, a subtle bulging in the shaft of a column to prevent it from looking thin or "waisted" to the human eye.</note> and be drawn back [tapered] toward the top. In its thickness, it would be one foot wider at the bottom than at the very top of the head. 

I believe the column was originally invented for the sake of supporting roofs. Afterward, we see that the interests of men advanced, excited by the desire of achieving the most worthy things: so that they labored as much as they could so that what mortals built should be as eternal and immortal as possible. Therefore, they placed columns and beams, and even floors and roofs, made out of solid marble. Yet in establishing these sorts of things, the ancient architects imitated the nature of things themselves so that they appeared not to have departed from the common usage of buildings; and in every way they strove that their works might be at once fit for use and most firm, as well as most beautiful to the sight. 

Nature doubtless first provided wooden and round columns; afterward, usage brought it about that in some places they were made four-sided. Therefore, if I interpret the matter correctly, because they saw rings of either iron or bronze cast onto the ends of wooden columns to ensure that the columns themselves would not split under the persistence of weight, 

<margin>The ring on columns.</margin>
architects also fixed a wide ring on the bottom foot of marble columns in the likeness of a **small band** <note>original: *fasceola*; in architecture, this is the "fillet" or "astragal" that separates parts of the column.</note>. This was done so that they might also be defended from the splashes of falling drops; and likewise at the top they placed a small band and a collar-ring <note>original: *torques*</note> added above, by which...

<meta>This page continues Alberti's detailed breakdown of architectural components, moving from the foundation and "small wall" (the arula) to the specific geometry of column bases and capitals. It then transitions into a discussion of the wall (paries) and structural integrity, using a famous contemporary example—the leaning walls of the Old St. Peter's Basilica in Rome—as a cautionary tale.</meta>

# Leon Battista Alberti

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely concluding a thought on how early builders modeled their stone structures on wooden precedents.</note> ...they saw that the wooden column was reinforced. But in the **bases** of columns, they observed this: that their lowest part should consist of straight lines and right angles. The top surface, however, should terminate according to the circumference of its own column. And they observed that this base should be wider than it is high in every direction; then they also wanted it to be wider than the column by a certain proportion, and they wanted the very bottom surface of the base itself to be wider than its top. And they intended that the **small wall** <note>original: *murulum*; referring to the pedestal or 'arula' mentioned on the previous page</note> likewise be larger than the base by a certain part. And they wanted the **foundation** also to be wider than the small wall by a certain part. And whatever things of this kind they placed one upon another, they aligned to the **plumb line** <term>plumb line: a cord with a weight used to ensure a structure is perfectly vertical</term> of the central point. 

But on the contrary, all **capitals** agree in this: that at their base they should imitate the lines of their column. At the top, however, they should end in a four-sided surface. And indeed, the top part of the capital will never be anything but wider than the bottom. 

<margin>The Wall.</margin> These things regarding columns. As for the **wall** <note>original: *paries*</note> itself, it shall be raised according to the proportions of the columns, so that if its height is to be as great as the column with its capital, its thickness should be as great as the column is at its bottom. Then they also observed this: that there should be no column, base, capital, or wall that was not most similar to others of its **order** <term>order: a specific style of architecture (like Doric or Ionic) that dictates the proportions of all parts</term> in every part—in height, width, and finally in every dimension and shape. 

And since it is a defect to have made a wall either thinner or thicker, or lower or higher, than reason and proportion require, I would nevertheless prefer to err on the side where something can be taken away rather than where something must be added. Here it will be helpful not to overlook even the defects of buildings, so that we may be more cautious in the matter. For the first praise is to be free of all defect. 

Yet I have noticed in the **Basilica of Peter in Rome** <note>Alberti refers here to the Old St. Peter's Basilica, built by Constantine, which was in a state of decay during the 15th century before its eventual demolition and reconstruction.</note> what the thing itself makes plain: it was done most unwisely, that they built a very long and very high wall above frequent and continuous openings <note>original: *apertiones*; referring to the arches of the nave</note>, reinforced by no curved lines and fortified by no supports. It ought to have been considered that the whole wing of the wall, undermined by too frequent openings, stretched and stood so high that it was exposed to catch the most violent **north winds** <note>original: *aquilonibus*</note>. 

By which it happened that, even then, the constant annoyance of the winds caused it to lean forward more than six feet from the straightness of the plumb line. Nor do I doubt that one day it will collapse with a light touch or a modest movement. Unless it were held up by the beams of the roofs, it would undoubtedly have fallen of its own accord already, given the lean that has begun. 

But I should blame the architect less, since, following the necessity of the place and site, he perhaps thought himself safe enough from the winds because of the hill <note>The Vatican Hill</note> that stands before the temple. I would have preferred, however, that all those wings on this side and that were made stronger.

XIIII.
On Outlines. Book I.

# On Outlines. Book I. Folio XIIII.

¶ How useful roofs are: both to the inhabitants themselves and to the other parts of buildings; and their diverse species and forms. Chapter 11.

<margin>The Roof.</margin>
**T**he utility of roofs is the first and greatest of all. For they contribute not only to the safety of the inhabitants, while they repel and exclude the night, the rain, and especially the burning sun. But they also wonderfully protect the entire building. Remove the roof, and the timber will rot, the wall will decay, the sides will crack, and finally the whole structure will gradually dissolve. Even the very foundations are strengthened by the protection of the roofs—though you may hardly believe it. Nor have so many buildings fallen into ruin by the force of fire, iron, the hands of enemies, or all other disasters, as have collapsed for no other reason than the negligence of citizens, because they were left naked and destitute of the help of roofs. Indeed, roofs are the armor of buildings against the injuries and assaults of storms. Since these things are so, our ancestors seem to me to have acted excellently both in other matters and in this: they wished to bestow such great honors upon the roof that they almost exhausted every art of decoration in adorning and beautifying them. For we see roofs made of bronze, glass, and gold, with gilded panels and plates of gold, and further distinguished most elegantly with sculptures of garlands and flowers, and even statues. Some roofs are under the open sky <note>original: *sub divo*</note>; others are not. Those "under the open sky" are those which are placed not for any use of walking, but solely to catch the rain. Those not under the open sky are the intermediate spans of **floor-timbers** <term>floor-timbers: horizontal beams supporting a floor or ceiling; original: *contignationum*</term> and vaults, by which it happens that one building is, as it were, placed upon another. In these, therefore, it happens that the work itself is a roof to the lower members of the building, and likewise a floor <note>original: *area*</note> for the upper ones. But of these floor-timbers, that part which hangs stretched above the head shall rightly be called the roof, 
<margin>The Ceiling</margin>
which we shall also call the **ceiling** <note>original: *celum*, literally "heaven" or "sky"</note>. That which is trodden by the feet of those walking shall be called the pavement or the **flooring** <note>original: *tectura*</note>. Whether the outermost coverings "under the open sky," which are placed to catch rain, should be considered as a type of pavement will be discussed elsewhere. 
<margin>Roofing.</margin>
As for the roofs that are under the open sky, even if their surfaces are perhaps flat in themselves, they will never be parallel to the floor they cover. Instead, they will always be sloping and slanted in some direction for the sake of pouring off the rain. But for roofs that are not under the open sky, it is necessary that their flat surfaces be parallel to the floor. All roofs must accommodate themselves in their angles and lines to the shape of the floor-plan and the form of the walls for which they are to be the covering. And...

<summary>Alberti discusses the essential protective function of the roof, describing it as the 'armor' of a building that preserves the walls and foundations. He distinguishes between external roofs designed for drainage and internal ceilings/floors that divide stories.</summary>
<keywords>roof, ceiling, architectural protection, drainage, floors, floor-timbers, structural preservation</keywords>

--- Page 59 ---
<meta>This page continues Leon Battista Alberti’s discussion on the design and function of roofs, concluding Chapter 11 and beginning Chapter 12 of Book 1, which focuses on the "outlines" or basic components of a building.</meta>

->Leonis Baptistae Alberti.<-

These roofs vary among themselves in succession: for some are formed with all lines curved, others with straight lines, and others mixed, and so forth. From this, it follows that various and manifold forms of coverings have also arisen. For roofs themselves are diverse by their very nature. Some are hemispheres <note>domes</note>, some are vaulted, some arched, and others are composed of several small arches. Likewise, some are called keel-shaped <note>original: *carinae*; roofs resembling the inverted hull of a ship</note>, while others are called <term>displuvia|roofs that slope away from the center to shed water outward</term>. But whatever the form may be, every roof must be such that its shadow protects its own floor and that it entirely directs rainwater away from the whole building for which it serves as a covering. For rain is always ready to do harm and is prone to mischief, never failing to exploit even the smallest openings; indeed, by its thinness it pierces through, by its softness it stains, and by its persistence it wears away all the "sinews" <note>original: *nervos*; the structural bonds or joints</note> of the building, and finally it vitiates and destroys the structure from its foundations. For this reason, skilled architects have rightly observed that they should prepare a free course for rains to flow away, and take care that water does not stand in any place, nor penetrate anywhere to cause damage. Hence, in snowy places, they wanted roofs to be primarily <term>displuvia|outward-sloping</term> and raised upward at an acute angle, so that the accumulation of snow would increase less and melt away more smoothly. In "summer-like" places (if I may call them that) <note>referring to warmer climates with less snow</note>, they placed roofs with a less sudden slope. Furthermore, care must be taken that the roof be made as much as possible as one single, equal, and entire piece; and, having considered the placement of windows and walls, it should cover the whole building far and wide, so that the water falling from the eaves does not dampen any part of the walls. Then, the roof should also be placed so that it does not rain from one roof into another. Also, the surfaces of a roof should not be vast and immense in their descent. For in the final channels of the tiles, the rain would overflow due to the abundance of many showers and flow into the building. This would cause great detriment to the work. Therefore, where there is a very large area, the roof should be divided into several surfaces and flow down into various parts. For this pertains both to convenience and to grace. If it happens in any place that several roofs must be placed, they shall be joined together there; so that those who have once been received under a roof may walk through the whole house protected by a covering.

### ¶ On openings: namely windows, doors, and others which do not penetrate the whole thickness of the wall: what kind, how many, and how large. Chapter XII.

**S**ince this is the case, we must now speak of openings. There are two kinds of openings. For some provide entrance and exit to the building for light and winds. Others do so for things and inhabitants. Windows serve the light; doors, stairs, and the spaces between columns serve things...

<meta>This page continues Alberti’s discussion on the "outlines" or structural components of a building, specifically moving from roofs into the necessity and placement of various types of openings.</meta>

Fo.XV.

# On Outlines.

...Likewise, those through which water and smoke pass—such as wells, sewers, and the mouths <note>original: *gula*; literally "throats"</note> of fireplaces, as I might call them—as well as oven openings and steam vents, are considered types of openings. Moreover, every part of the house should have windows, through which the enclosed air "breathes" and is renewed hourly. For otherwise, it will stagnate and bring corruption. <margin>Pay attention</margin> The historian Capitolinus <note>Julius Capitolinus, one of the authors of the *Historia Augusta*</note> relates that in Babylon, in the temple of Apollo, a very ancient golden casket was found. When it was broken open, a corrupt and poisonous air that had been trapped inside poured out. ☚ <margin>A wondrous thing concerning the golden box.</margin> It not only killed those who were nearby at the time but also spread a most terrible plague through its contagion across all of Asia as far as the Parthians. We also read in the historian Ammianus Marcellinus <note>A 4th-century Roman soldier and historian</note> that in the times of Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Verus <note>Roman co-emperors, 161–169 AD</note>, at Seleucia—after the temple had been plundered and the statue of Cominian Apollo <note>Apollo Comaeus</note> had been carried off to Rome—soldiers found a narrow opening that had previously been sealed by the priests <note>original: *vatib⁹*; seers or prophets</note> of the Chaldeans. <margin>Vapor</margin> When they forced it open in their greed for plunder, a pestilential vapor leaped out—so fierce and detestable <margin>Formerly at Seleucia</margin> that from the borders of the Persians all the way into Gaul, everything was infected with a foul and fatal disease. <margin>Pestilential.</margin> Therefore, there must be windows in every room. This is both for the sake of receiving light and for renewing the air; <margin>Windows: how they should be made.</margin> and they should be suited to the use of the place and the size of the wall, so that they receive neither more nor less light than necessary, and they should be neither more frequent nor sparser than use requires. Then one must also consider which winds the windows themselves are open to receive. For those that face healthy breezes can be made much wider in every direction. It will also be helpful to open them in such a way that the incoming breeze surrounds the bodies of the inhabitants. This will happen best if the sills <note>original: *spondæ*; the frames or ledges</note> of the windows are low enough that you can see and be seen by those walking through the streets. However, windows that are not facing the healthiest wind regions should be placed so that they receive as much light as is appropriate, but no more than can be spared. These should be placed high up, so that the intervening wall blocks the winds from hitting the bodies of the inhabitants directly. For in this way they will still have winds to refresh the air, but the winds will be "broken" <note>diffused or weakened by the height</note> and therefore not altogether unhealthy. One must also foresee how much sunlight will penetrate the house; depending on the convenience of different rooms, windows should be wider or narrower. For summer quarters or vast halls, windows should be placed to the north; or if they face south and are exposed to the suns, it will be beneficial to place the openings very low and of moderate size, since the former receive more refreshing breezes, while the latter are less troubled by the path of the sun's rays.

<meta>This page continues Alberti’s technical discussion on the "outlines" of a building, specifically focusing on the placement and proportions of openings like windows and doors to balance light, air, and structural strength.</meta>

# Leon Battista Alberti

And that place will have sufficient light from the constantly shining sun, where people have gathered more for the sake of shade than for the light itself. Conversely, in winter rooms, the windows will be open to the direct sun; if they are open, they will not be so exposed to the winds if they are placed high up, for the winds blowing in a straight course will not strike the inhabitants. Moreover, from wherever you intend to receive light, it is easy to obtain it from where you can look out upon the open sky. And it is by no means appropriate to place any openings made for the purpose of receiving light at the very bottom of the wall. For light is viewed with the face <note>original: *vultu*; literally "expression" or "face," implying the eyes' level</note>, not the feet; furthermore, it happens that the light is blocked by the presence of one or two people, and the rest of the room is thereafter rendered darker. This inconvenience does not occur when the light is brought in from a high position. <margin>Doors.</margin> Doors <note>original: *hostia*; usually meaning entrances or mouths of a building</note> should imitate windows: let more or fewer, larger or smaller ones be used according to the frequency of use and the purpose of the place. But in both cases, I see it observed that in public buildings, many of these <margin>Theaters.</margin> openings of the first kind were made. Theaters attest to this fact for us. <margin>Openings.</margin> Which, if we interpret them correctly, consist entirely of openings, both of stairs and especially of windows and doors. However, it is necessary to place openings in such a way that they are not placed in the smallest amount in the larger walls, nor are they driven into the modest fronts of walls any larger than necessity requires. Regarding such openings, different men have approved different outlines <note>original: *lineamenta*; the structural design or "lines" of the building</note>. But the most esteemed architects, where it was permitted, used only quadrangular and straight-lined shapes. Finally, everyone agrees on this: that they should be adapted in whatever way suits the size and shape of the building. Furthermore, they consider that the openings for doors should be so established that they are altogether taller than they are wide. Of these, those that are taller should contain two continuous circles <note>Alberti is describing a 2:1 ratio for the door's height relative to its width</note>. Those that are lower, however, should have a height equal to the diagonal of that square whose side is the bottom width of the door itself <note>The "square root of two" proportion</note>. And it is appropriate to place doors where the most convenient access possible is provided to all parts of the building. Furthermore, one must strive for grace in such openings, so that by equalizing the sizes, the right side corresponds to the left. Moreover, they were accustomed to set the number of windows and doors as an odd number. But this was done so that the parts on either side corresponded in pairs, while the central ones were a little larger. And they took the greatest care to preserve the strength of the buildings; for that reason, they placed the openings far from the corners and the projections of columns, specifically in the weaker parts of the wall: but those which were not needed for sustaining the load. And they ensured that as many parts of the wall as possible rose from the ground all the way to the roof whole and without being broken or interrupted.

# On Outlines. Book I. Folio XVI.

...to the plumb line. There is a certain kind of opening that imitates doors and windows in position and shape, but does not penetrate the entire thickness of the wall. <margin>A type of opening that does not penetrate the wall.</margin> Instead, like hollowed-out niches <note>original: *scaphis*; literally "skiffs" or "bowls," used here to describe the concave shape of an architectural niche</note>, they provide worthy and suitable spaces and seats for statues and paintings. Where these should be placed, how frequent they should be, and how large they are to be established, we will discuss more distinctly when we deal with the ornaments <note>Alberti dedicates later books of this treatise specifically to "Ornament," or the decorative finish of buildings</note> of buildings; even though this contributes no less to the calculation of expense than to the beauty of the work, because less stone and mortar is consumed in filling the wall. Let this much suffice for the matter: these arrangements of niches ought to be suitable in number, not excessive in size, and of a decent shape, so that they completely imitate the windows of their own order. 

And indeed, I have noticed from the works of the ancients that openings of this kind, whatever they may be, were usually placed no larger than to occupy a seventh part of their wall, but not smaller than to take up a ninth part. The spaces between columns <term>intercolumniation: the distance between two adjacent columns</term> are certainly to be counted among the primary openings. These are also pre-established variously according to the variety of buildings. But we will speak of these more distinctly when we reason in the proper place specifically about preparing sacred buildings. 

Here let it suffice to have advised that these openings should be placed so that the proportion of the columns, which are left to support the roofs, is held most diligently: lest they be left too slender or too sparse to comfortably bear the weight of the roofs; nor indeed thicker or more frequent than needed, so that the spaces of the area and the entrances remain clear for the practical uses of things and times. 

Furthermore, some openings appear when columns are frequent, others when they are rare <note>meaning "widely spaced"</note>. For a beam <note>original: *trabs*; a horizontal lintel</note> is placed over frequent columns; an arch is added over rare ones. But in all openings where an arch is drawn, care must be taken that the arch is no less than half a circle plus a part added equal to a seventh of the semi-diameter. For they affirm it is found among experts that this one shape of all is the most suitable for permanence. Indeed, they think all other arches are weak for bearing weight, and prone and exposed to ruin. 

Furthermore, we judge the semicircular arch to be the only one that does not require a tie-rod <note>original: *corda*; a structural member like a tension rod used to prevent the arch from spreading</note> or external supports. As for all others, unless you apply either a tie-rod or counterweights with which they may contend, we see them crack and fail by their own force. I will not omit here that excellent and most praiseworthy thing which I noted among the ancients: that such openings and the arches of vaults <note>original: *testudinum*; literally "tortoises," referring to the arched shell of a masonry vault</note> were so placed by those best architects in temples that even if you were to remove all the inner columns, nevertheless the arches of the openings and the vaults of the roofs would remain standing, and...

Leon Battista Alberti.

...at least they do not collapse. In the same way, all the lines of the arches upon which the <term>vaults</term> <note>original: *testudines*; literally "tortoise shells," used here to describe curved masonry ceilings</note> rest are brought all the way down to the ground with wonderful skill, known to few, so that the work stands by resting on arches alone. For since the earth is most firm beneath their centers, if the arches themselves are most firm, why should they not persist forever?

# Chapter XIII. On stairs and their types. On the odd number of steps, their dimensions, and the landings placed between them; on the exit for smoke and water, hearths, the placement and openings of well-mouths and sewers.

<margin>Stairs.</margin>
**S**etting stairs in place involves more difficulty than can be handled unless they are positioned correctly through mature and well-considered planning. For in a single set of stairs, three openings come together. The first of these is the doorway, which provides access to the stairs for those climbing. The second is the window, which allows light in so that the recessed edge of each step can be seen clearly. The third is the opening in the floor and roof, through which we pass to the upper floor and the covering of the building. For this reason, it is said that the layout of a work is certainly hindered by stairs. But let those who wish the stairs not to be a hindrance ensure that they do not hinder the stairs themselves. They should designate a certain and appropriate space on the ground plan where a free and unobstructed passage is available all the way to the highest roofs that are under the open sky. Do not be begrudging that so much area is occupied by the stairs. For they will provide enough convenience there, provided they cause the least inconvenience to the other parts of the building. Furthermore, the vaults and empty spaces left under the stairs will not be lacking for very useful purposes.

Among us, there are two types of stairs. For I do not intend to speak here of the stairs used in military expeditions and fortifications. One type is not climbed by steps, but by a sloping incline. The other type is that by which we ascend to the heights by means of steps. Our ancestors used to place the inclines as easy and low-pressed as possible. Indeed, as I have noted from their buildings, they considered those to be sufficiently convenient which were designed so that the vertical line of height corresponded to a sixth part of the horizontal line of length. In the matter of steps, especially in temples, they favored an odd number; for they say it is so arranged that we may enter the temple with the right foot, which they believed contributed to religious devotion.

<margin>☞</margin>
In these matters, I have noticed that good architects observed that they should almost never drive more than seven or nine continuous steps into a single flight. I believe they were imitating the number of either the planets or the cities <note>Alberti likely refers to the seven classical planets and perhaps the nine Muses or legendary city-founding numbers common in classical lore</note>. But at every such interval of seven or nine steps, they most wisely wove in a small <term>landing</term> <note>original: *areolam*; literally a "small open space" or garden bed, here meaning a flat resting place between flights of stairs</note>, so that those who were tired or weak might have intermittent rests from the labor of climbing. And if any accident should happen, such that those climbing should fall, they would have spaces where their bodies...

<page-num>XVII</page-num>
<header>Book I. On Design. Folio XVII.</header>
<sig>c</sig>

# Book I. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; On Design. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Folio XVII.

...stop the force of a fall and allow a person to recover and steady themselves. And I myself strongly approve of this: that stairs be interrupted by their own landings, be well-lit, and be ample and spacious according to the dignity of the place.

<margin>Steps.</margin>
Indeed, they used to think that the steps of stairs should be so dimensioned that they were neither thicker than a <term>sixth of a foot</term> <note>original: *sextante*; approximately 2 inches, though Alberti's measurements here may refer to the height or "rise" of the step in proportion to a larger unit</note>, nor thinner than <term>three-quarters of a foot</term> <note>original: *dodrante*; approximately 9 inches</note>. The depth <note>original: *retractiones*; the "tread" of the step</note> of the steps should be placed no less than a foot and a half, nor more than two feet. In the whole building, the fewer the number of stairs there are, and the less area they occupy, the more convenient they will be.

<margin>The exit of smoke and water.</margin>
Outlets for smoke and water must be unobstructed and directed so that they do not pool, overflow, stain, cause offense, or bring danger to the building. Hence, it is necessary to separate the <term>throats of the hearths</term> <note>the flues or chimneys</note> far from any combustible material, lest a spark or the intensity of the heat set fire to a nearby beam or timber. They also command that the channels of flowing water be so directed that excess is driven away, and that they cause no damage to the building through either erosion or dampness. For if any of these cause harm, even if it is very small, yet through length of time and the persistence of the irritation, the damage accumulates. In these water conduits, I have noticed that the most skilled architects ensured that rainwater from <term>dripping eaves</term> <note>original: *stillicidiorum*</note> was either led away through extended pipes so as not to splash those approaching, or collected in <term>basins</term> <note>original: *impluviis*; a Roman architectural feature for catching rainwater</note> to be stored in cisterns for human use, or forced to flow to certain spots where private waste might be washed away, so that people’s noses and eyes would be least offended. Above all, they seemed to take care to keep all rainwater far from the building and to remove it, both for other reasons and especially to prevent the ground beneath the building from becoming damp. In all openings, they also seemed to ensure that they placed them in the most suitable spots to provide the most benefit to the whole building. Especially regarding wells, I determine they should be placed in a public and open part of the house, provided they do not occupy spaces more worthy than themselves. Philosophers <note>original: *physici*; here meaning natural scientists or observers of nature</note> affirm that those placed under the open sky yield purer and cleaner water. But in whatever part of the house wells are dug, or sewers laid beneath, or water and moisture pour in, there must be openings of such a kind that plenty of air may breathe in, so that the damp exhalations of the floor may be wiped away and driven out by the blowing of the winds and the movement of the air.

¶ Thus far, we have touched upon the <term>outlines</term> <note>original: *lineamentis*; the conceptual design or plan of a building, which is the subject of Book I</note> of buildings which seemed to pertain to the work as a whole, noting each of the kinds of things to be discussed. Now we must speak of the construction and structure of buildings. But first, we must speak of materials and those things which it is necessary to prepare regarding materials.

<header>Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.</header>

# THE SECOND BOOK OF LEON BATTISTA ALBERTI: ON MATERIALS.

¶ One must often and at length revolve a plan in the soul and mind, prefiguring the whole work and each of its parts using <term>small boards and tablets</term> <note>original: *asserula/tabella*; these refer to early drafting surfaces or flat models</note> or any other kind of <term>scale models</term> <note>original: *modulis*; Alberti was a pioneer in advocating for 3D architectural models to test designs before construction</note>. One should freely add or subtract from these until the future building is determined in its type, quality, and size: lest, when the work is finished, you should repent of the deed and have to say: "I would not have wanted this; I would have preferred that." Chapter One.

<margin>c</margin> **I** believe that the labor and expense of buildings should not be started rashly, not only for many other reasons, but especially so that it does not damage one's honor and reputation. For just as a well-ordered work brings praise to all those who contributed their counsel, labor, or zeal to the project, so too, if there is anything in which you find a lack of the author's wisdom or the craftsman's skill in any part, it will greatly detract from their praise and name. Indeed, the merits and flaws of buildings are public and readily apparent; for some reason, that which is unseemly draws more attention to itself—leading to scorn—than that which is beautifully perfected and complete in every part draws to itself for admiration. 

It is indeed a wonder why it is so, that by the warning of nature, both the learned and the unlearned immediately sense what is right or wrong in the arts and the principles of things. In such matters, the sense of the eyes is the sharpest of all. Thus, if anything presents itself that is stunted, limping, redundant, empty, or disorganized, we are instantly troubled and desire something more elegant. Why this happens, we do not all understand; yet if we were asked, no one would deny that it could be amended and corrected. However, the precise method for carrying out such a correction is not for everyone to explain, but only for those who are well-consulted in the matter. 

It is the mark of a well-consulted person to have pre-planned and pre-defined everything in the soul and mind, so that during the execution of the work, or once it is finished, one does not have to say: "I would not have wanted this instead of that." And it is truly a wonder that we do not pay the lightest of penalties for a poorly constructed work. For what we did not weigh at the start—having attacked the task rashly and without consultation—we eventually recognize through the passage of time. From this, it follows that one either repents eternally because of the offense of the error (if it is not destroyed and amended), or, if it is demolished, the account of the expenses and loss—as well as the lightness and inconstancy of your judgment—is condemned. 

<margin>Julius Caesar</margin> Julius Caesar <note>The Roman dictator and general, 100–44 BCE</note> [demolished] a temple <note>original: *ædem*; here Alberti likely refers to a villa or manor house</note> from its foundations at <term>Nemi</term> <note>Lake Nemi, near Rome, where Caesar famously built a luxurious villa only to tear it down because it did not perfectly suit his tastes</note>...

<header>Book II. On Materials. Leaf XVIII.</header>
<sig>c iii</sig>

# Book II. On Materials. Leaf XVIII.

<margin>
He demolished a work completed at great expense so that he might rebuild it.
</margin>
Suetonius <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus (c. 69 – 122 AD), a Roman historian; this refers to his biography of Julius Caesar.</note> affirms that Caesar demolished a villa that had been both begun and finished at great expense because it did not entirely correspond to his expectations. In this matter, he deserves to be criticized by us, his posterity, if he failed to sufficiently pre-plan what was necessary for the task, or if perhaps he came to hate through a fickle error what had been correctly established at the time. For this reason, the ancient custom of the best builders will always be approved by me: that we should weigh the entire work and the individual dimensions of every part again and again, not only through <term>drafting</term> <note>original: *prescriptione*; refers to technical drawing</note> and painting, but also by using <term>scale models</term> <note>original: *modulis*; 3D physical representations</note> made of <term>small wooden slats</term> <note>original: *asserula*; thin pieces of wood used to construct models</note> or any other material. These should be examined before you attempt anything else that requires expense or care. In the construction of these models, the opportunity will be given to beautifully observe and consider the site of the region, the perimeter of the area, the number and order of the parts, the appearance of the walls, the strength of the roofs, and finally the logic and configuration of all those things we discussed in the previous book. And it will be permitted there to add, diminish, change, innovate, and completely overturn things without penalty until everything fits correctly and is approved. Add to this that the manner and total of the future expense—a matter by no means to be neglected—will be more certainly grasped from the width, height, thickness, number, size, form, appearance, and quality of individual items, weighed according to their importance and the labor of the craftsmen. For the logic and the total calculation of columns, capitals, bases, cornices, pediments, <term>cladding</term> <note>original: *crustationum*; decorative stone or marble facing</note>, pavements, and statues of this kind—which pertain either to the structure or the decoration of the building—will be held more certainly. I believe it should by no means be overlooked that producing models that are colored and (so to speak) tricked out with the <term>allurements of painting</term> <note>original: *picturae lenociniis*; Alberti warns that pretty colors can distract from structural flaws</note> is not the mark of an architect seeking to teach his craft, but rather of an ambitious one striving to entice and occupy the eyes of the viewer, attempting to divert the mind from a correct investigation of the parts to be weighed toward an admiration of himself. Therefore, I would wish for models to be provided that are not finished with exact craftsmanship, polished, or illustrated, but rather naked and simple, in which you approve the genius of the inventor rather than the hand of the craftsman. There is this difference between the <term>drafting</term> of a painter and that of an architect: the painter strives to show <margin>The drafting of the painter and the architect.</margin> projections from a panel by means of shadows, lines, and tapered angles. The architect, scorning shadows, places projections here based on the description of the <term>ground plan</term> <note>original: *fundamenti descriptione*</note>. He teaches the spaces and figures of each facade and the sides elsewhere with consistent lines and true angles, as one who wishes his work to be judged not by apparent sights, but by certain and calculated dimensions.

<summary>Alberti argues for the use of simple, unpainted 3D models to test architectural designs and estimate costs before construction. He distinguishes the architect's technical drawing style—focused on precise measurement—from the painter's use of perspective and shadow.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Alberti's discussion on the necessity of architectural models. It concludes his initial warnings about the "lust for building" and begins Chapter II, which focuses on the limitations imposed by human strength and the laws of nature.</meta>

# Leon Battista Alberti: On the Art of Building.

...review. Therefore, it is necessary to have made models of this kind; and to have examined them most diligently both by yourself and together with several others; and to have reviewed them again and again, so that there will be nothing in the work, even the smallest detail, of which you do not understand what and of what sort it is, what place and how much space it will occupy, and what uses it will serve. And especially, care must be taken above all that the logic of the roofs be as well-resolved as possible. For indeed, the roof by its very nature—if I interpret correctly—was the first among all building elements for mortals that served the purpose of rest; so much so that for the sake of the roofs, they do not deny that not only the wall (and those things that rise and follow with the walls) but even those things under the ground itself were invented, such as the drainage and diversion of waters from rain, sewers, and the like. 

I, however, being well-taught by experience in these matters, remember how difficult it is to bring a work to the point where the conveniences of its parts are joined with dignity and beauty; that is, so that while they have all other things that are approved, they also possess a refined variety of parts such as the logic of proportions and <term>harmony</term> <note>original: *concinnitas*; Alberti's central aesthetic concept of the rhythmic harmony of parts within a whole</note> shall have defined. It is a great thing indeed, O gods <note>original: *superi*; a classical invocation to the "gods above," reflecting Alberti's humanist blending of Christian and pagan terminology</note>, but I affirm that to cover all these things with a manageable, predetermined, decent, and fitting roof is a work only for a skillful and exceedingly circumspect intellect and craft. 

Finally, when the entire appearance of the work and the <term>design</term> <note>original: *proiectatio*; the architectural "projection" or layout</note> please you and other experts so much that nothing offers itself for you to hesitate over, and you determine there is nothing in which better counsel could be taken, I warn you not to hasten to begin the work out of a "lust for building" by demolishing old buildings or laying the massive foundations of the whole work; which is what the inconsiderate and precipitous do. But if you listen to me, you will wait for some time until the fresh approval of your own intellect has "cooled down," so that you may finally review everything more accurately; when it will be given not to the love of the invention but to the reasons of counsel, so that you may judge the matter more considerately. For in all things to be done, time will bring many things to your attention and consideration which would have escaped even the most skillful man.

### That nothing be done beyond one's strength or against nature, but consider who you are, what you are doing, and in what place. **Chapter II.**

When you are about to review your models, these considerations must be turned over among the reasons to be weighed. First, do not attempt anything beyond the strength of men. Nor undertake anything that will immediately be at war with the nature of things. For the force of Nature—even if it is sometimes interrupted by an obstructing mass or twisted by some pressure—is of such a kind that it never fails to overcome and shatter whatever opposes or hinders it. And all...

He warns architects to let their initial designs "cool" before building to avoid the errors of haste and to respect the limits of human power and nature.</summary>

<header>Book II. On Materials. Leaf XIX.</header>

### Book II. On Materials.

Indeed, nature, through its long and tireless persistence in attacking, eventually weakens and overthrows the stubbornness of things (if I may put it that way) set against it. We read of and see many man-made works that have failed to last for no other reason than that they contended against the nature of things. Who would not laugh at—or rather, who would not hate the insanity of—that insolent man <note>Alberti likely refers to the Emperor Caligula, who famously built a bridge of ships across the bay of Baiae to defy a prophecy</note> who determined to ride his horse over a bridge of ships extended across the sea?

<margin>The Port of Claudius.</margin>
The Port of Claudius at Ostia <note>original: *hostia*; the ancient harbor city of Rome</note> and the Port of Hadrian at Terracina were works otherwise intended to be eternal in every respect; yet we see that for some time now they have utterly failed. Their entrances are blocked by sand and their basins filled up, for the sea never ceases its constant struggle, daily harrying and eventually overcoming them. What then do you think will happen when you attempt to completely block or push back the force of rushing waters or the mass of falling cliffs? Since these things are so, one must take care not to undertake anything of the kind that does not properly agree with the nature of things. The next thing to beware of is that you do not take upon yourself a task in which you fail yourself, leaving the work unfinished.

<margin>The Port of Hadrian.</margin>
<margin>Tarquin</margin>
Who would not have blamed Tarquin, the King of the Romans, if the gods above had not favored the greatness of the city, and if the growing empire had not supplied enough wealth for such a magnificent undertaking? For in laying the foundations of the temple, he had already exhausted the entire estimated cost of the future work.

<margin>Rhodope the harlot built a royal tomb for herself.</margin>
Added to this is the fact that one must consider not only what you *can* do, but also what is *becoming* or appropriate. I do not praise that famous Thracian harlot Rhodope <note>A legendary wealthy courtesan in Egypt; Herodotus mentions a story that she built a pyramid, which Alberti here critiques as socially inappropriate</note>, whose memory has lasted to our times. She ordered a tomb to be built for herself at an incredible expense. For even if she had acquired royal wealth through her trade as a prostitute, she was in no way worthy of a royal tomb. 

<margin>Artemisia, Queen of Caria.</margin>
On the other hand, I do not find fault with Artemisia, the Queen of Caria, who built a most magnificent tomb <note>The Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World</note> for her most beloved and worthy husband. In these matters, I also approve of modesty. Horace scolded Maecenas <note>Maecenas was a wealthy patron of the arts; Horace’s Odes often critiqued the Roman obsession with luxurious villas</note> because he was "insane with building." 

<margin>Mad for building</margin>
Indeed, I find favor with the account in Cornelius Tacitus of the man who placed a modest tomb for Otho <note>Roman Emperor for three months in 69 AD; his simple tomb was praised for being durable and unpretentious</note>, yet one that would endure. 

<margin>Otho’s tomb: modest but lasting.</margin>
And although they require modesty in private monuments and magnificence in public ones, even the modesty of private citizens is sometimes highly praised within the public sphere. 

<margin>The Theater of Pompey.</margin>
We follow the Theater of Pompey with praise and admiration because of the extraordinary size and dignity of the work. It was a work worthy of both Pompey and of victorious Rome. 

<margin>Nero.</margin>
But not everyone approves of Nero’s insanity for building, nor his fury for undertaking the most vast works merely to spend money. Nor do they approve of him who, with so many thousands of men, [attempted to cut through] the mountain at Puteoli <note>The modern Pozzuoli; Nero attempted various massive engineering projects in this volcanic region near Naples</note>...

The canal navigable by five-banked galleys <note>original: *quinque remibus*; referring to quinqueremes, the heavy warships of the Roman era</note> from Lake Avernus to Ostia, begun by Nero, I condemn for several reasons, but especially because its maintenance would have required the perpetual and eternal prosperity of the Empire and a continuous line of princes devoted to such a project. Since these things are so, it will be your duty to have considered those points we have reviewed: namely, what it is you are doing, in what place you are doing it, and who you are that does it. To establish the whole matter according to its dignity and use will surely be the mark of a well-advised and considerate man. By the counsel and example of experts, it should first be clear to you where the funds will come from for everything necessary to complete the work, once the preparations are made.

### Chapter III.

Having noted and observed these things, you must examine the rest: whether each element is rightly defined and aptly distributed in its proper place. In performing this duty, you must so prepare yourself that, in every consideration of these matters, you would think it a disgrace not to achieve your goal as far as it lies within your power. You should strive so that no other work elsewhere, produced with equal expense and similar opportunity, can be either more gladly looked upon or more abundantly praised. For in matters of this kind, it is not enough simply not to be despised; rather, it is fitting to be especially approved, and likewise to be held up as a model for others to imitate. Therefore, we must be strict and very diligent investigators of these things. And care must be taken that, while nothing is introduced that is not elegant and highly approved, all parts should also mutually agree with one another in dignity and grace—to such an extent that whatever you might add, change, or take away would make the result more flawed and worse <note>This is Alberti's classic definition of beauty as a harmony of parts where nothing can be altered without destroying the whole</note>. But regarding these matters—I warn you again and again—make sure that the prudence of experts is your guide, along with the counsel of those who will view the work with a correct and sincere judgment. For it is through their knowledge and principles, rather than through private will and feeling, that it will be granted that what you do is either the best, or similar to the best. Finally, it is profitable for what you do to be approved by the voice of experts...

# Leon Battista Alberti: On the Art of Building

I believe that those who are not at all fickle should be selected, to whom you may diligently entrust and commend the work properly prescribed <note>original: "praescriptum"; referring to the architectural plans or specifications</note> so that they might finish it well and complete it in a timely manner. In evaluating all these things, it will be helpful to draw arguments and conjectures from nearby works that are readily available elsewhere. Advised by these, you can decide what needs to be done in your own project. For if you note the faults and merits in those, you can judge that very similar things will occur in your own future work. 

When the Prince Nero had decided to place a colossus of one hundred and twenty feet in Rome for the worship of the Sun—in which he would surpass the scale and magnificence of previous ones—Pliny writes that he did not award the contract for its making to 

<margin>
Zenodarus, a famous craftsman.
</margin>

Zenodarus (a craftsman famous and singular in those times) until he had seen sufficient proof of what he could achieve in a work of such great skill, through a colossus of wonderful weight he had made in Gaul among the Arverni. With these things established, let us pursue the rest. And indeed, in reviewing such things as are useful for the work of building, let us report what the learned ancients have handed down. 

<margin>
Authors on the art of building.
</margin>

Especially Theophrastus, Aristotle, Cato, Varro, Pliny, and Vitruvius <note>Alberti lists his primary sources: Greek philosophers and Roman writers on agriculture and architecture.</note>. For these matters are known more through long observation than by any arts of the intellect, and thus must be sought from those who have noted such things with the greatest diligence. We shall follow them, therefore, by collecting what the most esteemed ancients have discussed in many different places. We shall also add, according to our custom, anything we ourselves have noted from the works of our ancestors or from the advice of skilled craftsmen that might contribute in any way to what is being discussed. 

For I think it will be most convenient if, following the nature of the things themselves, we begin with those very things which men first employed for this business of building. Unless we are mistaken, these were felled trees and timber from the forests, even though I find among authors that they disagree about these matters. 

<margin>
Gelius Taxius built a mud dwelling for himself.

Vesta.

The descendants of Protogenes devised dwellings for mortals.
</margin>

There are those who say that men first lived in caves, so that the cattle and the master were enclosed in a common shade. From this they believe what is reported in Pliny: that a certain Gelius Taxius was the first of all to build a mud structure for himself in imitation of nature. Diodorus says that the goddess Vesta, daughter of Saturn, first invented dwellings. Eusebius Pamphilus, an elegant investigator of antiquities, asserts from the testimonies of the ancients that the descendants of Protogenes <note>The "first-born" or early inhabitants of the world in ancient Phoenician mythology cited by Eusebius.</note> devised homes for men which were woven from the leaves of reeds and papyrus. 

But let us return to the matter. The ancients, and especially Theophrastus, command that a tree should be cut—especially the silver fir, the pitch pine, and the pine—as soon as they have first begun to bud and put forth tender shoots. At that time, because of the abundance of moisture, the bark <unclear>is easily stripped</unclear>...

At what time fir, spruce, and pine should be cut for timber. Also, how trees are best seasoned and when they are fresh.

...you might have removed the sap. However, there are some trees cut after the vintage which are more suitable for felling, such as the maple, elm, ash, and linden. Likewise, they testify that if oaks are cut in the spring, they become worm-eaten <term>teredinosa</term> <note>original: "teredinosa"; referring to damage caused by wood-boring larvae</note>. But if the same trees are cut in midwinter <term>bruma</term>, they are neither spoiled nor warped. And it supports this point what they have noted: indeed, timber that is cut during midwinter while the north wind <term>borea</term> is blowing—even when green—burns very well and is almost free of smoke. This fact is an indication that the sappy moisture is not raw but digested <note>Alberti uses "digested" in the Aristotelian sense, meaning the sap has been chemically matured or "cooked" by the tree’s natural heat</note>. Vitruvius favored cutting timber from the beginning of autumn until the West Wind <term>Favonius</term> begins to blow. Hesiod says when the sun, hanging over our heads, burns with great force and men's color is darkened, then the harvest is at hand. But when the leaves begin to fall, then you should cut the wood. But Cato regulates the whole matter thus: He says if the timber is oak, cut it when the [winter] solstice has occurred. For toward midwinter it is always unseasonable; other timber that has seed should be cut when the seed is ripe; that which has none, when you please. That which has both ripe and green seed at once, cut it then when the seed has fallen. But cut elm when the leaves fall. And they say it matters greatly under which phase of the moon you apply the iron

From this it comes that they say: to sell grain, reap it during a fuller moon, for then the grains themselves are quite full; but to preserve it, reap it when the moon is "thirsty" <note>original: "sitiente"; meaning a dry or waning moon</note>. It is also established that tree foliage prepared during a waning moon does not rot. Vegetius favored the tree being split from the fifteenth to the twenty-second moon; he thinks a religious observance arose from this, so that for the sake of eternity they celebrate only on these days, because things cut during them last forever...
