<meta>This page continues Alberti's discussion on the harvesting of timber, moving from seasonal considerations to the specific influence of the moon and the preparation of wood after it has been cut. He transitions from Chapter 4 into Chapter 5, which deals with preservation techniques.</meta>

->Leone Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.<-

...they add that the moon should be observed as it sets. But Pliny thinks the best time to cut a tree is when the Dog Star <note>original: "Cane sidere"; the star Sirius, whose rising was associated with the hottest part of summer</note> is rising at its peak, and when the moon is in conjunction with the sun—a day called the new moon <term>interlunium</term>. He considers that the night of that very day should be awaited until the moon is beneath the earth. Astronomers declare the reason for this to be that all moisture in living things is moved by the power of the moon. Therefore, when the moisture is either drawn back toward the moon or left behind in the furthest fibers of the root, the remaining timber is left much cleaner. 

Add to this that they think the trees will be much more reliable if they are not felled immediately, but rather girdled <note>The practice of cutting a ring through the bark and sapwood to kill the tree and dry it out while it stands</note> so that they may dry out while standing. Indeed, they affirm that even the fir tree—which otherwise is not at all firm against the rot of moisture—will not be corrupted by water if it is debarked while the moon is waning. There are those who testify that heavy timbers like sessile oak and common oak, which by nature sink in water, will be made to float for up to ninety days if they are girdled in early spring and felled after they have lost their leaves. Others order that the thickness of the standing tree be cut deeper, right into the pith, so that the "gore" <note>original: "sanies"; referring to the watery, decomposing sap</note> and bad sap may be drained away more abundantly by dripping. To these things they add that you should not fell any tree to be hewn or cut before it has produced its fruit and the seed is mature. They advise that once the tree is struck, especially those that bear fruit, it must be stripped entirely of its bark.

# ¶ How the timber itself should be cared for once the trees are felled; where it is best preserved; and how it may be more suitably placed to last longer. Chapter V.

<margin>
Timber should be smeared with ox dung.
</margin>
**F**or indeed, timber is easily contaminated while under the inner bark, as long as it remains covered by the outer bark. Felled timber ought to be stored in a place where harsh suns and the blasts of sharp winds do not reach it; and especially those woods that are soft by nature <note>original: "sponte dantur"; likely referring to woods that are naturally less durable</note> should be completely protected by shade. For this reason, ancient architects made a point of smearing the wood with dung, specifically ox dung. Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle, often called the "father of botany"</note> explained that this was done so that, with the exits closed off, the thick phlegm <term>pituita</term> and the excessive force of vapors might gradually trickle and breathe through the pith, which results in the rest of the wood's dryness being condensed by uniform drying. 

They also think that timber dries more conveniently if stood with the top inverted. Then, they apply various remedies against age and future diseases. Theophrastus believes that buried timber lasts much longer. Cato <note>Cato the Elder, author of "De Agricultura," a key Roman source for farming and building materials</note> orders felled timber to be smeared with the dregs of oil <term>amurca</term> <note>original: "amurca"; the bitter, watery sediment left after pressing olives, used in antiquity as a pesticide and preservative</note> so that it may be immune to woodworms and rot. 

<margin>
Likewise with oil dregs, pitch, oil, and birdlime.
</margin>
It is well known that things damaged by water and the sea can be protected with pitch. They also report that wood soaked in oil dregs burns without the annoyance of smoke. They say that in the Egyptian labyrinth, beams made of Egyptian thorn were set after being treated with oil...

Page XXII.
## Book II. On Materials.

<margin>Mithridates' tower with alum</margin>
<margin>How it is treated:</margin>
<margin>Citrus wood, chestnut, and Egyptian wood are seasoned.</margin>
Pliny writes that Theophrastus says wood smeared with birdlime <term>visco</term> <note>original: "Visco"; a sticky substance made from holly bark or mistletoe used to catch birds, here suggested as a coating</note> does not burn. I should not omit this either: it is recorded in Gellius, from the annals of Quintus Claudius, that a wooden tower at Piraeus did not burn at all when Sulla was attacking it, because Archelaus, the prefect of Mithridates, had smeared it with a great deal of alum <note>original: "alumine"; a mineral salt used historically as a fire retardant</note>. There are, furthermore, various ways in which wood is toughened and strengthened against the injuries of the weather. Indeed, they bury citrus wood <note>original: "citream materiem"; likely referring to the North African Thuja tree, highly prized in antiquity for luxury furniture</note> in the earth and smear it with wax, then place it in heaps of grain for seven days, with as many days in between. This makes it firmer and more manageable when applied to a task. It is wonderful how much weight is removed by this; they also affirm that this same wood, once dried, acquires a dense and incorruptible hardness from the sea. It is well known that chestnut is cleansed by seawater. Pliny writes that they submerge Egyptian fig <note>original: "Ficum ægyptiam"; the sycamore fig</note> in a pool so that it may be dried and smoothed, for that wood otherwise sinks in water. We see our own skilled craftsmen keep wood submerged in water and mud for thirty days, especially that which they use on a lathe; they believe that when it is dried later, it becomes more seasoned and more fit for all uses. There are those who assert that this happens to any wood: if you bury it in a damp place while it is still green, it becomes eternal. But whether you bury it, keep it smeared in the light, or store it away, all experts agree on this opinion: it should not be touched until after three months. For it must "rest" and be imbued with a certain maturity of firmness before it is brought into a work. Cato orders that wood handled in this way be taken out and brought into the sun when the moon is waning and after midday; he disapproves of the four days immediately following the full moon, and warns that it should not be brought out while the south wind is blowing. And when you have brought it out, care must be taken that you do not drag it through the dew, nor should you hew or saw it while it is dewy, or frozen, or not entirely dry.

### ¶ Trees most suitable for buildings, which for what purpose, in which places they are more eternal, firmer, and of the greatest duration: Chapter VI.

**T**heophrastus seems to have thought that timber would not be well-dried for use as boards and especially for doors before three years. They consider these trees to be most suitable for the work of buildings: the Turkey oak <term>Cerrum</term>, the Oak, the Hard-oak <term>robora</term>, the Italian oak <term>esculum</term>, the Poplar, the Lime <note>or Linden</note>, the Willow, the Alder, the Ash, the Pine, the Cypress, the Wild Olive, the Olive, the Chestnut, the Larch, the Boxwood, the Cedar, as well as Ebony and even the Vine. But the nature of all these is varied, and they are to be employed for various uses accordingly. For some excel others in the open air, some are preserved in the shade, and some shine...

### Leon Battista Alberti. *On the Art of Building*.

...in the open air: others harden among the waters and are more eternal when buried. For that reason, some are used for veneers, planks, carvings, and interior works; others for beams and rafters; the rest for supporting outdoor pavements and roofings.
<margin>Alder.</margin>
And especially the **Alder** <note>original: "Alnus"</note> excels all others for river and marsh piling in foundations; it is most enduring of moisture. The same wood does not last in the air and the sun.
<margin>Winter oak.</margin>
On the contrary, the **Winter oak** <note>original: "Esculus"</note> is impatient of moisture.
<margin>Elm.</margin>
The **Elm** <note>original: "Vlmus"</note> becomes dense in the air and in the open; elsewhere it spreads and does not hold its shape.
<margin>Spruce.</margin>
The **Spruce** <note>original: "Picea"</note> and likewise the **Pine** <note>original: "Pinus"</note> are eternal if buried in the earth.
<margin>Pine.</margin>
But as for the **Hard oak** <note>original: "Robur"; specifically the sessile or pedunculate oak known for its density</note>, since it is so thick, sinewy, dense, and endowed with tiny pores, it does not absorb moisture, making it most suitable for all sorts of earthen buildings.
<margin>Hard oak.</margin>
It is especially useful if placed to bear weights, being then quite the strongest support for a column. However, although nature has instilled such hardness in it that it cannot be drilled unless soaked, they nevertheless assert that above ground it is unstable, becoming cracked <note>original: "rituosam"; likely meaning prone to fissures or "grinning"</note> and twisting itself; it is also easily corrupted by seawater. This does not happen to the **Olive**, the **Holm oak** <note>original: "ilici"</note>, and the **Wild olive**, which agree with the Hard oak in other respects but do not rot in the water.
<margin>Oak.</margin>
The **Oak** <note>original: "Quercus"</note> is never worn out by old age, because it is juicy deep inside and possesses its own strength.
<margin>Beech.</margin>
Likewise, the **Beech** <note>original: "Fagus"</note> and the **Walnut** <note>original: "Iuglans"</note> are not quickly destroyed by water and are counted among the principal woods to be buried.
<margin>Walnut.</margin>
Furthermore, the **Cork oak** <note>original: "Suber"</note> for use in columns, and the **Wild pine**, the **Mulberry** <note>original: "morus"</note>, the **Maple** <note>original: "acer"</note>, and the **Elm** are not useless trees.
<margin>Cork and other trees...</margin>
He considers them fit for rafters and beams. Theophrastus <note>a Greek philosopher and the "father of botany"</note> mentions the **Euboean nut** <note>original: "nucem euboicam"; likely the chestnut</note>: for it gives a signal with a sound before it breaks.
<margin>...fit for use as columns.</margin>
Because of this, it once happened that everyone inside a bathhouse at Andros escaped unharmed from a subsequent collapse of the roofs.
<margin>Euboean nut.</margin>
But the best of all is the **Fir** <note>original: "Abies"</note>.
<margin>Fir.</margin>
For while it is foremost in height and girth, being content with its natural stiffness, it does not easily bend under heavy loads, but remains straight and unconquered. Add to this that it is easy to work and not burdensome to walls due to its own weight. To this tree alone are many praises ascribed; they affirm it provides more uses than any other. Yet they do not deny it has one flaw: it very easily catches flames and is an enemy to fires.
<margin>Cypress.</margin>
Not second to this for timbering houses is the **Cypress** tree, which otherwise claims for itself the primary and chief praise among our trees. The ancients reckoned this among the most famous, not far behind cedar and ebony. Among the Indians, the cypress is venerated almost as an aromatic; and they might rightly praise it who want the **Chian** and **Cyrenaic** varieties, which Theophrastus declares to be eternal. Whether for its scent, shine, strength, size, straightness, or longevity. In all these...

# Book II. On Materials. Folio 23.

...among the praised trees, what tree will you compare to it? They affirm that the **cypress** <note>original: "cupressum"</note> feels absolutely no decay or old age, and it never develops cracks of its own accord. For this very reason, **Plato** <note>Greek philosopher, c. 427–347 BC</note> believed that public laws and sacred institutions should be inscribed on cypress tablets, because he thought they might be more eternal than bronze. This passage reminds me to relate things worth remembering that I have read and seen regarding the cypress itself. They testify that the cypress doors in the **Temple of Diana at Ephesus** <note>one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World</note> lasted four hundred years and preserved their luster so well that you would have called them new forever. We ourselves saw at **St. Peter's Basilica** in Rome—when the doors were being restored by Pope **Eugenius IV** <note>reigned 1431–1447</note>—that where the injury of men's hands (in stealing the silver they were once covered with) had not reached, they had remained solid and perfectly intact for over five hundred and fifty years. For if we interpret the annals of the Popes of the city of Rome correctly, there are that many years from the time of Pope **Adrian III** <note>reigned 884–885</note>, who installed them, to the time of Eugenius IV.

Thus, for making floorings and timber frames, they approve of **fir** <note>original: "Abiete"</note> and cypress; they perhaps prefer the latter for one reason: that it is more eternal. But cypress is heavier than fir. They also approve of **pine** <note>original: "pinum"</note> and **spruce** <note>original: "piceam"</note>. For they think the pine is very similar to the fir in resisting an imposed weight. But between pine and fir, there is this difference among others: the fir is less damaged by wood-borers <note>original: "terebina", referring to wood-eating larvae</note> because the pine has a more bitter sap, whereas the fir has a sweeter one.

I personally think the **larch** <note>original: "Laricem"</note> is second to none; I have noted that it has supported the weights of structures most firmly and for the longest time, both elsewhere and particularly in **Venice** in the ancient works of the forum.
<margin>Larch.</margin>
And they affirm that it provides all the benefits that other trees do. It is sinewy, tenacious of strength, very firm in storms, and unharmed by decay. There is an old opinion that this wood remains unconquered and almost unharmed by the damage of fire. Indeed, they even order that planks of larch be placed facing the direction from which you fear the coming danger of fire. But we have seen it burn when set on fire, yet in such a way that it seemed to disdain the flames and wished to shake them off. It is agreed to have one flaw: for it is made vulnerable to the **shipworm** <note>original: "teredini", a marine borer</note> by seawater.

They predict that **hard oak** <note>original: "robora"</note> and **olive** <note>original: "oleam"</note> will be useless for beam-work, because they are heavy, they yield to weight, and they bend almost of their own accord. Furthermore, woods that break more easily than they split are not useful for such beam-work, such as the olive, the **fig**, the **linden**, and the **willow**, and the like.

It is a wonder what they assert about the **palm** <note>original: "palma"</note>:
<margin>Palm.</margin>
that it resists a weight placed upon it and curves in the opposite direction <note>a classical belief that palm wood arches upward against a load, symbolizing resilience</note>. For outdoor beam-work and roofing, they prefer the **juniper** <note>original: "iuniperum"</note> above all others; and **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist, 23–79 AD</note> says its nature is the same as that of the **cedar**. But...

For other internal joinery—such as doors, beds, tables, benches, and the like—**fir** <note>original: "abies"</note> is excellent, especially that which grows on the Italian side of the Alps. 
For this tree is by nature very dry and its glue is most tenacious. **Spruce** <note>original: "picea"</note> and **cypress** are also very convenient for these things. <margin>Ash.</margin>

<margin>Mulberry.</margin>
They praise the **mulberry** <note>original: "Morum"</note> both for its eternity and because it blackens with age day by day and becomes more pleasing. **Theophrastus** <note>Greek philosopher and 'father of botany', c. 371–287 BC</note> mentions that the wealthy were accustomed to install doors made of **lotus** <note>likely the nettle tree, 'Celtis australis'</note>, holm oak, or boxwood. For this reason, they used it for making the statues of the gods. And then they used...

...used **Lotus** <note>original: "Lotho"; likely the Mediterranean nettle tree, prized for its dark, hard wood</note>, **Boxwood** <note>original: "Buxo"</note>, and **Cedar**; and likewise **Cypress**; and also the thicker part of the **olive root**, and the **Egyptian peach** tree, which they say is similar to the lotus. If any work needed to be turned on a lathe <note>term: lathe <gloss>a machine for shaping wood by rotating it against a cutting tool</gloss></note> to be made rounded: they used **Beech**, **Mulberry**, **Turpentine tree**, and especially **Boxwood**, which is the densest of all and excellently suited for turning; they also used **ebony**, the finest of all. Nor did they reject **white poplar**, or **black poplar**, **willow**, **hornbeam**, **rowan**, **elder**, and **fig** for making statues and panels.
<margin>Trees suitable for making and shaping statues.</margin>
These trees, due to their dryness and uniformity, are useful for receiving and preserving the painters' adhesives <note>original: "glutiniamenta"</note> and under-coatings <note>original: "illiniamenta"</note>. Moreover, they are pliable and quite easy for expressing shapes. Truly, among these, it is well known that the **lime tree** <note>original: "tiliam"</note> is the softest of all. There are some who approve of the **jujube** for making statues. Contrary to these is the **oak** <note>original: "robur"</note>; for indeed it is entirely incompatible with itself and all other materials of this kind, and it rejects all glue. They say the same defect exists in all milky and curly <note>original: "crispis"; referring to highly figured or burled grain</note> woods, so that they reject every kind of adhesive. Likewise, any wood that is smooth and dense sticks poorly with glue. Those that are different in nature, such as **Ivy**, **Laurel**, and **Lime**, because they are "hot" <note>This refers to the ancient theory of humors, where materials were classified as hot, cold, moist, or dry</note>, do not bond well with glue for long when joined with those that grow in damp places, because all such are "cold" by nature.
<margin>☛</margin> **Elm**, **Ash**, **Mulberry**, and **Cherry**, because they are dry, do not go well with **plane** and **alder**, which are wet by nature. Indeed, the ancients were so careful that they forbade joining things by glue that were not congruent in nature or were contrary. They even forbade joining together pieces that were not paired but merely stuck. Here is that advice of **Vitruvius**: that axles of **winter oak** <note>original: "esculeos"</note> should not be joined to **common oak** <note>original: "querquinis"</note>.

### ¶ On trees again, summarized and in general. Chapter VII.

**B**ut to report on all these matters summarily: It is agreed among all authors that infertile trees are stronger than fertile ones. Wild trees, not cultivated by hand or iron, are harder than domestic ones. For **Theophrastus** <note>Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle, known as the "father of botany"</note> denies that wild trees fall into diseases that kill them. But they declare that domestic ones, especially those that bear fruit, are subject to the gravest diseases. And among the fertile ones, they determine that the early-ripening are weaker than the late-ripening, and the sweet weaker than the sharp. And among the sharp and harsh ones, they consider those that produce more bitter and rarer fruit to be more solid. Those that bear fruit in alternate years, or are entirely sterile, are knottier than the fertile ones. And among these, the shorter the wood, the more difficult <note>likely meaning harder to work or more stubborn</note> it is. And sterile trees grow more than fertile ones. They add that those which grow in the open and are not sheltered by mountains...

### Leon Battista Alberti: On the Art of Building

...nor from forests: but those which have grown agitated by frequent winds and storms are indeed stronger and thicker, but shorter and more knotty than those which grew in a valley and a place safe from the winds. Moreover, trees grown in moist and shaded places are thought to be softer than those that have matured in sunny and dry spots. And those that grow toward the north are more suitable than those that decline from the north toward the south. And those born in places alien to their nature, they reject them just like miscarriages. And southern-facing parts will indeed be very hard: but they are twisted in their marrow <note>term: marrow <gloss>the pith or central core of the tree trunk; Alberti uses the Latin 'medulla' to draw an analogy to animal bones</gloss></note> and prove less uniform for executing the work. Furthermore, those naturally dry and slow to grow are stronger than those that are loose and fertile. 

For Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar whose agricultural writings were a primary source for Renaissance architects</note> thought that in these there was a female nature, but in the others a male nature; and that any white wood is less dense and more manageable than those into which any color has been infused. 

<margin>The quality of materials.</margin> 
And every heavy material is thicker and harder than light wood. And the lighter each is, the more fragile it is: and the curlier, the more compact. Then, to those whom nature has granted a longer life, she has also granted that once cut down, they decay more slowly. In every wood, also, the less marrow it contains, the sharper and stronger its nature is: those parts which are closest to the marrow are indeed harder and denser than the others, while those closer to the bark have a tougher fiber. 

<margin>A comparison of trees [to animals].</margin> 
For in trees, as in animals, they establish that the outer bark is for skin, that which lies beneath the skin is for flesh, and that which wraps around the marrow is for bone; and Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher, who wrote extensively on botany and biology</note> thought that the nodes in plants were very similar to nerves. 

<margin>Sapwood.</margin> 
They consider the **alburnum** <note>term: alburnum <gloss>the soft, living sapwood between the bark and the heartwood, often prone to decay</gloss></note> the worst part of all wood, both for other reasons and because it is prone to wood-eating worms. Add to this that the parts of the timber which were pressed by the midday sun while the tree stood will be drier than the rest, and more slender, and thinner, yet denser; they will have the marrow closer to the bark on that side. And likewise, those parts which were closest to the earth and roots will stand heavier than the rest; the sign of this is that they will float in water with difficulty. And the middle part of any tree is curlier, and wherever there are knots, the closer they are to the roots, the more winding they are; yet they consider the innermost parts more consistent and useful than the outer ones. 

Truly, among the types of trees, I find some about which the best writers report quite wonderful things. 

<margin>The vine surpasses the eternity of ages.</margin> 
For they affirm that the **vine** indeed surpasses the eternity of ages. A statue of **Jupiter** <note>the king of the Roman gods</note> made from vine-wood was seen in the city of **Populonia** <note>an ancient Etruscan city on the coast of Tuscany known for its metalworking and history</note> for many centuries, uncorrupted until the time of Caesar. All declare that there is no wood with a nature more thoroughly eternal. In the Indian territory of Arriana...

### On Stones: when they should be quarried and placed into the work; which are easier, more tolerant, better, and more durable. Chapter VIII.

**S**tone must also be prepared to be used for walls; it will be of two kinds. One for fitting and binding together rubble-work <term>rubble-work <gloss>original: "cementis", referring to 'caementa', unhewn stones or broken shards used to fill the core of a wall, rather than modern liquid cement</gloss></term>; the other which is suitable for the facing structure. First, concerning that which is for the structure. But many things, both for the sake of brevity and because they are too common, I shall pass over. Nor shall I insist here on disputing those physical theories about the beginnings and origin of stones: whether from mixtures of water and earth those viscous principles first hardened into mud and thereafter into stone; whether by the force of cold, or—as they claim concerning gems—by the force of heat and the sun's rays they grew thick and congealed; or rather, as with other things, the seeds of stones were likewise implanted into the earth by nature. Whether colors are in stones from a certain proportion of earthy particles mixed with liquid water. Or from the innate power of the seed itself. Or whether they are present from the received impression of a ray of light. Therefore, although all such things might perhaps contribute something to the ornamentation of the subject, I shall nonetheless pass them over; I shall pursue the architectural matter itself as if among craftsmen proven in practice and art, more freely and loosely than perhaps the most exacting philosophers demand. <margin>At what time it should be held.</margin> Cato <note>Cato the Elder, author of the agricultural treatise 'De Re Rustica'</note> says: quarry stone in summer; keep it in the open air. Do not put it into the work before two years have passed; so that in summer, during which time the stones are unaccustomed to washing, and frosts, and rains, or the remaining injuries of the seasons, they might gradually become seasoned. <margin>Stone to be quarried.</margin> For if you expose a stone recently taken from the quarry, pregnant with native moisture and sap <note>original: "succo", implying the stone contains a vital liquid or moisture like a plant</note>, to the bitterness of winds and sudden frosts, it will split and dissolve. In the open air, let it be proven how strong each stone is, and how steadfast against adverse and provoking things. Let it be tested by this sort of preliminary to its future contest with the eternity of time. Not before two years, so that those weak by nature and those which would have developed a flaw in the work may not remain hidden from you and may be separated from the stronger ones. For it is certain that in every kind of stone, they are found to vary among themselves, so that some harden in the air, while others by frost—

<margin>
The qualities
of stones
are worth
knowing.
</margin>
...[when] sprinkled [with water] they contract rust and dissolve, and other things of this kind. Truly, what these qualities are, according to the variety and nature of their locations, is most beautifully revealed through use and experience. So that you might have learned the force and virtue of each stone more fully from the buildings of the ancients than from the writings and monuments of philosophers. Nevertheless, to speak summarily of the whole genus of stones, one may establish this: every white stone is easier to work than a dark one. A translucent stone is more ductile <note>Easier to shape or lead with a tool</note> than an opaque one. And the more any stone resembles salt, the more unmanageable it will be.

A stone sprinkled with sand is rough when viewed in the light. If golden sparks glimmer within, it is stubborn. If it swarms with blackish spots—so to speak—it is wild <note>original: "indomitus", meaning untamable or impossible to carve cleanly</note>. That which is sprinkled with angular droplets will be stronger than that with round ones; and the smaller the droplets, the more tolerant the stone will be. And the purer and clearer the color of each, the more eternal it is. The fewer veins a stone has, the more whole it is. And where the vein itself is more congruent in color to the surrounding stone, the more uniform it is; the thinner the vein, the more difficult; the more winding and twisting, the harsher; and the more knotted, the more troublesome.

Those veins are most prone to splitting which have a line of red ochre <note>original: "rubrica", a red earth pigment</note> drawn through their middle; or very close to these will be the ones darkened here and there with a thin, whitish, grassy color. The most difficult of all are those that resemble ice, especially blue ice. They indicate a discordant and inconstant number of veins; and the straighter they are, the more untrustworthy. The more a stone gives a sharper and cleaner edge when its fragments are broken, the more compact it will be.

And a stone which, when its surface is broken, stands out less roughly, will be more manageable than a coarse one. But the whiter the coarse ones are, the less compliant they will be. Conversely, every dark stone, where the grain <note>original: "luna", literally 'moon', used here to describe the crystalline structure or 'shimmer' of the stone's grain</note> is finer, will more strongly resist the edge of the iron tool. Every base stone is harder the more porous it is. And that which, when sprinkled with water on the surface, dries more slowly, is more raw <note>original: "crudior", implying the stone has not 'ripened' or seasoned properly</note>. Every heavy stone is more solid and polishable than a light one; and every light stone is more crumbly than a heavy one.

A stone that rings when you strike it is denser than a "deaf" <note>original: "furdo", a stone that produces a dull thud rather than a clear ring</note> one. That which smells of sulfur when rubbed hard is sharper than one that gives off no scent. Finally, the more stubborn it is against the chisel, the more rigid and constant it will be against attacking storms. At the mouth of the quarry, the stone which preserves itself in larger blocks despite being exposed to the weather is considered the stronger. Likewise, almost every stone is softer when it is first dug up than after it has been kept in the open air; and a stone sprinkled or soaked with moisture is more manageable by the iron tool than when it has dried out. And the wetter the place in the quarry from which each stone is taken, the denser it will be when it has dried. They believe stones are easier to hew when the South wind <note>original: "austro"</note> blows than when the North wind <note>original: "borea"</note> blows; and

### Chapter IX.

**F**or it will indeed not be irrelevant to have understood how much variety and wonder they contain, so that each may be more appropriately suited to its proper uses. <margin>Volscinian stone.</margin> They declare that around Volscinii <note>Modern Bolsena in Italy</note> and in the territory of Statonia there is a stone most suitable for all building uses; neither fire nor any violence of storms harms it. And it is completely eternal and incorruptible against storms, while preserving the outlines of statues for a very long time. When Nero was rebuilding the city after the fires, Tacitus writes that he used Gabine and Alban stone for beams, because that stone is impervious to fire. <margin>Stone from Liguria.</margin> Among the Ligurians and in Venice, in Umbria, Picenum, and among the Belgae, a white stone is available <margin>A stone that can be worked with iron.</margin> which you can saw with a toothed iron saw and plane very easily. And if it were not otherwise weak and feeble by nature, it would surpass all others in works. But it is broken by frost, ice, and spray; and it is not at all robust against the sea air. <margin>Istrian stone.</margin> History mentions a stone not unlike marble <note>original: "histricus", referring to Istrian stone from the Adriatic coast</note>. But when touched by steam and flames, it immediately splits and bursts; they assert this very thing happens to any stone that is strong, especially white flint and also black, so that fire produces no benefit. <margin>Campanian stone.</margin> In Campania there is a stone very similar to dark ash, in which you would even think coals were mixed and interspersed; it is light in weight beyond what you could imagine and can be shaped with iron, and is thoroughly tenacious, and also stable; it is not weak against fires or storms; but it is so dry and thirsty that it immediately absorbs the moisture of the lime and burns it. Once the moisture is exhausted and vanished like dust, it leaves the mortar <note>original: "illimenta", the binding material or slurry</note> ruined. From this, the joints are soon dissolved, and the work weakens and collapses of its own accord. But contrary in nature to this stone is the rounded stone, especially that which is from a river; for it is always wet and does not adhere to cement. What of the fact that they have found in marble quarries that marbles grow? <margin>Marble grows. A fissure grows.</margin> In Rome during these times, small pieces of porous Tiburtine stone <note>Travertine, a common Roman building stone</note> were found beneath the earth, growing together into a single solid stone over time.

... [moisture] of the earth and its nourishing heat, so to speak, have grown together. At Lake Reate <note>modern Rieti</note>, <margin>☛</margin> you will see the place where the overflowing water falls headlong over a precipice into the river Nar <note>the Nera</note>; the upper edge of the bank grows daily, so that some have taken this as proof that by this kind of addition and the increase of stone, the valley itself was closed off at its narrow mouth and formed into a lake. In the Lucanian territory, not far from the Silari river <note>the Sele</note>, in the part facing East where dripping water flows down from high cliffs, you will see large masses of hanging stone <term>glacconia</term> <note>stalactites, likely named for their icy or glassy appearance</note> growing daily; they reach such a size that each of them is a load for many wagons. This stone, when fresh and wet with its "maternal juice," is quite soft. But when it has dried, it becomes very hard and most suitable for all uses. I have observed the same thing happening in some ancient aqueducts: the sides of the channels are encrusted by a certain petrifying gumming of the stone. In Gaul <note>France</note>, two things worthy of mention can be seen in our time. For in the territory of Corneliano, there is a very high bank of a torrent from which large and numerous spherical stones, conceived in the deep bowels of the earth, are birthed daily in many places. In the territory of Faenza, <margin>Stones born spontaneously</margin> near the bank of the river Lamone, there are vast stones stretched out by nature which vomit forth no small amount of salt daily, and they are thought to petrify over time. In the territory of Florence in Etruria, near the river Clanis <note>Alberti likely refers to the Chiana or a similar local stream</note>, there is a field in which, every seven years, the very hard stones with which it is abundantly strewn turn back into clods of earth. Pliny reports that among the Cassandrians and also around Cassandreia, cloddy earth turns into stone. At Puteoli <note>Pozzuoli</note>, a dust <note>pozzolana, a volcanic ash</note> is found which hardens in seawater and becomes stone. Also, along the entire shore from Oropus to Aulis, they report that whatever the sea washes over becomes stone and is rendered solid. In Arabia, Diodorus says there are clods of earth dug up that are sweet-smelling, which, like metals melted by fire, turn into stone. He adds that these stones are such that when raindrops fall on them, the joints melt together and they become a single united stone throughout the entire wall. They say a "sarcophagus" stone <margin>the miraculous sarcophagus stone</margin> is also dug up near Troas in Asia, which is joined by a fissile vein. They assert that bodies of the deceased placed in this stone are entirely consumed, except for the teeth, before the fortieth day; and what you might find more amazing, <margin>☛</margin> they claim that clothing, shoes, and such things brought in with the bodies are also turned into stone. Contrary to this is the *chernites* stone <note>original: "comites", likely a transcription error for "chernites"</note>, which they say preserved Darius <note>Darius the Great of Persia</note>. For it keeps bodies perfectly whole. But so much for these things.

# Book II. On Materials. Leaf XXVII.

**But** those who consistently used stone in place [of brick], as the ancients very gladly did: I believe indeed that men, led by a lack of things and by necessity, first made use of [clay] so that they might construct brick buildings. Later, when it was noticed that this kind of structural material was easy to work, convenient for use, fit for beauty, and firm and stable for eternity, they followed through to build not only other things but even royal palaces of brick. Finally, after they perceived—whether by chance or industry—that fire had the power to strengthen and densify bricks, they persevered in raising all things everywhere with fired-tile work <term>testaceo</term> <note>original: "testaceo... opere" - refers to kiln-fired ceramic or terracotta work as opposed to sun-dried mud bricks</note>. And as much as I have noted from the most ancient structures: I would certainly dare to say this, that nothing is found more convenient for all the uses of building you might wish than brick—not raw <note>original: "crudo" - sun-dried</note>, but fired: provided that a diligent method of firing and shaping is applied.

But concerning the praise of brickwork, another time. To the matter at hand: they say that in making bricks, that earth is approved which is whitish and chalky. Likewise, that which is reddish is also approved, and that which is called "male" sand <note>likely a reference to a coarse, gritty type of sand</note>. But they decide that sandy and thoroughly gravelly soil is to be avoided, and especially pebbly soil is to be driven away altogether: because things of this sort are distorted and split apart during firing, and then they crumble of their own accord once they have been thoroughly baked.

<margin>For making bricks</margin>
They think that bricks should not be shaped immediately from excavated earth: but they command that the earth be dug in autumn, soaked throughout the winter, and shaped in early spring. 

<margin>suitable.</margin>
For if you shape them in midwinter, it is likely they will become <margin>cracked</margin> cracked by frost; but if at the solstice <note>the height of summer</note>, they will split from the sharp heat by drying out <margin>mostly</margin> on the surface. But if necessity compels you to mold bricks during the winter chills: cover them immediately with very dry sand. If during the burning summer, cover with wet straw: for handled thus, they do not split or warp. There are some who want bricks to have a glazed surface. If that is desired, care must be taken that they are not shaped from sandy or too meager and dry earth, for they would absorb the glaze.

<margin>Bricks to be shaped</margin>
Truly, they are to be shaped from whitish and chalky and tough [clay]: and they should be kept thin, for those that happen to be thicker are poorly fired through and do not escape being immune to cracks. But if it is necessary to make them thicker, the disadvantage will be largely provided for if they are pierced through the middle of their thickness in one and then another place with a stylus, so that they may be more conveniently able to dry and bake through, with the sweat and vapor breathing out through these very vents, as if they were pores. Potters smear a white chalk over their earthenwares, by which it happens that the glaze melts most evenly onto the surface. This will also be beneficial for brickwork. I have noticed from ancient buildings that some part of sand, especially red, was mixed into the bricks: and that it was the custom to mix in red earth and marble by discovery. We have experienced that much firmer bricks are returned from the same single earth if, as it were...

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

Just as if we were about to make loaves of bread, we should first let the dough ferment, as it were; then, having kneaded it again and again, we should render it like wax and thoroughly purged of even the smallest pebbles. They harden by firing to such an extent that through much flame they are turned into a flint-like hardness. And whether it happens by fire while they are being baked, or perhaps by the air while they are drying—the same thing that happens to bread—bricks and tiles develop a solid crust. It will be helpful, therefore, to make them thin, so that there is more crust and less pith <note>original: "medullae" - refers to the softer, porous interior of the brick compared to the hardened outer surface</note>. And in these matters, one may observe that if they are laid in a clean and polished state, they will endure against the weather; the same is true for any stone, that if they are polished, they are not eaten away by roughness. 

Indeed, some believe that tiles should be scoured either just after being taken from the kiln before they become damp, or if they are already wet, before they dry out. For once a tile has been moistened and dried again, it hardens to such a degree that it will dull and consume the edge of an iron tool. But we find it more convenient to scrape them immediately after they are formed and while they are still being dried for firing. 

<margin>Three types of bricks.</margin>
Among the ancients, there were three types of bricks. The first was one and a half feet long and one foot wide. The second was five palms <note>A "palm" was a Roman unit of measurement based on the width of the hand, roughly 3 inches or 7.4 centimeters</note> on every side. The third was no more than four palms. We see in buildings, especially for arches and joints <note>original: "nexuras" - points where structural elements interlace or connect</note>, tiles that are two feet wide on every side. Writers record that the ancients did not use these equally for public and private works, but rather built public works with the larger ones and private buildings with the smaller. Regarding these, I have noted both elsewhere among the monuments of the ancients and specifically along the Appian Way <note>The most famous ancient Roman road, running from Rome to Brindisi, lined with monumental brick tombs</note> that various types of larger and smaller bricks exist, which they used in different ways. I believe they did this because they earnestly wished to accomplish not only whatever was useful, but also whatever occurred to the mind as fitting and graceful. To omit other examples, I have seen bricks no more than six fingers <note>original: "digitos" - finger-widths, roughly 0.75 inches each</note> long, one thick, and three wide. But these were used primarily for laying herringbone-patterned pavements <term>spicatim</term> <note>original: "spicatim" - a "spike" or "ear of grain" pattern, known today as herringbone</note>. 

Beyond all others, I approve of the triangular ones, which they made in this manner: they would form a brick one foot square and one and a half fingers thick; while it was still "green" <note>original: "virebat" - literally "green," meaning the clay was still wet and unforced</note>, they would mark it with two diagonal lines from corner to opposite corner with a deep score that cut through to half the thickness of the brick. From this, therefore, four equal triangles were obtained. 

<margin>Triangular bricks and their utility.</margin>
These bricks offered several advantages. They took up less mortar <note>original: "cretae" - likely referring here to the lime-binder or mortar</note>, they fit together better in the kiln, and they were more manageable to remove and carry to the work site—consider that one could hold four in one hand. The mason, with a light strike while building, would separate one from the other. He would then lay these in courses along the faces of the walls so that the one-foot side was exposed on the outside, while the corner was directed inward. From this, the expense was indeed less, the work more pleasing, and the structure firmer...

### ¶ The various species and natures of Lime and Gypsum, their similarities and differences; and several things regarding these not unworthy of knowing. Chapter XI.

<margin>
Cato.
Lime.
</margin>
**C**ato the Censor <note>Marcus Porcius Cato (234–149 BC), a Roman statesman who wrote 'De Agricultura', the oldest surviving work of Latin prose</note> disapproves of **lime** made from varied stones. And Cato condemns lime which is made from flint for every kind of work. Furthermore, any stone is exceedingly useless for making lime if it is exhausted, parched, or crumbling, in which the fire, during the baking process, finds nothing to consume; such are the tufa-like stones and those which are reddish or pale in the countryside around Rome, at Fidenae and Alba. For the lime which experts approve ought to be lighter by a third part of its weight than the stone from which it was made. Moreover, stone that is too flinty and naturally moist is by no means useful for making lime, because it turns to glass under fire. Green stone <note>original: "Viridis lapis" - likely referring to raw or unseasoned stone</note> (says Pliny) strongly resists fire. But we have found concerning porphyry stone that it is not only not baked by flames, but it even causes whatever contiguous stones are around it within the kiln to be given back <note>i.e., to fail or crack</note>, so that they are not sufficiently baked by the fires. Furthermore, they reject earthy stone because it yields impure lime. 

But the ancient architects especially praise lime which is made from stone that is very hard, quite dense, and particularly white. For they consider this not only useful for other purposes, but most firm especially for <term>vaults</term> <note>original: "testudinibus" - literally 'tortoise shells', a common architectural term for arched ceilings or vaults</note>. In the second place, they approve of that lime which is made from stone that is otherwise not light and crumbling, but porous. For they believe this to be the most excellent of all for the work of plastering and more ductile than the others, and that it renders works more splendid. We have also seen architects in Gaul <note>Modern-day France</note> use no other lime than that made from rounded stones gathered from mountain torrents, which are dark, very hard, and of such a kind that you might think them to be flint; yet in their work, both with stone and with bricks over many ages...

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

...it is established that it has provided excellent stability. I find in Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (Pliny the Elder), author of Natural History, a primary source for Alberti</note> that the lime made from millstone is naturally fatty: therefore it is very convenient for all uses. We have understood by experience that the millstone which is sprinkled drop by drop with salt, since it is coarser and therefore drier, does not succeed as well. But that other kind not mixed with salt, which is denser and breaks like snail shells with a finer powder, does succeed. But whatever the stone may be, that dug up specifically for lime will be more useful than that which is gathered from the surface; and that taken from a shady and damp quarry is better than that from a dry one; and that from white stone is more ductile than that from dark. In Gaul, among the maritime regions of the Aedui <note>A Celtic tribe in eastern France</note>, for lack of stone, they make lime from oyster and shellfish shells.

<margin>Gypsum.</margin> There is also a type of lime called <term>gypsum</term> <note>gipsum: a soft sulfate mineral used for plaster</note>: for it too is made from burnt stone, although they report that in Cyprus and Thebes gypsum is dug up from the surface of the earth, scorched by the sun. But every gypsum stone differs from limestone because it is very soft and crumbly, except for one which is dug in Syria. For that one is indeed very hard. They also differ in that gypsum stone is cooked for no more than twenty hours; whereas the stone for lime is cooked for no less than sixty hours. I have noticed four species of gypsum throughout Italy: two of these are translucent, and two are not translucent. Of the translucent ones, one is similar to lumps of alum, or rather to alabaster; this they call 

<margin>Squameola.</margin> **Squameola** <note>literally "Little Scale"</note> because it consists of very thin scales, as it were, clinging together and compressed like pages. The other is also scaly, but more similar to dark salt than to alum. Both species of the non-translucent ones imitate thickened chalk. But one is whitish and somewhat pale; the other has a reddish color spread over its paleness. The latter ones are inferior to the former; among the latter, the reddish one is more tenacious. Among the former, that which is purer provides whiter and more splendid <term>sigilla</term> <note>small relief figures or seals</note> and <term>coronas</term> <note>cornices or crown moldings</note> in plastering work. 

<margin>Gypsum.</margin> 
<margin>Rimini.</margin> 
At Rimini <note>original: Ariminum</note> you will find solid gypsum, so that you would say it is marble or alabaster; I ordered slabs to be sawn from it with a toothed saw, which are very convenient for the work of <term>crustationum</term> <note>veneering or decorative surface plating</note>. 

<margin>The preparation of Gypsum.</margin> 
So that I omit nothing, every gypsum stone ought to be beaten and crushed with wooden hammers until it is reduced to flour: it must be stored in a very dry place, applied immediately, mixed very quickly with water, and at once driven into the work. 

<margin>Likewise of lime.</margin> 
Lime, on the contrary, should not be crushed, but rather soaked as a lump; and indeed it should be slaked <note>macerated in water</note> long beforehand with plenty of water before you mix it into the work, especially for plastering, so that if any lump perhaps was insufficiently cooked by the fires, it may be dissolved and liquefied by long soaking. For when it is used fresh and not thoroughly washed and pre-soaked, because there may be some raw pebbles hidden in it, it happens that these pebbles, day by day...

# Book II. On Materials.
## Folio XXIX.

...lest they rot and subsequently emit pustules <note>original: "pustulas"; these are small blisters or pits that form in plaster if the lime is not properly aged or slaked</note>, by which all polishing of the work would be spoiled. Add to this that the lime should not be soaked all at once in a single "rain," so to speak, but it is necessary to moisten it gradually with repeated and successive sprinklings until it is rendered plainly drunk <note>original: "ebria"; a metaphor for being fully saturated with water</note>. From then on, it must be kept in a damp place and under pure shade without any mixture of other things, and covered with nothing more than a thin layer of light sand on the surface, until it ferments more smoothly through the passage of time. And it is indeed well established that lime increases greatly in strength through this kind of long-lasting fermentation.

<margin>☞</margin> We ourselves have seen some lime recently found in an old, long-abandoned pit which, as was clearly evident from many clues, had been left there for five hundred years. It was found to be moist and liquid, and so to speak "ripe," so much so that in its softness it far surpassed honey or the marrow of bones. Indeed, you could not imagine anything more convenient for any use. When kept in this way, it takes twice as much sand as that lime which is mixed when recently slaked.

In these matters, therefore, lime and gypsum do not agree; in other things, they do. For you should take gypsum out of the furnace immediately; keep it in the shade and in a dry place, and you must use it quickly. For whether it is kept in the furnace itself or elsewhere—exposed to the air, the moon, or the sun—especially in summer, it very quickly dissolves into ash and becomes useless. So much for these matters.

Regarding the furnaces, they warn that you should not put stone inside unless you have broken it, so that the pieces are no smaller than clods, as this allows them to be cooked more easily. It is indeed established that inside stones, especially round ones, there are sometimes certain empty cavities in which trapped air causes a great deal of damage. For when the fire is lit in the furnaces, it happens that either the air is compressed by the cold retreating inward, or as the stone eventually heats up, that same air expands into steam; it then swells up and, having broken the prison in which it was confined, it bursts out with a massive sound and sharp force in every direction, disturbing and overturning the entire heap within the furnace.

<margin>Worms in stones.</margin> And there are those who have seen living creatures thriving deep inside such stones—not only various other kinds but also worms with hairy backs and many feet—which are accustomed to causing loss to the furnaces.

<margin>A snake found with its breathing holes blocked.</margin> Nor should I fail to add here certain things worthy of mention regarding such matters which have been seen in our time. For we do not write these things only for craftsmen, but also for those devoted to the study of worthy subjects. For this reason, it is helpful to intersperse occasionally things that delight, provided they are not foreign to our subject and purpose. During the time of Pope Martin V <note>Martin V (reigned 1417–1431) was the pope who returned the papacy to Rome after the Great Schism; Alberti served in his papal chancery</note>, a snake was brought forth, found by craftsmen in the mines living inside a vast stone with all its air-holes blocked up. Several frogs were also found, and likewise...

What of that?

<margin>Veronese stones</margin>
From the territory of Verona, stones are gathered daily that are laid bare by the sky <note>likely referring to stones found on the surface or eroded by the elements</note>, marked most appropriately with a five-leaf design <term>quincfolio</term> <note>a cinquefoil or clover-like pattern often found in fossilized crinoids or similar prehistoric life</note> in certain and matching lines and most beautifully overlapping by the wonderful and perfect art of nature, such that no mortal whatever could imitate the subtlety of the work. And what you might wonder at more: you will find no stone of this kind except inverted, covering the impressed form of the design: so that you might easily think nature created such delights of her craftsmanship not for the admiration of men, but for herself. I return to the matter at hand.

I will not dwell here on describing how the hearth, the entrance, and the mouth of the furnace <term>praefurnium</term> <note>the area in front of the kiln where fuel is fed</note> ought to be vaulted, and how the interior seat of the fires should be fitted together so that the seething flame may breathe, be restrained as if by its own boundaries, and so that the whole force of the fires may flow together and breathe as one for the task of cooking <note>the process of heating limestone to create lime</note>. Nor will I follow up on how the fire must succeed gradually and not be interrupted until the flame comes out at the very top not at all smoky, and the stones inside the furnace glow white through the smoke; and the stone is not cooked until the furnace, which had gaped open while swollen with flames, has withdrawn and tightened itself. It is a wonderful thing in which you might observe the nature of the element. For if you remove the fire from cooked lime, the lime kiln will gradually become less hot at the bottom, but will be rendered much more ignited at the top. Now, since in completing these works not only lime but also sand is needed, we must speak of sand itself.

### ¶ Three different kinds of sand and various building materials in different places. Chapter XII.

<margin>Sand</margin>
There are three kinds of sand: Pit sand, River sand, and Sea sand. Of all, the best is pit sand <term>fossicea</term> <note>sand excavated from the ground rather than gathered from water</note>. And it is indeed diverse: Black, Gray, Red, "carbunculus" <note>a term used by ancient authors for a red, volcanic, or burnt-looking earth</note>, and Gravelly. If anyone should ask me what I would define sand to be, I might perhaps say that it consists of very tiny little stones broken from larger stones. Although it pleased Vitruvius <note>the Roman architect whose 1st-century BCE treatise "De architectura" was Alberti's primary model</note> that sand—and especially in Etruria what they call *carbunculus*—is a certain kind of earth thoroughly burnt by fires of nature enclosed within mountains and rendered such that the earth is now more solid than when uncooked and softer than the rock itself. Truly, among all these sands they prefer *carbunculus*. I have noticed that in the public buildings of Rome they used red sand especially. Deep-dug sand is the last among the pit sands. Gravelly sands are...

...is suitable for filling foundations. But among the primary materials, they next count thinner gravel <term>glarea</term> <note>a coarse sand or fine pebble mixture used to give bulk to mortar</note>, especially that which is angular and free from any mixture of earth; such as that which is supplied in abundance among the Insubres <note>original: "Visumbros"; a Celtic people of Cisalpine Gaul, modern-day Milan/Lombardy</note>. Next, they approve of sand <term>harena</term> which is taken from a stream after the first upper layer has been removed. Among the river sands, that of mountain torrents is more useful, especially that which has settled from swifter flows within the mountains. In the last place comes sand that has been taken from the sea; and among the maritime sands, they do not entirely reject the blackish and glassy varieties. Among the Picenes <note>the people of Picenum, an ancient region of Italy</note> in the Salernitan territory, they do not rank sand taken from the sea below pit-sand <term>fossicea</term> <note>sand dug from a pit or quarry, usually considered the strongest for building</note>. However, they do not approve of all sand taken from the shores of that region. For they have indeed found that on shores which lie open to the south winds <note>original: "austros"</note>, the sand is the worst of all. But those shores which look toward Libya <note>i.e., the North African coast/south-west</note> produce sand that is by no means the worst. Moreover, among maritime sands, that which settles near rocks and has a coarser grain is better. 

Yet sands have certain qualities by which they differ among themselves. For sea sand dries with difficulty and, being soluble due to its saltiness <note>original: "falsugine"</note>, it remains constantly moist and flows away. Therefore, it bears loads with difficulty and is never entirely trustworthy. River sand is also more moist than pit-sand; for that reason, it is more "ductile" and better suited for plastering <term>tectoriis</term> <note>the smooth finish or stucco layers on a wall</note>. Pit-sand is more tenacious on account of its "fatness" <note>clay or organic content that makes it sticky</note>, but it causes cracks; for that reason, they use it for vaulting <term>concamerationibus</term>, but not for plaster. But the best sand of any kind will be that which, when rubbed and pressed in the hands, makes a creaking sound <note>a classic test from Vitruvius to ensure the sand is clean and free of dirt</note>; and that which, when caught in a white garment, will not stain it nor leave any earth behind. On the other hand, sand will be bad if it is smooth to the touch and lacks any roughness, and mimics muddy earth in color and smell; or that which, when stirred in water, makes the water very turbulent and muddy; or that which, when left in an open space, immediately grows grass. It will also be bad if, having been recently gathered, it remains for a long time under the open sky exposed to the sun, moon, and frost: for it becomes earthy and rotten. As such, it is ready for producing shrubs and wild fig trees <term>caprificos</term>, but is very weak for holding a structure together. 

We have spoken of timber <term>materia</term>, stone, lime, and sand, which were approved by our ancestors. But it will not be possible in all places to find these things convenient and available for the tasks we intend to do. Cicero used to say that Asia <note>referring to the Roman province of Asia, modern Turkey</note>, on account of its abundance of marble, always flourished in the glory of its buildings and statues. But you will not find marble in all places; elsewhere, there is either no stone at all, or if there is, it is not suitable for every use. They testify that in the whole of Italy, on that side which turns toward the south, pit-sand is found; but on this side of the Apennines <note>the mountain range forming the spine of Italy</note>, it is not found. The Babylonians, he says...

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

Pliny states that the Carthaginians use bitumen <term>bitumine</term> <note>a naturally occurring petroleum-based tar used as an adhesive or sealant</note> while others use mud. Elsewhere, where there is an absolute lack of stone, they build with wattle and clay. Herodotus reports that the Budini <note>an ancient people of Scythia, in modern-day Ukraine/Russia</note> build both their private and public houses of nothing but wood, so that even the city walls and the very statues of their gods are wooden among them. Mella <note>Pomponius Mella, a Roman geographer</note> says that the Neuri <note>a tribe neighboring the Budini</note> lack wood entirely, so that they are forced to use bones in place of wood. In Egypt, they maintain their hearths with the dung <note>original: "segestionibus"; refers to dried animal waste used as fuel</note> of beasts of burden. Thus it is that different peoples are forced to have different shelters for themselves according to necessity and the opportunity of things. Among the Egyptians, there are those who build even royal houses from reeds; among the Indians, there are those who build for themselves from the ribs of whales <note>original: "caetarũ costis"; likely referring to large marine mammals</note>. Diodorus Siculus writes that in Dedalia, in the region of Sardis, people live by digging into the earth. In Carrhae, a town of Arabia, they construct walls and houses from blocks of salt. But more on these things elsewhere. Therefore, as we have said, the same supply of stone, sand, and such things is not found in every place. But in different places, there exists a different reason, method, and measure for both nature and materials. For that reason, one must use those things which are supplied; and in these very things, caution must be applied: first, so that we may have more suitable and convenient materials, selected and prepared; and next, so that we may use the more appropriate ones for building, distributing everything correctly in its proper place.

### Chapter. XIII.

**S**ince the materials we have reviewed—timber, stone, lime, and sand—are now prepared, it follows that we should settle the reasoning and method for constructing the building. For as for iron, bronze, lead, glass, and other things of this sort, no more industry is needed to prepare them than to buy them and gather them into one place, so that they are not lacking while the work is being completed; although we shall speak of selecting and distributing these in their own place, as they pertain to the completion of the work and its ornamentation. And as if we were about to perform the work and build with our own hands, we shall begin the matter from the foundations themselves. But here it is necessary that I first warn you once more that times must be weighed—both public times and our own private circumstances—so that we do not undertake anything in which, amidst troubled affairs, you might incur envy if you persevere in building, or financial loss if you abandon it. Add to this that the seasons of nature must be observed above all. For one may indeed see that those things built during the winter, especially in cold places, freeze. Truly, those built during the summer, especially in sweltering places, dry out before they can bond together. For this reason, the architect Frontinus <note>Sextus Julius Frontinus, a Roman civil engineer and author of 'De aquaeductu'</note> used to advise that there are fit and accommodated times for executing work: which are from the Kalends of April <note>April 1st</note> until the Kalends of November <note>November 1st</note>, with the heat of the summer...

Lucius Tarutius <note>a Roman mathematician and philosopher, friend of Cicero, known for casting the horoscope of Rome</note> is said to have discovered the birthday of the city of Rome by noting the successes of its fortune. The wisest of the ancients thought this moment of beginning had such great power over future events that Julius Firmicus Maternus <note>a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer</note> reports there were those who discovered the "birth-chart" <term>genituram</term> of the world from the outcome of events, and they wrote most accurately about that matter. <margin>Note on what the city’s birthday ought to be.</margin> For Aesculapius and Anubis, and those who followed them—Petosiris and Necepso <note>legendary founders of Hellenistic astrology</note>—affirm that it was thus: with Cancer rising from the horizon, and the moon halfway from the sun in Leo, Saturn in Capricorn, Jupiter in Sagittarius, Mars in Scorpio, Venus in Libra, and Mercury in Virgo. And indeed, if we interpret times correctly, they have great power in most things. For what of that which they say: that on a winter's day dried pennyroyal <note>a medicinal herb of the mint family</note> blossoms, inflated bladders burst, and the leaves of willow trees turn over? That the seeds of apples turn and move around, and the fibers in the little livers of mice match in number day by day with the number <note>likely referring to the phase/age</note> of the moon? 

I, however, although I do not grant so much to the professors of that discipline and the observers of times that I think they can guarantee a certain fortune for things by their arts; yet it is not that I think they should be despised if they ever argue that such prescribed times, by the warning of the heavens, can have a very great effect for better or worse. But however that matter may be, to have observed what they advise: either it will be very beneficial if they are true, or it will do very little harm if they are false. I would add here some laughable things which the ancients approved for beginning tasks; but do not interpret this otherwise than the matter warrants. And indeed they were ridiculous, who ordered that for a good omen one should begin other things, and especially the laying out of the site. <margin>Superstitions of the ancients.</margin> The ancients were so devoted to these superstitions that they took care that the first soldier enrolled in a draft did not have a name that was in any way unlucky; then also, for purifying a colony or an army, they chose those with "good names" to lead the sacrificial victims; and the censors did the same for farming out taxes. They established Lake Lucrinus <note>from *lucrum*, meaning profit or gain</note> as the first of all because of the "happiness" of its name. Then, moved by the bad omen of a name, they wanted that which was previously called Epidamnus <note>resembling the Latin *damnum*, meaning "loss" or "injury"</note> to be called Dyrrachium, lest those sailing there be said to go "into loss." For the same reason they named it Beneventum <note>"Good Outcome"</note>, which was previously called Maleventum <note>"Bad Outcome"</note>. I laugh...

One should especially offer those prayers to the gods above by which one asks that they provide help and assistance to the work and favor the undertaking until the matter turns out auspiciously, happily, and prosperously; and that the building may last for a long time, bringing health and well-being to the owner, his kin, and his guests; along with the stability of the structure, equanimity of mind, increase of fortune, the fruit of industry, the propagation of glory, and the permanence of all good things for posterity. So much for these matters.

Folio XXXII

# Book III. On the Work.

There are many parts to a building, and various lines and orders belong to those parts. The parts required to complete a structure are not at all obscure. For the top and bottom, the right and left, the near and the distant, as well as the middle sections that run between these extremes, are evident in themselves. But not everyone understands what belongs to each part or why they differ from one another. For the work is not, as the unlearned <note>original: "imperiti"</note> suppose, merely the lifting of stone upon stone and the piling of mortar upon mortar. Since the parts are diverse, they require very different materials and different levels of skill. One thing is required for foundations; another for the wall-girts <term>procinctuí</term> <note>These are horizontal reinforcements or "belts" that wrap around a building to provide structural integrity.</note> and cornices. One thing is needed for the corners and the edges of openings, another for the outer skins <term>extremis cutibus</term> <note>This refers to the facing or veneer of a wall, distinguished from the internal core.</note> of the building, and yet another for the internal recesses and the thickening of the walls. It will be our task to explain what is owed to each. In completing these matters, we shall begin from the foundations themselves, imitating those who are about to perform the work with their own hands.

The foundation, unless I am mistaken, is not actually a part of the structure, but rather the place and the seat in which the structure itself is to be raised and set. <margin>Foundations</margin> For if a site is provided that is entirely solid and perhaps consisting of nothing but stone—such as some you might find near Veii <note>An ancient Etruscan city near Rome, known for its rocky terrain.</note>—what foundations would you need to build there, rather than simply raising the structure itself? In Siena, one can see the massive weights of towers placed directly upon the bare, primary ground. For there, the mountain is solid, with a base of tufa <term>tofo</term> <note>A soft, porous volcanic rock common in Italy, used since antiquity for building.</note>. Therefore, a foundation—that is, the act of going into the ground and digging—is only necessary where a firm and stable soil must be sought by cutting and sinking a trench. This is a practice that is appropriate in almost all locations, which we will discuss later. 

<margin>What the soil should be like</margin>
The following signs will indicate that the soil is suitable: if no herbs are present that usually grow in damp places; if it bears no trees at all, or only those that cannot grow except in very hard and dense ground; if all the surrounding area is very dry and thoroughly parched; if the ground is stony, with stones that are not small or rounded, but angular and solid, especially flint-like stone. Furthermore, the soil is good if no springs well up beneath it and no stream passes through. For it is the nature of a stream either to carry things away forever, so long as its motion is strong, or to bring debris in. For this reason, the plains through which a river runs do not provide solid stability until you have descended below the level of the riverbed.

Before you begin to dig anything, you must very carefully mark out the angles of the plots and all the lines of the sides, over and over again, determining what they will be like and where they will be placed. To set these angles, you need a square <term>norma</term> <note>A tool used by masons and architects to ensure perfectly right angles.</note> that is not small, but very large, so that the lines of the layout may be followed more accurately. <margin>The square of the ancient architects</margin> The ancients made a square by joining three straight rules into a single triangle, one of which was three cubits long, another...

...the other was four; the third was five cubits. <note>Alberti is describing the 3-4-5 Pythagorean triple used to ensure a perfectly square corner.</note> Yet the unskilled <note>original: "imperiti"</note> do not know how to set these corners unless they have first removed everything occupying the area, leaving the ground empty and completely leveled. For this reason, acting as if they were in a hostile field, they suddenly seize their pickaxes and send in "builder-destroyers" to tear down and demolish everything. Their error must be corrected. For many things—the injury of fortune, the adversity of time, or the accidents and necessities of affairs—may occur to warn or even forbid you from pursuing what you have begun. Meanwhile, it is surely unseemly not to spare the labors of the ancients, and to fail to consult the convenience of the citizens who take pleasure in the accustomed hearths of their ancestors. ### Chapter II.

In describing foundations, one must remember that the first beginnings of the walls and the plinths <term>soccos</term> <note>Literally "shoes"; these are the widened bases of the walls that distribute weight.</note>—which are also called foundations—must be made wider than the future wall will be. This should be done in imitation of those who walk through the snow in the mountains of Etruria <note>The Apennines.</note>. For these people bind to their feet sieves woven with cords for that very purpose; by their width, their footprints sink less deeply. Exactly how the corners themselves are to be marked out would not be easy to pursue in words alone, for the method of capturing them is drawn from mathematics and requires the example of lines. This is a matter somewhat outside our current purpose, and one which we have dealt with elsewhere in our mathematical commentaries. <note>Alberti refers here to his own lost or separate mathematical treatises, possibly "De punctis et lineis apud pictores."</note> I will nonetheless try and strive to speak in a way that is helpful here, so that you, being of sound intellect, may easily understand many things from which you may afterwards master the whole matter for yourself. Those things which perhaps seem more obscure you may, if you wish, perceive perfectly by seeking them from those same commentaries. 

<margin>The method of defining the foundation.</margin> We, indeed, when defining foundations, have become accustomed to directing lines—which we call "roots"—in this manner: From the middle of the front of the work, I stretch a line to the back. At the midpoint of this length, I fix a nail into the ground. Through this, following the instructions of geometers, I draw a transverse perpendicular line. Thus, I reduce whatever must be measured to these two lines. Everything then follows most beautifully: the parallel lines are ready, the corners are most certainly defined, and parts correspond to parts and are fitly shaped. But if it should happen that, due to the interference of the walls of old buildings...
