<page-num>Fo.XXXIII.</page-num>
->### Book III. On the Work.<-

If you are unable to determine the boundary and seat for capturing the angle by a line of sight <note>original: "radio visus"; literally "a ray of vision," referring to the straight-line visual survey</note>, you must draw parallel lines along whatever path is free and unobstructed. From there, by marking the point of intersection—whether by the extension of the gnomon <note>A rod used in surveying to cast shadows or determine perpendicularity.</note> or the diameter, or even by other parallel lines leveled to the square <term>normam</term>—we shall achieve our purpose most beautifully. Nor will it be anything but most convenient to terminate lines of sight at elevated places with a line, so that from there, by dropping a plumb line <term>perpendiculo</term>, certain direction and progress may be assured. 

<margin>☛</margin> Once the lines and angles of the excavations have been marked accordingly, it would indeed be beneficial to possess a power of vision and intuition such as they say a certain Spaniard possessed in these times. He could discern veins of water creeping through the innermost parts of the earth no differently than if they were flowing in the open. So many unknown things occur beneath the earth that you cannot safely commit the burden and expense of building to them. And truly, it is necessary to neglect nothing in the whole building, but especially in the foundations themselves, where the reason and diligence of a cautious and circumspect builder might be found wanting. For in other parts, if any error is made, it causes less harm, is corrected more easily, and is endured more comfortably than in the foundations, where no excuse for error should be admitted. 

But the ancients say: dig—and may it be auspicious and fortunate <note>Alberti uses the traditional Roman prayer formula: "quod faustum et felix sit."</note>—until you find solid ground. For the earth has various and multiple "skins": some are sandy <term>fabulosas</term> <note>From "sabulum," referring to coarse sand or gravel.</note>, some are gritty, others are pebbly, and the like. Beneath these, in various and uncertain order, lies a dense and solid skin, most strong for supporting buildings. This layer itself is also varied, and is hardly similar to others of its kind in any respect. In some places it is extremely hard and almost impenetrable to iron; in others thicker; in others blackish; in others whitish, which most people consider weaker than the rest. In some places it is chalky; in others like tufa <note>A porous volcanic rock common in Italy.</note>; in others made of a certain kind of clay mixed with gravel. 

Regarding all of these, no other certain judgment can be given as to which is best except this one: that they approve the one which resists iron with difficulty <note>meaning the soil is hard to penetrate with a pickaxe</note> and which, when water is poured on it, dissolves the least. And for that reason, they believe no solid ground is found more certainly and consistently than that which lies beneath water gushing through the bowels of the earth. We, however, believe that all learned and skilled residents and neighboring architects should be consulted. For they, through the example of old buildings and the daily practice of constructing new ones, have been able to learn easily what the soil of that region is like and what it can bear. Nevertheless, there are proofs for testing and recognizing the firmness of the soil. For when you roll something heavy across the ground, or drop it from a height, and the place does not tremble, or if water in a bowl placed there does not show ripples...

...does not yield: we shall interpret this as a promise of stability in that spot. However, you will not always find solid ground in every location. You will encounter regions—such as those by the Adriatic and at Venice—where beneath the piled-up soil <note>Refers to the reclaimed land or alluvial deposits typical of the Venetian lagoon.</note> you will find almost nothing besides loose mud.

¶ Various types of locations: one should not trust them immediately. Instead, first of all, cisterns and wells must be dug. In marshy places, stakes and piles—inverted and charred at the tips—should be driven in with hammers that are not overly heavy, but with frequent blows, until they are firmly fixed right up to the top.

### Chapter III.

<margin>
The Tower of Mestre.
</margin>
**T**herefore, you must employ different methods for foundations, to be carried out according to the diversity of the locations. One place may be elevated, another low-lying; another may be in between, such as a slope. Furthermore, one may be drier and more arid, as is particularly the case with mountain ridges and peaks. Another may be completely soaked and flooded, such as those near the sea, near lagoons, or sitting within valleys. Another is situated so that it is neither entirely dry nor always wet, as is the nature of slopes; on these, water does not remain stagnant and rot the ground, but is carried away by the incline. In no place should you immediately trust the discovery of ground that resists the iron tool <note>original: "ferrum respuat"; meaning ground so hard it turns back a pickaxe or shovel.</note>. It could happen in a flat area that such ground is weak, from which the greatest loss and the ruin of the entire work would eventually follow. We ourselves saw a tower at Mestre, a town of the Venetians, which a few years after its completion sank under its own weight into the thin and feeble soil upon which it rested—as the outcome proved—until it was submerged right up to its highest battlements. Those people are all the more to be blamed who do not rely on a solid substrate provided by nature specifically to bear buildings; instead, finding some masonry <term>macerie</term> from an old ruin, they do not investigate how deep or of what quality it is, but inconsiderately raise high walls upon it. Out of a greedy desire to reduce expenses, they wantonly destroy the entire building. It is therefore excellently advised that wells be dug before anything else. This is done for many reasons, but especially so that it may be clearly revealed how much the "skin" <note>original: "cutis"; here referring to the geological layer or stratum of the earth.</note> of the earth is capable of supporting or undermining the work. Additionally, water may be found for the many conveniences of the work to be done, and the material dug out will be of use. Furthermore, the opening provides a "breathing space" <note>original: "respiratio"; Alberti follows the ancient belief that trapped underground vapors or "exhalations" could cause tremors or destabilize foundations.</note> against the movements of subterranean exhalations, ensuring safe and unharmed stability for the building. Therefore, whether by a well, a cistern, a sewer, or any other deep excavation, once the layers hidden beneath the earth have been examined, the most suitable one must be chosen to which you may entrust the work. Then, whether in an elevated spot or any other place where flowing water might undermine or carry anything away, a much deeper trench should be dug...

Folio XXXIIII.
Book III. On the Work. Folio XXXIIII.

# Book III. On the Work.

...will be beneficial. For there is evidence that the mountains themselves are washed and worn away by the constant repetition of rains, and are thereby diminished; this is shown by the fact that protruding lookout points <note>original: "speculae"; these are high vantage points or peaks that become more visible as the surrounding terrain erodes.</note> are seen more easily every day, which previously did not appear because the mountain was in the way.
<margin>
Mount Morello
</margin>
**Mount Morello**, which is above Florence, was green with many fir trees in our fathers' generation. But now it is left bare and rugged, if I am not mistaken, by the scouring of the rains. On sloping sites, **Junius Columella** <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella (4–70 AD), a celebrated Roman writer on agriculture whose works were rediscovered in the Renaissance.</note> ordered that we should begin the foundations from the lower part and in the deeper place. This was indeed done skillfully. For, besides the fact that the things cast and built there will remain firmly fitted in their own places, they will also resist like a strong support <note>original: "fultura"; a buttress or structural prop.</note> against those parts which you may later wish to place and build, which will then be joined to the upper section. It will also happen that any defects which might occasionally follow such excavations—with the soil gaping and slipping—will be less hidden from you and do less harm. 

In marshy places, it is appropriate to open a wide trench; the sides of the trench must be reinforced on both sides with stakes, wickerwork, planks, seaweed, mud, and things of that sort, so that water does not seep in from below. Then, any remaining water within the defenses must be drained, the sand cleared out, and the muddy bed <note>original: "lotosus alueus"; a bed filled with silt or muck.</note> must be completely scoured away until you find a place where the foot may stand on a firm track. This very same thing must be done in sandy soil <note>original: "fabuloso in solo"; soil containing "fabulum" or gravelly sand.</note> as far as the situation requires. Furthermore, the bottom of every excavation must be made completely even with a <term>level</term> <note>original: "libella"; a tool used by masons to ensure a perfectly horizontal surface.</note>, so that it is not sloped in any part, so that the weight to be placed upon it may be balanced with equal pressures. For weight has this ingrained and innate quality: it always seeks out and presses upon the lower points. 

There are some who order certain things to be done in marshes, but these pertain more to the structure itself than to the matter of the foundation. And they order them thus: Fix a large number of stakes and piles with their tips charred <note>original: "cacumine p̄uſto"; charring the wood was a common Roman technique to prevent rot in wet soil.</note> and their "feet" turned upward toward the sky. Let the area of this work be twice as wide as the future wall is to be. Let the piles be as long as one-eighth the height of the future wall, and let their thickness be at least one-twelfth of their own length. Finally, let them be driven in so closely together that there is no room left to drive any more between them. 

The machines for driving these piles—whatever kind they may be—ought to have hammers <note>original: "malleos"; in this context, the heavy weights used in a pile-driver.</note> that are not excessively heavy, but which strike with frequent blows. For when they are too heavy in weight and immense in their impact, they immediately shatter the timber. However, the frequency of the blows tires out and masters all the defiance and stubbornness of the soil through persistence. You may see this when you wish to fix a thin nail into hard wood: if you use a heavy hammer, it does not succeed; but if you use a small and suitable one, it will penetrate. So much for excavations for now, unless perhaps this should be added: that sometimes, either for the sake of thrift or to avoid the instability of the intervening soil, it is helpful not to have one continuous...

### ¶ A brief summary regarding the nature of stones: the excavation, the condition, the bond of lime and support, and the bindings that pertain to the matter. Chapter IV.

It remains for us to approach the construction itself. But since the whole art and order of building of a craftsman depends partly on the nature of the stones—their form and condition—and partly on the bond and bindings of the lime and the support, those things which pertain to the matter must first be reviewed very briefly.
<margin>Variety of stones.</margin>
Some stones are lively, strong, and full of sap, such as flint, marbles, and the like, which are naturally heavy and resonant. Others are exhausted, light, and "deaf" <note>original: "surdi"; refers to a stone that makes a dull thud when struck rather than a clear ring, indicating it is porous or structurally weak.</note>, such as tufa <note>original: "tofinei"; a porous rock formed from volcanic ash.</note> and sandy stones. Likewise, some stones have flat surfaces, straight lines, and equal angles; these are called "squared" <term>quadratos</term> stones. Others have multiple and varied surfaces, lines, and angles; these we shall call "uncertain" or irregular stones. Again, some stones are very large: that is, those which the bare hands of men cannot move at will without a sled, a lever, a roller <note>original: "rutulo"; a tool or cylinder for moving heavy weights.</note>, and porters and such things. Others are small: those which you can lift and place with one hand as you wish. A third type of stone is between these: those which are medium in weight and size, we call "just" stones. Every stone ought to be whole, least of all muddy, and well-soaked. Whether it is whole or cracked will be indicated by the sound it returns when struck. It will be washed nowhere more purely than in a torrent. It is well established that a "just" stone is not rendered sufficiently moist by water before the ninth day; a very large stone, even more slowly. A stone recently taken from the quarry is far more convenient than an old one. A stone that has once experienced lime does not love "second marriages" <note>Alberti uses the metaphor "secunda non amat coiugia" to explain that stones salvaged from old buildings do not bond well with new mortar.</note>. These things are concerning the stone itself.
<margin>The work of lime.</margin>
They reject lime which, when brought from the kiln, is not in whole lumps but is broken up and quite powdery; they say it will not be strong for the work. They approve of that which, being thoroughly purified by the fires, is white, light, and resonant; and which, when you sprinkle it, breathes out a sharp force of vapor with much crackling. It is established that because the former type is weak, it requires less sand. But to this stronger type, more sand is owed. **Cato** <note>Marcus Porcius Cato (234–149 BC), whose work 'De Agri Cultura' provided early Roman technical advice on building.</note> established that for every foot, one modius <note>a Roman dry measure, roughly 2 gallons or 8.7 liters.</note> of lime should be given to two of sand. Others say otherwise. **Vitruvius** <note>The primary Roman authority on architecture whose rediscovered texts fueled the Renaissance.</note> and likewise **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of 'Natural History', which contains extensive sections on minerals and building materials.</note> order the sand to be mixed...

...to be mixed: as it is done, for pit sand <note>original: "fossiceas"; sand dug from the earth rather than taken from water sources.</note> a fourth part is used; for river and sea sand, a third. Furthermore, where the material is to be more liquid and soft—as we shall soon relate—depending on the nature and quality of the stones, the sand shall be passed through sieves <note>original: "incerniculis"; a tool for sifting to ensure fine texture.</note>. But where it is thicker, then angular gravel and small fragments of broken stone shall be mixed in together with half the sand. Everyone affirms that if you add a third part of crushed pottery <note>original: "tunsae testae"; ground ceramic or brick, which helps the mortar harden and resist moisture.</note>, it will be much more tenacious. But however you mix it, you must work it over again and again until it is blended into a body of the smallest particles. For this reason, there are those who, for the sake of proper mixing, turn and pound the mortar for a long time in troughs. And so much for lime. Unless perhaps this is missing from what we have said: that lime bonds more tenaciously with its own stones—especially those from the same quarry—than it does with foreign stones.

### Some doctrines from the monuments and examples of the ancients regarding the filling of footings up to the ground level. Chapter V.

<margin>Asithis</margin>
<margin>Ctesiphon</margin>
<margin>Diverse types of foundations among the ancients.</margin>
**R**egarding the construction of footings <note>original: "pedamentis"; the structural supports or "feet" of the building below ground level.</note>—that is, the filling of foundations up to the ground level—I find nothing among the ancient writers that they advise, except for this one thing: that you should cast into the foundations any stone which, having been kept in the open air for two years (as we said above), has shown some defect. For just as in military service the lazy and cowardly, who cannot endure the sun and dust, are sent home to their people with a mark of shame, so too here they reject soft and weak stones, so that they may rest ignobly in their former leisure and accustomed shade. However, I find in historical accounts that the ancients were accustomed to exert every industry and diligence in placing footings in the earth, striving so that the structure there might be, as far as possible, no less solid in every part than in the rest of the wall. Asithis, King of the Egyptians (the son of Mykerinos <note>original: "Nicerini"; referring to the Pharaoh Menkaure.</note>), whose decree it was that those held by debt should give their father’s corpse as security, when he was about to build a brick pyramid, fixed beams into the marsh for laying the foundations, and over these he laid the bricks. It is also recorded in memory that the excellent Ctesiphon—who built the famous Temple of Diana at Ephesus—having chosen a level and cleared site that would eventually be immune to earthquakes, first laid down trodden charcoal <note>original: "carbonibus"; used to create a stable, rot-resistant layer in soft soil.</note>—lest foundations of such mass be placed rashly on slippery and unstable ground. Then, they say, the intermediate spaces were filled with the fleeces of shorn sheep <note>original: "velleribus pasorum"; wool fleeces used as a cushioning layer to absorb seismic shocks.</note> and packed with very frequent charcoal, and soon after, squared stones were extended over them with the longest possible joints. I also find that at Jerusalem, in the foundations of public works, there were those who placed stones...

...twenty [cubits] long, and no less than ten cubits deep. However, elsewhere in the most extensive works of the most experienced ancients, I have observed that they had various methods and practices for filling foundations. At the **Tomb of the Antonines**, they filled [the foundations] with fragments of very hard stone no larger than would fill a hand, using "floating" cement <note>original: "natante cemento"; likely a reference to a liquid grout or mortar into which stones were dropped</note>. In the **Forum Argentarium** <note>The "Money-Changers' Forum" in Rome, located near the Capitoline Hill</note>, they used cement made of all kinds of broken stones. At the **Comitium** <note>The open-air public meeting space of ancient Rome</note>, they built the substructure with fragments and clods of common stone <note>original: "lapide ignobili"; literal "ignoble stone," meaning cheap or non-ornamental stone used for structural purposes</note>.

But those who imitated nature at the **Tarpeian Rock** <note>A steep cliff on the south side of the Capitoline Hill</note> pleased me most, with a work especially suited for hills. For just as nature, in building mountains, mixes softer material with solid stones, so these men laid a substructure of two feet of the best squared stone they could find. Over this, they poured about two feet of a cement-like paste <note>original: "pultem cementitiam"; a thick mixture or "porridge" of mortar and rubble</note>; and thus, with alternating layers of stones and paste, they filled the foundations. 

Elsewhere, I have seen very firm works of foundations and structures of this kind, made by our ancestors with pit gravel <note>original: "glarea fossili"</note> and also with gathered stone, standing after many ages. At **Bologna**, when a very high and strong tower was being demolished, the foundations were found to be stuffed with round stones and clay <note>original: "saxo globoso & creta"; round river stones and stiff clay or chalky earth</note> for nearly six cubits. The rest of the structure above was then built with lime. 

Thus, there is a variety of methods in these things; and which of these I should approve above the others, I could not easily say, since I find examples from every one of these types that stand as by far the firmest and strongest. However, I determine that economy should be observed, provided you do not pour in rubbish or things that might rot.

There are also other kinds of footings. One indeed is suitable for **porticos** and those places where rows of columns are set up. Another is used in **maritime** places, where the certain ability to reach solid ground at will is not available. We shall speak of maritime matters then, when we treat of the harbor and the pier <note>original: "mole"; a massive stone structure or breakwater</note> to be placed within the deep sea. For that pertains not to the general work of all buildings, which is what we are discussing here, but to a specific part of the city; of which we shall treat together with others of its kind when we report on public works of that sort part by part.

For rows of columns, therefore, there is no need to fill the entire oblong trench with a continuous line of masonry; rather, it is appropriate first to strengthen the seat and beds of the columns themselves. From here, from one to the other, arches are to be drawn—with the curve <note>original: "dorso"; literally "back," meaning the extrados or convex side</note> inverted into the depth, so that the flat surface of the area serves as its chord <note>original: "corda"; the straight line connecting the ends of an arch</note>. For in this way, several weights added from here and there onto one place will be less likely to pierce the ground, because of the resistance of such a support of arches. And since columns are prone to piercing the ground; and because...

### Chapter VI.

Once the foundations are laid, the wall follows in readiness. Here, I would not wish to overlook a point that pertains both to the completion of foundations and the finishing of the entire wall. In vast buildings, where the mass of the walls is to be quite thick, suitable <term>estuaries</term> <note>original: "estuaria"; vents or breathing holes</note> and air-holes should be left from the foundations themselves, through the middle of the work up to the very top, not entirely buried. Thus, if any condensed or compressed vapor moves beneath the earth, it may exhale freely and profusely without any destruction to the structure. In several places, the ancients used to lead a <term>spiral staircase</term> <note>original: "scalam cocleam"; literally a "snail-shell" staircase</note> through the interior, partly for this very reason, partly for convenience—to provide a way to ascend to the top of the work—and perhaps also to reduce the expense of materials. I return to the matter at hand. 

<margin>Footing.</margin> The difference between the <term>footing</term> <note>original: "pedamentum"</note> and the ready wall is this: the footing, being aided by the sides of the trench, can consist of simple infill; whereas the wall is usually composed of several parts, as I shall soon describe. 

<margin>Wall.</margin> There are primary parts in a wall: 

<margin>Podium.</margin> The lowest part, which rises immediately above the infill of the foundation; if it is permitted, we shall call this the <term>podium</term> or the <term>platform</term>. <margin>Platform.</margin>

<margin>Cincture.</margin> The middle part, which goes around and embraces the wall; this they call the <term>cincture</term> <note>original: "procinctus"; a course of masonry that binds the structure like a belt</note>. 

<margin>Crown.</margin> The highest part, which holds the final roofing of the wall; this they finally name the <term>crown</term>. 

Among the primary parts of the walls, the most important are the angles and the inserted reinforcements <note>original: "concepteque"</note>, whether they be pillars, columns, or anything of that sort. These stand in the place of columns for sustaining the beams and arches of the roofs; all of these come under the name of <term>bones</term> <note>original: "ossium"; Alberti views the structural supports as the skeleton of the building</note>. There are also the standing "lips" on either side of openings <note>the doorposts or jambs</note>, which share the nature of both angles and columns. Furthermore, the covering of the openings—that is, the <term>lintel</term> <note>original: "superliminare"</note>—whether it be placed as a straight beam or as an arch, shall be counted among the bones. For an arch is indeed...

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

...I would say nothing other than that an arch is a bent beam, and what is a beam but a column placed crosswise? Those parts which run between and extend among these primary parts <note>referring to the "bones" or structural framework mentioned on the previous page</note> will be rightly called the **fillings**. Within the wall as a whole, there is also something that applies to all the parts we have recounted: this is the internal **filling** <note>original: "infarcinatio"; the rubble or grout core of a wall</note> of the wall, and the two sides on either hand, which you may call "skins" <note>original: "coria" or "cortices"</note> or "shells." One of these faces the external winds and sun, while the other fosters the internal shade of the area. But the proportion between the shell and the filling varies according to the variety of the construction.

The types of construction are these: **regular**, **reticulated**, and **uncertain**. Here, that observation of **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar and writer on agriculture</note> will be of no small use to the matter: he reports that the Tusculans <note>residents of Tusculum, near Rome</note> build enclosures for their villas out of stone masonry. In the Gallic territory, however, they build from baked bricks. Among the Sabines, they use raw <note>original: "crudo"; sun-dried rather than kiln-fired</note> brick, and throughout the Spains, they build with earth composed of small pebbles <note>likely referring to "formacei" or rammed earth walls</note>. But of these, more later.

**Regular** construction <note>original: "ordinaria"</note> is that in which squared stones, whether of standard size or rather very large, are joined together so that they are placed in their lines in order according to the ruler, the level, and the plumb-line. No construction is firmer or more stable than this.

**Reticulated** construction <note>original: "rheticulata"; literally "net-like"</note> is that in which squared stones, whether of standard size or rather small, are placed not lying on their sides, but standing on their corners <note>forming a diamond pattern</note>, with the face set according to the ruler and the plumb-line.

**Uncertain** construction <note>original: "incerta"; often called opus incertum</note> is that in which irregular stone is inserted such that each side, as far as its lines allow, sticks perfectly <note>original: "ad unguem"; literally "to the fingernail," a metaphor for a flawless joint</note> to the sides of the adjacent stone. We use this kind of stone joining in the flint-stone paving of roads. 

Furthermore, we use these various types in various places. For the facing of the <term>podium</term> <note>the raised base or platform supporting the wall</note>, we shall use nothing but very large and very hard squared stone; for that part of the construction, as we said, must be as whole and solid as possible. In the entire wall itself, there is nowhere a greater need for solidity and strength than there. Indeed, if you can, you should strengthen it with a single stone, or certainly with a number of stones that comes closest to the integrity and continuity of a single one. By what method a very large stone may be handled and moved—since that kind especially concerns ornament—we shall speak in its proper place. 

But "let it be built," says **Cato** <note>Cato the Elder, in his work "On Agriculture"</note>, "of firm stone and lime so that the work stands [two] feet <note>original: "pedes"; Cato's text specifies two feet</note> above the ground"; but the rest of the wall, they do not forbid making even of raw brick if one pleases. The reason for this is clear: because that part of the wall <note>the base</note> is worn away by the dripping of rainwater from the roofs. But when we revisit and examine the buildings of the ancients, we see that while elsewhere these parts of well-provided buildings were everywhere substituted with very hard stone, also among those nations where the injury of rains is not...

<meta>This page continues Alberti's technical exploration of masonry, moving from the general types of wall construction discussed on the previous page to the physical properties of stone and the environmental stresses that cause decay, specifically focusing on the foundation or "podium."</meta>

Book III. On Construction.
Fo. XXXVII.

...be observed: there were those who laid the entire base for a pyramid in Egypt using a very hard black stone <note>likely referring to the granite casing found on the lower levels of the pyramids of Khafre or Menkaure</note>. This leads me to interpret the matter more broadly. For just as with iron, bronze, and other such materials, if they are bent back and forth repeatedly in opposite directions, they grow weary and eventually break from fatigue. In the same way, bodies <note>structural elements</note> are most damaged and corrupted when harassed by alternating stresses. I have noticed this specifically in bridges, especially wooden ones. For those parts which, through the changes of the seasons, are now dried by the sun's rays and the blowing of the winds, and now soaked by nocturnal vapors or water, we see become eaten away and thoroughly rotten very quickly. The same thing can be seen in the parts of walls that stand at the very bottom near the ground. For they are worn down and eroded by alternating contaminations of moisture and dust. For this reason, I myself decree that the **podium** <note>the platform or continuous base of a building</note> of the entire structure should be built of hard, very firm, and very large stone, so that it may remain safest against the frequent insults of these opposing forces. As for what types of stones are the hardest, we have reviewed that sufficiently in the second book.

### ¶ Chapter VII. On the arrangement and connection of stones, which are rendered stronger or weaker by their creation or generation; and on the proper corners and "bones" of walls.

**I**ndeed, it is of the greatest importance, both here and elsewhere, with what arrangement and connection the stones themselves are placed in the work. For just as in wood, so too in stone there are both veins and knots, as well as parts that are weaker than others. Indeed, it is a common observation that marble can warp and twist. Stones contain "abscesses" and collections of rotten matter, which I believe swell over time as they drink in moisture from the air they have inhaled; from this follow serious blisters and the shattering of columns and beams. Therefore, in addition to what we have already discussed regarding stone in its proper place, one must know that stone is created by nature, as we see, lying flat <note>referring to sedimentary layers or strata</note>, from material that (as they interpret it) was liquid and fluid. When this material gradually thickened and hardened, the mass itself preserved the original shapes of its parts. Hence, in such stone, the particles of the lowest part consist of larger and heavier elements than those at the top; and veins run through them according to how the material, poured and spread over other material, adhered together. Those things that lie in the vein—whether they be the dross of the earlier material mixed with the dregs of the material added on top, or something else—since nature did not allow these disparate parts to be perfectly united, the stone is inevitably **fissile** <term>fissile: having a natural grain that allows it to be split easily into layers</term>. Furthermore, as is evident and clear from the "insults" <note>original: "contumelia"; damage caused by exposure</note> of the weather, lest we build anything with materials whose inner nature is hidden: all bodies are fashioned from compacted and accreted matter, and are dissolved...

<summary>Alberti discusses how environmental stresses like alternating moisture and heat decay structures, recommending large, hard stones for the building's base. He also explains the geological formation of stone in layers, which creates a natural "grain" or weakness that architects must consider.</summary>

<page-num>LIV</page-num>
<header>Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.</header>

...tance. Thus, also in stone, those parts which have been exposed to enduring the seasons are more wasted and prone to rot. Since this is the case, they <note>ancient builders</note> command that one pay attention when placing stones, especially in those parts of the building which must be the most robust: that the firmest and least brittle faces of the stones be set against the opposing assaults of the elements. Therefore, the **grain** <term>vena: the natural layering or "bedding" of the stone formed during its geological creation</term> should not be placed standing on its side, lest it peel away due to the weather; rather, it should lie flat, so that under the weight of the structure pressing down from above, it may never split open. And the interior face, which had been hidden in the quarry <note>original: *fodina*</note>, should be set so that it faces outward. For it is more "juicy" <note>original: *succosior*. Alberti believed that stone freshly taken from the earth contained a "quarry sap" or moisture that made it more vital and strong before it became parched and brittle by exposure</note> and more powerful. Truly, no face in the entire cut stone will be considered more enduring than that which did not follow the line of the quarry track, but rather that which cut across the transverse extension of the laying mass.

Furthermore, the **corners** throughout the entire building—since they must indeed be exceptionally strong—must be fortified with a very solid structure. For surely, if I interpret correctly, every corner of the whole building is half of the structure, since the failure of even one corner cannot occur without the loss of two walls <note>literally "sides"</note>. If you look into this, you will undoubtedly find that almost no buildings have begun to fail for any other reason than from the weakness of some corner. Rightly, therefore, the ancients were accustomed to make the corners much thicker than the walls, and in colonnaded porticos, to apply firmer supports at the corners.

Therefore, the strength of the corner is not desired only so that it may bear the roof—for that is the work of columns even more than corners—but especially so that the walls may be kept in their proper place <note>original: *in officio*, literally "in their duty"</note>, lest they deflect in any direction from the vertical line of the plumb-bob. Therefore, the corner should have very hard stones, long in length, so that like arms and forearms they may be carried through the extension of the joined walls. And these stones should be as wide as the thickness of the wall, so that there is no need for any internal filling <term>infarcinatione: the rubble or mortar core used to fill the middle of a thick wall between two outer faces</term>. It is fitting that the "bones" <note>Alberti's term for structural reinforcements</note> within the wall and the sides of openings be similar to corners; and they should be firmer in proportion to the greater weights they might have to support. And above all, it is necessary that they extend "hands"—that is, some stones here and there in alternating courses—as if they were supports to sustain the remaining filling of the wall.

### ¶ Chapter VIII. On the parts of the filling, the "skins" (facings), the rubble cores, and their various types.

But of the skins, some are outermost, and others are placed on the inner side. If you use a harder stone for the outermost skin, it will contribute to the building's durability—

# Book III. On the Work. Folio XXVIII. #

...[solidity] which is otherwise found in full reinforcements. As for the work, whether you apply **net-like work** <term>opus reticulatum: a style of masonry using diamond-shaped stones that resemble a net</term> or **irregular work** <term>opus incertum: masonry using stones of various shapes and sizes placed randomly</term>, I shall not find fault with it, provided that where the wall is attacked and sharply provoked by the sun’s heat, the force of the winds, or even by fire or frost, you set stone that is by nature most capable of withstanding such assault, mass, and injury. And especially in those places where heavy rains falling from roof-pipes or gutters are dashed against the wall by the wind, the most robust material must be used. Indeed, in ancient buildings one may see everywhere how, due to the fury of such spraying, even marble itself has been—if I may put it this way—eaten away and deeply pitted. <note>original: "peressum atque penitus exesum"</note>

Nevertheless, almost all skilled architects, to provide against this damage, have made it a habit to collect the rain from the roofs and lead it away through drainage systems <note>original: "impluvia"</note> to be divided and dispersed. What of that which our ancestors noted: that the leaves usually fall sooner in the autumn from that part of the tree which faces the South and the midday sun? <margin>The South-facing side falls sooner</margin> We ourselves have observed that all buildings collapsing from old age begin to fail toward the South. The cause of this perhaps is that the heat and force of the sun, while the work was still "green" <note>original: "virebat" - referring to fresh, wet masonry</note>, prematurely consumed the juices of the lime. Add to this that a wall, repeatedly dampened by southern winds and then made to boil by the sun’s scorching, becomes soaked through and rots away. Therefore, a material that is suitable and most powerful must be set against these and similar injuries.

This I judge especially important to observe: that you should lead the courses <note>horizontal layers of stone or brick</note> you have begun equally around the whole circuit of the structure and not unevenly. Do not let the wall consist of very large stones on the right and tiny ones on the left. For they say that a structure is indeed pressed down when the final weight is added, and that the lime ceases to yield to pressure while drying; because of this, it is inevitable that cracks will form throughout the work if it is uneven.

However, I will not forbid you from building the **internal skin** <term>cortex intestinum: the interior facing of a wall, as opposed to the exterior "skin"</term> together with the whole face of its wall using a softer stone. But whichever you use, whether internal or external, the skin must be raised so that it stands extended and finished according to its line and plumb-rule. This "line" will be that which corresponds equally to the perimeter of the plan, so that it is thoroughly, in every part, never bulging, never hollow, never wavy, never crooked, but well-fitted and finished. If you apply the first coat of **sanded plaster** <term>harenationem: a base coat of mortar mixed with sand</term> while the wall is still "green" <note>damp and fresh</note>, it will follow that whatever **cladding** or **white-finish** <term>albarium: a fine white plaster or stucco finish</term> you add will result in an'indestructible work.

There are two kinds of **core-fillings** <term>infarcinamentorum: the rubble and mortar used to fill the space between the two outer facings of a wall</term>. One is that which they use to fill the empty space between the skins by piling in rubble <note>original: "cementis"</note>. The other is that which they build up using common, though low-quality, stone rather than simply filling it. Both appear to have been invented for the sake of economy. Since...

## Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

Any small and common stone is assigned to this part of the walls. For if an abundance of very large and squared stone were supplied, who would voluntarily use small or broken stone? Yet in this one thing the **bones** <note>original: "ossa" — Alberti uses the metaphor of bones to describe the structural framework or load-bearing elements of a wall</note> themselves differ from the **fillings**. In the latter, they stuff the middle between the **shells** <term>crustas: the outer layers or facings of a wall</term> with whatever broken and mangled stone is available, in a work that is almost piled up and haphazard. In the former [the bones], no irregular stones, or very few, are mixed in; but they weave that whole interior with regular, orderly work. For the sake of eternity, I would prefer that they made the entire wall complete with squared stone in full courses. However you decide to fill that void between the shells with stone, as far as the matter allows, take care that the leveled courses are connected with an even line.

Then it will also be a matter of duty to lead certain regular stones from one outer shell to the other inner shell, at intervals that are not too sparse, through the middle of the wall’s thickness, in order to bind the shells to each other. This is done so that the internal **rubble-core** <term>infarciationes: the stuffing or filling material used between two masonry skins</term> does not push out the "sides" of the shells. 

<margin>
The method of rubble-core filling among the ancients.
</margin>The ancients observed a practice of raising these rubble-core fillings with a single, continuous leveling course <note>original: "refusionem"</note>; this was done in layers no higher than what would allow them to extend the courses every five feet. By this means, the structure is rendered taut and girded, as if by nerves and ligaments. Furthermore, if it happens that any part of the filling settles—either through some fault of the craftsmen or by accident—it will not immediately drag down the weight of the remaining material pressing from above. Instead, the upper parts will have, as it were, a renewed base upon which to stand.

Moreover, they give a warning—which I see was well observed among all the ancients—that no stones should be inserted during the filling that are larger than what would complete the weight of a **libra** <term>libra: an ancient Roman unit of weight, roughly 329 grams; here used to mean a small, manageable size</term>. For they believe that smaller stones are more easily unified and fitted to the joints than very large ones. This is supported by what is related in Plutarch concerning King Minos. For when he was dividing the common people by their trades, he judged that the more a body is divided into minute parts, the more easily it can be managed and leveled according to one's will. 

I think this also should not be neglected: that all hollows must be filled, leaving no empty space anywhere. This is important for many reasons, but especially so that animals do not enter there, which, by nesting and accumulating filth and seeds, might cause **wild fig trees** <term>caprificos: the wild fig, known in antiquity for its invasive roots that could crack masonry</term> to spring up throughout the wall. It is incredible to say what great masses of stone and what heaps I have seen moved by a single root of a tree. Therefore, everything you build must be diligently bound together and filled.

<header>Book III. On Work. Folio XXXIX.</header>

# Book III. On Work. Folio XXXIX.

**B**etween the structural courses <note>original: "procinctus" — horizontal reinforcement layers or "belts" built into the masonry to ensure stability</note>, certain bonds of larger stones are also introduced. These make the exterior shells <term>crustas: the outer facings or skins of a wall</term> entwined with the interior shells, and even the bones <note>original: "ossa" — the load-bearing structural framework within a wall</note> entwined with bones. Such are those stones which we said should be inserted every five feet.

Others, however, are the primary structural courses: these are extended through the entire length of the wall for the sake of reinforcing the corners and steadying the work. But these latter ones are used more rarely; I have hardly ever seen more than two or sometimes three of them in a wall. Their primary position and seat is at the top of the wall like a **cornice** <note>original: "corona" — literally a 'crown', referring here to a continuous capping or projecting course</note>, free from those more frequent reinforcements that occur every five feet. If thinner stones are available, it will not be unseemly. But in these others, which we call cornices—as they are rarer and involve more labor—it is proper to use stronger and thicker stones. In both types, the longest, widest, and firmest stones of their kind are required. However, the smaller stones shall be placed so that, together with the other facings of the wall, they meet the plumb-line and the rule.

These others, imitating cornices, will stand out with a projection of the face. Stones of this kind, very long and quite wide, are placed according to the level and are well-connected in rows, so that they cover the structures beneath like a pavement added on top. The bonding of the stones here is such that each new stone is now laid on top and so joined and fitted into those already laid beneath that it lies in the middle of the joint of the two underlying stones with an even and balanced extension. While this bonding of stones should by no means be neglected in the general structure, it must be observed to an even greater degree in structural courses of this kind. 

I have noticed that the ancients were accustomed to introduce a structural course into **reticulated work** <term>reticulatis operibus: a Roman masonry style using diamond-shaped tuff stones</term>, so that it consisted of five rows of bricks <note>original: "laterculorum"</note>, or no fewer than three; among these, while the others were standard, at least one row was made of stone no thicker than the others joined there, but longer and wider. In ordinary brick structures, we have also seen that for the purpose of bonding every five feet, they were content with a single row of a larger **two-foot brick** <note>original: "bipedalis" — a large Roman square brick approx. 59cm wide</note>. We have even seen cases where very long **lead sheets** <note>original: "laminas plumbeas"</note>, equal in width to the walls, were interspersed for the sake of bonding. But in building with very large stone, I see them content with a rarer structural course, or almost with the cornices alone. In completing the cornices, since these also encircle the wall with a very firm bonding, nothing ought to be neglected of those things which we have said so far regarding the structural course itself, so that in these none but very long and extremely wide [stones are used...]

...of all, the firmest stones should be inserted: and let the continuous bond be fitted together and rightly compacted, with the courses made exact to the level, and reduced and leveled to the rule according to the logic of each. The matter itself demands that you apply greater care and diligence here, because the cornices <note>original: "coronae" — the projecting top courses of a wall</note> gird the work in that very place which is more prone to slipping. Moreover, they perform their duty for the roof upon the walls. 

Hence it is said that for walls of sun-dried brick, you should add a fired-tile <term>testaceam: made of kiln-fired brick or terracotta</term> cornice, so that if any rain falls from the top of the roof or from dripping eaves, it does not cause damage, but the overhang protects it. For that reason, this must be observed in every remaining part of the wall: that a well-constructed cornice stands before the roof to repel every injury from rain-showers. 

Again, one must consider by what support or by what aids many stones may be gathered and held together into a single solid wall. To the observer, it surely occurs that first of all, there is a need for lime in this matter; although I would not rule that every stone should be joined with lime. <margin>Note by what things marble is stained.</margin> For marble, by contact with lime, not only loses its whiteness but is even sullied by foul spots of gore <note>original: "maculis cruoris" — Alberti uses the word for blood to describe the reddish-brown staining caused by the chemical reaction between lime and certain minerals in marble</note>. Such is the pride of whiteness in marble that it can hardly bear anything other than itself. What do you think? It disdains smoke; when smeared with oil, it turns pale; if soaked in dark wine, it becomes muddy; water drawn from chestnut wood darkens it to the core and so penetrates it that the marks of these things cannot even be erased by scraping. Hence the ancients used "naked" marbles in their work—as far as they could—driven together with no coating of lime smeared on. But about these things later.

## Chapter X. On the proper method of constructing a wall, by which it is raised with stone and made hardened with lime.

**S**ince it pertains to the duty of a skilled craftsman not so much to select the most convenient materials as to use those which are supplied aptly and appropriately, we shall proceed in this manner. Understand that lime should be thoroughly burnt until you approve of it: which, when drenched and then slaked after its heat, rises up imitating the froth of milk and swells in all its lumps. Pebbles encountered during the mixing with sand will be a sign of lime that has not been sufficiently soaked. If by chance you mix in more sand than is equal, it will not cohere because of its roughness. But if less than its nature and power can bear, it will resist like birdlime <term>viscus: a sticky substance used to catch birds, here meaning the mortar becomes too tacky and unworkable</term> with an improper slowness and will hardly yield. <margin>The soaking and utility of lime.</margin> You should assign lime that is not fully soaked, or is otherwise weaker, to foundations rather than to the rest of the wall, and among the rubble-fillings <note>original: "farcinamenta" — the loose stone and mortar core of a wall</note> within the facings. But all lime in which there is even the slightest defect must be driven far away from corners, structural "bones," and binding courses, and especially from arches.

<header>Book III. On the Work. Folio XI.</header>

...the firmest stones should be mixed in. Corners, structural frames <note>original: "ossa" — literally "bones," referring to the load-bearing skeleton of the building</note>, projections <note>original: "procictus"</note>, and cornices require a thinner, more slender, and purer sand, especially where they are to be finished with polished stone. Infill <note>original: "infarcinamenta" — the rubble or coarse material used to fill the center of a wall</note> will not reject a more pebbly <note>original: "glandulosiorem" — literally "acorn-shaped," referring to lumpy or coarse textures</note> material. Stone that is dry by nature and "thirsty" will pair quite well with river sand. Stone that is naturally damp and moist will prefer pit sands <note>original: "harenas fossiceas"</note>. I would not want you to expose sand taken from the sea to the south wind; perhaps it will be more conveniently set toward the north. 

A denser mortar is required for small stones. For dry and parched stones, a coarser mixture is needed. Although the ancients, in overall construction <note>original: "astructione"</note>, considered a coarser paste <note>original: "pultem"</note> of this kind to be more tenacious than a thin one. Very large stones do not settle by choice except through a liquid and flowing mortar, perhaps more for the sake of lubricating the bed <note>original: "lubricandi cubilis"</note>—so that they are easy to move by hand while being fitted—rather than for the purpose of bonding; such is the appearance of the mortar applied. 

And yet, it will be altogether very beneficial to place a soft and leveled bed of this sort underneath, so that stones laboring under an uneven weight do not snap. There are those who, seeing very large stones in ancient works with joints marked with red ochre <note>original: "rubrica"</note>, interpret this as having been used in place of lime. That does not seem likely to me, especially for this reason: I see only one of the two joining surfaces marked, not both. 

There is also something regarding walls that it would not be helpful to neglect. For a wall should not be heaped up with headlong haste and a chaotic hand, nor should the work ever be interrupted by lazy sluggishness, as if you were building against your will; nor should the begun work be procrastinated. Instead, one ought to pursue the matter with method and reason, in which speed is joined with the maturity of counsel and diligence. 

Experts forbid the work to be raised higher until the part finished so far <note>original: "hactenus"</note> has hardened. For since fresh and soft work is weak and unstable, it will by no means support what you build on top of it. One may indeed see swallows, taught by nature when they build their nests, making the first plasterings <note>original: "illutationes"</note> against the beams—which serve as the foundations and roots of the work—and likewise adding the next piles of material to these not at all haphazardly; instead, with the work paused, they build maturely and gradually until the beginnings of the work have gained firmness.

<margin>
See the method of building a wall.
How many [feet] to build at a time.
</margin>

They judge the lime to have hardened when it has "sweated out" the downy fuzz and "flowers" <note>original: "flosculos" — referring to efflorescence, the white mineral powder that forms on drying masonry</note> known to craftsmen. The thickness of the wall itself, along with the temperature of the place and sky, will advise how many feet high a pause should be made <note>original: "intercalandum"</note>. When you decide a pause is necessary, cover the top of the work with mats <note>original: "strumentis"</note>, lest the moisture <note>original: "succus" — literally "juice" or "sap"</note> be drained from the mortar by the wind and sun.

# Book III. On the Work. #

### Page XLI ###

-> f <-

...with gypsum or even with silver-chalk <note>original: "creta argentaria" — a fine white earth or clay often used as a polishing agent or fine plaster</note>. To ensure that it bonds more aptly during the assembly, fragments of earthenware <note>shards of terracotta or tile</note> should be inserted sparingly into the narrow cracks of the joints; these should protrude like little teeth so that the outer casing <note>original: "crustula" — the veneer or surface layer of stone</note> is held more firmly. As for the bare stone, it ought to be squared, and above all large, solid, and very firm. In this type of work, no infill <note>original: "infarcinamenta" — the rubble or loose material used to fill the center of a wall</note> is used; instead, perfectly level courses and a continuous bonding are required, and frequent connections using cramps and pins are owed to the structure.

<margin>Cramps are joined together in a continuous row.</margin>
**Cramps** <term>ansa: a metal or wooden fastener used to join two stones side-by-side</term> are those by which stones placed level to one another are joined in pairs. **Pins** <term>clauiculus: a vertical dowel or peg used to prevent stones from sliding</term> are those which, being fixed into both the lower and upper stones of the walls, ensure that the courses do not happen to be pushed out or pulled apart from one another. 

<margin>Likewise, Pins.</margin>
They do not reject iron **cramps and pins**. But we have learned from the works of the ancients that iron is corrupted <note>by rust</note> and does not last; whereas bronze lasts and is nearly eternal. Indeed, it has been observed that marbles are wasted away and broken all around by the rust of iron. **Wooden cramps** have also been seen inserted into the stones of the most ancient works; these I consider by no means inferior to iron ones. Bronze and iron cramps are secured with lead; wooden ones are sufficiently firm by their own shape, which are carved so that, for the sake of the resemblance, they are called **swallow-tails** <note>original: "caudæ hirundineæ" — known today as dovetail joints</note>. Cramps should be inserted in such a way that raindrops do not penetrate to rot them. They believe bronze is strengthened against age if a thirtieth part of tin is mixed in during the casting. 

<margin>Lest rust should grow.</margin>
They will fear rust less if they are smeared with bitumen or even oil. They assert that iron should be tempered with white lead, gypsum, and liquid pitch so that it does not feel the rust. Wooden cramps smeared with pure wax and olive oil lees <note>original: "amurca" — the watery, bitter liquid that settles from olive oil</note> do not rot. I see that a great deal of molten and very hot lead was poured into the sockets made for the cramps in the stones. You will find walls built everywhere in ancient buildings consisting solely of **infill** <note>original: "infarctura" — a method similar to modern concrete where a core is poured between two faces</note>, and they are very firm. These are constructed just like the earthen walls used in **Africa** and **Spain**, with two frames of either boards or wickerwork driven in on both sides to stand in place of the casing until the poured work has hardened. But they differ in this: here they pour in a nearly flowing cement-like paste <note>original: "cemētītiam pultem"</note>; there they trample down a tough earth, made ductile by moistening and kneading, using their feet and leveling rammers. In the former, for the sake of bonding, they also lay down larger stones as if they were rubble <note>original: "ruderamēta"</note>, especially stones in regular courses or even broken angular ones. For a rounded stone, even if it is quite strong against damage, will behave in a most untrustworthy manner in any structure unless it is bound by much supporting material.

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

<margin>Veneers</margin>
<margin>Note the laws for constructing walls</margin>
Indeed, in the earth walls of Africa, it is a marvelous method of construction to mix esparto <note>a tough fiber from Spanish and North African grasses</note> or sea-rush with mud; this remains unspoiled and durable against winds and rains. Up until the time of Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and naturalist</note>, earth towers and watchtowers placed on mountain ridges—dating back to the time of Hannibal—were still visible. We apply only thin **veneers** <note>original: "crustulae" — thin decorative or protective surface layers</note> so that I might call them "shards" rather than "husks." Using wattle-work <term>craticium: a framework of woven laths or reeds</term> and mats made of old reeds is a mean or "unfree" type of work <note>original: "opus illiberale" — work considered beneath a refined architect, associated with the lower classes</note>. Yet, the ancient Roman commoners used it everywhere. These wattle frames are smeared with mud and straw that has been kneaded for three days; afterward, they are dressed—as I mentioned recently—with lime or even gypsum. Finally, they are dignified with paintings or statues. If you mix gypsum with a third part of crushed tile <note>original: "testa rusam"</note>, it will resist dampness <note>original: "asperugo" — a term for roughness or rising damp</note> quite well. When mixed with lime, it becomes significantly stronger; however, in damp places, frost, and ice, gypsum is completely useless. It remains for me to provide a sort of summary—a most ancient law among architects which I decree should be observed as if it were an oracle. It is as follows:

Provide the wall with a very firm base. Let the upper parts correspond perpendicularly to the lower parts through the center point. Strengthen the **corners** and the **bones** <term>ossa: the structural framework or load-bearing elements of a wall</term> from the ground to the top with stronger stone. Use well-soaked lime. Do not place a stone in the work unless it is soaking wet. Oppose the harder stones against the most hostile forces <note>such as weight or weathering</note>. Carry out the construction according to the rule, the level, and the plumb line. See to it that the subsequent stones sit over the middle of the joints of the preceding stones <note>this refers to "breaking the joints" for structural bonding</note>. Lay full stones in regular courses; fill the middle of the wall with broken pieces <note>rubble infill</note>. Bind the courses together with frequent transverse stones <note>headers that span the thickness of the wall to tie the faces together</note. So much for walls. I come now to the roof.

<margin>Lightning does not strike the Laurel, the Eagle, or the Sea-calf.</margin>
But I would not wish to pass over this: I understand that certain arguments were greatly observed by the ancients. There are things in nature which undoubtedly possess a power not to be despised. They say that lightning does not strike the **laurel** tree, the **eagle**, or the **sea-calf** <note>original: "vitulum marinum" — a seal</note>. If these are incorporated into the work, there are some who perhaps think the building will remain untouched and immune to lightning. For my part, I seem to be able to hope for this just as much as I believe what they say about a red toad <note>original: "rana rubeta"</note> enclosed in a clay pot and buried in the middle of a field to keep birds away from the seeds. Or that the *ostrim* tree <insert>☞</insert> <note>possibly the box-tree or a specific maple</note>, if brought into a house, makes childbirth difficult. And that the Lesbian leaf *enomion*, kept under roofs, causes a loosening of the bowels and brings the plague through emptiness. I return to the matter. Here it is necessary to repeat what we touched upon earlier when we discussed the **design** <term>lineamenta: the conceptual layout and lines of a building</term> of buildings.

...[materials] placed on the roof, whether of wood or stone. We shall begin this matter here, taking this principle: let us establish that something exists which pertains to the reasoning of the whole roof, and is of this sort: just as in a wall, we interpret a roof to have bones, ligaments <term>nervos: Alberti uses "nerves" or "ligaments" to describe structural elements that bind things together, like rafters or joints</term>, fillings, rinds, and veneers <note>original: "crustulas"</note>; yet let us consider whether this is indeed the case in practice. 

To begin, let us start with those roofs which consist of straight lines made from the timber of the forests. To support roofs, it is necessary to set firm beams <note>original: "trabes"</note> from wall to wall; and we shall not deny that these are—as we were just discussing—effectively columns placed horizontally. Therefore, the beam takes the place of the **bone**. Indeed, if the principles of the work allowed, who would not desire the entire structure to be, so to speak, "bony" and extremely solid? That is, a structure joined and strengthened by continuous columns and united beams. But we look to economy <note>original: "parsimoniae" — thrift or practical management of resources</note>, considering anything superfluous that can be removed while maintaining the structural stability; for this reason, the intervals between the beams are limited here. 

From these beams, transverse rafters <note>original: "tigna"</note> are placed, and smaller square battens are led down, and whatever else is similar to these. It is by no means unfitting to think of all these as **ligaments**. Finally, onto these, boards and larger planks are fitted, which naturally take the role of the **filling**; by the same logic, we judge the pavement and the tiles to be the outer **rind**. We shall not deny that the "sky" <note>original: "coelum" — a common term for a ceiling or inner canopy</note> of the roof, which hangs above the head, is the inner **rind**. Therefore, if it is agreed that these things are so, let us investigate what is owed to each of them; once these are reviewed, we may more easily understand what is appropriate for stone roofs.

¶ We shall deal with these matters as briefly as the subject requires. But let this be relevant: I do not praise the architects of this age who, for the purpose of holding the floor timbers <note>original: "contignationibus"</note>, leave vast, gaping holes in the very **bones** of the walls, into which they insert the ends of the beams once the wall is finished. Because of this, the wall is made weaker and the building is poorly protected against the devastation of fire, as an entrance for fire is opened through to the next room. For this reason, I approve of the ancients who

For if you wish to link the walls together with the timberwork, there will be no lack of bronze loops and buckles and protrusions extending from the corbel, which you may use most conveniently for that purpose. 

A beam must be entirely whole and quite sound, and especially in the middle of its length, it should be free of any defect. If an ear is placed at one end and blows struck at the other end are heard to be shaky and dull, they indicate an internal "disease" <note>original: "morbum" — rot or internal decay</note>.

When the surface of a beam is to be squared, besides the bark, either nothing or as little as possible should be removed. On whichever side any transverse defect appears: place it so that it stands at the top. If any long crack runs straight through the beam, do not entrust it to the sides. Instead, assign it to either the top or, preferably, the bottom surface. If the beam must be bored through or perhaps "wounded" <note>original: "convulneranda" — Alberti often uses surgical or bodily metaphors for cutting into structural materials</note> by cutting, spare the middle of its length, and do not damage the bottom surface. If, however, as they have observed in the construction of basilicas, beams are to be placed in pairs, leave a gap of several fingers between them so they may breathe, lest they infect each other by heating up together <note>Alberti believed that wood "breathed" and that trapped heat or moisture between two touching beams caused rapid rot</note>. And it will indeed be beneficial to place the pairs of beams in an alternating fashion, so that their "heads" <note>original: "capita" — the narrower top end of the tree trunk</note> do not both rest in the same bed side-by-side. Instead, where the "foot" <note>original: "pes" — the thicker butt end of the trunk</note> of one lies, let the head of the other rest. For in this way, they will mutually assist the weakness of the lighter part with the firmer strength of the foot. It is also necessary that the beams themselves be "related"—that is, of the same species of wood, from the same forest, grown facing the same side of the sky, and, if possible, cut on the same day.

<margin>What the beds for beams ought to be like.</margin>

In this way, with equal natural strengths, they may perform an equal duty. Lay out the beds <term>cubilia: the recessed sockets or ledge in a wall where the end of a beam rests</term> for the beams according to the level, so that each of them is solid and very firm. Beware when placing the beams that the wood does not touch lime <note>Lime mortar was known to be corrosive to certain types of wood</note>; and leave the vents around them open and free, lest the wood be corrupted by any internal contact or waste away if enclosed. Under the "cushion" <note>original: "pulvillum" — the bearing point or block under the beam end</note> of the beam, spread dried fern, or charcoal, or rather olive-dregs <term>amurca: the bitter, watery liquid that settles out of olive oil, used in antiquity as a pesticide and wood preservative</term> mixed with its own pits. But if the trees are smaller than would allow you to place a whole beam from a single trunk: join several together into one assembly, so that they maintain their strength more tightly within themselves. That is, so that the upper line of the joined beam cannot be shortened by the pressure of weights, and conversely, the lower line cannot become longer. But let it stand like a cord <note>original: "corda" — referring to a bowstring or tension cord</note> with a sinewy grip to secure the trunks driven above, which push against each other with opposing faces. Rafters <term>tigna: smaller horizontal or sloped timbers</term> and all other remaining lumber which are prepared by being sawn from a beam shall be judged by the soundness and integrity of the original beam.

<margin>Planks on rafters.</margin>

They believe that planks that are too thick are not suitable, because when they begin to warp, they may force out the nails. They order double nails to be applied even to thinner boards, especially under outdoor <term>sub divalibus: "under the sky," referring to areas exposed to the elements</term> floorings, by which the corners and the middle of the sides of the planks may be secured.

<margin>Nails.</margin>

They order nails that bear weights transversely to be made thicker. But where others are more slender, they do not disapprove of them. However, it is fitting for these to be longer and wider in the head. I have found that bronze nails are more enduring <note>original: "penniores" — likely a contraction for "perenniores," meaning more lasting or durable</note> outdoors and in wet places; while iron ones are stronger <note>original: "nervosiores"</note> for interior work and dry conditions. Where by experience to strengthen...

<page-num>XLIII</page-num>
->### Book III. On Building.<-

...come into the framing, they <note>likely referring to carpenters or builders</note> take pleasure in small wooden pins. What we have said concerning wooden roofs shall also be observed in stone beams. For transverse veins and defects shall be rejected for use in beams or for the construction of columns; or, if the defects are moderate and slight, the sides of the stone where they appear shall be turned downward when placed into the work. Veins running lengthwise will be considered more tolerable for strength in beams than transverse ones. Likewise, stone slabs, for various reasons but especially for the sake of weight, should be made as thin as possible. Finally, the rafters, joists, and beams that are placed in either wooden or stone roofs should neither be so slender nor so far apart that they are too weak to bear their own load. Conversely, they should not be so thick or so crowded together that they make the work unpleasant and shapeless. But we shall discuss the form and grace of the work elsewhere. Therefore, let what has been said so far regarding straight-lined roofs suffice, unless perhaps one thing is missing that I should advise—which I believe must be strictly observed in every work:

<margin>Bones to be joined to bones</margin>
Naturalists <note>original: "physici" — here referring to those who study the natural world or physicians</note> have observed that in the bodies of living creatures, Nature is accustomed to finish her work in such a way that she never intended bones to be separated or disconnected from other bones. Thus, we too shall join bones to bones, and we shall bind them together most beautifully with "nerves" and "ligaments" <note>original: "nervuis / illigamentisque" — Alberti uses these anatomical terms to describe the joints, metal clamps, and fasteners that hold a structure together</note>, so that there is a continuous series and compaction of bones. Even if everything else were removed, the work would still stand, completed by its own members and strengths.

### Chapter XIII. On curved roofs, the differences of their arches, and their construction.

**I** come now to curved roofs. Let us consider how these correspond fully in all their proportions to straight-lined roofs. Arches constitute a curved roof, and we have suggested that an arch is essentially a bent beam <note>Alberti defines the arch not as a new structural type, but as a "flexed" version of the post-and-lintel system</note>. Here, too, ligaments come forward; they also add elements to fill the empty spaces. But I would like it to be more clearly understood what an arch itself is, and of what parts it consists. Indeed, I believe men derived the method for drawing arches from this: when they saw that two beams with their heads joined could be spread apart at their feet and so braced that, by mutual interlacing and equal weights against each other, they stood firm. This discovery was pleasing, and they began to use this method to place gabled roofs <note>original: "displuvia" — roofs designed to shed rainwater in two directions</note> upon buildings. After this, perhaps when they were unable to cover a larger area according to the plan because of the shortness of the beams, they interposed something between the high heads of the trunks, so that it looked nearly like the Greek letter $\Pi$ <note>Pi</note>. This inserted piece itself they perhaps called a "wedge" <note>original: "cuneum" — the ancestor of the modern voussoir</note>. Proceeding from that logic, by multiplying wedges of this kind, they observed the effect of an arch-like shape and approved of it. Transferring that method of drawing an arch to stone works, they created a complete arch with these additions; so that it must now be confessed...

# Leon Battista Alberti: On the Art of Building

...[bones should be joined to bones], and that the arch itself consists of the joining of several wedge-shaped stones <term>voussoirs<note>original: "cuneorum" — the wedge-shaped stones that make up an arch</note></term>. Some of these, with their lowest ends, settle toward the arch itself <note>referring to the inner curve or soffit</note>; others, sitting at the back, occupy the knot of the spine <note>the crown or keystone</note>; while others fill out the remaining circuit of the ribs. It is not out of place to repeat here what I reviewed in the first book: Arches differ from one another. For there is the **straight arch** <note>original: "rectus" — Alberti uses "straight" to describe the full, upright semicircular arch</note>, which is formed by a complete semicircle; its chord <note>the horizontal line connecting the base of the arch</note> passes directly through the center of the circle. There is also an arch that tastes more of the nature of a beam than an arch; we call this a **diminished arch** <note>original: "comminutum" — known today as a segmental arch</note> because it is not a full semicircle, but only some portion of one; its chord is distant from the center and sits above it. There is also the **composite arch**, which some call the **angular arch** <note>the pointed or Gothic arch</note>, which is composed of two diminished arches; it has on its chord two centers for the two curved lines that intersect one another.

<margin>The straight arch</margin>
That the **straight arch** <note>the semicircular arch</note> is the strongest of all is judged by experience and demonstrated by reason and argument. Indeed, I do not see how it could ever fall apart of its own accord, unless one wedge-stone should thrust out another; they are so far removed from such an injury that they are actually strengthened by one another's support. Furthermore, if they should by chance attempt to shift, the very nature of the weights—by which the stones are either held in place or which the stones themselves possess—prevents it. Hence that saying of **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar</note>, who said that in arched works the right side stands no more by the left than the left by the right. And one may observe this in practice. Indeed, how could the highest wedge-stone, which is unique at the middle of the spine <note>the keystone</note>, be strong enough to propel the side stones out? Or, when those side stones are themselves pressing in, how could that keystone ever be thrust out from the seat it already occupies? Those stones that follow next along the ribs are easily kept in their place by the balance of the weights. Finally, as for the stones that settle at either base, why should they move so long as the upper ones persist in their duty?

Therefore, for **straight arches**, which easily protect themselves, we do not require a chord <note>a tie-rod or tension member</note>; but in **diminished arches** we must secure them with an iron chain, or something that has the power of a chord, and by extending the walls on either side. We desire these wall extensions to be no shorter than the distance required to complete the missing part of the semicircle. The ancient architects never neglected to do this: they never failed to integrate all diminished arches within the thickness of the walls wherever it was permitted.

<margin>Diminished arches</margin>
Indeed, they also excellently observed that where the occasion allowed, they would place a **diminished arch** over straight beams. Furthermore, they would even drive **straight arches** over those diminished arches, so that the upper arch would support the diminished one below it and intercept the burden of the weights. **Composite arches** <note>pointed arches</note> are not seen among the ancients. There are those who think they should be introduced for the openings of towers, where the excessive weights placed above...

<summary>Alberti defines the three types of arches—semicircular, segmental, and pointed—and argues that the semicircular arch is the strongest due to the mutual support of its wedge-stones (voussoirs). He notes that segmental arches require extra support like iron chains or thick walls, and observes that pointed arches were not used by the ancients.</summary>
