Page XLIIII.
Header: Book III. On Construction.

...as if they were a prow set against the current to split it. However, arches of this kind are strengthened by the weights placed upon them rather than being crushed by them. I would wish that all the wedge-shaped stones <term>voussoirs<note>original: "cuneos" — the tapered stones that form the curve of an arch</note></term> by which the arch is drawn should be broad and, as much as possible, cut from very large stone. Indeed, the part of any body of voussoirs that was solidified and joined together by nature is more inseparable than what has been joined and compacted in arches by human hand and skill. The composition also ought to be mutually equal so that, as if on a scale, the right side corresponds to the left in appearance, size, weight, and the like. If you lead several arches for porticos through continuous connections from columns and capitals, make sure the voussoir from which two or more joined arches rise is not two separate stones, nor as many stones as there are arches, but one and the same single, whole stone, by which the heads of both arches are held together. However, if the second voussoirs that rise next upon these first ones are of very large stone, let both be treated so that one adheres to the other along the line of their joints at the haunches <note>original: "renibus" — the "kidneys" or haunches of the arch, where the curve begins to straighten</note>. A third stone will cover these second ones and will be fitted according to the rules of wall-building with a matching bond measured by the level <note>original: "libella"</note>, so that it serves both joined arches and holds the voussoirs of both in its grasp. Throughout the entire arch, see to it that the contact points of the joints and the closures are directed toward their center. Skilled builders have always placed the spine's wedge <note>the keystone at the crown of the arch</note> with a single, whole, and very large stone. But if the thickness of the wall is too great for you to place such whole voussoirs, it then begins to be not an arch but rather a **vault** <note>original: "testudo"</note>, which we shall call a **barrel vault** <note>original: "fornicem"</note>.

### ¶ The types of vaults: what they are, how many, what kind, and how they may be more correctly and usefully completed. Chapter XIIII.

**T**here are various kinds of vaults. We must investigate how they differ from one another and by what lines they are formed. I shall have to devise names so that I might be what I have especially intended to be in these books: easy to follow and not at all obscure. It does not escape me that the poet Ennius called the highest reaches of the sky "vaults" <note>original: "fornices"</note> and that Servius said they were "caverns" <note>original: "cavernas"</note> made in the manner of ship hulls. But I ask this indulgence: that in these books we consider it sufficiently well-said in English if it is both suited to the matter and understood most clearly. <margin>The types of vaults</margin> These are the types of vaults: the **barrel vault**, the **coved vault**, and the **spherical vault** <note>original: "fornix, camera, et recta spherica"</note>, and whatever parts there are of these. Of these, the **spherical vault** <note>a dome</note> by its nature is placed only on walls rising from a circular area. But the **coved vault** is suited to square areas. For **barrel vaults**, however, the areas have four angles, whether they are short or elongated, such as the covered walkways <term>cryptoporticos<note>original: "criptoporticus" — a vaulted, semi-subterranean gallery</note></term> we see being built. A vault is that which is drawn in the likeness of a perforated mountain.

# Book III. On Construction. Folio XLVI.

...[the builder] may grip it between the fingers of his left hand. And to fill the middle spaces, they have been accustomed to do so with an accumulation of **pumice** <term>pumice<note>original: "pumex" — a lightweight, porous volcanic rock ideal for reducing the weight of large vaults</note></term>; and especially pumice, which all experts declare to be the most convenient stone of all for filling vaults. But for the building of arches and **vaults** <term>vaults<note>original: "testudinibus" — literally "tortoise shells," the standard term for vaulted ceilings</note></term>, there is need for **centering** <term>centering<note>original: "armamento" — the temporary wooden support structure or scaffolding used to hold masonry in place until the mortar sets</note></term>; this is a certain rough and temporary timbering defined according to the circuit of the curved line.

<margin>
We shall make vaults.
</margin>

Upon this centering, instead of leather or skin, either wicker-work or reeds or common materials of this sort are spread, to support the mass in the vault until it has hardened. There is, however, among vaults one—the true **spherical vault**—which does not require centering.

<margin>
The stability of the true spherical vault is complete.
</margin>

This is because it consists not only of arches, but also of **rings** <term>rings<note>original: "coronis" — horizontal courses of masonry that form a complete circle, providing hoop strength to a dome</note></term>. And who could recount or imagine how many of each of these there are—clinging, driven in, intersecting each other, at right angles and at unequal angles? So that at whatever place you intersect any such stone throughout the whole vault, you realize that you have placed a **voussoir** <term>voussoir<note>original: "cuneum" — a wedge-shaped stone</note></term> of many arches and rings: a ring that has been built upon another ring, and an arch that has extended from another arch. Imagine that you wanted this work to fail; where would it begin? Especially since all the voussoirs seek a single center with equal strength and pressure. Many among the ancients took such advantage of the strength of this vault that they only laid down simple brick rings every few feet. But the rest of the vault they completed by pouring in a rubble-work masonry material. 

However, I far more approve of those who, during the progress of the work, took care that by the same art with which stones are bound together in a wall, here the lower rings are bound to those immediately above, and the arches are connected to each other in many places—especially if a supply of dry pit-sand is not available, or if the work is exposed to the southern sea winds <note>Alberti often warns that sea air and poor sand weaken mortar, requiring better physical bonding of stones</note>.

<margin>
A cornered spherical vault.
</margin>

You may also raise a **cornered spherical vault** <note>This likely refers to a cloister vault or a vault on pendentives</note> without any centering, provided you interpose a true spherical vault through its thickness. But there, a binding is especially needed, by which the weaker parts of this vault may be bound most tightly to the stronger parts of that one. Nevertheless, it will be helpful, once one or two stone rings have been led and hardened, to fasten light ties and hooks there, to which you may commit as much centering as is sufficient to support those rings which are built up a few feet from there, until they become dry. And thereafter, when these parts have also hardened, to transfer these supports of the centering to every few rows to complete the uppermost parts, until you have rendered the work finished. 

A <term>vault<note>original: "testudo"</note></term>, a <term>curved ceiling<note>original: "camura"</note></term>, and likewise an <term>archway<note>original: "fornix"</note></term> must be brought in with centering substituted. But I would wish the first rows of these, and the heads of the arch, to be entrusted to the firmest foundations. Nor indeed...

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

☞ I find fault with those who first raise all the walls, leaving only small projecting **mutules** <term>mutules<note>original: "mutulozꝝ" — stone projections or brackets intended to support later construction</note></term> behind, upon which they promise to place a vault at a later time; this results in a weak and unstable work. Therefore, if they listen to me, these arches will indeed be raised together in equal rows with their own wall to which they are attached. By this method, the work is joined together by very many and very strong bonds, as much as can possibly be done. The empty spaces left between the rising curves of the vaults and the wall to which they adhere—a place builders call the **haunches** <term>haunches<note>original: "fabricoxam" / "coxarum" — the 'hips' or side portions of an arch or vault where it starts to curve over</note></term>—should be filled up, not with earth or loose, dry rubble, but rather with regular and stable masonry, connected to the wall again and again. Some people like to insert empty ceramic water vessels, cracked and turned upside down, within the thickness of the haunches for the sake of lightening the load, so that no weight is added by moisture collecting there. Then, pour over **rubble work** <term>rubble work<note>original: "cementa" — a mixture of small stones and mortar used as fill</note></term> made of very light but otherwise tenacious stone. Finally, in the whole vault, whatever its shape, we shall imitate nature: for just as she has joined bone to bone, so she has also interwoven the flesh itself with small fibers for a binding through all diameters, drawn across in length, width, depth, and diagonally. I believe we should imitate this craftsmanship of nature by interspersing stones for the vaults.

Once these things are finished, the next task is the covering—the primary matter in all building—and no more necessary than it is difficult; in attaining and perfecting this, all the care and diligence of everyone has struggled again and again. We must now speak of these things. But first it is helpful to interject this point, which pertains primarily to the work of vaults. For indeed, there is a difference in how vaults are completed. For an arch or vault that must be made with **centering** <term>centering<note>original: "armamētis" — temporary wooden supports used during construction</note></term> underneath must be built with continuous and never-interrupted labor. But that which is made without centering requires intervals, almost between every course, until the parts already built are firm; otherwise, the newest parts added on top, if the earlier ones are not sufficiently firm, might loosen and slide off.

Furthermore, for vaults built with centering, it is helpful as soon as they have been closed up with the top **keystones** <term>keystones<note>original: "cuneis" — wedge-shaped stones; the final stone at the top of an arch</note></term>, to—so to speak—slightly slacken the supports by which the centering is held up. This is done so that while the work is still fresh, the joined wedges do not "float" between the packing and the support of the lime. Instead, they should occupy a level seat for resting among themselves, balanced by their own weights. Otherwise, during the drying process, the built parts would not settle and pack together as the work requires, but would leave cracks as they settle. Therefore, let it be done thus: do not remove the supports entirely, but let the centering be slackened gradually day by day; for if you do not lower them with careful timing, the fresh work may sag. After some days, however, depending on the size of the work, slacken them a little more. Do this thereafter until the stone wedges of the vault fit themselves together and the work hardens.

The method of slackening.
</margin>

Leaf XLVI.

### Book III. On the Construction.

...you drive into the heads of the scaffolding itself wooden wedges, sharpened to a point in the likeness of an axe. Therefore, when it pleases you to loosen the work, you may tap out these wedges bit by bit with a small mallet for as long as you wish, without any danger. Finally, I maintain this: the scaffolding should not be removed before a full winter has been endured. This is partly for other reasons, but also so that the work, weakened and loosened by the soaking of rains, does not collapse. And yet, nothing better can be given to **vaults** <note>original: "testudinibus" — literally "tortoises," a common term for arched or vaulted ceilings</note> than that they should drink their fill of water and never feel "thirst." So much for these matters.

### ¶ On the outer layers of roofs: their utility; types, shapes, and materials of tiles; gutter-tiles and eaves. Chapter XV.

**I** return to the outer shell of the roof. Indeed, if we interpret it correctly, nothing in the whole building is more primary than having a place where you may be received, fleeing from the burning suns and the storms falling from the sky. This benefit is like a wing to you; it is provided not by the wall, not by the floor, nor any of those other things, but primarily by that which is visible: the outermost shell of the roof. To have this shell remain strong against all the injuries of the seasons—as the necessity of the matter demands—is something that human industry and the arts, having tested all materials, have scarcely yet made sufficiently reliable. Nor do I believe it can easily be found. For since not only rain, but also frosts, heats, and that most hostile of all things, the wind, never cease to harass it, who could anywhere long endure such constant and indeed bitter enemies? From this it follows that some materials rot immediately, others dissolve, some weigh down the walls, others split or break, and others are stripped away; so much so that even metals, which are elsewhere invincible against the injuries of storms, cannot endure so many assaults in this position. But men, not scorning the abundance of things provided by the nature of their locations which came to hand, provided for necessity as far as they were able.

<margin>The custom of covering houses among various nations</margin>
Therefore, various methods of covering works arose. **Pyrges** <note>A legendary figure or group mentioned by Vitruvius</note>—so says **Vitruvius** <term>Vitruvius<note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, a Roman architect and engineer whose "Ten Books on Architecture" was the primary source for Renaissance builders like Alberti</note></term>—covered them with reeds; and at **Marseilles** <note>original: "Massiliam"</note> they cover the work with earth mixed with straw. Among the **Garamantes** <note>A powerful ancient Berber tribe of the Sahara</note>, the **Thelophagi** <note>A people mentioned by Pliny, possibly "the sun-eaters"</note>—as **Pliny** <term>Pliny<note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and naturalist</note></term> relates—cover their roofs with the shells of tortoises. The greatest part of **Germany** uses various small wooden slats. In the province of **Belgium**, they cut a white stone more easily than wood into thin sheets, which they set out as tiles. The **Ligurians** and **Etruscans** <note>Peoples of northern and central Italy</note> use broad slabs of flaky stone for covering their houses. Others, having tried **pavements** <term>pavements<note>original: "pauimenta" — here referring to flat terrace roofs made of masonry</note></term> (of which I shall soon speak), found that after all trials, human wit and industry have not yet found anything more convenient than the baked clay **tile** <term>tile<note>original: "tegula testacea" — a terracotta or ceramic tile</note></term>. For the work of pavements becomes rough from frost, splits, and sags. **Lead** melts in the heat of the sun. **Bronze**, if it is heavy, is expensive to place; if it is thin, it is disturbed by the winds and, growing thin from rust, is torn away. Tile...

# Leone Battista Alberti: On the Art of Building.

<margin>
Crinias of Cyprus is said to have invented the tile.
</margin>

They say that a certain Crinias of Cyprus, the son of a farmer, first invented the tile <note>original: "tegula"</note>. Of these, there are two types. One is flat, a foot wide and a cubit long, with flanges <note>original: "spodis" — the raised edges on a flat roof tile</note> protruding here and there to a ninth part of its width. The other is curved <note>original: "aduolutū" — referring to the *imbrex* or semi-cylindrical tile</note>, imitating the armor used to protect the legs. Both should be wider where they receive the flowing rain and narrower where they discharge it. However, flat tiles are more convenient, provided they are joined according to the rule and the level, so that they do not tilt to the side, nor allow hollows to run between them, nor let bumps protrude; this ensures nothing interferes with the cross-flow of the rain and no empty space is left. If the surface of the roof is vast, larger tiles will be required, lest the streams of rain overflow because the channels cannot contain them. To prevent whirlwinds from carrying the tiles away, I would wish for every tile to be secured with a bedding of lime mortar, especially in public works. In private buildings, it will suffice if you secure the first rows of the eaves <note>original: "stillicidia" — the dripping edge of the roof</note> against the force of the winds; then, the loose tiles can be more easily repaired when a defect occurs. Otherwise, the work is most fitly done in this manner: on wooden roofs, instead of the usual boards, small ceramic tablets <note>original: "testaceæ tabellulæ"</note> should be laid out and bound with plaster <note>original: "gypso"</note> over the descending rafters. Upon these tablets, the flat tiles should be laid and secured with lime.

☞ This method is very safe against fires and most comfortable for the use of the inhabitants. It can also be done at less expense if you lay down "Greek reed" <note>likely a type of giant cane or *Arundo donax*</note> in place of the ceramic tablets and secure it with lime. I would prefer that you do not use tiles—especially those secured with lime for public works—unless they have been seasoned for two years under the frost and the sun. For if a weak tile is laid, it cannot be removed without great expense to the work. It occurs to me to mention what we read in the historian Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BC</note> regarding those famous hanging gardens of Syria, which were built with a novel and by no means useless invention. Upon the beams, they placed reeds smeared with bitumen <note>original: "asphalto"</note>; upon these, they fitted baked stones in a double layer bound with plaster. In the third place, they added lead tiles, so cast and joined together that no moisture could penetrate to the first layers of brick.

<margin>
Hanging gardens in Syria.
</margin>

# Book III. On the Work. Leaf XLVII.

...flowing: it should either be collected in cisterns, or diverted into sewers.
<margin>Pay attention</margin>
If the water cannot be discharged from these sewers into the sea or into rivers, dig wells in suitable places down to the flowing water, and fill the trench with round stones. Finally, if that is not possible, they say to make pits of <margin>The method of making a sewer</margin> sufficient capacity and put in charcoal; then fill them with sand; these will soak up and consume the excess moisture. Furthermore, if the floor of the area is made of moved earth, it shall be rammed most carefully with a heavy beetle <note>original: "festucabitur" — the use of a heavy wooden rammer to compact earth</note> and a layer of rubble <term>rudus</term> <note>a layer of stones and lime</note> shall be laid over a foundation of stones. But if it is a suspended floor of timber, then another layer of planks is laid crosswise over the first, and it should be bedded with stones and a layer of rubble a foot thick should be applied. Some think that esparto grass or fern should be spread under the rubble, so that the timber is not damaged by contact with the lime. If the rubble is new, one part of lime should be mixed with three parts of stone; if it is reused material, two parts of lime to five. Once applied, it should be compacted by pounding it very frequently with rammers. To this, at a thickness of six fingers, a paste <note>original: "puls" — a fine mortar or bedding layer</note> made from crushed tile should be added, which has one part of lime mixed with three parts of the tile. Finally, the inlays <note>original: "sertilia"</note>, or herringbone tiling <term>testa spicacea</term> <note>bricks laid in a V-shape resembling an ear of grain</note>, or mosaic pieces <note>original: "tessere"</note> should be inserted according to the line and the rule. The work will be safer if, between the foundation and the paste, overlapping roof tiles joined with oil-based lime are laid down. For a floor not exposed to the open air—which <margin>Varro.</margin> Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar</note> highly approves of for its dryness—he orders it to be done thus: dig to two feet and ram the ground; then lay either rubble or a tiled floor. Leave open vents through which moisture may drip away via its own channels; heap up charcoal; and after these have been trampled down and well compacted, apply a layer half a foot thick made of a mixture of sand, lime, and ash. These things which we have reviewed thus far, we have interpreted from Pliny and especially <margin>Pavements</margin> Vitruvius. Now I shall relate what I have collected with the greatest care and diligence concerning floors from the works of the ancients, from whom I profess to have learned far more than from writers. And yet I shall begin with the top crust, though it is quite difficult to keep it from being weak and crack-prone. For when it is pregnant with moisture, whether by sun or winds, it dries on the surface. From this, as we see in the mud left by a flood, the skin of the dirt contracts and opens irremediable cracks. For those parts that have dried will no longer cohere by any artifice. But the damp parts easily yield and follow those that contract. I see the ancients applied either a ceramic or a stone crust. For I have seen tiles—especially where they are not trodden by feet—laid a cubit wide in every direction and joined with oil-based lime; and one sees small bricks, a finger thick, two fingers wide, and twice as long as they are wide, joined standing on their sides in imitation of ears of grain <note>the herringbone pattern mentioned earlier</note>.

Stone veneers <note>original: "crustas" — refers to the decorative or functional top layer of a floor or wall</note> can be seen everywhere made from larger marble slabs; and likewise from smaller cut pieces and little tesserae. Furthermore, ancient veneers are observed that are made of mortar alone; this is made by joining lime and sand with finely crushed tile, much like the third layer used by a painter. I have found that these veneers will be firmer and more excellent if you add a fourth part of crushed Tyburn stone <term>Travertine</term> <note>Lapis Tyburninus: a light-colored limestone used extensively in Roman architecture</note>. There are those who provide Puteolan powder <term>Pozzolana</term> <note>puluerē puteolanū: a volcanic ash from Pozzuoli that allows mortar to set even underwater</note>—which they call gravel <gloss>rapillus</gloss>—to this work in a marvelous way.

Veneers which are faced only with mortar can be tested by frequent beating, and by repeating this daily, they acquire a thickness and hardness that almost surpasses stone. And it is beneficial for veneers of this kind if they are sprinkled with a lime wash, or if they are smeared with linseed oil; they then take on a certain glassy hardness and remain unharmed by the weather. They affirm that lime worked with oil admits nothing harmful to the pavement. 

Under the veneer, I see a material poured of lime and very small bits of broken tile to the thickness of two or three fingers. Under that is found a sort of stuffing, partly of broken tile, and partly of small stone chips which the craftsmen struck off with a chisel; and I find this is generally a foot thick. Beneath this upper section, I find brick tiles laid down; finally, at the very bottom, stones no larger than a fist settle. One can see in a torrent that stones which are called "male"—such as the rounded, flinty, and glassy ones—are dried immediately upon leaving the water. But tile and tufa <note>a porous rock formed from volcanic ash</note> and things of that sort keep the moisture they have taken in for a long time. For this reason, there are those who claim that moisture from the earth does not penetrate much to the veneers where the pavement is laid over such "male" stone. 

We have also seen those who placed tile slabs on small pillars, a foot and a half high, arranged in a square pattern every two feet, upon which they built the kind of pavement we described. But this type of pavement belongs especially to the baths <note>This refers to a hypocaust system, where floors were raised on pillars to allow hot air to circulate underneath</note>, about which we will speak in its proper place. 

Pavements enjoy moisture and humid air while they are being made. In shady and damp places, they are preserved firmer and more intact. The things especially harmful to pavements are the weakness of the ground and sudden drying out. For just as the earth in the fields is packed down by repeated rains, so too are pavements, when abundantly moistened, welded into a single and complete solidity. In a place where rain falling from the roof pipes is received, it is necessary to place a stone veneer that is entirely whole and very solid, so that it is not dug out and spoiled by the constant (so to speak) persistence <note>original: "improbitate" — literally "wickedness" or "relentlessness," used here to describe the wearing power of water</note> of the forceful drops. Furthermore, for a pavement which is spread over mortar and timber framing <gloss>contignato</gloss>, care must be taken that the "bones" <note>the joists or structural beams</note> by which it is supported are strong in their power and equalized among themselves...

<margin>
The observation of the year and the weather is not to be neglected.
</margin>

...materials. If this is not the case—for instance, if a wall or a beam that is much stronger than the others is placed beneath a certain spot—the pavement will crack in that place and be spoiled. For since material does not always remain in the same state and strength, but is moved by the variations of the seasons, it softens with moisture; in dry conditions, it returns to rigidity and hardens. For this reason, when the weaker parts struggle under weight and settle, it inevitably cracks. So much for these matters.

But do not overlook what would be very useful to the task. For some times of the year and specific weather patterns are required for digging foundations, others for filling them, others for raising walls, others for placing vaults <note>testudinibus: literally "tortoise shells," referring here to arched or vaulted ceilings</note>, and others for applying veneers. Indeed, digging is most conveniently done during the dog days <note>caniculam: the hottest days of summer, associated with the rising of the Dog Star, Sirius</note> and in autumn itself, when the earth is dry and an abundance of moisture does not hinder the digging. They are also filled quite conveniently at the beginning of spring, especially where they are deep, for they will be sufficiently protected from summer heat by the surrounding earth. But they will be filled far more conveniently at the beginning of midwinter <term>Bruma</term> <note>original: "brumę" — the winter solstice or the shortest days of the year</note>, provided that region is not under a part of the sky where it freezes immediately rather than binding together.

A wall also hates excessive heat, as well as sharp cold and sudden frosts, and above all others, it hates the north winds <term>Aquilones</term>. And especially a vault, most of all, desires the most steady and temperate weather until the work has hardened and set itself. We shall apply veneers most appropriately at the rising of the Pleiades <note>vergiliarũ ortũ: the constellation whose appearance in the morning sky signaled the start of spring for ancient farmers and builders</note>, and specifically during those days when the south winds <term>Austri</term> blow with great moisture. For unless the surface to be covered with a veneer or plasterwork <term>Opus Dealbarium</term> <note>original: "opedealbario" — a fine white lime-plastering or whitewashing</note> is thoroughly moist, the applications will not bond; instead, they will crack and fall away in various places, and the work will be spoiled by frequent roughness. But veneers and plasterwork will be discussed more extensively in their own place. Now, having completed these types of subjects, let us pass on to consider the remaining matters more distinctly. And first, we shall deal with the types and variety of buildings and what is due to each; next, with the ornaments of buildings; and finally, we shall settle the correction or restoration of their defects, whether caused by the craftsman's error or the injury of time.

# Leon Battista Alberti. On Building.

**I**t is perfectly clear that buildings were established for the sake of men <note>original: "hominum" - though the OCR suggests "nominum" (of names), the context of the opening of Book IV clearly refers to human needs</note>. For in the beginning, if we interpret it correctly, men began to build works so that they might protect themselves and their property from adverse weather. Soon after, they followed this path not only wanting what was necessary for their safety, but they also did not wish to overlook anything that might contribute to achieving various convenient comforts. From there, prompted and enticed by the suitability of things, they reached the point where they even devised—and used daily—things that served to fulfill their pleasures. Thus, if someone were to say that some buildings are defined by the necessity of life, others by the convenience of use, and others by the pleasure of the times, he might perhaps say something quite appropriate to the matter. 

But when we look around at the abundance and variety of buildings, we easily understand that not all of these were prepared for use alone, nor solely for the sake of one thing or another. Instead, they are made primarily according to the variety of men, so that we have diverse and manifold works. If we wish to note the types of buildings and the parts of those types—just as we have intended—every method of investigation must be taken up and started from this point: that we more carefully consider how men (for whose sake buildings exist and according to whose use they vary) differ among themselves. In this way, each type of building can be more clearly recognized and more distinctly treated. Let us recall, on this subject, what those ancient founders of republics and laws—men of great skill—thought regarding the community of men. They were occupied with searching out and recounting such matters with the highest praise and the admiration of their discoveries.

Solon <note>An Athenian lawmaker and poet</note> distributed the orders of his citizens according to a census and the abundance and measure of their wealth; so much so, that they did not think those who received fewer than 300 measures annually from their fields should even be counted in the number of citizens.

...leaders of the flock. <margin>Britons</margin> The Britons divided their people into four classes. The first Britons were those from whom kings were made; the second were priests; in the third place were soldiers; and finally, the common people. <margin>Egyptians</margin> The Egyptians gave the first rank to the priesthood; beneath them they placed kings and prefects; in the third order they placed warriors; and the multitude was likewise divided among farmers, cattle-breeders, and craftsmen; and also (as Herodotus <note>A 5th-century BCE Greek historian.</note> says) the mercenary and the sailor.

<margin>Hippodamus</margin>
They say that Hippodamus <note>Hippodamus of Miletus, an ancient Greek architect and the father of urban planning.</note> also divided his own republic into three parts: the craftsman, the farmer, and the defender in war. <margin>Aristotle</margin> Aristotle did not seem to disapprove of those who selected from the multitude those worthy to be placed in charge of councils, magistracies, or judgments. But the rest of the common people they left divided among farmers, craftsmen, merchants, mercenaries, cavalry, infantry, and the "naval crowd." <margin>Indians</margin> It appears from the historian Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a 1st-century BCE Greek historian who described the social castes of India.</note> that the republic among the Indians was not much different from this. For there [were] the priest, the plowman, the shepherd, the craftsman, the soldier, the overseers <note>original: "effori" — likely referring to the *episkopoi* or inspectors described in ancient accounts of India.</note>, and those who preside over public councils. <margin>Plato</margin> Plato said that one type of republic was peaceful and desirous of leisure and quiet, while the other was fiery and warlike, according to the spirits of those who were in charge of affairs. From these parts of the soul, he divided the entire multitude of citizens. One part consisted of those who manage all things with reason and counsel. Another of those who pursue injuries with arms. The third of those who provide and supply the nourishment by which the fathers <note>referring to the elders or governing body.</note> and soldiers are sustained. I have briefly touched upon these excerpts from many commentaries of the ancients. From these, I am reminded to establish all the parts of republics that I have collected, and to judge that individual types of buildings are owed to each part. But so that we may conduct the whole matter more distinctly according to our purpose, it may be helpful to have discussed it thus: If someone were to divide the number of mortals into parts, what else would first come to his mind than to realize that they should not be judged as the same if you consider all the inhabitants of some place together, as if you review them separated and distinguished into parts? Having looked closely at nature itself, will he not feel that in whatever thing one differs most from another, from that thing he must seize the signs by which he may distinguish some from others? <margin>By reason, knowledge of the arts, and prosperity of fortune, man differs from the beast.</margin> And yet there is nothing by which one man differs more from another than in that one thing by which he is furthest removed from the race of beasts: reason and the knowledge of the best arts; add, if you wish, the prosperity of fortune. In all these gifts, a few among mortals stand out and excel together. From here, therefore, the first division will be open to us: that we select a few from the whole multitude, of whom some are illustrious in wisdom, counsel, and genius; others proven by the use of things and skill; others [wealthy in] resources... <note>The sentence concludes on the following page.</note>

### Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.
<sig>S 3</sig>

...[and they] are renowned for their abundant wealth and flow of fortune. Who would deny that the primary parts of the republic should be committed to them? <margin>☛</margin> Therefore, the primary care and management of affairs shall be entrusted to excellent men who are powerful in counsel. These men shall establish divine matters through religion; they shall determine the measure of justice and equity by law; they shall show the way to living well and blessedly; they shall watch daily over the defense and increase of the authority and dignity of their citizens. 

And when they sense that something would be convenient, useful, or necessary—since they themselves, perhaps weary with age, might prefer to be occupied in contemplating things rather than executing them—they will delegate to those skilled in the use of things and ready for action, so that they may continue to deserve well of the fatherland. These others, once the business is undertaken, shall manage the matter according to their duty, with skill and solicitude at home, and with labor and endurance abroad: they shall declare the law; they shall lead the soldier; they shall exercise themselves and the hands and industry of their people. 

Finally, they will understand that it is in vain to strive for the completion of things unless resources <note>original: "facultates" — referring to the financial means and materials necessary for large-scale construction.</note> are also present. Next to those [the leaders and doers], therefore, are those for whom resources are supplied either from the field <note>landowners</note> or from trade <note>merchants</note>. All the remaining hands and numbers of men <note>the laboring class</note> shall obey and serve these primary groups as use demands.

If these divisions are sufficiently appropriate, we have indeed discovered that some types of buildings are owed to the whole assembly of citizens; others to the leading men; others to the multitude. Then even among the leading men, some buildings are for those who preside at home and in counsels; others for those engaged in business; others for those who amass resources. Since a certain part of all these buildings relates to necessity, as we have said, and another part to convenience, let it also be fitting for us who comment upon buildings to have given something for the sake of the mind's pleasure; while in place of a reward, I have decided that the origins of such partitions should be sought from the basic principles of the philosophers. Therefore, we must speak of these things: what is suitable for everyone together; what for the fewer primary citizens; and what for the multitude of lesser people. 

But from where shall we take the beginning for such great matters? Should it be as men have proceeded to provide these things for themselves daily? Thus we also shall enter into the matter starting from the private little huts of the needy, and from there we shall arrive at those most magnificent works we see: of theaters, baths, and temples.

<margin>Nations formerly without cities.</margin>
For it is indeed established that the nations of the world lived for a long time surrounded by no walls of cities. Indeed, historians write that when Dionysus <note>Dionysus was often depicted in Renaissance texts as a civilizer and mythical conqueror of India.</note> traveled through India, there were no cities surrounded by walls among those peoples. Thucydides <note>A 5th-century BCE Greek historian.</note> writes that Greece was also once unfortified by walls. And likewise throughout Gaul until the time of Caesar, the entire nation of the Burgundians was not gathered into cities, but met here and there in villages. Indeed, I find that the first city was...

### Chapter II.

<margin>Wilderness of the Germans</margin>
All public things are owed to the whole city and to those parts which belong to it. If we establish from the opinion of philosophers that the purpose and cause of having a city is this: that the inhabitants may lead a peaceful life there, and as much as possible, one free from inconveniences and thus liberated from trouble. Surely, one must think again and again: in what place, site, and circuit of lines <note>original: "linearum ambitu" — the city's perimeter or footprint</note> it should be placed. <margin>Ligurians</margin>

But as usually happens with a rich field, it breeds sluggish men. In contrast, the Ligurians, who inhabit a stony land where they must be exercised by constant labor and drag out their days with the most extreme scarcity of food, are thoroughly industrious and very robust. Since these things are so, there will perhaps be some who do not find fault with such harsh and difficult regions for founding cities. Others feel otherwise. For they will indeed hope that things go well for them by the benefit and gift of nature, so that nothing more can be added, whether for necessity or for pleasure and delights.

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

For that we might use good things well can be granted by laws and the institutions of our ancestors. But truly, those things which contribute to a more pleasant life are certainly better if they are found at home, rather than needing to be sought from elsewhere. And they will certainly desire a territory <margin>The territory of Memphis</margin> like the one at Memphis <note>original: "Memphiticus ager". Memphis was the ancient capital of Inpu-hedj, Egypt.</note>: which Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar</note> writes enjoys a climate so mild that the leaves of no trees, not even vines, fall throughout the entire year. Or like those places beneath Mount Taurus looking toward the north; for there Strabo <note>Greek geographer and historian</note> testifies <margin>Grape clusters two cubits long.</margin> that clusters of grapes are produced two cubits <note>about 3 feet</note> long: and from single vines come single jars of wine: and from a single fig tree seventy measures <margin>Land</margin> are collected. Or like the land India and the Hyperboreans <note>A mythical people of the far north in Greek legend</note> inhabit on an island by the ocean: whose fields Herodotus <margin>Herodotus and the Hyperboreans.</margin> declares yield fruit twice a year. Or like among the Lusitanians <note>People of the Roman province in the west of the Iberian Peninsula</note> <margin>Also among the Lusitanians.</margin>: where they gather harvest after harvest from the seeds that fall. Or rather like at Talge <margin>Talge.</margin> on the Caspian mountain: a field which provides crops even when uncultivated. These are rare things: and those which you might more easily wish for than find. Therefore, the most excellent ancients, who committed to writing things received from others and devised by themselves, established that a city <margin>How a city should be placed.</margin> ought to be so positioned that it is content with its own territory: as far as the reason and condition of human affairs allow, it should lack nothing that must be sought from elsewhere. And so fortified within the circuit of its borders that while it cannot be easily invaded by an enemy, it is also strong enough to send soldiers into a foreign province at will, even against the enemy's wishes. For they agree that a city so inhabited can protect its liberty and greatly extend itself and its empire. But why should I say this here? Egypt <margin>Praise of Egypt for its position and other factors.</margin> is given primary praise for being wonderfully fortified on every side and completely inaccessible—here by the sea, there by the vastness of the desert: on the right by the steepest mountains: on the left by the widest marshes. Furthermore, the fertility of the land is so great that the ancients called Egypt the public granary of the world. And they say the gods themselves used to flee there for the sake of their spirit and safety. Yet Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note> testifies that this region—so fortified and so fertile that it is boasted to feed all mortals and to be able to receive and save the gods themselves—was never entirely free from someone [ruling it]. Rightly, therefore, do they warn us who tell the fable that mortal affairs, even if safe in the lap of Jove <note>Jupiter</note> himself, would be so in vain. Therefore, it may be helpful to imitate that saying of Plato: when he was asked where that famous city he had imagined for himself was to be found, he said: we are not discussing that; rather, we are investigating what kind of city it is proper to establish as the best of all: you should consider that one to be preferred above the rest which wanders least from the likeness of this one. So we too, bringing forth examples as it were, shall prescribe that city which the most learned judge will be convenient in every part: in other respects following the time and the necessity of things. That saying of Socrates...

### Book IV. On the Universal Work. Folio 51.

...we will maintain: that a thing which is so well-constituted in itself that it cannot be changed except for the worse, we should consider to be the best. ¶Therefore, we establish that a city ought to be of such a kind that none of the inconveniences which we reviewed in the first book are present at all. And if any things are desired for the necessities of life, none should be lacking. <margin>Where a city should be placed and what it ought to have</margin> It will have a territory that is healthy, very wide, varied, pleasant, fertile, fortified, well-stocked, and adorned with every abundance of fruits and every overflowing of springs. <margin>Also other things</margin> Rivers and lakes will be present, and the opportunity of the sea will be open: from whence whatever is lacking may be most conveniently brought in, and whatever is surplus may be exported. Finally, all things will be supplied for the excellent establishment and increase of civil and military affairs: which will serve as a protection for its own people, an ornament for the city, a pleasure for friends, and a terror to enemies. And indeed, I would consider it well for that city which is able to cultivate some good part of its land even against the will of an enemy.

Furthermore, it is necessary to place the city in the middle of its territory: from where it can look out over its borders and discern opportunities, and be ready in a balanced way wherever necessity demands; from where the farm manager and the plowman may frequently go out to work and return from the field in a moment, laden with fruit and harvest.

But whether you place it in an open plain, on the shore, or in the mountains is of the greatest importance. For each of these has something to recommend it, and conversely, something you might approve of less. When Dionysius <note>Likely referring to Dionysius I of Syracuse, or a legendary account of a general in the East</note> was leading his army through India, he led them, exhausted by the heat, to the mountains; immediately, having caught a healthy breeze, they recovered. And the founders of cities seem to have occupied mountains because they understood they would perhaps be safer there. But they lack water. A plain will provide the conveniences of rivers and waters. But the same is covered by a thicker atmosphere, which burns in summer and is immoderately cold in winter; and the same is less strong against hostile attacks.

Shores are convenient for bringing in merchandise. But as they say, every maritime city, stirred up and troubled by the allurements of new things and the excessive force of merchants, fluctuates constantly; and it is exposed to many accidents and dangers of foreign fleets. Therefore, I decide thus: <margin>☞</margin> in whatever place you locate a city, one must strive that it may share in all these conveniences and be free from the inconveniences. And I would wish that a plain be given to mountains, and hills to plains, where I might establish a city. If it is not possible to achieve this by choice through the variety of locations, we shall use arguments of this kind to secure the necessary things: <margin>How a city should be placed near the sea.</margin> so that in maritime regions, a city should not be left too close to the shore if it is on a plain, nor too remote if it is situated on a mountain. 

Many cities elsewhere testify that shores change, especially in Italy, <margin>Baiae.</margin> where Baiae <note>original: "Baiæ". A famous Roman resort town near Naples; due to volcanic activity (bradyseism), much of the ancient city is now underwater.</note> was submerged by the sea. In Egypt, <margin>Pharos.</margin> Pharos <note>The island in Alexandria famous for its lighthouse; it became a peninsula after a causeway was built.</note>, which had previously been surrounded by the sea, now clings to the mainland like a <term>peninsula</term> <note>original: "Chersonessus", a Greek term for a peninsula.</note>. So also Tyre...

<margin>Tyre. Clazomenae.</margin>
...and Strabo <note>Strabo (c. 64 BC–24 AD) was a Greek geographer whose work *Geographica* described the known world.</note> writes that Tyre and Clazomenae were once like this. Indeed, they say that the temple of Ammon <note>The Oracle of Amun at the Siwa Oasis. Ancient writers noticed sea shells in the desert there and concluded the sea had once reached the area.</note> was once by a retreat of the sea, though it now remains far inland. However, they advise that you place a city either right on the shore or far from the sea. For one can see that the sea breeze is heavy with salt and harsh. Therefore, when it reaches the inland plains, you will find the air there damp with dissolved salt; it surely makes the sky thick and almost slimy, so that in many places of this kind you may sometimes see things like spiderwebs <note>Alberti refers here to "gossamer," the fine silk of small spiders that can drift in the air, which he interprets as a physical manifestation of thick, salty atmosphere.</note> flying in the air. They say that the air is affected no differently than water, which is easily corrupted by the mixing of salt until it even offends with a stench. The ancients, especially Plato, approve of a city that is ten miles distant from the sea. But if it is not possible to place it far from the sea, it should be situated where such breezes do not arrive unless they are broken, weary, and purified. It should be placed behind [higher ground], so that by the intervention of mountains, all noxious force from the sea is intercepted and frustrated. From the shore, the view of the sea is very pleasant; nor is it bathed in unhealthful air. Aristotle thinks those regions are the healthiest which, agitated by constant winds, breathe in every moment. But let them beware that the sea there is not grassy with a shallow and submerged shore, but deep, rigid with cliffs of living rock and shaggy banks. Setting the city itself upon a "proud ridge"—as they say—of a mountain confers dignity, beauty, and especially health and safety. For wherever mountains overhang the sea, the sea is never shallow. Then, if any thickness of vapors rises from the sea, it fails in its ascent. And if a sudden hostile hand brings trouble, they [the residents] see it from further off...

<margin>In what way on a hill.</margin>
...more foresightedly, and remove it more safely. The ancients approve of a city placed on hills that face the east. They also approve of one where the North Wind <note>original: "boreas"</note> reaches a warm region. Others perhaps will approve of one that slopes to the west, led by the feeling that crops are more fertile under that aspect of the sky. Yet below Mount Taurus, those parts which face the north are far healthier than others, especially for the same reason that historians declare them fertile.

<margin>In what way in the mountains.</margin>
Finally, if a town is to be placed in the mountains, first one must take care that—as usually happens in such places, especially where other higher hills rise around—a heavy and long-lasting collection of mists does not create a dark day and a murky, constantly harsh sky. Then, care must be taken against the immoderate rushing and nuisance of winds, lest something too monstrous vexes [the city], and especially the North Wind there. For that wind, says Hesiod <note>Hesiod was an 8th-century BC Greek poet; his work *Works and Days* describes the biting cold of the winter winds.</note>, makes everyone—but especially the elderly—numb and bent. The site of a city will be inconvenient in which...

->Folio LII.<-
->Book IV. On the works of all.<-

...where an overhanging rock might reflect the vapors gathered from the sun, or where infernal <note>original: "avernae." Alberti refers to Lake Avernus, which ancient writers associated with the toxic vapors of the underworld.</note> valleys pour out air too sharply. Others advise that the side of a city should be bounded by the precipices of the location. But nearly all precipices show themselves to be weak against movements <note>Alberti likely refers to landslides or seismic activity.</note> and storms, as seen in many towns elsewhere and especially in **Volaterrae** <note>Modern Volterra. The city is famous for its "Balze," dramatic cliffs caused by erosion that have indeed swallowed parts of the ancient city over centuries.</note> in Etruria; for they slip away over time and drag down whatever you have built upon them. <margin>Volaterrae.</margin>

And indeed one must take care that no contiguous mountain hangs above, which a hostile enemy could occupy to press the attack; nor should any safe plain lie below for the enemy that is large enough to allow them to fortify a camp for a siege or draw up a battle line for an assault. We read that **Daedalus** built the city of **Agrigentum** <note>Modern Agrigento in Sicily.</note> on a steep rock with difficult access, so that it could be guarded by no more than **three men** <margin>Agrigentum. Three men could guard it.</margin>—a fitting stronghold, provided the exit is not blocked and entry prevented by equally few armed men.

Military experts strongly approve of **Cingulum** <margin>Cingulum, a town.</margin> in Picenum, founded by **Labienus** <note>Titus Labienus, a lieutenant of Julius Caesar.</note>, for other reasons and because—unlike almost all other mountain towns where the fighting becomes equal once you have climbed up—that is not the case there. For they are repelled by the high and steep rock. Nor does the enemy have a very safe position from which they could plunder and devastate the fields at will in a single excursion; nor will they be able to besiege all the approaches at once, nor retreat safely to a nearby camp. Nor will they send out parties for fodder, wood, or water without danger.

The opposite is true for the townspeople: for with hills lying below and connected on this side and that, with frequent valleys between, they have ways to march out immediately to harass the enemy; and they can burst forth and overwhelm them unexpectedly at every sudden hope and opportunity. No less do they approve of the town of **Bisseium** <margin>Bisseium, a very safe town.</margin> among the **Marsi**, located at the very junction of rivers flowing together from this side and that; also with a narrow entrance from the valleys, difficult access, and rough, pathless mountains rising around it, so that the enemy can neither settle in the place nor watch all the valley passes. Meanwhile, the townspeople are excellently situated for receiving and bringing in supplies and reinforcements, as well as for launching attacks.

¶ So much for mountains. But if you place a city in a level spot <margin>Where a city should not be placed in a level spot.</margin>—and as is common, near a stream, so that it might even pass through the middle of the walls—ensure that the water does not flow from the south or toward the south. For in the former case, moisture, and in the latter, coldness increased by the vapors of the river, will arrive more troublesome and harmful.

If, however, it flows past outside the city enclosure, the region must be considered; and where the access for winds is made easier, walls should be set against them, keeping the river behind. In other matters, the observation of sailors will be relevant: they believe that winds, by their very nature, tend to follow the sun and the eastern breezes. Natural philosophers say that the morning air of the day is purer...

Finally, one must provide again and again that no mountain, rock, lake, marsh, river, spring, or any of these things be situated such that they could fortify and protect an enemy, or bring any disadvantage to the city and its citizens. It was a custom to mark the intended line of the walls with a white line, which they called "pure." <margin>Pharos planned by Alexander.</margin> It is said that when Alexander <note>Alexander the Great (356–323 BCE).</note> was marking the site for this land, specifically while he was laying out Pharos <note>Pharos: An island off Alexandria, later famous for its lighthouse.</note>, he substituted flour when the "pure" [lime] ran out. This event gave the seers an opportunity to predict the future, for they believed that through such omens noted on the birthdays of cities, certain outcomes of time could be predicted. Among the Etruscans, these things were taught in their ritual books: <margin>☞ Etruscan teaching regarding the birthdays of cities.</margin> exactly what ages would follow from the birthday of a city. This was done not by observing the heavens—a matter we discussed above in the second book—but by taking evidence and conjecture from present events. Censorinus <note>A 3rd-century Roman grammarian who wrote *De Die Natali* (On the Birthday).</note> recalls that they wrote in this manner: on the day cities are founded, from those born on that day, the one who lived the longest would, upon the day of his death, mark the end of the first *saeculum* <term>saeculum: a period of time representing a "generation" or the longest possible human life, used by the Etruscans to track the lifespan of their civilization</term>. Of those remaining in the city on that day, the death of the one who reached the greatest age would mark the end of the second age. Thus, in turn, the time of the remaining ages was determined; portents were sent by the gods by which we might be warned that an age had ended. These were their beliefs. They also add that from these signs, the Etruscans learned the sequence of their own ages very clearly. For they committed to memory that the first four of their ages were 100 years each. The fifth was 123. The sixth was 120, and the seventh was the same number of years. The eighth was then passing through the time of the Caesars. The ninth and tenth were yet to come.

They also believed that the nature of these ages could be known through these signs. Indeed, they conjectured that Rome would possess the empire of the world because, on the day it was founded, one of those born on that day obtained the kingship. <margin>Numa shared the same birthday as the city of Rome.</margin> I find that this was Numa <note>Numa Pompilius: The legendary second king of Rome, known for establishing its religious laws.</note>; for Plutarch records that the city was founded and Numa was born on the 14th of the Calends of May <note>original: "xiiij. calendas maias." Relying on the arms and strength of their citizens, they thought themselves sufficiently fortified by their laws. The Egyptians and Persians, however, thought on the contrary that their cities should be fortified with the protection of walls in the grandest manner. For others, and likewise Nineveh and Semiramis <note>Semiramis: A legendary queen of Babylon often credited with massive building projects.</note>, desired the thickness of the walls for their cities to be such that joined chariots could be driven along the top of the work’s breadth. <margin>Cities surrounded by the most magnificent walls.</margin> They raised the height so far that it exceeded one hundred cubits. Arrian <note>A Greek historian (c. 86–160 CE) who wrote the *Anabasis of Alexander*.</note> records that at Tyre the walls were 150 feet high. And some have been found who were not content with only a single wall. The Carthaginians encircled their city with a triple wall. Herodotus says that Deioces <note>The first king of the Medes.</note> encircled the city of Ecbatana with seven rings, even though it was situated on an elevation. As for us, since we understand that the most essential protection lies in the walls themselves for the preservation of safety and liberty when enemies surpass us in luck or in number, we do not approve of those who wish for a city to be entirely naked—

### Chapter IV. On walls, ramparts, towers, and gates.

<margin>How walls are to be placed.</margin>
**B**ut I return to the walls. Regarding their construction, the ancients advise thus: two walls should be built on the inside with an interval of twenty feet placed between them; then, the earth removed from the ditches should be placed in between and packed down with rams; and these walls should be raised in such a way that from the level ground of the city, one might ascend to the ramparts along a gentle slope, as if by a likeness of steps. Others say that the earth taken out from the ditch should be placed as a rampart around the circuit of the city; and one wall should be raised from the very bed of the ditch, of such thickness that it can strongly withstand the weight of the pressing earth. From this, likewise, another higher wall should be led out toward the inside of the city, separated from the first by a space that is not narrow, but large enough so that <term>cohorts</term> <note>A cohort was a standard tactical unit of a Roman legion, numbering roughly 480 men.</note> formed into a line of battle there may have unimpeded space for fighting. Likewise, throw across transverse walls from the outer to the inner wall; by their connection and support, the primary walls joined together by these may be held fast, and they may more strongly endure the pressing force of the earth placed between them. But for our part, besides these, we approve of those walls which are so established that if they are finally overthrown by the force of attacking machines, they have an area of substitute space where the heaps of ruins may settle, and they do not fill up the ditches with their own ruin. In other matters, Vitruvius is very pleasing. 

<margin>Vitruvius</margin>
"I think," he says <note>Alberti is quoting from Vitruvius's *De architectura*, Book 1, Chapter 5.</note>, "the work of a wall should be made thus: so that through its thickness, charred olive-wood planks are very frequently laid between; so that both faces of the wall, bound together among themselves just like dovetail ties, may have eternal firmness."

<margin>Walls of Plataea.</margin>
Thucydides <note>The Greek historian Thucydides (c. 460–400 BCE) describes the siege of Plataea in Book 2 of his *History of the Peloponnesian War*.</note> records that the Plataeans, when besieged by the Peloponnesians, opposed the enemy with a wall of almost this kind. For they indeed intermingled wood with bricks and strengthened it greatly. 

And Caesar <note>Julius Caesar describes this "Gallic wall" (*murus gallicus*) in his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*, Book 7, Chapter 23.</note> says that almost all walls among the Gauls are of this form: continuous straight beams are tied back on the inside at equal intervals in length, and they are packed with large stones, so that beam does not touch beam; by joining such orders together, they reach the proper height of a wall. 

<margin>Gallic walls from the description of Caesar.</margin>
This work is not unsightly in appearance and is strong for defense; for the stone protects from fire, and the timber from the <term>battering ram</term> <note>original: "ariete"; a heavy engine used to breach walls.</note>. Then, if it happens that the work is attacked by the missiles of machines, they say it will happen that the interconnected mass of the entire wall, having been shaken, is moved forward; and together...

### Book IV. On the Work of All Buildings. Folio LV.

...is made prone to collapse. But we consider that walls are most beautifully strengthened against the damage caused by projectiles in this way: <margin>Counterforts</margin> We shall raise **counterforts** <note>original: "anterides"; these are reinforcing piers or buttresses built against a wall to strengthen it.</note> with a triangular base, with one angle projected toward the enemy, at intervals of ten <term>cubits</term> <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger (about 18 inches).</note> from each other along the course of the wall. We shall lead arches from one of these to the next and provide them with **vaulted ceilings**. And the empty spaces that were left there, shaped like the hulls of ships, we shall fill up by tamping down clay mixed with straw using levers.

In this way, the force and impact of the siege engines <note>original: "tormentorum"; referring to catapults or ballistae</note> hitting the wall will be frustrated by the softness of the clay. It will also ensure that the wall can only be weakened in scattered spots by the persistence of the engines, and any breaches can be blocked immediately. Among the Sicilians, an abundance of pumice will provide this quality beautifully, which is what we seek here. Elsewhere, in place of pumice and clay, they use <term>tufa</term> <note>A light, porous rock formed from volcanic ash, often used in ancient construction.</note> to good effect. We shall also not refuse gypsum for this work. Finally, if any of these materials are used and are exposed to the moisture of the south wind or the vapors of the night, they should be covered with a stone crust or facing.

It will also be particularly helpful to place the outer bank of the ditch a little higher in its slope than the rest of the surrounding field. For in this way, the aim of the projectiles will not reach the city walls, but will fly over them. And there are those who think the safest wall against siege engines is one drawn in a line that imitates the teeth of a saw. 

However, the walls at the city of Rome are pleasing, in which there is a **walkway** <note>original: "decursorium"</note> at middle height. Throughout the wall, slits are left at suitable places, from which the unwary and hurrying enemy might be secretly wounded by archers. And towers should be driven into the wall every fifty cubits, acting like counterforts, with rounded fronts projecting and standing taller than the wall; so that whoever approaches closer exposes an unprotected side to the projectiles and may be finished off. In this way, the wall is defended by the towers, and one tower is defended by another.

<margin>Towers.</margin> 
Place the towers on the side facing the city open and bare of walls, lest they perhaps provide cover for an enemy who has managed to enter. **Cornices** <note>original: "coronae"; decorative and functional projecting moldings.</note> provide both ornament to the towers and walls and bring strength through their binding; they also prevent the secret climbing of ladders placed against them. There are some who wish for gaps to be left along the walls, especially under the towers themselves, to be crossed by wooden bridges; these can be immediately either pulled back or thrown down as the situation demands, for use or for safety.

<margin>Gates.</margin> 
On both sides of the gates, the ancients were accustomed to set up twin larger towers, built solid for a great part of their height; these, like arms, protect the bay and the "throat" of the entrance. Let no stone vaulting be built into the towers, but rather wooden floors, which can be both torn up and consumed by fire when necessary. They forbid the floors of the towers to be fixed with nails, so that they can be more quickly thrown down if the enemy prevails. Roofs and retreats will not be lacking, by which...

# ¶ The size, form, and logic of roads, both military and urban, as well as of other matters. Chapter V.

<margin>The width of the road according to the decree of the Twelve Tables.</margin>
**T**he design of gates should be determined according to the number of military roads. For some roads are military, while others are not. I shall not pursue here the definitions of legal experts—such as whether I should establish that a cattle path <note>original: "actus"</note> or a footpath <note>original: "iter"</note> are both comprised under the term "road" <note>original: "via"</note> for the sake of the movement of beasts and men. Certainly, military roads are those by which we set out into a province with an army and baggage. Therefore, a military road must be much more spacious than non-military ones. It was common practice for the ancients to set them at no less than eight <term>cubits</term> <note>A cubit is approximately 18 inches; eight cubits would be about 12 feet.</note>. According to the law of the **Twelve Tables** <note>The ancient foundation of Roman law, dating to the 5th century BC.</note>, they define a road así: that which is straight should have a width of twelve feet; where it turns—that is, where there is a bend—sixteen feet. Non-military roads are those by which we depart from a military one, either into a villa or a town, or equally from one villa to another, just as there are paths through the fields or side-streets through the city.

<margin>Military road</margin>
There is furthermore a certain type of road which shares the nature of a broad street <note>original: "platea"</note>; these are those used for certain specific purposes, especially public ones: for example, those leading to a temple, a racetrack, or a <term>basilica</term> <note>A large public building used for legal proceedings and public business.</note>. The layout of military roads should not be the same through the countryside as it is within the city. Outside the city, these rules must be entirely observed: that it be wide and very open for a complete view in all directions; that it be free and most unimpeded by obstructions of both water and ruins; that no hiding places or retreats at all be left for bandits to set ambushes; and that there be no access points here and there from which raids might be launched. Finally, let it be direct and the shortest; it will be the shortest of all, not by being the straightest, but by being the safest. I prefer it to be a little longer rather than poorly suited. There are those who think the Privernate territory <note>original: "agrum priuernatem"; referring to the area around the ancient Italian city of Privernum.</note> is safest because deep roads—like submerged ditches—crisscross it, which are ambiguous to enter, uncertain to travel, and not at all safe: with overhanging banks from which an enemy can easily be crushed. More skilled men think that road safest which is led across the "backs" or ridges of small hills. Closest to this is the road which, according to ancient custom, is directed through the middle of the fields upon a built-up embankment <note>original: "agger"</note>. Indeed, the ancients called it an "embankment road" for that reason; and a road protected and led in this way will offer many advantages: for since from a prospect...

## Book 4. On the Work of the Whole. Folio 56.

...so that by the pleasantness of the view from a raised embankment <note>original: "celsam exaggerationem"; a reference to the 'agger', the built-up foundation of a Roman road.</note>, travelers may be greatly relieved from the labor and annoyance of the journey. Furthermore, it is of great importance to have seen the enemy from afar, and to have the means by which you can either hold back a pressing assault with a modest force, or retreat with no loss to your own men if they are overwhelmed. This is relevant to what I noted regarding the **Portuensian Way** <note>The road connecting Rome to its harbor, Portus.</note>. For when a vast number of people and a great quantity of goods from Egypt, Africa, Libya, Spain, Germany, and the islands converged there, they constructed a double paved road. In the middle, a raised row of stones stood out like a boundary <note>original: "limes"</note>, so that people could go out by one side and return by the other, avoiding the collision of those in a hurry. A military road <term>via militaris</term> <note>A state-maintained highway designed for the rapid movement of armies and official messengers.</note> outside the city ought to be of this kind: unobstructed, direct, and very safe.

When the road reaches the city, if it is a famous and powerful city, it is fitting to have very wide, straight roads, which contribute to the dignity and majesty of the city. But if it is a colony or a fortified town, it will provide the safest access if the road does not lead directly to the gate, but is drawn to the right or left near the walls, and especially beneath the very defensive towers of the walls. Inside the city, however, it is fitting for the roads not to be straight, but to be winding like a flowing river, turning this way and that, and again back upon themselves with a gentle curve. For besides the fact that where the road appears longer, it will increase the perceived size of the city, it truly contributes greatly to beauty, convenience, and the needs of various times and situations. For how great a benefit it will be to those walking along, that at every step, new faces of buildings are gradually presented to them, so that the entrance and view from each house is directed from the middle of the road's width itself! While excessive openness is unsightly elsewhere and even unhealthy, here the vastness itself might be beneficial. **Cornelius** <note>Referring to the Roman historian Tacitus, who wrote about the aftermath of the Great Fire of Rome.</note> <margin>Nero made the city of Rome hotter by widening the roads.</margin> writes that the city of **Rome** was made hotter by the roads widened by **Nero**, and for that reason less healthy. Elsewhere, by contrast, conditions grow harsher in narrow streets; in summer, there will never be a lack of shade, and there will be no house that the sun's rays do not enter. And the breeze will never be absent. For wherever a strong wind strikes, it will find a straight and mostly unobstructed area to flow through. And yet, one will never experience the winds as harmful there, for they will immediately be broken by the obstruction of the walls. Add to this that if an enemy enters, he will be in danger, harassed no less from the front and sides than from the rear.

Regarding military roads, so much for now. Non-military roads will imitate these, unless perhaps this difference exists: that in the latter case, they will indeed be made straight to a line, so as to better align with the corners of the walls and parts of the buildings. But within...

...I find that it pleased the ancients that there should be some inextricable paths in city streets <term>vici</term> <note>While 'vici' can mean neighborhoods, here Alberti refers to the physical streets and alleys within them.</note> and some with no exit, so that an entering enemy or wrongdoer would be hesitant, uncertain of himself, and fearful; or, if he were bold enough to persist, he would rightly be in greater danger. It is also beneficial to have smaller streets that are not long and extended, but rather end at the first cross-street, so that they do not appear to be a public or easy path, but rather provide an entrance to the houses. For this provides better light to the homes and offers the city a hindrance against hostile incursions.

<margin>Plato’s opinion on city streets.</margin>
Curtius writes that Babylon was inhabited with scattered and non-continuous streets. Plato, on the contrary, liked not only the streets but even the walls of the houses to be joined together, and he wanted this arrangement to serve as a wall for the city.

### ¶ Chapter VI. On wooden and stone bridges: their piers, vaults, and arches; their angles and bank-abutments; their wedges or cutwaters; their paving and crowning.

<margin>Where a bridge should be located.</margin>
A **bridge** is certainly the most important part of a road. However, not every location is suitable for a bridge. For besides the fact that it should not be left in some remote or secluded corner for the convenience of only a few, but should rather be open for the use of everyone in central regions, it must certainly be located where it is easy to build, where it can be completed without excessive expense, and where one can hope it will last forever. Therefore, one must seek out shallows that are not too deep, not steep, not uncertain, and not shifting, but rather level and stable. One must avoid whirlpools, eddies, abysses, and similar hazards found in flowing waters. One must especially avoid the "elbows" or bends of the banks; for in those places, as one can see, the banks are prone to collapse. Furthermore, through those very bends, timber, trunks, and forest debris swept from the fields during floods are not carried down in a straight and easy flow, but are spun around; they collide with one another and, slowing down, they gather into a massive heap against the piers. From this, the openings of the arches become blocked and give way until the entire structure is overthrown and destroyed by the massive pressure of the water. 

<margin>Wooden bridges.</margin>
But some bridges are made of stone, others of wood. We shall speak of wooden ones first, as they are easier to construct, and afterwards we will deal with those of stone. Both types must be exceptionally firm. Therefore, a wooden bridge shall be strengthened with a large and sturdy supply of timber.

<margin>Caesar’s method in bridge construction.</margin>
To execute this task beautifully, the example of **Caesar** <note>Alberti is citing Julius Caesar’s famous description of his bridge over the Rhine in "The Gallic War" (Book 4).</note> is of great benefit. For he established the method of building a bridge in this manner: He joined together two beams, each a foot and a half thick <note>original: "tigna bina sexquipedalia"</note>, sharpened slightly at the bottom according to the depth of the river, at an interval of two feet from each other. When he had fixed these into the river using machines...
