...and he had driven them in, not straight down perpendicularly, but slanting and sloping, so that they leaned in the direction of the river's current. Opposite these, he placed two more joined in the same way, forty feet apart at the lower end, turned against the force and rush of the river. These two sets, once positioned as we described, he joined with two-foot beams <note>original: "bipedalibus trabibus"</note> laid across, spaced as far apart as the width of the joining timbers required. These transverse beams were secured at each end by two fasteners <term>fibulae</term> <note>These 'fibulae' were likely iron or wooden braces or clamps used to lock the timbers together under tension.</note>; because these were spread apart and braced in opposite directions, the strength of the work and the nature of the structure was such that the greater the force of the water, the more tightly the joints were held together. This framework was then covered with long poles and overlaid with wickerwork. Furthermore, smaller beams, which they call support-piles <term>subucas</term> <note>These are secondary piles driven in at an angle to provide additional bracing against the current.</note>, were driven in diagonally on the downstream side of the bridge to act as a buttress and, being joined to the whole work, they could withstand the force of the river. Other piles were also placed a short distance upstream from the bridge, so that if the barbarians sent tree trunks or ships downstream to destroy the work, these defenders would lessen the force of such things and prevent them from damaging the bridge. These are the words of Caesar. It is also not out of place to mention that in Verona they were accustomed to deck wooden bridges with iron rods, especially in the section where wagons and carts were drawn.

<margin>Stone bridge.</margin>
¶ Next follows the **stone bridge**, the parts of which are: the bank-abutments, the piers, the vault <note>original: "fornix," referring to the arched structure itself.</note>, and the paving. There is this difference between bank-abutments and piers: it is necessary that the former stand with a deep and powerful resistance. For they must not only support the weight of the vault laid upon them, just as the piers do, but they must also serve as the primary heads of the bridge to repel the force of the arches and hold them together so that they do not spread. Therefore, one must choose banks or rather rocky cliffs, which are the most firm, to which the heads of the bridge may be committed. The number of piers will be determined by the width of the river. Arches of an uneven number are both pleasing to the eye and contribute to stability. For the middle of the stream’s course is faster and more impetuous the further it is from the restriction of the banks, and the more free it is, the more forcefully it rolls down. Therefore, this central path should be left clear and unobstructed, so that it does not hinder the stability of the piers by struggling against them. Piers should be placed throughout the river where the waters glide past more restrained and, so to speak, more sluggishly. The evidence for discerning such a location will be shown by the alluvial deposits; otherwise, we shall grasp the matter in this way: imitating those who scattered nuts in the stream so that the besieged might gather and eat them <note>This refers to a famous incident during the Second Punic War at the siege of Casilinum, where the Romans floated nuts down the Volturnus river to feed the starving inhabitants.</note>, we should observe the continuous passage of the river for a long distance—say, fifteen hundred paces—especially at a time when...

# Leon Battista Alberti, On the Art of Building.

...if the river has swollen, we should throw in something that floats on the water. This will be a sign that the waters are rushing with greater force in the places where the objects you threw gather most. In placing the piers, therefore, we shall avoid this location; we shall instead choose the spot where the things thrown reach more <margin>King Menes</margin> sparsely and slowly. When King Menes <note>original: "Mina rex"; Alberti refers to the legendary first Pharaoh of Egypt, Menes.</note> had decided to build a bridge at Memphis, he diverted the Nile elsewhere through the mountains, and once the work was finished, he restored it to its channel. <margin>Queen Nitocris.</margin> Queen Nitocris of the Assyrians, having prepared everything necessary for the construction of a bridge, diverted the river into a very large lake she had excavated; in the meantime, while the lake was filling, she constructed the piers in the dry bed of the river. These were their methods. ¶ But we shall proceed in this way. The foundations of the piers shall be fixed during the autumn when the waters are low, by means of a surrounding enclosure <term>septum</term> <note>A 'septum' here refers to a cofferdam—a temporary watertight enclosure pumped dry to allow construction work below the waterline.</note>. The method of making this enclosure is as follows: stakes are driven in at frequent intervals in a double row, so that their heads emerge from the water like a palisade. On the inside, facing the piers, they are covered with wickerwork according to the circuit of the palisades, and the intervals between the rows are filled with algae and mud. These are thickened by treading them down so that the water can no longer flow through. Soon, whatever remains within the fold of the enclosure—whether it be water, or besides water, mud or sand, or anything else inconvenient to the work—is removed. The rest is completed as I described in the previous book. For one must dig down to solid ground, or rather, the soil should be very tightly thickened with charred stakes <note>original: "palis pręustis"; Charring the tips of wooden piles was a common Roman technique to prevent rot and harden the wood before driving it into wet ground.</note>. I have noticed that excellent architects were accustomed, in the continuous stretch of the bridge itself, to substitute a single continuous base <margin>How the bases of the piers are to be built.</margin> rather than building each one individually while the river was closed off by a single enclosure. However, they did this by adding new sections to those already positioned. For the total force of the water can by no means be entirely barred and contained. Therefore, while we are conducting the work, sluices <term>aestuaria</term> must be left for the current, through which the stubbornness of the surging waves may be exhausted. These sluices will either be left open in the ford itself, or, where it is advantageous, wooden molds and hanging channels will be prepared, through which the overflowing water of the current may glide away. But if one begrudges such great expense, place simple bases for each individual pier, shaped like a galley <term>liburna</term> <note>A 'liburna' was a fast, pointed Roman warship; Alberti is describing what modern engineers call a 'starlings' or 'cutwaters'—the pointed ends of bridge piers.</note>—long, with the prow and stern projected into an angle and finished off—and align them with the flow of the water itself, so that by dividing the force of the unruly waters, they may diminish it. One must remember that the waves are more hostile to the "sterns" of the piers than to the "prows." This is shown by the fact that the water struggles more fruitfully <note>original: "fecūdior illuctatur"; i.e., with more turbulence or violent churning.</note> at the sterns of the piers than at the prows. Furthermore, whirlpools are seen to be excavated there into the depths, while the prows themselves stand in a channel more filled with sand. Since these things are so, these parts must be the most fortified in the whole mass of the work...

# Book IV. On the Work of All Parts. Folio LVIII.

...and they must be extremely firm to withstand the constant harassment of the waters. It is therefore greatly beneficial to the matter if the deep foundation of the piling <note>original: "pedamenti"; refers to the underwater support structure or piles</note> itself is extended far in every direction, and especially toward the downstream end <note>original: "puppim," literally "the stern"</note>, so that even if some part of the pilings is removed by any accident, plenty remains to support the weight of the piers without failing. It also helps significantly to extend the base there from the very beginning on a gentle incline, so that the waters passing over it do not rush in with a sheer drop, but flow away easily with a soft descent. For water falling headlong disturbs the bottom, and having become more turbulent, it carries away what it has moved, and in moments hollows out the site.

We shall build the piers <margin>Materials for building piers.</margin> of stone of great length and exceptional width, which by its nature resists frosts, is not softened by water, nor otherwise easily dissolved, nor cracks under weight; and it shall be joined with all diligence according to the ruler, the plumb-line, and the level, with joints never interrupted, longways and crossways with mutually interlocking connections, rejecting all fragments of smaller stones.

Frequent copper pins <term>acus</term> and cramps <term>ansae</term> shall be driven in, with their sockets so pressed and arranged that the stones are not weakened by these "wounds" <note>the cut-outs made in the stone for the metal</note> but are strengthened by the grip. The work shall be raised high, with an angular upstream end <note>original: "prora," literally "the bow"</note> and downstream end, with the entire top projecting so far that the fronts of the piers are higher than even the most overflowing floods. The thickness of the piers shall be about one-fourth the height of the bridge. 

There have been some who finished these "bows" and "sterns" <note>Alberti uses nautical terms for the cutwaters of the piers.</note> not in an angle but in a semicircle, led, I believe, by the beauty of the design. And although I might say a circle has the strength of an angle, I nevertheless primarily approve of the angle here—provided it is not so sharp that it is marred by being chipped away by any slight damage. Indeed, even an angle that is blunted and shorn by a circle will be pleasing, if it is not left too obtuse and resists the hostile speed of the attacking wave. We shall establish that the proper angle for piers is one where the right angle is in a ratio of four-to-three <term>sesquitertius</term> <note>A 4:3 ratio</note>, or if that pleases less, three-to-two <term>sesquialter</term> <note>A 3:2 ratio</note>. So much for the piers.

¶ If the nature of the place does not provide the kind of riverbank foundations <term>subices</term> we desire, we shall strengthen them with pier-work. We shall extend the last piers and some arches <margin>Arches</margin> onto the dry land at the bank, so that if the persistence of the waves over time should wash away part of the bank, the road will by no means be cut off, as the bridge is extended into the field. The vaults and arches must be exceptionally strong and wonderfully reinforced, both for other reasons and because of the sharp and never-ceasing vibrations from carts. Add to this that sometimes perhaps vast weights of colossi <note>large statues or heavy loads</note> must be dragged across the bridge—

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

...of obelisks and the like; and just as happened to Scaurus when dragging a boundary stone <note>referring to Marcus Aemilius Scaurus, a Roman official known for massive public works; the anecdote likely refers to the legal liability for damaging public property during transport</note>: public contractors fear the damages of incomplete work. For this reason, the bridge must be adapted in its design and every part of its construction for permanence, to withstand the frequent and troublesome jolts of carts. Reason dictates that bridges should be built with whole, very large stones; we can easily understand this through the example of an anvil. For if the anvil is large and heavy, it easily withstands the blows of hammers; but if it is lighter, it recoils and is moved by the strikes.

We have said that a vault is composed of arches and fillings <term>complementa</term>, and that the strongest arch is the one that is straight <note>original: "rectus"; in this context, Alberti refers to the semi-circular arch, which he considers the ideal or "true" arch shape</note>. But if, because of the arrangement of the piers, a straight arch would be so high in its curvature that it becomes an obstacle, we shall use a diminished one <note>a segmental or flattened arch, which allows for a lower road profile</note>, with the supports on the banks reinforced with much greater thickness.

<margin>The Arch.</margin> Finally, any arch that projects from the faces of that vault should be fitted together from very hard and very large stone, no less than those you thought should be committed to the piers. Nor will the stones in the arch be more pleasing than if their thickness corresponds to one-tenth of their span <term>corda</term> <note>original: "corda," literally "string"; referring to the horizontal distance between the springings of the arch</note>. The span should be no longer than six times the thickness of the pier, nor shorter than four times. 

There shall be bronze inserts and strong clamps <term>ansae</term> to interlock these wedge-shaped stones <term>cunei</term> <note>the voussoirs that form the arch</note> with one another. Then, for the arch, the topmost wedge—which is called the spine <note>original: "spina"; the keystone</note>—will be hewn to match the lines of the others, but it will have a bit more thickness at one end, so that it can only be inserted <unclear>firmly</unclear> and driven in with a light ram. In this way, the remaining wedges placed throughout the arch will be squeezed more tightly together and remain more firmly in their place. 

All the fillings <term>complementa</term> should be built in with stone, so that no bond <term>nexura</term> could be made more whole, nor any joint tighter. But if a supply of the strongest stone is not available everywhere for completing the fillings, I will not necessarily refuse weaker stones, provided that along the entire back of the vault, the keystone and the rows driven in next to it on both sides are chosen from nothing but very hard stone.

It follows that the work must be paved; the ground must be packed down and sprinkled with gravel to the thickness of a cubit <note>approximately 18 inches or 45 centimeters</note>, no less for bridges than for permanent roads. Afterward, the stone paving is to be laid, supported by pure river or sea sand. On bridges, however, the bedding and the floor must be leveled with rubble work <term>caementio</term> to a thickness equal to that of the arches. After this, the layers you have spread must be reinforced with lime. In other respects, the method for both [roads and bridges] will be the same. For the sides shall be protected with the strongest structure and paved over with stone...

LIX
# Book IV. On Public Works.

...[the paving stones should be] neither too small nor prone to shifting—lest they be torn away by a light impact—nor yet so large that they become slippery, causing a pack animal to fall before it can find a firm grip for its hoof. <margin>☚</margin> Furthermore, it matters greatly what stone is used for the paving. Do you not consider what happens from the long and constant wear of animals and wheels, when we are reminded that even ants can hollow out a path in flint <note>original: "silice"</note> by the wear of their feet? 

But I have observed that the ancients, both elsewhere and specifically on the road to Tivoli <note>The Via Tiburtina</note>, paved the center of the road with flint stones <term>siliceo lapide</term>. The sides, however, they covered with small gravel. This was done so that the wheels would be less likely to break the paving stones, and to provide a softer surface for the hooves of the animals. In other places, and especially on bridges, they built raised stone walkways along the parapets <term>spondas</term> for the entire length of the bridge, so that pedestrians might walk more cleanly. The middle was left for wagons and horsemen. 

Furthermore, the ancients highly approved of flint stone for this work. Among flints, the porous variety <note>original: "fistulosus," meaning pitted or full of small holes</note> is more suitable—not because it is harder, but because it is less slippery underfoot. We shall use whatever stone is available according to the local supply, provided that the hardest are selected to pave at least that part of the road where the animals most frequently tread. And animals certainly seek the more level path, while utterly refusing the steeper ones. Whether flint or any other stone is used, it should be broad and a cubit thick, or at least no less than a foot. The top surface should be level and the sides joined tightly with no gaps left between them, arranged with a slope <term>fastigiatio</term> so that the collected rain may flow off. 

<margin>The slope.</margin> This crowning or sloping is of three types. For either the incline runs toward the middle of the paved way—which is appropriate for wider roads—or it slopes toward the sides, which is less of an obstacle for narrower roads, or it is directed straight along the length. These arrangements are managed according to whether the outlets of the sewers and channels lead into the sea, a lake, or a running stream. A proper slope will be half a finger's width for every two cubits. I noticed that on the inclines where the ancients ascended mountains, they sloped the road one foot for every thirty feet of length. And in some places, such as at the heads of bridges, slopes are seen with a height of one palm for every cubit; but these are short distances, which a loaded animal can cross with a single surge of effort.

### ¶ On sewers, their use, and types; and on rivers and canals serving for navigation. ->Chapter VII.<-

**S**ewers are considered to belong to the work of roads, as they are to be led beneath the middle of the paths, serving to keep the roads paved, level, and cleaner. For this reason, we should not neglect them here. Indeed, what else should I call a sewer but a bridge, or rather a very wide arch?

### Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

Certainly, for that reason, in establishing these sewers, everything we have reviewed so far regarding the construction of the bridge itself will be strictly observed. Indeed, the ancients held the use of sewers in such high regard that in no other completed work do they seem to have applied so much expense and diligence. They count the sewers among the foremost of the wonderful works of the city of Rome. I do not dwell here on how many benefits sewers bring: to the elegance of the city, to the cleanliness of public and private buildings, and to keeping the air healthy and pure, rather than tainted. 

<margin>Smyrna.</margin> They say that the city of Smyrna <note>Modern-day İzmir, Turkey</note>—where Dolabella liberated Trebonius from a siege <note>original: "Trebonium Dolobella obidione liberavit." This refers to a conflict in 43 BC; Alberti uses the historical anecdote to emphasize that even a grand city is diminished by poor sanitation.</note>—was otherwise very beautiful in the layout of its streets and the decoration of its works. However, because there were no sewers to carry away the discharged waste, the foulness used to offend visitors. 

<margin>Siena.</margin> In Siena, in Tuscany <note>original: "Senis in Ethruria"</note>, elegance is lacking because sewers are lacking. Because of this, it happens that not only during the first and last watches of the night—the hours when the vessels of collected filth are poured out of the windows—does the whole city stink, but the ground there is also sometimes foul and heavily dampened. 

Of sewers, some are what I call diffusing <term>diffusoriae</term>, which pour the incoming waters into a lake or into the sea. Others are open-ground <term>subdivae</term> <note>These function as soakaways or drainage pits</note>, through which the received waste is not vomited elsewhere but is instead neutralized, as if swallowed and digested by the belly of the earth. 

<margin>Diffusing sewers.</margin> Diffusing sewers ought to be built upon a bed that is sloping, downward-facing, and solid, so that the flow runs as freely as possible and the structures built there are not softened by constant moisture. It is beneficial to have these raised above the level of the river, so that they are not filled up by turbid floods and are not obstructed by silt. For the open-ground sewers, we shall be content with the bare soil itself. 

<margin>The earth devours and consumes all things.</margin> For indeed, the poets declare the earth to be Cerberus <note>The three-headed hound of the underworld</note>, and the philosophers call it the "wolf of the gods," because it devours and consumes all things. Therefore, the filth and whatever is received into the ground will vanish as the earth processes it, and fewer vapors will exhale to create a foul stench. But I would wish for sewers into which urine is to be poured to be led far away from walls. For by the heat of the sun, they are infected and spoiled to a greater degree. 

Furthermore, I believe that rivers and water canals—especially those serving to carry vessels—should be considered alongside the logic of roads, since the ship is certainly counted among the types of vehicles. Then, too, what is the sea itself by its nature but a widely open road? But there is nothing more at this point that would be useful to discuss at length. If it should happen that these resources are insufficient for human needs, then any faults that might cause offense must be corrected by hand and skill, and whatever conveniences are lacking must be provided; the method for these things will be treated in its proper place.

¶ Of harbors: where and how they are better constructed; and of squares.

## On the division and assignment of public places in the city. Chapter VIII

**N**ow if there is any part of the city that aligns with those matters we must discuss here, it is surely the harbor. And yet, a harbor will seem like the <term>starting gate <note>original: "carcer". In a Roman racecourse, the carcer was the starting stall from which horses or chariots began the race.</note></term> in a racecourse: the point from which you begin the course of a journey, or where you end and rest once the excursion is complete. Others will perhaps interpret a harbor as a "stable" for shipping. Let it be what you wish: a starting gate, a stable, or a receptacle. Certainly, if it is the defining purpose of a harbor to receive a ship into itself from the force of storms, it must surely offer protection; thus, let there be strong and high sides.

Furthermore, it is necessary to have an appropriately fitted space, so that ships both large and laden can be received there conveniently and rest safely. If the natural favor of the location provides these things of its own accord, there is nothing further you could desire—<margin>Athens has three natural harbors.</margin> unless perhaps, as at Athens (which <term>Thucydides <note>A Greek historian (c. 460 – c. 400 BC) famous for his 'History of the Peloponnesian War'.</note></term> writes had three natural harbors), you are of a doubtful mind as to which of the three harbors you should choose as the principal one.

But it is established from what we said in the first book that there are some regions where all winds cannot reach, and others where some winds are troublesome and constantly active. Therefore, we shall prefer that harbor which breathes milder and cleaner breezes at its entrance, and where you do not have to wait a long time for the winds when you wish to enter or depart. Everyone considers <term>Boreas <note>The North Wind.</note></term> to be the calmest among the winds; they also assert that the sea, once stirred by the <term>Aquilo <note>The North-East Wind.</note></term>, grows quiet immediately when the wind stops, but after the <term>Auster <note>The South Wind.</note></term> stops, the waves continue to toss for a long time. 

However, because of the variety of locations, those features that are more convenient and ready for the use of ships should be chosen. Depth is also desired, both in the mouth, the bay, and at the banks, so that it does not reject a heavy merchant ship when it is loaded with goods. It is also fitting for the bottom to be clean and not at all grassy. Although the dense and tangled roots of grasses sometimes bring much convenience for securing anchors, I would nevertheless prefer a harbor of such a kind that it contains nothing within itself that might contaminate the purity of the air or damage the ships—such as seaweed and grasses born in the waters. For these stir up the most harmful shipworms, moths, and little grubs for <term>hulls <note>original: "carinis". Literally the keels or bottoms of the ships.</note></term>, and they provoke pestilential stenches from the rotting shores. 

The mixing in of fresh waters will also make a harbor wasting and pestilential, especially those waters which the mountains yield from rainstorms. Nevertheless, it should have nearby and neighboring springs and streams from which you may take pure water capable of being preserved on a ship. And I would wish it to have ready, direct, and certain exits, immune from <term>sandbanks <note>original: "syrtibus". Referring to the Syrtes, dangerous shallow gulfs off the coast of North Africa, often used generally for any hidden shoals.</note></term>, free from impediments, and safe from the ambushes of enemies and pirates. Moreover, at the headland nearby...

He warns against the biological and environmental dangers of stagnant water and seaweed which can rot wooden hulls and cause disease.</summary>

I would wish for some **high and conspicuous mountain peaks** to loom over the site—notable and distinguished landmarks—which sailors, recognizing from afar, might seek as a designated sign for their navigation. Inside the harbor, a quay and a <term>bridge <note>original: "pons". Here, Alberti likely refers to a pier or a docking platform rather than a bridge over a river.</note></term> should be constructed, so that the convenience of unloading the ship is more immediate. The ancients built such works, though some did so in one way and others in another; this is not the place to discourse upon those variations. For the design of such things pertains to the dredging of harbors and the construction of the <term>mole <note>original: "molem". A large stone structure used as a breakwater or causeway.</note></term>, which will be discussed in its proper place. 

The harbor should also feature a promenade, a portico, and a temple, so that those disembarking from the ship may be properly received. There will be no lack of columns, handles, and iron rings to which the ships may be tied. Numerous vaults shall be established in which the imported goods may be stored. High and fortified towers shall be raised at the mouth of the harbor, so that from these watchtowers they may foresee the arrival of sails; by night, they shall show a certain path to sailors with fires, and with battlements they shall protect the ships of allies. Transverse chains shall also be added, by which the enemy may be excluded. 

From the harbor and through the middle of the city, a <term>military road <note>original: "via militaris". In Roman planning, these were the major state-maintained highways designed for the rapid movement of troops and commerce.</note></term> shall be directed. Many neighborhoods will converge there, so that from every side an attack may be launched against any insolent enemy fleet. Further inland, the harbor will have smaller, secluded bays where damaged vessels may be repaired. But let this matter concerning the harbor not be omitted: many famous cities were, and are, safer because the entrance through the mouth is uncertain, with shifts in the channels that are barely visible and known only to those who navigate them every hour.

<margin>Squares.</margin> These are the things that seemed worth saying about the public affairs of the community—unless one adds that they should order the <term>squares <note>original: "plateas". Open public spaces or plazas used for markets and assembly.</note></term> to be divided. In these squares, goods brought in during peacetime may be traded, the youth may exercise, and in wartime, supplies of wood, fodder, and similar remedies for enduring a siege may be kept. 

Truly, the temple, the shrines, the <term>basilica <note>original: "basilica". In the classical sense, a large public hall for legal and business matters, rather than strictly a religious building.</note></term>, the theater, and such things are more common than private; but they belong to the priests or the magistrates. These things, therefore, will be discussed in their own place.

# Book V. On the Works of Individuals. Page LXI. #

-> **Book V** <-

**W**e discussed in the previous book how the variety of buildings—both within the city and in the countryside—must be adapted to the requirements of the citizens and inhabitants. We established that certain buildings are owed to the entire community of citizens, others to those of higher rank, and others to those of lower status. Having completed our treatment of those things that serve the general public, this fifth book will be dedicated to the needs and conveniences of individuals. In explaining this subject, which is varied, extensive, and difficult, I will strive with all my talent and industry. I want you to understand that I have intended to omit nothing that anyone might reasonably desire for the matter at hand, and to include nothing that serves more to decorate my speech than to fulfill my purpose. 

We must indeed begin with those of higher rank. The most worthy of all are those to whom the supreme governance and moderation of affairs are entrusted. These may be many people, or just one. Truly, the one who presides alone over the others must be the most worthy of all. Let us consider, therefore, those things which are made for the sake of that one individual. 

It is of the greatest importance to consider what kind of person we are establishing this ruler to be. Shall he be like one who rules holily and piously over a willing people—one who is moved no more by his own profit than by the safety and benefit of his citizens? Or, on the contrary, shall he be the kind of man who wishes to have a state of war with his subjects, so that he rules even over those who are unwilling? For while most other buildings and the city itself should differ, the city of those whom they call <term>tyrants <note>original: "tyrannos". In the Renaissance context, this refers to an absolute ruler who governs without legal right or against the will of the people.</note></term> should not be the same as the city of those who enter upon and protect their power as if it were a granted magistracy. 

For a city belonging to kings will be fortified just enough to be able to keep out a foreign enemy. But since a tyrant's own subjects are no less his enemies than foreigners are, he must fortify his city on both sides: against foreigners and against his own people. It must be fortified in such a way that he can use foreign help against his own people, and even use some of his people against the rest. 

In the previous book, we made the city fortified against enemies; let us now consider what is useful against one's own people. <term>Euripides <note>An ancient Greek playwright (c. 480–406 BCE) often cited by Renaissance humanists for his political insights.</note></term> believes that the multitude is by its very nature a powerful adversary, and if it combines fraud and craft into one, it becomes entirely invincible. 

<margin>Carras, a most populous city of Egypt.</margin> 

They say that <term>Carras <note>original: "Carras". Alberti is referring to Cairo, Egypt. In the Middle Ages and Renaissance, Cairo was famous for its immense population and its system of canals.</note></term> in Egypt is so populous a city that if no more than a thousand heads of the deceased are carried out in a day, the city is considered healthy and doing very well. Wise kings divided this city with frequent water-filled ditches (canals) so that you would say it is no longer one city, but many small cities joined together. I believe they did this so that the convenience of water would be spread everywhere. But by this means, they primarily achieved a situation where they do not fear the heavy uprisings of the many; for those who would move to revolt...

...are most easily suppressed: just as if someone made two or more manageable and portable statues out of one great colossus. The Romans sent no senator as proconsul <note>A governor of a province in the Roman Republic and Empire.</note> to Egypt, but instead distributed men of the equestrian rank <note>The *equites*, a social class below senators, often serving as administrators or military officers.</note> to various locations. Arrian <note>A Greek historian and philosopher (c. 86–160 AD) who wrote on military and historical matters.</note> stated they instituted this practice so that a province so well-suited for revolution <note>original: "res nouas", literally "new things," a common Roman idiom for political upheaval or revolution.</note> would not be brought under the command of a single man. 

And it has indeed been noted that no city is granted immunity from civil dissensions if its site is divided by nature—for instance, if a river flows through it, or if several hills stand out, or if one part lies on a hill and another on a plain. In such cases, the city will be most conveniently divided by an intervening wall. I believe this wall should be drawn not as a transverse diameter across the area, but rather like a circle enclosing another circle. For the wealthier citizens, who delight in more spacious areas, will easily allow themselves to be excluded by the first wall. They will not be unwilling to leave the meat market <term>macellum: a specialized Roman market for provisions, particularly meat and fish</term> and the central workshops of the city to the suburban purveyors of delicacies. That idle crowd of Terence’s Gnatho <note>Gnatho is a "parasite" or sycophant character from the Roman playwright Terence's play *The Eunuch*. Alberti uses him here to represent the lower-class service workers and social hangers-on.</note>—the tailors, butchers, cooks, and the like—will bring more security and less suspicion than if the leading citizens were not excluded from their company. 

It is not irrelevant what we read in Festus <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian whose work preserved many historical details.</note>: that Servius Tullius <note>The legendary sixth king of Rome, known for his social and administrative reforms.</note> ordered the patricians <term>patricians: the hereditary aristocratic class of ancient Rome</term> to live in a specific street, so that if they attempted any plot, he could overwhelm them from a higher position. This 

<margin>The inner city wall.</margin>
**inner wall** must be drawn in such a way that there is no region of the city that it does not reach. It is necessary to raise this wall—along with the other walls of the city, but especially this one—to be the strongest in thickness and in every craft of workmanship. It should be sublime in height, so that it stands above the private roofs of all. It is fitting to fortify it with battlements and ramparts, and perhaps even a ditch on both sides, so that the guards, protected on each side, may defend it. 

Furthermore, the towers should not be open on the inside, but enclosed by a wall; and they must be positioned so as to be exposed both to internal and external enemies, especially where roads or the high roofs of temples are directed. I would have no ascent into the towers except through the wall itself. And no access should lie open to the wall except where the prince permits. From the citadel through the city toward the streets, no arches or towers should be left—they should be prohibited—nor any wall projections, from which soldiers running through the streets could be driven back by missiles. 

Finally, the entire construction of these things must be so prepared that he who rules alone possesses all the high places; and no one may hinder his men’s ability to run throughout the entire city. In these ways, therefore, the city of tyrants differs from the city of kings. Perhaps they also differ in this: that for free peoples, flat lands are more convenient. A tyrant is safer on a mountain. As for the other buildings they inhabit, those of both the king and the tyrant, in most matters they [differ] not only from each other but also from private buildings of the commoners...

### ¶ On the portico, vestibule, atrium, hall, stairs, passages, openings, entrances with one or more recesses, and the hidden escapes of princes and private citizens; the distinction between houses; and also the separate or joined living quarters of the prince and his wife. Chapter II.

<margin>Portico and Vestibule</margin>
We believe that the portico and the vestibule <term>vestibulum: the entrance court or space between the street and the door of a house</term> were established not so much for the sake of servants—as Diodorus <note>Likely referring to Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BC.</note> thinks—but for the sake of all the citizens. Inside the house, the walkway, the courtyard, the atrium <term>atrium: the central open hall of a Roman house</term>, and the hall—which I think is called a *sala* from *dancing* <note>original: "a saltando". Alberti suggests the word 'sala' (hall) derives from the Italian 'saltare' or Latin 'saltare', to dance.</note> because the joy of weddings and banquets is celebrated within it—belong not to the public, but rather to the inhabitants. It is well known that some dining rooms belong to the children and others to the servants; furthermore, the sleeping quarters of the matrons, the maidens, and the guests are almost entirely for individuals. We spoke concerning the universal division of these parts, insofar as it pertains to them generally, in the first book: for it is necessary that they be appropriately arranged in terms of their outlines, number, size, and site according to the use of each. Now we shall pursue these matters in detail.

The portico and the vestibule will ennoble the entrance. An entrance brings honor both through the path by which it opens and by the dignity of the construction, by which the interior dining rooms and chambers are bounded. These shall be arranged in suitable locations so that the light let in may be conveniently preserved: so that they harmonize well with the air, sun, and winds, and are accommodated to their desired uses. They shall be distinguished so that no social interactions—whether of guests or of those who are constantly present—diminish their dignity, convenience, or pleasure, or increase the insolence of the visitors. And just as the forum <note>The central public square of a Roman city.</note> and the broad streets function in a city, so the atrium, the hall, and things of that kind will function in a house: they should not be in a rejected, hidden, or narrow place, but should be prominent so that the other members of the house may flow into them most easily. In these spaces, the arrangements of stairs and passages shall end; in these, the greetings and congratulations of guests shall conclude. Again, the house shall have entrances that are not multiple, but a single one, so that no one can enter or carry anything out without the doorkeeper's knowledge.

<margin>Openings</margin>
Regarding openings—both of doors and of windows—we will take care that they do not lie open to thieves, nor likewise to neighbors for the purpose of disturbing, watching, or learning what is happening within.

### Leon Battista Alberti. On Architecture.

...that are said or done within. The Egyptians build private houses in such a way that no window openings are visible from the outside.

<margin>Back door.</margin>
Someone might perhaps wish for a back door <term>postica: a rear entrance or postern gate</term> to be present, through which harvests, carriages, or beasts of burden might be brought in, so that the primary vestibules are not defiled by filth. They might also add a more secret little back door, through which the master alone, without the household's knowledge, could admit hidden couriers and messengers, and depart at his own discretion, as the times and the nature of affairs might require. I do not disapprove of these; indeed, I would very much wish for the existence of the most secret hiding places, the most hidden recesses, and concealed escape routes—hardly known even to the father of the family himself—by which, in adverse circumstances, he might save his silver, his clothing, and himself, should a "foul storm" <note>A metaphor for political or social upheaval or personal danger.</note> so require. 

<margin>Treasures in David's tomb.</margin>
They had made chambers <term>loculi: small compartments or niches</term> at the tomb of David, in which they stored treasures from the king's inheritance with marvelous skill, so that they could in no way be discovered. 

<margin>Hyrcanus the High Priest.</margin>
Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note> says that after 1,300 years, the High Priest Hyrcanus drew three thousand talents of gold from one of these to free the city from the siege of Antiochus. They also relate that later, Herod also seized a great quantity of gold from another. In these matters, then, the houses of princes agree with those of private citizens. The greatest difference between the houses of princes and private citizens is that each primarily reflects its own nature. In the former [princely houses], which are dedicated to the use of many people, it is appropriate that they excel in number and scale; in the latter [private houses], which are for a few or for individuals, they should be more refined <note>original: "cultiora"</note> rather than very large. 

There is also this difference: in the former, even the retreats of individuals must reflect the nature of princes, which are indeed for many people, since a multitude is never lacking in the homes of kings. In other private houses, however, it is helpful to place the parts intended for many people in such a way that the royal house does not have more thoroughly distinct members—for the wife, the husband, and the servants—so that each part serves not only utility but also dignity <note>original: "majestatem," meaning majesty or social standing.</note>, provides for everything everywhere, and no confusion overflows from the multitude of the household staff. 

This is certainly difficult, and something you can hardly achieve under a single roof. Therefore, each should be given their own region and area, and their own complete roof space and structure. But they shall be joined by the roof and by walkways <term>itiones: paths or passages</term> so that the hands of the servants and household members, while hurrying to perform their duties, do not appear as if summoned from some neighboring house, but are present, at hand, and ready. And the noise of the little children, the maidservants, and the "chattering flock" <note>original: "graculaeque cohortis" - literally a "flock of jackdaws," referring to the noisy nature of a large household staff.</note> shall be secluded from the dealings of the men, and all the uncleanness <term>illautities: lack of elegance, or the mess associated with service work</term> of the servants shall be separated.

Book 5. On the works of individuals.

The meeting rooms and dining halls of princes shall be established in the most dignified place. Height of the site will bring dignity, as will having the sea, the hills, and a wide region in view before one's eyes. The entire house of the wife shall be completely separated from the house of the prince himself: except that the innermost chamber and the sleeping quarters of the nuptial bed shall be open to both as common areas. The houses of both shall be closed and guarded by the same single entrance and doorkeeper. The other ways in which these differ from other buildings are more characteristic of private citizens than of princes; therefore, we shall speak of those in their proper place. Again, the houses of princes agree among themselves in this regard: for besides those things required for their private uses, it is certainly necessary to have an entrance directly from the public highway, and especially from a river or the sea; then, instead of a simple vestibule, there should be spacious reception areas where the arrivals of ambassadors and nobles—whether arriving by carriage or by beast of burden—may be received.

### ¶ Porticos of the atrium; or of the basilica, of the summer or winter council-chamber; the conveniences of places and observation points; and how the structure of royal palaces must necessarily differ from the fortresses of tyrants. Chapter 3.

---

**I** would wish for a portico and roofs to be present not only for the sake of men, but also for beasts of burden, so they might be protected from the sun and rain. 
<margin>Portico</margin>
At the vestibule, a portico, a walking-place, a place for exercise <term>gestatio: a space designed for light exercise, often by being carried in a litter or walking slowly</term>, and the like are very pleasant: where the youth, waiting for the elders returning from their conversation at the prince's vestibule, may exercise themselves in jumping, ball-games, the discus, and wrestling. 
<margin>Atrium. Basilica.</margin>
Next to the inner rooms, there should be an atrium <note>The central hall of a Roman house.</note> or a basilica <note>In this context, a large hall for public business or legal matters.</note>: where clients may wait for their patrons while discussing matters, and where the prince, about to pronounce the law, may take his seat at a tribunal. 
<margin>Council-chamber.</margin>
Then comes the council-chamber <note>original: "concenaculum", which literally means a dining room or upper room, but here Alberti uses it to mean a place for formal assembly and deliberation.</note>: where the elders may assemble to greet the prince and, when asked, give their opinion. It is perhaps fitting that one such room be for summer and another for winter; and altogether, care must be taken for the weary age and comforts of the "fathers" <note>Referring to the elder advisors or senators.</note> who have assembled, lest anything there should negatively affect their health. They should be able to stay there for as long as reason and the necessity of the times require for debating and deciding matters, without any or even the slightest hindrance. I find in Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC – 65 AD), the Roman Stoic philosopher.</note> that first of all Gracchus <note>Gaius Gracchus (154–121 BC), a Roman politician known for his social reforms.</note>, and soon after Livius Drusus, established the practice of not hearing everyone in one place, but having the crowd separated: they received some in secret, others with a few people, and others with everyone together, so that in this way they might distinguish between "first-rank" and "second-rank" friends. If such a thing is either permitted or pleasing in a man's fortune, various and multiple doors shall be made, through which they may receive people in different parts and dismiss those they have received, and exclude those they do not wish to see without causing offense <term>contumacia: here meaning a social slight or perceived insolence</term>.

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

...they agree in similar matters. But these are the things in which they differ. For it is fitting that the <margin>Royal house.</margin> houses of kings be situated in the center of the city, easy to access, beautiful in their decoration, and elegant in their luxury rather than being arrogant. For a tyrant, one must locate not so much a house as a fortress, so that it is neither entirely within the city nor entirely outside of it. Add to this that theaters, temples, and the houses of the nobility are most beautifully joined to the house of a king. <margin>Seat of the tyrant.</margin> The seat of a tyrant, on the other hand, must be contained within its own space, separated from all other buildings by a moderate distance. The most honorable building, and one which would suit and benefit both types of ruler, will be one where the royal palace is not so exposed and open that it cannot repel the insolent, nor the fortress so isolated that it seems more like a prison than the lodging of an elegant prince. One thing here I would not wish to overlook. For most convenient to tyrants are hidden and secret <margin>Listening pipes.</margin> listening pipes <note>original: "fistulæ auscultatoriæ"; these were acoustic conduits built into the thickness of walls to allow a ruler to eavesdrop</note> concealed within the thickness of the walls, by which they may stealthily catch what guests or household members are saying among themselves. But since it is characteristic of the royal house to be different from the fortress in almost all things, and especially in the most important ones, it will be the architect's duty to join the royal house to a fortress, so that the king may use it in sudden emergencies. The ancients established fortresses in cities so that they might have a refuge in adverse times, where they might protect the modesty of virgins and matrons along with the sanctity of sacred rites. Indeed, Festus <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian</note> mentions that among the ancients the fortress was consecrated to religion and was usually called "augurial," and that a certain secret sacrifice was customarily performed there by virgins, hidden and far removed from the knowledge of the common people. For that reason, you will find no fortress of the ancients that is empty of temples. But tyrants have usurped the fortress for themselves; they have turned the piety and religion of the place toward crime and monstrosity, and they have turned that holy refuge from calamity into a breeding ground for miseries. Let us continue the matter. <margin>Fortress of the Amonians.</margin> At the Ammonians <note>likely referring to the temple-fortress of Ammon at the Siwa Oasis described by ancient historians</note>, the fortress was surrounded by a triple wall near the temple. The first fortification stood for the tyrants. The next was for the wives and children. The last was the seat of the <term>guards</term> <note>original: "satellitū"; specifically the armed retainers or bodyguards of a ruler</note>. And it would be a fitting work, were it not intended more for one who suffers violence than one who inflicts it. And just as I do not approve of a soldier's bravery if he achieves nothing more than stubbornly enduring an insulting enemy, so I think it should be expected of a fortress that it be able not only to withstand an attacker, but also to restrain those who assault it. Both, however, must be managed so that you seem to have sought the site itself with great effort. To achieve these things, the location and the plan of the walls will be paramount. I see that those skilled in military matters debate whether a fortress should be made most firm by placing it on a hill or on a plain.

# Book V. On Individual Works.
...situated on a plain. And concerning the piles, ditches, bridges, and towers of the same.

->Chapter IIlI<-

**I**ndeed, I do not argue that there are any hills of such a nature that they cannot be besieged and destroyed by force, nor are there plains that cannot be attacked by arms with impunity if they are correctly fortified. Truly, the whole matter must be weighed by the opportunities of the locations, so that all the principles we mentioned regarding the city are applied to the placement of the fortress. By all means, it is necessary that the fortress have unobstructed routes for sorties: from which it can freely seek and admit its own and external reinforcements by land, river, lake, or sea—whether against enemies, against citizens, or against its own garrison, should any sedition or treachery require it. The design of a fortress will be very convenient if it joins itself to all the city walls in the manner of the letter "O," as if catching huge "C" shapes with bent horns, rather than completely enclosing them. It may be shaped thus, or in a way from which many rays extend as if to a circumference; for in this way, as I was just saying is necessary, the fortress will neither be entirely inside the city, nor entirely outside of it.

<margin>The fortress as the back door of the city.</margin>
Because if anyone wishes to describe a fortress most briefly, perhaps he will not err if he says it is a "back door" <note>original: "postica"; Alberti uses this term to describe the fortress as the city's ultimate fallback point or rear defensive exit</note> for the city, most extraordinarily fortified in every part. But let it be indeed, as they wish, the highest peak of the works and the knot of the city: it ought to be threatening, rough, and rigid. It should be stubborn and unconquered; a small fortress will be safer than a large one. For in a small one, we shall need the loyalty of a few, whereas in a large one, we shall require the service of many. And as that character in Euripides <note>Alberti refers to the Greek playwright Euripides, likely referencing a sentiment from his plays regarding the danger of the masses</note> says: "never was a multitude not stuffed with evil characters." Thus, in a small group, loyalty will be less uncertain than treachery will be among many. The platform <term>podium: the sloped base or "batter" of a wall</term> of the fortress shall be placed 

<margin>The platform of the fortress.</margin>
solidly, built with vast stones and with an external line slanting at an angle. By this, any ladders brought against it are weakened by the curvature, and an enemy who clings to the wall cannot avoid stones dropped from above. Furthermore, missiles sent by engines do not strike with the full force of a ram, but spring off at an angle. The courtyard <margin>The courtyard.</margin> inside shall be paved everywhere with very wide and thick stones laid in double or even triple layers, so that besiegers cannot creep in stealthily through tunnels <note>original: "cuniculis"; these were mines or subterranean passages dug by attackers to collapse walls or enter a fort</note>.

<margin>The wall.</margin>
The wall, very high, very solid, and very thick, should be raised all the way to the uppermost cornices. It should be of a type that most beautifully repels the force of machines and missiles, and which can be least easily equaled by ladders or even an earthwork <note>original: "aggere"; a mound of earth built up by besiegers to reach the height of a wall</note>, as far as lies in our power. The rest shall be completed as we said regarding city walls. The primary method for protecting the city and fortress walls will be this: that you take care entirely that the enemy cannot approach closer with impunity. This will be achieved both by the ditch, which we said should be deep and wide, and also through 

<margin>Stealthy slits.</margin>
"stealthy slits," if I may call them that, arranged through the very bottom of the platform. Whence, while the enemy protects himself from above with a shield, he may be pierced through in whatever part he is not covered...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of military architecture from Book V, specifically focusing on the defensive advantages of verticality and the specific construction of the central tower or keep (arx) and its internal provisions.</meta>

<header>Leon Battista Alberti: On the Art of Building.</header>

...it would carry. This kind of defense is superior to all others. For there, the defenders seize the opportunity to finish off the enemy more safely; they act along a shorter line; they rarely strike at the enemy in vain, for it is difficult for the attackers to shield their whole body. If a missile misses one oncoming enemy, it will strike the next, or perhaps another and another behind him. Missiles thrown from above, however, are not aimed without danger to the thrower. They barely strike a single man, who might foresee the shot and dodge with a slight movement, or deflect the missile with a small shield. 

If the fortress is by the sea, the surrounding waters should be obstructed with stakes and stones, so that siege engines <term>machinamēta</term> cannot be brought closer. If it is on a plain, it should be surrounded by a water-filled moat; but to prevent this from creating foul air <note>Alberti frequently warns against "miasma" or stagnant air as a cause of disease</note>, it should be dug deep enough to reach bubbling, "living" water. If it is on a mountain, it will be protected by precipices. We shall use all these methods wherever possible. In those places where projectiles from siege engines <term>tormentorum</term> might strike, the walls should project in sharp angles, like the prows of ships, rather than being built in a curve. 

I am well aware that some experienced in warfare argue that very high walls are not useful against the force of missiles. They claim that the rubble from such walls fills the ditches and provides an easy path for the charging enemy. This will not occur if the precautions I mentioned above are followed. I return to the matter at hand.

<margin>A primary tower is to be raised for the fortress.</margin>
¶ For the fortress, one primary tower <note>the keep or donjon, which served as the final stronghold</note> shall be raised. It should be solid in many of its parts, robust in its entire construction, fortified on all sides, and higher than the others. Access to it should be difficult, and entry permitted only by a movable bridge. 

There are two types of movable bridges. One is the kind that swings upward to block the exit. The other is extended and retracted, used especially where fierce winds blow; this latter type is more practical. Any towers within range that could strike this main tower with missiles should be left open on the side facing it, or built with only a very thin wall <note>original: "muro... gracili"; this ensures that if an enemy captures the outer towers, they have no cover from which to attack the main keep</note>.

## Watch-stations in the fortress, platforms, beams, roofs, water, soldiers, arms, grain, salted meat, vinegar, wood, cisterns, storage, entrances, tunnels, sewers, secret places, and other requirements of a ruler. Chapter V.

**E** xcubiarum <note>watch-stations</note> — The positions for the guards and the platforms for the defenders must be distributed so that some manage the lowest parts of the fortress, others the highest, and others different sections, each with distinct duties and posts. Ultimately, every entrance, exit, and division must be so prepared and fortified that neither the treachery of friends nor the force or fraud of enemies can cause harm. 

To prevent the roofs of the fortress from being crushed by the weight of projectiles, they should be finished at a sharp angle or reinforced with sturdy construction and very thick beams. A protective layer should then be added, containing pipes <note>tubuli</note> to drain away rainwater; this layer should be laid down without any lime or mud mortar. Finally, use fragments of pottery, or rather—

...they should be covered with pumice scattered over them, two cubits <term>cubit</term> <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of measurement, roughly the length of a forearm, or about 18–22 inches.</note> in thickness. Thus they will fear neither the weight of falling objects nor the damage of fires.

In short, the citadel <term>arx</term> <note>The 'arx' is the fortified stronghold or 'keep' of a city, usually its highest and most defensible point.</note> must be completed as if you were building a small city; it must therefore be constructed with the same defensive work and skill as the city itself, and everything else useful should be fitted into it. There must be no lack of water; there must be places to station soldiers and store arms, grain, salted meat, vinegar, and especially wood, so that it is available and preserved. And within the citadel itself, this primary tower we mentioned <margin>they should be mentioned.</margin> will stand like a smaller citadel; it must lack nothing of those things required for fortresses. It will have a cistern and storage for things to feed and protect itself abundantly. It will have entrances from which it can burst out even against its own people <note>original: "in suos etiam invitos," implying a ruler's need to suppress a domestic uprising</note>, if they turn hostile, and from which it can bring in requested reinforcements. 

Here, I will not omit that citadels have sometimes been defended by water tunnels <term>cuniculis</term>; while cities have sometimes been captured through sewers. Both of these are useful for sending out messengers. But care must be taken that such things cause far less harm than benefit. They should therefore be made most suitable: they shall be led in twists and turns, and terminate in a deep pit, so that neither an armed man can penetrate nor an unarmed man escape into the citadel unless called and admitted. The sewers should end very well, or rather in deserted and unknown sandpits, or in the secret recesses and burial grounds of temples. 

Then, if human misfortunes are not to be neglected, it will surely help to have known entrances into the inner citadel; so that if the ruler is ever shut out, he can break back in at the right time with armed men. Perhaps it will contribute to this end to have some very hidden part of the walls blocked not with mortar but with clay <note>So that it can be easily broken through in an emergency.</note>. We have now said what ought to be done for the sake of the one person who rules over others, whether he be a king or a tyrant.

¶ What kind of dwellings are suitable for those who administer the republic <term>res publica</term>, and where. Whether the senate house, the basilica, the governor's palace, the camp, the temples, the shrines, and the chapels should be located apart.

**I**t follows that we should settle those matters required by those who do not rule alone, but where several govern the state together. To these, either the whole republic is entrusted as if to a single magistrate, or it is distributed in parts. The republic consists of sacred things by which we worship the gods—over these the high priests <term>pontifices</term> preside—and secular things by which human society and safety are maintained. Over these, at home, are the senator and the judge; abroad, the commander of the camps, the prefect of the fleet, and the like. To any of these, two types of dwelling are owed: one which pertains to his office, and another into which he may withdraw himself and his family. Indeed, each shall have a family home <term>larem familiarem</term> <note>The 'Lares' were Roman guardian deities of the household; Alberti uses the term to mean the private family residence.</note> according to his status, just as he might wish to be similar in his way of life either to a king or a tyrant...

<meta>This page continues Alberti's discussion on the residential needs of different social classes. Having previously discussed the fortified dwellings of rulers (the citadel), he now moves to the houses of the elite and the placement of temples.</meta>

...or finally to a private citizen. There are, however, some things that are especially owed to this class of men. Virgil [the poet] stated it excellently:
> The house of his father Anchises stood apart, 
> and had retreated, hidden by trees. <note>original: "Secreta inquit erat patris Anchisae domus: arboribusque obtecta recesserat." From Virgil's *Aeneid*, 2.299-300.</note>

He understood indeed that the houses of the elite—for their own sake and for the sake of their families—should be far removed from the ignobility of the common crowd and the noise of craftsmen. This is appropriate for several reasons: for pleasure, for the convenience of large spaces, for the beauty of gardens, and also to prevent trouble within such a large, multifaceted, and diverse household. In such homes, the playful youth—since almost none of them live for themselves but are usually driven mad by someone else's food and drink—might provoke the complaints of husbands; furthermore, it ensures that the excessive ambition of those coming to pay their respects does not disturb the patrons more than is necessary. I see that the wisest princes have withdrawn not only from the crowded masses but even from the city, so that no common person, unless driven by a great matter, might annoy them with troublesome persistence. Otherwise, what value would their wealth have if they were not allowed to be at leisure and relax from time to time?

Whatever the nature of their houses, they must have sufficiently spacious reception rooms for those paying their respects, and a way and exit for proceeding to the forum that is not at all narrow; this is so that the household servants, clients <term>clientuli</term>, and attendants who follow them, and those who gather to increase the number of "toga-wearers" <note>original: "togatuli," referring to lower-ranking citizens or clients who sought favor by attending a patron in public.</note>, might not be hindered by crowding in their eagerness to accompany the master.

As for the activities these leaders perform according to their office, it is obvious: the senate has the senate house <term>curia</term>, the judge has the basilica or praetorium, the general has the camps and the fleet, and so on. What of the high priest <term>pontifex</term>? To him, not only the temple is suitable, but also those things which are like military camps, because both the high priest and those appointed under him to administer sacred rites wage a kind of "citadel" and laborious campaign <note>Alberti uses "militia" here to describe the disciplined, defensive life of the clergy against vice.</note>—such as we reviewed in the book titled *The High Priest*: a struggle of virtue against vice. 

<margin>The Temple.</margin>
There is one Greatest Temple where the supreme prelate performs fixed ceremonies and sacred rites with solemn ritual. There are others over which lesser priests preside, including the small chapels <term>facella</term> throughout the city districts and the shrines <term>delubra</term> in the countryside. 

A Greatest Temple is perhaps more convenient in the middle of the city, but it is more honorable if set apart from the dense crowd and bustle of citizens. It is more dignified on a hill, though it will be placed more stably on a plain because of earthquakes. Finally, the temple must be placed in a location where it will be treated with the highest veneration and majesty. From there, all filth, impurities, and indecencies of every kind must be driven far away from sight, so that fathers, matrons, and virgins coming to pray are neither offended nor distracted from their purpose of performing holy duties. 

<margin>The architect Nigrigeneus</margin>
In the works of the architect Nigrigeneus <note>Nigrigeneus is likely an obscure ancient author on land surveying or boundaries often cited in technical Latin treatises.</note>, who wrote about boundaries, I find the following: that ancient architects thought the dwellings of the gods were correctly situated when their fronts faced the west...

### Book V. On the works of individuals. Folio LXVI.

...inclined; but it pleased later generations to change all that religious practice. They thought that temples and their boundaries should be placed toward that part of the sky where the earth is first illuminated: so that the temple would immediately behold the sun rising out of the dawn. However, I see that the ancients approved of this for shrines and small chapels: that their fronts should be extended toward those approaching from the sea, or from a river, or from a public road. Finally, the building itself should be such, and so prepared in every part, that it entices those at a distance to come see it, delights those present, and holds them fast through admiration of the work and its rarity. A vaulted <term>testudunatum</term> <note>Literally "tortoise-shelled," referring to a stone or brick arched ceiling.</note> building will be safer from fire; a timber-framed one more unharmed by earthquakes; but while the former is more robust against the passage of time, the latter is more graceful in its charm. So much for temples for now. For many things that seemed necessary to say belong more to the decoration than the use of temples, which we shall deal with elsewhere. Smaller temples and chapels will imitate the proportions of the greatest temple, according to the dignity and use of the place.

The cloisters of the priests for piety, and by virtue of their office, "camps" for philosophy, virtue, and mercy. The types of cloisters: namely for men and for women; either in the city or outside; theaters, circuses, and plazas for the sake of preaching.

->### Chapter VII.<-

**PO**ntiffs' "camps" are indeed the cloisters in which many have gathered for the sake of either piety or virtue: such as those who have dedicated themselves to sacred rites, and those who have vowed virginity to the powers above. There are also priestly camps in which the talents of students are engaged in attaining knowledge of human and divine matters. For if it is the priest’s duty to lead the assembly of men toward a life perfect in every part, as much as lies within his power, this will be done through nothing more beautifully than through philosophy. For since there are two things in human nature that can provide this for us: namely, virtue and truth. <margin>Virtue and truth.</margin> It will indeed happen that truth settles and excludes the disturbances of the soul, while virtue explains the works and reasons of nature and communicates them to us; through these things, the talent is purged of ignorance and the mind is purified from the contagion of the body. Through this, surely, we enter a most blessed life, almost as if we were rendered very similar to the gods. Add to this that it is the mark of good men—as priests wish both to be and to be considered—to meditate upon, study, and pursue those things which they understand are owed to the human race by man: by relieving and helping the sick, the weak, and the destitute through duty, kindness, and mercy. For it is the priest's duty to exercise himself and his followers in these things. Concerning these matters, we must speak, whether they pertain to the higher priests or rather to the lower ones.

<margin>
Types of cloisters

...it seems. But we shall begin with the cloisters. There are different types of cloisters: some are so secluded that the inhabitants never go out into public, except perhaps in the temple or during the procession of <term>lustrations</term> <note>original: "lustrationum" — religious purification rituals or solemn processions.</note>. Others are not so strictly enclosed that they are barred for all time. Furthermore, of these, some house men and others women. I do not find fault with the cloisters for virgins <note>nuns</note> if they are placed within the city; nor do I entirely praise them if they are situated outside the city. In the latter, indeed, solitude will offer fewer harassers; but those who do force their way in will have more leisure and freedom for their crime where no witnesses are present than here in the city, in the midst of many spectators and those who would discourage such wickedness. In both cases, care must be taken that they do not wish to act against their chastity—but primarily that they **cannot**. For this reason, all entrances must be so closed off that they offer no opportunity for observation, so that no harasser can hover about without the suspicion of immediate disgrace. Legionary camps do not need to be as fortified with ramparts and ditches as these enclosures must be protected by walls—high, solid, and leaving no openings anywhere through which, I will not say the conquerors of chastity, but not even the sparks and lures of eyes or words can be sent to undermine their souls. Windows will receive light from the interior through an open <term>area</term> <note>original: "area subdivale" — a courtyard open to the sky.</note>. Around the courtyard, a portico, a walking path, cells, a <term>cenaculum</term> <note>a dining hall</note>, a <term>conclave</term> <note>a private chamber</note>, and other things that are necessary will be arranged in suitable places according to the layout of private houses. I would not want small garden spaces and meadows to be missing, which serve more to refresh the spirit than to nourish pleasures; since this is the case, they will be removed not without reason from the midst of the crowded inhabitants.

If the enclosures for both <note>men and women</note> are moved out of the city, it will indeed be beneficial. For the constant devotion to their vows of holiness and the peaceful religious spirit to which they have dedicated themselves entirely will be less disturbed by the frequency of visitors. But whether these houses be for men or women, I would want them to occupy the most healthful locations possible, lest those enclosed in the cloister—while they have leisure for the mind but grow numb in body, affected by much thinness and vigils—drag out a life more burdened by illness than is right. Finally, for those whom the city has excluded, I would want the place to be primarily fortified by nature, so that the sudden violence of bandits or a raiding enemy with a light hand cannot pillage it at will; and for that reason, it shall be beautifully fortified with a rampart, a wall, and a tower, as the religious nature of the place allows. As for the residences of those enclosed who combine the study of the liberal arts with religion—so that they may more conveniently look after the affairs of men in accordance with their undertaken duty—it is necessary that they be not entirely in the midst of the tumult and noise of craftsmen, yet also not removed far from the crowd of citizens; this is because, among other reasons, they are [the families...]

### ¶ Chapter VIII. On gymnasiums and buildings for debate; on public auditoriums and schools; on places for the weak and hospitals; and on lodgings for the sick, both male and female.

<margin>Gymnasiums</margin>
**A**mong the ancients, especially the Greeks, it was the custom to place buildings in the middle of the city which they called <term>palaestrae</term> <note>original: "palestras" — ancient Greek wrestling schools that evolved into general centers for education and social interaction.</note>, where citizens would occupy themselves in debate. In those places, there were windowed spaces and views through openings; there were rows of seats and porticoes surrounding an area green with grass and clothed in flowers. Works of this kind are very well suited to this class of religious men; and indeed, I would wish that those who delight in good studies should stay diligently with the professors of the arts, with the highest pleasure and no distaste or satiety for the matters at hand. Therefore, I will provide there both a portico and an open area, and the like, so that you would desire nothing more for the use of lodging. They will receive gentle sun in winter, and in summer, shade and the most pleasant breeze possible. ¶ But we shall follow up on these architectural delights more distinctly in their proper place.

<margin>Schools</margin>
If it is pleasing to establish public auditoriums and schools where you may meet wise teachers, place them in a location that is equally convenient for all residents. Let the noise of craftsmen cease; let smells and stenches be absent; let it not admit the playfulness of the idle; let it savor of a solitude worthy of serious men occupied with the greatest and rarest matters; and let it possess more authority in itself than charm. Furthermore, that the **pontiff** <note>original: "pontifex" — here referring to a high religious official or civic leader responsible for public welfare.</note> may exercise piety toward the weak and the destitute,

<margin>Hospitals</margin>
there will be a place both varied and to be established with the highest diligence. For it is necessary to receive and cherish the destitute in one place and the sick in another; moreover, among the sick, there are those for whom care must be taken lest, while providing for a few useless ones, you bring danger to many useful ones. There have been princes in Italy who forbade in their cities that class of men—torn in garment and limb, whom they call **vagabonds** <term>errones</term> <note>original: "errones" — wanderers or beggars.</note>—from begging at doors with prayers. For as soon as they arrived, they were warned not to allow themselves to be seen idle in the city for more than three days; [arguing] that no one is so broken that he cannot provide his labor to the company of men in some matter...

...be lacking; indeed, even the blind are useful at least for helping the rope-makers. <note>Alberti suggests that even those with disabilities should be given productive roles in society, such as assisting in trades that rely on touch or stationary labor.</note> Those, however, whom some more serious disease had completely overcome: the magistrates of the gathered guests used to distribute them in groups among the minor priests.
