In Tuscany <note>original: "Etrichiam" — likely a variation of Etruria</note>, by that ancient cult of sanctity and most true religion for which it has always been famous, wonderful hospitals are seen, built at incredible expense; where any of the citizens or foreigners feel that nothing pertaining to health will be lacking for them. 

But since some of the sick are diseased—those who infect the healthy with the poisons of leprosy, plague, and such contagions—while others are, so to speak, curable, I would wish these to have distinct lodgings. The ancients used to build temples to Aesculapius, Apollo, and the Goddess of Health <note>original: "Aesculapio, Apollini, salutique dijs" — Aesculapius was the god of medicine; Apollo was his father and also a healer; Salus was the personification of health and well-being.</note>—by whose arts and power they thought the human race recovered and preserved good health—only in the most healthy locations <margin>☞</margin>, where pure air and the clearest waters were supplied; so that the sick brought there might recover more quickly, not only by the help of the gods, but also by the benefit of the place. 

And certainly, we shall desire the healthiest places above all, where you keep the sick, whether publicly or privately. A dry and perhaps rocky place for this purpose, constantly swept by winds, and not scorched by the sun but illuminated by a gentle season, would be suitable, since dampness provides fuel for rots. But it is clear that nature in every matter delights in temperament <term>temperament</term> <note>original: "temperamento" — in Renaissance medicine, this refers to the balance of the four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>; indeed, health itself is nothing other than the temperament of the complexions <term>complexions</term> <note>original: "complexi" — the specific makeup of bodily humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) in an individual.</note> of which we are composed; and moderate things always delight. 

In other cases, the contagious shall be excluded not only from the city, but also far from the public road <margin>☞</margin>; the remainder will be kept in the city. Let the roofs of all these be divided and distributed so that those who are being cured are received in one place, and in another those whom you have taken in to be cared for <note>This refers to palliative care or hospice care.</note> rather than saved, as long as their fates bear them thus—such as the decrepit and the mentally incapacitated <note>original: "capti mente" — literally "captured in mind."</note>. Add that females in one place, males in another, whether they are sick or caring for them, must be kept separately. Add also that, just as with servants, so too with these: it is fitting that some parts of the lodging be more private and others more common, according as the very logic and manner of curing and living together shall demonstrate; of which it is not our purpose to pursue more at length. Let it suffice that all such things are to be defined in all their parts by the uses of private individuals. Enough on these things for now. Now let us pursue what remains in the order we had established. <margin>-</margin>

# Book V. On the works of individuals.
## On the courthouse and its requirements. Chapter IX.

**W**e have said that there are indeed two parts of the Republic <note>original: "R.P." (Res Publica)</note>: one sacred and the other profane. The sacred part has been completed, and the profane has already been touched upon in part where we discussed holding the senate and legal judgments within the prince's palace. What remains to be added to those points we shall list here very briefly; soon we shall come to military camps and the navy; finally, private matters will be explained. The ancients were accustomed to gather the Senate in temples. Later, the custom grew for them to meet outside the city. Finally, because it was better for the majesty of the state and the conduct of business, they desired to have buildings specifically dedicated to this duty. This was so that the "Fathers" <note>A traditional term for Senators.</note>, weary with age, would not be deterred by the frailty of long life nor prevented by the inconvenience of the location<margin>Senatorial House</margin> from meeting frequently and staying together longer. For this reason, they placed the Senatorial House in the middle of the city. They thought a courthouse and a temple should be joined closely to it, not only so that those held by political ambitions or occupied with legal cases in the forum could more conveniently fulfill both duties without interrupting their studies or offices, but also so that the Fathers themselves—who, being mostly older, are usually very devoted to religion—could move conveniently from the temple to business after greeting the gods. Add to this that if the Senate should ever be asked to grant an audience to ambassadors or princes of foreign nations, it is in the interest of the Republic to have a place where you can receive the waiting guest with a dignity that honors both the visitor and the city. 

Furthermore, in public lodgings of this kind, nothing should be neglected that helps in comfortably receiving, honorably hosting, and conveniently dismissing the multitude of citizens. Special care must be taken that paths, lighting, spaces, and similar features intended for use lack no convenience whatsoever. As for the Praetorium <margin>Praetorium</margin> <note>In this context, the Praetorium refers to the seat of justice or a courthouse.</note>, where many people come to argue their cases, the openings <note>doors and windows</note> must be more numerous, larger, and more accessible than for either a temple or a senate house. Furthermore, the entrance to the senate must be protected, though in a way that remains honorable. This is necessary for many reasons, but especially so that a reckless mob of rioters, stirred up from the "insane" common people by some seditious leader, cannot break in at will to the destruction of the Fathers. Indeed, for this very reason, porticoes, walkways, and such features should be added, where the servants of the clientele and the family, waiting for their masters, might serve as a defense in unforeseen emergencies. I must not omit this: in all places where the voice of those reciting, singing, or debating must be heard, vaulted ceilings <term>vaulted ceilings</term> <note>original: "testudinata" — literally "tortoise-shelled," referring to arched or masonry vaults.</note> are not at all suitable because they blunt the voice; timbered ceilings <term>timbered ceilings</term> <note>original: "contignata" — ceilings made of wooden beams and planks.</note> are suitable because they are resonant.

## On setting up land camps and their three types: temporary, stationary, and sustaining; and this indeed is based mostly on the opinions of others. Chapter X.

<margin>Three types of camps.</margin>
**I**n setting up camps, we must certainly repeat and weigh all those principles which we discussed in the previous books regarding the methods of establishing cities. For camps are, as it were, the nurseries of cities; indeed, you will find no small number of established cities in the very places where skilled military leaders once laid out their grounds. In the matter of camps, however, these are the main points: we must understand what the camps themselves are intended for. Camps would surely not be established if men did not fear sudden clashes of arms and the greater force of enemies. Since such work would be considered entirely unnecessary otherwise, the nature of the enemy must therefore be taken into account. One enemy may be an equal match in arms and strength; another may be more impetuous and powerful. From this, we shall establish three types of camps. 

The first is the temporary land camp, changeable in a moment, which we use while managing and preparing an affair against an armed foe, partly to keep the soldier in safety, and partly for the sake of arranging and seizing a needed opportunity so that you may brilliantly complete what has been started. The second type of camp is the stationary one, intended for when you plan to press and occupy an enemy who lacks confidence in their own forces while they keep themselves within some fortified place. The third type of camp is perhaps that by which you sustain an attacking and pressing enemy until, affected by the exhaustion of provoking you or the boredom of the siege, they depart and go away. 

In all of these, exceptional care must be taken and provision made first and foremost that they are so situated in every part that they lack nothing of all those things suited for safety, for self-defense, and for enduring and breaking the enemy. Conversely, you must ensure that nothing—so far as it depends on you—is supplied to the enemy by which they might either provoke you or move about without inconvenience and danger. Therefore, the advantages of the location must be sought out first: a place where supplies and reinforcements can be found in abundance, transported quickly, and received at your discretion. In such a place, fodder <note>original: "papulum"</note> will not be lacking, wood will be nearby, and there will be a free and ready exit for your troops to move against the enemy. For the enemy, on the contrary, everything should be left hindered and difficult. 

I would wish the camp to stand out so that you look down upon the entire region of the enemy, lest anyone attempt or begin anything that is not immediately seen and known to you. Slopes, open ground, steep heights, and precipices should surround the place on all sides. This is so that the enemy cannot surround you with a large force or break in from any side without grave danger. Furthermore, when the enemy finally approaches, they should not be able to freely launch war engines <term>tormenta</term> <note>This refers to various types of heavy artillery, ranging from classical catapults to early Renaissance cannons.</note> or persist in their position without great harm to themselves. If these natural advantages of a location are available, they should be used. Otherwise, it will be necessary to have considered both what kind of camp you need and in what lo— <note>The text cuts off mid-word "locis" (locations), continuing on the next page.</note>

Book V. On the works of individuals. Folio LXIX.

...must be placed for carrying out an expedition. For stationary <term>stataria; permanent military bases</term> camps must be much more fortified than temporary ones: and in flat places, they require more intricate skill and greater resources than on hills. We shall begin with temporary ones, since the use of these is more frequent. Indeed, it is thought that changing camps very often benefits the health of the soldiers. But in placing camps, this point perhaps comes to mind: whether we should consider it more convenient to have them within our own borders or in foreign territory. Xenophon <note>original: "Zenophon"; a Greek philosopher and military commander known for his writings on leadership and tactics.</note> used to say that the enemy is harmed by the changing of camps; doing so will undoubtedly benefit your own men's honor for bravery. To trample upon foreign lands will contribute to your advantage, while security is found in having retreated into your own soil. But let us establish it such that we think of the camp as something like a citadel to a city for the entire region that lies under and obeys it: it must necessarily have a contiguous retreat for its own people and a ready and prepared advance against outsiders. 

Furthermore, the method of surrounding camps with a rampart is varied.
<margin>Various methods of ramparting.</margin>
The Britons surround themselves with ten-foot stakes, burnt and sharpened at the tip, with one end fixed into the ground and trampled down, and the other standing out and projecting so that they face the oncoming enemy. Caesar reports that the Gauls <note>People of the region covering modern France, Belgium, and parts of Germany.</note> were accustomed to throw wagons in the way of the enemy to serve as a rampart. He remembers that the Thracians used the same against Alexander. The Nervii <note>A powerful Belgic tribe in northeastern Gaul.</note>—specifically to hinder cavalry—draw a hedge of cut young trees, bent towards each other, with numerous branches joined together. Arrian mentions that Nearchus, the prefect of Alexander sailing through the Indian Sea, fortified his camp with a wall so that he might be safer from the barbarians. 

It was the Roman custom to provide for every single mishap, fortune, and time, so that there would never be cause for regret.
<margin>The Roman custom regarding camps.</margin>
Indeed, they exercised the soldier no less in fortifying camps than in all other military duties. They did not value the destruction of the enemy as much as they took care to protect their own men excellently, and to be able to endure the enemy, and by enduring, to frustrate and repel them. This, in the end, they considered no small part of victory. For that reason, they adopted and carried out everything that anyone could report or devise for their own advantage and safety. If high and steep places were lacking, they would imitate precipices with very deep ditches and a built-up mound <note>original: "agger"; an embankment of earth.</note>, and they would surround them with a rampart <note>original: "vallo"</note> and wickerwork.

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

<margin>Where and in what manner land-based and stationary camps should be located.</margin>
**W**e shall follow their principles in this way: we will plan for a location that is not only convenient, but more suitable than any other for the tasks at hand. In addition to the qualities we have already listed, the site should be dry, not at all muddy, and unaffected by floods, but situated so that it is in no way obstructed for your own side. To the enemy, however, it should offer nothing that is safe; it should not allow unhealthy water to be nearby, nor permit healthy water to be far away. It will take in the purest springs or streams within the camp, or place rivers in front of the camp for protection. If this is less possible, care must be taken that a convenient water source is nearby. Furthermore, the camp shall be proportioned to the number of soldiers—not so large that it cannot be guarded by the distribution of watchword tokens <term>tesserae; small tablets used to circulate secret passwords among sentries</term> and defended by soldiers in alternating shifts of fighting without exhaustion. Conversely, they shall not be so narrow and cramped that they do not provide enough space for the soldiers' business. Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta, renowned for his military and social reforms.</note> thought angles in camps were useless and arranged them in a circle, unless he had a mountain, a river, or walls behind him. Others preferred a quadrangular area for the camp; but we shall adapt the positions and boundaries of the camps to the conditions of the times and the nature of the locations, as the reasoning for the actions to be performed—and the requirements of attacking or enduring the enemy—shall demand. We shall dig a ditch so wide that it can only be leveled with the greatest effort of a rampart and over a long period of time; or rather, two ditches will be cut with a space left between them. The ancients thought that even in such matters, an odd number of feet was significant for religious reasons <note>Likely referring to ancient Roman or Pythagorean beliefs that odd numbers were more auspicious and favored by the gods.</note> and were accustomed to making the ditch fifteen feet wide and nine feet deep. The ditch shall be cut with straight sides so that it is as wide at the bottom as the distance between the top edges. But where the ground is loose and prone to sliding, the depth shall be carved gradually, with a slope that narrows toward the bottom. In flat and low-lying places, these ditches shall be filled with water drawn and diverted from a stream, a lake, or the sea. If this is not possible, the bed of the ditch will be made hazardous by sowing it with stakes, hewn and sharpened trunks, and likewise with spikes and caltrops <term>murices; iron spikes or jagged stones used to injure the feet of horses or men</term> scattered throughout.

<margin>Ditches for stationary camps.</margin>
Once the ditches of the camp have been thus produced and prepared, a rampart <term>agger; a defensive embankment made of earth</term> shall be set up. It should be so thick that it cannot be disturbed by protective sheds <term>musculi; mobile mantlets or "mussels" used by besiegers for cover</term>, and so high that not only can grappling hooks <note>original: "falces"; literally "sickles" or hooks used to tear down fortifications.</note> not be driven in to dismantle it, but even weapons cannot easily be thrown by hand to deter the soldiers. It is practical that the material removed from the ditches should be piled up to form the rampart. For this work, the ancients approved of using "the skin of the earth" [sod] cut from meadows, which is held together by the roots of grasses. Others place green willow wicker-work interspersed within the structure, which by sprouting...

Book V. On Individual Works. Folio LXX.

...and they should strengthen the raised work with a tangle of roots and fibers <note>original: "fibrarum complicatu"; Alberti refers to using organic matter to bind the earth of the rampart together</note> along the inner edges of the ditch and the outer edge of the mound. Thorns, hedgehog-stakes <term>stili erinatij; defensive spikes or sharpened poles resembling the quills of a hedgehog</term>, hooks, and other items of the same kind should be fixed in place to delay the enemy's ascent. The top of the mound shall be surrounded by a crown of sturdy stakes fixed in place and joined by transverse beams; these will be enclosed by wickerwork and doubled mantlets <term>pluteis; portable screens or wooden breastworks used to protect soldiers</term>, and filled with chalk interspersed and trodden down. Pinnacles and "stags" <note>original: "cerui"; these were forked branches resembling stag antlers, placed as obstacles to hinder an enemy's advance</note> shall be stretched out above. Finally, everything should be brought into the work so that it can be less easily undermined or cut through, and less easily climbed; and so that the soldier behind the rampart <note>original: "pugnaculo"; a defensive parapet or battlement</note> is better covered and safer.

<margin>Towers.</margin>
Towers shall be raised at intervals of one hundred feet along the edges; and especially in those places subject to attack, they shall be prepared more frequently and higher, so that they can strike down even an enemy breaking into the camp. The **Praetorium** <note>the general's tent or headquarters</note>, the **Quintan gate**, and the **Decuman gate** <note>the Quintan was the side gate near the market area; the Decuman was the rear gate, usually furthest from the enemy</note>—and those things called by their camp names—shall be held in the safest locations; they shall be most ready for launching sorties, for bringing in supplies, and for recovering the soldiers.

Now, these things, as I said, are more necessary for stationary camps than for temporary ones; but since it is a duty to fear all accidents that either chance or the times might bring, even in momentary camps, the things we have mentioned should by no means be neglected as far as they are useful. Moreover, those things which pertain to stationary camps specifically placed to withstand sieges are very similar to those we will discuss regarding the citadels of tyrants. A citadel 
<margin>Citadel.</margin>
is a kind of work meant for a siege, since the citizens pursue it with eternal hatred. The most bitter kind of siege is to watch perpetually and wait at every moment for an opportunity to satisfy the provocations of hatred by destroying it. For that reason, as we have said, care must be taken that it be powerful, strong, stable, and ready to defend itself; for frustrating and repelling the enemy; and safe and unharmed against all assaults and the persistence of a siege. 

Furthermore, in those camps where you press and harass a cornered enemy, none of these things should be observed with any less diligence. And they say rightly that the reality of war is such that those who conduct sieges are often, in turn, besieged themselves. Wherefore one must not only take care of how to conquer, but also beware lest you be overwhelmed either by the audacity and skill of the enemy or by the negligence of your own men. 

<margin>Attack. Defense.</margin>
To conquer, two things contribute: the **attack** and the **circumvallation** <term>the building of a continuous line of fortifications around a besieged city to cut off its supplies and escape</term>. To avoid being overwhelmed, likewise two things contribute: the **defense** and the **pre-fortification**. Every effort of the attacks will tend toward that end, so that in the tow-

...until you break through the fortifications. I am not speaking here of the ladders by which you might climb even while the enemy resists, nor of tunnels, nor of mobile towers <term>ambulatorijs turribus; large wooden towers on wheels or rollers used to overlook city walls</term>, nor of engines of war <term>tormentis; mechanical artillery like catapults or ballistae</term>, nor of the rest of every kind of harm we inflict using fire, water, and every abundance of nature. It is not my place here, I say, to follow these matters; we shall pursue these military machines more distinctly elsewhere. However, this is relevant to the matter: they advise that against the force of missiles, you should throw up beams, timber, screens <term>pluteos; wooden shields or breastworks</term>, hurdles, ropes, bundles, and sacks filled with wool, seaweed, or hay. Place these especially so that they hang down and overlap. Against fire, dampen these same things—most effectively with vinegar—or cover them with mud and raw brick <note>Vinegar was believed in antiquity to be more fire-resistant than water and was frequently used to soak hides or blankets to protect wooden structures from incendiary arrows.</note>. Against water, stretch hides over them so the rain does not wash away the brick; conversely, against impacts, so that the hides are not pierced and torn to pieces, add soaked and wet patchwork quilts.

<margin>Circumvallation.</margin>
It is not unwise to establish a **circumvallation** <note>a line of fortifications built by the besiegers to completely surround a city, both to block supplies and to protect themselves from relief armies</note> close to the besieged walls for several reasons. It will be completed with a shorter length, with less labor from the soldiers, and with a lighter supply of materials and expense; once finished, it will require fewer guards. However, it must not be pushed so far inside the boundaries <term>pomerium; the open space or sacred boundary inside or outside a city wall</term> that the townspeople can overwhelm the soldiers in the camps or at work with wall-mounted engines. If a circumvallation is indeed built, so that the defenses of the besieged are cut off and supplies sought from elsewhere are intercepted, it will certainly be most convenient if you achieve this very thing by design, blocking off approaches wherever you wish. Whether you seize the bridges, or elsewhere block off the fords and roads with beams or stone walls, or whether you link marshes, lakes, swamps, rivers, or hills together with a constructed work, or if you take care that the force of water increases and fills the slopes: to these must be added things that are effective for the use of resistance and fortification. For one must fortify with a ditch, a mound, a tower, and similar works, both against the townspeople and against the relief forces of the provincials <note>The "subsidiarias prouincialiū manus" refers to external armies coming from the surrounding territory to break the siege.</note>. This is to prevent the former from hindering with a sally <note>original: "eruptione"; a sudden charge out of a besieged place</note>, or the latter with a combined attack and invasion. Furthermore, castles and watchtowers shall be placed in suitable spots, so that gathering water, wood, and fodder may be safer, freer, and more convenient for the soldier and the pack animals. But the forces should not be so scattered into various parts that they cannot be ruled by one command, fight with combined strength, and be able to help one another instantly with a single purpose. It helps here to recall a noteworthy story from the historian **Appian**. At Perugia, 

<margin>Octavian.</margin>
while **Octavian** <note>The future Emperor Augustus, during the Perusine War (41–40 BC).</note> was besieging Lucius, he dug a ditch fifty-six stades <note>A stade was approximately 600 feet; this ditch would be roughly 6.4 miles long.</note> long stretching all the way to the Tiber; it was thirty feet wide and thirty feet deep. He added, furthermore, a high wall and one thousand and fifty wooden towers standing sixty feet high, and so he fortified the work.

...so that the besieged are not only kept at bay but also excluded <note>prevented from leaving or receiving supplies</note>, so that they cannot harm the army from any direction. Thus far for land-based camps, unless perhaps this point is missing: that a most worthy and visible location must be selected where the standards of the republic may be placed with supreme majesty, and where divine services may be performed with the greatest veneration; and where the military magistrates, when called to the tribunal and the council, may gather.

### ¶ Maritime camps, the fleet: ports: ships: the parts and shapes of ships, and also the fortifications of ports. Chapter XII.

**T**here will perhaps be those who deny that maritime camps are held by fleets, and they will say that for a ship—being like a sort of aquatic elephant <note>original: "aquatico elephanto"; Alberti compares the massive, steered nature of a ship to the war elephants of antiquity</note> which they guide with its own reins—ports are more relevant to the use of camps than ships themselves. Others, on the contrary, will affirm that a ship is nothing other than a certain moving fortress. Let us set these disputes aside and thus determine that there are two things by which this our reasoning and art of building may provide safety and victory for naval commanders and troops: one in the fitting out of ships, the other in the fortifying of ports, whether you attack the enemy or keep them away. The primary use of ships is that they transport you and your belongings; the next is that they provide aid in war without danger. Dangers will either be present from within the ship itself, as if joined to its body and innate, or they will be imported from without. External dangers are the force of the winds, the mass of the waves, and encounters with rocks and shoals; all of which will be avoided early enough through experience in maritime affairs and the knowledge and skill of places and winds. Innate defects <note>original: "innata... vitia"</note>, however, are caused either by the design <term>liniamenta; the geometric plan or "lines" of the vessel</term> or the material; provision must be made against these defects. They reject all material that is prone to splitting, brittle, porous, or rotting. They prefer bronze nails and pins to iron ones. From the ship of Trajan <note>Alberti refers here to the "Nemi Ships," massive Roman vessels submerged in Lake Nemi. Alberti personally led an early archaeological attempt to raise them in 1446. He mistakenly attributed them to the Emperor Trajan; they were actually built by Caligula.</note>—which was raised from Lake Nemi <margin>A ship raised from Lake Nemi: [it lay there] more than 1,300 years.</margin> during these days while I was reflecting on what I have written, where it had lain submerged and abandoned for more than one thousand three hundred years—I observed from the lake that pine and cypress wood had lasted remarkably well. On its planks on the outside, they had glued linen cloths with pitch, stretched double and drenched in black pitch; and above that, they had secured lead sheeting with small bronze nails. In the building of ships, ancient architects took their designs from fish: so that what is the spine in the fish becomes the keel <term>carina; the "backbone" of the ship's hull</term> in the ship; what is the head becomes the prow; then the tail serves for the rudder, and the fins and wings for the oars. There are two kinds of ships: cargo ships <term>onerariæ; heavy transport vessels</term> and fast ships <term>fugaces; literally "fleeting" ships, referring to light, swift warships or scouts</term>. The length of the ship contributes primarily to straight courses; brevity will make it responsive to the commands of the rudder. I would have the length of a cargo ship be no less than triple its width, and for a fast ship no more than nine times its width. Elsewhere of the cargo ship...

## Leonis Baptistæ Alber. De re ædificatoria.

I have pursued the principles of ships more extensively in that little book titled *The Ship* <note>original: "Navis"; a lost treatise by Alberti on naval architecture</note>; but here I shall say how much relates to the undertaking at hand. These are the parts of ships: the keel, the stern, the prow; add the sides on either hand, and if you wish, the rudder and sails, and what pertains to the ship's course. However much the weight of water would be required to fill the hollow of the ship to its proper level, it will sustain that same weight of cargo according to the rule of foundations. <margin>Keel.</margin> The keel <term>carina</term><note>the structural "backbone" of the ship's hull</note> ought to be flat; all other parts shall be carved according to the curve of a bent line. The wider the keel, the more weight it will tolerate, but it will be slower in its course; a narrowed and drawn-back keel is faster, but unless you put in a great deal of ballast <term>saburra</term><note>heavy material like sand or stones placed in the hold to provide stability</note>, it will wobble. A broad keel is suited for shallow waters; a slender one is safer on the high seas. <margin>Prow.</margin> High and raised sides and a prow are stubborn against attacking waves, but are overcome by heavier winds. The sharper the line of the prow, the readier and more gliding it is for sailing. <margin>Stern.</margin> The more slender the stern <term>puppis</term>, the more persistent it is in holding the intended furrows <note>the "furrows" refer to the ship's wake or its ability to stay on course</note>. For the ship, the bosses and the breasts <note>the forward-bulging parts of the hull</note> ought to be strong and slightly forward-leaning, so that they might drive forward against the drag of the sails or the impact and force of the waves; immediately toward the stern it should become slender, so that it might fly out, as if by its own accord, in a slippery escape. A greater number of rudders increases the ship's stability but decreases its speed. An equal length will be given to the mast and the ship. Let the other small things—oars, anchors, ropes, beaks <term>rostra</term><note>the pointed prows used for ramming</note>, towers, bridges, and such minor details—be passed over. To the matter belong the beams and timbers hanging from the railings and sides, and likewise those extended forward. These serve as a defense in place of beaks and against opposing attacks; then also the masts raised in place of towers; yards and skiffs raised onto the yards will serve excellently as bridges. The ancients used "ravens" <note>original: "corvos"; a Roman boarding device consisting of a spiked bridge</note> on the prow; our people have learned very well to raise towers on the prow and stern near the mast, and to throw up patchwork coverings, ropes, sacks, and such like as a wall and roof; and they have learned to keep off those climbing aboard by means of a net drawn over with ropes. And regarding the decks of ships: I have devised and noted elsewhere how you can render them entirely filled with frequent rising spikes <note>likely caltrops or concealed sharpened stakes</note> in a single moment of time during a fight, so that the enemy cannot move his foot even a little without receiving a wound; and on the contrary, ☞ where it might be useful, how the deck can be cleared of every such annoyance with the removal of those things in another brief moment. But I do not wish to repeat those things here. It should suffice to have prompted talented minds. Then too, I have discovered by what art I might, with a single light strike of a small hammer, dissolve the entire planking of the deck and throw down the whole multitude that has climbed up; and immediately, with a light hand in a brief moment, restore the whole work to use. These things I have also devised...

### Book V. On the works of individuals. Page LXXII.

...for sinking and burning the ships of the enemy, for throwing them into confusion, and for killing the naval crowd with a miserable slaughter, there is no need for me to recount here. Perhaps these things will be discussed elsewhere. 

However, let this not be overlooked: the same length, height, or breadth is not appropriate for ships in every location. In the sea between the windings of islands, massive hulls—which you cannot command without a great many hands—fare poorly when the winds rage a little more fiercely. Conversely, near Cadiz <note>original: "Gades"; a port city in Spain on the Atlantic coast</note>, where the ocean is vast, a tiny vessel is swallowed by the waves. 

Furthermore, it pertains to naval matters to protect or obstruct harbors. This we shall most excellently achieve by a mole <term>moles</term><note>a massive stone structure used as a pier, breakwater, or causeway</note> led into the deep, and by a mound, chains, and similar objects placed in the way, which we dealt with in the previous book. Stakes shall be fixed in front; obstacles of stone shall be thrown in. Then, frames made of planks and wicker, empty but filled with heavy weights, shall be sunk. 

But if the nature of the place or the magnitude of the expense should prevent these things from being done—for instance, if there is fluid sliminess or too profound a depth—then do as follows: with casks placed beneath in order and joined together, fit beams and timbers laid straight and others across one another, and bind them together. Add to this, so that they project from the raft against the enemy, high and very sharp beaks <term>rostra</term> and stakes, which they call *tonsillas* <note>original: "tonsillas"; these were likely pointed mooring-posts or defensive spikes fixed in the water</note>, with iron tips, lest any smooth ship of the enemy dare to attack the work with full sails or glide past. Cover the raft with earth to protect it from the injury of fires; drive wickerwork and screens around it like a rampart; build towers on it in suitable places; and fasten it against the waves with frequent anchors in stable spots that may be hidden from the enemy. It will be helpful to draw the work in a curve, bent like an arch against the waves, so that it may bear the force of the water more robustly and strongly, and so the anchors of the defenses may be less strained from the outside. So much for these things.

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

<margin>Granary and treasury</margin>
...rising up and extending themselves beyond the roofs, it is necessary to build walls throughout the whole building to intercept the devastating flames of fires, and to ensure that water flows more profusely over the roofs as in ancient times. Markets <margin>Emporium</margin> shall be established by the sea, at the mouths of rivers, or at the intersections of military roads. Regarding naval yards <margin>Naval yard</margin>, these shall be joined to inlets and basins where the fleet may be hauled out, restored, and returned to the sea. In such places, care must be taken that the water is kept in constant motion; for ships rot under the influence of the south wind, decay in the midday heat, but are preserved by the rays of the rising sun. Furthermore, storehouses of any kind for preserving goods should be added; these locations are known to benefit primarily from dryness of the air. But we shall speak of these more extensively when we discuss the affairs of private citizens, as these matters pertain most especially to their concerns—with the exception of salt-houses <margin>Salt-house</margin>. Indeed, you should establish salt-houses in this way:

Lay the ground with charcoal to the depth of one cubit <term>cubit</term><note>an ancient unit of length based on the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, roughly 18 inches</note> and level it. Then, sprinkle over it sand mixed with pure chalk <note>original: "creta"; likely referring to a fine clay or pipeclay used for lining</note> to a depth of three palms <term>palms</term><note>a unit of measurement based on the width of the hand, approximately 3 inches</note> and smooth it. Finally, pave it with brick that has been baked until it is black. For the inner faces of the walls—where such brick is not available—use squared stone, not tufa <note>a porous volcanic rock</note> nor reclaimed stone, but stone that is exceptionally hard and preserved with mortar. Recess the work one cubit inward from the main wall, and establish a partition made of joined timbers and bronze nails, or rather, fastened into panels. Fill the interval between the timber and the wall with reeds. It will be of great help to have soaked the wood in clay mixed with oil dregs <term>amurca</term><note>the watery, bitter liquid that remains after pressing olives; it was used in antiquity as a preservative and pesticide</note> and diluted with crushed esparto grass and rushes. Furthermore, any such public building must be entirely fortified with walls, towers, and garrisons against the plots, insolence, and attacks of thieves, enemies, and seditious citizens.

I believe I have treated the subject of public works abundantly, unless this one thing is lacking—which indeed pertains to the magistrates themselves in no small measure: that they should have a place to commit those whom they judge must be punished for defiance, treachery, and wickedness. Let us not, therefore, neglect the prison <margin>Prison</margin>. I find that there were three types of prisons among the ancients. The first was where the unruly and unrefined were driven so that, at night, they might be instructed by learned and highly esteemed professors of the liberal arts in what pertains to good morals and a proper way of life. The second was where debtors and those who must be deterred from their accustomed insolence by the tediousness of confinement were held. The third was where the monstrously wicked—unworthy of the sun and the company of men—were committed, soon to be punished and delivered over to darkness and filth. Finally, regarding this last type of prison, if anyone should see fit to create a subterranean pit resembling a horrific tomb, he would indeed be looking toward the punishment of the guilty far more than the law itself or human reason requires.

# Book V. On the Works of Individuals. Folio 73.

## Book V. On the Works of Individuals. Folio 73.

For even if degenerate men deserve the worst of all things for their crimes, it will nevertheless be the duty of the state and the prince to lose nothing of their sense of piety <note>original: "pietate"; here referring to a sense of duty, mercy, or moral obligation</note>. Therefore, it is necessary to strengthen the work with walls, openings, and vaulting so that a person confined within can never easily escape. To this end, the thickness, depth, and height of the structure will contribute greatly, especially if built with levels of very hard stone joined by iron and bronze. Add, if you wish, beams and high openings protected by gratings and the like; yet all these things are weaker than a man’s memory of his own liberty and safety, which he will seek to reclaim unless you allow the work to be completed with all the strength of nature and human ingenuity. Indeed, those seem to me to remind us most excellently who say that the "adamantine" <term>adamantine</term><note>meaning unbreakable or like a diamond; from the Greek 'adamas'</note> prison is the eye of a watchful guard. But let us follow the customs and institutions of the ancients in other matters. It should be a priority for prisons to have a place where they may serve the stomach <note>original: "ventri pareant"; meaning a place to eat</note>, and where they may also be refreshed by a hearth without the injury of smoke or stench. Regarding the whole matter of the prison, you should decide thus: an area in a safe and well-attended part of the city is to be surrounded by a strong, high wall, unbroken by any openings, and fortified with towers and walkways. From this wall, one must retreat three cubits <term>cubits</term><note>an ancient unit of length, about 18 inches</note> inward to the walls of the cells, so that guards walking about at night may intercept the escapes of conspirators. The middle space within the area should be divided so that the entrance hall appears as little gloomy as possible, where those sent for discipline are first gathered. After this, armed guards should occupy the first entrances within the railings and defensive barriers. Immediately following, an open-air courtyard <note>original: "area subdiualis"; a courtyard open to the sky</note> shall be established. On either side, there shall be porticoes through which a clear view into many cells is provided by numerous openings. Within these cells, bankrupts <note>original: "decoctores"; literally "those who have boiled away their wealth"</note> and those liable for debt shall be kept, not all together, but separated. At the front, the prison shall be more confined, where those guilty of minor crimes are held. In the innermost chambers, capital offenders shall be secured.

### Chapter XIV.

<margin>Private house.</margin>
I come now to private buildings. We have said elsewhere that a house is a small city. It will therefore be necessary to consider almost all the same things in its construction as pertain to the work of a city: that it be as healthy as possible, that it possess opportunities, and that it provide conveniences. These are the things that make for a life led peacefully, tranquilly, and elegantly. What all these things are by their own nature, what they should be like, and of what sort they ought to be, I seem to have discussed for the most part in the previous books. But here, taking a new beginning from another point, we shall order the matter thus. A private house is for a family.

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

...must be established for the sake of pleasure <note>original: "gratia"; in this context, it refers to the aesthetic grace or the delight a building provides</note>: so that one may rest within it most comfortably. No dwelling, however convenient, will be of any use unless everything required for the sake of the inhabitants is held under the same roof. There is a great number of people in a household and a great quantity of things which you cannot arrange at your whim in the city in the same way as you can in the country. For it happens in urban buildings that a neighbor's wall, the eaves-drop <note>original: "stillicidium"; a legal and architectural term regarding the runoff of rainwater from a roof onto a neighbor's property</note>, a public square, a road, and many such things hinder you from satisfying your own requirements. This does not happen in rural settings. There, everything is freer, whereas in the city, everything is restricted. Therefore, for many other reasons as well as for this one, it is helpful to distinguish matters such that some are urban and others are rural.

I shall speak of private buildings in both categories. Poorer citizens require one thing; wealthier ones another. For the poorer sort measure their way of living by necessity, while the more elegant <note>original: "lautiores"; referring to the wealthy or refined upper class</note> hardly set limits to their desires, even when they have reached satiety. But let us relate what moderation a well-advised man would approve in each case; I believe we should begin with the easier ones. Rural buildings are more straightforward, and the wealthy are more ready to spend money in the country. But first, let us very briefly repeat a few things that pertain to the primary principles of a villa. 

They are as follows: one must flee a disastrous climate and "rotten" <note>original: "cariosam"; meaning crumbly, decayed, or poor-quality soil</note> land. One should build in the middle of a field at the foot of a mountain, in a watery, sunny, and healthy region, and in a healthy part of that region. They consider a gloomy and unhealthy sky to be present when the other disadvantages we discussed in the first book are there, as well as dense forests, especially those filled with trees with bitter leaves, where the air—untouched by either wind or sun—grows raw <note>original: "incrudescant"; becomes harsh, thick, or stagnant</note>. Then also consider a sterile and unhealthy soil, from which if you finally manage to harvest anything, it will only be woods.

<margin>Where a villa should be located.</margin> I think a villa should be placed in that part of the field which most beautifully suits the master’s urban house. According to Xenophon <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and historian whose "Oeconomicus" was a primary source for Renaissance ideas on estate management</note>, one should go to the villa on foot for the sake of exercise and return on horseback. Therefore, it shall not be entirely remote from the city; and the road should not be difficult or obstructed, but suitable and very convenient for winter and summer travel and for transporting goods, whether one pleases to use a carriage <term>reda</term><note>A four-wheeled traveling carriage used in antiquity and the Renaissance</note>, or go on foot, or perhaps even travel by boat. 

It will be beneficial if it is not far from a city gate but rather near one, so that you can frequently return to either city or villa at your whim with your wife and children, more conveniently and quickly, without a great display of clothing <note>meaning without the need for formal traveling attire or the luggage required for a long journey</note> and without the public acting as commentators <note>original: "populo interprete"; without being the subject of public observation or gossip during a long trek</note>. It is fitting to have a villa situated so that the morning rays are not hostile to the eyes of those setting out, and the evening sun does not trouble those returning home. Again, a villa should be held in a place that is not entirely destitute, neglected, or ignoble, but of such a kind that people are enticed to live there by the hope of profit and the pleasantness of the climate, with an abundance of things, a joy of life, and without danger. A villa should certainly be built in a very popular location, or near a city, or joined to a military road or a port where a number of ships might dock; but it shall be situated appropriately so that while the pleasure of these things is not lacking, the family estate is not overly disturbed by the frequency of passing guests.

<margin>if they are remote from the sea</margin>
**Windy** places, the ancients say, are usually free of **rust** <note>original: "rubigine"; in an agricultural context, this refers to mildew, blight, or fungal diseases that thrive in stagnant, damp air</note>: but dewy places and valleys that have no through-draft are frequently corrupted by such harms. I do not always and everywhere approve of what they say: that a villa should be built to face the rising sun at the equinox. For those things that are said about the sun and the breezes are prone to change according to the region; 
<margin>for often the wind takes on the quality of the place through which it passes</margin>
thus, the north wind <note>original: "aquilo"</note> is not always light, nor the south wind <note>original: "auster"</note> everywhere unhealthy. **Very learnedly**, Celsus the physician <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus, a Roman medical encyclopedist</note> used to assert that all winds are denser because they fall from the sea; but those that come from inland are never anything but lighter. And for the sake of the winds, I judge that the very mouths of valleys should be avoided; for there the winds are too freezing if they come through the shade, or too sweltering when they arrive through a flat area that is scorched and illuminated by much sun.

**B**ut since some villa roofs are those where the freeborn dwell, and others where the bonded laborers reside, and the latter seem to be established primarily for the sake of profit, while the former are perhaps brought about for the sake of the mind's pleasure: let us discuss those things which especially concern the field. Their dwellings ought not to be far from the master's, so that they <note>the masters</note> may understand every hour what each person is doing and what work needs to be done. The proper purpose of this part of the buildings is that the fruits which can be taken from the field are prepared, gathered, and preserved through it. This last part—that is, that you preserve what is collected—you may think belongs more to the duties of a master's or urban house than to a rustic estate; but that is accomplished by the hand of men, the abundance of tools, and especially by the industry and diligence of the **steward** <term>villicus: the farm manager or bailiff responsible for the daily productivity of the estate</term>.

The **bailiff** <note>original: "villicus"; the manager of a rural estate</note> should be stationed at the primary gate: so that no one may go out or carry anything away at night without his knowledge. **chamber** where the troughs, baskets, pulleys, ropes, hoes, two-pronged mattocks, and tools of that kind may be stored and repaired. On the crossbeams and joists of the shed, crates should be spread; there, the levers, poles, stakes, rods, brushwood, foliage, fodder for the oxen, hemp, and raw flax and such things shall be placed. There are two kinds of four-footed animals: the **working** kind, such as the ox and the beast of burden; and the **productive** kind <note>original: "fructuarium"; animals kept for their "fruit" or products like milk, wool, and meat</note>, such as the sow, sheep, goat, and all such herds.
<margin>Working four-footed animals.</margin>
Regarding the working animals first, since they are primarily in the place of tools; then later we shall speak of the productive animals, which pertain to the bailiff's industry. You must take care that the
<margin>Ox-stall.</margin>
**ox-stalls** and 
<margin>Horse-stable.</margin>
**horse-stables** are not freezing during the winter. Enclose the mangers so they do not scatter their fodder. For horses, make sure the bedding <note>original: "stramenta"; likely referring here to the fodder or hay racks</note> hangs from a high position, so that as they stand with their necks raised, they must pluck it down with some effort; for this results in a leaner head and more agile shoulders. Conversely, provide their barley and seeds so that they draw them from the bottom of a pit; for they will gorge themselves less immoderately and will swallow fewer whole seeds; furthermore, they will be rendered firmer and more robust in their muscles and chests.
<margin>☞</margin>
One must absolutely provide that the wall facing the front of the manger is not damp; a horse has a thin skull and is impatient of moisture and cold. For this reason, take care that the windows do not admit the **rays of the moon**; for the moon brings a white film <note>cataracts or moon blindness</note> over the eye and a heavy cough; indeed, the rays of the moon are a plague to the throats of cattle. For oxen, place things low down so they may eat while lying down. If beasts of burden look toward a fire, they will become shaggy; an ox, however, grows cheerful when people are present. A mule kept in a hot or dark place goes mad. There are those who think a mule is sufficiently covered by a roof if its head is covered, while the rest of the body is exposed to the air and cold. For oxen, lay down **stone pavements** so that their hooves do not rot from filth. For horses, dig out the floors and cover the trench with planks or robust boards, so that they do not become soaked by the mud of their urine, and so the hooves do not become worn down by the vibration of a hard pavement.

### Chapter XVI.

<margin>For the cattle shed.</margin>
The **bailiff's** <note>original: "villici"; the estate manager</note> industry will be occupied not only in gathering from the field, but also—and primarily—with the "animate" <note>Living creatures, as opposed to "mute" tools like plows</note> four-footed beasts, birds, and fish, about which I shall speak very briefly. Place the **cattle pens** <note>original: "armentaria septa"</note> in a dry and minimally marshy location; the ground should be cleared of rubble and sloped so that it can be swept and easily made clean. Cover them in part, and in part leave them open to the sky; take care that the south wind or the damp night air does not reach the cattle, and provide that other winds do not trouble them excessively.

<margin>For the hare-warren.</margin>
For the **hare**, build a stone wall deep down to the water level <note>to prevent the hares from burrowing out</note>. Surface the area with "male" sand <note>original: "sabulo masculo"; a term for coarse, gritty sand</note> and raise mounds in several places made of **Cimolean earth** <note>original: "creta cimolea"; a type of fuller's earth or medicinal clay used in antiquity</note>.

<margin>For the poultry house.</margin>
Give the **hens** a small portico in the courtyard facing south, sprinkled with plenty of ash and dust <note>for the birds to "bathe" in to remove parasites</note>. Above this, fix the nesting area and a perch where they may gather at night. There are those who order that hens be kept in large, enclosed cages facing the east. But because they are kept for the sake of eggs and offspring, just as they are more spirited in freedom, so too are they more fertile; in the shade and in confinement, the laid egg is often wasted.

<margin>Dovecotes.</margin>
Place the **dovecote** <note>specifically for wood-pigeons or "palumbes"</note> near water where it is visible and moderately high. There, the winged bird may fly over the "moat" and play as if in a wrestling-school of wings and clapping; gliding with spread wings, it delights to land. There are those who say that the more distance and labor the wood-pigeon endures returning to its young after taking food from the field, the fatter the chicks it produces. This is because the food brought in the mother's throat—with which she feeds the brood—becomes semi-digested during the delay. For this reason, they approve of a dovecote placed in a high, steep place. Then again, some perhaps think it better to have the dovecote far from water, lest the birds chill the eggs with wet feet. If you shut a **kestrel** <note>original: "tinunculum"; a small bird of prey</note> in the corners of the tower, the dovecote will be safer from the attacks of hawks. If you bury a **wolf's head** sprinkled with cumin inside a cracked jar near the entrance so that it breathes out a scent <note>this reflects an ancient folk-belief or "sympathetic magic" recorded by Roman authors</note>, it will cause a great many pigeons to flock there, leaving their larger homes. If you make the floor out of clay and sprinkle it repeatedly with human urine, it will increase their number. In front of the windows, stone ledges or olive-wood boards should be attached, projecting a **cubit** <note>about 18 inches</note>, where the bird may land from its flight and fly out again.

<margin>On small birds.</margin>
¶ Smaller **caged birds** waste away if they are denied a view of the trees and the sky. Nests and small plots for birds should be fitted in warm places. For those birds that walk more than they fly, these should be placed low, right on the ground; for the others, they should be positioned higher up. Each should be secured with **rims** <note>original: "spondulis"; circular dividers or borders</note> for the sake of keeping the eggs and chicks in place. For the construction of these chambers, mud is more suitable than lime...

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

...and lime mixed with gypsum. Every reused stone is harmful; brick is more useful than tufa <note>A soft, porous volcanic rock common in Italy</note> if it is moderately baked. Timber from poplar or fir is the most useful. For all birds, the stalls ought to be bright, pure, and clean—especially for pigeons. Indeed, even four-footed animals will become scabby if they lie in the filthiest conditions. Therefore, let the structures be vaulted, the walls entirely coated and smoothed with marble plaster <note>original: "tectorio marmorato"; a high-quality finish made of lime and crushed marble</note>, and let them be diligently blocked up so that cats, mice, lizards, and similar harmful little beasts are not a nuisance to the eggs and chicks, or to the walls. Feeding and watering troughs shall be added. Furthermore, a ditch shall be led around the villa in which geese, ducks, pigs, and oxen can be washed and submerged; care should be taken where they take their food so that even in rainy and turbulent weather they may be most cleanly sated. For the stalls of smaller birds, watering and feeding receptacles shall be fixed to the wall with pipes, so that the birds are able neither to scatter nor foul what is put inside. From these, tubes shall open to the outside through which food may be supplied; in the middle, there shall be a bath into which an abundance of clean water flows.

<margin>Fish pond.</margin>
Dig the **fish pond** <note>original: "piscina"</note> in clayey soil, deeper than the sun's rays can reach to overheat it, or than it might freeze from the cold. Then, open up caverns along the side where the fish may flee from sudden disturbances or tumult, lest they waste away from fear. A fish is nourished by the "juice of the earth" <note>An ancient biological concept that fish absorbed nutrients directly from the water and soil</note>; it languishes in sharper heat, will die in the frost, but is restored to vigor by the midday sun. They believe that muddy rainwater is sometimes received not without benefit, but the first rains after the **Dog Days** <note>original: "caniculum"; the hottest days of summer associated with the star Sirius</note> should be excluded, for they taste of lime and kill the fish. Thereafter, water should be admitted only rarely, lest it infect the water and the fish with the sluggishness of foul-smelling moss. Care must be taken that water breathes in and out perpetually from a spring, river, lake, or the sea. Regarding maritime fish ponds, the ancients give more convenient warnings: they say a muddy region supports "flat" fish, such as sole and shellfish; a sandy region better feeds other deep-sea fish, such as **giltheads** <note>original: "auratas"</note> and **dentex** <note>original: "dentices"; a type of Mediterranean sea bream</note>.

<margin>Stagnant pond.</margin>
Rocks support thrushes, blackbirds <note>Ancient names for certain species of wrasse or rock-dwelling fish</note>, and those born among the stones. Finally, they say the best **pond** <note>original: "stagnum"</note> for fish is one positioned so that the incoming sea wave pushes out the previous one, and does not allow the old, sluggish water to remain within the basin. For they believe that waters which are gradually renewed become less overheated. Thus far on the industry and diligence of the **bailiff** <note>original: "villici"</note> in many matters; but he also approves of what is done early for the gathering and storing of harvests and fruits. For the sake of these, it is necessary to have prepared a **threshing floor** <note>original: "areā frumētariā"</note>, open to the sun and winds and not far from the shed of which we recently spoke, so that if sudden clouds arise, you may withdraw the servants and the gathered grain to cover in a light moment.

<margin>Threshing floor.</margin>
Where you make the threshing floor, level the ground—not perfectly flat, but slightly sloped—and dig it over; afterward sprinkle it with **olive dregs** <note>original: "amurca"; the bitter, watery residue left over from pressing olives, used in antiquity as a pesticide and to harden earthen floors</note>...

Then sprinkle it again with the dregs of oil <note>original: "amurca"; the bitter, watery residue of olive oil production, used as a natural pesticide and herbicide</note>. ### ¶ The master's and the freeborn's villa, its structure and individual parts: where, how many, which, of what sort, and how large the lodgings or storage places for men, beasts of burden, and crops should be. Chapter XVII.

**T**here are those who say the master's villa should be twofold: one for summer and another for winter. They define them thus: that winter bedrooms <margin>Bedroom</margin> should face the winter sunrise <note>the South-East</note>, and the dining room <margin>Dining room</margin> the equinoctial sunset <note>the West</note>. But summer bedrooms <margin>Walk</margin> should face south, and the dining room the winter sunrise; the walk should be exposed to the midday sun. However, we believe these should be positioned differently according to the climate and region, so that the cold is tempered by warmth and the wet by dryness.

Furthermore, I would wish the dwellings of the freeborn to occupy a spot in the field that is not the most fertile, but otherwise the most dignified, from which every benefit and pleasure of air, sun, and prospect may be freely taken, and which offers easy access from the fields. It should receive the arriving guest with most honorable spaces; it will look out upon, and be looked upon by, the city, towns, the sea, the spreading plain, and the well-known peaks of hills and mountains. It will have the delights of gardens and the allurements of fishing and hunting laid out before its eyes. 

Since (as we have said) some parts of the house belong to everyone, some to many, and some to individuals, the houses of prominent men will imitate the princely style, using very large spaces before the gates for races and equestrian contests—spaces that far exceed the reach of a youth's javelin or arrow. Within the gates, where many gather, there shall be no lack of walks, paths for carriage exercise <term>gestationes; paths intended for being carried in a litter or light exercise</term>, swimming pools, and courtyards—both grassy and paved—as well as porticos and semicircles <note>original: "emicycli"; semicircular seating areas</note>, where the elderly may converse in the pleasant winter sun, and the household <margin>Household</margin> may spend its festival days and enjoy the summer shade. 

Yet it is established that in a house some things are owed to the household, and others to the things that the household finds pleasing. The household consists of the husband and wife, children and parents, and those who live together for their service: stewards, ministers, and servants; the household does not exclude the guest either. For the sake of the household, things must be kept for sustenance, such as food, and for use, such as clothing, weapons, books, and even the horse. The primary part of all these is what you might think of as the "hollow of the house" <margin>Inner court</margin> or the "atrium" <margin>Atrium</margin>; we shall call it the "sinus" <margin>Inner hall</margin> <note>original: "sinus"; literally a fold, bay, or heart, used here to describe the central focal point of the home</note>. Closely following are the dining rooms, and then the private bedrooms which belong to individuals. Finally, let there be chambers...

...is most <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion on the best climate</note>. For by the purity of the air which flourishes under that region of the sky, being perpetually serene, and by the brilliance of the sun with which it is bathed, it is rendered illustrious and wonderfully pleasant to behold. The mountains to the east, 
<margin>From the east</margin>

<margin>North.</margin>

Likewise with rivers and lakes: they are neither convenient when too close, nor are they pleasant when they are too distant. On the other hand, the sea at a moderate distance blows "impure suns" <note>likely referring to hazy, salt-heavy vapors or humid heat</note>; yet from very close it harms less, as the air remains more stable. From a distance, 
<margin>Of the sea</margin> 
it adds further to the charm by exciting a longing for itself. However, it matters which part of the sky the sea reveals itself to. For a sea open to the south burns the sight; under the east it moistens; to the west it grows misty; and from the north it is biting cold. From the central hall <note>original: "sinu"; literally a fold or bay, here referring to the inner courtyard or entryway</note> access will be given to the dining rooms <note>original: "cenacula"; while this can mean upper rooms, in this architectural context it refers to dining or living suites</note>. These will be, according to the necessity of use, some for summer, others for winter, and others, so to speak, 
<margin>Dining room.</margin> 
in-between. For summer dining rooms, they primarily require water and the greenery of gardens; for winter ones, warmth and a hearth <term>focus<explanation>the central fireplace or hearth of a Roman home, serving as both a heat source and a symbolic center of domestic life</explanation></term>. In both, spaciousness, cheerfulness, and elegance are desired. There are arguments by which you might easily be persuaded that the hearths among the ancestors were not such as we are accustomed to have. *And the rooftops of the house smoke,* as the poet says <note>original: "Et fumant... culmina tecti"; a quote from Virgil’s Eclogues, I.82, suggesting smoke rose through the roof rather than a chimney</note>. We see that throughout all of Italy, except for Tuscany and Gaul, this was observed up to these times: that no "throats" <note>original: "gulae"; a technical term for chimney flues</note> for smoke were built into the roofs. Vitruvius 
<margin>Dining room</margin> 
used to say that for winter dining rooms <note>original: "tricliniis"; rooms with three couches for reclining at meals</note>, subtle ornamentation of the vaulted ceilings with crown-work is not useful, because they would be ruined by the smoke of the fire and frequent soot. Indeed, they even smeared the vault above the hearth with black pigment, so that it might appear black by design rather than being stained by smoke. Elsewhere I find they were accustomed to use cleaned woods so they would be free of smoke; these were called "cooked" <note>original: "cocta"; likely referring to charcoal or wood that had been pre-dried or charred to prevent smoking</note>. For this reason, legal experts decided that "cooked" wood did not fall under the general legal definition of "wood." Thus you might judge they used portable hearths made of bronze or iron, as each person's wealth and status required. And perhaps that kind of men, being of the camp and hardened by military service—as they were almost to a man—used the hearth less. Nor do the physicians <note>original: "physici"; referring to natural philosophers or medical authorities</note> allow that we use much fire continually. 
<margin>Continuous fire must not be used.</margin> 
Aristotle said that the solidity of flesh in a living being is established by cold. And those who profess these things have noted that smiths who work in shops with fire are almost all rendered with very wrinkled and shriveled faces and skin. They attest this happens because the channels <note>original: "cloacas"; used here metaphorically for the pores or vessels of the body</note>, the smoothness, and the vital juices by which flesh is formed are liquefied by fire and vanish into vapors. Among the Germans and Colchians <note>people of the Caucasus region</note>, or elsewhere where the help of fires is needed against the harshness of the cold, they use a 
<margin>Hearth.</margin> 
heated room <note>original: "concale-facto conclaui"; likely referring to a stove-heated room or a hypocaust system</note>; which will be discussed in its proper place. Let me return to the hearth.

# Leon Battista Alberti. On Architecture.

<margin>Smoke-vent</margin>
...between the couches. These are the things that pertain to the use of the hearth: that it be ready for use, that it may warm many people at once, that it has enough light, and no wind. Yet it must have a place for the smoke to breathe; otherwise, it would not ascend. Therefore, it shall not be forced into a corner, nor deep within the wall; yet it shall not occupy the foremost space of the dining tables. It shall not be troubled by the drafts of the doorways; its lowest opening <note>original: "faucibus"; literally "throats" or "jaws," referring to the fireplace opening</note> shall not project much from the wall. The throat <note>The "gula" is the narrow passage of the chimney flue</note> shall be capacious, and wide from right to left, raised to a plumb-line, and tall enough to exceed all the heights of the roof ridges. This is certainly done because of the danger of fires, and also so that the wind, being obstructed by the edges of the roof, does not gather aerial waves and retard or beat back the smoke with eddies. Smoke ascends of its own accord by its inherent heat, but from there it is propelled more swiftly by the heat of the flames and the hearth. Therefore, once received by the throat of the chimney, it is narrowed as if in a pipe, and is thrust out by the force of the increasing flames, not unlike the sound from a trumpet. For just as in a trumpet, if it is too wide it becomes "deaf" <note>meaning the draft becomes weak or ineffective</note> by the air turning back within it; so it is with smoke. The peak of the top cap shall be covered because of rain, and shall be made with wide-open nostrils <note>ventilation holes</note> and surrounded by partitions, yet with a wing-like screen <note>original: "alamento"</note> by which the nuisance of the wind may be kept away. Between the screens and the wide nostrils, space will be left for the streams of smoke to be vomited out. Where this is not possible, I recommend what I call a "revolving cap" <note>original: "vertula"</note>, which I would like to be placed upon an upright needle. This is a bronze box, wide enough to encompass the uppermost jaws of the throat within itself. A crest shall stand projecting from the front of this, which, driven like a rudder, turns its back to the attacking winds. Most conveniently, bronze horns or those made of ample and suitable hollow earthenware may be placed around the heads of the throats, because with the upper mouth turned toward the throat itself, they vomit out the smoke through the upper opening while protecting it from the wind with the lower "cheek."

<margin>Kitchen</margin>
A kitchen and a pantry <note>original: "cella obsonaria"; a room for storing meat and provisions</note> are owed to the dining rooms, where the remains of the dinner, the vessels, and the linens may be brought. The kitchen is neither to be held in the very lap of the couches <note>the seating area</note>, nor moved further away so that the hot dishes requested for the couches grow cold during the passage; it will be enough to exclude the noise and filth of the kettles, pans, and pots. One shall see to it that the carrying of wood is not hindered by rain, nor by unpleasant winding paths, nor by the uncleanness of the locations, lest the more dignified parts of the house be disgraced by these things. From the dining rooms, the bedchambers are reached. It is a mark of the greatest refinement not to have the same dining rooms

<margin>Saying of Lucullus</margin>
in summer as in winter. That saying of Lucullus <note>Lucius Licinius Lucullus (c. 118–57 BC) was a Roman general famous for his extreme luxury and magnificent villas</note> comes to mind: that a noble man ought not to be in a worse condition than cranes and swallows <note>who migrate to find the best climate</note>. However, we shall report those things which reason approves as well-moderated in every respect. I remember from Aemilius Probus <note>Often confused in the Renaissance with Cornelius Nepos, a Roman biographer</note>, the historian, that among the Greeks it was not customary for wives to be present except at the banquets of close relatives, and that there were certain parts of the houses where the women sat, which no man was permitted to enter except for the closer kinsmen.

# Book V. On the works of individuals. Folio 78

And truly, where it is appropriate for women to be, I think the places ought to be no different than those dedicated to religion and purity. Furthermore, I would wish for elegant lodgings of this kind to be assigned to girls and virgins, so that in their delicacy they might keep themselves within such a chamber with less boredom. <margin>Room.</margin> A most useful matron shall sit nearby, from where she may understand what each person is doing in the house. But let us follow what is advocated for the ancestral customs of each. For a husband and wife, separate sleeping quarters should be provided for each; not only so that a woman who is about to give birth or is unwell is not a nuisance to the husband, but also so that they may obtain more undisturbed summer sleep. For whoever wishes it, each shall have their own door; and besides that, a shared back door <note>original: "posticulum"</note> shall be available, through which they can seek each other out without an intermediary. Under the wife's chamber, a wardrobe <term>vestiaria<gloss>a room for storing clothing and textiles</gloss></term> shall be prepared; under the husband's, a library cell. Parents of a weary age who need leisure and rest shall have a warm, sheltered sleeping area, set apart from all the noise of the family and outsiders. Above all, they shall have the <margin>Look to happiness</margin> happiness of a small hearth, and whatever else the grace of a weary mind and body requires. Under <insert>beautiful</insert> this chamber shall be the silver-storage cell. In this area, the young boys and <margin>The Family</margin> youths will be placed. In the wardrobe, the young girls. In the nearest area, the nurses shall stay the night. <margin>We shall place the guest</margin> We shall place the guest in that part which is nearest to the vestibule, so that they may more freely receive visitors who come to greet them, and disturb the rest of the family less. Boys of noble birth <note>original: "praetextati"; referring to children wearing the toga praetexta</note> shall stay opposite or not far from the guest, for the sake of enjoying and fostering familiarity. The guest shall have a sub-chamber where he may store more secret and precious things, and return to them in private at his will. For the noble boy, there shall be an armory cell beneath his chamber. The overseers and servants shall be separated from the quarters of the free-born in such a way that a decent and suitable place is assigned according to each person's duty. Maidservants and chamberlains, permitted in their own places, shall not be further away than is necessary to hear instantly and be ready at the commands of the one ordering. The steward of the dining room <note>original: "curator triclinii"</note> shall possess access to the wine cellar and the pantry. Those who care for the four-legged animals shall sleep near the stables. The master's horses shall be separated from the pack animals; and they shall be kept in a place where they do not offend the house with stenches or disturb each other with brawls, or where any fire hazard might cause harm. <margin>On wheat and seed</margin> Wheat and seed rot from moisture, turn pale from heat, are thinned by being moved about, and <margin>and on preserving seed.</margin> are spoiled by contact with lime. Therefore, wherever you decide they must be stored—whether in caves, or pits, or on a boarded floor, or heaped on the bare ground—take care that they are kept in a very dry and thoroughly fresh place. Josephus is a witness <note>referring to the historian Flavius Josephus, who recorded finding ancient, preserved stores of grain at the fortress of Masada</note> that grain was found whole and intact at Sebaste <note>The text says "Siboli," likely a corruption of Sebaste or referring to a specific site in Judea</note> after a hundred years from when it had been buried. There are those who think barley is not spoiled by a warm place; yet after a year it is more quickly spoiled. Natural philosophers <note>original: "phisici"</note> affirm that bodies are corrupted by moisture in one way, and corrupted by heat in another.
