All things are spoiled by inconsistency in the air; for this reason, all blasts of wind should be kept out. Furthermore, they say that fruits are disfigured with wrinkles by the north wind. <margin>The Wine Cellar.</margin> They approve of a wine cellar that is subterranean and enclosed; however, there are some wines that languish in the shade. Wine is disturbed when touched by any winds coming from the east, south, or west, especially in winter and spring; during the rising of the Dog Star <note>The "caniculae syderis" refers to the hottest days of summer when the star Sirius rises.</note>, it is even moved by the north wind; it dries out in the sun's rays, grows dull by the influence of the moon, and becomes soft and faint by movement. Wine is a greedy taker of scents; it is weakened and ruined by a stench. It lasts for years in a dry, cold, and constant state. Columella <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella, a Roman writer on agriculture whose works were rediscovered in the Renaissance.</note> says: "As long as the wine remains cold, so long will it remain good." Therefore, place the wine cellar in a stable location, free from the rumbling of carts; turn its side and windows from the east toward the north. Cleanse away, drive far off, and completely exclude all filth and foul-smelling things: dampness, thick vapor, smoke, garden exhalations from onions, cabbage, figs, or wild figs. Level the floor of the cellar with a pavement like that used for open-air courts; sink a small pit in the middle so that if anything is spilled due to a defect in a jar, you may collect it. There are those who make jars of cement and masonry. <margin>Jars.</margin> But the larger the jars <term>dolia<gloss>large earthenware storage vessels, often partially buried in the ground</gloss></term>, the sharper and stronger the wine will be. <margin>Oil Storage.</margin> Oil-rooms love warm shadows; they hate cold breezes; furthermore, they are tainted by smoke and soot. <margin>Manure Pits.</margin> Let those impure things be set aside—though they say manure pits <term>sterquilinia<gloss>heaps or pits for dung and refuse</gloss></term> should be deep, where you may store new manure in some and old in others. They are usually enjoyed in a damp place and emptied by the winds. Let this be for things that fear fire, such as the hayloft; and let things that are offensive to sight and smell be driven away and banished from the land. In a manure heap made of oak, serpents will not arise. I do not think this should be passed over. For what evil is this, that in the field we place manure pits in a hidden and secluded spot, so that the stench does not offend the farm family; yet under our roofs, and almost under our pillows in the primary chambers—where we otherwise seek undisturbed rest—we choose to have private latrines, which are storehouses of the most pestilential stench.

¶ The difference between the villa of the wealthy and an urban lodging; that the buildings of the poorer sort should approach those of the wealthy as much as their resources permit; and that one should build more for summer than for winter use.

### Chapter XVIII.

**B**ut the villa and the urban lodgings of the wealthy differ among themselves in this: that for the fortunate, the villa is a summer resort, while they use urban roofs to endure the winters <note>original: "brumas," referring to the winter solstice or the shortest days of the year.</note> more comfortably. Accordingly, from the countryside, they capture every pleasantness of light, breeze, space, and view; from the city, they seek shaded and softer delights. It is enough, therefore, if what is suitable for civic use is provided within the city with dignity and healthfulness; however, as far as the narrowness of the locations and the abundance of light permit, urban houses will seize for themselves all the charm and pleasantness of a villa. They will indeed have, besides roomy recesses <note>original: "laxitatem sinus," referring to wide, comfortable interior spaces or architectural bays.</note>, also a portico, a place for walking, a carriage-drive, and the delights of gardens and such. 

But if that is less possible on level ground, they will provide proper spaces for the rooms even by piling buildings one on top of the other. The nature of the place permitting, underground areas will be dug out, in which you may place liquids <note>such as wine or oil</note>, firewood, and services alike; upon these, more honorable parts will be built. And yet other buildings may also be added to these if necessary, until there is abundant provision for the family's uses. The primary parts will be assigned to primary uses, and the more dignified parts to the more dignified uses. Finally, he will ensure that distinct and ready places are prepared, in which the harvest or fruits, as well as tools and finally all the household goods <term>supellectilis<gloss>a broad Latin term for domestic furniture, utensils, and equipment</gloss></term>, may be kept. # Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

Where they <note>Referring to valuable household goods or tools.</note> cannot be kept under lock and key, great care must be taken that they are kept in sight; and all the more so the less frequently they are to be used. For a thing that is seen every day clearly has less to fear from a thief. Building projects of a more modest sort, as far as their resources allow, will claim for themselves examples of the elegance of the wealthy to imitate; yet this moderation should be applied: that they never wish to put considerations of profit after pleasure. Therefore, the villa of such a man will look after the ox and the flock not much less than the wife. He will want a dovecote, a fishpond, and things of that kind for profit, not for luxury; yet he will prepare the villa a little better so that the mistress of the house may dwell there more willingly and become accustomed to looking after domestic affairs diligently. However, he will not look out for utility and profit without first consulting the health of the residents. Celsus <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus, a Roman encyclopedist known for his medical treatise "De Medicina."</note> advised that when it is necessary to change the air, you should do so in winter; for we become accustomed to enduring a heavy sky with less danger during the winter solstice <note>original: "bruma."</note> than in summer. But we seek out the villa most especially in summer. Therefore, care must be taken that the site is, indeed, by far the healthiest.

Within the city, under his lodgings, he will consider it more conducive to his hopes and desires to have a profitable shop rather than a well-appointed dining room; and he will seize a corner at a crossroads, a frontage in the forum, or a visible turn along a military road. He will be troubled by almost no other care than to hunt for customers by displaying the allurements of his wares. For internal works, he will use materials not indecently: sun-dried brick, wattle-and-daub, and <term>chaff-mixed mortar</term> <note>original: "creta acerata materia," a mixture of clay or lime with chaff or straw used for insulation and binding.</note>. In the exterior parts, however, he will consider that it is not always granted to have a frugal and convenient neighbor; for that reason, he will encircle the house with a wall strong enough against the injuries of men and the elements. He will place the bordering alleys either so wide that they are quickly dried by the breeze, or so narrow that the runoff from the eaves of both houses may be caught and discharged by a single channel. During rains, alleys of this sort, and even more so the channels themselves, shall be steeply sloped, so that water does not stand or flow back, but is cleared away as quickly as possible by the shortest path.

As for the rest of these matters, those which seem worth repeating in summary <margin>Note the things that are summarized here.</margin> from what we dealt with in the first book are these: Which parts of the building ought to be immune to the accidents of fire; which are exposed to the injuries of the weather; which ought to be more secluded; and which should lack noise.

**Let them be vaulted.** It is very pleasing for all ground-floor dwellings to be vaulted; those built above ground-floor rooms will be made healthier by the presence of a floor <note>original: "contignatione," referring to a timber-framed floor that separates the living space from ground dampness.</note>. Rooms for which light is useful at twilight, such as the greeting room, the walkway, and especially the library, should face the equinoctial east. Whatever fears moths, fading, mold, or rust—such as clothing, books, weapons, seeds, and all foodstuffs—should face south and west...

Against the heat, many things are required, but even then they do not always help much. Therefore, for winter rooms, let the area be modest, the height modest, and the fittings modest; for summer, on the other hand, have everything wide and open in every part. Make the room a seeker of cool breezes, but exclude the sun and the heat-blasts sent by the sun; a large volume of air enclosed in a wide hall, along with many bodies of water gathered together, keeps cool longer.

The designs and materials of works, the craftsman’s hand, and what seemed to pertain to the construction of public and private buildings—both sacred and profane—insofar as they were fit to withstand the damage of the seasons and adapted to their various uses according to the requirements of places, times, people, and circumstances, we have completed in the five previous books. Therefore, since things were so, I could not help but think often and long about writing a commentary on these matters. During my thinking, I determined that such great matters—so worthy, so useful, and so necessary in the lives of men—which offered themselves freely to a writer, should not be neglected; and I judged it to be the duty of a good and studious man to try to rescue from destruction this branch of learning, which our most wise ancestors always held in the highest esteem. Thus I was in two minds and uncertain of my plan, whether I should proceed or rather leave off.

The author writes of himself here most modestly.

Love for the work and affection for my studies prevailed; and what my talent could not sufficiently provide, ardent study and incredible diligence supplied. There was no ancient work anywhere in which some praise might shine forth that I did not immediately investigate to see if I could learn anything from it. In this way, I lightened the labor of writing with the desire and pleasure of learning. And truly, to gather into one place things so various, so disparate, so scattered, and so foreign to the practice and knowledge of writers—and to review them in a worthy manner, place them in a fitting order, treat them with accurate speech, and demonstrate them with certain reasoning—demands greater ability and learning than I profess to have in myself. Nevertheless, I do not at all regret my effort if I have achieved what I altogether intended: that those who read me should decide that I preferred to be easy to understand in my speaking rather than to appear eloquent. Those who have tried it know better how difficult this one thing is in writing commentaries on such matters than those who have not made the attempt might believe. And unless I am mistaken, what we have written, we have written in such a way that you would not deny it is Latin, and it may be understood well enough. ## On the dignity, grace, delight, beauty, and ornament of buildings; what they are, and how they differ from one another; how they must be built according to a certain rational method of art; and finally, on the parent of the art itself. Chapter II.

**E**OR indeed, it is thought that grace and delight flow from nowhere else but from beauty and ornament. For we see that no one can be found who is so gloomy and slow, so rude and rustic, that he is not moved in a greater way by beautiful things. Among all things, he seeks out the most adorned and leaves the rest behind; he is offended by the ugly, and he rejects everything that is unpolished or neglected. And however much ornament he perceives to be missing from a thing, he admits that it lacks just that much in grace and dignity. 
<margin>Ornament is to be sought</margin>Beauty, therefore, is most worthy and especially to be sought by those who wish to make their works anything but <margin>beautiful.</margin> unpleasant. How much our ancestors—who were the most prudent of men—believed was owed to this matter is proven by all their other achievements: their laws, their military service, their religion, and the entire Republic. It is incredible to say how much care they took to ensure these things were most highly adorned, as if they wished to show their judgment: that those very things without which human life could hardly exist would be a tasteless and saltless business if the display and pomp of ornament were removed. When we look at the heavens and their miraculous works, we certainly admire the gods more because they are beautiful than because we perceive them to be useful. Or why should I pursue these examples? Nature itself, as may be seen everywhere, does not cease daily to revel in an excess of beautiful pleasures—to say nothing of other things—even in the painting of flowers. But if there is any thing in which these qualities are desired, surely a building is such that it can in no way lack them without offending both the expert and the ignorant. For why should we be moved by a shapeless and disjointed pile of stones, except that the larger it becomes, the more we condemn the waste of expense, and detest the thoughtless lust for heaping up stones? To have satisfied necessity is a light and very small thing; to have provided for convenience is ungrateful if the inelegance of the work gives offense. Added to this is the fact that this one quality of which we speak brings the greatest help to convenience and even to permanence. For who will not affirm that he lives more comfortably when he finds himself within adorned walls rather than neglected ones? Or what else is so hardened that it could be achieved by any...

<meta>This page continues Alberti’s discussion on the necessity of beauty in architecture. In the previous section, he argued that beauty is not merely a luxury but a fundamental requirement. Here, he provides his famous definitions of "beauty" and "ornament," establishing that beauty is an inherent, mathematical harmony, while ornament is a secondary, added layer.</meta>

# Leon Battista Alberti: On the Art of Building

No work of human art will ever be so well-fortified as to be entirely safe from human malice. Yet 
<margin>The power of beauty.</margin>
**beauty** will even compel a hostile enemy to temper his anger and allow the work to remain inviolate. Indeed, I would go so far as to say that no work is as safe from human injury, or will remain as unscathed, as one distinguished by dignity and grace of form. To this end, every care, every diligence, and every calculation of expense must be directed: so that whatever you build is not only useful and convenient, but above all highly adorned and thus most pleasing. In this way, those who behold it would wish that no expense had been spent elsewhere so much as upon that very place.

But what beauty and ornament are in themselves, or how they differ from one another, we might perhaps understand more clearly in our minds than I can explain in words. Nevertheless, for the sake of brevity, we shall define them thus: **beauty** is a <term>certain reasoned harmony</term> <note>original: *concinnitas*; Alberti’s term for the perfect integration of parts based on mathematical ratios</note> of all the parts within the body to which they belong, such that nothing could be added, diminished, or altered without making it less pleasing. This is a great and divine thing, in the pursuit of which all the powers of art and intellect are consumed; it is rarely granted even to Nature herself to produce something that is completely absolute and perfect in every part. "How few," says the character in Cicero, "are the beautiful youths <note>original: *ephebus*; a term for a young man of military age</note> to be found in Athens!" That observer of forms understood that there was something missing, or something in excess, in those he did not approve of—something that did not harmonize with the most beautiful principles. If I am not mistaken, had **ornaments** been applied to these, they would have contributed by masking or covering whatever was deformed, or by grooming and polishing the more graceful parts, so that the unpleasing aspects would offend less and the lovely ones would delight more. 

If this is accepted, then **ornament** will be, as it were, a kind of subsidiary light to beauty, or even a complement to it. From this, I believe it is clear that beauty is suffused throughout the entire body of that which is beautiful, as if it were its own innate quality; ornament, however, has the character of something attached and added rather than innate. 

Again, let me proceed in this way. Those who build in such a way that they wish their works to be approved—as those who possess any wit <note>original: *salem*; literally "salt," used here as a metaphor for intelligence or taste</note> ought to—must surely be moved by a certain reason. Indeed, to do anything according to a certain reason is the very essence of art. Who then will deny that correct and approved building can be derived from anything but art? Since this very part of the work, which deals with beauty and ornament, is the primary part of all, there will surely be some certain and constant reason and art behind it, and he who neglects it is most foolish. 

Yet there are some who do not approve of these things, saying that the judgment by which we evaluate beauty and all building is a loose and wandering opinion, and that the form of buildings is varied and changeable according to each person's whim...

<summary>Alberti defines beauty as an inherent, perfect harmony of parts (concinnitas) and ornament as an added quality that can mask defects. He argues that architectural beauty is not a matter of subjective whim but is governed by a rational, teachable art.</summary>

Book VI. On Ornament. Folio 82.

to be bound by the rules of the arts. This is a common fault of ignorance: to claim that what you do not know is of no value. I have decided that this error must be removed; however, I do not take it upon myself to think that we must investigate too extensively the origins from which the arts first flowed, by what reasoning they were guided, or by what nourishment they grew. Let it suffice to say, as they do, that the parent of the arts was chance and observation <note>original: *casum atque aduersionem*; literally "accident and turning toward [observation]"</note>, their foster-child was usage and experience, and they grew to maturity through knowledge and reasoning. Thus they say that over a thousand years, through the efforts of a thousand thousand men, medicine was discovered; likewise, navigation and almost all arts of this kind grew through small additions.

The adolescence of the art of building among the Asians. Luxury among the Greeks. But its flowery maturity among the Italians, taken up with the care and administration of kings. Some of its precepts are universal, some particular.

### Chapter III.

**A**rchitecture—so far as we can perceive from the monuments of the ancients—spent its first adolescence, so to speak, in a profusion of luxury in Asia <note>By "Asia," Alberti refers to the ancient Near East, including the Assyrians and Babylonians</note>. Soon after, it flourished among the Greeks. Finally, it attained its most proven maturity in Italy. For this seems likely to me: those kings, abounding in the flow of resources and leisure, when they looked upon themselves, their wealth, the majesty of their scepter, and their greatness, understood that they had need of grander roofs and more honorable walls. They began to pursue and collect everything that contributed to that end, so that they might use the largest and most honorable buildings. They perhaps placed roofs using the largest trees and took to building walls from nobler stone; the work earned admiration and even favor. 

From this, they perhaps sensed that vast works were praised; and since each one thought it especially the duty of a king to do those things which private citizens could not—delighted by the sheer scale of the works—the kings themselves began to compete more zealously among one another, reaching even the madness of raising pyramids <note>Alberti often contrasts the "madness" of sheer size (like the Pyramids) with the "reasoned harmony" of true beauty</note>. I believe, indeed, that the practice of building provided the occasion for them to see, in large part, what difference number, order, position, and appearance <note>original: *facieve*; appearance or outward form</note> make; they would have combined one or two of these things as they were added. And so, being delighted by more pleasing things, they learned to reject those that were less harmonious <note>original: *inconcinniora*; things lacking *concinnitas* or reasoned harmony</note>. 

Greece followed: a land that flourished with fine and learned talents and burned with the desire for self-adornment. Along with other things, they took care to build temples above all. From this, they began to inspect the works of the Assyrians and Egyptians more diligently, until they understood that in works of this kind, the skill of the craftsmen was more to be praised...

<meta>This page continues the historical narrative of architecture's development, specifically focusing on how the Greeks refined the art through intellectual rigour and how the Romans later balanced this refined beauty with their traditional sense of practical utility and vast imperial resources.</meta>

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

...hands than royal riches. For indeed, being able to do great things is the mark of the fortunate; but to produce things that the skilled cannot find fault with belongs to those who deserve praise. For this reason, Greece took it upon itself as its duty to strive, in its works, so that those whom it could not equal in material wealth, it might surpass, so far as was in its power, through the gifts of intellect <term>intellect|Alberti uses the word *ingenium*, referring to innate talent, creative power, and mental acuity</term>. 

And it began, just as with other arts, to seek out and draw this art of building from the very bosom of nature, to handle it in its entirety, and to know it through and through with sagacious skill, looking ahead and weighing what distinguishes those buildings that are praised from those that are less favored. In that investigation, it omitted nothing. It tried everything, surveying and retracing the footprints of nature. By mixing like with like, straight with curved, and the obvious with the more obscure, it looked forward as if a third thing might arise from the union of male and female <note>Alberti frequently uses biological metaphors to explain architectural harmony and the "marriage" of different design elements</note>, which would fulfill the promise of the task at hand. 

Nor did it cease to consider individual parts over and over again, even in the smallest details: how the right side might match the left, the upright with the level, or the near with the distant. It added, subtracted, and balanced the large with the small, the similar with the dissimilar, the first with the last, until it discovered that one quality is praised in those things built for endurance over time <note>original: *vetustatem perferendam*, referring to structural longevity</note>, while another is praised in those built for nothing so much as for beauty <term>beauty|*Venustas*, a classical term for aesthetic grace and charm</term>. 

So much for the Greeks. Italy, meanwhile, following its innate frugality, first established that the same principles apply to a building as to a living creature. For instance, in a horse, it recognized that the very shape of the limbs which one approves for functional use is almost always the most convenient for the animal's purposes; thus it believed that the grace of form <note>original: *gratiam formae*</note> is never found excluded or separated from the proven convenience of use. 

But once dominion over nations was won, Rome burned with no less a passion than Greece for the adornment of the city and itself. Within thirty years, what had been the most beautiful house in the entire city could no longer claim even the hundredth place. Since there was an incredible abundance of talented men practiced in this field, I find that there were seven hundred architects in Rome at one time, whose works we can scarcely praise enough for their merits. 

<margin>Tatius gave the people of Ostia baths built with a hundred Numidian columns.</margin> 
And as the power of the Empire supplied sufficient means to inspire universal admiration, they report that a certain Tatius <note>likely referring to a Roman official or benefactor, though the name may vary in different historical manuscripts</note> donated baths to the people of Ostia at his own private expense, constructed with one hundred Numidian columns <note>Numidian marble, or *giallo antico*, was a prestigious yellow-tinted marble highly prized in Rome</note>. Given these circumstances, it was decided to combine the grandeur of the most powerful kings with ancient frugality, so that parsimony would not detract from utility, nor would utility be hindered by a lack of resources. In both cases, whatever could be devised for elegance and beauty...

<summary>Alberti describes the transition of architecture from Greek intellectual refinement to Roman practical grandeur, highlighting how the Romans combined functional utility with immense material wealth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the evolution of architectural theory, moving from the intellectual foundations laid by the Greeks to the practical and ornamental mastery achieved by the Romans and the ancient inhabitants of Italy.</meta>

<page-num>LXXXIII</page-num>
->Book VI. On Ornament. Folio LXXXIII.<-

...might be added. Moreover, through unceasing care and diligence for building projects, this architectural art was rendered so thoroughly analyzed that it contained nothing so recondite, so hidden, or so deeply concealed that it was not tracked down, drawn out, and brought into the light—the gods being willing and the art itself offering no resistance. For since the art of building had an ancient home in Italy, especially among the Etruscans <note>The Etruscans were a powerful civilization in ancient Italy (modern Tuscany) before the rise of Rome, known for their advanced engineering and temple designs</note>—among whom, besides those royal wonders of which we read, there remain very ancient and highly esteemed written records of monuments and temples built for the use of old Etruria—since, I say, it had an ancient home in Italy and realized how greatly it was desired, this art seemed to strive with all its might to ensure that the world, which all other virtues had already honored, might be rendered far more admirable through its own ornaments. 

Therefore, the art offered itself to be thoroughly understood and mastered. It deemed it an utter disgrace that the citadel of the world and the glory of nations <note>Alberti is referring to the city of Rome at the height of its power</note> should be equaled in the splendor of its buildings by those peoples whom it had already surpassed in every other form of virtuous achievement. And why should I mention here the porticos, temples, harbors, theaters, and the gigantic works of the public baths <term>public baths|Latin: *thermae*, massive Roman bathing complexes that served as social and cultural hubs</term>? In these, they achieved such a level of wonder that even the most skilled architects of foreign nations, when beholding them in person, would sometimes declare that such things were impossible to build. 

What more? I will say no more than this: even in the construction of sewers <note>original: *cloacis*; Alberti notes that even the utilitarian Roman sewer system, like the Cloaca Maxima, was built with aesthetic consideration</note>, they could not endure a lack of beauty. They were so delighted by ornaments that they considered it a most noble thing to pour out the very resources of the Empire for that purpose alone—building, of course, so that they might have structures to which ornaments could be appropriately applied. 

Thus, from the examples of our predecessors, the advice of experts, and the frequent practice of creating admirable works, a most complete knowledge now exists. From this knowledge, highly tested precepts have been derived; anyone who wishes—as we all should—not to be utterly incompetent in the art of building should by no means neglect these rules in any part. 

It is my task, having undertaken this province of study, to collect these precepts and explain them to the best of my intellectual ability <term>intellectual ability|Latin: *ingenium*, meaning innate talent and creative power</term>. Some of these rules concern the universal beauty and ornament of the entire building as a whole; others follow the individual parts, piece by piece. The first set of rules is drawn from the very heart of philosophy and has been adapted to guide and shape the method and path of this art. The next set, arising from the practical knowledge we have mentioned, has been "hewn," so to speak, to the standard of philosophy to produce the systematic order of the craft. I shall speak first of those matters that relate more directly to the technical skill of the art; I shall use those that encompass the subject as a whole as an epilogue.

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

## All beauty and ornament in things arises from talent, hand, or nature; and though a region itself can scarcely be decorated by the hand or talent of man, many other things, both worthy of admiration and hard to believe, can be aided and adorned by human industry. ### Chapter IV.

<margin>
Repetition from the first book.
</margin>

**T**hose things that please in the most beautiful and ornate objects indeed arise either from the invention and reasoning of the mind, or from the hand of the craftsman, or are instilled in the things themselves by nature. To the mind <note>original: "ingenij" – referring to the intellectual design or "wit" of the architect</note> belong choice, distribution, arrangement, and the like, which bring dignity to the work. To the hand belong piling up, joining, pruning, trimming, polishing, and similar tasks which bring grace to the work. In things derived from nature, there will be weight, lightness, density, purity, resistance against age, and similar qualities, which bring admiration to the work. These three must be adapted to the parts according to the use and function of each.

There are many ways to categorize the parts to be noted. But here it pleases us to divide the building thus: either by that in which all buildings agree, or by that in which they are different. From the first book, we understood that every building requires a region, a plot, partitioning, a wall, a roof, and an opening. In these things, therefore, they agree. They differ in that some are sacred, some profane <note>In the Renaissance context, "profane" simply means secular or non-religious buildings</note>, some public, some private; some are prepared for necessity, others for pleasure, and the like. 

Let us begin with those in which they agree. As for the region, it is hardly clear what grace or dignity the hand or talent of man can bring to it, unless perhaps he contributes this: if we imitate those who devised the superstitious wonders of works about which we read. Wise men, however, do not blame such people if they set out to make things useful, and they do not praise them if the works are unnecessary. And rightly so. 

<margin>
Stasicrates or Dinocrates promised to make an image of Alexander out of Mount Athos.
</margin>

For who would dare—whoever he might have been, whether Stasicrates as Plutarch reports, or Dinocrates as Vitruvius <note>Vitruvius was a Roman architect whose 1st-century BCE treatise was the primary inspiration for Alberti</note> reports—who promised he would carve an image of Alexander the Great out of Mount Athos, in whose hand a city would sit upon the mountain, capable of holding ten thousand men? But as for Queen Nitocris <note>A legendary queen of Babylon mentioned by Herodotus</note>, who by vast excavations and a great circuit forced the Euphrates—having been turned three times—to approach the village of the Assyrians, I shall indeed praise her if she rendered the region both most fortified by the depth of the trench and most fertile by the abundance of waters. 

But let such things delight most powerful kings. Let them join seas to seas, having cut through the space that lies between both. Let them level mountains with valleys. Let them create new islands and restore islands again to the continent; let them leave nothing for others to imitate, and in that way recommend themselves to posterity. Certainly, where...

Indeed, the more their works are joined with utility, the more they will be approved. The ancients were accustomed to bring dignity to places and groves, as well as to a region, through religion. We read that all of Sicily was sacred to Ceres <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture and grain</note>; but let those things be passed over. It will be most pleasing if a region is endowed with some wonderful thing that is singular in rarity, admirable in virtue, and outstanding in its kind—as, for instance, if it happens to have a climate milder than all others and persisting with incredible consistency. <margin>Take note</margin> Such as at Meroë <note>An ancient city on the Nile; classical authors often claimed its inhabitants lived to extreme old age</note>, where it is said men live as long as they wish. <margin>as long as they wish.</margin> Especially if that region produces something seen nowhere else, and which is desirable and healthy for the human race. Such is the land that yields frankincense, cinnamon, or balsam. Especially if some divine power dwells within it. <margin>The island of Euboea.</margin> Such as in the soil of the island of Euboea, which they say is entirely immune to everything harmful. 

Since the plot <note>original: "Area" — the specific piece of ground where the building stands</note> is a part of the region, all these things will honor it and contribute to the ornament of the region; but many more ready conveniences are provided by nature for making a plot famous than for a region. For there are everywhere promontories, rocks, peaks, volcanic lakes <note>original: "averni" — referring to Lake Avernus or similar craters believed to be entrances to the underworld</note>, caves, springs, and the like, which offer various and manifold reasons for admiration; it is better to build in these places for the sake of inspiring wonder than elsewhere. 

Nor are traces of ancient memory lacking, where time and the condition of things and men have brought about what might move eyes and minds with admiration. I pass over those things: the place where Troy was, and fields soaked with blood like Leuctra, Trasimene <note>Sites of famous ancient battles</note>, and a thousand of that kind. I cannot easily say how much human hands and talent contribute to this matter. I pass over other things that are simpler. <margin>Note: The olive of Neptune and [Minerva]</margin> Such as plane trees carried across the sea even to the island of Diomedes for the sake of decorating the site. And columns, obelisks, and trees planted by the greatest men, which posterity might venerate. Such as the olive tree that stood for a long time at the citadel in Athens, planted by Neptune and Minerva. I also pass over things preserved for many ages and handed down by our ancestors to posterity. Such as the terebinth tree <note>A species of Mediterranean flowering plant</note> at Hebron, which they say lasted from the beginning of the world until the time of the historian Josephus. 

This will serve beautifully to honor the matter in an exceeding way: an elegant and very clever device, namely those things forbidden by law—such as that no male should enter the temple of the Good Goddess <note>original: "Bonae Deae" — a Roman goddess whose rites were strictly restricted to women</note>, nor the shrine of Diana at the Patrician Portico. <margin>Note how they were honored in ceremony and religion.</margin> And at Tanagra, that no woman should enter the grove; nor likewise should anyone penetrate the inner parts of the Temple of Jerusalem; and further, that no one except the priest, and only for the sake of sacrifice and...

As for the other things which generally pertain to the beautification of the **area** <note>The ground-plot or platform of a building.</note>—such as the perimeter, the outline, the mounding, the leveling, the stabilization, and the like—I have nothing further to say, except that you should seek them from the first and likewise the third of the preceding books. ## A brief repetition on partition; and on the wall, the roof, and the remaining material: their composition, order, and the method by which they are to be adorned. Chapter 5.

**P**artition <note>The "distribution" or layout of rooms and spaces within a building's plan.</note>, likewise, even if it was treated for the most part in the first book, we will nevertheless repeat it very briefly in this way. In every matter, the primary ornament is to be free of all **indecency** <note>original: "indecentia" — referring to a lack of fitness, proportion, or appropriateness for the building's function.</note>. A partition will therefore be decent if it is not interrupted, not confused, not disturbed, not dissolved, and not compacted from ill-fitting parts; and it will consist of members that are not too many, not too minute, not too vast, and not too disso[lute]...

<meta>This page follows Alberti’s discussion of the psychological and historical power of architectural elements. He is now transitioning into the technical and aesthetic principles of "Concinnitas" (harmony) and the use of rare, monumental materials—particularly monolithic stones—to evoke awe. -># Leon Battista Alberti: On the Art of Building<-

...[parts that are] small and deformed, not as if they were torn away and scattered from the rest of the body; but instead, everything shall be so defined—by nature, utility, and the management of things to be done—and so explained by order, number, size, placement, and form, that we may understand no part of the entire work to have been made without some necessity, without great convenience, and without a most pleasing <term>harmony</term> <note>original: "concinnitate" — This is Alberti's central aesthetic concept, referring to the perfect integration of parts so that nothing can be added or taken away without destroying the whole.</note> of the parts. For indeed, if the entire partitioning <note>The distribution and arrangement of spaces within a building.</note> agrees well with these principles, then the pleasantness and grace of the ornaments will not only be established correctly but will shine forth more clearly. If it does not agree, the work will undoubtedly be unable to preserve any dignity. Therefore, it is necessary that the whole formation of the members be spread out and perfected toward a certain consensus of necessity and convenience; so that the delight comes not so much from the fact that these or those parts are present, but rather that those very parts are placed there in that specific order, site, connection, arrangement, and shape. 

Regarding the decorating of the wall and roof, there will be more room for you to display the rarest gifts of nature, the skill of art, the diligence of the craftsman, and the power of genius. And if perhaps the opportunity is given that you can <margin>Osiris built two golden temples.</margin> imitate that ancient Osiris <note>The Egyptian god of the afterlife, whom Renaissance humanists often viewed as a historical king and bringer of civilization.</note>, who they say built two golden temples: one to the Celestial Jupiter, the other to the Royal Jupiter. Or perhaps you may be able to raise a stone of greatest size, beyond human belief, such as the one Semiramis <note>The legendary Queen of Babylon, famous for her massive building projects.</note> brought down from the mountains of Arabia: twenty cubits wide and up to one hundred and fifty long. Or if such a magnitude of stones is granted that you can complete from it some entire part of the whole work, such as they say existed in Egypt: <margin>A shrine made from a single, whole stone.</margin> a shrine at the temple of Latona <note>The goddess Leto. Herodotus describes this monolithic shrine at Buto.</note>, forty cubits wide at the front, carved from a single, whole stone, and covered by another single stone. 

Truly, such a thing will bring much admiration to the work, and all the more so if it was brought from a foreign land by a difficult path, like the one Herodotus <note>The 5th-century BC Greek historian, often called the "Father of History."</note> writes was sought from the city of Elephantine <note>An island in the Nile that served as a border city and a source of granite.</note>: more than twenty cubits wide and fifteen high, dragged for a journey of twenty days. It will also contribute excellently to the logic of the ornaments if a stone worthy of admiration is placed in a noble and distinguished location. At the island of Chemmis in Egypt, there is a shrine not so much wonderful because it is roofed with a single stone, but because that stone was placed upon walls so high and of so many cubits. The rarity and elegance of the stone itself will also provide ornament: for example, if it is of that kind <margin>A translucent statue.</margin> of marble <note>likely "Phengites," a translucent stone used by Nero.</note> from which they say the Prince Nero built the Temple of Fortune in his "Golden House": pure, white, and translucent, so that even with no doors open, the light seemed to be enclosed within. Finally, of that...

<meta>This page continues Alberti's discussion from Book VI, moving from the general necessity of harmony (concinnitas) in architecture to the specific methods of wall decoration and the engineering required to handle the massive materials used in such ornaments.</meta>

...ways everything will contribute. But whatever these things may be, they will be inept unless an accurate order and measure is preserved in the composition. For each individual thing must be reduced to a number, so that like corresponds to like: right to left, top to bottom; nothing should be mixed in that would disturb either the objects or the order. Everything must be leveled with equal lines at fixed angles. Indeed, one may see that sometimes humble material treated with art brings more grace than noble material piled up elsewhere in confusion. Take the wall at Athens, which <term>Thucydides</term> <note>Greek historian (c. 460–400 BC). Alberti is referencing his account of the walls of Athens being rebuilt in haste using any available material, including gravestones, after the Persian Wars.</note> writes was built in a hurried labor: who will say it is beautiful for being filled with the ruin of statues seized even from tombs? On the other hand, it is pleasing to look at walls piled up in the rustic buildings of the ancients—made of irregular, small stones and rubble-work—where they stand in level rows, distinguished by alternating white and black colors, so that, given the modesty of the work, nothing more is desired. But these things perhaps relate more to that part of the wall called <term>cladding</term> <note>original: "crustatio" — the ornamental outer layer or veneer of a wall, such as marble or stucco.</note> than to the raising of the main walls themselves. Furthermore, all materials shall be so distributed that nothing is begun except by the design of art and deliberation; nothing added except by the logic of the undertaking; nothing left as finished that has not itself been worked and perfected with the utmost diligence and care. But the primary ornament of the wall and roof—especially a vaulted roof—will be the cladding itself, always excepting the colonnade. This will indeed be of many types: pure <term>stucco</term> <note>original: "albaria"</note>, decorated stucco, paintings, wood paneling, <term>marquetry</term> <note>original: "sectilis" — work made of pieces cut to fit together, like mosaic or inlay</note>, glass, and mixtures consisting of these parts.

<margin>Archimedes.</margin>

...they might not obscurely perceive for themselves. From <term>Pliny</term> <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the *Natural History*, a primary source for ancient technology.</note> I find it thus:
<margin>Obelisks transported.</margin>
that an obelisk was brought down to Thebes by allies through a canal drawn from the Nile. It was done by a wonderful method: they sent ships full of small bricks <note>original: "laterculo" — referring to small baked bricks used as ballast.</note> under the stone; soon, by emptying them, the ships rose, so that by some art of transport they might lift and carry the burden of the stone. From the historian <term>Ammianus Marcellinus</term> <note>A 4th-century Roman historian who described the transport of the Lateran Obelisk to Rome.</note> I find it thus: an obelisk was brought from the Nile placed on a ship of three hundred rowers, and dragged from the third milestone of the city from the Ostian gate into the <term>Circus Maximus</term> <note>The largest stadium in ancient Rome, often adorned with Egyptian obelisks.</note>. In erecting it, many thousands of men labored; the entire Circus was filled with machines of the highest beams and most massive ropes. From <term>Vitruvius</term> <note>The most influential Roman writer on architecture (1st century BC).</note> we read that <margin>Chersiphron</margin> the father and Metagenes the son moved columns and architraves <note>original: "epistilia" — the horizontal beams resting on the columns.</note> to Ephesus by a device borrowed from the rollers <note>original: "chylindris"</note> which the ancients ordered to be used for leveling the ground. For he fixed and secured with lead into each end of the stones iron pins projecting out, which stood out as the axle for wheels; he drove wheels on either side onto these axles, of such great width that the stones themselves hung from those iron axles; thus, by the turning of the wheels, they were moved and transported. They say the Egyptian <margin>Chemmis</margin> <note>Likely referring to the Pharaoh Cheops or the city of Chemmis associated with stone-working.</note>, in constructing a pyramid that was a work more than six <term>stades</term> <note>A Greek unit of distance; six stades is roughly 1,100 meters, here perhaps referring to height or volume in a literary exaggeration.</note> high, brought the most massive stones by means of mounds he had built. <margin>Cheops</margin> <note>OCR: "Cleopas". Referring to the Pharaoh of the Great Pyramid.</note> the son of Rhampsinitus, <term>Herodotus</term> <note>The Greek "Father of History" (5th century BC).</note> writes, in that pyramid for the building of which he had exhausted a hundred thousand men for many years, left steps on the outside, by which the most massive stones were moved using short timbers and suitable machines. Then they also recorded this in writing: elsewhere, most massive stone beams were placed upon high columns in this manner. For in the middle length of the beam, they placed two transverse <term>rollers</term> <note>original: "thorulos" — small cylindrical supports acting as a fulcrum.</note> touching each other; soon, on one end of the beam, they piled baskets full of sand, so that by this pressure the other end, which was bare, would be raised; and the other roller would be left free of weight. Then, by moving the baskets back and forth, and alternately piling them onto the already raised end, and substituting higher rollers as the gap opened wider, they achieved the result that the stone gradually climbed, as if of its own accord. <margin>☛</margin> These things, most briefly collected, we leave to be learned more extensively from the authors themselves. But for the purpose of this work, a few things relevant to the matter must be succinctly repeated. I do not insist here on explaining the nature of weight—that it continually presses down, obstinately seeks the lower parts, resists being raised with all its strength, and never yields its place except as a conquered thing, either overcome by a greater weight or by a powerful contrary force. Nor do I repeat that motions are various: from center to center, around the center...

...and some are carried, others dragged, others pushed, and the like; concerning these inquiries I have written more extensively elsewhere. Let this principle stand among us: weights are never moved more easily than when they descend, for they move of their own accord. They are never moved with more difficulty than when they ascend, for nature resists. There is, however, a third type of motion intermediate between these, which perhaps partakes of the nature of both: it neither moves by its own power nor resists compliance, such as when it is dragged across a level and unimpeded <term>pathway</term> <note>original: "vado" — literally a shallow or ford, used here by Alberti as a metaphor for the surface or track upon which a load is moved.</note>. All other motions are either easier or more difficult depending on how close they are to one or the other of these extremes. By what means immense weights can be moved, the very nature of things seems to have shown in many ways. For one may see that those things which are placed upon a standing column 
<margin>On things to be moved</margin>
are easily disturbed by a light touch; and once they have begun to move toward a fall, they can be restrained by no force at all. Then, one may also observe that rounded columns, the circles of wheels, and rolling things move easily, but if they are rotating, they are difficult to stop; yet if you try to drag these same things so that they do not rotate, they do not follow easily. Furthermore, it is evident that the greatest weights of ships are moved through stagnant waters by a light pull, if you persist in the dragging. Yet if you strike them with <term>battering rams</term> <note>original: "arietes"</note>, they do not move where you wish even with the greatest sudden blow; and conversely, some things move by a sudden and rapid impulse that would otherwise not be displaced without the greatest force of weight. Upon ice, too, heavy things follow the one dragging them without any resistance. Likewise, we see that things tied to a very long rope and suspended are ready for movement across a certain distance. It will be useful to have noticed and imitated the principles of these things; let us go through them briefly. The <term>keel</term> <note>original: "carina" — Alberti uses the nautical term for the bottom of a ship to describe the base of a sledge or the underside of the stone being moved.</note> of the weight must be entirely solid and level: the wider it is, the less it will wear down the underlying pathway; the narrower it is, the more agile it will be, but it will furrow the path and be swallowed up. If there are corners on the keel of the weight, it will use them like claws to grip and resist the path. If the pathway is slippery, firm, level, constant, never dipping, never rising, and never sweating moisture to cause an obstruction, then undoubtedly that weight will have nothing to struggle against or refuse to obey—except for the fact that the weight is naturally a lover of rest, and thus sluggish and stubborn. Perhaps observing things similar to these 
<margin>The saying of Archimedes.</margin>
and reflecting deeply on the power of the matters we have reviewed, <term>Archimedes</term> <note>The famous Greek mathematician and engineer (c. 287–212 BC) known for his work on levers and pulleys.</note> was moved to say: "If a base were given for such a mass, I could certainly move the world." In preparing the keel and the path, we shall conveniently achieve what we seek here. Dra...

<meta>This page continues Alberti's discussion on the mechanics of moving heavy weights. In the previous section, he established the basic principles of motion on level ground. Here, he moves into the practical lubricants and mechanical devices—cylinders, wheels, and pulleys—required to overcome friction and the physical limitations of materials.</meta>

Leon Battista Alberti: On the Art of Building.

For bases will indeed be laid down according to the vastness of the weight, with numerous, firm, and uniform timbers, never rough and never interrupted by joints. Between the <term>keel</term> <note>original: "carinam" — Alberti uses nautical metaphors for architecture; here "keel" refers to the bottom surface of the weight being moved.</note> and the <term>pathway</term> <note>original: "vado" — literally a ford or shallow water; here it means the prepared track or ground.</note>, there must be something intermediate to make the journey slippery. 
<margin>Types of lubrication</margin>
They make it slippery with soap, or tallow, or the lees of oil, or perhaps with a wet wash of chalk. There is also another type of lubrication which is created by substituting <term>cylinders</term> <note>original: "chilindris" — rollers.</note> placed crosswise. If these are many in number, it will be difficult to fit them so they are aligned with the parallel lines and markers used for guiding the path. This alignment is entirely necessary so that they do not become disordered or scrape against the track, shifting the weight to one side; rather, they should follow their duty with a single, harmonious breath. If there are too few of them, they will either fail and shatter under the weight, slowing the progress as they break apart; or, because they touch the underlying surface of the path in only one line and touch the "keel" of the weight above in another single line, the cylinders will be driven in and stuck as if they were penetrating with a sharp blade. This happens because the body of a cylinder is composed of many equal circles stacked one after another. It is a established fact, asserted by mathematicians, that a circle cannot touch a straight line at more than one point. For this reason, we call that single line where the weight presses upon the cylinder the "edge" <note>original: "aciem".</note>. One must provide for these issues by using dense materials and by marking the lines according to a square and a straight edge.

### On pulleys, levers, rollers, wheels and their parts, and the sizes, forms, and shapes most suitable for them. Chapter 7.

**B**ut since, in addition to these, there are also things which are proven by use—wheels, pulleys, screws, and levers—these must be treated more accurately. Indeed, wheels are in many respects similar to rollers. For they always press upon a single point perpendicularly. But this is the difference: rollers are more efficient, whereas wheels are slowed by the friction of their axles. 
<margin>The Wheel.</margin>
The parts of a wheel are three: the outer, widest rim of the circle; the middle axle; and the circle in which the axle is inserted, like a bracelet. Others might perhaps call this the "pole" <note>original: "polum".</note>, but since it stands still in some machines and moves in others, we shall call it—if it be permitted—the <term>axle-sleeve</term> <note>original: "axecla" — likely Alberti’s own term for a bearing or axle-box.</note>. If the wheel turns on a thick axle, it will be moved with greater difficulty; if it turns on a thin one, it will not tolerate the weights. If the outer circumference of the wheels is narrow, it will sink into the path (as we said of the rollers); if it is wide, it will wobble from side to side. And if it must perhaps be turned to the right or the left, 
<margin>Axle-sleeve.</margin>
they obey with difficulty. If the axle-sleeve is more open than is proper, it causes wear by grinding; if it is too tight, it becomes stubborn. The space between the axle and the axle-sleeve ought to be slippery. For one of these acts as the path, and the other as the keel of the weight. 
<margin>The Roller.</margin>
Rollers and wheels are made from elm or holm-oak. Axles are made from holly and cornel-wood.

# Leaf LXXXVIII.
## Book VI. On Ornament.

...or rather an <term>axle-sleeve</term> <note>original: "Axecla" — likely a bearing plate or a metal lining for an axle-hole to reduce wear.</note> is best made of bronze mixed with a third part of tin. <term>Small pulleys</term> <note>original: "Cicleolæ" — literally "little circles" or small wheels.</note> are little wheels. A <term>lever</term> <note>original: "Vectis"</note> follows the spokes of a wheel. But whatever all such things may be—whether they are massive wheels that men turn by walking inside them, or <term>cranes</term> <note>original: "erganæ"</note> or <term>lifting screws</term> <note>original: "cocleæ"</note> in which the lever is of primary importance, or pulleys and anything of that kind—the principle of all of them is derived from the mechanics of the <term>balance</term> <note>original: "libræ" — a set of scales.</note>. They say that Mercury was considered divine mainly for this reason: that he used no hand signals, but used only words to say what he meant so that he was clearly understood. If I fear I cannot achieve that same clarity, I will nonetheless try my best. For I have determined to speak of these things not as a mathematician, but as a <term>craftsman</term> <note>original: "faber"</note>: providing no more than what must not be overlooked.

Let us take a <term>javelin</term> <note>original: "iaculum"</note> in hand for the sake of learning; I would have you consider three spots on it, which I call "points." The two ends are the iron head and the <term>fins</term> <note>original: "pynnulas" — the stabilizing feathers or flights.</note>; the third is the middle <term>throwing-strap</term> <note>original: "amentum" — a leather thong used to impart spin and leverage when throwing.</note>. I call the spaces between these points—from the strap to the ends—"radii." I will not argue why this is so, but the thing itself will be clear through experiment. <margin>☞</margin> For if the strap is fixed in the middle of the shaft, and weights equal to the fins match the iron head, then both ends of the javelin will stand in mutual resistance and be balanced. But if the iron-clad head is perhaps heavier, the fins will be overcome. Yet there will be a certain spot on the javelin closer to the heavier head where, if you move the strap back to it, the weights will immediately balance each other. That will be the point from which this longer radius exceeds the shorter one by as much as this lighter weight is exceeded by the heavier one.

For those who have investigated these matters have found that radii that are not equal are balanced by weights that are not equal, provided that the number of parts collected together from the radius and the weight on the right side corresponds to the opposite numbers on the left. <note>Alberti is describing the Law of the Lever: Equilibrium is reached when the weight multiplied by the distance from the fulcrum is equal on both sides.</note> For if the iron is three units and the fins are two, the radius to the iron must be two, and the other radius to the fins must be three. From this, since this number of five will match the other five <note>original: "numerus quinque alteris quinque" — Alberti uses a simple additive logic (3+2 = 2+3) to illustrate the inverse proportion needed for balance.</note>, the ratios of the radii and weights being equalized, they will rest level and balanced. If the numbers do not match, the side where they exceed will prevail.

I do not overlook this: if equal radii extend from the same strap, they will mark out equal circles in the air as the ends move. But if they are unequal, they will also describe unequal circles. We have said that wheels are contained within circles; thus it is shown that if two contiguous wheels attached to a single axle are moved with one and the same motion, so that when one moves the other does not remain still...

He uses a javelin and its throwing strap as a practical model to demonstrate how shifting a fulcrum allows unequal weights to reach equilibrium.</summary>

<margin>On pulleys.</margin>
...and if one part remains still while the other moves, we will understand what force exists in each based on the length of the spokes in both. One must note the length of the spoke from the middle point of the innermost axis. If these things are sufficiently understood, the entire principle we seek for machines of this kind is clear, especially concerning wheels and the <term>lever</term><note>original: "vectis"</note>. In <term>pulleys</term><note>original: "trocleis" — blocks containing one or more wheels used to redirect force or gain mechanical advantage.</note>, there is a little more for us to consider. For both the rope drawn through the pulley and the <term>sheaves</term><note>original: "orbiculi" — the small wheels inside the pulley block.</note> themselves move along a path in the pulley; in this, there is a "middle motion," which we said was between the most difficult and the easiest, because it neither ascends nor descends, but resists equally upon its own center.

But so that you may understand the reality of the matter: imagine a statue weighing 1,000 pounds <note>original: "M," the Roman numeral for 1,000.</note>. If this hangs from the trunk of a tree tied by a rope, it is certain that this single rope supports the full thousand. Now, attach a pulley to the statue and draw the rope through it—the same rope by which the statue was hanging—and lead it back up to the tree trunk so that it hangs a second time. It is evident that the statue's weight now hangs by a doubled rope, and the pulley is squeezed in the middle by the balance of forces. Continue by adding another pulley to the tree trunk and draw the rope through it as well. I ask you: what portion of the weight will the part of the rope support after being led back up and then drawn through? "Five hundred," you will say <note>original: "V," the Roman numeral for 500.</note>. Do you not then understand that no greater weight can be given to this second pulley by the rope itself than what the rope itself holds? It will have, therefore, 500. I will proceed no further with this example. Up to here, I think it has been sufficiently shown that weight is divided by pulleys, and from this, greater weights can be moved by a smaller force. However many such doublings of the rope there are, that is how many divisions of weight there will be. From this it follows that the more sheaves are used, the more the weight is, as it were, cut up and dispersed into parts, making it easier to handle.

¶ Regarding the pulley and its wheels, regarding weights to be dragged by rope, pushed by lever, or carried by wheel—whether using only one of these methods or several together—it must be approached with skill, experience, and by following examples, yet always proceeding gradually and with mature consideration.

-># Chapter VIII.<-

<margin>The screw.</margin>
**W**e have spoken of the wheel, the pulley, and the lever. Now I would like you to understand that the <term>screw</term><note>original: "coclea" — literally "snail shell," used here for the mechanical screw.</note> consists of <term>threads</term><note>original: "anulis" — literally "rings." Alberti is describing the continuous spiral of a screw as a series of rings.</note> which themselves take up the weight to be supported. If these "rings" were complete circles and not cut so that the end of one joined the beginning of the next, the weight moved upon them would undoubtedly neither ascend nor descend, but would be dragged along a level path through the circuit of the circle. Therefore, by the force of a lever, the weight is forced to glide along the slants of the ring. Again, if these rings were very small in circumference and too close to the center, the weight would be moved by a shorter lever and with less strength. Here I will not remain silent about what...

-># Book VI. On Ornament. Folio LXXXIX.<-

...I did not think I would say more. If you prepare the matter so that the weight of the keel—as far as the hand and the craftsman's art can achieve—is reduced to nearly a single point, and it sits stable in the water <note>original: "vado" — here referring to the bed of a waterway or the surface upon which a vessel rests</note>, it may be moved in such a way that it creates no ripples in the water by its motion. I testify to this: you will move the ship of Archimedes <note>A reference to the *Syracusia*, a massive ship of antiquity that Archimedes supposedly moved single-handedly using a system of pulleys.</note> and achieve whatever else of that kind you desire. But of these things, I shall speak elsewhere. Each of these things we have reviewed is, by itself, extremely powerful for moving weight. But if they are all joined into one, they will be marvelously effective.

Among the Germans, you will everywhere find youth playing upon the ice, supported by a slender iron shoe <note>An early description of ice skates</note> that has been smoothed underneath; with a light push, and because of the slipperiness of the surface, they glide over it with such speed of motion that they do not even allow themselves to be overtaken by a swift bird. 

But as weights are either drawn, pushed, or carried, perhaps we may define them thus: weights are drawn by rope, pushed by <term>lever</term><note>original: "vecte"</note>, or carried by wheels and the like. How we can use all of these together is readily apparent. But in all such things, there must be present something constant and most firmly fixed, from which the other parts are moved. 

If the weight is to be drawn, there must be another, greater weight to which the cables of the machines are committed; if no such weight is present, drive a strong, three-cubit <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches; thus, a spike about four and a half feet long.</note> iron spike deep into the compacted ground, or secure it with transverse logs. To the head of the spike that projects from the ground, wind the cables of the <term>pulleys</term><note>original: "troclearum"</note> and the <term>winch</term><note>original: "erganae" — a mechanical device for hauling or lifting.</note>. If, however, the ground is sandy, lay down very long, whole beams upon which the tracks may be fitted, and tie the cables at the ends to the spike. 

I will say something that the unskilled will not agree with until they understand the whole matter: 

<margin>Two weights pulled at once</margin>

two weights together are moved more conveniently across a flat plane than a single one. This is done as follows: once the first weight is moved to the very end of the laid track, I shall secure it with small wedges until it sticks firmly; then I shall attach the machine by which the second weight is to be drawn to this fixed weight. It will happen that, on the same track, the second weight is moved by the first, which is now acting as a fixed anchor. 

If a weight is to be lifted on high, we will most conveniently use a single beam or a ship’s mast that is not at all weak. If we raise this, we will firm its base at a spike or some other stable thing. At the top end, ropes shall be tied, no fewer than three: one to the right, another to the left, and a third extended along the length of the beam to the front. Then, at some distance from the base of the mast, a pulley or winch shall be fixed in the ground; the rope stretched through them shall be pulled. As it is pulled, the mast will raise itself by its head, while we guide it with those twin ropes tied to the head, moving it here and there...

...if we control it with leather straps: so that it stands as long as we wish, and hangs in the direction needed to place the load. These side ropes, if other larger weights are not available to steady them, shall be secured in this manner: A square trench will be dug deep into the ground; a timber trunk will be laid at the very bottom; to this, bindings will be attached so that they rise up from the ground. Planks <note>original: "plutei" — here meaning heavy wooden covers or shields</note> will be laid crosswise over the trunk; soon the trench will be filled with earth and packed down tight. Then, if you soak the area with water, it becomes even heavier and more stable; all other things will be prepared as we described for moving loads on a level surface. For at the head of the beam, and to the weight itself, blocks <note>original: "talleae" — a term for a block-and-pulley assembly</note> will be driven; and near the foot, a <term>windlass</term><note>original: "ergana" — a heavy machine used for winding rope to pull or lift weights</note> will be secured, or whatever you wish of that kind in which the force of a lever is present. In all these things for practical use, this must be observed: that for moving the most massive weights, means of this kind should be employed that are neither small nor weak. One must avoid any length in the rope, in the spoke, or in any tool we use for moving that suggests frailty. For length is naturally associated with thinness; and conversely, thickness is gained from shortness. If the ropes are thin, let them be doubled through the pulleys <note>original: "cicleolis"</note>. If the ropes are larger, let large pulleys also be used, lest the rope be cut through by the sharp edge of too small a circle. Let thick iron axles be inserted, so that they are no less than a sixth part of the pulley’s semi-diameter, and no more than an eighth part of the total diameter. 

A wetted rope is safer from catching fire, which can happen through the heat of friction and constant motion. It is also better prepared for turning in the pulleys. Add to this that it also uncoils less. It is more useful to soak it with vinegar than with water, and with seawater rather than river water; a rope wetted with fresh water and left in the hot sun rots most quickly. Coiling ropes is safer than knotting them. In all cases, one must take care that rope does not rub against and cut rope. The ancients used an iron rod to which they fastened the primary knots of the ropes and blocks; especially for grasping a stone weight, they used iron <term>tongs</term><note>original: "forcipes"</note>. The shape of the tongs was fashioned like the letter X, with the lowest "fingers" hooked inward, so that they might grip the weight like the bite of a crab. The two upper ends were fitted with rings; the rope was passed through these rings and tied back, so that by its own tension, the rope tightened the grip of the tongs. We have also seen on vast stones, especially on the mid-sections of columns that are otherwise smoothed and polished, protruding "navels" <note>original: "umbiliculos" — these are small stone bosses or lugs left by the masons to provide a grip for ropes</note> left like handles, by which the loops of the ropes were held so they would not slip off. They also use <term>cramps</term><note>original: "impleolae"</note> especially for the cornices. 
<margin>
Cramps.
</margin>
For I give the name "cramps" to those which are made thus: a cavity is hollowed into the stone in the likeness of an empty purse, proportionate to the size of the stone, several palms deep...

# Book VI. On Ornament. Folio XC

...with a narrower mouth and a wider base inside. We have seen <term>sockets</term><note>original: "impleolas" — holes carved into a stone to receive lifting tools</note> a foot deep; they fill these with small iron <term>wedges</term><note>original: "cuneolis"</note>, two of which are shaped on the sides to resemble the letter D. These are inserted to fill the interior spaces at the sides of the socket. Then a middle wedge is driven in last to fill the empty space between the two, completing the fit. The "ears" or lugs of each wedge protrude from the opening. An iron pin is passed through the holes in these ears, and a strong handle is attached to which the hauling rope is looped. We have secured columns, the lintels of gates, and similar objects that must be set upright in this fashion. 

We also constructed an iron or wooden <term>lifting frame</term><note>original: "ergaſculum" — here referring to a protective cradle or hoist structure</note> made very sturdy to withstand the vast weight. With this, we encircled the column, gripping it in its proper place, and secured it with slender, long wedges driven in with a light hammer. Finally, we attached "breeches" <note>original: "brachas" — rope slings</note> made of rope to the frame in such a way that we damaged neither the stone with the "wounds" of carved sockets, nor the sharp corners of the stone with the pressure of the ropes. It should be added that this method of binding is the most efficient, suitable, and reliable of all. Many other things pertaining to these uses will be explained more fully elsewhere. 

But here it is appropriate to define <margin>What machines are.</margin> **machines** simply as being like living beings with extremely powerful hands, moving weights in much the same way as we move them ourselves. For this reason, the same tensions of limbs and nerves that we apply when letting go, pushing, pulling, or transferring loads must be imitated by machines. 

I offer one warning: whenever you prepare to move the most massive weights, it is beneficial to approach the task gradually, cautiously, and with maturity. This is due to the various, unpredictable, and irrecoverable accidents and dangers that tend to happen in such work, even to the most experienced, and often against all expectation. For the praise and approval of your talent that follows a success will never be as great as the detestation and hatred of your recklessness that will overflow should the attempt fail. Enough on these matters for now. Now I return to wall-claddings.

### ### In cladding walls, at least three coats of sand-rendering are needed. Their duties and materials. Types of applied and driven claddings. Preparing the lime; a new invention for pictorial cladding. Chapter IX.

<insert>O</insert>n all claddings, it is necessary to have applied at least three coats of <term>sand-rendering</term><note>original: "harenationū" — plaster or mortar layers made with sand and lime</note>. The duty of the first coat is to grip the surface of the wall as tightly as possible and to hold the subsequent layers against the wall. The duty of the final coat is to bring forth the beauty of the polishing, the colors, and the <term>outlines</term><note>original: "lineamētorūqʒ"</note>...

# Leone Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

The function of the middle layers is to correct and prevent the defects of both the first and the last. These defects are as follows: for if the final and uppermost layers are "sharp"—or, if I may put it this way, "biting" against the walls, as the first layers ought to be—they will crack with numerous small fissures as they dry out due to their own sharpness. Conversely, if those first layers are softer—as the final layers should be—they will not grip the wall with a tenacious bite but will peel away. The more <term>sand-renderings</term><note>original: "harenationes" — layers of mortar or plaster mixed with sand, often called "rendering"</note> there are, the more brilliantly the surface will be polished, and the more solidly they will endure against the passage of time. <margin>Sand-rendering.</margin> We have seen instances among the ancients who added up to nine layers of sand-rendering. The first of these should be entirely rough, made from <term>quarry sand</term><note>original: "harena fossili"</note> and crushed brick, not finely ground but chunky like acorns, to a thickness of a few fingers, or sometimes up to a palm’s breadth. For the middle coats, river sand is more suitable because it cracks less. These middle layers must also be left rough, for additional coats will not stick to a smoothed surface. The final layer of all will be a most brilliant <term>marble-finish</term><note>original: "marmorata" — a plaster made with lime and marble dust instead of sand</note>; that is, one where finely crushed white stone is used instead of sand. It is sufficient to make this final part half a finger thick, for if it is applied any thicker, it dries with difficulty. We have seen some who, for the sake of thrift, spread the final "skin" no thicker than the leather of a shoe. The middle layers should be adjusted in succession depending on which of the other layers they are closest to. 

Certain veins very similar to translucent alabaster are found in rocky mountains; these are neither marble nor gypsum, but something in between, and are naturally quite crumbly. This stone, when crushed and mixed instead of sand, will wonderfully reflect glittering sparks of marble-like whiteness. Nails fixed into walls for the purpose of holding the <term>facings</term><note>original: "crustationum" — decorative or protective outer layers of stone, plaster, or tile</note> are seen everywhere; experience has shown that bronze ones are superior. <margin>Nails fixed into walls.</margin> It is very pleasing when, in place of small nails, they fix protruding bits of flint into small holes made between the joints of the wall courses, using a wooden mallet. Indeed, the fresher or rougher a wall is, the more densely it will hold the sand-renderings. Therefore, if you apply the first layer of sand-rendering (however thin) during construction while the work is "green" <note>original: "dum viret opus" — meaning while the mortar is still fresh and damp</note>, the grip will provide a tenacious and indelible bond for the layers to be applied on top. All facing work is best applied after the south winds <note>Which bring warmth and humidity, preventing the plaster from drying too quickly and cracking</note>; those applied during north winds, cold, or intense heat—especially the final "skin"—will suddenly become rough and uneven. Furthermore, some facings are "laid on" and others are "attached." Those that are laid on consist of gypsum or lime. However, gypsum is only useful in a very dry place. <margin>Types of facings.</margin> For any type of facing, moisture seeping from an old wall is an enemy. Stone, glass, and similar materials are "attached." These are the types of facings that are laid on:
