### Book VI. On Ornament.

<note>original: "albaria/pura/infignita/pictoria"</note> **White-plaster** may be plain, decorated, or pictorial. Of those applied over a surface, they are: **boarded**, **cut-out**, or **tessellated**. <margin>How lime should be prepared.</margin> Regarding the layers, the <term>lime</term><note>original: "Calx" — the essential ingredient for traditional plaster, created by heating limestone</note> shall be prepared thus: it should be slaked abundantly and left to soak for a long time in a covered pit with pure water. Then it shall be worked with an iron tool, just as wood is hewn with an adze. A sign that it is well-soaked will be when the tool encounters no pebbles while hewing. They consider it not yet "mature" enough if it is before the third month. It ought to be tough and very sticky when tested. For if the iron comes out dry, it is a sign that the lime is faint and "thirsty." When you mix in sand or crushed material, stir it for a long time and vigorously, and then again for a long time; indeed, turn it over repeatedly until it almost foams. The ancients used to pound this mixture in a mortar when they were about to apply the "final skin." They tempered this very mixture so that it would not stick to the iron tool while being applied. While one layer is already applied and becoming dry—yet still "green"—another shall be applied. Care will be taken so that all the "skins" dry out at the same pace. While the <term>plaster-finishes</term><note>original: "crustationes"</note> are still green, they are compacted by being beaten with smooth planers and rods. <margin>☞</margin> The final skin in pure white-plaster, if diligently rubbed, will give the brilliance of a mirror. Furthermore, once it is completely dry, if you coat it with a mixture of wax, mastic, and a little oil melted together, and then heat the coated wall with glowing coals from a basin so that it "drinks in" the ointment, it will surpass marble in its luster. We have found by experience that such plaster-finishes remain free from cracks if, during the application, you beat the appearing fissures with bundles of <term>marshmallow twigs</term><note>original: "ibisçi"</note> or raw broom. If you must apply it during the <term>Dog Days</term><note>original: "caniculā" — the hottest days of summer</note> or in a sweltering place, pound and chop old ropes very finely and mix them into the paste. Then it will be smoothed most beautifully if, during the polishing, you sprinkle on a little white soap dissolved in warm water; however, too much oiling makes it grow pale. <term>Relief-figures</term><note>original: "Signa"</note> will be attached most easily with stamps. These small figures will be drawn from carvings by pouring wet plaster over them. Once these have dried and are coated with the ointment we mentioned, they will imitate the texture of marble. <margin>Two kinds of figures.</margin> There are two types of such figures: one is **prominent** <note>high relief</note>, the other is **restrained and blunted** <note>low relief</note>. High relief is not inconveniently adopted on a straight wall. However, for the "sky" of vaulted ceilings, low reliefs are more suitable. For if high reliefs hang down, they are easily brought down by their own weight and pose a danger to the inhabitants. They rightly advise that where there will be much dust, you should not use carved and protruding cornices, but flat and restrained ones, so they may be more easily wiped clean. <margin>Pictorial finishes.</margin> **Pictorial finishes** are of two types: some are "in the wet" <note>fresco</note> and others "in the dry" <note>secco</note>. For the wet, every natural color derived from stone, earth, minerals, and the like is suitable. However, dyed colors...

Every color—and especially those that change when placed in fire—requires the driest conditions; it hates <term>lime</term><note>original: "calcem" — basic lime is chemically reactive and can destroy certain pigments</note>, the moon, and the south wind. There is a **new invention** for using **linseed oil** to apply whatever colors you wish, making them eternal against all injuries of the air and sky, provided the wall where they are applied is dry and not at all damp. Nevertheless, I find that ancient painters used liquid wax as a binder for painting the hulls of ships. Furthermore, we have seen in ancient works colors of gemstones applied to the wall—if I understand the matter correctly—rendered by **wax** or perhaps **white bitumen** to such hardness by age that they could be dissolved by neither fire nor water; you might say it was fused glass. We have also seen those who, with the <term>milky flower of lime</term><note>original: "lacteo calcis flore" — the finest, cream-like surface of the lime slaking process</note>, fixed glass-like colors to the wall while it was still "green" <note>freshly applied and damp</note>. So much for these matters.

# A
s for applied veneers and paneling, whether they are plain or carved, the method for both is the same. It is wonderful to say how much diligence the ancients applied to cutting and polishing marble slabs. I have indeed seen marble slabs more than four cubits long, two wide, and **scarcely half a finger thick**, joined with a wavy line to better deceive the viewers. **Pliny** writes that for cutting marbles, the ancients primarily approved of *Ethiopian sand*; *Indian sand* was a close second, but *Egyptian* was softer, and both surpass our own. However, they say a sand found in a certain shallow of the Adriatic Sea was used by the ancients. We collect sand from the shores of **Pozzuoli**, which is not least useful for this work. Angular sand taken from any mountain stream is useful; but the coarser it is, the wider the segments it grinds and the more sharply it "bites." The more lightly it clears the sludge, the closer it is to a polished finish. Polishing begins from the coarsest files and ends in that which "licks" rather than bites. *Thebaic stone* is approved for rubbing and polishing marbles.

For thinner panels, after the second rendering of sand, instead of <term>lime</term><note>original: "calcis"</note>, one should use a mixture of wax, pitch, resin, mastic, and any number of gums, all melted together. The panel should be heated gradually so that it does not crack from the sudden stress of the fire. In placing the panels, praise will be given if the harmony of the appearance is reflected in their arrangement and sequence. For spots should be matched to spots, and colors to colors, and like things to like, so that one bestows grace upon the other. I greatly like the cleverness of the ancients: they made those things closest to the eye exceedingly bright and polished. However, in those things that were to be distant or high up, they spared the labor. Indeed, in some places they did not even apply smoothed stones, as those would scarcely be noticed even by the most curious; only the broad <margin>Marbles.</margin> edges were intended to be inspected.

<margin>Tesserae</margin>
<margin>Also, cut-out work</margin>
Cut-out work <note>original: "circumexsecta" — known today as *opus sectile*, where larger pieces of stone are cut into shapes to form a pattern</note> and tessellated work <note>original: "tessellulata" — standard mosaic work using small cubes</note> agree in this: that in both we imitate painting by using various colors of stone, glass, or shells, arranged in a suitable layout. 

<margin>Mother-of-pearl veneers</margin>
They say that **Nero** was the first to institute the cutting of mother-of-pearl shells and mixing them into <term>veneers</term><note>original: "crustationibus" — the decorative "crust" or skin of marble applied to a wall</note>. These techniques differ in that in cut-out work, we use the largest pieces of paneling we can. In tessellated work, small square pieces no larger than beans are inserted; for the smaller they are, the more extensively they reflect sparkles of light. Because the surfaces of the small <term>tesserae</term> reflect the light they receive in various directions, they differ also in their adhesive: a paste of gums is more convenient for fixing the larger cut pieces, but for these tessellated mosaics, lime is more useful when mixed with the very finely ground powder of **Travertine stone**. 

There are some who order the lime for tessellated work to be washed again and again with boiling water, so that it might be softer and more pliable once the sharpness of the salts has been removed. I see that in "circles" of cut-out work, very hard pebbles were ground down, whereas in tessellated work, gold is painted onto glass using <term>lead-oxide</term><note>original: "calce plumbi" — litharge or lead glass, which has a lower melting point and high brilliance</note>, than which no glass is more fluid.

<margin>👉</margin>
¶ Almost everything we have said regarding wall veneers applies to **floor work** <note>original: "opus pavimenti"</note>, which we promised to discuss; except that floors do not accept such painterly or remarkably fine veneers, unless perhaps that "painterly" effect is achieved by dyeing the mortar paste with various colors and pouring it into spaces enclosed by marble borders to imitate a painting. 

The mixture is dyed with red ochre, burnt tile, flint, and iron dross; and when these crusted pavements have dried, the work is "scoured" <note>original: "dispumabitur" — literally 'defrothes', referring to the polishing process that brings up a shine</note>. It is done like this: a flint stone, or rather a five-pound lead weight with a flattened surface, is dragged back and forth with cords across the pavement with very coarse sand and water until it is beautifully smoothed by the scraping. It will not be smooth, however, unless the angles and lines of the mosaic pieces are flush. Once it has been coated and soaked with oil, especially **linseed oil**, it acquires a glassy skin. Olive oil dregs... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence at the bottom of the page</note>

### Chapter XI: On the timber-framing of roofs: vaulting, and open-air pavings; and whether panels are made from cedar, bronze, or lead, or if the tiles are glazed, which is more convenient and how.

<margin>
The Portico of Agrippa.
<gloss>made of bronze</gloss>
</margin>
**H**aving discussed walls, the roof also has its own delights and beauties of timber-framing, vaulting, and open-air pavings. There exist to this day at the **Portico of Agrippa** <note>Built by Marcus Agrippa in Rome, known for its massive scale</note> timber-framings with bronze beams forty feet long: a work in which you would not know whether to wonder more at the expense or the genius of the craftsman. We have related elsewhere that the roof of the **Ephesian Diana** <note>The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World</note> stood for very many years made of cedar.

<margin>Salauces, King of the Colchians.</margin>
Pliny mentions that **Salauces**, king of the Colchians, having been conquered by Sesostris, king of the Egyptians, possessed beams of gold and silver. Then too, temples are seen covered with marble panels: such as they say were at the **Temple of Jerusalem**, most magnificent and gleaming with the highest luster, so that to those viewing that roof from afar, it seemed to be a mountain of snow.

<margin>Catulus. The Pantheon. Honorius, Supreme Pontiff.</margin>
**Catulus** was the first at Rome to gild the bronze tiles of the Capitol. Not long after, I find that the **Pantheon** at Rome was covered with bronze in the form of gilded scales. And I find that **Honorius**, the Supreme Pontiff <note>Pope Honorius I, reigned 625–638 AD</note>—in whose time Muhammad instituted a new religion and sacred rites for the Egyptians and Libyans—covered the entire **Basilica of Saint Peter** with bronze panels. Germany shines with glazed tiles.

<margin>
The use of lead in open-air timber-framing.
</margin>
We use lead everywhere; a material indeed suited for durability and especially for grace, nor is the expense immoderate. But in it, there are these disadvantages: for if it is applied to **masonry work** <note>original: "cementitio operi" — concrete or rubble-fill construction</note>, because it cannot "breathe" from below, but grows excessively hot from the heat of the sun resting on the stones it lies upon, it melts.

<margin>👈</margin>
Let this experiment serve the point: A lead vessel will not be melted by fire if it is full of water; but throw in a small stone, and it will immediately melt and be pierced at the point of contact. There is the added fact that

<margin><gloss>Regarding the lead vessel</gloss></margin>
where it does not have frequent and very firm fastenings by which the sheets are held, it is easily stripped away by the winds. Furthermore, it is soon spoiled and eaten away by the salts of the lime; thus it is committed much more safely to timber, unless perhaps you fear fire. But there, too, the nails are a nuisance, especially iron ones, because the sun heats them more violently than the stones themselves...

XCIII

Liber VI. On Ornament.

...they boil and are corroded by rust. Therefore, the handles and needles for the vaulted sections should be made of lead, so that the plates and tiles may be soldered with a red-hot iron. It is also necessary to provide the work underneath with a light coating made from the washed ash of willow trees mixed with white chalk. Nails made of bronze <term>bronze</term><note>original: "ex ære" — referring to copper alloys like bronze or brass</note> boil less and are less damaged by rust. Lead is spoiled if smeared with dung. Therefore, care must be taken that birds flying there do not have perches where they can settle; or a thicker material must be substituted in those places where falling dung accumulates. On the summit of the **Temple of Solomon**, **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian and bishop</note> reports they had stretched chains from which four hundred bronze vessels hung, to frighten away the birds with their sound. On roofs, the gables, the edges of the gutters, and the corners are also decorated. For balls, flowers, statues, two-horse chariots, and such things are added, of which we shall speak part by part in their proper place. Now, regarding everything encompassing this type of ornament, nothing else occurs to me, except that everything should be placed in fitting locations that suit the work. The ornaments of openings bring a great deal of delight and dignity to a project.

### Chapter XII: On the ornaments of openings, their difficulties, the attachment of skeletons, and the raising of columns, whether the work is attached, adhering, or free-standing.

**B**ut they have many heavy difficulties, which can only be provided for with great diligence by the craftsman and heavy expense. For they require stones that are vast, whole, matching, elegant, and rare—none of which are easily found, nor are they easily handled, directed, carved, or composed exactly as one wishes. **Cicero** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator whose writings often touched on the ethics of craftsmanship</note> used to say that it was necessary for architects to be able to set columns to a **plumb line** <term>plumb line</term><note>original: "ad perpendiculum" — perfectly vertical, measured by a weighted cord</note>; this is absolutely necessary in openings, both for the sake of stability and for grace. There are also other inconveniences, but we shall provide for all of them as far as our ingenuity allows. An opening by its nature is a passage, but sometimes a wall is propped against another wall like a skin against a garment; and a certain type of opening is fashioned, not small, but closed off by an opposing wall, which for that reason may not inaptly be called **attached** <term>attached</term><note>original: "affictum" — decorative elements like half-columns or pilasters that are fixed to a solid wall rather than supporting a void</note>. This type of ornament, like almost all others, was first invented by carpenters for the sake of strengthening the work and reducing expense. Stonemasons, imitating this, brought exceptional beauty to their works. Any of these will be more beautiful if it has its **skeleton** <term>skeleton</term><note>original: "ossa" — the structural frame or main members</note> whole, made from a single stone. The next best thing will be when it has all its parts so joined that it does not appear where they meet. The ancients used to erect the largest stones for columns and other duties even for attached openings, and set them on their bases, before they raised the wall. This was indeed a prudent counsel. For the use of machines...

->Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.<-

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

...[of the columns] was made more manageable, and the plumb lines <note>original: "perpendicula"—weighted strings used by builders to ensure vertical alignment</note> were observed more freely. To use a plumb line, a column should be positioned on its base in this manner: the centers of the circles must be marked on both the bottom and the top of the column. In the center of the base, an iron needle <note>original: "acus ferreus"—a metal pin or dowel used to center the shaft on the base</note> shall be fixed with lead. The center of the bottom of the column will then be bored out so that it receives the needle projecting from the base within itself. Above the top of the machine, a point will be marked from which a plumb line may fall exactly into the center of the needle on the base. Once these things are prepared, it will not be difficult to nudge the upper shaft of the column until the center of its own circle is positioned directly under the point marked by the plumb line.

I have learned from the works of the ancients that softer marbles can be smoothed with the same iron tools with which timber is scraped. They also observed this practice: they would install stones that were still rough, except for the hewn <term>heads</term><note>original: "capitibus"—referring here to the joining surfaces or "beds" of the stones</note> and the edges <note>original: "labris"—literally "lips," the outer edges of the contact surface</note> where they were to be joined together in the work. Once the structure was built, they would then trim and polish the parts that remained rough. I believe they did this so that they would risk the least possible expense during the dangers of the hoisting machines. They would have suffered a much heavier loss from a polished and perfectly finished stone if it had been broken by some accident than from an unfinished one. Add to this that they were very far-sighted regarding time; for there is one time for constructing a work, and another for facing and polishing it.

<margin>Two types of attached works.</margin> There are two types of attached works. One which so adheres to the wall that a certain portion of it lies hidden within, while the rest protrudes from the wall. The other consists of whole columns and stands free from the wall, appearing as if it intended to imitate a portico. Let the former be called "protruding" and the latter "detached." 

Among the protruding type, the columns will be either round or quadrangular. Round columns should protrude no more and no less than a semi-diameter <note>exactly half of the column's thickness</note>. Quadrangular ones should protrude no more than a fourth part of their side, and no less than a sixth. In the case of detached columns, they shall nowhere stand further from the wall than the width of their whole base plus a fourth part; and nowhere shall they stand closer than the distance required for the entire column and base to be clear of the wall. In those cases where they stand back by the width of the whole base and a fourth part, it is necessary that a quadrangular column protruding from the wall should correspond to them. 

In detached works, the beam <term>architrave</term><note>original: "trabs"—the primary horizontal member spanning the gap between columns</note> will not be extended continuously across the face of the wall; instead, it will be joined at right angles and leveled against the columns, so that the ends of the inner beams breaking out from the wall may reach out to meet the individual capitals <term>capitula</term> of the columns. The cornices <note>original: "coronae"—the projecting moldings at the top of the entablature</note> that ornament the beam of the wall will also decorate the perimeter of these projecting beam-ends. However, in protruding works, you may choose whether to use a continuous beam and cornices without interruption along the entire length of the building, or to imitate the logic of detached works by creating a simulated breakout and protrusion of the inner beams. We have spoken of the ornaments that belong to those parts...

->Book VI. On Ornament. Page XCIIII.<-

[of] buildings; in which all buildings agree; but of those in which they do not agree, we shall speak in the next book. For this one has enough breadth. But since this book has taken upon itself the task of inquiring into those things which belong to the ornaments of these parts, let nothing be neglected which may contribute to that matter. In the whole art of building, the primary ornament is certainly found in the columns.

¶ That the primary ornament is in the columns; their lines, axis, boundary, circle diameters, positions, projection, recession, swelling, thinning, ring, the axis itself, and the parts and small portions of the diameter. Chapter XIII.

<margin>Theodorus and Tholus, excellent craftsmen of columns.</margin>
**F**or when several are placed together, they adorn porticos, walls, and every kind of opening; and even single ones are by no means unbecoming. For they grace crossroads, theaters, and squares; they preserve trophies, serve as monuments, possess grace, and bring dignity. It is difficult to say how much expense the ancients poured into this most elegant feature. For some, by no means content with Parian or Numidian marble and alabaster <note>Parian marble was famous for its whiteness; Numidian was a yellow marble from North Africa; alabaster was prized for its translucency</note>, even added the hand of the most outstanding craftsmen; they made them filled with statues and images, such as are said to have been in the temple of the Ephesian Diana, numbering more than one hundred and twenty. Others added bronze and gilded bases and capitals, such as were placed in the double portico at Rome during the consulship of Octavius, he who triumphed over Persius <note>Gnaeus Octavius, who defeated King Perseus of Macedon in 168 BCE</note>. Others made entire columns of bronze; others rendered them clothed in silver. But let those things be passed over. It is entirely necessary that columns be smooth and turned as if on a lathe. I find that certain architects, Theodorus and Tholus, in their workshops at Lemnos <note>an island in the Aegean Sea</note>, allowed the wheels to spin, and there they balanced hanging columns in such a way that they were turned while a boy rotated them. This is from Greek history. Let this be enough for the matter.

<margin>Calculations for the diameters in a column.</margin>
In a column, we weigh these longest lines: the axis and the <term>boundary</term> <note>original: "finitorem"—the line defining the outer profile or slant height of the column</note>. Shorter, however, are the diameters of the circles which gird the column in various places. Among these circles, the most well-known are the flat surface which is at the very top of the column, and likewise the other flat surface which is at the bottom, which we also call the <term>plane</term> <note>original: "planam"—the flat horizontal surface of the column's ends</note>. The axis, moreover, is the straight line drawn through the marrow <note>the core or internal center</note> of the column from the center of the topmost circle to the center of the lowest; this same line is called the middle plumb line <note>original: "perpendiculum"</note> of the column. On this very axis line, the centers of all the circles are fixed. The boundary, however, is the line drawn from the outer rim of the top circle to the point on the bottom rim opposite to it. This defines the extension of all the diameters that exist through the thickness of the column, and from this, the proportions are derived.

Leonis Baptistæ Alber. De re ædificatoria.

# Leon Battista Alberti’s *On the Art of Building*.

The line [of the column profile] is not a single straight line like an axis, but is composed of many lines, partly straight and partly curved, as we shall soon explain. There are five places along the column for measuring the diameters of the circles. These are the names of the locations: the **projection**, the **retraction**, and the **belly**. There is a double projection: one at the top of the column and another at the bottom. These are so named because they project and stand out more than the rest. There are also two retractions that follow immediately after the projections, both at the bottom and at the top. They are called so because through them the projections are drawn back to the solid thickness of the shaft. The diameter of the **belly** <note>original: "venter"; this refers to the swelling of the column shaft, technically called entasis, which prevents the column from looking thin or "waisted" from a distance</note> is marked below the midpoint of the column’s length, named so because the column appears to swell out there. Furthermore, the projections differ from one another. For the one at the bottom consists only of a **nextrum** <term>nextrum: a thin fillet or square-edged band at the base of a column shaft</term> and the curve by which it is drawn back from the fillet to the solid column. However, the projection at the top of the shaft, besides the fillet and this sloping curve, also has a **collar** <note>original: "torquem"; a ring-like molding</note>. We promised that we would try, as far as we are able, to speak in Latin and in such a way as to be entirely understood. Therefore, it is necessary to coin words where common ones are not available, and it is helpful to take similar names from things that are not dissimilar. 
<margin>What a "nextrum" is.</margin>Among us Etruscans <note>Alberti refers to his Tuscan heritage here</note>, they call a very thin band with which young maidens bind and weave their hair a *nextrum*. Therefore, if it be permitted, let us call the small band—which, like a curved ruler, travels around the base of the column like a ring—a *nextrum*. Moreover, the ring at the top, which, besides the *nextrum*, binds the uppermost part of the shaft like a wound cord, let us call a **collar**. Finally, the "finitor" <note>the boundary or profile line of the column</note> line will be prepared in this way: on the floor or on some leveled wall (a place which I call the "drawing" <note>original: "picturam"; here meaning a full-scale plan or template</note>), a straight line is inscribed as long as the future column will be, which the craftsmen are to cut from the rock; this line is called the **axis**. We shall divide this axis into certain parts according to the logic of the future work and the variety of columns (which will be discussed in its proper place). Based on the measure of these parts, the diameter of the lowest base will be made, which we draw there in the drawing as a small transverse line at right angles to the bottom head of the axis. We divide this diameter into twenty-four parts. We give one of these parts to the height of the little fillet [*nextruli*]; which height we certainly describe in the drawing as a tiny line. Again, from the twenty-four parts of the base, we take three, and at that height we place the center of the nearest retraction on the axis. Through this center, we draw a line at right angles, parallel to the base. This line, therefore, will be the diameter of the lowest retraction, the length of which is made shorter than the diameter of the base by one-seventh of that diameter. Having marked these...

<meta>This page continues the technical geometric construction of a column shaft, specifically detailing the mathematical proportions for the "belly" (entasis) and the upper moldings, and concluding Book VI.</meta>

<page-num>XCV</page-num>
<header>Book VI. On Ornament. Folio XCV.</header>

...with two lines—that is, the diameter of the retraction and the **fillet** <note>original: nextrum; a thin, flat molding at the base of the shaft</note>—from the edge of the fillet released to the edge of the retraction, we draw a curved line with its back toward the axis, using a curve as soft and pleasing as possible. The beginning of this curve will take up a quarter of a small circle, the radius of which is the height of the fillet. After this, we divide the entire length of the axis into seven equal parts and mark these divisions with points. Starting to count from the base <note>original: planta</note>, at the fourth point I shall establish the center of the **belly** <note>original: venter; the point of maximum swelling or entasis in a column</note>, through which you should draw its diameter, the length of which should be equal to the diameter of the lower retraction.

Next, the upper retraction and projection are established as follows: based on the size of the column (which we will discuss in its proper place), the diameter of the top circle is derived from the diameter of the bottom base and noted in the drawing <note>original: pictura</note> at the very top of the axis. Once this diameter has been drawn, we divide it into twelve small parts. One whole of these parts will be taken up by one **collar** <note>original: torquis; a ring-like molding</note> and the fillet of the upper projection. For this collar will take two-thirds of this twelfth part, and the remainder it will give to the fillet. But within this projection there will be a **retraction**, the center of which will be distant from the center of the top circle of the projection by one and a half of those twelve parts. The diameter of the retraction itself will be less than the largest diameter of the projection by one-ninth of it. After this, a curved line is drawn with the same stroke as we used for the bottom curve.

Finally, once the projections, retractions, slanted curves, and the diameter of the belly have been marked in the drawing, a straight line is drawn from the edge of the upper retraction and likewise from the edge of the lower retraction to the edge of the diameter we marked for the belly. And so, by these descriptions we have reviewed, the line called the **boundary** <note>original: finitor; the profile or silhouette of the column</note> is composed. According to the measure of this line, a thin **template** <note>original: tabula gracilis</note> is fashioned, by which the stonecutters may determine and fix the proper girth and boundaries of the column. If the column is well turned, the surface of the bottom of the **shaft** <note>original: scapi</note> will be equalized at equal angles on both sides of the central perpendicular line, by drawing a radius from the center of the circle at the top surface of the column. These things we have not found handed down in the writings of the ancients, but we have noted them with diligence and study from the finest works. What follows will pertain for the most part to the principles of these kinds of outlines; they will be most worthy and will contribute wonderfully to the delights of painters.

Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

# THE SEVENTH BOOK OF LEON BATTISTA ALBERTI ON
# THE ART OF BUILDING, WHICH IS ENTITLED
# THE ORNAMENT OF SACRED BUILDINGS.

¶ Having resumed the divisions of architecture, he demonstrates, through examples and reasoning, the sacred reverence of walls, temples, and basilicas, as well as the religious sanctity of the site and the dignity and grace of the city. ->Chapter One.<-

**W**e have said <note>referring to his earlier books where he established the fundamental requirements of a building: necessity, convenience, and pleasure</note> that the art of building consists of parts, and that some of these parts are those which comprise every type of building, whatever it may be: such as the site, the roof, and things of this sort. Others, however, are those by which buildings themselves differ from one another. Regarding the ornaments of the former, we have reviewed them up to this point as far as seemed relevant to our purpose. Now we must speak of these latter parts. This investigation will indeed possess such utility that even painters—the most exquisite seekers of beauties—would declare that they should by no means be without it. It will also possess such delight that I would not say one would repent of having read more. But I would wish you not to disapprove if, having set forth new goals, we approach the matter with new beginnings. Indeed, the beginnings and the approaches are most correctly opened through the division, description, or notation of the parts from which the whole case is established. For just as in a statue cast from a mixture of bronze, gold, and silver, the smith considers one thing regarding weight, the sculptor another regarding the lines and proportions <note>original: lineamentis</note>, and others perhaps seek yet another thing; so too have we elsewhere said that these parts of the art of building should be distributed in such a way that they provide a sufficiently fit and ready order for reviewing what was relevant to that matter there. Now we shall define a partition that satisfies the beauty and decorum of buildings more than their utility and firmness. Although all praises of this kind agree so well among themselves that in a matter where you find one of these lacking, the others will certainly not be approved either. Buildings, therefore, are either public or private. Yet both public and private buildings are either sacred or profane.

<margin>
Walls dedicated to the gods.
</margin>

¶ I shall speak first of public buildings. The ancients established the walls of cities with the highest religious devotion and dedicated them to a deity under whose protection they would remain. Nor indeed did they think that by any human reason could the affairs of mortals be sufficiently moderated by anyone to prevent insult and treachery from circulating among men; they thought that a city was always as close to misfortune—either through the negligence of its own people or the envy of neighbors—as a ship upon the open sea.

Book VII. On the Ornaments of Sacred Buildings. Folio XCVI.

...and exposed to dangers. For this reason, I interpret the fables which claim that <term>Saturn</term><note>The mythical Roman god of agriculture and the Golden Age; Alberti treats these myths as allegories for early political wisdom.</note>, to provide for human affairs, once put heroes and demigods in charge of cities, so that their wisdom might protect them; for we stand in great need not only of <term>walls</term><note>original: *moenibus*</note> to protect us, but also of the help of the gods. But they proclaim that Saturn did this because, just as we put a shepherd, not a beast, over a flock, so he understood that over men should be placed another kind of living being, far superior in wisdom and virtue.

Therefore, walls are dedicated to the gods. Others proclaim it was by the providence of the Best and Greatest God <note>original: *optimi & maximi dei*—a title originally for Jupiter, used here by Alberti to refer to the Divine Creator.</note> that <term>guardian spirits</term><note>original: *fatales genij*</note> were assigned both to the souls of men and to peoples. Therefore, the walls by which citizens are gathered into one and protected were undoubtedly held sacred. Indeed, when they were about to capture a besieged city, lest they seem to act against the veneration of religions, they would call out the tutelary gods of that city with a specific sacred song <note>original: *sacro carmine*—Alberti refers to the Roman ritual of *evocatio*, where an attacking general invited the enemy's gods to leave their city and come to Rome.</note> so that they might migrate elsewhere not against their will.

Who would doubt that a temple is a religious place, both for other reasons and especially because there, due thanks and veneration are given to those of the human race who have deserved best from the gods? Such piety is a primary part of <term>justice</term><note>original: *iustitiae*</note>; and who would not agree that justice itself is a kind of divine gift? There is also a part of justice closely related to this higher one, chief in dignity, most pleasing to the gods, and thus most sacred: that which we use toward men for the sake of peace and tranquility, when we wish to see each person receive their due according to their merits. Therefore, we shall assign the <term>basilica</term><note>In the Renaissance, the 'basilica' was understood as a hall of justice where law was administered, modeled on Roman civil buildings.</note>, where authority must be exercised, to religion. 

What of the monuments of worthy things, which are dedicated to eternity and commended to posterity? These, if I am not mistaken, consist entirely of the principles of justice and religion. We must therefore speak of walls, temples, basilicas, and monuments; but before we touch upon these, a few things must be briefly mentioned regarding the cities themselves, which should not be omitted. 

The region and site of a city will be greatly honored by an abundance of buildings distributed and placed in the most suitable locations. 
<margin>Plato on the constitution of the city.</margin>
<term>Plato</term><note>Specifically referring to the urban planning described in Plato’s *Laws*.</note> approved of the land and site being divided into twelve classes; and in each he established individual temples or shrines. We shall add shrines at crossroads, the seats of lesser judges, garrisons, racetracks, and spaces for games, and whatever else might be appropriate to these, provided that the land flourishes everywhere with an abundance of roofs. 

Moreover, some cities are very large, others smaller, such as fortresses and tiny towns. There is an opinion among ancient writers that cities built on the plain are not at all ancient, and therefore possess less authority. For they interpret them as having been built long after the <term>flood</term><note>original: *diluvium*—the Great Deluge mentioned in both classical and biblical traditions.</note>. But certainly, flat and open places are more suitable for cities, while steep and more difficult places are better for fortresses...

...conduce to grace and pleasantness. In these matters, however, I would wish for this: that flat areas should rise into a very slight mound for the sake of cleanliness <note>original: *munditiae gratia* — Alberti emphasizes that a slight slope prevents the accumulation of waste and stagnant water, a key concern in Renaissance hygiene.</note>, and mountainous areas should occupy for themselves a flattened and level area.

<margin>Capua.</margin>
For the sake of its streets and buildings, Cicero seemed to prefer the city of Capua to the city of Rome, for the reason that it was not suspended on hills and interrupted by valleys, but was open and leveled. At the island of Pharos, Alexander <note>Alexander the Great.</note> desisted from founding a city in a place otherwise fortified and very convenient, because he realized the space would not be sufficiently ample for the future city. Nor do I think this should be passed over: the distinguished ornament of a city stands out where there is an abundance of citizens. 

<margin>Tigranes.</margin>
We read that when Tigranes <note>Tigranes the Great, King of Armenia (c. 140–55 BCE), who founded the capital Tigranocerta.</note> was founding the city of Tigranocerta, he compelled a very great number of the most honorable and illustrious men to gather there with all their fortunes; he issued an edict that whatever they did not bring to that place would be confiscated by the treasury if found elsewhere. This same thing neighbors and even mortals of foreign nations will do of their own accord when they believe they can lead a life there that is both very healthy and very refined among honest and well-mannered people. But the chief ornament to cities will be brought by the site, the layout, the shapes, and the arrangements of the streets, the forum, and subsequently each individual work; so that everything is correctly prepared and distributed according to the use, dignity, and convenience of each. For indeed, if order <note>original: *ordine* — a central concept for Alberti, referring to the rational arrangement of parts to form a harmonious whole.</note> is removed, there will be nothing at all that presents itself as either convenient, or pleasing, or worthy. Plato used to say that a well-mannered and well-constituted republic ought to provide by law that the luxuries of foreign nations should not be brought into the city, nor should any citizen 

<margin>☛</margin>
*whoever is younger than forty years old travel abroad.* And those guests who had come to the city for the sake of virtue, when they had been imbued with good disciplines for a time, should be sent back to their own people. This is because, through the contagion of such foreigners, citizens daily unlearn the old parsimony of their fathers and begin to hate ancient customs—a thing which, above all others, renders cities most wretched. Plutarch relates that the people of Epidauros, having noticed that their citizens were becoming wicked through commerce with the Illyrians, and remembering that revolutions <note>original: *res novas* — literally "new things," the standard Latin term for political upheaval or revolution.</note> are stirred up in states by bad morals, 

<margin>Epidauros</margin>
fearing this, chose from the multitude of all citizens one man each year, especially serious and circumspect, who would go to the Illyrians and purchase and contract for whatever each of his fellow citizens had commissioned. Finally, all experts are of this opinion: that they command care to be taken most diligently, lest the city be corrupted by the admixture of foreign things. Yet I do not think those should be imitated who would exclude every kind of guest. 

<margin>The custom of the Greeks.</margin>
Among the Greeks, according to an ancient custom, peoples were not joined...

...otherwise peaceful people, however, not enemies, if ever they arrived armed, they <note>The Carthaginians.</note> asserted they would neither receive them into the city nor drive them away through inhospitality; but they established a market for selling goods not far from the city boundaries <note>original: *pomerium* — the sacred and legal boundary of a city, where building was often forbidden for religious and defensive reasons.</note> where the newcomers could refresh themselves and buy what they needed, so that the citizens would be immune from the suspicion of danger. And to me, indeed, the Carthaginians are approved. 

<margin>The custom of the arriving Carthaginians.</margin>
For they did not refuse to receive foreign guests, nor did they wish all things to be held in common with the citizens. The road to the forum lay open to the outsider, but to the more secret parts of the city, to the shipyards and such, even a sight of them was not granted. 

Advised by this, we shall divide the city area in such a way that not only should foreigners have their own distinct lodgings suitable for them and not inconvenient for the citizens, but even the citizens themselves should live suitably and conveniently among themselves according to each person's duty and dignity. It will contribute exceptionally to the grace of the city if various workshops of craftsmen occupy various streets and regions for themselves in suitable places. For indeed, the money-changers, painters, and jewelers <note>original: *anularii* — literally 'ring-makers'.</note> should be by the forum. Nearby should be the spice shops, clothing shops, and whatever might finally be considered more honorable. 

In the outermost places, the filth and stench of obscene things, especially the dunghills of the tanners, shall be secluded; and they shall be driven to the north, because there the winds are either rare into the city, or so strong that they are swept away rather than brought in. There would perhaps be some who would like the neighborhoods of the nobles to be free and purged of all the dregs of the common people. Others might prefer all the regions of the city to be so adorned that whatever use demands, everything is supplied everywhere; for that reason, they would not refuse to have shops for hire mixed in with the houses of the most worthy. But enough on these things. One thing is surely owed to utility, another to dignity. I return to the matter.

## ¶ On the primary construction of walls and temples among the ancients.
### Chapter II.

**F**or walls, the ancients—especially the people of Etruria <note>The Etruscans, a pre-Roman civilization in Italy known for their advanced engineering and massive stone walls.</note>—approved squared and extremely massive stone. This very thing the 
<margin>Walls to be built.</margin>
Athenians also used at the Piraeus <note>The port city of Athens.</note>, at the urging of Themistocles. Ancient towns are also seen, both in Etruria and Umbria, and even among the Hernici <note>An ancient Italic tribe of Latium.</note>, built with very large stone, irregular and vast: a work which I certainly approve of vehemently. For it displays a certain rigidity of the most severe antiquity, which is an ornament to cities. And I would indeed wish the city wall to be of such a kind that, having seen it, the enemy would shudder and soon depart in despair. A very wide and deep ditch, confined by banks steepened by a wall, will bring majesty.

Such as they say existed at Babylon, fifty royal cubits <note>original: *cubitus regius* — an ancient unit of length, approximately 20 inches, longer than the standard cubit.</note> wide...

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

...fifty, and more than a hundred deep. The height and thickness of the walls will increase their majesty: such as we read that Ninus, Semiramis, Tigranes, and almost all those who were inclined toward magnificence of spirit, constructed. In the towers and galleries of the walls of Rome, we have seen floors decorated with **tessellated work** <note>original: *opere tessellata* — mosaic patterns made of small squares of stone or glass.</note>, and walls most elegantly veneered. But not all things will be approved for all cities. Indeed, the delights of cornices and veneers do not belong on defensive walls; instead of cornices, some slightly more polished, very long stones shall project according to the rule and the level. Moreover, regarding the veneering, although the roughness of the front will persist of its own accord, stubborn and as if threatening, I would nevertheless wish the stones to be so joined at their mutual angles and lines that the construction is nowhere disgraced by gaps. 

<margin>
The Doric Rule.
</margin>
We shall achieve this most conveniently by the **Doric rule**: which Aristotle used to say the law ought to resemble. For that rule was made of lead and was flexible. For since those ancient builders had stones that were very hard and intractable, and they wished to spare expense and labor, they did not hew the blocks into right angles; instead, they placed them in irregular rows, just as each stone might find its own seat. Because it would be most laborious to move the stone around until it found suitable places and a fit position, they would apply a flexible rule of this kind: they would wrap it around the angle and the sides of the stone to be joined, and use the bent lead as a square <note>original: *norma* — a carpenter's square.</note>. With this, they could test the gaps between the stones already in the structure and identify the places where they could confirm the stone was a match and subsequently insert it. 

Then, for the sake of veneration, I would wish a wide path to be marked out within the <term>pomerium</term> <note>A sacred and legal boundary of a city, traditionally kept clear of all buildings.</note> and before the walls, and dedicated to public liberty; which indeed no man whatsoever may obstruct with impunity with a ditch, a wall, a fence, or even a shrub. 

<margin>
Concerning the temple. Note who first established temples in ancient times.
</margin>
¶ I come to **temples**. I find that the first founders of temples were Father Janus in Italy. And for that reason, the ancients were accustomed to always mention the god Janus first in their sacrifices. There are some who say that Jupiter first dedicated temples among the Cretans; and for that reason, Jupiter is thought to be the primary god among those who are worshipped. Among the Phoenicians, they proclaim that Uso first erected images to fire and wind, and built temples. Others say that when Dionysius traveled among the Indians—at a time when no cities yet existed in those regions—having established towns himself, he added temples and handed down certain religious cults. Others affirm that in Achaia, Cecrops first built for Ops <note>An ancient Roman/Sabine goddess of the earth and fertility.</note>, and the Arcadians were the first to build temples for Jupiter. They say also that Isis—whom they called the "law-giving" goddess because she was the first of the race of gods to establish living by her own laws—built a temple for her parents, Jupiter and Juno...

<header>Book VII. On the Ornaments of Sacred Things. Page 98.</header>

<margin>He consumed the temples with flames.</margin>
...they report that they were made in the beginning, and that the priests decreed them. However, it is not entirely clear what kind of temple existed among various peoples through that later age. I, for one, would easily be persuaded that they were like that on the citadel in Athens, or like the one on the Capitol in Rome. Even when the city was flourishing, they had temples covered with straw and thatch. For thus they believed that the ancient **frugality of the fathers** <note>original: *pristinam illam patrum parsimoniam* — a reference to the Roman ideal of "mos maiorum," or the unpretentious customs of their ancestors.</note> ought to be expressed. But when the wealth of kings and other citizens had suggested that they should honor themselves and their city with the greatness of buildings, it seemed shameful that the houses of the gods, in terms of the praise of beauty, should be surpassed by the roofs of mortals. The matter soon progressed to the point where, in a most frugal city, **King Numa** <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome, who established many of the city's religious institutions.</note> spent four million pounds of silver <note>original: *libras argenti quatercentenas decies*</note> on the foundations of a single temple. I strongly praise this ruler's institution, as he looked to the dignity of the city and attributed it to the veneration of the gods to whom we owe everything. 

Although there was indeed an opinion among some who were held to be wise that they did not approve of temples being built for the gods above. On their advice, **Xerxes** <note>The Persian King who invaded Greece in 480 BCE.</note> is said to have set fire to the temples of Greece because they enclosed the gods within walls—gods to whom all things ought to be open, and for whom the world itself serves as a temple. But I return to the established purpose.

### ¶ With how much genius, care, industry, and diligence a temple must be established and adorned; for which gods, where, and what kind of temples. Chapter III.

**I**n the whole matter of building, there is nothing in which there is need for greater genius, care, industry, and diligence than in the establishing and adorning of a temple. Not to mention that a temple well-maintained and well-adorned is surely the greatest and primary ornament of a city. A temple is truly the lodging of the gods. If we decorate houses for kings and great men as guests, and prepare them most sumptuously, what shall we do for the immortal gods? Whom we certainly wish to be present when called to sacrifice, and to hear our prayers and supplications? 

But even if the gods do not care for these fleeting things that men make, they may be moved by the purity of those who strive and by the veneration of the divine power. Without a doubt, it is of the greatest importance for the **cult of piety** <note>original: *pietatis cultum* — the practice of religious devotion and duty.</note> to have temples that wonderfully delight the soul and hold it with grace and admiration for themselves. The ancients asserted that piety was only then truly cultivated when the temples of the gods were frequented. For these reasons, I would wish that so much beauty be present in a temple that no more ornate appearance could even be imagined; and I desire it to be so prepared in every part that those who enter are struck with awe and shudder with admiration for worthy things, and can hardly restrain themselves from professing aloud: that this place is surely worthy of God.

<margin>Miletian temple. Samian temple.</margin>
...let them look upon these. **Strabo** <note>A Greek geographer and historian (c. 64 BC – 24 AD) known for his work "Geographica."</note> says that the Milesians built a temple which, on account of its sheer size, remained without a roof. I do not praise this. The Samians boasted that the temple among them was the largest of all; I will not deny that such things should be established in such a way that they can hardly be increased in size. For ornament is an infinite matter; something is always left over even in tiny temples, so that it seems something both could and should be added. However, I will approve of those things which you would not wish to be larger relative to the size of the city; meanwhile, I am offended by the vastness of roofs <note>Alberti often argues for "concinnitas," or a sense of appropriate proportion and harmony; he dislikes buildings that are over-ambitious to the point of being impractical or structurally unsound.</note>. But I especially desire this in temples: that whatever meets the eye, all should be of such a kind that you could not easily decide whether the **skill and hands of the craftsmen**, or the **zeal of the citizens** in providing and displaying the rarest and most excellent things, are more worthy of praise; and whether these same things contribute more to grace and beauty, or to the permanence of eternity. This matter, as in other works both public and private, must be considered again and again and in a greater way, especially in constructing temples. For it is fitting that such great expenses, once paid out, should be most strongly fortified against adverse events lest they perish. And we consider that **antiquity** brings no less authority than it brings the dignity of ornament to temples.

<margin>To which gods and in what places temples should be placed.</margin>
But the ancients, advised by the **Etruscan discipline** <note>original: "disciplina Aetruscorum" — the body of religious and divinatory knowledge used by the Romans, inherited from the Etruscans, which dictated how cities and temples should be oriented.</note>, decided that temples should not be placed for all gods in every location. For they thought that gods who presided over peace, modesty, and the good arts should be placed within the enclosure of the city walls. Those who stirred up pleasures, quarrels, or fires—namely **Venus, Mars, and Vulcan**—they thought should be excluded outside the walls. **Vesta, Jupiter, and Minerva**, whom **Plato** said were the guardians of cities, they placed at the center of the town and on the citadel. **Pallas [Athena]**, the goddess of craftsmen; **Mercury**, to whom merchants made offerings in the month of May; and **Isis**, they placed at the forum. They situated **Neptune** at the seashore, and **Janus** on high mountains. For **Aesculapius**, they located a temple on the Tiber Island, because they believed that the sick especially required water. **Plutarch** <note>A Greek philosopher and biographer (c. 46 – 119 AD).</note> said they were accustomed to placing shrines for this god elsewhere outside the city because the air there was healthier. Furthermore, they believed that different forms of temples were owed to various gods.

<margin>Various forms of temples to be established for various gods.</margin>
For they approved a round shrine for the **Sun and Liber Pater** <note>original: "Liberiq. patris" — an ancient Italian god of fertility and wine, later identified with the Greek Dionysus or Roman Bacchus.</note>; and **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a prolific Roman scholar.</note> said the temple of Jupiter, because it reveals the "seeds" of all things, ought to stand with a **perforated roof** <note>original: "perforato" — referring to an "hypaethral" temple, one open to the sky to represent the heavens.</note>. The shrine of **Vesta**, whom they thought to be the earth itself, they made round in the likeness of a ball. For other celestial gods, they raised buildings high from the earth. For the gods of the underworld, they placed them beneath the earth. For terrestrial gods, they placed them on the middle ground. It also happens that I interpret it thus: that they invented various temple buildings for themselves based on the various requirements of their sacrifices. For some indeed drenched the altars with blood. Others with wine and...

But our own people <note>Referring to the early Christians.</note> have widely adopted the use of **basilicas** <note>Originally Roman public buildings for law and commerce, which Christians adapted into churches.</note> for the purpose of sacrifice. This was done partly because from the beginning they were accustomed to meeting and gathering in the basilicas of private citizens, and partly because within them the altar could be placed before the **tribunal** <note>The raised platform where a Roman magistrate sat, which became the site of the Christian altar.</note> with the greatest dignity, and a choir could be beautifully arranged around the altars. The remainder of the basilica, such as the walkway and the portico, was open to the people, whether walking about or standing by for the sacrifice. Furthermore, the voice of the preaching prelate was heard more clearly in a timber-roofed basilica than in a **vaulted temple** <term>testudinato (literally "tortoise-shelled," referring to a stone vault or dome)</term>. But more on these things elsewhere. Let the saying be applied to the matter: that temples for **Venus, Diana, the Muses, and the Nymphs**, and the more delicate goddesses, should be dedicated in a way that imitates **virginal slenderness** and the flowery tenderness of youth. For **Hercules, Mars**, and the greatest gods, the buildings should be so placed that they offer more authority through their gravity than grace through their age. Finally, where you locate a temple, it ought to be a place that is frequented, illustrious, and—as they say—**proud**; and it should be free from all contagion of the profane. For this reason, it shall have a large and worthy square in front of it. It should be surrounded by wider streets, or rather, most dignified squares, so that it may be clearly seen from every direction.

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

The ancestors observed that for temples, the floor plan should be extended: so that it might be longer by more than a half than it is wide. Others established that the width should be exceeded by the length by a third part. Others wished the length to comprise two full widths. In rectangular floor plans, the greatest defect of deformity will be if the angles are not all right angles. The ancients used a number of angles: either six, or eight, or likewise even ten. All floor plans of this kind must necessarily have their angles terminate at the circumference of a circle. And they are correctly derived from the circle itself: for half of the diameter in a circle will provide the side for a floor plan of six angles <note>Alberti is describing the geometric fact that the radius of a circle is equal to the side of an inscribed regular hexagon.</note>. If you draw straight lines from the center cutting through the middle of each side of the hexagon, it is easy to see how you can create a floor plan of twelve angles. Then from the twelve-angled shape it is also obvious how to make a square and even an octagon; although there exists another very convenient method for drawing octagons. For once an equilateral and right-angled square has been drawn, I extend the diameters <note>In this context, Alberti refers to the diagonals of the square.</note> to each angle of the square; and from the point of intersection, I draw the half-parts of each diameter so that they cut the sides of the square on this side and that. The middle portion that remains between these two sections made on the side will be the side of the octagon. We shall likewise produce a floor plan of ten angles from the circle. For we shall draw two diameters of the circle intersecting each other at equal angles on both sides. Then from the semi-diameters themselves, whichever you prefer, we shall divide it into two equal parts. From there, from the point of that division, we shall lead a straight line in an oblique path to the high top of the other diameter. If from this line thus drawn you subtract as much as is the fourth part of the entire diameter <note>original: "quarta totius diametri pars"; this refers to half of the radius.</note>, what remains there will be the side of the ten-angled plan. <margin>Tribunes.</margin> **Tribunes** <term>tribunalia (semi-circular or polygonal recesses, often called apses, intended for the altar or seats of dignity)</term> are added to temples: but to some more, and to others fewer. For in rectangular temples, almost nowhere is there more than a single one, and that is placed at the innermost head: so that to those entering the door, it presents itself directly opposite. Or if they are finally added to the sides as well, that may be done without indecency in those rectangular floor plans which are twice as long as they are wide: and no more than one should be placed on each of those sides; or if it would be helpful to add many, it is fitting if the number be odd. In round floor plans and likewise—if I may speak thus—in polygonal ones, a number of tribunes will be very conveniently added. For according to the number of sides, either a single tribune will be added to each individual side, or alternately, one side will be left free while the next will be given a tribune. In round plans, six or even eight tribunes are very conveniently added. In floor plans of many sides, care must be taken that the angles are not in...

...should ensure they are comparable and conforming to each other. Again, a <term>tribunal</term> <note>original: "tribunal"; in this architectural context, Alberti refers to a raised platform, an apse, or a recessed chapel</note> will be either rectangular or drawn to a semicircular perimeter. If only a single tribunal is to be placed at the head of the temple, it will be most highly approved if its curve ends in a semicircle. A rectangular shape is the next best option. However, where a great number of tribunals are to be present, it will contribute to the beauty if rectangles are mixed with semicircles in an alternating arrangement, with their fronts corresponding to one another across the space. 

In these tribunals, the opening of the <term>throats</term> <note>original: "faucium"; the narrow entrance or opening of a recess</note> shall be established as follows: for when there is to be a single tribunal in a rectangular area, I will divide the width of the temple into four parts, and of these, I will give two parts to the "throats" of the tribunal. Or, if we prefer a more spacious design, I will divide the width into six parts, and of these, I will give four parts to the opening. In this way, the ornaments of the columns, the windows, and such features will be most conveniently fitted into their proper places. 

If, however, you place several tribunals around the central area, it is permissible to make those along the sides of the same width as the primary tribunal. Yet, for the sake of dignity, I would prefer the primary one to be larger than the others by one-twelfth. This is also important in rectangular tribunals: if the primary tribunal is made equal on all sides, it will not be disapproved; but in others, the lines drawn from right to left <note>the width</note> ought to have double the length of those that extend into the recess <note>the depth</note>. 

The solid part of the walls—that is, the <term>bones of the building</term> <note>original: "ossa aedificii"; Alberti's metaphor for the structural piers or load-bearing wall segments</note>—which separate the openings of the various tribunals in temples, shall be constructed so that they are never less than a fifth of the width of the opening, and never larger than a third; or, where you wish the space to feel most enclosed, a half. In round floor plans, if the number of tribunals is six, you shall make these gaps—that is, the "bones" and the solid wall—equal to half of the opening. If there are eight openings, then you should make these solids equal in width to the tribunals, especially in the largest temples. If the number of angles is very high, the solid wall shall be one-third the width of the tribunal. 

In some temples, here and there, according to the ancient <term>Etruscan</term> <note>original: "Aetruscorum"; referring to the pre-Roman civilization of Italy known for specific architectural proportions</note> custom, there are not tribunals along the sides, but rather <term>small cells</term> <note>original: "cellulae minusculae"; small side-chapels or rooms</note>; the proportion for these is as follows: They took an area whose length, divided into six parts, exceeded the width by one part <note>a 6:5 ratio</note>. From that total length, they gave two parts to the width of the portico, which projected across the vestibule of the temple; the remaining length they divided into three parts, which were assigned to the depths of the three cells. Again, they divided the width of the temple itself into ten parts. From these they gave three parts to the cells on each side...

### Chapter V. Temple porticos: approaches: steps: and the fitting and intervals of the portico itself.

<margin>
How and where a portico is to be placed in a temple.
</margin>
**T**hus far concerning the internal areas. A <term>portico</term> <note>a porch or covered walkway supported by columns</note> for rectangular temples shall be placed either across the front, or likewise across both the front and the rear; or it shall support the <term>cella</term> <note>the inner sanctum or main chamber</note> all around. On the side where a tribunal projects, a portico shall not be added to the front. Nowhere shall a portico be held shorter in rectangular temples than what is required to span the entire width of the temple: and nowhere shall it be wider than one-third of the total length. In porticos that are at the sides of temples, the columns shall be distant from the walls of the cella by the space of one <term>intercolumniation</term> <note>original: "intercolūnij"; the proportional distance between two adjacent columns</note>. In the rear, the portico will imitate whichever of these styles I have already described. For round temples, we will either surround them with a portico or establish a portico only in the front. In both cases, the ratio of width will be derived from the rules for rectangular temples. But porticos that project in the front shall never be made unless they are rectangular; their length shall either take up the whole width of the inner area, or be reduced by one-eighth, or finally never be shorter than one-fourth.

<margin>
The institution of the Hebrews concerning the placing of temples.
</margin>
Among the Hebrews, it was written in the law of the fathers: "Let there be for you one primary and sacred city in a suitable and convenient place. In it, build one temple and one altar from stones not hewn by hand, but gathered, white and most shining. Let the access to the temple be not by steps." <note>Alberti refers here to Mosaic law, specifically Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy, regarding the construction of altars and the unity of the place of worship</note> For one nation, dedicated to religion by one consensus and institution, will be safe and fortified by one God. Neither of these rules do I approve. For the first is foreign to use and convenience, especially for those who visit temples frequently, such as old women and the weak. The other is vehemently foreign to the majesty of a temple: which we have seen elsewhere in sacred structures built in the recent age of our fathers; where one must climb some steps through the doors to reach the threshold, and then descend from there by just as many steps to the floor of the sacred place—I will not say it was an inept institution, but I do not know why it was instituted. In my opinion indeed, the area of the portico and the whole temple, since it contributes greatly to dignity, ought to be raised and standing out from the rest of the city's ground. But just as in a living creature the head, the foot, and whatever member you wish must be related to the other members and to the whole remaining body: so too in a building, and especially in a temple, the universal parts must be conformed...

[...of the] body: so that all parts correspond among themselves: so that when any one of them is taken, the same measurement allows all the other parts to be appropriately measured. Thus I find that almost all the best ancient <term>architects</term> <note>original: "architectos"</note> established the height of the <term>platform</term> <note>original: "suggesti"; the raised base or pedestal upon which a temple or altar stands</note> by taking it from the width of the temple. For they divided the width into six parts, and gave one of these to the height of the platform. There were also those who, in larger temples, wanted that elevation to be a seventh of the width; and in the largest, a ninth. A <term>portico</term> <note>a porch or covered walkway supported by columns</note> by its very nature consists of only one whole and continuous wall; while on the other sides, it lies open and is passable through its openings. 

One must therefore consider what kind of openings you wish to use. For there is a certain kind of colonnade where the columns are placed sparsely and somewhat far apart from each other; another where they are crowded and set closer to one another. In both of these there are flaws. For in the sparser ones, because of the wideness of the intervals, if you use a <term>beam</term> <note>original: "trabe"; the horizontal architrave spanning the gap between columns</note>, it breaks. <note>The following phrase is underlined in red ink in the original manuscript</note> *If, however, an arch is used, it is not sufficiently conveniently supported by the columns.* In the more crowded ones, however, because of the narrow intervals, the passages, views, and light are impeded. For that reason, a third type was found, a middle and elegant one, which avoids the faults of those others, serves convenience, and is approved above the rest. We could have been content with these three types.

<margin>
Because the number of columns might be lacking for the size of the area, the architect deviates from the best middle-ground.
</margin>
But the skill of craftsmen added two more types in the same way; of which I think as follows. For since perhaps the number of columns was lacking for the size of the area, they turned from that best middle-ground to imitate the sparser ones. But when there was a surplus of columns, it pleased them to place them somewhat more crowded. Therefore, five types of intervals are counted, which it is helpful to call: **widespread**, **crowded**, **elegant**, **somewhat widespread**, and **somewhat crowded**. Furthermore, I think it also happened that when perhaps a supply of very long stone was not available, the architect was forced to make the work with shorter columns. Understanding that this beginning was not succeeding well enough for the grace of the work, he substituted <term>little walls</term> <note>original: "murulos"; likely referring to pedestals or plinths</note> under the columns, by which he might achieve the proper height of the work. 

For from the observation and examination of works, he had discovered that columns in porticos have no grace unless they are brought to certain ratios of height and thickness. Regarding what pertains to these ratios, they advise thus: Make the <term>intercolumniations</term> <note>original: "intercolūnia"; the spaces between columns</note> an odd number. Do not place columns except in pairs. Make the middle of the openings, which stands directly opposite the door, wider than the rest. Where the intercolumniations must be held narrower, employ more graceful columns. With wider intervals, use thicker columns. Therefore, of columns...

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

Thicknesses will be regulated by the intervals, and the intervals by the columns, following these laws in particular. For in "crowded" <note>original: "confertis"; referring to the pycnostyle arrangement where columns are very close together</note> works, the intervals of the columns shall not be narrower than what is required to contain one and a half thicknesses of a column. In "widely spaced" <note>original: "dispansis"; or araeostyle</note> works, however, the interval shall contain no more than three thicknesses plus an additional three-eighths of a single column. In "elegant" <note>original: "elegantibus"; likely referring to the eustyle or "well-proportioned" spacing</note> works, the interval will contain two thicknesses and a quarter part of one. Under the crowded arrangement, two thicknesses are given; under the widely spaced, three full thicknesses are granted. As for the middle intervals in their respective rows: these shall indeed be made wider, so that they exceed the others by a fourth part of themselves. This is what those authorities advise. But we, from the measurements of ancient buildings, have noticed that the middle openings of this kind are not placed according to the same ratios everywhere. For in widely spaced colonnades, none of the best <term>architects</term> <note>original: "optimoꝝ nemo"</note> used the fourth part; instead, most used a twelfth, surely by a prudent plan: lest a beam of immoderate length should fail to support itself and break. Finally, many used a sixth in the remaining cases; and not a few used a twelfth, especially in those openings which we call elegant.

### Columns: the parts of the colonnade portico: capitals: and the types of capitals. Chapter VI.

<margin>
Parts of the
colonnades.
</margin>
<insert>P</insert>aving established the intervals, the columns must be raised to support the roofs. It is of great importance whether you raise columns or <term>piers</term> <note>original: "pilas"; square or rectangular supports as opposed to round columns</note>, and whether you use arched or <term>beamed</term> <note>original: "trabeatis"; horizontal architraves</note> openings. Arched openings and piers are appropriate for theaters; and even in <term>basilicas</term> <note>large public halls used for legal and business matters</note>, arches are not rejected. But in the most dignified works, such as temples, nothing is ever seen except beamed <term>porticos</term> <note>covered walkways with a roof supported by columns</note>. We must speak of these. The parts of the colonnade are the lowest platform, and upon it the <term>base</term>; upon the base the column; then the <term>capital</term>; then the <term>beam</term> <note>original: "trabs"; the architrave</note>; and upon the beam the joists or the <term>fascia</term> <note>a flat horizontal band</note>. Once these are cut, the ends of the joists are either covered or finished. In the highest place is the <term>cornice</term> <note>original: "corona"</note>.

<margin>
Capitals
of the
colonnades.
</margin>
I believe we should begin with the capitals, by which colonnades are most varied. Here I ask of those who would transcribe this work of ours: let them record the numbers which shall be reviewed not with figures, but with Latin names and letters; like so: "twelve," "twenty," "forty," and the like, and not "xii," "xx," "xl." <note>Alberti was famously concerned that copyists would misread Roman numerals, leading to architectural errors; he insisted on writing numbers out in full.</note> Necessity taught us to place capitals upon columns so that the ends of the joined beams might sit upon them. But that raw and square-cut wood had an ugly appearance. Therefore, at the beginning among the <term>Dorians</term> <note>one of the primary Greek tribes, credited with the oldest of the classical orders</note>—if we believe everything the Greeks say—they thought to devise something similar by imitating a <term>lathe</term> <note>a machine for shaping wood or stone by rotating it</note>: so that a round shape, like a dish, would appear to be placed under a small square lid; and because this appeared too compressed, they added a neck a little higher...
