## Book VII. On the Ornaments of Sacred Buildings. Folio CII.

...having substituted a [support], they raised it up. The Ionians, having examined Doric works, approved of the <term>dishes</term> <note>original: "lances"; likely referring to the abacus, the flat slab on top of a capital</note> on the capitals. But they did not approve of that bareness of the <term>neck</term> <note>original: "colli"; the transition between the column shaft and the capital</note> and the joining of the [basin]; for that reason, they added the bark of a tree, which, hanging down on both sides and curling into a spiral, would clothe the sides of the dishes. <note>This describes the characteristic "scrolls" or volutes of the Ionic order, which Alberti poetically compares to curling bark.</note> Then came the Corinthians, under the leadership of Callimachus: who, not using flattened dishes like the others, but a very tall vessel covered around with leaves, had been very pleased when he saw such a thing at the tomb of a young girl, where an <term>acanthus</term> <note>A Mediterranean plant with jagged leaves that became the standard decoration for Corinthian capitals.</note> plant had grown up and clothed it in that way.

<margin>Three types of capitals: Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian.</margin>
There were therefore three types of capitals invented that the experience of experts would accept. Although I find this very thing was in use among the most ancient Etruscans—I mean the Doric, the Ionic, and the Corinthian. And what do you think is the reason? A number of different capitals are found here and there, which were produced with great care and exquisite diligence by those who studied to invent new things.

<margin>None.</margin>
¶ Yet none of these presents itself as being worth approving over the others, except for one—so that we do not attribute everything we have received to foreigners—which I call the <margin>Italic.</margin> <term>Italic</term> <note>original: "italicum"; Alberti’s name for the Composite order, which combines elements of the other three.</note>. Indeed, it added Ionic delights to the festivity of the Corinthians: and in place of handles, it attached hanging spirals—a pleasing and very well-regarded work. They established columns that would contribute to the elegance of the work in this way. For they said those columns are owed to Doric capitals whose length, measured from the top to the bottom, equals seven times the thickness of their base. For Ionic columns, they wanted the base thickness to be a ninth part of their length. For Corinthian capitals, they substituted a column eight times its thickness in length. For all these columns, they thought the bases should be equal in height to each other, but varied in their <term>contours</term> <note>original: "lineamentis"; the specific profile and decorative moldings of the base.</note>. What more? They were different from each other in almost all the contours of their parts. However, they agreed for the most part on the logic of the columns. For the Ionic, Corinthian, and Doric styles all approved of the column contours we spoke of in the previous book; and in this they also agreed, imitating nature: that they thought the shafts of the columns should never be anything but more slender at the top than at the bottom. There were some who said they should be placed a fourth part thicker at the bottom than at the top. Others—because they understood that objects seen from a distance appear smaller to the eye—very wisely thought that very long columns should be made less slender at the top than those that were equally short; and they established the following rules for them. Where a column is to be fifteen feet long, the bottom thickness should be divided into six parts; and having cast aside one of these parts, the remaining five should be given to the top...

...to the thickness. Regarding the column, they thought that for those from fifteen to twenty feet in height, the shaft should be so proportioned that out of thirteen parts at the bottom, eleven should be left at the top. From twenty to thirty feet, the columns should have seven parts at the bottom and six at the top. Then, for those up to forty feet, out of fifteen parts of the lower column, thirteen are left at the top and two are removed; the rest are discarded. Finally, up to fifty feet, it is necessary for the column to be eight parts thick at the base and seven at the top. Following this deduction, one must reason that the higher the head of the column is, the thicker it should be left. Thus, in these matters, all things reached a consensus. But we have found from measuring actual works that these rules were not strictly observed among our Latin <note>Roman</note> ancestors.

¶ A useful repetition regarding the outlines of columns and their parts. Regarding the base, the <term>tori</term> <note>rounded, cushion-like moldings</note>, the rings, the fillets, and the <term>plinth</term> <note>original: "latastro"; the square slab at the very bottom of a column base</note>. On the small components of the outlines: the little band, the step, the rough-work, the cord, the flute, the little throat, and the little wave.

### Chapter VII.

**I** shall therefore repeat regarding the outlines of columns almost the same things we dealt with in the previous book, though not by the same method, but one that is otherwise useful. I will take from the columns that the ancestors were accustomed to place in public works one that is halfway between the largest and the smaller ones; I establish this to be thirty feet. In this one, you divide the greatest diameter of the footprint into nine equal parts: from which you will give eight parts to the greatest diameter of the top <term>surface</term> <note>original: "picturę"; Alberti uses this to mean the cross-section or face of the column</note>. The proportion of these will be as nine to eight, which they call <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>A ratio of 1 plus 1/8</note>; and I will place it in the same proportion so that the diameter of the lowest recession is to the diameter of the footprint. For while the footprint is nine, this recession is eight. Again, I will set the greatest diameter of the top surface to the top recession as a <term>sesquiseptima</term> <note>A ratio of 1 plus 1/7, or 8 to 7.</note> proportion.

<margin>Parts of the base.</margin>
¶ I come to the outlines of the parts in which they differ. In the bases, these are the parts: the plinth, the tori, and the rings.

<margin>What a plinth is.</margin>
The <term>plinth</term> <note>latastrum</note> is a quadrangular part placed at the very bottom: I call it so because it spreads out in width in every direction.

<margin>The torus.</margin>
The <term>tori</term> <note>singular: thorus</note> are thick rings in the base: one of which is pressed down by the column itself, while the other sits upon the plinth.

<margin>The ring.</margin>
The <term>ring</term> <note>original: "orbiculus"; refers to the scotia or trochilus</note> is a hollowed-out circle which, like a pulley-wheel, is pressed there between the tori.

<margin>The Doric method for measuring column parts.</margin>
They derived every part to be measured for their calculation from the diameter of the bottom of the column: and thus they established the Doric principle first. For they made the base half as thick as the diameter of the bottom of the column; in this, they wanted the plinth to extend in every direction...

# Book VII. On Sacred Ornaments.

...width should be such that it captures the full diameter of the lower column, and in addition no more than half of that diameter, and no less than a third <note>Alberti is defining the width of the square plinth as being between 1.33 and 1.5 times the column's bottom diameter</note>. They divided the height of the entire base into three parts, one of which they gave to the thickness of the **plinth** <term>latastrum</term> <note>original: "latastri"; the square slab at the very bottom of a column base</note>. Thus, the thickness of the entire base was three times the thickness of the plinth, and the width of the plinth was also three times the thickness of the base. Aside from the plinth, they divided the remaining thickness of the base into four parts, the highest of which they gave to the **upper torus** <term>thoro</term> <note>original: "thoro"; a large, rounded, cushion-like molding</note>. Again, that middle portion of thickness between the upper torus and the bottom plinth was divided into two parts: the lower they gave to the **lower torus**, and they carved the upper part into a **scotia** <term>orbiculo</term> <note>original: "orbiculo"; a concave, recessed molding, also known as a "trochilus"</note> that sits between the two tori. This scotia consists of a hollowed channel and two **fillets** <term>nextrulis</term> <note>original: "nextrulis"; small, flat decorative bands or rings</note> which surround the edges of the channel. They gave the fillets one-seventh of the space, and hollowed out the rest. 

In every building, we have said that one must notice that whatever is built on top must rest upon a solid foundation. It will not be solid if a **plumb line** <note>a weight on a string used to determine a perfectly vertical line</note> falling from the foot of the stone placed above finds air or empty space beneath it. Therefore, when they carved the channels of the scotias, they were careful that the plumb lines of the parts to be built above did not meet those hollows in the carving. The tori will project out from half their thickness by an additional eighth part. Furthermore, the widest circle of the thicker torus will, by its plumb line, equal the outermost line of the plinth. 

<margin>
The Ionic method.
</margin>
These are the Doric rules. The Ionics indeed approved of the Doric thickness, but they doubled the scotias and added two rings between the scotias. Thus, they made the bases as high as half the diameter of the lower column; they divided this height into four parts, and gave one of these to the thickness of the plinth. To the width of the plinth, however, they gave eleven of these same quarter-parts. Therefore, the total thickness of the base was four parts and the width was eleven. Having marked out the plinth, they divided the rest of the height into seven parts: of these, they gave two to the thickness of the lower torus. Again, whatever thickness remained besides the torus and the plinth, they divided into three parts: the top one they gave to the upper torus; the middle two they gave to two scotias and two rings which are pressed between both tori. The proportion of the scotias and rings was as follows: they divided the space itself between the tori into seven parts, giving one to each ring; the scotias took the remaining portions in equal shares. They observed the same projections in the tori as the Dorics did, and in carving the scotias, they were careful not to disturb the plumb lines of the parts added above.

<margin>The Corinthian method</margin> approved of the Ionic and also the Doric base, and used both throughout. ### On the capital and its parts in the Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian manners. Chapter VIII.

<margin>The Doric capital.</margin>
**N**ow I return to the capitals. For the Doric capital, they made it as thick as the base, and they divided its entire thickness into three parts: the first they gave to the **abacus** <term>operculo</term> <note>original: "operculo"; the flat slab at the very top of a capital</note>; the second was occupied by the **echinus** <term>lanx</term> <note>original: "lanx"; the bowl-like molding below the abacus</note> along with the neck of the capital that sits beneath the echinus. The final third was left for the width of the abacus, which, toward the edge, had a full diameter plus a sixth part of the semi-diameter of the bottom of the column. These are the parts of this abacus: the **cymatium** <term>cimatiū</term> and the **fascia** <term>lataſtrũ</term> <note>original: "lataſtrũ"; a broad flat band</note>; and the cymatium here is an **ogee** <term>gulula</term>: it takes up two parts out of five of the abacus. The lip of the echinus reached the outer lines of the abacus. Around the bottom of the echinus, some encircled it with three small rings for the sake of ornament, others with an ogee. This ornament occupied no more than a third part of the echinus. The diameter of the neck—that is, the lowest part of the capital, which is observed in all capitals—did not exceed the solid thickness of the column. Others, as we have gathered from the designs of buildings, made the Doric capital with a height of three-quarters <note>original: "ex dimidia atq; item ex quarta"; literally "from a half and also from a fourth"</note> of the diameter of the lower column; and they divided this entire height of the capital into eleven parts: of which they gave four to the abacus, likewise four to the echinus, and three parts to the neck. Soon they divided the abacus into two equal parts: of which the upper part was an ogee and the lower a fascia. Again, they divided the echinus into two equal parts, the lowest of which they gave either to rings or to an ogee, which would gird the echinus from below. To the neck, indeed, some attached roses, others rising leaves. These are the Doric rules.
<margin>The Ionic capital.</margin>
We shall make the Ionic capital thus. The total thickness of the capital shall be half the thickness of the column at its bottom. Divide this thickness of the capital for yourself into twenty-one **modules** <term>modulos</term>. To the abacus, therefore, you shall give three modules. [Of these parts] you shall give four to the **abacus** <note>The OCR "tici" is likely the end of "abaci"</note>; to the **echinus** <term>lanci</term> <note>original: "lanci"; literally "dish," referring here to the rounded molding beneath the abacus</note> you shall give six. Leave the remaining six at the bottom for the **volutes** <term>volutis</term> <note>the spiral scrolls of an Ionic capital</note>, which the hanging **cushion** <term>cortex</term> <note>original: "cortex"; literally "bark" or "shell," referring to the side of the Ionic capital</note> shall form on this side and that. The width of the **abacus** <term>operculi</term> <note>original: "operculi"; literally "lid"</note> in every direction shall be equal to the diameter of the top of the shaft of its column. The width of the cushion, from the front of the capital to the back, shall equal the abacus. The length of this cushion shall flow out from the sides and hang down, winding itself into a spiral line. The **eye** <term>vmbilicus</term> <note>original: "vmbilicus"; literally "navel," the center point of the spiral</note> of the spiral on the right side shall be twenty-two modules distant from the corresponding eye on the left. And it shall be twelve modules distant from the top line of the abacus.
<margin>How the spiral is to be drawn.</margin>
Draw the spiral itself in this way: in the point of the center of the eye, describe a tiny point whose radius <note>original: "semidiameter"</note> is one module. And mark another point opposite it, and likewise another below in the upper arc. And mark another opposite it below in the lower arc. Then, place the fixed foot of the compass on the upper point of this kind; draw the moving foot from the line that divides the abacus from the cushion, and descend, driving it toward the outer part of the capital until it completes a full semicircle and meets the region below the point of the tiny circle. There, tighten the compass and place the fixed foot below on the lowest point of the tiny circle. Lead the moving foot from the start of the spiral already described, and ascend inwards until you touch the top lip of the echinus. Thus, with two unequal semicircles, you will have created one full turn of the spiral. Next, resuming the drawing in this manner, fold the spiral—that is, the windings of the drawn line—toward the eye, that is, toward the tiny circle. The lip of the echinus shall expand so that it projects two modules from the cushion at the front; but its base shall equal the width of the top of the column. The **recesses** <term>cõtracturę</term> of the volutes, which join the front volutes to the back ones along the sides of the capital, shall be made slender, to the thickness of the echinus plus half a module. An ornament shall be added to the abacus: a **cymatium** <term>cimatium</term> with an **ogee** <term>gulula</term> of one module. The thickness of the cushion shall be hollowed out with a channel to the depth of half a module. The width of the **fillet** <term>nextruli</term> at the channel shall be a fourth part. In the middle of the front, through the channel, leaves and seeds shall be carved. The parts of the echinus which project through the front of the capital are made with **egg-and-dart** <term>ouiculatas</term> <note>original: "ouiculatas"; literally "little eggs"</note>; and beneath the eggs, they spread out **beads** <term>baccas</term>. They clothe the recesses of the sides between the volutes with scales or leaves. Such, then, is the Ionic capital.
<margin>The Corinthian Capital.</margin>
The height of the Corinthian capital, however, takes two semi-diameters of the bottom of the column. This entire height shall be divided into seven modules. The thickness of the abacus takes one module; the remaining [six...]

### Book 7. On the Ornaments of Sacred Buildings. Folio 105.

The **vase** <term>vas</term> <note>original: "vas"; the "bell" or central core of the Corinthian capital</note> occupies the space: the width of its base is as great as the column is at the top, excluding the projections; its **rim** <term>labrum</term> at the top equals in width the thickness of the column at its bottom. The width of the **lid** <term>operculi</term> <note>The abacus</note> fills ten modules. But the corners are cut back <note>original: "decussantur"</note> by half a module on each side. The lids of other capitals consist of straight lines. The lids of the **Corinthian** <term>Corynthiorum</term> are curved inward until the distance between the curves is equal to the width of the vase’s base. The **molding** <term>cimatium</term> of the lid will be defined by one-third of the thickness: its outlines will be like those we apply with the finest chisels to the tops of columns. A small binding <note>original: "nextrulum"</note> and a cord clothe the vase with two rising rows of leaves: and they grant eight leaves to each row. The first leaves are two modules long. The second row likewise rises to two modules. The remaining modules are given to the **stalks** <term>canaliculis</term> <note>original: "canaliculis"; usually termed "caulicoli" in modern architectural English—the stalks from which the small volutes emerge</note> emerging from the leaves and climbing up to the height of the vase. The number of stalks is sixteen: on each face of the capital, four are wound; two to the right from a single node, and two to the left from another single node, leading themselves in such a way that the ends hang under the corners of the lid, imitating a **snail** <note>original: "cocleam"; referring to the spiral of a snail shell or volute</note>. The middle ones are joined at the center of the face, their heads also entangling in a curve. Near these middle stalks, a distinguished flower stands out from the vase, not exceeding the thickness of the lid. The thickness of the rim appears around the vase where the stalks do not cover it—that part is one module: the curls of the leaves are divided into five "fingers," or seven if preferred. The tips of the leaves hang forward by half a module; it is most graceful with leaves of this kind, as in every carving, that the lines are carved deeply and sharply. Thus are the Corinthians. The **Italic Capital** <term>Italici Capitulum</term> <note>The Composite order, which Alberti calls "Italic"</note> has added to its own capitals whatever ornaments were in the others. 

<margin>The Italic Order.</margin> 

For they have the same proportion for the vase, the lid, the leaves, and the flower as the Corinthians. But in place of the stalks, they have **handles** <note>original: "anfas" (ansae); referring to the large Ionic-style volutes</note> projecting under the four corners of the lid, which fill two whole modules. The face of the capital, which would otherwise be bare, took its ornaments from the Ionic. For it pours out a small channel for the curled handles: and like a dish <note>the echinus</note>, it has the rim of the vase decorated with **eggs** <note>original: "ouiclatum"; the egg-and-dart motif</note>. It also has beads <note>original: "baccas"; the bead-and-reel molding</note> stretched underneath. Besides these, many mixed capitals are seen, with lines from these styles and parts either increased or diminished. But these are not approved by the learned. Thus far for capitals; unless that part is missing which is usually placed above the lid of the capital: another small quadrangular lid, hidden in the work, so that the capital might breathe and not be entirely buried...

## Chapter IX. On the beams of the capitals, joists, planks, bands, modules, fillets, tiles, grooves, and other such things pertaining to colonnades.

Once the capitals are set, the **beam** <term>trabs</term> <note>the architrave, the lowest part of the entablature</note> is placed upon them; on the beam are the **joists** <term>tigna</term>, planks, and such things as pertain to supporting the roof. In all these, other orders differ greatly from the Ionic, and the Ionic from the Doric, although in some aspects they all agree. For they arrange the beam in such a way that they want its lowest width not to exceed the solid part of the top of the column; but they make the top width of the beam equal to the diameter of the bottom of the column.

<margin>What cornices are.</margin>
We call the **cornices** <term>coronices</term> those topmost parts which project above the joists. In these, they also observed what we said should be done in all projections: that however much the height of that part was, so much should it project from the wall. They also observed to place this work of the cornices with a slight inclination <note>a "weathering" or slope to shed water</note> of a twelfth part, because they had found that these parts appear to tilt backward when they are extended at right angles. Here again I ask those who will transcribe these things—and I ask it again and again—that they express the numbers to be listed not with figures <note>Roman or Arabic numerals</note> but with their full names, so that the text is less corrupted by errors. <note>Alberti was deeply concerned that copyists would misread numbers, leading to structural failures in buildings designed from his book.</note>

<margin>The Doric beam and its module.</margin>
The Doric [architects], therefore, made the beam no less thick than the semi-diameter of the bottom of the column. On it are three **bands** <term>fasciae</term>; and under the first upper band, certain short **fillets** <term>regulae</term> are stretched, from each of which hang six small **pegs** <term>claviculi</term> <note>known in modern architecture as "guttae" or drops</note> attached beneath for the sake of holding the joists: their heads project from the wall to the fillets themselves, so they do not slide backward. They divided the entire thickness of this beam into twelve **modules** <term>moduli</term>: by which modules all the following small parts are measured. To the first, lowest band they gave four modules. To the one next to this, which is the middle, they gave six. To the topmost, two modules were left. And of the six modules of the middle band, the top module was given to the fillets and another to the hanging pegs. The length of the fillets was twice six <note>twelve</note> modules. The spaces left clear between the ends of the fillets were eighteen modules wide.

<margin>Joists.</margin>
On the beams are the **joists** <term>tigna</term> <note>which form the "triglyphs" in the Doric order</note>: whose ends, cut perpendicularly, appear on the outside from half a module. The width of the joists will equal the thickness of the beam; to the height, however, they add half of itself until it is twice nine <note>eighteen</note> modules. Through...

# Book VII. On the Ornaments of Sacred Buildings. Folio 106.

On the height of the front of the joists <note>referring here to the ends of the beams that form the "triglyphs" in the Doric order</note>, three straight, equidistant grooves are marked, cut at a right angle, so that their opening spreads to the width of one module. From here and there, the edges of the margins are trimmed back until half a module remains vacant. Where the work is intended to be elegant, the empty spaces between the joists are filled with tablets of equal width <note>these are the "metopes," the panels between the grooved triglyphs</note>; and the joists are placed vertically so that they sit firmly over the center of their respective columns. The ends of the joists, however, project from the tablets by half a module; the vertical line of the tablets <margin>**Tablets.**</margin> aligns with the lowest band of the beam placed beneath. On tablets of this kind, there are carved the heads of oxen, plates, or wheels <note>original: "capita vitulorum/ patinę/ rotęve"; these are traditional Doric motifs: bucrania, paterae, and wheels</note>, and things of that sort. Upon each of the joists and tablets, a small band is placed in the position of a molding <term>cimatium</term> <note>a crowning decorative molding, often with an S-curve profile</note>, two modules wide. When these are finished, a shelf <term>pluteus</term> <margin>**The Shelf.**</margin> is placed on top, two modules thick, decorated with small channels or grooves. On this shelf—for so I interpret the "pavement"—a layer is spread three modules thick; its ornament consists of a "small sheep" <note>original: "ovicula"; likely referring to an egg-and-dart or bead-and-reel molding pattern</note> derived, unless I am mistaken, from the variation of stones that emerge from a support of lime within a pavement. Above this, one places the **mutules** <term>mutuli</term> <note>projecting blocks under the cornice that resemble the ends of rafters</note>, as wide as the joists and as thick as the pavement. Each one is positioned so that they correspond to the individual joists below them. They project forward by twelve modules; their fronts are cut off vertically, and a molding is painted or carved upon them: a small "throat" <term>gulula</term> <note>a "gola" or ogee molding, named for its throat-like curve</note> made of a half and a quarter module. In the spaces that appear hanging between the mutules, roses and acanthus leaves are carved. Above the mutules, the face of the work <note>the corona or drip-stone</note> is applied, occupying four modules. This face consists of a band and a "throat" molding. For the throat molding occupies one and a half modules. At this point, if a **pediment** <term>fastigium</term> <note>the triangular gable forming the roof end</note> is to be placed on the work, all the cornices are repeated within the pediment itself. In each of these, at the predefined angles, the individual parts belonging to its type are fitted so that they correspond exactly to the vertical lines and are bounded by their own proper lines. The work of the pediment differs from the primary cornices in this: that on a pediment, a drip-edge <term>stillicidium</term> <note>a gutter or projecting molding to shed rainwater</note> is always applied at the very top; in the Doric order, this is a wave-like molding four modules thick. However, in those cornices that are intended to support a pediment, it is not applied; whereas in those that will not have a pediment, it is applied. But we shall speak of pediments soon.

<margin>**Ionic Beam.**</margin>
Such are the Doric matters. The Ionians, indeed not without skill, established that a thicker beam <note>architrave</note> is owed to taller columns—a rule that is observed quite appropriately in the Doric order as well. For this reason, they decided it should be defined thus: where a column is to be twenty feet high, the beam shall be made from one-thirteenth part of the column's height. But if it is up to twenty-five feet, then the beam shall be made one-twelfth part of the column's length. But if...

...if a column is to be thirty feet long, the beam <note>original: "trabs"; the architrave, the lowest part of the entablature resting directly on the columns</note> shall be given one-eleventh of its length. Finally, the remaining parts shall be determined by the following graduation. An Ionic beam consists of three bands <term>fasciae</term> besides the molding <term>cimatium</term>. The profile of the molding was a "little throat" <term>gulula</term> <note>a cyma reversa molding, which has an S-shaped profile</note>. Again, what was beneath the molding they divided into twelve modules: of which they gave three to the lowest band, four to the middle, and the remaining five modules they gave to the uppermost band, which sits directly beneath the molding. There are some who gave no molding to the bands, and some who did; of these, some placed a "little throat" <note>original: "gululam"</note> at one-fifth the height of its band, and others a "little rope" <note>original: "funiculum"; a bead-like or cable molding</note> at one-seventh.

You will furthermore find in the works of the ancients that profiles were either transferred or mixed from various systems of work; which you should not entirely disparage, but of all of them, they seem to have most approved of a beam in which no more than two bands are present. I interpret this as being the Doric beam, once the "rules" <note>regulae</note> and "little pegs" <note>clauiculis; referring to the guttae or drop-like ornaments</note> are removed. This they made as follows: they divided the entire thickness into nine modules, of which they gave one module and two-thirds of a module to the molding. Beneath that, they gave three and one-third modules to the middle band. To the lowest band, they gave the remaining two modules. The molding of this beam had, in its upper half, a small channel <note>canaliculum</note> with a "right-hand tool" <note>dextrulo</note> and in the other half a "cabled" <note>rudentem</note> pattern. Indeed, in this case, the middle band was given a "little rope" <note>funiculus</note> beneath the cable pattern in place of a molding, at one-eighth the height of the whole band; and the lowest band was given a "little throat" molding at one-third of its own width. Above this Royal Band they placed a "little throat" molding no more than four modules high, and no less than three. # Book VII. On the Ornaments of Sacred Buildings. Folio CVII.

The height at the front takes four modules. The part which covers the base of the <term>mutules</term> <note>rectangular blocks projecting under the cornice, resembling the ends of wooden rafters</note> is six and a half modules wide. Above the front of such mutules, tiles <note>original: "imbrices"</note> were placed, two modules thick; their ornament was a "little throat" <term>gulula</term> <note>an S-shaped molding</note> or a "rope" <term>rudens</term>. In the highest position was a "little wave" <term>undula</term> of three modules, or four where it was preferred. Upon this wave, both the Ionics and the Dorics used to carve lion heads vomiting out the collected rainwater. They took care that the falling water would not splash those entering the temple or the interior of the temple itself. For this reason, the mouths of those heads that hung over openings were kept closed. The Corinthians

<margin>Corinthian beam.</margin>
added nothing to the work of the beams and floor-frames except, if I interpret correctly, that they did not place the mutules so they projected far out; nor did they place them according to a plumb line like the Dorics, but kept them bare and shaped to the line of the "little wave." These are spaced apart by as much as they project from the wall at their fronts. In other matters, however, they followed the Ionics. Thus far concerning beamed <term>trabeated</term> colonnades. We shall speak of arched ones soon, when we treat the basilica. There are some things pertaining to colonnades of this sort that must not be neglected. For it has indeed been discovered that columns placed in the open air appear thinner than those placed in an enclosed space. And the greater the number of flutes <term>striae</term>, the thicker the columns seem to be. For that reason, they give this advice: make the corner columns thicker, because they are more constricted by the perspective of the open air than the others;

<margin>Small channels.</margin>
or increase the number of flutes. But columns are fluted either with

<margin>Flutes.</margin>
channels drawn in a straight line to the bottom, or with channels wound around the column <note>referring to spiral fluting</note>. Among the Dorics, the channels are excavated straight down the column; these channels the architects called <term>striae</term> <note>flutes</note>. Among the Dorics, the number of flutes is twenty; among the others, twenty-four. The others distinguish the channels by an intervening "little joint" <term>nextrulo</term> <note>the flat fillet between the grooves</note>. This is made no less than a third and no more than a fourth of the width of the channel's opening. They are hollowed out to the shape of a semicircle. The Dorics, however, having removed the fillet, draw simple flutes, sometimes flat, or rather hollow them out to no more than a quarter of a circle, and they terminate the continuous excavations at an angle. Almost all designers fill the bottom third of the flutes' length with a "rope" <note>original: "rudente"; this is known as cabling, where the bottom of the flute is filled with a convex molding to protect the edges</note> so that the column may be more resistant to blows and injury. A flute that is drawn straight through the length of the column from top to bottom makes the column appear thicker to viewers than it actually is. One that is wound around, however, will create variety. But the less it diverges from a straight perpendicular line, the thicker the column will appear. The windings of the flutes should be no more than three, and...

<meta>This page continues Alberti's discussion on the ornamentation of columns, specifically the technical methods for carving flutes (striae) and the proportional math for spacing columns in the Doric and Ionic orders. # Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

...they were never accustomed to placing less than one whole [flute]. Whatever kind of flute <term>stria</term> <note>the vertical grooves carved into a column shaft</note> you draw, it is proper for it to be continued and brought down in a consistent and matching line from top to bottom, so that the excavations do not clash. The angle of a square <note>original: "norma"</note> will provide the method for the excavation. Mathematicians hold that a line drawn from any point you choose on the circumference of a semicircle to the ends of the diameter forms a right angle for that square. Therefore, once the sides of the flutes have been carved, the trench must be sunk so deep that the angle of the square may settle into it freely. However, on any fluted columns, a decent interval must be left at both ends, so that the empty space of the flutes is distinguished from the neighboring small knots <note>original: "nextrulis"</note> that bind the crown <note>original: "coronam," here referring to the capital or molding</note>. So much for these matters. Near Memphis, they say that around the temple they used colossi twelve cubits high instead of columns. Elsewhere they placed columns that could be turned <note>original: "volubiles," perhaps referring to columns on pivots or with spiral designs</note>, clothed in vine-shoots and filled with scattered little birds. But for the majesty of temples, a column that is smooth and clean is more becoming.

<margin>
Dimensions for the arrangement of columns.
</margin>
Certain dimensions are collected which provide much skill and ease for arranging columns in a work. For indeed, the columns that will be present in the work are numbered, and the method of arrangement is derived from that number. Now, in the Doric order—to begin with these—if there are to be four columns, the front of the area shall be divided into twenty-seven parts. If there are to be six, it shall be divided into forty-one parts. But if there are to be eight, it shall be divided into fifty-six parts. From these, two parts shall be given to each column thickness. In Ionic works, however, where four columns are to be placed, the front of the area shall be divided into eleven and a half parts. Where six columns are placed, it shall be divided into eighteen parts. But if it is necessary to have placed eight columns, it shall be divided into twenty-four and a half parts; from these, one part shall be given to the thickness of the column.

### ¶ On the temple floor, the interior spaces of the area, the site of the walls, and the wall ornaments. Chapter X.

**T**he floor <term>pavimentum</term> of the temple and the interior spaces are those which provide a place where people may ascend by some step; and they require the place where the altar of sacrifice is to be stationed to be higher than all else. As for the entrances and the throats <note>original: "fauces," the narrow passages</note> of the inner chambers <term>cellae</term> which are at the sides, some left them entirely open and completely unobstructed, with no part of a wall drawn across. Others placed two columns between them, following the ratios of the beams and ornaments from the portico of which we spoke recently. The remaining void that was there above the crowns <note>the moldings or cornices</note> was left for the holding of statues and candelabra.

<page-num>CVIII.</page-num>
<header>Book VII. On Sacred Ornaments. Folio CVIII.</header>

...they were [extending the walls]; others restricted the openings of the entry to the cells by extending the wall on either side.

<margin>Wall</margin>
¶ Anyone who believes that temple walls ought to be raised to an extreme thickness for the sake of dignity is mistaken. For who would not criticize a body whose limbs swell more than is proper? Furthermore, the advantage of natural light is taken away by the thickness of the sides.

<margin>Pantheon</margin>
In the Pantheon temple, the most excellent architect, although the wall needed to be thick, used only solid ribs <note>original: "assis," here referring to the structural brick arches or "ribs" that form the skeleton of the Pantheon's wall</note>; he rejected other fillers. The spaces there which the unskilled would have filled in, he occupied with niches and openings; by that method, he reduced the expense, sustained the burden of the weights, and added elegance to the work.

A wall’s thickness should be determined by the proportions of the column: so that in a wall, the ratio of the height to its own thickness corresponds just as it does in columns. I have noted that the ancients were accustomed to dividing the front of the site in temples into twelve parts—or where they desired the work to be most robust, into nine—and from these, they gave one part to the thickness of the wall. In round temples, no one took the wall height as less than half [the diameter]; many took two parts out of three of the diameter; some took three parts out of four, to which height they would raise the interior wall as far as the vault <term>testudo</term> <note>literally "tortoise," a term for a dome or vaulted ceiling</note>.

But the more skilled divided the circumference of that circular area into four parts and extended a line equal to one of them; they raised the innermost wall there to a height corresponding to that length, which responds in a ratio of eleven to four. Many have imitated this same rule in quadrangular buildings, whether temples or any vaulted works. Where, however, there are cells to be placed on either side of the area so that the breadth of the space appears more open to the eye, they sometimes raised the height of the wall to match the height of the area.

But in round buildings, the height of the interior wall will not be the same as the exterior. For the top of the interior wall will provide the starting point for the vault. Indeed, it is fitting for the exterior part of the wall to be raised as high as the eaves <term>subgrundia</term>. Therefore, this part will occupy one-third of the total height of the vault that is placed upon the walls, if the roof is indeed led down in steps. But if the roof is made with straight and sloping lines <note>original: "displuviatis," referring to a roof that sheds water away from the center</note>, then the exterior wall there will occupy half the height of the vault.

<margin>Note</margin>
In temples, a wall made of brick <term>testaceus</term> <note>referring to fired brick or tile</note> will be most convenient, but it should be decorated with the ornaments of cladding.

In Elis <note>a region in the Peloponnese</note>, at the temple of Minerva <note>Athena</note>, the brother of Phidias applied a plaster coating made of lime kneaded with saffron and...

...milk. The monument of Osymandyas <note>original: "Simandium", referring to the Pharaoh Ramses II</note> in which the concubines of Jove were said to be buried. The kings of the Egyptians encircled it with a golden ring one cubit <term>cubit</term> <note>an ancient unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18 inches</note> thick and three hundred and sixty-five cubits in circumference: in which for every cubit, a single day of the year was inscribed. So they say. Others, on the contrary, following Plato, believed their people should be cautioned by law that, in temples, they should reject a variety of ornaments and allurements and prize whiteness <note>original: "candorem," implying both physical white color and moral purity</note> above all. Nevertheless, he said, "let it be a model." I am easily persuaded that purity and simplicity of color, just like purity and simplicity of life, is most pleasing to the supreme gods; and it is not fitting to have things in temples that distract the mind from religious meditation toward various allurements and pleasures of the senses.

But I believe that, both in other public affairs and especially in sacred buildings, one should never depart from dignity <note>original: "gravitate"</note>. He is to be praised who wishes the wall, the roof, and the floor to be most exquisitely carved by every art and most elegant—and above all, as far as lies in your power, enduring. Therefore, an internal cladding <term>crustatio</term> <note>a decorative facing or veneering of a wall</note> under the roof made of marble, glass, or paneled wood, or carved around, will be very suitable. Truly, according to the custom of the ancients, a coating of lime plaster <term>calce</term> sprinkled with small figures <term>sigillis</term> will be approved as excellent. In both cases, care shall be taken that suitable and most decent places and positions be assigned to statues <note>original: "signis"</note> and paintings. And especially in the portico, monuments of great deeds will be most beautifully commended through paintings.

<margin>The dictator Caesar bought two paintings for ninety talents.</margin> Inside the temple, however, I prefer to have painted panels <note>original: "tabulas," referring to movable paintings on wood panels</note> rather than paintings applied directly to the walls themselves; or I shall be delighted by statues rather than panels, unless they are of such a kind as those which Caesar the dictator bought for ninety talents to adorn the temple of Venus Genetrix. And I shall contemplate a good painting—for to paint something poorly is to defile the wall—with no less pleasure of the mind than when I read a good history. Each is a painter: the former paints with words; the latter teaches the subject with a brush. In other respects, both are equal and have much in common. In both, there is a need for the greatest talent and incredible diligence. But I would wish that in temples, both on the wall and on the floor, nothing be present that does not savor of pure philosophy.

<margin>Roman laws inscribed on bronze tablets.</margin> I find that in the Capitol there were laws inscribed on bronze tablets by which they governed the empire; and when the temple burned, they were restored by the Emperor Vespasian to the number of three thousand. They record that on the threshold of Delian Apollo there were verses inscribed by which men were taught what composition of herbs they might use against all poisons. 

<margin>☞</margin> We shall consider that those admonitions should be displayed by which [men become] more just, more modest, more fruit[ful]...

### Book VII. On Sacred Ornaments.

...and that we might be rendered more graceful and adorned by every virtue. Like those sayings that are read: **Be such as you would wish to seem** <note>original: "Talis esto / qualis videri velis"</note>. **Love, and you will be loved** <note>original: "Ama / et amabere"</note>, and others of this kind. Especially, I would wish the floor to be filled with lines and figures pertaining to musical and geometric matters, so that from every side we might be stimulated toward the cultivation of the soul. The ancients were accustomed to place the rarest things for the sake of ornament, both in temples and in porticos. Such was that in the temple of Hercules: horns of ants brought from India; and those of Vespasian, who placed <margin>Cinnamon crowns.</margin> crowns of cinnamon in the Capitol; and of Augusta <note>likely Livia, the wife of Augustus</note>, who placed a very large cinnamon root in a golden bowl in the primary temple of the Palatine. <margin>Horns of ants.</margin> Among the people of Thermum in Aetolia <note>an ancient Greek city and religious center</note>, which Philip <margin>Philip broke the weapons and tablets at Thermum.</margin> ravaged, they say there were in the temple porticos more than fifteen thousand weapons, and more than two thousand statues for the sake of ornament—all of which Polybius <note>a Greek historian of the Hellenistic period</note> records that Philip broke into pieces, except for those that bore the name or image of the gods. And perhaps it is not the number of such things that should be weighed so much as the variety. Among the Ciculi <note>likely referring to a tribe mentioned by Solinus, perhaps the Sicels or a North African group</note> there were those who set about fashioning statues out of salt, according to Solinus <note>a 3rd-century Roman grammarian and compiler</note>. And Pliny says a statue was made out of <margin>Statues of salt and glass.</margin> glass. Truly, such very rare things will be most worthy of admiration for nature and human ingenuity. But regarding statues, I speak elsewhere.

Columns are applied to walls and placed between openings. Their use here is not the same as in a portico. I have noticed in the greatest temples that where columns might perhaps not have corresponded to such a vastness of work, they extended the "horns" of the vaults <term>camurarum</term> <note>referring to the curved ribs or the arching profile of the ceiling</note> so that the rise <note>original: "sagitta," literally 'the arrow,' the vertical distance from the base of the arch to its highest point</note> in their arches exceeded the semi-radius by a third; this also added to the beauty. For a vaulted ceiling <term>testudinatio</term> <note>literally 'tortoise-shelling,' referring to masonry vaulting</note> that raises itself high into the air is more "agile," if I may put it that way, and more open. I think I should not pass over this point: in the vaulting of arches, the heads must be made at least longer than the semi-radius by as much as the prominence of the cornices occupies for the spectators, so that they cannot be seen from the middle of the temple.

The Amazons burned the Temple of Ephesus while Sylvius Postumius was reigning. It was burned once more at the time Socrates drank the poison in Athens. And we read that the temple at Argos perished by fire during the year Plato was born in Athens, while Tarquin reigned at Rome. Why should I mention the sacred porticos in Jerusalem? Or the temple of Minerva at Miletus? Or the temple of Serapis at Alexandria? They say that almost all other temples have fallen into such a calamity. Caesar used to say that **Alexandria** was immune from fires while he was besieging it because it was <term>vaulted</term> <note>original: "testudinata", meaning built with stone arches or "tortoise-shell" vaults rather than wooden beams</note>.

And indeed, the vault itself has its own ornaments. Among the ancients, the same kind of ornaments that silversmiths made for sacrificial <term>paterae</term> <note>shallow libation bowls used in ancient rituals</note>, architects transferred to the decoration of spherical vaults. And those designs which were common on the woven coverings of beds, they imitated on arches and curved ceilings. For this reason, one sees quadrangular and octagonal patterns and similar works spread across the vault, drawn with matching angles and equal lines, distinguished by radii and circles, so that nothing more could be added for the sake of beauty. 

And this certainly pertains to our subject: the ornaments of vaults are undoubtedly most worthy, such as we see everywhere else and especially in the **Pantheon**, set into the hollows of the <term>coffers</term> <note>original: "formarum", referring to the recessed panels in the dome</note>; however, the ancients did not leave a written record of how they made them. We have attempted to produce these with little labor and expense. For we trace the outlines of the future shapes—whether they be quadrangular, hexagonal, or octagonal—directly upon the <term>centering</term> <note>the temporary wooden framework used to support an arch during construction</note>. Then, in those parts of the vault where I wish there to be hollows, I fill them up to the established height by applying raw brick instead of a layer of lime. Thus, over these "mounds" built along the back of the centering, I construct the vault out of brick and lime...

**T**HE openings of windows in temples ought to be moderate and high, so that you see nothing except the sky; and so that those who perform the sacred rite, or those who pray, are in no way distracted from the divine matter. Add to this that the fires <note>the ritual lamps or candles</note> which are required in temples—than which you have nothing more divine for the practice of religion and ornament—grow faint in too much light. The ancients, for that reason, were for the most part content with the opening of the door alone. But for my part, I would approve of a temple where the entrance is entirely bright, and the interior walk is not at all gloomy; but where the altar is placed, I would wish the place to display majesty rather than beauty. # Leone Battista Alberti: On the Art of Building.

Regarding the opening, the sides, and the lintel: the ancients never made windows and doors <margin>Door of the temple.</margin> except in a rectangular shape. But let us speak of doors first. For doors, the best architects—whether **Ionian**, **Doric**, or <margin><unclear>construction</unclear></margin> **Corinthian**—made the sides at the very top thinner by one-fourteenth part than they were at the bottom. To the <term>lintel</term> <note>original: "superliminari", the horizontal beam across the top of a door</note> they gave the same thickness that they found at the very top of the side-post; they made the lines of the ornaments match on both, and they joined the connections <term>to the fingernail</term> <note>original: "ad unguem", a Latin idiom meaning perfectly or with extreme precision, as a sculptor checks a seam with a fingernail</note>. Furthermore, they made the highest <term>cornice</term> <note>original: "coronam", the crowning molding</note> of the door, which supports the lintel, level with the tops of the column capitals found in the portico. Thus, in these matters, they all observed what we have said.

In other respects, however, they differ greatly from one another. For the **Dorians** divided that entire height into sixteen parts: from these, they gave ten parts to the height of the opening—which the ancients also called the <term>light</term> <note>original: "lumen", referring to the clear space of the window or door</note>—and five parts to the width; to the side, they gave one part. These are the Doric rules.

The **Ionians**, however, divided that first whole height—which is leveled with the tops of the column capitals—into nineteen parts: from these, they gave twelve parts to the height of the opening, six to the width, and one to the side.

The **Corinthians** divided it into nineteen parts: from these, seven parts were given to the width of the opening, and they made the height of the light double the width <note>i.e., 14 parts</note>; the side of the door was one-seventh of the width of the opening. In each case, this side is the <term>jamb</term> <note>original: "antipagmentum", the decorative frame or casing of a door</note> or beam. And unless we are mistaken, the Ionians delighted in their own beam adorned with three <term>fasciae</term> <note>flat, horizontal bands</note>; the Dorians in theirs, with the <term>regulae</term> <note>narrow strips</note> and <term>guttae</term> <note>original: "clauiculis", literally "little keys" or pegs; the small water-shedding ornaments under a triglyph</note> removed, and for the sake of ornament on the lintel beam, each added his own beautiful cornices for the most part.

But the Dorians did not place the visible "three-furrowed" heads of the beams <note>original: "capita tignorū trisulcata", referring to <term>triglyphs</term></note> upon the beam; instead, in that place, they used a wide "royal" fascia, according to the thickness of the side standing by the door. To the fascia they added a <term>cymatium</term> <note>a wave-shaped molding</note>, a <term>gorge</term> <note>original: "gululam", a small concave molding</note>, and above that a plain <term>plinth</term> <note>original: "gradum Plutei"</note>; and upon that, <term>ovolo</term> <note>original: "ouicula", egg-shaped carvings</note>, then <term>mutules</term> <note>rectangular blocks under the cornice</note> covered with their own cymatium; and in the highest place, a <term>cyma recta</term> <note>original: "undulam", a "little wave" molding</note>, taking the dimensions of the small parts from those which we read above concerning Doric <term>entablatures</term> <note>original: "trabeationibus"</note>.

The Ionians, by contrast, did not use the royal fascia which they had placed on the beams; instead of the fascia, they imposed a swelling <term>frieze</term> <note>original: "fasciculum", here a pulvinated or rounded frieze</note> of leafy branches, as thick as the beam minus a third part of the beam, bound with a strap. Above that, a cymatium, and <term>dentils</term> <note>small tooth-like blocks</note>, and ovolo, and a thick row of mutules covered by a fascia with its own cymatium on the front, and a final "little wave" molding. ### Book VII. On Sacred Ornaments. Folio CXI.

With the thick step of the roof <term>modillions</term> <note>original: "mutulorum", blocks or brackets supporting a ledge</note>, they added what I might call "leading ears," a name drawn from their resemblance to the well-eared, keen-scented hounds. The outline of these <term>consoles</term> <note>original: "auricularum", literally 'little ears'</note> was like a large, oblong letter **S**, with its ends winding themselves into a curled spiral in this manner. The thickness of these consoles at the top cluster matched their width; at the bottom, they were narrower by one-fourth. The length of the consoles hung down as far as the level of the upper opening. 

The **Corinthians** transferred the entire design of colonnades from the portico to the doors themselves. Doors are also decorated in places that are especially open to the sky—to ensure these designs are not repeated elsewhere—by attaching a small portico in this manner: having set the sides and the lintel, they attach a free-standing column on either side, and sometimes these even project forward. <margin>Door ornamentation</margin> The bases of these columns are spaced so that the entire work of the <term>door-case</term> <note>original: "antipagmentorum", the decorative frame or architrave around a door</note> is contained within that span. The height of the columns, including the capitals, is equal to the distance from the outer corner of the right base to the outer corner of the left base. Upon these columns, the architrave, the frieze, the cornice, and the pediment are placed according to the rules of the portico, which we have already discussed in its proper place above. 

There were those who, instead of an architrave, fixed cornice ornaments to the sides of the doors, which created a very wide opening for the door; this work is better suited to the delights of private houses—especially for windows—than it is becoming to the authority of temples. In the largest temples, especially those where there are no other openings, the height of the space is divided into three parts: one and the same part at the very top is left to serve as a window, and it is decorated with a bronze grate; the remainder is given to the <term>door-leaves</term> <note>original: "valuis", the swinging panels of a folding door</note>. 

The <margin>Door-leaves and hinges</margin> individual parts of the door-leaves have their own rules. Among these parts, the most important is the **hinge**; there are two ways to handle this. For either iron hooks and <term>pintles</term> <note>original: "arpicones", a type of hook-and-eye hinge system</note> are fixed to the side of the door-frame, or a shaft is extended from the corner of the door-leaf, and the door turns upon the point where that shaft is set. Because the door-leaves of temples are made of bronze for the sake of permanence and are of immense weight, they are moved more safely by an **axis** <note>original: "axe", a pivot or spindle</note> than by hooks. 

I will not recount here the doors I have read about in the works of historians and poets—those covered in gold, ivory, and statues, so heavy that they required crowds of men to open them and struck terror with their noise. In such things, I instead praise the ease of opening and closing. Therefore, at the bottom point of the axis, a bronze socket mixed with tin should be placed. Both the socket and the head of the axis (to which the door-leaf is joined like a box) should be deeply hollowed out into the curved shape of a bowl, so that they may enclose between them a perfectly smooth and well-rounded **iron ball**.

<meta>This page continues Alberti's technical specifications for temple entrances, specifically focusing on the mechanical fittings of the door pivots and the decorative moldings of the door leaves, before transitioning to the design and materials of temple windows and the introduction of Chapter XIII regarding altars and temple furnishings.</meta>

### Leon Battista Alberti: On the Art of Building

...polished. At the very top of the axle <note>original: "axis", referring to the vertical pivot on which the door turns</note> which is at the summit of the door leaf, there shall be a bronze plate <note>original: "samella", likely a variant of "lamella"</note> inserted into the lintel. In addition to this, the axle will be fitted with a movable iron ring, polished and smoothed all over. In this way, the door leaf will never be stubborn, but will play along and move easily at the slightest touch. Each doorway will have double door leaves, one of which may fold back to one side and the other to the opposite side.

<margin>Ornaments of the door leaves.</margin>
The thickness of the door leaf shall be one-twelfth of its width. The ornaments on the door leaves are bands <term>fasciae</term> <note>flat, decorative strips of molding</note> which surround the width of the door, attached in a number according to choice—either double, triple, or even single. If they are double and arranged like steps one above the other, both together shall take up no more than a fourth and no less than a sixth of the door's width. The first band, which is attached and stands out, shall be wider than the one beneath it by one-fifth. If they are triple, they shall take their outlines from the Ionic architrave <note>the main beam resting on the columns</note>. But if the bands around it are simple, they shall be between one-fifth and one-seventh of the width. The molding on the inside of the bands shall be a "little throat" <term>gulula</term> <note>original: "gulula", a small concave or wave-shaped molding</note>. The length of the door leaf shall be divided by horizontal bands so that the uppermost spaces occupy one-fifth of the total height.

<margin>Windows of temples.</margin>
In temples, windows are decorated just as much as the doors. However, their opening—which should occupy the highest part of the wall nearest the vault <note>the arched ceiling</note> and terminate at its corners against the upper curve of the vault—is handled differently under an arch than in the doorways. For they are indeed twice as wide as they are high, and they divide the entire width with two small columns placed between them, according to the proportions of a portico. But in these cases, the columns are almost always rectangular. The outlines of the frames <term>scaphorum</term> <note>recesses or niches</note> in which painted panels and statues are placed are taken from the designs of the doors; they fill one-third of the height of their wall. At the windows of temples, to provide light while guarding against frost and the force of the winds, they used to place stationary panels of thin, translucent alabaster instead of door-leaves; or they used bronze or marble mesh. They filled the intermediate spaces of the mesh not with fragile glass, but with transparent stone <term>lapis specularis</term> <note>likely mica or selenite, used before clear glass was common</note> sought especially from the town of Segobriga <note>original: "Sogobria", an ancient Roman city in Hispania</note> in Spain, or likewise from Bologna in Gaul <note>original: "Bononia galliae", possibly referring to Boulogne-sur-Mer</note>. This is a layer of translucent and very pure gypsum, rarely larger than a foot wide, to which nature has given the unique quality of not showing its age.

# Book VII. On the Ornaments of Temples.
-> Folio 112 <-

**P**ost these things, it will indeed pertain to the design of the temple to establish the altar on which they may sacrifice in the most worthy place; certainly, it should sit justly before the tribunal <note>the "tribunal" refers to the raised platform or apse at the head of the temple where the high altar or seat of authority is placed</note>. The ancients used to make the altar six feet high and twelve feet wide, upon which they would place a statue <note>original: "signum", referring to a cult image or sacred representation</note>. 

Whether it is proper to scatter many altars throughout the temple for the sake of sacrifice, let that be for others to judge. Among our ancestors, during those beginnings of our religion, the best men would come together for the communion of the supper <note>original: "communionem cœnæ", a reference to the Early Christian agape feast or Eucharist</note>; not for the purpose of filling their bodies with feasts, but so that they might become mild through mutual fellowship, and return home with minds filled with good advice, most eager for virtue. 

<margin>Note</margin>
<margin>The ancient custom of feasting.</margin>
There, having tasted rather than consumed what was set out for the supper with the greatest frugality according to the ancient custom, both a reading and a sermon on divine matters were held. The studies of all were burning toward the common salvation of everyone and the cultivation of virtue. At last, each person, according to what their means could supply, offered into the middle a kind of tax owed to piety, and from this collection for the deserving—that is, through the priest <term>antistes</term> <note>a term for a high-ranking cleric or bishop</note>—it was distributed to those who were in need of help. 

In this way, all things were held in common among them, as if among the most loving brothers. After that time, when it was permitted by the princes to practice publicly, they did not deviate much from the old institute of the fathers; but with a larger crowd flocking together, they used smaller offerings <note>original: "libamento", here referring to the bread and wine of the sacrament</note>. The eloquent sermons which the priests <term>pontifices</term> <note>Alberti uses the classical term for high priests to describe Christian bishops</note> used in those times may be seen everywhere in the commentaries of the fathers. 

Therefore, there was at that time only a single altar at which they would meet, as they were about to celebrate a single sacrifice daily. These times have followed, which I wish some grave man—with the popes' permission—might consider worthy of reproach; for while they themselves, for the sake of maintaining their dignity, hardly grant the people the power of seeing them on the annual festivals, they have made everything so crowded with altars that—I will say no more. 

I affirm this: among mortals, nothing can be found or even thought of that is worthier or holier than the sacrifice. Indeed, I think no one is well-advised who wants the most worthy things to become cheap through too much ease of access. 

There are also certain other types of ornaments that are not fixed, with which the sacrifice may be adorned. There are also others by which temples are otherwise honored, the reasoning for which should be looked to by the architect. It is asked: what is the most beautiful thing of all? 

<margin>Pay attention.</margin>
A crossroads made joyful by playful youth? A sea filled with a fleet? A field filled with soldiers and victorious banners? A forum filled with senators in togas and the like? Or a temple brilliant with the brightness of lights? 

But indeed, I would wish the lights in temples to have majesty. This majesty is not found in the tiny sparks of little torches, which...

...which we use today is not the same. I do not deny they will have charm if they are adapted to some beautiful arrangement of lines, or if they are extended with lamps along the lines of the cornices. But the ancients please me much more; they burned fragrant flames in rather large basins <note>original: "conculas", literally small shells or bowls used as oil reservoirs</note> atop their candelabra. <margin>Candelabrum.</margin> The length of the candelabrum was divided into seven parts. Two parts were given to the base; this base was triangular, being longer in one dimension than it was wide. At the bottom, it was indeed wider than at the top. The shaft of the candelabrum was raised by pitcher-like vessels <note>original: "vasis gutturijs", vessels with narrow necks for pouring</note> set one upon another. At the very top was placed a basin packed with gums and fragrant woods. <margin>Balsam</margin> They have recorded in memory how much balsam, taken from public tributes, the princes ordered to be burned daily on solemn feast days for incense in the greatest basilicas of Rome. This amounted to about five hundred and eighty pounds.

<margin>Gyges.</margin> ¶ So much for candelabra. I come now to the remaining things with which temples are excellently adorned. We read that Gyges gave six mixing bowls <term>crateras</term> <note>large vessels used for mixing wine and water, often dedicated as trophies</note> as a gift to Pythian Apollo, made of solid gold and weighing thirty thousand pounds. <margin>Note on vessels and things of that kind</margin> And at Delphi, there were vessels of solid gold and silver, each of which held six *amphorae* <note>a standard Roman liquid measure, roughly 26 liters each</note>. There were also those who once valued the hand and invention of the artist in temples more than the gold itself. Among the Samians, in the temple of Juno, they say there was an iron bowl dedicated, <margin>Most precious.</margin> surrounded by figures, which the Spartans had once sent to Croesus as a gift; it was of such great size that it held three hundred *amphorae*. I find also that the Samians sent to Delphi an iron tripod-cauldron <term>cortinam</term> on which the heads of animals were sculpted with marvelous skill, which colossi seven cubits high supported on bended knees. It is a wonder, too, that the Egyptian Samniticus built a temple to the god Apis most adorned with columns and various figures, and inside a statue of the god Apis, which they intended to be viewed continuously in the sun. And there is that even more <margin>Cupid's weapon.</margin> wonderful thing: the weapon of Cupid hung in the temple of Diana at Ephesus, held up by no visible cords. Concerning statues of this sort, I have nothing to say, except that they should be placed in their own proper and decent spot so that they are viewed with admiration and dignity.

**I**t is well established that the Basilica was originally a place where leaders would meet under a roof to administer justice. # Book VII. On the Ornament of Sacred Buildings.

...another walkway, which we call the "pleading-walk" <note>original: "causidicam", a term Alberti uses for a transverse walkway where lawyers (causidici) gathered</note> <margin>The Basilica.</margin> because crowds of rhetoricians and lawyers would frequent it. And they joined these walkways together with a line drawn in the likeness of the letter T. Then they interpret that exterior porticoes were added for the sake of servants. Therefore, a <term>basilica</term> <note>a large public building for legal and business affairs, which served as the structural model for early Christian churches</note> consists of a walkway and porticoes. And yet, because a <term>basilica</term> shares something of the nature of a temple, it will claim for itself in many respects all the ornaments owed to temples. However, it will use them in such a way that it makes clear it preferred to imitate temples rather than equal them. It will be raised up on a platform <note>original: "exaggerabitur", referring to an "agger" or mound of earth/masonry used as a base</note> in the manner of temples. But from the height of the platform owed to temples, one-eighth shall be taken away, so that for the sake of veneration it may yield to the worthier building; furthermore, the other things applied for ornament shall by no means possess that gravity which those placed upon temples have. Furthermore, the difference between a <term>basilica</term> and a <term>temple</term> <margin>How the basilica differs from a temple.</margin> is this: that [the basilica]—on account of the crowd of almost tumultuous litigants and for the purpose of reviewing and signing documents—ought to be very accessible for passage and extremely well-lit by openings; and it will be approved if it is prepared so that those who come seeking their patrons or clients may find where they are at first glance. For these reasons, columns are required more sparingly there; moreover, arched structures are most suitable, and they do not refuse even trabeated <note>post-and-beam construction with horizontal lintels</note> ones.

But we shall define a <term>basilica</term> thus: that it is indeed a very spacious and quite unencumbered <term>walkway</term> enclosed under a roof by inner <term>porticoes</term>. For one that is devoid of porticoes, we judge to belong more to the nature of a <term>senate house</term> <note>original: "curia" or "senatus"</note> than to a <term>basilica</term>. And regarding that, it will be discussed in its proper place. <term>Basilicas</term> ought to have a floor plan arranged such that their length is double their width. It will also be convenient to have a central <term>walkway</term> and certainly a pleading-walk that is free and unencumbered. But if by chance the pleading-walk is removed and it is only to have simple porticoes on this side and that, it shall be defined in this manner: the width of the area shall be divided into nine parts, of which five shall be given to the central <term>walkway</term>, and two to each of the porticoes. Then the length likewise shall be divided into nine parts. Of these, one shall be given to the curve of the <term>tribunal</term> <note>the semicircular apse or raised platform for judges</note>. For the width of the <term>tribunal</term> at its opening <note>original: "faucibus", literally "throats"</note>, two parts shall be given. But if, besides the <term>portico</term>, a pleading-walk is to be added, then the width of the area shall be divided into four parts: two shall be given to the central <term>walkway</term>, and one each to the individual porticoes. Again, the length shall be divided thus: for the curve of the <term>tribunal</term> will take for itself inwardly [cur—] <note>catchword: "cur", the start of "curvaturam" or "curvam" on the following page</note>

...[from its height] a twelfth part of its length. The opening of the interval <note>likely referring to the spacing between columns or the width of the entryway</note> shall take twice a twelfth and a half on top of that. The width of the pleading-area <note>original: "causidicae"; the side aisles or walkways where legal business was conducted</note> shall take for itself a sixth part of the length of the floor area. But if one building is to have both a pleading-area and double porticoes: the width shall indeed be divided into ten parts: of which you will give four parts <note>inferred from the remaining six</note> to the middle walkway, while three on the right and another three on the left shall be occupied by the porticoes, with the spaces divided between them in half. But the length indeed will be divided into twenty parts: from which one and a half parts shall be given to the curvature of the tribunal <note>the semi-circular apse or judgment seat</note>. To the opening of the tribunal itself, three and a third parts shall be given. To the pleading-area, no more than three whole parts shall be given. The walls of basilicas shall not be as thick as those of temples. 

<margin>
The walls of basilicas
</margin>

For they are not raised to support the weight of vaults <note>original: "testudinum", literally "tortoise shells", used here to mean heavy stone vaulted ceilings</note>, but to support the beams and rafters of the roofs. They shall therefore be made thick to the extent of a twentieth part of their height. The height of the walls for the front, relative to the width of the space, shall add a half more, and nowhere more than that. In the corners of the walkways, piers <note>original: "pilae"; square structural supports</note> shall be extended, stretching themselves along the wall in line with the colonnades of the wall, so that they occupy no less than twice, and no more than three times, the thickness of that wall. There are also those who, in the middle of the length, also raise a pier in order among the columns for the sake of stability. Its width takes either three thicknesses of a single column, or at most four. The colonnades <note>the arrangement of columns</note> shall also by no means have the same weight and gravity as those applied to temples. For which reason, if we use a beamed <term>trabeated</term> <note>a style of architecture using horizontal beams rather than arches</note> colonnade especially, we will calculate thus: For if they are indeed Corinthian, a twelfth part shall be taken from their thickness <note>making them more slender than temple columns</note>. But if they are Ionic, a tenth shall be taken away. But if Doric, a ninth. In other matters—the capitals, the beam, the fascia <note>the flat bands on an architrave</note>, the corona <note>the projecting part of a cornice</note>, and fittings of this sort—they shall imitate temples.
