...[a square] quadrilateral <note>likely referring to the abacus, the flat slab at the very top of a column capital</note> height, in some places a fourth, in others a fifth of its column's diameter. For the line of the *undula* <note>original: "undulae", a wave-like or "cymatium" molding</note> of this added quadrangle, the width equaled the maximum extension of the capital. At the top, there were projections equal to the height; by this arrangement, the faces and the corners of the arch had more convenient and firmer seats. Arched colonnades, as well as those with entablatures <note>original: "trabeatae", referring to the horizontal beams or lintels resting on columns</note>, vary among themselves. For some are indeed "spread out" (*dispansae*), while others are "crowded" (*confertae*), and so on. In the crowded ones, the height of the open void will take half of its width's appearance. In the spread out ones, the height will have five-thirds of the width. In those that are moderately spread out, this width will be half the length. 

<margin>
Arched colonnades.
</margin>

In those that are moderately crowded, it will be a third. We have said elsewhere that an arch is a bent beam. Therefore, the same ornaments shall be given to arches that would be given to beams, if they were placed upon such columns. Furthermore, those who wish the work to be most ornate will additionally draw straight lines continuously along the wall above the highest ridge of such an arch. They will design the beam, the fascias, and the cornices <note>the decorative horizontal moldings that crown a wall or colonnade</note> such as they understand are owed to the colonnades at that height. 

<margin>
Columns given to the beam.
</margin>

But since some basilicas are surrounded by a single portico and others by a double one, the placement of the cornices above the columns and arches will therefore vary. For in those that are enclosed by only a single portico, the arrangement of the cornices will take up five-ninths, or up to four-sevenths, of the entire height of its wall. In those where double porticoes are present, the cornices will ascend no less than a third, and no more than three-eighths. 

Furthermore, for the sake of ornament as well as utility, other very large rectangular columns <note>these are likely "pilasters," or rectangular columns attached to the wall for decoration and support</note> shall be applied to the wall above the first cornices; these should rest with their centers directly over the primary columns substituted below. For this is indeed beneficial because, while maintaining the solidity of the structure and increasing the dignity of the work, it will lighten the weight and the great expense of the wall; and the prominence of the cornices will also drive these uppermost colonnades, as the logic of the work there requires. 

Add to this that in basilicas with two porticoes, the colonnades will be placed one above the other, three in number from the roof to the bottom. In others, however, there are two. Where you have placed three levels of colonnades, you shall divide that space of the wall—which is above the first columns up to the highest ceiling of the roof—into two parts; and at that place, the second cornices shall end. Between the first cornices and the second, the wall shall be kept solid and decorated with designs of "crustation" <note>original: "crustationum", referring to the practice of facing walls with thin slabs of marble or decorative stone</note>.

...[corresponding] to yours. Their width shall not be narrower than to take three-quarters of the entire interval that exists between the columns. The height of the windows, quite appropriately, will take two of these widths. The same lintel will equal the tops of the columns, excluding the capital, if they are quadrangular. But if the windows themselves are arched, it will be permitted to raise the back of the arch nearly up to the beam; and even with a diminished arch <note>a "diminished" or "segmental" arch is one that is less than a full semicircle</note>, it will be permitted to use one's judgment there. Beneath the windows shall be placed a windowsill <term>pluteus</term> <note>a low wall or parapet used here as a sill</note> with a molding of a small "throat" <term>gulula</term> <note>original: "gulula", a concave molding known as a gola or cyma recta</note> or "little eggs" <term>oviculis</term> <note>an egg-and-dart motif</note>. The empty spaces of the windows shall be latticed; but they shall not be blocked up with the plaster plates common in temples. It is indeed fitting that they have something to break and intercept the biting winds and hostile frosts as they approach, so that no discomfort is brought in. On the other hand, it is necessary for them to breathe continuously and very freely, lest the dust raised by the frequent movement of feet harm the lungs or eyes. For this reason, I strongly approve of thin plates made of bronze or lead, decorated—so to speak—with frequent and minute holes, through which light may penetrate and the air may be purified by the movement of the breeze.

### Chapter XVI.

<margin>☞ Boundary markers in-</margin>
**I** come now to the monuments of things. It pleases me here, for the sake of the mind, to be a little more pleasant than I have been until now, while all our discourse was occupied with the numbers of measurements. However, I shall be as concise and brief in my speaking as I can. Our ancestors, when they sought to extend the borders of the empire by force and strength after defeating their enemies, established signs and boundary markers <term>termini</term> by which they might indicate the course of victory, and render the land won by arms marked and distinct from that of their neighbors. From this arose the goal markers <term>metae</term> <note>conical pillars used to mark turning points or boundaries</note>, columns, and similar marks for distinguishing things. After this, to show gratitude to the gods above, they moved forward to bestow a portion of the spoils upon sacred rites and commended public joys to religion. From this arose altars, chapels, and things of that sort which served that purpose. They also decided to provide for their name and posterity; they took pains to have their faces known and their virtues proclaimed among the race of men. From this they devised spoils, statues, inscriptions, and trophies <term>trophea</term> <note>monuments consisting of captured arms and standards</note>, which served to celebrate their fame. Not only those who had helped their country in some way followed these practices, but also the happy and fortunate, as far as their wealth allowed them to show. But in the 
<margin>Boundary markers</margin>
execution of the work, different things pleased different people. The boundary markers of Father Liber <note>the Roman god Bacchus</note>, which he placed as a sign of his journey to the borders of India, were stones arranged at frequent intervals and tall trees whose trunks were covered with ivy. # Book VII. On Sacred Ornaments.

...truth hangs suspended, nodding with closed eyes. In the middle is a heap of books with an inscribed title: "These are the true medicines of the soul." <note>Alberti is likely quoting a description of the library of the Egyptian King Osymandias, as recorded by Diodorus Siculus.</note>

<margin>Inventors of statues:</margin>
But of all these things, if I am not mistaken, the use of statues was the most excellent. Indeed, they serve as ornaments for both sacred and secular, public and private buildings; they provide a wonderful memory of both men and events. And truly, whoever it was who first invented statues was of a most outstanding genius. Some believe they arose together with religion. And they claim that the Etruscans <note>The ancient civilization of central Italy, renowned for their terracotta and bronze craftsmanship before the rise of Rome</note> were the inventors of statues. Others would argue that the Telchines of Rhodes <note>Mythical metalworkers and sorcerers often credited with the first images of the gods</note> were the first who fashioned statues of the gods. They write that these figures, once dedicated to magical rites, used to bring forth clouds, rain, and the like, and could change the forms of living creatures at will. Among the Greeks, Cadmus the son of Agenor <note>The legendary Phoenician prince and founder of Thebes</note> was the first to consecrate statues of the gods in a temple. 
<margin>Cadmus</margin>

They say that in Rome there was such an abundance of statues that another "stone people" was said to be present. Rampsinitus <note>A legendary Pharaoh mentioned by Herodotus</note>, a very ancient king of the Egyptians, set up stone statues for Vulcan <note>The Roman name for the Greek smith-god Hephaestus; Alberti refers here to the temple of Ptah in Memphis</note> that were twenty-five <term>cubits</term> <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters</note> high. Amasis <note>The Pharaoh Ahmose II</note> set up a reclining statue at Memphis; its size was forty-seven feet, and on the base stood two others, twenty feet high. Near [the tomb of] Osymandias <note>The text says "Simandum," referring to the Ramesseum</note>, three statues of Jupiter <note>Representing the Egyptian god Amun-Ra</note> were placed, a wonderful work. 
<margin>Memnon.</margin>
They were carved from a single stone; one of them, in a sitting position, was so large that its foot exceeded seven cubits. Beyond the hand of the craftsman and the vastness of the stone, what is amazing is that in such a great mass there was no joint or flaw. And since stones were not sufficient for such conceived magnitudes, later people began to cast bronze statues one hundred cubits tall. 

But above all others was Semiramis <note>A legendary Queen of Assyria</note>; when stone was lacking and she desired something greater than what could be achieved in bronze,

...Theodorus completed at Ephesus. <note>Theodorus of Samos was a Greek architect and sculptor credited with work on the great Temple of Artemis.</note> Let these things be said for the sake of interest; although they contribute much to the subject, I would nonetheless wish them to be considered as if borrowed from the next book, when we shall deal with the monuments of private individuals, to which these matters especially belong. For since private citizens could not easily allow themselves to be surpassed by princes in the magnitude of their expenses—as they themselves burned with a greed for glory and vehemently desired to spread the fame of their names by whatever means possible—they did not spare any expense in that regard, so far as their fortune allowed. However, what was within the power of the craftsmen and could be achieved through the strength of genius, they pursued with all their zeal. Therefore, by striving to be equal to the greatest kings in the **elegance of their lines** and the **propriety of their work**, they attained, in my judgment, a position in this matter that is not far behind. Thus, let these things be reserved for the next book. This I promise: they will bring pleasure when you read them. But let us not skip over what pertains to our current subject here.

### ¶ Whether statues should be placed in temples, and which, what kind, where, and how many. Chapter XVII.

<margin>¶</margin> **T**here are those who deny that statues should be placed in temples. It is said that King Numa, <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome, known for establishing religious rites.</note> following the discipline of the **Pythagoreans**, <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who often emphasized abstract or mathematical truths over physical representations.</note> forbade any image to be placed in temples. Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, the Stoic philosopher and advisor to Nero.</note> thereafter mocked himself and his fellow citizens: "And yet," he said, "we play with dolls like children." But those who established these practices for their elders, bringing forth a reason, argued thus: "Who will be so foolish regarding the gods as not to understand that they must be defined by the *mind*, not the *eyes*?" And it is certain that no forms can be given at all by which such a great matter might be imitated or fashioned in even the smallest part. Indeed, they believe it is beneficial if no hand-made forms are present at all; by this, we achieve a state where each person may fashion in his mind, according to the strength of his own genius, those things concerning the First Principle of things <note>The "First Principle" refers to the supreme divine source or God.</note> and the intelligences of the beings above. For in this way, they will more readily venerate the majesty of the Highest Name. Others think differently. For they say that the likenesses of men were attributed to the gods by a certain excellent and wise counsel, so that the minds of the unlearned might be more easily turned away from the depravity of life when images were present, so that those approaching them might believe they were approaching the gods themselves. Others granted that the effigies of those who had deserved well of the human race—whom they judged worthy of being consecrated in memory among the number of the gods—should be placed in sacred places to be seen. By this, posterity, in venerating them, would be incited to the imitation of virtue by the pursuit of glory. But regarding statues, especially in temples, it is of the greatest importance what kind they are, in what places they are crowded, and also from what material they are made...

# Book VII.
## On the Ornaments of Sacred Buildings.

...we decorate. For we do not think they should be like those ridiculous statues of the god Priapus <note>original: "Priapus"; the Greek god of fertility, often depicted as a crude, ithyphallic scarecrow-like figure used as a guardian in gardens.</note> found in gardens, nor like those of warriors and such in porticoes. Nor do I think they should be placed in narrow or ignoble places. But first let us settle the matter of the material, and then the rest. ¶ The ancients (says Plutarch), <margin>Statues from wood.</margin> made images from wood, such as the Apollo in Delos; and in the city of Populonia, <note>An ancient Etruscan city.</note> a Jupiter made from vine-wood, which many say has remained uncorrupted. Similarly, the Diana of Ephesus, which some say is of ebony. Mutianus <note>Gaius Licinius Mucianus, a Roman general and author cited by Pliny.</note> records that it was made of vine-wood. <margin>Peras.</margin> Peras, who founded the Argive temple and consecrated his daughter as the priestess, fashioned a Jupiter from the trunk of a pear tree. There were those who forbade the gods to be fashioned from stone, which is hard and monstrous. Likewise, they rejected gold ☞ and silver, as being from an unfruitful and unhappy earth, or because its color was sickly. And yet Jupiter (he says) stood upright with difficulty in a narrow temple. And in Jupiter's right hand was a lightning bolt of clay <note>original: "fictile fulmen"; referring to the early Roman practice of using terracotta for religious statues before the influx of Greek luxury.</note>. Among the Egyptians, there were those who thought god was fiery and inhabited the ethereal fire, and could not be grasped by human sense; for that reason, they wanted gods made of crystal. Others thought gods were most aptly fashioned from black stone, because they considered that color to be incomprehensible. Finally, others used gold, as it would match the stars. Truly, I have doubted from what material the statues of the gods should be made. Certainly, you will say the material ought to be most worthy for fashioning a god; but rarity is closest to dignity. However, I am not one who would wish them to be made from salt, as Solinus <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Latin geographer.</note> records the Sicilians were accustomed to doing, or from glass, as Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the *Natural History*.</note> mentions. Nor likewise from pure gold or silver; not indeed for the reason of those who rejected them as arising from sterile earth and having a sickly color. Many things move me, among which is that which I have persuaded myself pertains to religion: that those whom we place to be adored in the stead of gods, we should make as similar as possible to the gods themselves, so far as that may be achieved. Therefore, I judge they should be held as immortal in their permanence, as far as can be done by mortals. Or what reason should I give why people value the opinion received from their ancestors about such things so highly? For you might hear that there is a painted image of a god in one place, but in another place nearby, they do not think the statue of that same god hears prayers and the vows of the righteous any less. Moreover, if you move those statues which the common people venerate excessively, you will not find anyone who would trust them more or commend their vows to them, just as they treat bankrupts <note>original: "decoctoribus"; literally those who have "boiled away" their assets; spendthrifts or bankrupts who have lost their public credit.</note>. Therefore, they ought to have stable, proper, specifically dedicated, and most worthy seats. They say that nowhere in human memory has an elegant work of gold been seen, as if the prince of metals disdains to be honored by deceitful artifice. If this is so, the statues of the gods which...

...even if we desire them to be most graceful, it is not fitting to make them of gold. Add to this that men driven by greed might easily steal a golden beard, or rather, melt down the gods in their entirety if they were made of gold. Bronze will be very pleasing, unless the brightness of the purest marble entices me. But there will be something in bronze that I especially approve of for the benefit of its permanence—provided we make them in such a way that the reason for such a detestable crime <note>Referring to the theft or melting down of statues for their metal value.</note> is greater if one destroys it, than the profit if one melts it down for other uses. Such statues will be those which we have shaped with a hammer or by casting as a thin leaf, as if led by the skin alone. They write of a statue made of ivory <note>likely the colossal statue of Zeus at Olympia or Athena Parthenos.</note> of such great size that the roof of the temple could scarcely contain it. I do not praise this. For it is necessary for it to be appropriate in size, in the lines of its form, and in the proportion of its parts. And perhaps the faces of the greatest gods, more severe with beard and brow, do not harmonize well with the softer image of virgins. Furthermore, unless I am mistaken, the rarity of the gods will increase the veneration. It will be very convenient to place two on the altar, or no more than three. The rest of the number shall be arranged in most suitable seats along the sides. I demand that each of these gods and heroes express his own life and character through his habit and gesture, as far as you are able through the skill of the artist. I do not want him to perform as a wrestler or a stage-player (which some consider beautiful), but I would wish him to offer from his countenance and the whole appearance of his body a grace and majesty worthy of a god to those approaching: so that he may seem to receive them most kindly with a nod and a hand, and to be willing to grant favors to those who pray. I decree that statues of this kind are to be placed in temples; but the rest are to be assigned to theaters and profane <note>In the architectural sense, "profane" refers to any building that is not a consecrated religious site, such as civic or private buildings.</note> buildings.

For one must labor with all art and industry to render sacred works, especially public ones, most ornate, for they are prepared for the gods above; whereas profane ones are only for men.

<header>Book VIII. On the ornamentation of public secular buildings. Leaf 118</header>

# Book VIII. On the ornamentation of public secular buildings.

Therefore, it is fitting that less worthy things yield to those more worthy; yet they shall still be honored with their own appropriate decorations. In the previous book, we discussed what public sacred buildings <note>Alberti uses "sacra" to refer specifically to temples and religious structures.</note> should be like. It follows now that secular <note>original: "profana"</note> ones be reviewed. We shall explain, therefore, what ornament should be bestowed upon each.

<margin>The Road.</margin>
I consider the road to be the most pre-eminent of public works. For it is prepared for the convenience of both citizens and foreigners alike. But since some travelers move by land and others by water, we must speak of both. I would like you to recall what I have said elsewhere: that some roads are military, and others are not. Furthermore, a road must be treated one way within the city, and another way through the countryside. A military road through the countryside is greatly adorned by the land through which it is directed: if it is well-cultivated, planted, and filled with villas, inns, and an abundance of beautiful things; if it reveals now the sea, now mountains, now a flowing lake or springs, now arid rock or a plain, and now a grove and a valley. It will also be an ornament if it is not steep, not difficult, and not unkempt, but (so to speak) winding and level, and completely open to the view. 

To achieve these things, what did our ancestors not attempt? I do not only refer to those roads paved with the hardest stone for up to a hundred miles, and built up with piles of massive stones. They paved the Appian Way <note>The "Queen of Roads," the oldest and most important Roman road, connecting Rome to Brindisi.</note> from Rome all the way to Brundisium. Everywhere along the military roads, one sees rocks cut through, mountains leveled <note>original: "delumbati," literally meaning hamstrung or weakened.</note>, hills tunneled, and valleys filled—all at incredible expense and through miraculous labor. All these things serve both utility and, certainly, ornament. Furthermore, a most worthy ornament is provided if travelers frequently encounter opportunities for conversation, especially regarding noteworthy matters.

-> "An eloquent companion on the road," as Laberius <note>Decimus Laberius, a Roman knight and famous writer of mimes in the 1st century BC.</note> used to say, "is as good as a carriage." <-

And truly, we are relieved of the boredom of a journey in no small measure by conversation. For this reason, while I have always highly valued the wisdom of our ancestors in their other institutions, I especially praise them for the invention I am about to discuss—even if they had greater goals in mind than merely pleasing those traveling abroad.

<margin>On the site among the Romans.</margin>
-> "Do not bury or burn a man within the city," says the Law of the Twelve Tables <note>The earliest code of Roman law, dating to the 5th century BC.</note>. <-

Furthermore, it had been provided by a very ancient decree of the Senate regarding burial that no dead person should be buried within the city walls, except for the Vestal Virgins and the Emperor, as these were not bound by the laws. Plutarch says the Valerii and the Fabritii were permitted to be buried in the Forum as a mark of honor; but when their descendants had placed the body there, they would immediately carry it away after applying a torch, indicating that they possessed the right but chose not to use it. Therefore, tombs...

<page-num>XVIII</page-num>

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

...they placed their monuments throughout the countryside in suitable and conspicuous places near the road. They made them, as far as their resources and the skill of the craftsmen allowed, extremely rich in ornaments. Therefore, they stood built with the most exquisite <term>outlines<gloss>original: "lineamentis," a key term for Alberti referring to the intellectual design and proportions of a building</gloss></term>. There was no lack of an abundance of columns. Marble <term>veneers<gloss>original: "crustationes," thin slabs of decorative stone used to face a wall</gloss></term> shone. Statues, sculptures, and tablets were gleaming. Faces cast in bronze or marble were viewed with very elegant artistry. It is not necessary for me to pursue at length how much those most wise men looked out for both the republic and good morals with this institution. I will only touch upon those things which pertain to our matter. 

For what do you think travelers thought when they journeyed along the Appian Way, or any other military road, and saw them so wonderfully filled with an abundance of monuments? Were they not delighted in the highest degree as this and that, and then another, and yet another most ornate tomb presented itself? From these, the inscriptions <note>original: "titulus"</note> and images of illustrious men could be recognized. What an opportunity it provided, from so many signs of ancient memory, to recall the deeds of the greatest men! They could lighten the journey with conversation while simultaneously increasing the dignity of the city. 

But that was the least of the benefits. This was a more important consideration: that the fortunes and safety of the fatherland and the citizens were very well provided for by this practice. <margin>☞</margin> The historian Appian <note>Appian of Alexandria (c. 95–165 AD), a Roman historian of Greek origin.</note> testifies that among the chief reasons why the rich refused the <term>Agrarian Law<gloss>The Lex Agraria, Roman laws proposed to redistribute public land to the poor, which the wealthy elite fiercely resisted</gloss></term> was that they considered it impious for the monuments of their ancestors to pass to strangers. How many estates do we think reached great-grandsons through this single veneration and observance of either affection, piety, or religion—estates which spendthrifts and bankrupts would otherwise have lost to gambling? Add to this that it was an ornament to the name and posterity of both families and the city, by which the living might be stirred again and again to prefer imitating the virtues of the most praised men. 

Finally, consider this: with what eyes could they look upon an arrogant and rampaging enemy among the monuments of their own kin, if such a thing ever happened? What coward or fool would not immediately burn with the desire to avenge both his fatherland and his honor? How much courage would the indignation, piety, or grief then felt have instilled in the minds of men! 

Therefore, the ancients are to be praised. Yet I would not dare to blame our own people, who bury the dead in the most sacred places within the city, provided they do not bring the corpse inside the temple where the fathers and magistrates assemble at the altar to call upon the gods. From this practice it sometimes happens that the purity of the sacrifice is contaminated by the foulness of <term>corrupt vapor<gloss>referring to the "miasma" or foul air believed to cause disease from decaying matter</gloss></term>. How much more convenient were those who established the practice of cremating bodies!

<summary>Alberti argues that placing ornate tombs along public roads served to inspire travelers, preserve family estates from being sold, and provide a psychological defense against invaders. He concludes by critiquing the unhygienic practice of burying bodies inside churches, favoring the ancient preference for cremation or outdoor burial.</summary>

# Book VIII. On the Ornament of Public Secular Structures.

## ¶ On tombs, and the many various reasons and methods of burial. Chapter II.

**B**ut it is helpful here not to overlook the considerations regarding tombs that seem worth mentioning. For they come very close to being considered public works when they are entrusted to religious care. "Where you inter the body of a deceased person," says the law, "let that place be sacred." <note>Alberti quotes a Roman legal principle, likely from the Twelve Tables, which established that a grave (locus religiosus) was protected by divine law and could not be bought or sold.</note> And we ourselves profess this same principle: that the laws governing tombs pertain to religious duty. Therefore, since religious matters should take precedence over all else, I believe I must discuss these—even though they often fall under the laws of private individuals—before I proceed to describe public secular works. 

There has been almost no nation anywhere so savage that it did not feel some regard for tombs should be maintained—except perhaps the <margin>Fish-eaters.</margin> Fish-eaters <note>original: "Ictyophagi"; ancient writers used this term for various coastal peoples along the Red Sea and Indian Ocean.</note>, whom they say from the farthest reaches of Indian barbarism are accustomed to cast their dead into the sea. They assert that it matters little whether a body is dissolved by earth, water, or fire. The <margin>Albanians.</margin> Albanians <note>This refers to the Caucasian Albanians of antiquity, an ancient people of the Caucasus region, rather than modern Albanians.</note> also considered it a sin to care for the dead. The <margin>Sabeans.</margin> Sabeans <note>An ancient South Arabian civilization in modern-day Yemen.</note> treated the bodies of the dead as nothing more than dung; they even discarded their kings onto dung heaps. The <margin>Troglodytes.</margin> Troglodytes <note>Literally "cave-dwellers"; ancient geographers used this name for various tribes in Africa and the Near East.</note> would bind the neck of the deceased to their feet and carry them out hurriedly with laughter and jokes; then, showing no regard for the site, they would commit the body to the earth and place a goat’s horn at the head. 

But no one with a sense of humanity would approve of such customs. Others, both among the Egyptians and the Greeks, built monuments not only for the physical body but also to honor the names of their friends—a display of piety that everyone praises. I believe we should especially listen to those among the Indians who claimed that the most magnificent of all monuments are those preserved in human memory and handed down to posterity, or those who celebrated the funerals of the most virtuous men by doing nothing else but singing their praises. Nevertheless, for the sake of the survivors, I maintain that we must also take the physical body into account. 

Furthermore, it is obvious that tombs are highly effective in preserving a name for posterity. Our ancestors, in order to show gratitude to those who served the republic excellently with their blood and their lives—and to inspire others to seek equal glory through virtue—were accustomed to grant both statues and tombs at public expense. Yet they perhaps gave statues to many and tombs to only a few, for they understood that statues might perish through the elements or old age. "The sanctity of tombs," as Cicero says, "resides in the soil itself, for it can neither be destroyed nor moved by any means." <note>Alberti is quoting Cicero’s *De Legibus* (On the Laws) 2.22.55, where Cicero argues that while a building might fall, the ground remains "religious" forever.</note> For while other things are extinguished by time, tombs become more sacred as they age. Moreover, they dedicated tombs to religious protection for this reason, if I am not mistaken: so that the memory of a man, once entrusted to the stability of a structure and the earth, might be guarded by the fear of the gods and religious awe, and thus remain inviolate by the hands of men.

Hence arises that provision from the **Law of the Twelve Tables** <note>The Twelve Tables (c. 450 BCE) were the foundation of Roman law. Alberti refers to a rule preventing the "vestibule" or entrance area of a tomb from being acquired through long-term use (usucapion), ensuring it remained forever attached to the grave.</note> that it was not permitted to take possession of the vestibule or the approach to a tomb by right of use. Add also the law by which a heavy penalty was imposed if anyone violated a pyre-site, or if they had thrown down or broken a column from a tomb. Finally, among all well-ordered nations, regard has been given to tombs. So great was the care for tombs among the **Athenians** that if any general neglected to honor those killed in war with burial, he would be punished by death. <note>This likely refers to the Battle of Arginusae (406 BCE), where Athenian commanders were executed for failing to recover the bodies of the fallen due to a storm.</note> Among the **Hebrews**, it was provided by law that they should not leave even an enemy unburied. Many things are reported about the various types of funerals and tombs, which it would be irrelevant to pursue here. For instance, there is that which is told of the 

<margin>Scythians.</margin>
**Scythians**: that some were accustomed, as a mark of honor, to eat the deceased during banquets, while others nourished dogs by whom the departed would be devoured. <note>Alberti draws here on ancient ethnographic accounts (like those of Herodotus or Pliny) regarding "sky burials" or ritual cannibalism, though these were often sensationalized by Roman authors.</note> But enough of these. Almost all who wished their republic to be well-constituted by their own laws took care, first of all, that both funerals and tombs should not be unnecessarily sumptuous. According to the law of **Pittacus**, <note>Pittacus of Mytilene (c. 640–568 BCE), one of the Seven Sages of Greece.</note> it was not permitted to place upon a mound of earth anything except three small columns, no more than three cubits high, or a similar fixed measure. For they judged it fitting that in a matter where the nature of all was common, there should be no distinction of fortune; instead, all things should be common to the common people and the wealthy alike. Thus, according to ancient custom, they were covered with pure clods of earth; and they interpreted this as being done rightly, since they were committing the body, which was from the earth, as if into a mother’s lap. They decreed that no one should make a tomb more laborious than what ten men could complete in three days. 

But those who 
<margin>Egyptian custom.</margin>
built tombs most carefully beyond all others were the **Egyptians**. For they declared that the human race was in error for building the most magnificent houses as lodgings for a very short time, while neglecting the tombs where they would rest for the longest time. But this seems likely to me: that the 

<margin>Custom of the Getae.</margin>
**Getae** <note>The Getae were a Thracian people living near the lower Danube.</note> then indeed established it so through that ancient posterity. For in the place where they had buried a corpse, they first placed either a stone or perhaps—what greatly pleased **Plato** in his *Laws*—a tree, for the sake of marking the spot. And soon they began to build something over or around it, lest some wild beast make a foul mess by digging it up or rooting it out. But when afterwards that season of the year returned, so that they saw the field either flowering or burdened with the harvest, just as it was when their loved ones had departed from life, naturally the longing for the dearest ones they had lost was awakened in their minds. Repeating their words and deeds, they would go to the place and honor the memory of the deceased with whatever means they could. From this, perhaps, arose the custom that others, and especially the **Greeks**, became accustomed to honor the mounds of those who had deserved well of them.

...at festivals. For **Thucydides** <note>original: "Tuchidides"; a Greek historian (c. 460–400 BCE) known for his history of the Peloponnesian War.</note> says they used to assemble there with a display of garments and bring the first-fruits of their crops. This work they considered both most pious and highly religious, so much so that they even did it publicly. From this, I follow this conjecture: that for tombs, they began to establish not just mounds or small columns for the purpose of marking or covering the site, but also to build shrines <note>original: "delubra"</note>, so they might have a place to perform these sacred rites with dignity. For this reason, they took care that these structures were indeed most becoming and highly adorned in every respect.

But the locations where such tombs were placed varied among the ancients. According to pontifical law <note>The religious laws of Rome administered by the High Priests or Pontifices.</note>, it was forbidden to make a tomb in a public place. **Plato** <note>The Greek philosopher; Alberti refers here to ideas found in Plato's *Laws*.</note> held the view that a man should be managed such that neither in life nor in death should he be in any way a burden to the gathering of men. For this reason, he decreed that they should be buried both outside the city and nowhere else but in land that was entirely barren. Those who designated a specific place for tombs under the open sky and excluded from the gathering of men followed him; these I strongly approve of.

Others, by contrast, kept bodies preserved in gypsum or salt at home. <margin>Mycerinus</margin> **Mycerinus**, king of the Egyptians, had placed his deceased daughter in a wooden cow; he kept her with him in the royal palace and ordered those who presided over the mysteries to make offerings to her every day. **Servius** <note>A 4th-century commentator on the works of Virgil.</note> records that the ancients were accustomed to place the tombs of their most excellent and noble sons on high and most conspicuous mountains.

<margin>Alexandrians</margin> The **Alexandrians**, during the time of the historian **Strabo**, had enclosures and gardens dedicated to burying bodies. In the age nearest to that of our fathers, they built small chapels attached to the larger temples for the sake of tombs; and throughout **Latium** <note>The central region of Italy including Rome.</note> one sees family <term>bustuaria</term> <note>original: "bustuaria"; places where bodies were both burned and buried.</note> dug into the earth, fitted with small individual niches along the wall in which they would store the remains of those cremated. There remains a brief inscription even for the baker, the barber, the cook, the <term>alipta</term> <note>original: "aliptę"; a slave responsible for anointing bathers or wrestlers with oil.</note>, and others of that kind who were part of the household.

Where they buried young infants, as a consolation to their mothers, they would enclose their likenesses, cast in gypsum, within the urn. They set up marble likenesses of their ancestors, especially those of great talent. These were their practices. But we shall not find fault with where they chose to bury the body, provided they committed the monuments of their name to the most worthy places. Moreover, the things that give pleasure in monuments of this kind are these: the form of the work and the inscription.

Which form of building the ancients thought most worthy of tombs above all others, I could not easily say. The **Tomb of Augustus** <note>The Mausoleum of Augustus in Rome, built in 28 BCE.</note> at **Rome** was built of squared marble stone and covered with trees [evergreen] through...

From this widespread custom and the zealous pursuit of tombs, with new designs being invented daily, they progressed so far that nothing more could be devised that they had not already employed and most beautifully perfected; and ultimately, all such works are of a kind that they are greatly admired. 

Yet from this great multitude of examples, we notice this: some cared for nothing more than to bring honor to the container of the body. Others, however, sought more extensively to build something upon which they might most beautifully commend their titles and the fame of their achievements. Therefore, the former were content either with just a marble chest, or they added a **small shrine** <note>original: "facellū"; usually "sacellum," a small chapel or shrine.</note> as the religious nature of the place required. ### ¶ On small shrines, pyramids, columns, altars, massive structures, and other things of that kind.

->Chapter III.<-

<gloss>N</gloss>ow, since the tombs of the ancients are admired, I see that in some places **small shrines** <note>original: "facella"; small chapels or votive structures.</note> were placed, in others pyramids, in others columns, and in others structures such as **massive monuments** <note>original: "moles"; large, heavy architectural masses like the Mausoleum of Hadrian.</note> and the like. I believe we should speak about each of these individually, and first concerning the small shrines. 

<margin>Small shrines.</margin>
I would wish these shrines to be like small models of temples. Nor will I object if you join together designs gathered from various different kinds of buildings, provided they contribute to grace and also to durability. Whether it is more beneficial to have built these monuments—which we desire to be eternal—from noble or ignoble materials is not entirely clear, because of the damage caused by those who carry things away. But **ornament** indeed delights; for as we have said elsewhere, nothing is more suitable for preserving things and commending them to posterity. Of the tombs of **Julius Caesar** and **Claudius**, those great princes—which were undoubtedly most famous—nothing more remains at this time...

<margin>☞</margin>
From this, I think those should be warned here who wish their own works to be truly perpetual: that they should build with stone that is not weak, yet not so elegant that someone would either easily covet it or lightly snatch it away. Furthermore, I think a measure should be kept in these things according to the dignity of each person, so that I would condemn even in kings a profuse insolence of expenditures. And certainly I detest those monstrous works which the Egyptians built for themselves, which are hateful even to the gods above; since none of them was actually buried in such boastful tombs.

And above that work rose four other pyramids, a hundred feet high. And upon these again others, incredible not only in their vastness but also in their **design** <note>original: "lineamento"; a central concept for Alberti, referring to the intellectual "lines" or geometric plan conceived in the architect's mind.</note>. square stone; some were even raised with bricks. ¶ Of columns, some are for building: which are used everywhere in structures. Others were of such a size that they were not at all fit for the use of building civil structures, but were devised only for the sake of memorializing and for posterity. We must therefore speak of these. Their parts are as follows: rising from the floor itself by a <term>propodium</term> <note>original: "ppodio"; a projecting base or pedestal</note> and a platform, there are steps. On these stands a quadrangular altar. Upon this, in turn, a second altar stands out, not much smaller than the first. In the third place is the base of the column: then the column itself: upon it the capital: and in the final place a statue positioned on a pedestal. There are those who, between the first and second altar, have interposed something like a <term>latastrum</term> <note>original: "latastrū"; likely referring here to a plinth or a thick slab serving as a transition piece</note> in place of a support, so that the work would be taller and more graceful. The measurements of all these parts are taken, as in the works of temples, from the diameter of the bottom of the column. But this base, where the works are made very vast, will have only one <term>torus</term> <note>original: "toros"; a large, rounded convex molding at the base of a column</note> and not several like other columns. Therefore, the thickness of the base is divided into five parts: you give two to the torus and three to the latastrum. The width of the latastrum on every side will take five times half of the half <note>i.e., one and a quarter diameters</note> of the diameter of the column. Furthermore, the altars on which the base sits will have these parts. In the highest place, which itself ought to project from all parts of the structure, will be the <term>cimatium</term> <note>original: "cimatiū"; a cymatium or crown molding, often S-shaped</note>: and at the bottom, there will be a <term>foccus</term> <note>original: "foccus"; literally a "hearth," but used here by Alberti to mean a socle or base molding</note>. For I call that ornament by this name for the sake of similarity, whether it is extended with steps, or a little wave, or a little throat <note>original: "vndula, aut gulula"; refers to specific molding profiles: the "wave" is a cyma, the "throat" is a cavetto or gola</note>, which is indeed the proper base of some part. But some things must be said regarding an altar of this kind, which we intentionally passed over in the previous book, having destined them for this place. ¶ I have said that it happened that they built little walls to support columns. When, therefore, they wished to have passages and exits once the little walls were placed, they removed the other intermediate parts and left only so much of the wall under the bases of the columns 
<margin>Altars.</margin>
as would suffice for supporting the columns themselves. This part that was left, we now call an "altar" <note>original: "aram"; Alberti uses the word for altar to describe what we would call a pedestal or "die"</note>. For this little wall, there was an ornament at the top, a cimatium: a little throat, or a little wave, or some such thing. Then a matching foccus corresponded at the bottom. With these two ornaments, then, they encircled the altar: and they made that cimatium itself to be one-fifth or one-sixth of the height of the altar itself. Moreover, they never made the altar thinner than what would correspond to the width of the base of the column, so that the superstructure of the latastrum would not hang in empty space. Others, for the sake of firmness, added an eighth of the latastrum to the thickness of the wall. However, the height of the little altar, besides the moldings...

Folio CXXII.

### Book VIII. On the Ornament of Public Secular Buildings.

<margin>On columns</margin>

...the [intermediate space] and the <term>plinth</term> <note>original: "soccum"; the lowest square member of a base or pedestal</note> was either equal to its width or exceeded it by a fifth. Thus, I have found that among the elegant ancients there were small walls and altars of this kind. I return to the column. Under the base of the column, an altar shall be placed, which should correspond to the base of the column with suitable dimensions, as we just said. For again: this will have a <term>cymatium</term> <note>original: "cimatium"; a molding with a wave-like profile</note> consisting of a complete cornice, specifically of the Ionic type, whose features you remember are these: at the lowest part a small throat; then a step; then a cable; then the protected face of the <term>mutules</term> <note>original: "mutulorum"; decorative blocks under a cornice</note>; and finally, in the highest position, a small wave with cords and a small knot in inverted orders.

Another altar placed beneath this one will likewise be drawn with similar lines, so that nothing added hangs over it into empty space. But to this one, steps will rise from the pavement floor itself, either three or five in number, with heights and setbacks unequal to each other. These steps together will equal in their total height no more than a fourth and no less than a sixth part of the altar placed above them. In that altar, a small door will be opened, and ornaments will be applied to it, either Doric or Ionic, of the kind we reviewed in the discussion on temples.

On the other elevation, the altar will have an inscription written upon it, and a heap of spoils <note>original: "exuuiarum"; referring to the "trophies" or captured armor often carved on victory monuments</note> will be carved. If anything is interposed between these two altars, it shall be made high by a third of its width; and that space will be occupied by fixed statues such as applauding goddesses: **Victory**, **Glory**, **Fame**, **Abundance**, and the like. There were some who covered the top altar with gilded bronze.

Once the altars are finished, the column will be raised above the base; its height will equal seven times its own diameter. At the top of the shaft, if the column is very large, it shall be made more slender than at the bottom by no more than a tenth part. In other smaller columns, we shall follow those rules we dealt with in the previous book. There were those who extended the height of the column to a hundred feet, and made the whole exterior rough with carved figures and the history of events; and inside they carved a spiral staircase <note>original: "gradus ad cocleam"; literally "steps like a snail shell"</note> by which you might climb all the way to the top.

On a column of this kind, they placed a Doric capital, removing the addition of the neck above the top covering of the capital. In smaller columns, a beam, bands, and ornaments of the cornice are placed surrounding it on every side. In the largest columns, however, these things will be omitted; for blocks of stone of such size would not be available, nor could they easily be set upon the work. In both cases, at the highest point, something shall be placed to serve as a base on which a statue is located. If by chance this is a square altar, then its corners shall not exceed the solid mass of the column. But if it is round, its size shall not go beyond the lines of that square. The size of the statue was one-third of its column. So much for columns.

## Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

<margin>Wall ornaments.</margin>
Regarding a monumental structure, the ancients were accustomed to draw the design outlines in this way. In the first place, a square area would rise up, built high in the manner of temples. From there, the wall was raised in height no less than one-sixth and no more than one-fourth of the length of the plan. Ornaments were applied to the wall either only at the very top and bottom, and also at the corners; or, in addition to that, attached colonnades projected along the wall. 

But if columns were placed only at the corners, then the height of the entire wall—excluding the steps of the <term>platform</term> <note>original: "crepidinum"; the base or foundation moldings of a building</note>—was divided into four parts. Three of these were given to the column together with its capital and base. The single remaining top part was assigned to the rest of the ornaments: that is, the <term>architrave</term> <note>original: "trabi"; the main horizontal beam</note>, the <term>frieze</term> <note>original: "fasciae"; literally a band or strip</note>, and the <term>cornice</term> <note>original: "coronae"</note>. 

This single top part was further divided into sixteen <term>modules</term> <note>original: "modulos"; a standard unit of measurement in classical architecture</note>: five modules were given to the architrave; likewise five to the frieze; and six were given to the cornice with its <term>wave molding</term> <note>original: "undula"; a small S-shaped decorative molding</note>. That which was below the architrave down to the platform of the foundation was divided into twenty-five parts: of these, three were given to the height of the capital, and two to the base; the remaining middle space was filled by the length of the column shaft. In the corners, these columns were always made square. The base was formed with a single <term>torus</term> <note>original: "thoro"; a large, convex, ring-shaped molding</note>, and this was made from half of the total height of the base. At the bottom, in the place of the <term>necking</term> <note>original: "nextruli"; the transition between the shaft and the capital or base</note>, the column had the same proportions for its projection as it did at the top of the shaft. The width of the column in these works was made from one-fourth of its length. 

However, where the wall was filled with a full order of colonnades, then the square columns placed at the corners were measured at one-sixth of their length in width. The other columns along the wall and their ornaments were drawn from the design principles of temples. Between these colonnades and the ones mentioned just before, there is this difference: in the former, from corner to corner along the entire length of the wall, both the base at the bottom and the collar and necking of the column at the top are carried through continuously beneath the architrave. This is not done where many attached columns project—though there have been some who have carried the design of the base around the entire work, as is done in temples.

Within this square circuit of walls, a round and conspicuous structure would rise, projecting higher than the walls already placed by no less than half of its own diameter, and no more than two-thirds. The width of this round structure took from the maximum diameter of that square area no less than a half, and no more than five-sixths. Most designers occupied three-fifths; they repeated round shapes over square ones, and in turn placed a second round shape upon a second square according to the ratios I have mentioned, up to the fourth level of construction. They decorated them with the elements we have reviewed so far. There was no lack of means of ascent through the monument itself...

...most suitable: both the sacred rites of small shrines, and colonnades rising high from the wall, and the beauty of statues placed between the columns, and <term>inscriptions</term> <note>original: "tituli"; here meaning formal inscriptions, titles, or commemorative plaques</note> arranged and located in fitting places.

### ¶ Chapter 4. On the inscriptions, marks, and sculptures of tombs.

<margin>The famous saying of a philosopher.</margin>
**B**ut now I come to inscriptions. Their use was both manifold and varied among the ancients. For they were used not only on tombs, but also on sacred temples and even private houses. Symmachus says <note>Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, a 4th-century Roman statesman known for his letters and oratory</note> they used to inscribe on the <term>pediments</term> <note>original: "fastigiis"; the triangular top of a classical building</note> of the temple the names of the gods to whom they were dedicated; our own ancestors were accustomed to inscribe on small shrines to whom and at what time of year they were dedicated. This pleases me greatly. And—lest this be irrelevant—when the philosopher Crates <note>Crates of Thebes, a Cynic philosopher</note> arrived at Cyzicus and found these verses inscribed everywhere on private houses: *The strongest man, Hercules, son of Jupiter, lived here; let no evil enter this house,* he mocked it; he suggested instead they should inscribe: *Here poverty dwells.* For he argued that this [poverty] would drive away every kind of monster more readily and effectively than Hercules would.

<margin>What sort of epigrams there ought to be.</margin>
But inscriptions will be either written—which they called <term>epigrams</term> <note>original: "epigrammata"; brief, pithy poems or inscriptions</note>—or marked with signs and images. Plato ordained that no more than four verses should be written on tombs. Yet [as the poet says]: *But place a poem for me in the middle of the column, but let it be brief, so that the traveler hurrying from the city may read it.* <note>original: "Atqui tu media mihi carmen pone columna: Sed breve: quod currens vector ab urbe legat"; a quote from the Roman poet Propertius (Elegies, 2.11)</note> And certainly excessive length is very annoying elsewhere, but especially in these [monuments]. Or if at last it is a little longer, let it be entirely elegant in expression; and let it contain something that moves the soul toward piety, mercy, or gratitude, or which one does not regret having read, and takes pleasure in committing to memory and reciting.

That inscription of Homonoea is praised: *If the cruel fates allowed souls to be exchanged, I would gladly exchange mine for yours, dear Homonoea. But now, all that remains for me is to flee the light and the gods, so that I may follow you through the Styx after your untimely death.* <note>original: "Si pensare animas sinerent crudelia fata: Pensarem pro te cara Omeneæ libens: At nunc/ quod superest/ fugiam lucemque deosque: Ut te immatura per styga morte sequar."</note> And elsewhere: *Behold, citizens, the urn of the image of old Ennius, who depicted the greatest deeds of your fathers. Let no one honor me with tears nor perform my funeral with weeping. Why? I fly, living, through the mouths of men.* <note>original: "Aspicite o Cives senis Ennij imaginis urnam... volito vivus per ora virum"; a famous self-epitaph attributed to the early Roman poet Ennius</note> At the tombs of those who fell at Thermopylae, the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> had inscribed: *Stranger, tell the Lacedaemonians that we lie here while following their commands.* <note>original: "Hospes nuncia lacedemonijs nos hic iacere dum eorum iussa sequimur"</note> Nor shall we reject it if it contains some wonder of wit.

<margin>Pay attention to the witty epigram.</margin>
*Hey, traveler: here husband and wife do not quarrel. You ask who we are? I will not say. But look, I'll say it myself: here Belbius Balbus calls me Brebia Peppa. Oh wife, do you still chatter even when dead?* <note>Alberti quotes a humorous ancient inscription; "Peppa" and "Brebia" are likely informal nicknames, and "magarris" (chatter) implies her nagging voice follows him from the grave.</note> Such things are very pleasing. They used to attach larger letters of gilded bronze to the marble. The Egyptians used signs...

...in this manner. For by an eye they signified God; by a vulture, nature; by a bee, a king; by a circle, time; by an ox, peace, and other things of this sort. They used to say that these letters were known only to themselves, and that one day the knowledge of them would perish completely—just as has happened among us with the Etruscans. Throughout Etruria, excavated from the ruins of towns and funeral pyres, we have seen tombs inscribed with letters that everyone is convinced are Etruscan. Their marks imitate the Greek, and also the Latin, but no one understands what they signify. Therefore, they claim it will likewise happen to others. However, they say the Egyptians' own method of notation <note>Alberti is referring to hieroglyphics, which were a source of great fascination and mystery during the Renaissance</note>, which they used there, can be very easily interpreted throughout the whole world by learned men—to whom alone such matters should most worthily be communicated. Many have imitated these and carved various things on tombs.

<margin>The tomb of Diogenes.</margin>
At the tomb of Diogenes the Cynic <note>The famous Greek philosopher known for his extreme poverty and for living in a ceramic jar</note>, a column was erected upon which they placed a dog made of Parian marble.

<margin>Cicero of Arpinum found the tomb of Archimedes for the citizens.</margin>
At Syracuse, Cicero of Arpinum <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator and statesman</note> boasted that he had found the tomb of Archimedes, which had been neglected by time and overgrown with briars, and remained unknown to the citizens. He identified it by a conjecture based on a **cylinder and a small sphere** <note>original: "chylindro & sphærula"; Archimedes requested these geometric shapes be placed on his tomb to commemorate his discovery of the ratio between the volume of a sphere and its circumscribed cylinder</note> which he had seen carved on a certain prominent column. At the tomb of Simandus <note>Probably Osymandyas, the name used by Diodorus Siculus for Ramesses II</note>, king of the Egyptians, his mother was sculpted in stone twenty cubits high, wearing three royal insignias above her head, by which she showed she had been the daughter, wife, and mother of a king.

<margin>The tomb of Sardanapalus.</margin>
At the tomb of Sardanapalus, king of the Assyrians, they placed a statue striking his hands together in applause, and they had inscribed below: *I built Tarsus and Anchiale in no more than one day. But you, my guest, come eat and drink with festivity and jest, since the other things of men are by no means worthy of this—that is, applause.* <note>original: "Tarsum Archileūq; cōdidi... haud quaq̄ hoc dıgna sunt id est plausu"</note> And so they used notes and signs of that kind. Our Latin ancestors, however, chose to express the deeds of the most famous men through carved history. Hence columns, hence triumphal arches, hence porticos filled with painted or carved history. But among these, I would wish you to commit only the most worthy and grave matters to monuments. We have said enough of these things. Inland roads and water crossings will enjoy the same decorations provided to land routes. But since watchtowers <term>speculae</term> <note>original: "specula"; these include both military watchtowers and maritime lighthouses</note> are owed to maritime and somewhat also to land routes, we must discuss them.

<margin>Wonders</margin>
I do not repeat here what we read in Herodotus <note>original: "apud Herodotū legimꝰ." Herodotus was a 5th-century BC Greek historian; Alberti is referencing his description of the Temple of Belus in Babylon</note>: that there was a watchtower in the middle of a temple at Babylon whose base filled a whole stadium <note>A stadium was a Greek unit of length, approximately 600 feet</note> on each side, consisting of eight structures built one upon another. I shall praise this kind of work in watchtowers. For structures piled high in that manner contribute to both grace and strength, since the binding of their vaulting is so interwoven that the walls are beautifully held together.

A watchtower shall be either square or round; in both, the height must correspond to the width according to a certain ratio. When a square tower is to be slender, its width shall be one-sixth of its height; a round one will have a diameter of one-fourth of its height. If it is to be very thick, and is square, it shall be no more in width than one-fourth of its height. If round, its diameter shall be one-third of the height. For the thickness of the wall, if it is forty cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit based on the length of the forearm, about 18 to 21 inches</note> high, you shall give it no less than four feet. If it is fifty cubits high, then you shall give it five feet. For sixty cubits, you shall give it six feet. And from then on, proceed with an equal progression. 

However, these rules apply to plain and simple watchtowers. But there have been some who added an external portico <note>A porch or walkway supported by columns</note> to towers at mid-height with detached columns; and some who wound this portico in a spiral line; and some who encircled the whole with porticos like crowns; and those who covered the whole with carved animals. In these, the system of columns will not deviate from other public works. Indeed, everything may be reduced to a slender form, except for the weight of the structure. But he who wishes to make a watchtower most safe against the force of storms, and most pleasant to the sight:
<margin>Watchtowers</margin>
he shall place round parts over square ones, or again square ones over round ones; and he shall reduce the work step-by-step so that it becomes slender according to the rule of columns. I shall describe what we consider to be the most becoming form. First, the bases of the square towers shall rise from the ground; their height shall take a portion...

...of the total height that the work will have from the highest summit to the lowest foot [should be] a tenth <note>Alberti is defining the thickness of the base relative to the total height of the tower</note>. The width of this [base] shall have a fourth of that same height. Columns shall be attached to the walls on each side of the pedestal: two in the middle, and one at each corner, distinguished by their ornaments, as we recently described for sepulchers. On a pedestal of this sort, a quadrangular structure, like a small chapel <term>sacellum</term> <note>A small shrine or enclosed space; here used to describe a specific architectural tier</note>, shall stand, whose breadth shall be twice the height of the pedestal. It shall be made as high as it is wide; and columns shall be attached to this on the outside, such as we described for temples in the third, fourth, and fifth orders. Next, round chapels shall be placed upon it. There will be three of these round chapels, and we—drawing a comparison from reeds—shall call them "knots" <note>original: "nodos." Alberti uses the analogy of the joints or nodes on a reed or stalk of grass to describe how the tower tapers and segments as it rises</note>.
<margin>What a "knot" in a watchtower is.</margin>
Therefore, the height of each knot shall be equal to its width, with an additional twelfth of that same width added. We want this [extra] part to serve as the base <term>soccus</term>. The width, however, shall be derived from the lowermost quadrangular chapel which was set upon the first pedestal, in this manner: For you shall divide the side of that quadrangular chapel into twelve parts; taking away one of these parts, you shall give what remains to the next, first knot. Again, divide the diameter of this first knot into twelve parts likewise; and from these parts, you shall give eleven parts to the second knot. In the same way, you shall make the third knot more slender than the second by an eleventh part of itself. By this gradation, we shall achieve what most learned ancients approved of in columns: that the trunk of the work be thicker at the lowest foot by a fourth than at the summit. Columns with their ornaments shall be attached to the knots, no more than an eighth [of the knot's thickness] and no less than a sixth. Then, windows and niches <unclear>scafic</unclear> <note>The OCR 'scafic' is likely a corruption of "scaphia," referring to shell-shaped niches or hollows</note> with the ornaments due to them shall be opened in suitable places in each knot and likewise in the chapel. The void of the window opening shall not take up more than half of its intercolumniation <note>The space between two adjacent columns</note>. The sixth and highest level of the work in this watchtower, which shall indeed be placed above the third knot I mentioned, will be a quadrangular work; its height and width shall be set so that it takes up no more than two-thirds of the diameter of the highest knot. For ornament, there shall only be corner columns fastened to the pillars <term>pilae</term>, upon which the vault <term>testudo</term> <note>Literally "tortoise," a common term for a vaulted ceiling or dome</note> rests. There will also be the beam [entablature], the capitals, and ornaments of this kind. But the middle spaces of these walls shall be made passable, like a crossroads. In the seventh and final level, a round portico, passable from every side, shall be raised with bare and unencumbered columns. The length of the columns with their ornaments shall be as great as the diameter of this area. The diameter itself shall take up three-fourths of the breadth of the chapel set beneath it. <margin>Ptolemy's watchtower.</margin>
Upon this circular colonnade, one should place a spherical dome. In the small chapels <term>facellis</term> <note>Alberti uses this term to describe the smaller architectural compartments or tiers that make up the height of the tower</note> which are rectilinear and four-sided, crests <term>cristae</term> shall rise at the far corners. In the first four-sided chapel, which sits in the lowest space above the base <term>crepidinem</term>, the middle space will occupy five-eighths of its total external width. But among the ancients, that of King Ptolemy on the island of Pharos <note>The Pharos of Alexandria, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, which served as the prototype for all later lighthouses</note> was most highly praised; he ordered fires to be kept in a high watchtower, suspended and constantly moving, for the use of ships at night, so that the flames would not be mistaken for stars from a distance. Also, moving images showing which way the wind blows, or where the sun is in the sky, and how much of the day has passed, would serve the purpose most beautifully there. So much for these things.

## ¶ The more distinguished ways of cities: how gates, harbors, bridges, arches, crossroads, and entrances are adorned. Chapter 6. ##

**I**t follows that we should enter within the city. But there are some roads that are much more distinguished, which by their nature can be both inside and outside the city: such as those leading to a temple, a basilica, or a theater. Therefore, regarding these first...

<margin>Heliogabalus.</margin>
<margin>Roads once miraculous in their structure.</margin>
We read that Heliogabalus <note>A Roman Emperor (r. 218–222 AD) known for his extravagant public expenditures</note> built wider and more distinguished roads of this kind using Macedonian and porphyry stone. Historians praise the road at Bubastis in Egypt that led to the temple; it was straight through the forum and paved with excellent stones. Its width filled four plethra <note>An ancient Greek unit of length; four plethra is roughly 400 feet or 120 meters</note>. On this side and that, most vast trees flourished. Aristeas <note>A historical figure associated with the "Letter of Aristeas," which describes the city of Jerusalem and its Temple</note> records that in Jerusalem there were elegant, elevated walkways through the city, through which the elders and more distinguished citizens might walk more honorably. This was done especially so that those carrying sacred objects would not be polluted by contact with profane things. Also famous in Plato <note>A reference to the opening of Plato's *Laws*, describing a walk through a cypress grove</note> is the road from Knossos to the cave and shrine of Jupiter, lined with cypress trees. I find that among others in Rome, there were two roads of this kind most worthy of admiration. One from the gate all the way to the Basilica of Paul <note>Saint Paul Outside the Walls</note>, about five stadia <note>Approximately 3,000 feet</note> long. The other from the bridge to the Basilica of Peter, 2,500 feet long, covered by a portico of marble columns and a lead roof. These ornaments are wonderfully suited to such roads. But I return to military roads. The head and, as it were, the boundary of roads—both those outside the city and those inside—is the gate for land routes and, unless I am mistaken, the harbor for sea routes. Unless, perhaps, it is a subterranean one, such as the Egyptians...

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

They say that in Thebes <note>Ancient Greek city</note> there were [secret roads] through which kings could send out armies without any of the townspeople noticing. I find that there were also many such paths excavated at Praeneste <note>Modern Palestrina</note> in Latium, running from the top of the mountain down to the plains with wondrous skill. They write that in one of these, Marius <note>Gaius Marius the Younger, who committed suicide in these tunnels during a siege in 82 BCE</note>, when hard-pressed by a siege, perished. From the author who wrote the life of Apollonius <note>Philostratus</note>, I found a road worthy of mention. For he says a Median woman at Babylon <note>Likely referring to the legendary Queen Nitocris</note> constructed a road of stone and bitumen led deep beneath the riverbed, by which one could cross on dry feet from the royal palace to another house positioned directly across the river. But let us be permitted not to believe everything from Greek historians.

<margin>Gates.
Harbors.</margin>
I return to the matter at hand. Gates shall be adorned no differently than triumphal arches, about which we shall speak soon. A harbor will be adorned by extended porticoes built around it, with a rugged quay <term>crepido</term> and wide, open spaces; also a prominent, famous, and spectacular temple; and in front of the temple, a broad, open forum; and in the very mouth of the harbor, colossi <note>colossal statues</note>, such as were in several other places and especially at Rhodes, where they say Herod placed three. Historians celebrate the massive mole <term>moles</term> <note>original: "moles" – a massive stone structure used as a pier or breakwater</note> at the harbor of Samos, which they say was twenty fathoms <term>orgias</term> high and extended two furlongs <term>stadia</term> into the sea. Therefore, these things will adorn a harbor if they are crafted with elegant art and uncommon materials. Furthermore, as for the road within the city—besides being well-paved and perfectly clean—it will be most beautifully adorned by porticoes of equal design, with houses on both sides balanced against each other, aligned by line and level. But the specific parts of the street to which ornaments are especially due are these:

<margin>Bridge.</margin>
The bridge and the crossroads. Indeed, a spectacle is nothing other than a forum surrounded by steps. ¶ I shall begin, therefore, with the bridge, since it is the most important part of a road. The parts of a bridge are the piers <term>pilae</term>, the arches, and the paving <term>instratura</term>. The parts of a bridge also include the central road where pack animals travel, and on either side, the walkways <term>decursoria</term> where those in togas <note>citizens</note> may walk; and for the

<margin>Hadrian’s Bridge.</margin>
sides, there are railings; for some, there is even a roof. Such as at Rome, on the most excellent of all bridges, the work of Hadrian <note>The Pons Aelius, now the Ponte Sant'Angelo</note>, which is worthy of mention, and whose "corpse" <note>original: "cadavera" – Alberti uses this striking term to refer to the majestic ruins of the bridge's upper structure</note>, so to speak, I used to gaze upon with veneration. For there had stood a roof raised upon forty-two marble columns with an entablature <term>opere trabeato</term>, a bronze roofing, and wondrous ornamentation. We shall make the bridge as wide as the road. The piers shall be equal to each other in number and size. To their thickness shall be given a third of the span <note>the width of the arch opening</note>. The prows <note>original: "prorae" – the triangular cutwaters or starlings of a bridge pier</note> on the piers shall be extended against the force of the water until they add half the width of the bridge to the structure; and they shall emerge even above the flood levels. The stern <note>the downstream end of the pier</note> shall likewise be extended; however, it would not be unbecoming...

# Book VIII. On the Ornamentation of Public Secular Buildings. Folio CXXVI.

...it will be pleasing if any [piers] are somewhat less pointed and, as it were, blunt. It will also be pleasing if buttresses <term>anterides</term> rise up from the "prow" and "stern" <note>the upstream and downstream ends of the pier</note> for the sake of strength to support the sides of the bridge; therefore, let the thickness at the base occupy no less than two-thirds of the width of the pier. The arches should stand with their heads <note>crowns</note> entirely out of the water. Their moldings should be derived from the Ionic or, better yet, the Doric beam <note>entablature</note>; and in large bridges, their thickness should never be less than one-fifteenth of the total opening. For the sake of strength, small square pedestals <term>arulae</term> <note>literally "little altars"</note> shall be arranged along the parapet <term>sponda</term> by line and level; upon these, if desired, you may raise columns to support a roof to be drawn over it. The height of the parapets, including the base and the molding, shall be four feet. You will fill the spaces between the pedestals with a screen <term>pluteo</term>. For the pedestals and the screen, the molding shall be a "throat" <term>gulula</term> <note>a concave molding or cyma recta</note>, or rather a "little wave" <term>undula</term> <note>a convex molding or cyma reversa</note> extending through the whole line of the parapet. A matching base shall correspond to the molding at the bottom. The walkways <term>decursoria</term>—which are added along the middle of the bridge path next to the parapet for the sake of women and pedestrians—shall stand one or two steps higher than the middle road itself, which is paved with flint <note>silice</note> for the sake of beasts of burden. The height of the columns with their ornaments shall be as great as the width of the bridge.

<margin>Crossroads (Trivium)</margin>
A crossroads <term>trivium</term> and a forum differ only in size. A crossroads is surely a tiny forum. Plato <note>In his *Laws*</note> commanded that there should be spaces at crossroads where nurses could meet with children and be together. I believe this was so that the children might be made stronger by the use of fresher air, and the nurses might be more elegant out of a desire for praise, and they would wander less into negligence under the observation of so many eyes. Certainly, it will be an ornament to both the crossroads and the forum if there is an elegant portico under which the magistrates presiding might sit or take a midday rest, or where people might wait to perform mutual duties for one another. Add to this that the presence of the elders will deter the youth—who are playing and <margin>☞</margin> competing in the wider spaces—from all the impudence and buffoonery of a frolicsome age.

<margin>Forum.</margin>
One forum is for money-changers <term>argentarium</term>, another for vegetables <term>olitorium</term>, another for cattle <term>boarium</term>, another for wood <term>lignarium</term>, and so on; for these, both a location in the city and their own proper ornaments are due. But it is agreed that the money-changers' forum is the most excellent of all. The Greeks established the forum as a square; they surrounded it with very large and double porticoes; they adorned it with stone columns and beams; and above, on the timber flooring, they made walkways. Among us Italians, the width of the forum was two-thirds of its length; and because, according to ancient custom, gladiatorial shows were watched there, the columns were placed further apart toward the portico. Around the portico, the money-changers' shops <term>tabernae</term> were situated, and above, on the floorings, balconies <term>meniana</term> <note>named after Maenius, these were projecting galleries for spectators</note> and rooms to serve public taxes were prepared. These...
