# Book VIII. On the Ornamentation of Public Secular Buildings. Page LVII.
## Leo Battista Alberti: On the Art of Building.

...to them. But we shall approve of a forum whose area completes two squares <note>meaning the length is twice the width, a classic Vitruvian proportion</note>. It is fitting that the porticoes and the structures built around it should correspond to the open-air area with specific dimensions: this prevents the space from appearing too vast if the surrounding buildings are too low, or too cramped if it is enclosed by a crowded pile of overly high buildings. The height of the roofs will be very convenient if it is set at one-third of the forum's width, or at the very least, no less than two-twelfths <note>one-sixth</note> of that width. 

<margin>**Forum porticoes.** I would wish the porticoes to be raised <note>exaggeratas</note> by a fifth of their own width.</margin>

Furthermore, the width of the portico will be the same as the height of the columns. The outlines of the colonnade shall be derived from the basilica <note>a large public hall used for legal and business matters</note>. But in these, the crown <term>corona</term>, the band <term>fascia</term>, and the beam <term>trabs</term> <note>the components of the entablature</note> together shall take up a fifth part of the column's height. If it is pleasing to build a second story of colonnades over the first, those shall be made more slender and shorter than the first by one-fourth. They shall be placed like a mound upon a pedestal <term>soccus</term>, the height of which should be half the height of the lower support.

## Triumphal Arches

<margin>**Triumphal Arches.**</margin>

But what ornaments the forums and crossroads in a grander way are the arches placed at the mouths of the streets. For an arch is, as it were, a perpetually open gate. I believe the arch was invented by those who extended the empire. For Tatius <note>likely referring to the historian Tacitus or a source regarding Titus Tatius</note> says that according to ancient custom, they would also expand the *pomerium* <note>the sacred boundary of a city</note>. They say that Claudius did this. Therefore, as the city grew, they decided that the ancient gates should be preserved for the sake of utility, for other reasons, and perhaps also so they might be safer in the event of misfortune against the force of invading enemies. Consequently, because that structure stood in a very famous place, they deposited there the spoils taken from the enemy and the marks of victory. From that point, the arch began to be decorated; titles, statues, and historical scenes were added. 

We shall most fitly build an arch in the place where a road ends in a square or a forum, and especially on a *via regia* <note>a "royal way," which Alberti uses to mean the most principal or dignified street in a city</note>. For an arch, not unlike a bridge, will have three passable ways. The middle one is for the soldiers. This side and that <note>the two side passages</note> are for the mothers and those who accompany their victorious army returning to salute their ancestral gods, and to applaud and congratulate those celebrating a triumph. 

Where you build an arch, the line of the ground-plan that runs <term>along the road</term> <note>original: secundum viam</note> shall be half the length of the line that intersects the cross-street from right to left. And the length of that transverse line shall be no less than fifty cubits <note>approximately 75 feet or 23 meters</note>. This work is very much like a bridge. However, it consists of no more than four piers and three openings. From the shorter line of the plan—that is, the one <term>along the road</term>—an eighth part shall be left on the side of the area facing the forum, and likewise an eighth for the other rear side of the area; these spaces are to be occupied by the little pedestals <term>arulae</term> <note>literally "little altars"</note> from which the columns for the arch will rise. Indeed, the other line of the area, which is <term>longer</term> <note>original: prolixior</note>, that is, the one which is transverse...

# Book VIII. On the Ornamentation of Public Buildings. Page CXXVII.

The structure placed across the road shall be divided into **eight modules**: from these, two modules are given to the central opening; then, one module shall be given to each of the piers, and likewise, one module to each of the side openings. 

The inner sides of the piers, which rise vertically to support the arch of the central opening, shall be made **two modules high**, with the addition of a **third part of a module**. The same ratio for the height of the sides will be applied in the remaining two side openings; for they shall be related to their own spans with a similar dimension <note>maintaining the same proportional relationship between height and width</note>. 

The ceiling for the smaller openings will be a vault <term>fornix</term>. The ornaments extending at the top of the piers, beneath the arch and vault, will imitate a **Doric capital**; but in place of the flat plate and lid <note>the abacus and echinus of a standard capital</note>, they will have projecting cornices in the **Corinthian** or even **Ionic** style. Below this cornice, like a neck, it will have a clear band <term>fascia</term>. 

Next, that which is joined to the tops of the column shafts will have a collar <term>torques</term> and a small bead <term>nextrulo</term>. All these ornaments together will be made from **one-ninth** of the height of the pier. This ninth part is further divided into nine small particles:
*   **Five** of these you shall give to the cornice;
*   **Three** you shall give to the band <term>fascia</term>;
*   **One** you shall give to the collar and bead.

The curved beam—that is, the arch which faces forward—shall take for its own thickness no more than a **twelfth** and no less than a **tenth** of the width of the opening. 

Columns shall be attached to the middle of the pier fronts properly and neatly; they shall be placed such that the top of the shaft is level with the peak of the opening. In their length <note>height</note>, they shall span as much as the width of the central opening. Beneath the column shall be placed a base, a small pedestal <term>arula</term>, and a plinth <term>soccus</term>. Above the column, there shall be a capital, either **Corinthian** or **Composite** <term>italicum</term>; and above that, a beam <term>trabs</term>, a band <term>fascia</term>, and a cornice <term>corona</term> in the Ionic or Corinthian style. Each of these shall be executed with their proper outlines, which we have discussed above. 

Above such colonnades shall rise the wings of the uppermost superstructure wall <note>the attic story</note>, until they add half as much again to the work as exists from the lowest base to the outer line of its cornice. The height of this added wall shall be divided into **eleven parts**:
*   The **topmost part** is given to plain cornices, with no band or beam placed beneath;
*   At the **bottom**, one and a half parts are given to the plinth <term>soccus</term>, which shall have an ornament of an inverted wave <term>undula</term> <note>a cyma reversa molding</note> comprising a third of its height.

Statues shall be neatly placed upon the ends of the beams which project from the work to meet the columns; they shall have beneath their feet a small pedestal <term>arula</term> as thick as the column is at its base. The total height of the statues, including the pedestal, shall take up **eight** of these eleven parts of the wall. Finally, on the topmost ledge of the work facing the forum, there are displayed four-horse chariots <term>quadrigae</term>, larger statues, animals, and such...

...images of things shall be arranged in various ways. In place of a pedestal <term>soccus</term> where they may rest, a small wall shall be substituted, three times as high as the cornice that is closest and adjacent below it. The height of the statues which are to be placed in this final and highest position shall exceed those previous statues which we placed upon the columns by no more than a sixth, and no less than a ninth. # VII. On Adorning Places of Spectacle, Theaters, and Racing-Courses, and How Great Their Usefulness Is.

<margin>
Spectacles.
The opinion of Epimenides on spectacles.
</margin>
**I** come now to spectacles. They say that Epimenides—the man who slept for fifty-seven years in a tomb <note>the legend usually specifies a cave, but Alberti uses *sepulchro*</note>—when he was in Athens while they were constructing a place for games, rebuked the citizens and said: "You are truly ignorant of how many disasters this place will cause; if you understood it, you would tear it apart with your teeth." And I do not dare to find fault with our own high priests and masters of morals if they have intentionally prohibited the use of spectacles. 

<margin>
The law of Moses.
</margin>
They praise Moses, who established that his entire people should gather for festivals in a single temple and celebrate feasts together at appointed times. What else should I say he intended by this, except that he wished the minds of the citizens to be softened by assembly and communion, and to make them more ready for the fruit of friendship? Thus I believe our ancestors established spectacles in cities not more for the sake of celebration and pleasure than for usefulness. And indeed, if we consider the matter carefully, many reasons will occur why you might grieve again and again that such a noble and useful institution has long since fallen into disuse. For since some spectacles were invented for the delights of peace and leisure, and others for the pursuits of war and business, in the former the vigor and power of the intellect and mind are certainly excited and nourished; in the latter, the strength and firmness of the spirit and physical powers are wonderfully increased. 

<margin>
The Arcadians, the inventors of games.
</margin>
In both, there is a certain and constant path which contributes greatly to the safety and honor of the fatherland. The Arcadians, because they were austere and harsh in their way of life, are said to have invented games in order to soften the minds of the citizens; those who later abandoned them lived so...

Fo.CXXVIII

# Book VIII. On the Ornamentation of Public Secular Buildings.

Polybius recalls that minds grew hard <note>The historian Polybius argued that the inhabitants of Cynethia became savage because they neglected the civilizing influence of music and games</note>; so that they were held as execrable throughout all Greece. But the memory of games is otherwise very ancient, and of various kinds. Various authors are said to have been their creators. For they say that Dionysus indeed instituted dancing and games of the lyre in the beginning. I find also that Hercules was the author of certain games. Then they proclaim that the contest <term>agon</term> <note>original: *agonem*, a Greek term for a public struggle or contest</note> was devised at Olympus, and its inventors were the Aetolians and Epeians after the return from Troy. Among the Greeks, they report that Dionysus Lenaeus <note>Dionysus of the Wine-press, associated with the Lenaia festival</note>, who first invented the choruses of tragedies, also first established the seating for spectacles.

In Italy, Lucius Mummius first gave theatrical games in a triumph two hundred years before the Prince Nero; and from here actors <term>histriones</term> migrated into the city from the Etruscans. Horse-racing contests were brought from the Tyrians; and from them nearly the rest of the variety of games arose from Asia and was carried over to the Italians. I could easily believe that those virtuous descendants—who used to mark Janus upon their bronze coins <note>referring to early Roman heavy bronze coinage, the *aes grave*</note>—watched games while standing under a beech or an elm tree. 

<margin>Verses of Ovid on the games.</margin>
Naso <note>The poet Ovid</note> says: "You first, Romulus, made the games anxious, when the abducted Sabine women delighted the single men. Then no awnings hung over a marble theater, nor were the stages red with liquid saffron. There, the foliage which the wooded Palatine had provided was simply placed; the stage was without art. The people sat on steps made of turf, with any leafy branch covering their shaggy hair." <note>original: *Primus solicitos inquit Naso fecisti Romule ludos...* from Ovid's *Ars Amatoria*</note> 

However, they say that Iolaus, the son of Iphicles, first established seats built with steps on the island of Sardinia, when he had received the Thespiades from Hercules. But according to ancient custom, theaters were then first made of wood. For this reason, they even accused Pompey for having placed a permanent seat for spectacles—not, as before, with sudden <note>meaning temporary or makeshift</note> steps, but with lasting ones. Afterwards they reached the point where three very large theaters were held within the city; and amphitheatres, along with many others, then one that could hold more than two hundred thousand men, and the greatest Circus of all. All these were distinguished by squared stone and marble columns. Add to this that, not content with these, they also raised temporary spectacles with marble and glass and an incredible abundance of statues. The most capacious of all spectacles up to that time burned during the war of Octavian at the city of Piacenza <note>original: *Placentia*</note> in Gaul. But so much for these things.

Spectacles are divided: some look toward leisure, others toward business <note>or "serious activity"</note>. Joined to leisure, which may delight, are poets, musicians, and actors. Those which indeed look toward the matter of war are wrestling, boxing, the weighted-glove <term>caestus</term>, javelins, racing-courses, and whatever preludes of arms there are of this sort; which Plato used to command every year, because they contribute wonderfully to the health of the republic and the honor of the city. Various labors are owed to these, and they are accordingly called by various names. For while there are indeed some in which poets, comic and tragic, and those of that sort are engaged, these we call theaters for the sake of dignity...

Fo. CXXVIII [verso]

<header>Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.</header>

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

<margin>Circus.</margin>
<margin>Amphitheater.</margin>
<margin>Monagus, inventor of the games.</margin>
<margin>Cavea.</margin>
<margin>Parts of the theater.</margin>
...tacles <note>continuing from the previous page</note> we shall call them. Others, truly, in which well-born youth may practice with racing-chariots, whether drawn by two horses <term>biga</term> or four horses <term>quadriga</term> <note>original: *biga / quadrigave*</note>: this shall be called a **Circus**. Still others, finally, in which hunts of enclosed wild beasts are held: this shall be called an **Amphitheater**. Nearly all such structures for spectacles imitate the horns of a battle line drawn up for war. They consist of a central floor <term>area</term> <note>original: *area mediana*</note> in which actors, boxers, teams of animals, and the like may perform, and tiers of steps <note>original: *gradationibus*</note> upon which the spectators may sit; but they differ in the layout of the central floor. For among these, that whose form is similar to a waning moon <note>original: *senescenti lune*</note> is called a **theater**. However, when it is extended into an oblong shape by its "horns," it is called a **Circus** for this reason: because within it, both two-horse and four-horse chariots circle around the turning-posts <term>metas</term> while competing. Furthermore, in these buildings naval battles were also held by letting in water, in some places from a stream and in others from an aqueduct.

There are those who say the ancients were accustomed to practice such games between swords and rivers <note>original: *inter enses et flumina*; a folk etymology for "Circenses"</note>, and for that reason they were named "Circensian." And they say that the inventor of these games was a certain **Monagus** at Elis in Asia. Those structures which were enclosed by two theaters joined face-to-face were called the hollow <term>cavea</term> <note>original: *caueam*, referring to the seating bowl</note>, and the work itself is called an **Amphitheater**. Above all, it is necessary that the sites for spectacles be chosen for their healthfulness, lest heavy breezes or the sun, or those other factors we reviewed in the first book, cause harm. This is especially true of the theater, which, because the people seek out poets and shaded, light-hearted delights of the mind during the month of August, ought to be entirely turned away from the sun and covered. For a sunbeam trapped within the circuit of the structure would bake the bodies of the audience, and once their humors began to boil, they would easily fall into disease. 

The place must also be resonant <note>original: *sonorus*</note>, and not at all "deaf" <note>original: *surdus*, meaning acoustically flat or prone to echoes that kill sound</note>. It is also appropriate to have porticos, either joined to the work or nearby, in which the people may take shelter from sudden rain and storms. **Plato** approved of the seating for the theater being within the city, but the horse-racing tracks being outside the city. The parts of the theater are these: the open bay of the central floor under the open sky; the tiers of seats <note>original: *subselliorum gradationes*</note> around this floor; and the raised structure of the stage <term>pulpiti</term> <note>original: *pulpiti*, the platform for performers</note> across the entrance-ways, where the elements pertaining to the play are coordinated. And at the highest circuit, there are porticos and roofs, by which the voice, as it spreads, may be contained and made more resonant. 

But Greek theaters differed from Latin ones in this respect: the Greeks, because they brought their choruses and stage-dancers into the middle of the central floor <note>the orchestra</note>, required a smaller stage; our people, because the entire cast performed the play on the stage, wished for it to be more spacious. On this point all agreed: that in the beginning, they should circumscribe a semicircle <note>original: *emiciclum*</note> in the floor and extend the horns of that semicircle. But some did this with straight lines, and others with curved ones. Those who used straight lines extended them parallel to one another until they had added to the horns of the semicircle a length equal to a quarter of the diameter. Those, however...

Fo. CXXIX.

Book VIII. On the Ornament of Public Buildings.

...those who used curved lines would indeed draw a complete circle, and from that full circumference of the cycle, they would subtract a fourth part. What remained, therefore, they left for the **theater**. Once the boundaries of the central floor <term>area</term> <note>original: *areae*</note> were established, the tiers of seating <term>subsellia</term> <note>original: *gradationes subselliorum*</note> were prepared. First, they determined how high they wished the tiers to be, and from that height, they defined how much space they would occupy at the base. Almost all builders made their theaters as high as the central floor was wide. For they had discovered that in lower theaters, voices tend to slip away and vanish, whereas in very high ones, they are strengthened but heard more harshly. Among the more refined architects, however, there were those who made the height of the theater four-fifths <note>original: *partem quintam... quater*</note> the width of the central floor. 

<margin>Steps.</margin>
Within this total height of the work, the tiers of seats never occupied less than half, nor more than two-thirds <note>original: *tertiam bis*</note>. For the steps of the seats, some made the width twice half the height <note>original: *dimidiam altitudinis bis*</note>; others made the height twice one-fifth of the width. We shall describe the method that we consider to be the most perfect and approved in every respect. 

<margin><unclear>Foundations.</unclear></margin>
The outer foundations of the tiers—that is, the walls where the highest row of seating ends—shall be cast at a distance from the center of the semicircle <term>emicicli</term> equal to the radius of the central floor plus one-third of that same radius. The first steps for ascending shall not begin from the ground level of the central floor itself. Instead, in the largest theaters, a high wall shall be raised at the very start of the lowest tiers, equal to one-ninth of the central floor's radius; in smaller theaters, this wall shall be raised no less than seven feet. From there, the steps for seating shall begin to ascend. These steps shall be established at a height of one and a half feet, and a width of one and a half to two feet. 

<margin>Passages.</margin>
The passages <term>itiones</term> <note>original: *itiones*, the walkways or corridors for spectator access</note> shall be vaulted beneath the steps, arranged and balanced so that some lead directly into the central floor, while others lead to the highest tiers. There shall be as many of these as the size and breadth of the theater requires. 

<margin><unclear>Royal</unclear></margin>
Of these, however, seven shall be primary passages, directed toward the center and entirely unobstructed. Their entrances shall be separated by equal intervals. One of these passages, located in the very middle of the semicircular curve, shall be more open than the rest. I call this the **Royal Opening** <note>original: *apertionem regiam*</note> because the royal way is led through it. There shall also be one passage at the right end of the diameter and another at the left. Furthermore, two intermediate passages shall be placed on this side and two on the opposite side through the semicircle. Between these, other paths may be placed, as many as the circumference of the theater will allow. In the largest theaters, the ancients divided the entire seating area into three sections, and around each...

# Leon Battista Alberti. On Architecture.

...for viewing, a step was placed there twice as wide as the others, which indeed would separate the upper steps from the lower ones by an intervening small circular path <note>original: *interiecta circuitionis areola*; this refers to a walkway or landing known as a *diazoma*</note>. Into these—if I may call them so—perfected arrangements, the various ways of ascent converged through vaulted passages <note>original: *subtestudinata gradationum*</note> beneath the seating. I have noticed in some theaters that excellent architects and well-advised craftsmen provided that for each primary entrance <note>original: *itiones*</note>, internal stairs were added on either side. One set of these allowed the more eager and agile to fly upward with a rough and rapid ascent via continuous steps. The other stairs, however, were more moderate and open, having intermediate landings <note>original: *areas interiectas*</note> and turnings <note>original: *refractiones*</note> where matrons and the elderly might carry themselves with a slow pace and rest while climbing. So much for the steps <note>original: *gradationibus*</note>.

Furthermore, in front of the narrow entrances <note>original: *faucibus*</note> of the theater, raised spaces were constructed where the masked actors <note>original: *personati*</note> would perform the play. In those places, it was the custom for the fathers <note>senators or elders</note> and magistrates to sit, separated from the common people in a specific and most honorable place—for instance, in the central floor itself <note>original: *area mediana*; the orchestra</note>, where benches <note>original: *subsellijs*</note> were placed with elegant decoration. 

<margin>The Stage.</margin>
The stage <note>original: *pulpitum*</note> was then made so large that players, musicians, and those performing dances would not require a much larger one. The floor of this stage extended to the very center of the semicircle <note>original: *emicicli*</note>; they raised it no more than five feet, so that the senators could most beautifully view all the gestures of the performers from the level ground. However, in theaters where it was not the custom for the central floor to be occupied by those wearing togas <note>citizens of high status</note>, but instead was given over entirely to dancers and singers, the area of the stage was made smaller. Yet it was raised higher, sometimes up to six cubits <note>approximately 9 feet</note>. 

Moreover, this part in both types of theater was adorned with columns and stories <note>original: *contignationibus*</note> placed one above the other in imitation of houses. It had folding doors in suitable places: one in the middle like a royal entrance, with the ornamentation of temples; and others nearby through which the stage actors <note>original: *proscæniti actores*</note> would have access to come forward or retreat, as the acts of the plays required. 

<margin>Three kinds of poets.</margin> 
And since there were three kinds of poets involved in the theater: the **Tragic**, who recited the miseries of tyrants; the **Comic**, who explained the cares and anxieties of fathers of families; and the **Satyric**, who sang of the delights of the countryside and the loves of shepherds. There was also a place where, by means of a revolving machine <note>original: *versatili machina*; likely a reference to *periaktoi*, triangular prisms rotated to change scenes</note>, a painted facade <note>original: *frons*</note> would immediately be presented, and there would appear either a hall <note>original: *atrium*</note>, a cottage, or even a forest, as it suited the theme and the plays being performed. 

Thus the floor, the steps, and the stages for the scenic artists were of this kind. We have said that one of the primary parts in a theater, invented for the sake of strengthening voices and sounds, is the portico. This was placed at the highest steps and was fitted with arrangements of columns for the sake of...

# Book VIII. On the Ornament of Public Secular Buildings. Folio 130.

...looked toward the central area of the theater <note>original: *area mediana*; the orchestra</note>. This is what we must discuss next. **Pay attention.** <note>original: *Attende*</note> From the philosophers, they had learned that the air, when struck by the voice, is moved by the breaking of sound into circles, not unlike how water is moved into rings when something has suddenly emerged within it. They understood that—just as with a lyre <note>original: *cythara*</note> and especially in wooded valleys—the sound and the voice are rendered much more sonorous and clear when the swelling rings of motion (if I may call them that) strike something. This occurs because the rays of the voice traveling out from the center are stopped by a wall, like a ball thrown against it, and are pushed back. From this rejection, those rings are rendered denser and stronger. 

Moved by this principle, they originally established that theaters should be built in a circle. And so that the voice should meet no obstacle in the meantime to prevent it from reaching the highest parts of the theater with a free flow, they placed the steps <note>the seating tiers</note> in such a way that a single straight line would touch all their extended corners. In the highest place of the tiers, they added a portico <note>a covered walkway with columns</note> which would contribute greatly, looking toward (as I said) the central area of the theater. Its front was to be completely unobstructed with openings. However, the rear part of that portico, opposite the openings of the spaces between the columns, was to be entirely closed off by a continuous wall. 

Then, as if for a pedestal <note>original: *socco*</note> for the structure, they raised a parapet <note>original: *spondam*; a rim or enclosure</note> below the colonnades and the wall, to collect the swelling rings of voices. For indeed, the air coming up from the portico would be received there most softly; it would not echo back whole with a full impact, but rather reinforce the sound. They also added, both for the sake of providing shade and for the quality of the voices, a canopy <note>original: *velum*; a massive cloth awning</note> above to serve as a ceiling for the theater. This, stretched out and adorned with stars <note>original: *stellis circumallaqueatum*</note>, would cover the central area, the tiers, and the spectators from above with its shadow. 

<margin>The Portico in the Theater.</margin>

This portico possessed a great deal of artifice. Indeed, for the sake of supporting this one, other colonnades and porticoes were placed beneath it, opening toward the exterior of the theater. In the largest theaters, these were made double, lest by chance if rain driven by a sharp wind or a storm should arise, those walking through the porticoes might be sprayed. The openings and colonnades of these first supporting porticoes were not of the kind we reviewed in temples or in basilicas, but were built with solid work and a very firm wall according to the designs taken from a triumphal arch. Regarding these lower parts, which are made for the sake of the upper ones, we must speak first. The ratio of the openings in these porticoes is such that a single opening is placed opposite each of the entrances <note>original: *itiones*</note> by which you reach the central area of the theater. Then it is necessary that other openings follow these in certain orders. It is proper for each of the openings to agree among themselves in height, width, and finally in all lines and ornaments.

...one part should correspond to the other. It is also necessary that the open passage along the length through that portico should be as wide as the empty space of the opening between the piers <note>original: *pilas*; the heavy square supports that carry the arches</note>. It is also fitting that the piers themselves in that location should be half the width of their own open aperture. To have cared for all these things with skillful industry and the greatest diligence is the duty of the architect. Moreover, the columns should not stand free and clear as they do in triumphal arches; instead, they shall be attached to the middle of the fronts of the piers. Small pedestals <note>original: *arulae*, literally "little altars"</note> shall be placed under the columns, equal to one-sixth of the height of the columned order. 

The rest of the ornaments will follow the pattern used in temples. However, the height of the column with all its ornaments and the cornice <note>original: *corone*</note> shall be half the vertical height of the inner seating tiers <note>original: *gradationū*</note>. Thus, there will be two orders of these external colonnades, the second vaulting of which will equal the total height of the seating tiers. At this very height, the floor of the portico—which, as I said, faces inward toward the central area of the theater—shall also be made level. The outline of the theater's central area <note>the orchestra</note> mimics the footprint <note>original: *vestigium*</note> of a horse’s hoof.

When these things are finished, the uppermost portico shall be placed above. Its front and colonnade will not receive light from the outside (like the structures placed beneath it which we have just reviewed); instead, as we said of it earlier, 

<margin>The Enclosure of the Theater <note>original: *Circūuallatio*</note>: what it is.</margin>

it will face the central area of the theater. Because this work is designed so that voices do not slip away but are gathered together and sent back fuller, we shall call it the **enclosure wall** <term>circuuvallatio: a surrounding wall designed for both structural enclosure and acoustic reflection</term>. The height of this enclosure will be three times half the height of the first external colonnade. It will have the following parts: a wall placed under the columns, which we shall call the **podium** <term>suggestum: a high base or platform wall</term>. This wall—measured from the highest steps of the theater to the very covering of its roof—should be no more than one-third of the total enclosure height in the largest theaters, and in smaller ones, no less than one-fourth. 

Upon this wall, columns shall be placed. The length of these columns, including their bases and capitals, shall be exactly half the total height of the enclosure. Above these columns will come the ornaments, and to mimic the style of basilicas <note>large public halls</note>, an attic wall <note>original: *alamentum*, a wall extension</note> will rise up, led along above the columns. This wall should occupy the remaining sixth part of the total enclosure height. The columns here will be free-standing, with their designs and outlines taken from those used in a basilica. In number, they will equal the columns that are attached to the external portico, and they shall be positioned upon the same radii. I call "radii" the straight lines drawn from the center of the theater to each of the exterior columns. In the wall of the enclosure that supports the columns (the same one we call the podium), openings <note>original: *vada*</note> shall be made for the lowest entrances into the theater, which should correspond exactly to the vertical lines of the passages below...

<page-num>CXXXI</page-num>

In [certain] places, niches <term>scafi</term> <note>original: *scafi*; concave recesses or "shells" used for acoustics</note> shall be formed; in these, if desired, bronze vessels may hang upside down, so that when the voice reaches them, its strike might return more resonant. Here I will not follow those things of Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman architect whose ten-volume work was Alberti's primary source and rival</note> which were taken from musical divisions, according to whose proportions he instructed that vessels be arranged throughout the theater to resonate with principal, middle, and highest <note>original: *superexcellentes*</note> voices and consonances. It is indeed a very easy thing to say, but how difficult it is to achieve in practice is known to those who have tried. However, we shall not despise that which even Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher; Alberti likely refers to the "Problems," a work attributed to Aristotle that discusses sound and resonance</note> is convinced of: that any empty vessels and even wells help the voice to resonate. 

<margin>Mark well</margin>

I return to the portico of the encircling wall <term>circumvallatio</term> itself. This portico indeed has a solid back wall by which the entire enclosure is shut in, so that voices striking it are not scattered. To the outer skin <note>the exterior face</note> of this wall of the theater, which faces those approaching, shall be applied ornaments of columns, corresponding in number, height, and alignment <note>original: *perpendiculis*</note> and such parts to the substituted colonnades <note>original: *columnationibus*</note> that are below them on the front of the porticoes. 

<margin>How the largest and smallest theaters differ.</margin>

From what has been said, it is readily apparent in what respects the largest theaters differ from the smaller ones. For in the former <note>the large theaters</note>, the outermost portico at the bottom is double; but in the latter <note>the smaller</note>, it is single. Again, in the former, only a second external portico is raised above the work; in the latter, even a third is added. They also differ in this: that in some tiny theaters, an innermost portico is not used; instead, the encircling wall is built up with only a wall and cornices <note>original: *coronis*</note>, so that the cornice there has the power to steady the voices, just as the encircling wall and its portico do in the largest theater. In some of the very largest theaters, however, this very upper portico is made double. 

Furthermore, for theaters that are covered, the open-air pavements <note>the floor of the upper portico</note> are finished with a crust <note>paving stones or plaster</note> and sloped so that the dripping water <note>original: *stillicidia*</note> flows down toward the seating tiers. But the streams of collected rainwater are swallowed by the catch-basins <term>impluvia</term> between the corners of the walls and are sent down through hidden pipes into secret sewers <term>cloacas</term> <note>original: *caecas cloacas*, literally "blind sewers"</note>. Around the highest outer cornice of the theater, sockets and brackets <term>mutuli</term> are fitted; to these, for the decoration of public games, naval masts <note>original: *mali*</note> are set to receive and hold the ropes and thongs of the extended awning <note>original: *veli*; the great velarium used to shade the audience from the sun</note>. 

But since such a great mass of structure must be raised to a proper height, the thickness <term>crassitudo</term> of the wall must therefore be aptly determined to bear the load. Therefore, at the first colonnades, the outermost wall shall be made thick to the extent of one-fifteenth part of the total future height of the work. The intermediate wall between both porticoes, which separates one portico from the other when the porticoes are double, shall be thinner than the outer one by one-fourth. Subsequently, the walls which are raised above these shall be thinner than those below them by one-twelfth of their thickness.

## ¶ On the ornaments of the Amphitheater, the Circus, the walkways, the resting-places, and the porticoes for legal disputes before minor judges. Chapter VIII.

<margin>Amphitheater</margin>
**T**hus far we have spoken of these theaters. It follows that we should explain the circus and the amphitheater. All buildings of this kind emanated from theaters. For a circus is indeed nothing else than a theater with its "horns" <note>the ends of the semicircular seating</note> extended in long, parallel lines; however, by its nature, it does not have attached porticoes. An amphitheater, truly, consists of two theaters joined together at the horns of their seating levels in a continuous circuit. They differ in that a theater is, as it were, a half-part of an amphitheater. They also differ because an amphitheater has an area in the middle that is empty of stage platforms <term>pulpitis scenicis</term> and entirely clear. In other matters, however—especially in the seating levels, the porticoes, and the entryways—they correspond in this fashion. We interpret that the amphitheater was established primarily for the sake of hunting-shows <term>venationes</term> <note>staged hunts or battles with wild beasts</note>: and for that reason, it was pleasing to make them round, so that a beast enclosed and harassed there, finding no corner in which to take refuge, might be more readily driven out by the combatants. For those who would fight against the most ferocious beasts in wondrous ways were sent into that space. Among them, some, raising themselves high with the help of a jump and a spear, would deceive a charging bull.

<margin>Read here about the games of the amphitheater.</margin>
Others, dressed in armor made of reed-spikes <note>original: *stimulis cannarum*; likely a protective suit designed to prick the animal when it attacked</note>, offered themselves up to be handled by bears. Others, withdrawing themselves through a crate <term>archa</term> provided with small doors and many turns, would irritate a lion. Others, relying on a cloak and an iron hammer, would taunt the animals. Finally, if anyone possessed an invention of wit for deceiving, or a preeminence of spirit and physical strength for enduring, they would risk themselves in the midst of the arena, according as each had set out to seek either rewards or praise. I find also that in theaters and amphitheaters, princes were accustomed to scatter fruit to the people and let loose small birds, which would excite the boyish brawls of those snatching them up. Although the central area of the amphitheater is walled around by two joined theaters, it shall not for that reason become entirely oblong, as would happen if the extended arms of both theaters were put into the work. Rather, it shall have a line of width drawn by a certain ratio from the length of the area. There were those among the ancestors who gave seven-eighths of the length to the width. There were also those who gave three-quarters of the width to the length. Other things they followed just as in theaters. For indeed, an exterior portico was applied around it, and likewise a portico on the highest seating level, which we have called the encircling wall <term>circumvallatio</term>.

<margin>The Circus</margin>
¶ The Circus follows. They report that this was established in imitation of the heavens. For indeed, they say twelve entrances <note>original: *hostiorum*; the *carceres* or starting gates</note> were present according to the twelve houses of the sky <note>the Zodiac</note>, and that it had seven distinguished turning-posts <term>metas</term> <note>the *metae* were the conical pillars at the ends of the central barrier that chariots turned around</note> placed there after the number of the seven planets.

<page-num>132</page-num>
<header>Book VIII. On Public and Secular Ornaments. Folio 132.</header>

...and that the boundaries were set at the east and at the west, separated by a long distance. Through the middle spaces of this circus, two-horse and four-horse chariots <note>original: "bigae & quadrigae"</note> would race and be set loose, just as the moon runs through the zodiac. They completed twenty-four heats <note>original: "missilibus," referring to the laps or starts</note> according to the number of hours in a day. Similarly, the competitors were divided into four factions, each having its own color at the starting gates: **green**, representing the grassy season of spring; **red**, representing the fiery air of summer; **white**, representing the pale autumn; and **dark**, signifying the somber winter. In these circuses, the central area was not left open as in an amphitheater, nor occupied by stages as in theaters. Instead, along a longitudinal line that divided the area into two tracks <term>curricula</term>—that is, two halves across its width—turning posts <term>metae</term> were erected in suitable places for the competitors, whether driving four-legged beasts or running on foot, to circle around.

<margin>Turning posts of the circus</margin> There were three primary turning posts. The central one was the most magnificent of all, being four-sided, tall, and gradually tapering. Because it tapered in this way, they called it an **obelisk**. The two remaining posts were either colossal statues or stone crests rising high with ship-prows <note>original: "rostris"</note>, shaped by craftsmen for beauty and grace. Between these, on both sides, two smaller columns or turning posts were placed. In the records of historians, I find that the **Circus Maximus** in Rome was three *stadia* <note>a Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet</note> long and one wide. Today it is in ruins, and not even the slightest hint remains of what it once was. But elsewhere, from the dimensions of similar works, I find this: the ancients were accustomed to making the central area of the circus at least sixty cubits wide, while the length was seven times the width. The width was divided into two equal parts, and a line was drawn lengthwise where the turning posts were placed in this manner: they divided that same length into seven parts. One part was given to the turn <note>original: "anfractui"</note>, where the competitors would swerve around the final post from the right-hand track into the left. Then they arranged the other posts along the same line so that they were spaced equally apart along the length of the circus, occupying five-sevenths of the total length. A raised platform <note>original: "crepido," here referring to the central barrier or 'spina'</note>, no less than six feet high, was built from post to post. This separated the two track spaces on either side so that whether the horses were harnessed together or running singly, if they should swerve, they would have no way to cross over. Seating tiers were added to the sides of the circus on both ends, occupying no more than a fifth and no less than a sixth of the total width of the central area. The steps of these tiers began from the raised platform, as in amphitheaters, for the sake of the spectators, so that they would not encounter any danger from the beasts.

...youth should be exercised with the ball, in jumping, and in the handling of arms; but let the fathers be refreshed by walking, or, if they are in poor health, by being carried about <note>original: "gestatione," referring to being moved in a litter or carriage for passive exercise</note>. Celsus the physician <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus, a famous Roman medical writer from the 1st century AD</note> used to say that we exercise more beneficially under the open sky than in the shade. But to make that shade more comfortable, porticos were added to enclose the open area. Some paved this area with marble and mosaic <term>tessellato</term>; others offered a view of greenery, filling it with myrtle, juniper, citron, and cypress trees. For this work, the porticos on three sides were simple and quite wide—doubling the width of the porticos found in a forum. 

On the fourth side, which faced south, the portico was made much more spacious and double-rowed. On the front, it had <term>Doric</term> columns as high as the portico itself. They ordered the interior columns—which separated the front portico from the inner one—to be made one-fifth higher than the primary columns for the sake of supporting the weight and for the drainage <note>original: "displuviandi," to allow water to run off</note> of the roof. For this reason, they taught that <term>Ionic</term> columns should be used there, because by their nature Ionic columns are taller than Doric ones. 

However, I do not see why, in these porticos, it would not be permitted to make the ceiling level <note>original: "ad libellam," perfectly horizontal</note> on both sides; it would certainly add to the grace of the building. In both sets of colonnades, the thickness of the columns was determined as follows: In the Doric order, the thickness of the column at its base was two-fifteenths <note>original: "quintamdecimam... bis," resulting in a ratio of 1:7.5</note> of its total height, including the capital and the base. In the Ionic and <term>Corinthian</term> orders, the thickness of the column at the bottom was given one part out of eight and a half parts of the total height of the shaft; other measurements were defined as they are in temples. 

Attached to the outermost wall of the portico were very dignified seating areas <term>sessiones</term>, where those dressed in togas <note>the formal garment of Roman citizens</note> and those practicing philosophy might dispute the most important matters. Some of these seating areas were for summer and others for winter. In the part where the north wind or the "aquilo" <note>the northeast wind</note> blew through, they placed the summer seats. For the winter seats, they sought out the most pleasant sun, sheltered from the winds. For this reason, the winter seats were enclosed with solid walls on all sides; the summer seats, however, had the walls removed here and there—leaving only enough to support the roof—and faced north with windows or rather an open colonnade, looking out freely upon the sea, mountains, a lake, or whatever beauties were available, admitting as much light as possible. 

To the right of the walking portico, and likewise to the left, other seating areas were attached, sheltered from external winds, which would receive the morning and afternoon sun from the open sky of the central area. The layouts of these seating areas varied: some were extended into a semi-circle <term>hemicycle</term>, others into straight lines; both types corresponded with suitable dimensions to the central area and the portico. The width of the work...

<meta>This page continues Alberti's architectural guidelines for the porticos (colonnaded walkways) surrounding a gymnasium or public square. [the walkway] had half of the total length. The width was divided into eight parts: six parts were given to the central area open to the sky, and one part was given to each individual portico. When they created a seating area <note>original: "sessionem," a place for sitting and conversation, often an exedra</note> in the shape of a semicircle <note>original: "emiciclum"</note>, its diameter took up two-fifths of the open area's width. But the rear wall in the portico was made accessible to the seating area itself through openings. The height of the semicircle for this seating area in the largest works was as great as its width. But in smaller works, it had a height equal to five-quarters of the width. Above the roof of the portico, at the front of the semicircle and the seating area, window openings stood out; through these, the sun would be received within the semicircle, and the place would be abundantly illuminated. If, however, rectangular seating areas were added, then they were made twice as wide as the portico, and the length was given double its own width. I call "length" here that which extends along the portico. Therefore, for those entering the seating area, its length extends from right to left.

<margin>The portico for legal disputes</margin>
There is also, among public works, the "litigious portico" <note>original: "porticus litigiosa," a place for legal proceedings</note> for the minor judges, which they used to build. Their size was considered not at all modest, according to the dignity of the city and the place; and contiguous rooms <note>original: "cellae"</note> were joined to the portico in a row, in which legal matters might be settled according to the judgment of those meeting together. What I have said up to now seemed to be "most public," because in these places both commoners and patricians <note>the lower and upper classes of Roman society</note> might meet everywhere and freely. But there are also some public things which are open only to the leading citizens and those conducting public business, such as the <term>comitium</term>, the <term>curia</term>, and the senate. We must now speak of these.

## On the adornment of the council-chambers of the assemblies and the senate; also on groves and bathing places; on books, libraries, schools, stables, naval stations, and mathematical instruments for ornamenting cities. Chapter IX.

<margin>The Comitium</margin>
**P**lato decreed that the <term>comitium</term> <note>original: "comitium," a place of assembly for political purposes and voting</note> should be held in a temple. # Leon Battista Alberti: On the Art of Building

[The priestly chamber shall be] vaulted <note>original: "testudinata," referring to a ceiling shaped like a tortoise shell or an arch</note>; the senatorial council chamber, however, shall have a timbered ceiling. In both of these, the summoned advisors will give speeches; therefore, consideration must be given to the acoustics of their voices. For this reason, it is necessary to provide a structure that does not allow the voice to drift away too high, especially in a vaulted room, so that the sound does not echo too harshly in the ear.

For the sake of beauty and, above all, utility, cornices <term>coronæ: decorative horizontal moldings that project from a wall</term> shall be attached to the walls. I have noted from the works of the ancients that council chambers were built in a rectangular shape. In those that are vaulted, the wall is made as high as the front of the building is wide; the chambers are then covered with an arched vault, deducting one-seventh from that height. Directly opposite the door as one enters, a tribunal <note>a raised platform for magistrates or judges</note> shall be open; the depth of its curve <note>original: "sagitta," literally "arrow"</note> shall take up one-third of the width of its opening <note>original: "corda," literally "string" or chord of an arc</note>. The width of the doorway takes up one-seventh of that wall's opening. 

Around half the height of the wall, with an additional eighth of that half added, projecting cornices shall stand out, along with a decorative band <note>original: "fascia"</note>, a beam, and columns. Some architects placed more columns and some fewer, depending on whether they preferred them crowded together or spread out; the calculation for these colonnades is drawn from the porticos of temples. Above the cornices, to the right and left in the wall, statues and items pertaining to religious matters shall be placed in niches <note>original: "scafis"</note>. But on the front wall of the work, at a height equal to the niches, a window was opened that was twice as wide as it was high, with two small columns <note>original: "colunnellis"</note> placed between them to support the lintel. Thus shall be the priestly chamber.

The senatorial council chamber <note>original: "senatoria curia"</note>, however, shall be made as follows. The width of the floor area will be two-thirds of the length; the height up to the roof beams will be equal to the width of the area plus an additional fourth of that width. Cornices will be attached around the wall in this manner: the height from the floor to the ceiling will be divided into nine parts. One part will be given to the solid base, which serves as the footing and the podium <note>original: "crepidine et podio"</note> upon which the columns are raised. This solid part of the wall will be occupied by the backs of the benches <note>original: "subselliorum renes"</note>. 

What remains above that will be divided into seven parts. Of these, you will give four full parts to the first tier of columns; upon these first columns, a second tier shall be placed, which will support the main beam <note>original: "trabs regia"</note> and the ornaments that follow. Both the first and second tiers of columns will have their own bases, capitals, cornices, and such, as we said were required for basilicas <note>large public halls used for legal and business matters</note>. The intervals between them on the right and left walls shall be an uneven number, preferably by one, and the spaces shall be equal. 

On the front walls, however, there shall be no more than three intervals, of which the middle one shall be wider than the others by one-fourth. Through each interval—whether of columns or of brackets <term>mutulorum: stone blocks projecting from a wall to support a cornice</term> which are above the middle cornices—windows shall be placed. For it is necessary that council chambers of this kind be most brilliantly lit <note>original: "illustrissimas"</note>. Low walls <note>original: "plutei"</note> shall be placed under the windows, as we described for the basilicas. And...

The ornaments of windows, which serve as their facade at the top of the wall, should not exceed the height of the neighboring columns, excluding the capitals. The height of the window opening shall be divided into eleven parts; of these, seven parts shall be given to the width. The "ears" <note>original: "auriculæ," referring to the decorative side-brackets or consoles of a door or window frame</note> here will hang down just as they do there. 

The proportion of these mutules is as follows: the width of the mutules themselves shall be equal to what the uppermost shaft of the column would have been in a colonnade, removing the ring <note>original: "torquis"</note> and the projection of the edge. Their length <note>original: "pendebit," literally "it shall hang"</note> shall be as great as the height of a Corinthian capital would have been, minus the "kiss" <note>original: "osculo," a technical term for the junction or necking of the capital</note> of the capital. The projection of this mutule shall not exceed the cymatium <term>cymatium: a molding with a wave-like S-curve profile</term> of the main beam <note>original: "trabis regiæ," the architrave or principal beam</note>.

<margin>Libraries were once abundant.</margin>
Pisistratus was the first to establish books for the public at Athens. Xerxes carried that abundance of books away into Persia. Seleucus restored them. I find that in the library of the Gordians, there were as many as sixty-two thousand books. In the territory of Laodicea, at the Temple of Nemesis, a very great school of physicians was frequented, which had been established by Zeuxis.

The City of the Sun, which they call Thebes, is said to have had one hundred public stables of such great size that two hundred horses were kept under a single roof. This is noteworthy.

<margin>Heliogabalus.</margin>

For me, it is not yet sufficiently clear whether they are more a private work or a public one. Certainly, as far as can be seen, they are a mixture of both. For they contain many things drawn from private buildings and many likewise drawn from public ones. The work of the baths, since it requires a very large area, will occupy parts of the city that are neither the most crowded nor the most neglected; for there both fathers and matrons gather for the sake of cleanliness. 

Squares surround the roofs of the baths; and a wall of no small height encloses the squares. Entry into the squares is provided only in certain and suitable places. But in the middle of the roofs is the atrium, like the center of the building, most spacious and noble, with chambers designed according to the layout of a temple...

Surrounding this entire circuit of roofs (as I have said) were very spacious plazas; these were indeed large enough to accommodate racing tracks for games. Nor were there lacking, in suitable locations, turning posts <margin>Turning posts of the baths</margin> <note>original: "metae", the conical pillars used as turning marks in a Roman circus</note> which competitors would race around.

At the southern plaza, which extends in front of the vestibule, a wide expanse of open ground was laid out, stretching toward the south and ending in a semicircle. Rising around this work were tiers of seating <margin>Sitting areas</margin> in imitation of a theater. A wall also rose high to block out the southern winds. In fact, a single, continuous outer wall enclosed and contained all these plazas, as if they were a small town.

Adjoining this enclosure wall were very noble sitting areas, both semicircular and rectangular in shape, which looked out upon the main roofs of the baths. In these seats, the citizens could enjoy either sun or shade—here in the morning, there in the evening—at their own discretion as the hours turned.

Furthermore, and particularly toward the north, beyond this great enclosure wall, were placed open-air areas of moderate height; these were oblong and bounded by a line slightly curved into an arc. A secluded portico surrounded these areas in a curve, closed by its back wall; it offered no view other than a small patch of sky, which was left there as a summer retreat within its open area between the enclosure wall and this curved portico. For in that spot, due to the narrowness of the area and the height of the walls, the sun hardly ever penetrated, even during the summer solstice.

In the corners of the great enclosure, there were vestibules and small shrines; in these, as some say, purifications were performed so that the matrons might find favor with the gods. This, then, was the full list of parts that made up the public baths. The designs for these parts were drawn from those we reviewed above, and likewise from those we are about to discuss, according to whether they were more suited to public or private use. The total area of the entire complex in almost every case occupied more than one million one hundred thousand square feet <note>original: "centenos decies centies"; Alberti is describing the massive scale of Roman Imperial baths, such as those of Caracalla or Diocletian</note>.

# Book IX. On the Ornamentation of Private Buildings.

It is necessary to remember that of private buildings, some are urban and others are rural. Furthermore, among these, some are used by the more humble <note>original: "tenuiores," referring to those of lower social or financial standing</note>, while others are used by the more wealthy. We shall treat the ornamentation of all these classes. But first, let us not omit several points that relate to the subject. Among our ancestors, I see that it greatly pleased the wisest and most modest men—both in other matters, public and private, and specifically in this one matter of building—that frugality and parsimony should be practiced. They believed that all luxury among citizens should be removed and restrained; I find that they provided for this with all zeal and industry through both warnings and laws.

Therefore, in the view of Plato, those were approved who had decreed (as we have said elsewhere) that no one should bring in more illustrious paintings than those which were held to have been painted in the temple by the ancients. 
<margin>Parsimony</margin>
He forbade a temple to be adorned with elaborate painting, unless it were such that a single painter could finish it in a single day. Likewise, he ordained that images of the gods should be made only of wood or stone; but bronze and iron he said should be left for the uses of war, for which they were the proper instruments.

Demosthenes preferred the customs of the ancient Athenians far above the customs of his own times. For he said they left us public buildings, and especially temples, so many, so magnificent, and so ornate that no room was left for them to be surpassed. But indeed, they built private houses with such moderation that even the homes of the most distinguished men did not differ much from the houses of ordinary citizens. For this reason, among mortals, they achieved a state where their glory surpassed any envy. 

But even these did not seem praiseworthy to the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note>, if by chance they had cultivated the city more through the skill of the craftsman than through the glory of their achievements; they believed themselves worthy of praise who possessed a city cultivated more by virtue than by structure. 
<margin>The law of Lycurgus</margin>
Among them, according to the law of Lycurgus, it was not permitted for roofs to be worked except with an axe, nor doors except with a saw <note>original: "ferra," literally "iron," referring here to the saw</note>. When Agesilaus saw squared beams in the houses in Asia, 
<margin>The saying of Agesilaus.</margin>
he laughed; he asked whether, if square trees grew among them, they would make them round? And he was right to do so: for according to the ancient modesty of his people, he believed a private house should be built for necessary use, not for beauty and luxury. 

Among the Germans in the time of Caesar, care was taken that they should not build too carefully, especially in the countryside, lest any cause for dissension arise among the citizens out of a desire for another's property. Valerius at Rome, when he had a very tall house on the Esquiline Hill, tore it down to avoid envy and rebuilt it on level ground. And so that virtuous posterity followed this frugality both publicly and privately as long as good morals allowed. Later, however, as wealth increased...

# Leonis Baptistae Alberti. On the Art of Building.

...luxury grew so much in nearly everyone except for **Octavian** <note>original: "Octaviano," referring to Emperor Augustus</note>; for he was actually burdened by too costly a building, and indeed, he even demolished a villa that had been built too lavishly. So much, 
<margin>
The structure and luxury of the Gordians
</margin>
I say, did luxury grow in the city that, among others, there were those of the **Gordian** family who built a house on the Praenestine Way with two hundred columns of a single style and equal size. I remember reading that fifty of these were Numidian, fifty Claudian, fifty Synnadic <note>original: "simiadas," a precious marble from Phrygia</note>, and fifty Carystian <note>original: "tisteas," likely referring to the green-veined marble from Karystos</note>. What of that which **Lucretius** also mentions? That there were *golden statues of youths throughout the halls, holding flaming torches in their right hands, so that they might provide light for nighttime banquets.* To what end do I mention these? So that from their preparation I may establish that very thing I have said elsewhere: those things please which are moderated according to each person's dignity. And if you listen to me, I would prefer that in private homes the most refined people should lack something that contributes to ornament, rather than having the most modest and frugal people find fault with luxury in any part. 

But since we all agree that a reputation for both wisdom and power must be left to posterity—and for that reason, as **Thucydides** <note>original: "Tuchidides"</note> said, we build great things so that we may appear great to those who come after us—and since we also ornament our possessions for the sake of honoring our country and family no less than for elegance (and who would deny that this is the duty of a good man?), it will surely be pleasing to one who wishes those parts which are most public, or which will especially gratify a guest—such as the front of the house, the vestibule, and the like—to be perfectly appropriate and becoming.

And although I profess that those who have exceeded moderation should be blamed, I judge those who have built at great expense in such a way that their works cannot be properly ornamented to be even more worthy of blame than those who have desired ornament at a slightly greater cost. But I maintain this: whoever wishes to correctly observe the true and certain ornament of buildings will surely understand that it is obtained and consists not in the expenditure of wealth, but most especially in the application of ingenuity <note>original: "ingenium," meaning the architect's creative talent and intellect</note>. I believe that a wise man, in preparing his private home, will not even want to differ remarkably from others; he will take care lest he provoke envy through expense and ostentation. 

But, on the contrary, he who is well-advised will want to be surpassed by no one in the craftsman's diligence and the excellence of his planning and judgment; from this, every division and the harmony of the design <note>original: "lineamenta," referring to the precise linear layout and proportions</note> are wonderfully approved, which is itself the chief and primary kind of ornament.

The royal house.
</margin>

# Book IX. On the Ornament of Private Buildings.

<margin>The vestibule and portico</margin>
In the previous part, we discussed how anything intended for public use should be adorned. Now, however, let us begin to address those things which are suited solely for private uses, so that they may be made ornate. I would wish the **vestibule** <note>original: "vestibulum," the entrance area between the street and the interior of the house</note> to present itself as most honorable and splendid, according to the dignity of each person. Let a most illustrious **portico** <note>a covered walkway supported by columns</note> follow. Nor should magnificent spaces be lacking. Finally, and thereafter, all other parts shall take from the imitation of public works as much as the matter itself allows, provided it contributes to grace and dignity. With this moderation applied, the house should show that its owner preferred to capture charms far more than to follow any pride. For this reason, just as in the previous book concerning public works, secular buildings yielded in dignity to sacred ones as was fitting: so here, private works will easily allow themselves to be surpassed by public ones in all elegance and abundance of ornament.

<margin>☞</margin>
The owner will not have acquired bronze or ivory doors for himself—an act which was once counted among the criminal charges against **Camillus** <note>original: "Camillo"; Marcus Furius Camillus was a Roman hero accused of taking bronze from the spoils of war for his own home</note>. **Coffered ceilings** <note>original: "lacunaria," sunken panels in a ceiling</note> will not shine with much gold and glass. Everything will not be illuminated with Hymettian or Parian marble <note>highly prized Greek marbles</note>. For those things belong to temples. Instead, he will use ordinary materials with elegance, and elegant materials with moderation. He will be content with cypress, larch, and boxwood. He will coat walls with **stucco** <note>original: "opere albario," a fine white plasterwork</note> and clothe them with simpler paintings. He will craft cornices from Luni <note>Carrara marble</note> or rather Tiburtine <note>travertine</note> stone. Yet he will not entirely renounce or banish all those magnificent things. Rather, like gems in a crown, he will place them most sparingly in the most worthy spots. 

If one wishes to define the whole matter briefly, I would state it thus: sacred things ought to be prepared so that nothing more can be added to their majesty and the admiration of their beauty. Private things, however, should be kept so that, conversely, it seems nothing can be taken away that is joined with exceptional dignity. For the rest, such as secular public buildings, I believe a middle ground between these two should be left. Therefore, in private ornaments, the builder will restrain himself most strictly; yet in most things, he will use a freer path. For if a column should happen to be somewhat thinner throughout its body, or perhaps somewhat more swollen in its **entasis** <note>original: "ventre," the slight curve or "belly" of a column</note>, or more slender in its tapering than the exact logic of public works permits: it will not be considered a flaw or disapproved, provided it has nothing shapeless or distorted. Indeed, what is not permitted in public works—namely, to deviate slightly from the weight and most calculated law of outlines—occasionally contributes to delight in these private works. 

And that which fell out quite charmingly, which the most jovial people were accustomed to do: to attach vast statues of slaves near the doors of dining rooms in place of doorposts, supporting the lintel upon their heads; 
<margin>Columns in gardens</margin>
and to place columns in porticos, especially of gardens, which look like tree trunks with knots...

<summary>Alberti argues that private architecture should be elegant and refined but always subordinate to public and sacred structures in magnificence. He suggests a "middle way" of moderation while allowing for more creative freedom and whim in private spaces like gardens.</summary>

...finished: or they might represent **fasces** <note>original: "fasces," bundles of rods bound with a leather strap, a Roman symbol of magisterial authority</note> bound with a thong; or those that were winding and palm-like, roughened with leaves and filled with little birds and streams. Then also for capitals, they might place either baskets hanging full of clusters of grapes and fruits, or a palm tree regrowing with its top stalks, or coils of snakes joined in various entwinements, or eagles flapping their wings, or Gorgon faces with serpents fighting among themselves; and similar things which would be long to pursue. 

But the craftsman, as far as he can, will maintain the most worthy forms of the parts by preserving the boundaries produced by the art of lines and angles; and he should seem to have wished not to defraud the work of a fitting harmony of members, but rather to play with a charming site for visitors, or rather to delight them with the wit of the invention. And since some of the dining rooms, passages, and reception rooms are for the public, while others are secluded and entirely intimate: in the former, he will serve public splendor with the city's communal pomp, which is by no means odious. In the latter, however, in more hidden places, it will be permitted to indulge a little in playfulness at one's discretion.

### The different ornament of urban and non-urban houses. However, in suburban houses, both the rustic and urban ornament will be approved. <margin>Chapter 2</margin>

<margin>
Aelius 
Aristides
</margin>

**B**ut since some private houses are urban and others are non-urban, let us consider what ornament suits each. Between urban houses and a villa, besides those things we said in previous books, there is this difference: that the ornaments of urban houses ought to savor of gravity much more than the others; to villas, however, all those allurements of festivity and pleasantness shall be granted. 

Then there is also this difference: that in urban houses you must moderate many things according to the rules of the neighborhood, which in a villa we will pursue with freer right. One must be careful against exaggeration, lest the building be much more haughty than the cohesion of a neighboring building requires. Porticos also will set a limit of width for themselves from the layout of the joined walls. 

The thickness and height of walls in Rome was not finished according to one's whim. For according to an old law, it was not permitted to build one thicker. **Julius Caesar** also took care, on account of the dangers of collapses, that nowhere within the city should a wall be raised higher. A villa is not bound by these laws. It was given as a point of praise to Babylonian citizens that they lived in houses of four **stories** <term>original: "contignationum," literally the framing of floors with timber</term>. The orator **Aelius Aristides** <note>A 2nd-century Greek orator known for his "Oration to Rome," a panegyric praising the Roman Empire</note>, praising Rome in a celebratory speech, proclaimed as something admirable in its layout that they had superimposed the largest houses upon the largest houses—a pleasing flattery. But he approved of that more because of the greatness of the people than for reasons of wealth.

# Book IX. On the Decoration of Private Buildings.

<margin>The danger arising from the excessive height of houses</margin>
...surpassed. They say that Tyre surpassed Rome in the height of its houses; and for that reason, Tyre was once not far from being entirely destroyed by earthquakes. A building will achieve both convenience and, especially, grace if it possesses no more necessity for climbing or descending than is sufficient. And indeed, those people offer correct advice 

<margin>stairs as the disturbers of buildings</margin>
who proclaim that stairs are the "disturbers of buildings"; I see that the ancients took great care to avoid their hindrance. But for a villa, no necessity forces one to place some buildings on top of others. For indeed, it will claim for itself the most becoming spaces with a more sprawling openness, in which various parts follow one another on an even level. This is a practice that would please me greatly even in cities, if only it were permitted. 

There is also a certain type of private building that requires both the dignity of a city house and the delights of a villa; we passed over this in the earlier books as it was destined for this place. 

<margin>suburban gardens</margin>
These are the **suburban gardens** <note>original: "horti suburbani," estates located just outside city walls that combined the luxury of a house with the productivity of a garden or small farm</note>: which I believe should by no means be neglected. Indeed, this will contribute to the brevity for which I am striving. For we shall explain at once what is appropriate for each of these types. But first, it is necessary that I report certain things about the garden itself that should not be omitted. Among the ancients, they say: "He who has prepared a field, let him sell his city house." "He who holds city things dear has no need for rural things." Perhaps they aim at this: to establish that a garden is most convenient. The natural philosophers <term>physici</term> <note>meaning those who study the physical world or medicine</note> warn us to enjoy air that is as free and pure as possible. I do not deny that a villa placed in a deep retreat will provide this. 

On the other hand, the logic of urban and civil business requires the head of the family to be frequently present in the forum, the senate house, or the temples. A city house will provide this most easily. But that house is at odds with health, just as the villa is at odds with business. Generals are accustomed to move their camps so that foul odors do not cause too much harm. What do you think will happen in a city, in which the accumulations of so much filth over so much time are kept, and evaporate from every side? 

Since these things are so, I determine that of all things built for use and convenience, the suburban garden is the most primary and healthy; it neither keeps one from conducting city business, nor is it subject to the impurity of the air. Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator and statesman</note> took care through Atticus to obtain gardens for himself in a place of equal fame. However, I would not want them so famous that one could never be outside the doors without a **toga** <note>the formal, heavy woolen garment required for public business in Rome, which Alberti suggests is too restrictive for the relaxation of a garden</note>. I would wish for that measure of convenience which the character in Terence <note>the Roman playwright</note> boasted of taking, saying: "So that no weariness of either the villa or the city may take hold of me." 

<margin>Martial Cocus</margin>
It is well put in Martial <note>original: "Martialis Coci," the Roman epigrammatist Valerius Martialis</note>: "Staying in the country, you ask what I do? I answer in few words: I dine, I drink, I sing, I play, I bathe, I sup, I rest. Then I read; I summon Phoebus <note>the god of poetry and light</note> and I challenge the Muse." 

<margin>What a villa should be like</margin>
And indeed, proximity to the city and easy retreats are pleasing: where whatever is liked is permitted according to one's whim. Proximity to the city will provide fame; the clarity of the road will provide accessibility; and the pleasantness of the region is essential. Building there will delight, if as soon as...
