...that as people leave the city, the villa's entire facade should offer a joyful sight, as if it were enticing and waiting for those setting out toward it. I would wish for it to be slightly elevated; and I would wish for the road to rise up to that place with a slope so gentle that it deceives those walking, until they realize they have ascended not by any effort but by looking around at the fields and sensing the height of the place. Flowery meadows all around, a very sunny field, the cool shadows of woods, the clearest springs and streams, and swimming pools, and all those things we said elsewhere were owed to villas will not be lacking for pleasure as well as for use. 

Furthermore, the entire facade and assembly of the house—which in every building repeatedly wins favor—I would very much wish to be thoroughly bright and very clear on every side, admitting plenty of light from the wide sky, plenty of sun, and plenty of healthy air. I do not want it to look out anywhere at something that offends with a gloomy shadow. Let everything smile upon and congratulate the guest on their arrival. Once inside the roofed areas, guests should be in doubt whether they prefer to linger there for the sake of their spirit where they are, or to seek further rooms, provoked by their cheerfulness and brightness. From square courtyards <term>areas</term><note>original: "areis," meaning the open floor spaces or courtyards</note> into round ones, from round ones back into angular ones; from these, passage should be given into those that are neither entirely round nor enclosed by all straight lines. And when you have entered the inner heart of the house, there will be no place where it is necessary to step down. Truly, one will penetrate to the very last chamber either on level ground or by very modest boundaries <note>referring to low thresholds or very slight inclines rather than steps</note>.

### ¶ That the parts and members of buildings differ as much in nature as in appearance, and ought to be decorated in various ways with outlines and ornament. Chapter III.

But since the parts of buildings differ greatly among themselves—namely in nature and appearance—I believe we must consider all those things about them which we left elsewhere, having destined them for this place. For there are indeed those which, whether you make them round or square, it matters very little, provided they contribute correctly to their use. But how large these same parts are, and in what places they are arranged, matters a great deal. 

And it is necessary that some of these be made larger, such as the central hearts of the houses; others require a smaller area, such as the bedchambers and all the inner rooms. Others are in the middle, such as the dining rooms <term>cenacula</term><note>upper-story dining rooms or apartments</note> and even the <term>vestibule</term><note>an entrance hall or passage between the street and the interior of a house</note>. What the appropriate arrangement for each member in a house should be, we have said elsewhere. As for how the courtyards differ among themselves, there is no need for me to report it. For many things are largely a matter of choice and are changed according to the varied manner of living in different places. The ancients added either a portico or a sitting-area to their houses; both were not always in straight lines, but curved in the manner of a theater. To the portico, almost all of them attached a round vestibule. ...round spaces will be measured according to the lineaments <note>The underlying geometric design and structural outlines</note> of temples, except that the height of the walls ought to be greater here than in temples; you will soon see why this is so. If the space is quadrangular, there will indeed be a way in which it differs from what we said concerning sacred and public secular buildings. Nevertheless, it will share some qualities with the senate house and the curia <note>original: "curia," the ancient Roman assembly house</note>.

<margin>How wide an atrium should be.</margin>
According to the common old custom of our ancestors, the atrium <note>The central hall or court of a Roman house</note> will either have a width of two-thirds of its length; or the length itself will be five-thirds of the width; or else the length will be seven-fifths of the width. In any of these, the ancients seem to have established that they would raise the wall in height until a third of the floor's length was given to the height four times <note>meaning a height equal to 4/3 of the length</note>. From our own measurements of buildings, we have found this: that the height of quadrangular floor areas <term>areas</term><note>The open floor space or courtyard</note> depends on the wall; one height is required where it is vaulted <term>testudinetur</term><note>from "testudo" (tortoise); a curved or arched ceiling resembling a shell</note>, and another where it is timber-beamed <term>contignetur</term><note>A flat ceiling supported by joists or beams</note>. Likewise, in the largest buildings, one thing must be provided, and another in smaller ones. For the proportion of the distances from the central point of the observer's eye to the extreme heights being viewed is not the same in both. But of these things we shall speak elsewhere. We define the size of floor areas based on the roof, and the roof based on the length of the beams required for the covering. I will call a roof "moderate" if a moderate tree and timber is sufficient to support it. And besides those we were reviewing, there are indeed many other most harmonious dimensions and correspondences of lines which we will try to explain succinctly and most clearly in this manner: if the length of the floor area to the width is...

<margin>Pay attention to what is written here about lines.</margin>
...double: then in timber-beamed rooms, the height will be equal to the width, with half of that width added on top <note>A 3:2 ratio of height to width</note>. In vaulted rooms, however, you will add a third of the width to the wall height. This applies to moderate buildings. But in the largest buildings, if they are vaulted, then the height from top to bottom will be five-quarters of the width; in timber-beamed ones, it will be seven-fifths. If the length of the area is triple the width: then if it is timber-beamed, three-quarters of the width will be added to the height. If it is vaulted, the height will be equal to the width plus an additional half. If it is quadruple: in vaulted rooms, the height will be half the length. In beamed rooms, the width is divided into four parts, and from these you will give seven parts to the height. If it is quintuple: the height will be the same as in the quadruple, but a sixth of that height itself will be added. If it is sextuple: it will be as in the previous case, but a fifth part will be added instead of a sixth. If the area has equal sides <note>A square</note>, the height of vaulted rooms will exceed as in the triple proportions; timbered ones, however, will not exceed the width. Moreover, in larger areas it will be permitted to lower the height so long as the width exceeds...

...from a fourth of the height. In those spaces where the length exceeds the width by a ninth part of itself, the height should likewise be exceeded by the width by a ninth part; we use this ratio only in beamed ceilings <term>trabeatis</term> <note>ceilings with exposed horizontal support beams</note>. When the length is four-thirds of the width, you shall raise the wall to a height equal to the full width plus an additional sixth part of that width in timbered ceilings <term>contignatis</term> <note>floors or ceilings constructed with joists</note>. But if it is to be vaulted <term>testudinabi</term> <note>from "testudo," meaning tortoise shell; referring to an arched or domed ceiling</note>, add further so that the height equals the full width plus a sixth part of the length. When you make the length three-halves of the width, then in timbered ceilings the height will exceed the width by a seventh part. In vaulted ones, however, you will add a seventh part of the longer line that encloses the floor area. Finally, if the floor has such combinations of lines that one side is five and the other seven, or one is three and the other five, and similar ratios—which either the necessity of the site, the variation of the designer's invention, or the logic of ornament might require—then both lines shall be joined together and half of that sum shall be given to the height.

I must not overlook this point: Atriums <note>The central reception halls of a house</note> should nowhere be made longer than double their width. Chambers <note>original: "conclavia," referring to private rooms or dining rooms</note> should never be made so long that their width is less than two-thirds of their length. Ratios of triple, quadruple, and longer dimensions of this kind are reserved for porticoes <note>covered walkways supported by columns</note>, which themselves should not exceed a sixfold ratio of length to width.

Openings for both windows and doors will be placed in the wall. If a window is opened in the wall of the width 

<margin>The horizontal window</margin>
—which is naturally shorter than the length of the room—then there shall be no more than one. And yet it shall be so placed that either its width is shorter than its height, or conversely, that its width is greater than its height; this latter kind of window is called "lying" <term>accubantium</term> <note>A "reclining" or horizontal window, often placed higher on a wall</note>. If, therefore, the width is narrower, as is typical in doors, then you will ensure that the empty space of the opening from right to left is no more than a third and no less than a fourth part of the entire inner wall. The lowest line of the opening <note>the window sill</note> shall be distant from the floor no more than four-ninths of the total wall height, and no less than two-ninths. The height of the opening shall be one and a half times its width. This is how it shall be if the width of the opening is shorter than its height. 

But if the opening is wider from right to left and shorter from bottom to top, then from the total length of the wall you shall give to the width of the window no less than a half and no more than two-thirds. The height in such a case shall likewise be either half the width or two-thirds of it. However, two small columns <term>colunnellae</term> <note>mullions or small upright supports</note> shall be placed between them for the purpose of supporting the lintel <term>superliminaris</term>.

But if windows are to be placed in the longer wall, then more shall be made, and they should be an odd number. I see that the ancients preferred the number three for these, and they shall be made in this manner: the entire longest line of the wall will be divided...

### ¶ With what things private houses, pavements, porticoes, courtyards, and gardens may be adorned with pictures, plants, or statues. Chapter IIII.

<margin>☞</margin>
**T**here are, besides, certain ornaments that you should apply to private houses which must not be overlooked. The ancients used to paint rectangular and circular labyrinths in the pavements of porticoes, in which children might exercise. We have seen floor surfaces <note>original: "pareas," likely referring to the paved areas or perhaps a specific type of mosaic tile</note> painted with winding herbs, with waving tendrils spread out widely. There are also seen those who represented carpets spread in bedrooms by means of marble mosaic <term>tessellatura</term>. Others have scattered them with little crowns and twigs. <margin>Oh, what a noble pavement!</margin> They praised the invention of that Sosus <note>original: "Osi"; referring to Sosus of Pergamon, the most famous mosaicist of antiquity</note> who laid a pavement at Pergamon in which the remains left over from dinner appeared <note>this refers to the famous "Unswept Floor" (asarotos oikos) mosaic, which realistically depicted crumbs and scraps</note>: a work not at all unbefitting for a dining room. I think Agrippa acted very suitably in constructing pavements from earthenware shards <term>crustis figulinis</term>. I hate extravagance. Those things delight me which bring ingenuity to beauty and charm. In the encrustation of walls, no projection of painting will be more pleasing or more remarkable than that which expresses stone colonnades. A portico in which Titus Caesar used to walk was distinguished by polished Phoenician stones <note>original: "fœniceis lapidib⁹," likely referring to reddish Phoenician marble or porphyry</note>, by whose splendor all things might be seen as if in a mirror. The prince Antoninus Caracalla painted the deeds and triumphs of his father in a portico. Severus also did this himself. Agathocles, however, did not paint his father's deeds, but his own. Among the Persians, it was not permitted by ancient law to paint or represent anything other than the killings of wild beasts by their kings. <margin>Of the Persians</margin> And certainly the brave and memorable deeds and faces of one's own citizens will be most aptly painted and applied both in porticoes and in dining rooms. Caius Caesar, with the highest approval of all, placed in his portico statues of those who had increased the glory of the republic. These indeed I approve of. But I would not want a wall to be excessively filled either with images or statues, or completely covered and occupied by a narrative <term>hystoria</term> <note>original: "hystoriaqꝫ," referring to a continuous narrative or historical painting</note>. One may see this in gems and especially in pearls: if they are packed together in a heap, they lose their luster <note>literally: "they grow dirty" or "become common"</note>. ...place, so that in certain fit and worthy locations, distinct stone frames are held within the walls, where both statues and panels may be positioned: such as those Pompey brought back in his triumph, in which the praises of his deeds performed by sea and land were seen painted. Or I would rather have present those things which poets have devised to encourage good morals: such as that of Daedalus, who painted the flying Icarus on the doors at Cumae <note>original: "Cumas"; an ancient city in Italy where, according to Virgil, Daedalus built a temple to Apollo and depicted his flight from Crete</note>. And since painting and poetry are varied—some expressing the deeds of the greatest princes most worthy of remembrance; others the manners of private citizens; others the life of the plowman—the first, which possesses majesty, shall be applied to public and the most excellent works. The last will especially suit gardens, which indeed is the most pleasant of all. We are cheered in mind in a greater way when we see painted the amenities of regions: ports, and fishing, and hunting, and swimming, and the games of country folk, and flowery and leafy scenes. <margin>Take note.</margin> That also of the prince Octavian <note>the Emperor Augustus</note> pertains to the matter: who indeed used to display the unseen, enormous bones of the greatest animals as ornament for his houses <note>Suetonius records that Augustus decorated his villas with these "giants' bones," which were likely fossils</note>. For grottoes and caves, the ancients were accustomed to apply a rough crust of plaster by industry, embedding small clumps of pumice or the foam of Tiburtine stone <term>travertine</term>, <margin>Tiburtine stone called "living pumice" by Ovid.</margin> which Ovid calls "living pumice." And we have seen those who applied green wax to imitate the mossy fuzz of a grotto. That which we saw at a cave where a spring of water broke out greatly delighted us: a crust made of various shells and sea oysters, some inverted, others overlapping, joined together by a variety of colors with truly most charming artifice. <margin>A crust of shells.</margin> Where men meet with their wives, they advise that only the most worthy and most handsome faces of men be painted. For they say that this has the greatest influence on the conception of matrons and the future appearance of the offspring <note>Alberti refers here to the "maternal impression," a historical belief that the visual environment of a pregnant woman could physically shape her child</note>. <margin>Take note of these things not unworthy of mention.</margin> To look upon painted springs of water and rivulets is especially beneficial for those suffering from fever. One may test this: if ever during the night sleep escapes one lying down, if you then persist in recalling to mind the most charming waters of springs, rivers, or lakes you have ever seen, immediately that dryness of wakefulness is moistened, and sleep creeps in, until you fall most sweetly asleep. The thickness of these columns was one-tenth of their length, following the Corinthian style. <margin>The Town House.</margin>

In both, a <term>vaulted roof<gloss>original: "testudinata"; literally "like a tortoise shell"</gloss></term> will be very pleasing. The ornaments of both the beams and the cornices placed upon the columns shall take up a fourth of the height of the colonnade. If a second set of columns is placed atop the first colonnade, the second shall be shorter than the first by a fourth. If a third level is raised, these will then be shorter by a fifth than those they stand upon. But where one is content with a single colonnade, it shall adapt itself to the proportions of public works that are secular. ### Chapter V.
### That the form, dignity, and beauty of buildings must be sought from the parts of the body, just as in animals; from which the gift of <term>harmony<gloss>original: "concinnitas"; Alberti's central concept of the perfect integration of parts so that nothing can be added or taken away without destroying the whole</gloss></term> arises, just as the nature of things consists of even or odd numbers, limits, and musical voices and tones.

**N**ow I come to those matters which we promised to discuss: the sources from which all kinds of beauty and ornament emerge, or rather, what has flowed forth when expressed from the whole logic of beauty. This is indeed a difficult investigation. For whatever that one thing is which must be selected and expressed from the whole number and nature of the parts—to be imparted to each part by a certain and equal logic, or to be held in such a way that it joins and contains many parts into one assembly and body with a right and stable cohesion and agreement—of which we are seeking something very similar here: surely that very thing must savor of the power and, as it were, the essence of all those things with which it either coheres or mingles; otherwise, they would fight with discord and divisions and be scattered.

While this inquiry and selection is by no means prompt or easy in other matters, it is especially uncertain and dangerous in all these things we are about to discuss. The art of building consists of so many parts, and each individual part—as you have seen—demands to be honored by such various kinds of ornaments. But we shall pursue the matter according to our plan and the strength of our wit, not repeating the method by which a solid knowledge of the whole is perceived from the number of parts. Rather, we shall begin here with what pertains to the matter, noting what it is that nature itself does to create beauty.

We are reminded by the reasoning of the most skilled of the ancients, and we have said elsewhere, that a building is like a living creature <note>original: "veluti animal"</note> in which it is necessary to imitate nature when completing it. Let us therefore investigate why it is so in bodies produced by nature that some are called more beautiful, others less beautiful, or even deformed. It is obvious from those things considered among the number of the beautiful that they are not all of such a kind that there is no difference between them; for...

...or by that very thing in which they do not agree, we feel that something is either impressed or infused into that same thing. ☞ Why should we declare that things which are very dissimilar are nevertheless together extremely charming? I will use an example. Someone might desire a girl who is slender in her tenderness. Another man, in the works of the comic poet <note>Likely referring to the Roman playwright Terence, who often contrasted different types of female beauty</note>, preferred over all other girls that maiden who was indeed more robust and full of color <note>original: "fuci plena"; literally "full of lichen-dye," implying a healthy, rosy complexion or the use of rouge</note>. To you, perhaps, the beauty of a wife will be pleasing: one who imitates neither the weak in her thinness nor rustic boxers in the thickness of her limbs. But let there be found in her just as much as can be added to the former or taken from the latter while preserving dignity. What then? Because you prefer one or the other of these, you will by no means decide that the others are of a form neither noble nor worthy.

But that she should please above the rest, something could effect—what sort of thing that is, I do not ask. However, so that you may judge beauty, it is not opinion, but a certain innate reason in our minds that will bring it about. That this is so is apparent: since there is no one who, upon seeing ugly, shapeless, or obscene things, is not immediately offended and hates them. Whence, however, that sense of the mind is excited and comes forth, I do not seek to the bottom. But let us consider from those things which offer themselves freely how much they contribute to the matter. For in the forms and shapes of buildings, there is indeed something excellent and perfected by nature that excites the mind and is immediately felt.

I believe indeed that beauty, dignity, charm, and any similar qualities consist in those things which, if you take away, diminish, or change them, are immediately corrupted and perish. If this is persuasive, it will not be tedious to review those things which can be taken away, increased, or changed, especially in forms and shapes. For it is certain that every body consists of certain parts of its own, from which, if you take one away, or reduce it to a larger or smaller size, or transpose it to unseemly places, it will happen that what was appropriate for the decency of the form in that body will be corrupted.

From which we can determine—lest I pursue the rest of these things too at length—that these three things are the most important in which the whole reason we seek is contained: **number**, and what we shall call **definition** <note>original: "finitio"; in Alberti's theory, this refers to the mathematical proportions of length, width, and height</note>, and **placement**. But there is something more besides, from all these things joined and linked together, by which the whole face of beauty shines forth wonderfully. That shall be called by us <term>harmony<gloss>original: "concinnitas"; Alberti's central concept of the perfect integration of parts so that nothing can be added or taken away without destroying the whole</gloss></term>, which we surely say is the foster-mother of all grace and decorum. And indeed it is the duty of harmony to arrange the parts of the parts—which otherwise are distinct from one another by nature—by a certain perfect rule, so that they correspond to one another in appearance. From this it happens that when they are brought to the mind, whether by sight, hearing, or any other way, harmonious things are immediately sensed. For by nature we desire the best things, and we cling to the best with pleasure; nor does beauty flourish in the whole body or its parts...

...more than <term>concinnitas: a central term for Alberti, often translated as "harmony," "congruity," or "perfect integration," referring to the ordered arrangement of parts</term> in itself and in its nature. Indeed, I interpret it to be the companion of the mind and of reason; it has the widest fields in which to exercise and flourish. It encompasses the whole of human life and its reasons, and it treats the whole nature of things. For whatever nature produces, it is all moderated by the law of *concinnitas*. Nor is there any greater zeal of nature than that what she produces should be absolutely perfect. This would be achieved by no means if *concinnitas* were removed, for the supreme consensus of the parts would perish. But enough on these things so far: if we have sufficiently established these points, we can define beauty as a certain consensus and "conspiracy" of parts <note>original: "conspirationẽ partiũ"; Alberti uses this word in its literal Latin sense—a "breathing together"—to describe how parts work in total harmony</note> in that thing of which they are parts, according to a certain **number**, **delimitation** <note>original: "finitio"; referring to the sizing and boundaries of the parts</note>, and **arrangement**, such that *concinnitas*—that is, the absolute primary 

<margin>The method and reason of building.</margin>
architectural reason—pursues it. From this, it claims for itself dignity, grace, and authority, and it is held in high value. Since our ancestors perceived from the nature of things that all these matters we have spoken of so far were so, and they did not doubt that by neglecting these they would achieve nothing that would contribute to the praise and beauty of a work, they declared, not without justice, that they must imitate nature as the best craftsman of forms. For that reason, they collected the laws which nature used in producing things, as far as human industry was able, and transferred them to their own architectural methods. Looking, therefore, at what nature was accustomed to do regarding the body as a whole and concerning individual parts, they understood from the first principles of things that bodies do not always consist of equal proportions. Thus, some bodies are produced slender, others thicker, and others in between. <margin>The bones of a building are even</margin>
In the same way, in other places, the **bones** <note>original: "ossa"; Alberti uses this biological metaphor to describe the essential structural framework, such as columns and corners</note> of a building follow the nature of things: for that reason, columns, corners, and such things were never placed in an **odd number**. Indeed, you will find no animal that stands or moves on an odd number of feet. Conversely, however, they never placed **openings** <note>original: "apertiones"; referring to doors, windows, or any voids in a wall</note> in an even number. That this same principle is observed in nature is readily apparent; for although in living creatures nature provides pairs of ears, eyes, and nostrils on either side, she placed the **mouth** as a single, open feature in the middle. Truly, among even and odd numbers, there are some that are more familiar to nature than others, and particularly celebrated among the wise. Architects have employed these in composing the parts of buildings, primarily because they possess certain inherent qualities for which they are judged most worthy. Indeed, all natural philosophers assert that nature itself consists of a **ternary** <note>the number three</note> principle. And regarding the **quinary** <note>the number five</note>, 

<margin>On the number five.</margin>
when I consider so many, so various, and such admirable things that either observe the number five within themselves or proceed from things that have five parts—such as the human hand—I agree, not without reason, that it is divine and justly dedicated to the gods of the arts and especially to **Mercury** <note>the Roman god of commerce, communication, and craftsmanship</note>. 

<margin>On the number seven.</margin>
It is also established that God, the great architect of the universe, is exceedingly delighted by the **septenary** <note>the number seven</note> number, having placed seven wandering stars in the heavens. Furthermore, He willed that man—whom He desired to be His own delight—should be so regulated that his conception, birth, growth, maturity, and all such stages of life return to this very number seven. **Aristotle** says that the ancients did not give a name to a newborn infant before the seventh day after birth, as if it were not yet destined for survival; for both the seed in the womb and the newborn infant are at the greatest risk during the first seven days after their origin. Among the odd numbers, 

<margin>On the number nine.</margin>
they also celebrate the **novenary** <note>the number nine</note>, according to which number skillful nature arranged the spheres in the heavens. Furthermore, it is established among natural philosophers that nature is accustomed to using a nine-part portion of a whole in many significant matters. For the ninth part of the sun's annual cycle is approximately forty days. **Hippocrates** <note>the ancient Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine"</note> used to say that the fetus in the womb is formed according to this number. Moreover, we observe everywhere that the movement from most serious illnesses toward recovery is concluded on the fortieth day. Mothers who have conceived cease their <term>purgation: the natural postnatal or menstrual cleansing of the body</term> if the child is male; and conversely, after birth, if a male is born, mothers begin their purgation on that same day. They also affirm that before the fortieth day, an infant has never been seen to laugh or shed tears while awake, though they report that infants do both while sleeping. So much for odd numbers. # Leon Battista Alberti: On the Art of Building

<margin>The number eight.</margin>
It is evident that the **number eight** has the greatest power in the nature of things. We see that no infants born in the eighth month survive, except in Egypt. Furthermore, they say that if a pregnant woman gives birth in the eighth month and the fetus is stillborn, the mother herself is likely to die soon after. Moreover, if a couple conceives in the eighth month, the infant will be filled with a mucous slime, and its skin will be rendered foul and very much like an **oyster** <note>original: "ostreacea"; a reference to a rough, scaly, or slimy skin texture attributed to premature or unhealthy births in Renaissance medical lore</note>, which is quite revolting. 

<margin>The number ten.</margin>
**Aristotle** thought the **number ten** was to be considered the most perfect of all. This was perhaps for the reason—as some interpret it—that its square is completed by the sum of four consecutive cubes <note>original: "quattuor cōtinuis collectis cubis"; Alberti is likely referring to the Pythagorean *Tetractys*, where 1+2+3+4 = 10, though he uses the term "cubis" (cubes/units) in a geometric sense</note>. Therefore, architects have used these numbers everywhere. Specifically, they did not exceed the number ten for even-numbered **openings** <note>windows or doors</note>, nor did they exceed the number nine for odd-numbered ones, especially in temples. 

Now it follows that we must speak of **Finishing** <note>original: "finitio"; this refers to the determination of proportions and the correspondence between the dimensions of length, width, and height</note>. 

<margin>What is Finishing?</margin>
**Finishing** is, for us, a certain correspondence of the lines among themselves by which dimensions are measured. One of these is of length; the second, of width; the third, of height. The method of Finishing is most aptly derived from those things in which nature shows herself to us as something to be observed and admired. Indeed, I affirm again and again that saying of **Pythagoras**: it is most certain that nature is consistent with itself in all things. So it is: those very same numbers that cause that **harmony** <note>original: "concinnitas"; a key term for Alberti meaning the rhythmic or musical integration of parts</note> of voices to be most pleasing to the ears are the very same numbers that cause the eyes and the mind to be filled with wonderful pleasure. Therefore, the entire method of Finishing will be derived from **musicians**, for whom such numbers are perfectly understood, and from those things furthermore in which nature provides something conspicuous and worthy of itself. But I shall not pursue this further than is useful for the architect. Let us leave aside what pertains to the arrangement of individual voices or the theories of **tetrachords** <note>a scale of four notes used in ancient Greek music</note>. 

<margin>On harmony.</margin>
Those things which pertain to our work are as follows. We say that **Harmony** is a sweet consonance of voices for the ears. Of voices, some are deep and others are high. A deeper voice resonates from a longer string; higher ones from shorter strings. From the various disparity of these voices, different harmonies are produced, which the ancients gathered into certain numbers by comparing the relationship of sounding strings. 

These are the names of the **consonances** <note>musical intervals that sound pleasing together</note>:
*   The **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"; also called "sesquialtera" (a ratio of 3:2)</note>.
*   The **Fourth** <note>original: "Diatesseron"; also called "sesquitertia" (a ratio of 4:3)</note>.
*   The **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"; which is a "double" (ratio of 2:1)</note>.
*   The **Twelfth** <note>original: "Diapason diapente"; which is a "triple" (ratio of 3:1)</note>.
*   The **Double Octave** <note>original: "Disdiapason"; which is called "quadruple" (ratio of 4:1)</note>.

To these they added the **Whole Tone**, which is also called the **one-and-an-eighth** <note>original: "sexquioctauus"; a ratio of 9:8</note>. These types of consonances that we have reviewed relate to the comparisons of strings to one another in this way: for the **one-and-a-half ratio** <note>sesquialtera/Fifth</note> is so called because the longer string contains the entire length of the shorter one plus another half-part of that shorter one within itself. For what was called "sesqui" among the ancients...

<summary>Alberti explains the mystical and natural significance of the numbers eight and ten before defining "Finitio" (Finishing/Proportion) as a system of architectural dimensions based on the mathematical ratios of musical harmony.</summary>

...we interpret the saying. In the **sesquialtera** <term>sesquialtera: a ratio of 3:2, where the larger value contains the smaller plus its half</term>, therefore, the number three is given to the longer string, and the number two to the shorter. The **sesquitertia** <term>sesquitertia: a ratio of 4:3, where the larger value contains the smaller plus its third part</term> is so called when the larger string contains the whole of the smaller one, plus a third part of that same smaller one. To the larger, therefore, you give the number four; to the smaller, three. 

In that consonance which is called **Diapason** <note>original: "Diapason"; the Greek musical term for an octave</note>, the corresponding numbers are held in a double ratio, such as two to one, or the whole to its half. In the **triple ratio** <note>3:1</note>, the number three relates to that same unit, or the whole to its third part; in the **quadruple ratio** <note>4:1</note>, the number four similarly relates to the unit, as the whole to its fourth part. Finally, the musical numbers themselves, to summarize them, are these: **one, two, three, four**. There is also, as I said, the **tone** <note>original: "tonus"; the 9:8 ratio which represents the interval between musical notes</note>, in which the larger string, compared to the smaller, exceeds it by an eighth part of the smaller. 

Architects use all these numbers very conveniently: they are taken in pairs when laying out marketplaces, squares, and open-air areas, where only two dimensions are considered—width and length. They are also used taken in threes, as in the arrangement of public seating, the senate house, the hall, and the like; in these, they relate width to length, and they want the height of both to correspond to the harmony.

## ¶ The correspondence of numbers in measuring areas; the principle of proportion is not innate to harmonies and bodies. Chapter VI.

<margin>The principle of areas.</margin>
We must speak of these things: first, concerning **areas** <note>referring to the ground plans or surface dimensions of rooms and buildings</note>, in which dimensions are joined in pairs. Some areas are short, others are longer, and others are of medium length. The shortest of all is the **square**, whose sides are equal to each other in length and whose angles are all right angles. Next to this is the **sesquialtera** [3:2], and then the **sesquitertia** [4:3] will also be counted among the short areas. Therefore, these three types of correspondence—which we call **simple**—are assigned to short areas. 

Likewise, three ratios are suitable for **medium** areas. The best of these is the **double** [2:1]; next to this is the one composed of a doubled *sesquialtera*. And it is produced thus: given the smallest number of the area, say four, the first *sesquialtera* is produced, which becomes six. To this you again add its [sesquialtera] part, and they become nine <note>Alberti is explaining a compound ratio: 4 to 6 is 2:3, and 6 to 9 is 2:3. The total ratio of 4:9 is a "doubled sesquialtera," or a musical fifth plus a fifth</note>. Therefore, the greatest length here will exceed the shortest by a double ratio, and even more by the tone of the double. For the medium areas, there will also be the **sesquitertia taken twice**, produced by a similar calculation as the next. From this calculation, the shorter line will be as nine, and the longest as sixteen <note>9 to 12 is 3:4, and 12 to 16 is 3:4. The total ratio is 9:16</note>. Therefore, here the larger line exceeds the double of the smaller by one tone less. In the longer areas, the method of derivation...

# Leon Battista Alberti’s On the Art of Building.

...follows in this way. For either the **double** <note>original: "dupla"; a 2:1 ratio</note> is joined with the **sesquialtera** <term>sesquialtera: a ratio of 3:2, where the larger value contains the smaller plus its half</term> and it becomes a **triple** <note>original: "tripla"; a 3:1 ratio</note>; or the **sesquitertia** <term>sesquitertia: a ratio of 4:3, where the larger value contains the smaller plus its third part</term> is also joined to the double, and the outer numbers become as three and eight <note>An 8:3 ratio</note>; or they are taken so that the **dimensions** <note>original: "diametri"; Alberti uses this to mean the lines of measurement across a space</note> correspond to each other from a **quadruple** <note>original: "quadrupla"; a 4:1 ratio</note>. We have spoken of the shorter areas in which the numbers correspond either equally, or as two to three, or as three to four. And of the medium-sized areas in which the numbers correspond: either from the double, or as four to nine, or as nine to sixteen. Finally, we reviewed the longer areas in which they correspond from the triple, or from the quadruple, or as three to eight. Moreover, we shall join together all the dimensions of the body—if I may speak thus—in groups of three, using these numbers: which are either innate to the harmonies themselves, or are taken from elsewhere by a certain and correct reasoning. In harmonies there are numbers from whose correspondences their proportions are completed, as in the double, triple, and quadruple. 

For the **double** is indeed obtained from the simple sesquialtera, to which a sesquitertia is also added, following an example of this kind: Let the smallest number of the double be two. From this, through the sesquialtera, I produce the number three; then from three, through the sesquitertia, the number four will be obtained—which is the same number that is double to two. Or likewise in this way: Let the smallest number be three; I produce a sesquitertia, which makes four; I add a sesquialtera, and six is obtained—which, related to three, completes the double. 

Then also the **triple** is composed from the double and the sesquialtera joined together. Let the smallest number here be two: from the double it will become four; to this I add the sesquialtera, and it becomes six—which indeed, as the number six, corresponds to two from the triple. Or in this way likewise: having placed the same two as the smaller, I take its sesquialtera, and it will become three. I also add the double of three: we have six itself, the triple of the smaller. 

By similar extensions, the **quadruple** is produced, from which the double is composed by adding another double to it. For that is indeed made from a duplicated double, which is also called the **double octave** <note>original: "disdiapason"; the musical interval of two octaves</note>. It is made in this manner: Let the smallest number here be two; double this, and it becomes an **octave** <note>original: "diapason"; the 2:1 ratio</note>, which corresponds as four to two. Double this again, and it becomes a double octave, in which eight corresponds to two. This quadruple is also composed by adding the sesquialtera and the sesquitertia together to the double. How that is done is clear from what was just said. For, so that this explanation may be more fit, having placed a pure two, through the sesquialtera it becomes three; which through the sesquitertia becomes four. Finally, that four through the double becomes eight. Or thus...

# Book IX. On the Decoration of Private Buildings. Leaf 145.

For once the number **three** is established, you obtain a **six** from its **double** <note>original: "dupla"; a 2:1 ratio</note>; to this you add another half of itself, which makes **nine**; to this you add its third part, which will give **twelve**: which, relative to its smallest part, is also a **triple** <note>original: "ternari⁹"; a 3:1 ratio</note> of four. Architects use these numbers we have reviewed, not in a confused or haphazard way, but with correspondences on both sides to achieve **harmony**. For example, if one wishes to raise walls upon a floor area whose length is perhaps **double** its width, one should use the correspondences for the double ratio there, and not those belonging to the **triple**; only those by which that same double is composed. The same logic follows for a **triple** area; for it too will use its own correspondences, and no others but its own. Thus, one will define the diagonal measurements <note>original: "diametros"; Alberti often uses this term to refer to the diagonal lines of a geometric shape</note> by the numbers I have listed, so that one understands they are perfectly suited to the work.

In defining these diagonal measurements, certain correspondences are innate that can by no means be determined by whole numbers, but are instead captured by **roots** and **powers**. 

<margin>Roots</margin> **Roots** <note>original: "radices"</note> are the sides of square numbers. 
<margin>Powers</margin> **Powers** <note>original: "potentiae"</note> are the areas of those squares themselves. From the accumulation of areas and powers, **cubes** are conceived. The first of the cubes, whose root is **unity** <note>the number one</note>, is dedicated to the **divinity** <note>original: "diuinitati dicata"; Alberti follows the Pythagorean tradition where the number one represents the source of all things and the Divine</note>; for this reason it is considered consecrated, because being produced from unity, it is itself entirely one in its areas. To this is added what they say: that **one** is the most stable of all figures, equally constant on every base, and enduring. But if unity is not a number itself, but the spring from which numbers flow, containing and pouring itself out, then it may perhaps be permitted to say that **duality** <note>the number two</note> is the first number. 

From this root [two], you produce a square **area of four**; if this is raised up to a height equal to the root, a **cube of eight** will be completed. From a cube of this kind, the arrangements of these definitions will be held. For first, the side of the cube itself presents itself here, which is called the **cubical root**; its area in numbers is **four**, and the total volume of the cube itself is **eight**. Added to these is the line from one corner of the area to the opposite corner: which, being drawn straight, divides the square area into two equal parts, which is why it is called the **diameter** <note>the diagonal of the square</note>. How much this line is in terms of a whole number is unknown <note>Alberti is referring to the fact that the diagonal of a square with side 2 is the square root of 8, an irrational number</note>. But it is established that this is the **root of an area of eight**. There is also the **diameter of the cube** <note>the diagonal through the center of the 3D cube</note>, which we know for certain is the **root of the number twelve**. Finally, there is the longest line in a **right-angled triangle**; if the two smaller sides of this triangle containing the right angle are such that one is the root of an area of four, and the other is the root of twelve, then the third and longest line stretched opposite the right angle <note>the hypotenuse</note> shall be the **root of the number sixteen**. Therefore, such correspondences of numbers and quantities as we have reviewed are innate for defining diagonal measurements. The use of all these is that the shortest line is given to the width of the area, and the longest corresponds to this...

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

...ing <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page</note> to the length. The middle values indeed should be given to the height. But sometimes these will be exchanged for the convenience of the buildings. 

¶ Now we must speak of that method of definition which is not innate to harmonies and bodies, but is taken from elsewhere to serve in joining the three diagonal measurements <note>original: "diametros"; here referring to the three dimensions of a room: length, width, and height</note> together. For there are indeed certain very useful annotations of the three dimensions to be fitted into the work, drawn both from musicians, geometers, and also from arithmeticians; it will be helpful to review these. Those who philosophize call these **means** <term>mediocritates: the mathematical "middle" value between two extremes, used to determine proportional heights</term>; their logic is both varied and manifold. 

<margin>
Categories of means.
</margin>
But first, among the wise, there are three modes of capturing these means: the goal of all of them is that, once two extremes are set, a certain middle number is found that corresponds to both those set terms with a fixed ratio. This is, so to speak, by a certain joining of affinity. 

<margin>
Arithmetic.
</margin>
In this inquiry we consider three terms: two of which, one on this side, is called the **greatest**; and on the other side, its opposite, the **smallest**. The third indeed is **intermediate** and corresponds to both by a mutual relation of the intervals—the distance by which this middle number stands apart from both. Out of the three that the philosophers primarily approved, the easiest mean to find is the one they call **arithmetic**. For once the extreme terms of the numbers are set: that is, the greatest on this side—say, **eight**—and the smallest directly opposite—say, **four**—one joins both into one sum: it will therefore become **twelve**. Half of this sum of the combined parts is taken: that will be **six** units. They establish this number **six** as the **arithmetic mean** here, which indeed stands at an equal interval between those set extremes of four and eight <note>In an arithmetic mean, the difference between the numbers is constant: 6 is 2 more than 4, and 8 is 2 more than 6</note>. 

<margin>
Geometric mean.
</margin>
The second mean indeed is the **geometric**; it is captured thus. For the smallest term—say, **four**—is multiplied by the greatest—say, **nine**. From these so multiplied, the sum of thirty-six units is made; the **root** of this sum (as they say)—that is, the number of the side which, when multiplied by itself, completes that area of thirty-six units. This root will therefore be **six**: for six taken six times will give that area of thirty-six. It is very difficult to find this mean <note>original: "arithmeticam"; the Latin text likely contains a scribal error here, as the author is clearly describing the geometric mean</note> everywhere in whole numbers; but it is explained most beautifully by lines, of which there is no need to report here. 

<margin>
Musical mean.
</margin>
The third mean, which is called **musical** <note>Also known as the harmonic mean</note>, is a little more laborious than the arithmetic; yet it is defined most beautifully by numbers. In this, the ratio that the smallest of the set terms has to the greatest must be the same ratio that the distances have: from the smallest to the middle on one side, and from the middle to the greatest on the other side... <note>catchword: ter</note>

...following the example of smaller numbers of this kind. Let the numbers be positioned: the smaller thirty; the larger indeed sixty: these indeed here have a **double** ratio <note>A 2:1 ratio</note>. I therefore take the smallest possible whole numbers in a double ratio: these are one on this side, and against it two; I join them and they become three. I then divide that whole interval which is between the greatest given number, sixty, and the smallest, thirty, into these same three parts; each of these three parts will be ten. For that reason, I add one of these parts (that is, ten) to the smaller term; it becomes forty. This will be the sought-after **musical mean** <term>mediocritas musica: today known as the harmonic mean. In the set 30, 40, 60, the middle term 40 is the harmonic mean because the differences (10 and 20) are in the same ratio as the extremes (30:60)</term>, which is distant from the greatest number by double the interval by which the middle number itself is distant from the smallest. For it was in this proportion that we proposed the greatest of the extremes should correspond to the minimum. By means of such means, architects have discovered many most worthy things both concerning the whole building and the parts of the work, which it would be long to pursue. But they used means of this kind especially for raising the height in relation to the diameter.

### ¶ On the manner and dimension of placing columns: their positioning and finishing. Chapter VII.

**S**ed <note>The letter 'S' is a decorative woodcut initial in the original</note> it will be beautiful to understand the manner and dimension of placing columns, which the ancients distinguished into three kinds according to the variety of three periods of time. For contemplating **man**, they judged that columns should be fashioned by them according to his likeness. 

<margin>
Man
</margin>

And so, they found the diameter of a man, measuring from one side to the other, to be a **sixth part** of his height; but from the navel to the loins to be a **tenth part** of his length <note>height</note>. Our interpreters of the sacred <note>Referring to Biblical commentators, such as St. Augustine, who compared Noah’s Ark to the human body</note>, noticing this very thing, assert that the **Ark** built during the flood was made according to the configuration of a man. Perhaps they originally placed columns at such dimensions: so that some were sixfold at the base, and others indeed tenfold. 

But because the sense of nature is innate in our minds—by which we said harmonies are perceived—architects were warned that such great thickness in the former and such great slenderness in the latter was not fitting, and they rejected both. Finally, they thought that what they sought lay between these excesses. For that reason, imitating the **arithmeticians** in the first place, they forced both those extremes into one, and divided the sum of the joined numbers by the middle. From which they found that the number which was distant from the number six and the number ten by equal spaces was the number **eight**. And so it pleased them for that reason to give the diameter of the base **eight times** to the length of the column, and they named them **Ionic**. Indeed, they held the **Doric** kind of columns, which is owed to thicker buildings, by that same reasoning by which they held the Ionic. For they joined that smallest of terms, which was six, to this middle value established for the Ionic, which was eight; and the sum made fourteen...

Page LXVIII

## Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

They divided this total sum into equal parts; from this, the number seven was assigned, according to which they fashioned the **Doric** columns, so that the bases of the shafts were one-seventh of their total length. Then, they established the more slender columns, which they called **Corinthian**, by taking that middle **Ionic** number <note>The number 8</note> and joining it with the greatest of the terms <note>The number 10</note>; this sum was also divided in half. For the Ionic number was eight, while the greatest of the terms was ten; these, when added together, gave a total of eighteen, half of which is nine. Therefore, they gave nine times the diameter of the lower shaft to the length of **Corinthian** columns. To the **Ionic**, however, they gave eight times, and to the **Doric**, seven times.

<margin>Placement.</margin> Thus much concerning these matters. It follows next that we must speak of **placement** <term>collocatio: the strategic arrangement and positioning of architectural components to ensure they fit their site and function</term>. Placement pertains to the site and the seating of the parts; its importance is felt more acutely when it is handled poorly than it is understood on its own merits when done decently. Indeed, a great part of this relies on a judgment implanted by nature in the minds of men. It also contributes significantly to the logic of **proportional definition** <note>original: "finitionis rationibus"</note>. Nevertheless, regarding the matter at hand, these are the general types. Even the smallest parts positioned in their proper places throughout a work bring beauty to the sight. But if they are placed in a foreign spot, or one unworthy and unbecoming of them, they become cheapened if they are elegant, and if they are not, they are even more severely criticized. We see this even in the works of nature: if, by chance, one were to attach the ear of a donkey to the forehead of a puppy; or if someone were to walk with an oversized foot, or with one hand larger than the other, or with one pupil larger than the other, he would be considered deformed. Even in beasts of burden, it is not approved to look out of one eye that is blue-grey and another that is black; it is so deeply rooted in nature that the right parts should correspond to the left in every **symmetry** <term>parilitate: a state of being equal or matching; the basis of classical architectural balance</term>.

<margin><note>A hand-drawn manicule (pointing finger) highlights the following lines on symmetry.</note></margin> Wherefore, we shall observe above all that every detail, even the most minute, be arranged according to the level, the line, the numbers, the form, and the appearance, so that the right mutually corresponds to the left, the highest to the lowest, the nearest to the nearest, and equals to equals—all most evenly fitted for the ornament of that body of which they are to be parts. Furthermore, statues, tablets, and whatever notable decoration is applied must be so fitted together that they seem to have grown naturally in the most suitable places, almost like twins. The Ancients valued this evening out of symmetry so highly that, even in placing marble tablets, they wanted them to correspond exactly in quantity, quality, outline, position, and colors. There is a remarkable thing among the Ancients in which I have often greatly admired the excellence of their art: in placing statues, both elsewhere and especially on the **pediments** <term>fastigiis: the triangular gable forming the roofline of a classical temple</term> of temples, they took care that those placed on one side did not differ in any part, lineament, or material from those placed directly opposite. Indeed, we see statues of two-horse and four-horse chariots, their drivers, and their attendants, which correspond to one another so perfectly...

...so that we can testify that in this matter [art] has surpassed nature; in whose works we do not see even a nose that is identical to another nose <note>original: "nasum quidem naso similem." Alberti argues that while nature creates variety and individual imperfections, the architect seeks a universal, idealized beauty.</note>. ### ¶ Certain Brief Summaries and Annotations, Serving as Laws for the Construction and Adornment of the Entire Work. Chapter VIII.

**I**t follows that I shall collect certain summary and brief admonitions, which must be observed as laws not only in the whole adornment and the comparison of beauties, but also in the entire business of building. This will also serve as the **epilogue** <term>epilogum: a concluding summary of the main points of the architectural treatise</term> we promised to collect. First, as we have said that all **vices** <term>vitia: architectural defects or errors, categorized here by whether they occur during planning or construction</term> of deformity are to be far avoided, we shall bring forward the particularly serious ones. Some vices arise from counsel and the mind, such as judgment and choice; others from the hand, such as those involving the craftsman’s labor. Errors and sins of counsel and judgment are prior in their nature and timing, and are more serious in themselves; likewise, once a sin is committed, it is far less corrigible than the others. Therefore, we shall begin with these.

<margin>Pay attention to the force and the vexed [nature of the site].</margin> It will be considered a vice if you choose an unhealthy, restless, infertile, unfortunate, or gloomy region to place your work—one subject to evils both obvious and hidden. It will also be a vice if you prescribe a measure for the **area** <note>original: "areae modum." Here meaning the building's footprint or site layout.</note> that is not apt or well-suited to the divided region. Or if you join member to member in a way that they do not mutually agree with one another for the use and convenience of the inhabitants. Or if the arrangements are not suitable for individuals.

<margin>A fault of the site.</margin> Or if the convenience of the whole family—children, servants, matrons, girls, urban and rural folk—has not been sufficiently provided for with the dignity of each, along with provisions for the guest and the visitor. It is a vice if you make things too vast or too small, too open or too secluded, too joined or too separated, or many more or fewer than the matter requires. It is a vice if there is a lack of means to ward off the heat and the cold without discomfort. If there are no lodgings where you may exercise and delight yourself for the sake of good health, or where you may shield those who are infirm or unwell from the offenses of the weather and the seasons. Add to this if the building is not sufficiently fortified and safe from the injury of men and sudden accidents. If a wall is either too thin to support itself and the roof, or far thicker than firmness requires. If the roofs "quarrel" with one another (if I may speak thus) with their **dripping gutters** <note>original: "stillicidijs." Referring to poor drainage design where water from one roof falls onto another.</note>. If they pour the force of the rains into the interior of the walls. If you have placed things too high or too low. If the gaps of the openings admit infected winds, troublesome frosts, or intrusive sun. Or, on the contrary, if you make them too obstructed...

...blindness has brought in hateful things. If they have not spared the **bones of the walls** <note>original: "ossibus parietum." <margin>Vices of Ornaments</margin>
Furthermore, those things among the **vices of ornaments** which must be hated above all others will be just as in the works of nature: if something happens to be backward, crippled, excessive, or in any part shapeless. For if this is indeed condemned in nature and held as a monster, what of the architect who has used parts indecently? And if there are indeed parts which are used regarding forms—lines, angles, extension, and such—then those are right who assert that no vice of deformity is found more obscene and detestable than to intermingle angles, lines, or surfaces that have not been diligently examined and compared among themselves in number, magnitude, and position, nor equalized and joined together. 

And who would not vehemently rebuke him who, where no necessity compels, draws the lines of a wall here and there in **imitation of a wandering worm** <note>original: "aberrantis lumbrici." This is a famous Alberti critique of floor plans that lack straight lines or clear geometric order, wandering aimlessly like a worm's trail.</note>, disordered and inconsiderate, some long, some tiny, with unequal angles and shapeless joining; and especially in the same area being here more obtuse, and there opposite more acute, with confused reasoning, disturbed order, and without forethought or correction. 

It will also be a vice to have managed the matter so that, although it might otherwise not be too bad regarding the logic of the foundations, yet it results that when ornaments are desired, it is nonetheless impossible for it to be made more refined by the elegance of ornaments. This happens when one has cared for nothing in the walls except that they support the roofs, leaving nothing anywhere where one might properly and distinctly impart either the dignity of columns, the grace of statues, the beauty of panels and painting, or the splendor of **revetments** <term>crustationum: decorative wall coverings, usually made of thin slabs of marble or precious stone</term>. 

Closely joined to this vice is this: if you could have achieved at equal expense things that were by far the most beautiful and most graceful, yet you did not strive with all your strength to attain it. For there is indeed in the forms and shapes of buildings something excellent and perfected by nature <note>This refers to Alberti's core concept of *concinnitas*, or the natural harmony of parts.</note> which stirs the soul and is felt immediately if it is present; but if it is absent, it is greatly longed for. 

And the eyes especially are by nature very greedy for beauty and **harmony** <term>concinnitatis: the absolute and fundamental rule of beauty consisting in the consensus and conspiracy of parts according to a specific number, outline, and arrangement</term>; and in this matter, they show themselves to be fastidious and quite difficult to please. Nor do I know why it happens that they demand more what is missing than they approve of what is present. For they continuously look for what could be added to the brilliance and splendor; and they are offended unless they see as much art, labor, and industry displayed as they judge could have been foreseen and done by the most careful, sharp-sighted, and diligent person. Indeed, sometimes they cannot even explain what it is that offends them, except for this one thing:

# Book IX. On the Ornament of Private Buildings. Folio CXLVIII.

...so that those who fully complete these works do not possess an immoderate desire for looking at beauty. Since these things are so, it will surely be the duty of all to strive with zeal, work, and diligence so that, as far as lies in us, those things we build are most ornate; especially since everyone desires those things to be ornate. In this class are public works and especially sacred ones. For no one can endure to have those exist bare of ornaments.

<margin>Another vice.</margin>
It will also be a vice if you attach to private buildings those ornaments which are owed to public ones; or conversely, if you apply to public buildings those belonging to private ones—especially if those ornaments are indeed of the smallest kind in their genre. It is also a vice if they are not meant to last, as with one who applies trivial, fleeting, and putrid smears of painting <note>original: "picturae illimenta." Alberti is likely referring to low-quality fresco or temporary pigments that flake away, which he finds unworthy of "eternal" public architecture.</note> to public works. For public things ought to be eternal. And it is surely a grave vice, which we see among some foolish people, who polish and finish works barely begun with the color of paint and the signs of sculpture.

<margin>Deioces, King of the Medes.</margin>
From this it happens that these fleeting things are destroyed before the work itself is brought forth. For it is necessary to finish the work bare <note>original: "Nudum... opus." A fundamental principle for Alberti: the structural integrity and geometric "nudity" of a building must be perfect before any decoration is applied.</note> before you clothe it: the last step will be to ornament it. For this, the opportunity and capacity of both time and materials will present itself only when you can do so most conveniently and without any hindrance. 

<margin>The city of Ecbatana, surrounded by a sevenfold wall of various colors.</margin>
But the ornaments you choose to add should for the most part be of such a kind that the hands of many average craftsmen may be employed in completing them. If any indeed are more elegant and refined—such as statues or panels like those of Phidias or Zeuxis <note>Phidias was a famous Greek sculptor; Zeuxis was a legendary Greek painter.</note>, which are considered rarer—they shall be placed in equally rare and most worthy locations.

<margin>Caligula had a marble and ivory manger.</margin>
I do not praise that Deioces, King of the Medes, who surrounded the city of Ecbatana with a sevenfold wall and distinguished them with colors so that some were white <note>The word "albi" (white) is implied by the context of the list of colors and the marginal correction.</note>, others purple, others blue, others covered in silver, and some even gilded. I also hate Caligula, who had a marble stable and an ivory manger. Everything Nero built was covered in gold and distinguished with gems.

<margin>Heliogabalus paved floors with gold.</margin>
Heliogabalus was even more insane, who paved floors with gold, grieving that he could not use amber <note>original: "electro." This refers to electrum, which could mean a natural gold-silver alloy or amber; in both cases, it represents extreme, impractical luxury.</note>. And these displayers of works—or rather of insanity—are surely to be blamed: they pour out the resources of mortals and the sweat of men on a matter which neither use nor the logic of the work begun required; nor would any admiration for talent honor it, nor the grace of invention commend it.

<margin>How a building should be considered.</margin>
Therefore, I advise again and again that these vices be avoided: before you undertake the work, weigh the whole matter with yourself and consult with experts once models <note>original: "exemplaribus ad modulos." Alberti was a pioneer in advocating for the use of precise, three-dimensional scale models rather than just drawings.</note> have been reduced to scale. From these I would wish that you repeat all parts of the future work two, three, four, seven, ten times—both with breaks and resuming at intervals—so that from the deepest foundations to the highest roof tile, nothing in the whole work, whether hidden or open, large or small, is not long and deeply pre-considered, pre-determined, and intended by you.

<summary>Alberti warns against the "vice" of misplaced or excessive ornament, citing ancient tyrants as examples of architectural insanity, and stresses the absolute necessity of using scale models for rigorous planning.</summary>

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

...by which matters, locations, order, and number <note>original: "qb⁹ rebus / locis / ordine / numeroq;"</note> it is fitting or better to have placed, joined, and prescribed. Thus the well-advised architect will proceed: he will approach the matter prepared and accurately. He will learn the strength and nature of the soil where he places the building. He will learn both from ancient buildings and from the use and custom of the inhabitants what the stone, the sand, the lime, and the timber <note>original: "materia." In Roman and Renaissance contexts, this specifically refers to structural wood/timber.</note> taken from that place—or even imported from elsewhere—can withstand against storms under that sky where the building is to be made. He will establish the width, height, and first beginnings of the foundations and footings. Then, for the wall, the facings, the infill, the joints, and the structural "bones," <note>original: "ossibus." Alberti often uses anatomical metaphors, viewing the load-bearing framework of a building as a skeleton.</note> he will repeatedly consider what is owed to each part and of what quality. He will also reconsider what is required for the fittings, the roof, the facing, the open-air pavement, and the interior work. He will prescribe the locations, paths, and methods by which superfluous, harmful, and foul things may be diverted, turned away, and restrained—such as sewers for carrying off rain, ditches for drying out areas, and fortifications for prohibiting moisture—as well as those things which frustrate and overcome the force, mass, and injury of rushing weights, attacking waves, and harassing winds. Finally, he will define everything; he will leave nothing for which he does not prescribe a measure as if by law. Although almost all these things seem primarily to pertain to firmness and utility, <note>These represent two of the three fundamental Vitruvian principles: *firmitas* (strength) and *utilitas* (function).</note> they nevertheless offer this of themselves: that if they are neglected, they bring about a flaw and the greatest deformity.

<margin>
Things which
lead to the
elegance of
ornament.
</margin>
These are the things which most especially lead to the elegance of ornament. The method of decorating the work must be exact and readily available for distinguished things—not too crowded together, not crammed in, and not forced into a single heap—but distributed and placed so definitely, suitably, and appropriately that whoever changes anything would feel the entire pleasantness of the harmony <note>original: "concinitatis." Concinnity is Alberti's most famous aesthetic concept: the rhythmic, musical harmony of all parts of a building so that nothing can be added or taken away without destroying the whole.</note> has been disturbed. Furthermore, nothing should be considered neglected in any part of the work or void of art; yet you would not wish everything to be brought to an equal state of exquisite ornament and filled with riches. Rather, he should use abundance no more than variety. He will place some things from the most excellent in the primary locations; he will place others in the middle among those less elegant; and others again among the last. In this matter he will take care not to join too much of the frivolous with the most precious, nor the tiniest with the grander, nor the very profuse and most ample with the more retracted and narrow. Instead, those things which are dissimilar in dignity and not equal in their kinds will be made equal by the arrangement of the artistic composition. So while some things display gravity and majesty, others exhibit pleasantness and festivity. The reason and order of all things should so match that they not only converge in a rivalry to honor the work, but that one part cannot even [stand] by itself without the others...

<summary>Alberti details the architect's responsibility to master local materials and structural engineering before introducing his central theory of "concinnitas" (harmony), which dictates how ornaments should be balanced and distributed.</summary>

<page-num>Leaf CXLIX.</page-num>
<header>Book IX. On the Ornamentation of Private Buildings.</header>

...[that the work] might seem to stand or maintain its dignity sufficiently; it will also help to intermix slightly more neglected parts in certain places: so that by comparison with them, the more polished parts appear more brilliant. He must completely beware that the principles of the lines <note>original: "lineamentorum." For Alberti, "lineaments" are the conceptual, geometric lines of the design that exist in the mind of the architect before the building is physically constructed.</note> are not subverted. This would happen if, as I said, Doric were mixed with Corinthian, or Corinthian with Doric, or Ionic with Doric, and things of that sort. To Order, also, its own parts shall be given: so that nothing is scattered in an interrupted or confused way, but is placed in its own and fitting locations. For middle parts will be balanced with middle parts, and those that are equally distant from the middle will be equally balanced. Finally, all things shall be measured, bound, and compacted by lines, angles, flow, cohesion, and comprehension <note>original: "comprehensione," referring to the overall unity or the way the parts are perceived as a single whole</note>: not by chance, but by certain and defined reason. They will present themselves so that the gaze <note>original: "intuitus"</note> may run freely and smoothly, as if flowing through the cornices, the gaps, and through the entire inner and outer face of the work, increasing pleasure from the pleasure of similar and dissimilar things; so that those who watch do not think they have looked long enough, because they look again and again and wonder, unless they look back even as they must depart. And when they have searched enough, they shall nowhere in the whole work encounter anything uneven, non-corresponding, and not consenting in all its numbers <note>original: "numeris." In Renaissance architectural theory, "numbers" refers to the mathematical proportions and ratios used to create harmony.</note> to beauty and grace.

Therefore, such things shall be devised and weighed from models <note>original: "modulis." This can refer to both mathematical units and physical scale models.</note>; and it is necessary that we pre-meditate and even prepare not only what you begin, but also what will be of use during the completion, warned by the models themselves. Once the work is begun, there must be no hesitating, no varying, no stopping: but the whole thing having been grasped in a brief and circumscribed explanation, those things which are fitting and convenient, sought out and collected, should be supplied promptly. Therefore, these are the things which the architect ought to have cared for with both counsel and judgment. However, it is not fitting to repeat the errors of the workmen; but he will take care that the craftsmen use the plumb-lines, the line, the rule, and the square <note>original: "norma"</note> correctly. Moreover, he will build at appropriate times, pause, and resume the work with moderation: he will place and arrange things that are pure, uncorrupted, unmixed, solid, sincere, convenient, suitable, and strong; he will set them in their own and fitting places and seats, so that they stand, lie, or lean, by the front or the side, whether in the open or the closed, as the nature and use of each requires.
