# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

...[he should consider] how much praise, how much profit, how much favor, and also how much fame with posterity he might attain if he performs his duty correctly. And on the contrary, if he begins anything impiously, unwisely, or without consideration: how much blame, how much hatred he will undergo, and what a telling, fitting, open, and constant testimony of his own foolishness he will exhibit to mankind. <term>Architecture</term> <note>original: "architectura." Alberti defines this not just as construction, but as a discipline of the mind and a civic responsibility.</note> is a grand undertaking; nor is it for everyone to attempt such a great matter. He who dares to profess himself an <term>architect</term> <note>original: "architectus"</note> must be endowed with the highest intellect, the keenest study, the best learning, and the greatest experience; and above all, with a serious and sincere judgment and wisdom. In the matter of building, the first praise of all is to judge well what is appropriate. For indeed, to have built is a matter of necessity; to have built conveniently is drawn both from necessity and from utility. But to have built in such a way that the refined approve and the frugal do not reject, can only proceed from the skill of a learned, well-advised, and highly considerate <term>artist</term> <note>original: "artificis"</note>. Furthermore, to do those things which seem convenient for use, and which you do not doubt can be done according to the plan and the help of fortune, is no more the part of an <term>architect</term> than of a manual <term>builder</term> <note>original: "fabri." Alberti famously distinguishes the architect (the intellectual designer) from the "faber" (the manual laborer or craftsman who works with his hands).</note>. But to have pre-thought and determined in the mind and judgment what will be perfect and complete in every part: this belongs to that one intellect of the kind we seek. Therefore, he must invent by intellect, learn by experience, select by judgment, compose by wisdom, and perfect by art whatever he undertakes. I establish that the foundation of all these things is prudence and maturity of counsel; but as for the other virtues—humanity, affability, modesty, and integrity—I do not require them in him more than in any other men devoted to any craft. For these are things that if a man lacks, I would not even think him a man. But he must entirely avoid levity, stubbornness, boasting, intemperance, and whatever else might diminish good favor among citizens or increase hatred. Moreover, I would wish him to conduct himself as people do in the study of literature. For no one will think he has given enough effort to literature unless he has read and known all authors, even the not-so-good ones, who have written anything in that field which they follow. So here, he will most diligently examine whatever works are anywhere present that are approved by the opinion and consensus of men; he will commit them to lines <note>original: "lineis," meaning he will draw them</note>, note them with numbers <note>original: "numeris," meaning he will record their measurements</note>, and wish to have them scaled down into models and examples. He will learn and repeat the order, locations, types, and numbers of individual things which they used, especially in those greatest and most worthy things they achieved. It is a conjecture that these were extraordinary men, since they were the directors of such great expenses; yet he shall not be moved by that vast exaggeration of works, as in...

# Book IX. On the Ornament of Private Buildings.

...let him rest content in that. It is a great thing, he says, that the farmer does; but above all, the architect will inquire into what is contained within any work that is thought out beforehand and hidden, or rare and admirable in its method of invention. He will accustom himself to approve of nothing unless it is entirely elegant and worthy of admiration for its wit; and whatever is commendable anywhere, he will take for himself to imitate. However, those things that he understands could be made much more refined, he will treat with skill and meditation so that he may correct and improve them. Indeed, those things which are otherwise not the worst, he will strive to make better through the strength of his intellect; and always, through a sharp and spirited investigation of the best things, desiring greater goals, he will exercise and increase his intellect. In this way, he will gather to himself all the praises—not only those scattered and, as it were, sown about, but even those hidden in the innermost secrets of nature, if I may put it that way. He will grasp them in his mind so that he may apply them to his own works with a wonderful harvest of praise and glory.

He will also rejoice to bring forth something from his own genius into the light of day that we may admire—perhaps like the invention of that man <margin>A sacred temple</margin> who built a sacred temple without using any iron tool <note>original: "nullo adhibito ferramento." This likely refers to the biblical account of the Temple of Solomon (1 Kings 6:7), which was built with stones finished at the quarry so no tool was heard at the site.</note>. Or like the man who moved the standing Colossus <note>original: "colossum." This refers to the "Colossus Neronis," a 100-foot bronze statue. After Nero's death, the architect Decrianus moved it to a new location near the Flavian Amphitheater using twenty-four elephants.</note> at Rome and kept it suspended; for which work he employed twenty-four elephants. Or like the man who made a labyrinth out of a quarry, <margin>building with tools</margin> or a temple, or anything useful for common needs beyond all expectation.

They report that Nero used prodigious architects to whom nothing came into <margin>Note this</margin> mind except what men could scarcely achieve. These I do not approve of at all. Rather, I would wish that they compose themselves so that in everything they always appear to have wanted to give the first priority to utility and frugality. And even when he has done everything for the sake of ornament, he will nonetheless arrange it so that you would not deny he did it primarily for the sake of utility. I will approve if the most proven principles of the ancients are found in new inventions of works; and new discoveries of wit will not be lacking in them. 

Therefore, in this manner, he will stir up the powers of his intellect through use and the handling of matters that lead to attaining this <term>learning</term> <note>original: "eruditionem." In the Renaissance sense, this implies a deep, humanistic education across many disciplines.</note> with much praise. He will consider it his duty not only to possess that faculty which, if he lacked it, he would not be who he professes to be, but he will also fortify himself with the knowledge and cultivation of all the good arts as much as they pertain to the subject. He will make himself ready and unencumbered, so that he does not lack the assistance of doctrine for more or greater things in this field. He will decide that he must never lay aside his study, never cease from <term>industry</term> <note>original: "industria," implying persistent hard work and diligence.</note>, until he feels he is most like those to whose praises nothing more can be added. 

☞ Nor will he think himself satisfied if there is anything anywhere contributing in any part that he can attain through art and intellect, until he has grasped it, held it deep within, and acted according to his strength, so that the credit for it in himself is reduced to the final form and appearance of its kind.

<header>Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.</header>

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

<margin>Note those things which are especially necessary for the architect to know.</margin>
¶ Now, as to which of the arts contribute—or rather, which are absolutely necessary—to the architect, they are these: Painting and mathematics. As for whether he is learned in the others, I do not greatly trouble myself. For when some say that an architect ought to be a jurist <note>A legal expert or lawyer.</note> because of the laws concerning the warding off of water, the marking of boundaries, the notification of works, and many such things defined by legal interdicts <note>original: "interdicto." In Roman law, an interdict was a specific remedy or order issued by a magistrate.</note> that are dealt with during building, I will not listen. Nor do I demand of him an exact expertise in the stars <note>Astronomy and astrology.</note> simply because it is appropriate to place libraries facing north and baths toward the setting sun. I would not even say he must be a musician just because sounding vessels <note>Alberti refers here to Vitruvius’s description of acoustic jars (echeia) placed in theaters to amplify sound.</note> are placed in theaters; nor a rhetorician because it might help him to have pre-instructed the contractor on what is to be done. Indeed, the consideration, expertise, counsel, and diligence regarding those things of which he is to speak will provide enough for him to speak appropriately, fittingly, and prudently about the matter. That very quality is primary and foremost in eloquence. I do not, of course, want him to be speechless; nor do I want his ears to be completely deaf to harmony. It will be enough if he does not build on public land or on another's property; if he does not obstruct lights; if he does not impose a servitude <note>A legal obligation on a property to benefit another, such as a right of way.</note> through dripping water, drainage, or pathways contrary to the law. It will be enough if he understands the winds, in what part of the world they blow, and by what names they are called. If, however, he should be more highly trained in these matters, I shall not object. But he can no more be without painting and mathematics than a poet can be without voice and syllables. And I am not sure whether it is enough to have mastered them only moderately.

<margin>On painting.</margin>
Regarding myself, I confess this: many conjectures for works have often come into my mind which I greatly approved of at the time; yet, when I reduced them to lines <note>Alberti refers to the process of making architectural drawings.</note>, I found errors in the very part that had most delighted me, and they were errors that required great correction. Again, when I weighed what I had drawn and set about measuring it by number, I recognized and rebuked my own negligence. Finally, when I had committed these same things to models and templates, it sometimes happened that upon re-examining the individual parts, I discovered that even the numbers had deceived me. But I do not wish him to be a Zeuxis <note>A famous Greek painter of the 5th century BCE known for his realism.</note> in painting, or a Nicomachus <note>A mathematician of the 1st/2nd century CE known for his "Introduction to Arithmetic."</note> in numbers, or an Archimedes <note>The famous Greek mathematician and engineer.</note> in the handling of angles and lines. It will be enough if he has mastered those elements of painting which we ourselves have written <note>Alberti is referring to his own earlier treatise, "De pictura" (On Painting), written in 1435.</note>. It is also enough if he has attained that expertise in mathematics which is devised for practical use, mixed of angles, numbers, and lines. Such are the things handed down concerning weights, and the measuring of surfaces and bodies, which they call *podismata* <note>original: "podīſmata." A Greek-derived term for linear measurements or surveying.</note> and *embada* <note>original: "embadaq̃." A Greek-derived term for the measurement of areas or floor space.</note>. By joining study and diligence to these arts, the architect will obtain favor, wealth, and a name for posterity and glory.

¶ It helps not to pass over one thing here that pertains to the architect: he should not freely promise his services to everyone who announces they intend to build...

<summary>Alberti identifies painting and mathematics as the two indispensable arts for an architect, emphasizing that technical drawing and modeling are essential tools for correcting design errors. He dismisses the need for deep expertise in law, music, or rhetoric, arguing that basic practical knowledge in these areas is sufficient.</summary>

# Book IX. On the Ornament of Private Buildings. Folio CLI.

<margin>How the architect's advice is to be shared.</margin>
...must be shown by you. This is something that those who are frivolous and more than enough greedy for glory do in competition. Indeed, I do not know but that one should wait until they ask again and again. For it is necessary that those who profess to want to use your advice believe in you of their own accord. Or why should I step forward to explain my worthy and useful thoughts of my own volition, with no thanks repaid, just so that one or another unskilled person might believe me? For to make you more skilled by my warnings in a matter in which I either relieve you of the greatest expense or contribute greatly to your convenience and pleasure, deserves no mediocre reward. 

Therefore, it is the mark of a wise man to have preserved his dignity; it is enough to have provided faithful advice to the one asking, and refined drawings <note>original: "lineamenta." Alberti uses this term to refer to the linear design, blueprints, or the conceptual structure of a building as opposed to its physical matter.</note>. But if by chance you take it upon yourself to be the supervisor and finisher of the work: it will be difficult for you to avoid all the faults and errors of others—whether committed through inexperience or negligence—being attributed to you alone. 

Such matters should indeed be demanded of skillful, circumspect, and rigid assistants <note>original: "adstitoribus." These are the foremen or site supervisors who manage the daily labor and material handling.</note>: who may attend to what needs doing with diligence, zeal, and assiduity. I would also wish that, as far as is permitted, you take care that your dealings are only with the splendid and those princes of cities most desirous of these things. For works performed for any who are unworthy become cheap. What do you think the authority of the highest men—whom you have judged should be served above all—confers upon you toward the fruit of praise? 

I indeed believe that, besides the fact that we almost all seem somehow, through the perception and judgment of the fortunate, to be far wiser than is common in such matters, I am one who believes that for any architect, those things which they require for finishing the work should be provided appropriately and abundantly. Men of lesser means, since they are very often less able, are also less willing to do this. Add to this what can be seen: where the genius and industry of the craftsman is otherwise equal, and compared here and there in a work; nevertheless, from the price and excellence of the materials of which that work consists, the favor and recognition will be much more accumulated in the one than the other. 

Finally, I warn you never to approach anything rashly out of a desire for glory, especially something unusual and unseen. Everything brought into the light should be weighed and digested down to the smallest detail. For it is a laborious thing to complete with the hands of others what you have devised with your own genius; and as for wanting to use the money of others at your own discretion—who does not understand that this will never be free of complaint? 

Then there is that common vice by which it happens quite often that almost none of the greatest works are without heavy and highly blameworthy errors; I would very much like you to drive this far away from you. How many will there be of all people who do not affect to seem the corrector, moderator, and director of your life, art, morals, and principles? Every great building, due to the brevity of human life and the magnitude of the work, will hardly ever allow that by the same [man it be finished...]

He also highlights the challenges of supervising labor and managing a patron's budget without incurring blame for errors.</summary>

...could be completed by the one who set it down. But we, boastful followers that we are, contend and glory in having innovated something entirely new. From this, it happens that the well-begun works of others are corrupted and finished poorly. I believe, indeed, that one should stand by the intentions of the original authors <note>Alberti is warning against the vanity of architects who change existing plans just to claim originality, often ruining the original design's logic.</note>, who thought those designs out with maturity. For it may be that something moved those first founders which will not be hidden from you as you search more diligently and for a longer time, and as you consult more correctly. Nevertheless, I warn you: whatever you resolve to attempt, do not undertake it except by the counsel or, rather, the decree of the most experienced men. In this way, you will best provide for both the convenience of the building and for your own reputation against the false accusations of detractors. We have spoken of public buildings, of private ones, of the sacred, and of the profane; those pertaining to use, to dignity, and to pleasure. Now, what remains—if any defect has crept into a building, either through the architect’s ignorance and negligence, the injury of time or men, or through sinister and unforeseen accidents—we shall say in what manner it can be corrected and restored. Favor these studies, O men of letters <note>original: "litterati." This refers to the humanist scholars and educated elite to whom Alberti addressed his work.</note>.

# LEON BATTISTA ALBERTI ON THE ART OF BUILDING, BOOK TEN AND THE LAST. WHICH IS ENTITLED THE RESTORATION OF WORKS.

## ¶ On the defects of works. From where they arise. Which can be amended by the architect, and which cannot. Which things make the air heavy. Chapter I.

<margin>Defects of the mind and of the hand.</margin>

If we are next to discuss the correction of defects in works, it is necessary to have considered what and of what sort those defects are which can be amended by the hand of man. For in this way, even physicians <note>original: "physici." Alberti frequently draws parallels between the "health" of a building and the health of a human body, a common trope in Renaissance architectural theory.</note> believe that the greatest part of remedies depends upon the knowledge of the disease. Of the defects of buildings, both public and private, some are, as it were, implanted and innate from the architect; others are brought in from outside. And again, of these, some can be corrected by art and ingenuity, while others cannot be corrected at all. From the architect come those which we showed in the previous book, as if pointing a finger. For some are defects of the mind, and others are of the hand. The mind's defects are: choice, partitioning, distribution, and definition—when they are preposterous, scattered, or confused. The hand's defects, however, are: preparation, collection, construction, and joining—when they are neglected and lazy, and other such faults into which the ill-advised and the negligent easily fall. But as for those defects which are brought in from outside, I think they can hardly be counted, so many and so varied are they; among which is that...

# Book 10. On the Restoration of Works. Folio 152.

<margin>All these lower things grow old with time.</margin>
As they say, **all things are conquered by time** <note>original: "omnia vinci aevo." A common classical sentiment, most famously expressed by Virgil.</note>; and the trials of old age are insidious and exceedingly powerful. Nor can physical bodies struggle against the laws of nature without undergoing old age. Indeed, some even consider the sky itself to be mortal for the reason that it is a body. We feel what the sun’s heat, the freezing of shadows, frost, and the winds can do. 

<margin>Time, the devourer of things, the stubborn subduer.</margin>
Driven by these trials, we see even the hardest flints crack and decay; and from high cliffs, immense rocks are torn away and pushed down by the weather, so that they fall along with a great part of the mountain. Add to these the injuries caused by men. By the gods, I sometimes cannot help but be indignant when I see things destroyed through the negligence—or, to avoid saying something more hateful, I shall say the greed—of some, which even a barbarian or thieving enemy would have spared because of their exceptional dignity. Yet stubborn time, the subduer of things, would easily have allowed them to be eternal. 

Add the sudden accidents of fires; add lightning, earthquakes, the force of waters and floods, and the many prodigious forces of nature that can bring about—daily—unheard of, unhoped for, and incredible things, by which every well-laid plan of the architect is spoiled and disturbed. 

<margin>Note. These things are not unworthy of knowledge, which formerly occurred or appeared.</margin>
Plato used to say that the island of **Atlantis**, no smaller than Epirus <note>Plato’s Timaeus and Critias describe Atlantis as much larger; Alberti or his source may be summarizing or comparing it to specific Greek regions for his readers.</note>, had vanished. We have learned from history that **Bura** and **Helice** <note>Two Greek cities in Achaea that were famously destroyed by an earthquake and tsunami in 373 BC.</note> were destroyed—one by a chasm in the earth, the other by the waves. And that the Tritonian marsh disappeared instantly. Conversely, at Argos, the Stymphalian marsh suddenly overflowed. And near Theramenes, an island with hot waters suddenly grew up. Out of the sea, between Thera and Therasia, a flame burst forth which kept the entire sea boiling and burning for four whole days; immediately afterward, an island of twelve stadia <note>A stadium was an ancient Greek unit of length, roughly 185 meters.</note> emerged, upon which the Rhodians built a temple to Neptune the Protector. 

Elsewhere, mice increased so greatly in number that a plague followed. And ambassadors were sent from the Spaniards to the Senate to seek aid against the injuries caused by "little hares" <note>original: "lepusculorum." This refers to a famous historical incident in which rabbits became a destructive pest in the Balearic Islands, leading the inhabitants to ask Emperor Augustus for military help.</note>. We have collected many such things in that little work entitled *Theogenius* <note>Alberti is referencing one of his own philosophical dialogues, written in the 1430s, which discusses the hardships of life and the vagaries of fortune.</note>. 

<margin>On the restoration of the city.</margin>
But not all defects brought in from elsewhere are of such a kind that they cannot be corrected. Nor will every defect be such that it can always be corrected by the architect. For things that are fundamentally corrupted and thoroughly depraved in every part do not admit of correction. Likewise, those things which are in such a state that they cannot be made better unless they are overturned in all their lines <note>That is, completely demolished and rebuilt from the foundations.</note> are not so much corrected as they are demolished so that you may build something new there. But I do not dwell on this. Let us pursue those things that can be made more convenient by the hand of man. And first, those which are public. The greatest and most extensive of these is the city, or rather, if one prefers to interpret it so, the region of the city. A region in which an unobservant architect has founded a city will perhaps suffer...

### Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

...defects were corrected. For otherwise, a site will either be insufficiently safe against sudden enemy raids, or the climate will be harsh and unhealthy, and the things necessary for use will not be supplied in abundance. We shall, therefore, settle these matters. The journey from Lydia into Cilicia is through a very narrow natural pass between mountains, so that you might say nature intended to create a gate for the region. In the throats of the ridge—which the Greeks call *pylae* <note>original: "pilas," a Latinization of the Greek word for "gates," often used for narrow mountain passes like the famous Thermopylae.</note>—there is also a path which three armed men could guard; the way is steep with frequent wandering streams that flow from the roots of the mountains. There are similar "saws" <note>original: "serræ," a term used for jagged, saw-toothed mountain ridges.</note> in Picenum, and those commonly called the Fossombrone, and many others elsewhere. But these naturally fortified entrances are not available everywhere at our whim; yet we seem <margin>Note these wonders.</margin> to be able to imitate nature in many respects. Indeed, the most prudent ancients performed these wonders in many places. For they prepared things in such a way as to render a region fortified against enemy raids. I shall recount very briefly from the deeds of the most excellent princes those things which are relevant to the matter. <margin>I shall recount the works.</margin> <margin>Artaxerxes.</margin> At the Euphrates, Artaxerxes excluded the enemy from his presence with a ditch sixty feet wide and ten miles long. The Caesars—among whom was <margin>Hadrian.</margin> Hadrian—built a wall eighty miles long through Britain to separate the barbarians from the Roman fields. <margin>Antoninus.</margin> Antoninus Pius also built a turf wall through the same island. Severus, after him, led a rampart <margin>Severus.</margin> across the island to the shores of the ocean for one hundred and twenty-two miles. In the Margian region of India, <margin>Antiochus</margin> Antiochus Soter—at the place where he founded Antioch—surrounded the perimeter of the region with a wall fifteen hundred stadia <note>A stadium was an ancient unit of length; 1,500 stadia is roughly 170 miles.</note> long. <margin>Sesostris.</margin> Sesostris <note>The OCR reads "Seofofis," likely a transcription error for the legendary Egyptian king Sesostris.</note> also built a wall on the side of Egypt toward Arabia, from Pelusium to the City of the Sun (which they call Thebes), through deserted places, likewise fifteen hundred stadia long. When Neritos had been continuous with Leucas, they cut through the isthmus and brought in the sea to make it an island. But the Chalcidians and Boeotians built a dike across the Euripus to join Euboea to Boeotia, so that one might be a help to the other. <margin>Alexander</margin> Near the Oxus River, Alexander founded six towns not far from each other, so that if harassed by sudden enemies, reinforcements would not have to be sought from afar. <margin>What "tyrses" are</margin> *Tyrses* <note>original: "tyrses," from the Greek word for a tower or turreted structure.</note> is the name given to defenses fortified with a high rampart, very similar to castles, which were used everywhere against the approach of enemies. <margin>Persians.</margin> The Persians had blocked the Tigris River by throwing in cataracts <note>In this context, cataracts refers to man-made weirs or obstructions designed to prevent enemy ships from sailing upstream.</note> so that no ship could sail up in a hostile manner. Alexander destroyed them, saying that it was the work of a cowardly spirit; he urged them instead to trust in the strength of their courage. There are those who, by bringing in a large quantity of water, made a region resemble Arabia, which they say was most highly fortified against enemy entry by marshes and stagnant pools from the Euphrates.

# Book 10. On the Restoration of Works.

...the region, therefore, they rendered fortified by such defenses against the enemy. By these same arts they ensured that the enemy's region was indeed weaker. 

What things they are that make the climate heavy and unhealthy, <margin>What things make the climate heavy.</margin> we have discussed more at length in their own place <note>Alberti refers here to Book I of this treatise, where he discusses site selection and environmental health.</note>: if you collect them, you will find they fall into these general kinds. For either immoderate suns, or raw shadows, or heavy blasts of wind will be encountered; or the earth will be infected by evil vapors; or there will be things from the sky itself which bring a harmful evil. Men believe the climate can hardly be corrected by any human arts, unless that which they write brings help: that by appeasing the high gods, or following the warnings of the gods—such as the nail driven by a consul <note>original: "clavo per consulem affixo." This refers to the ancient Roman ritual of the *Clavus Annalis*, where a nail was driven into the wall of the Temple of Jupiter to ward off plagues or mark time during crises.</note>—sharp plagues have sometimes been calmed. 

On the other hand, for the inhabitants of towns and villas, there will be no lack of things that might help against suns and winds. But we have found nothing that sufficiently helps an entire region; though I would not deny that defects brought from the air can be corrected in large part when it happens that noxious vapors are removed from the earth. For that reason, I will proceed with those matters. 

Whether by the power of the sun or by a heat conceived in its innermost vitals, the earth breathes out those two things: moist breath <term>anhelitus (moist exhalation)</term>, which, when raised into the air, is condensed by the cold into rain and snow; and dry spirit <term>spiritus (dry exhalation)</term>, by which they believe it happens that the impulses of the winds are moved. Let it be agreed among us that both breathe out from the earth; and just as we perceive the vapors exhaled from the bodies of living creatures to taste of the nature of the body from which they are poured out—from a pestilential one, pestiferous; from a fragrant one, sweet, and so forth. Sometimes it is also evident that a sweat or vapor which might otherwise be very little troublesome by its own nature, yet infected by the stench of clothing, smells foully. So it is in the earth. For a field that is neither well covered with water nor sufficiently dry, but becomes muddy from both, will for many reasons pour out infected and harmful breaths and spirits. 

And let this indeed be relevant to the matter. For where the sea is deep, we perceive cold waves being rolled, but in other places warm ones. They say this happens because the heat of the sun cannot be submerged more deeply or penetrate further. And just as if you happen to dip red-hot, glowing iron into oil, and if there is then only a little oil, it will immediately stir up acrid <margin>☛</margin> and turbulent smoke. If, however, a great deal of oil floats above it, it will be extinguished and will not produce smoke. 

But we shall proceed with these matters with the brevity we began. Servius <note>Servius was a famous 4th-century commentator on Virgil; Alberti often cites him for historical and mythological anecdotes.</note> writes that after a marsh near a certain town was dried up, and a pestilence had arisen from that act, Apollo was asked for advice, and he told them to dry it out completely. Near Tempe, water stood in a wide stagnation; <margin>Hydra.</margin> Hercules cleansed it by drawing a ditch. And the Hydra—the place from which they say eruptions of water devastated the nearby city—he burned out <note>Alberti provides a rationalist interpretation of the Myth of the Lernaean Hydra, suggesting it was actually a series of troublesome water springs or a swamp that Hercules "cured" through drainage and fire.</note>, as they tell it; in...

# Leon Battista Alberti: On the Art of Building

<margin>Mazara.</margin>
They say it happened that once the superfluous moisture was consumed and the soil made dense, the channels of the overflowing trickles were worn away. Formerly, the Nile had risen more than was right; without the silt, many and various creatures remained stuck together in the mud. When the soil dried, they rotted: from this, a great plague spread. In the city under Mount Argeus, says Strabo <note>Strabo (c. 64 BC – 24 AD) was a Greek geographer whose work was a primary source for Renaissance thinkers like Alberti.</note>, Mazara <note>A city in Sicily, modern Mazara del Vallo.</note> indeed abounds in good waters; but if in summer there is no path for them to flow, they make the air unhealthy and pestilential. Likewise in Libya to the north, and also in Ethiopia, it does not rain; because of this, lakes often become muddy due to drought. For that reason, not only do other such creatures arise from corruption, but especially a huge abundance of locusts prevails. Against such stenches and the power of rot, both remedies of Hercules <note>Alberti interprets the mythical labors of Hercules—specifically the cleaning of the Augean stables and the slaying of the Hydra—as allegories for hydraulic engineering: drainage and the "fire" of the sun.</note> will be very conveniently applied: first, a ditch is dug so that the soil does not become muddy from the delay of stagnant water; next, it is opened to the sun. For we interpret the use of fire by Hercules as the sun itself. And it helps to fill the area with rock, earth, or sand. By what means you can easily fill the hollows of stagnant waters with sand from a river will be told in its proper place. 

<margin>Ravenna</margin>
Strabo says that Ravenna, which in his time was flooded by the sea, was accustomed to be affected by a foul odor; yet the air was not pestilential. He wonders why this is: perhaps it is for the same reason they say occurs in the cities of Venice, because the surrounding marshes, driven by the winds and the tide of the sea, never stay still. They say Alexandria was very similar to this; but there, during the summer, the rising of the Nile removed that defect. We are therefore warned by nature as to what must be done. For it will help either to dry the land out completely, or to make it well-watered by letting in streams, currents, or the sea; or finally, to dig out the earth down to the innermost springs of the water. Enough on these matters.

### ¶ Chapter II. On things necessary for use, and especially water, which our ancestors always held in high regard; also the variety of waters.

Now, if anything is lacking for the necessity of use, let us provide so that it is not missing. I will not seek far for what things are necessary: they are ready at hand. Food, clothing, shelter, and especially water. Thales of Miletus <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher often cited as the first to propose a single underlying substance for the world—water.</note> said that water was the principle of things and of human society. Aristobolus says he saw more than a thousand villages 
<margin>See the utility of water.</margin> 
deserted because the Indus river had diverted elsewhere. Indeed, I do not deny that water is like food for the heat in living creatures, and the nourishment of life. Or why should I mention plants, or other things which mortals use? I believe that of all things that grow and take shape on earth, if you take away water, they would become nothing. Near the Euphrates, they drive the flocks away from grazing because they grow too fat on meadows that are more than sufficiently fertile; they believe the cause of this is...

<margin>Custom of the Spartans</margin>
Xenophon <note>Xenophon (c. 430–354 BC) was an Athenian historian and student of Socrates.</note> mentions that, for the sake of dignity, the Kings of the Spartans were granted a pond of water before the doors in front of their house. Rivers or springs will not always be available to lead water from. Alexander ordered wells to be dug along the Persian sea and shore so that he could water his fleet. In Epirus <note>A region in northwestern Greece.</note> there is a sacred spring in which burning torches are extinguished if plunged in, but once extinguished, they catch fire again. In Eleusis <note>The site of the famous Eleusinian Mysteries near Athens.</note>, a spring leaps at the sound of flutes. Foreign animals, if they drink from the Indus, change their colors. On the shore of the Red Sea <note>original: "maris Erytrei"</note> there is also a spring; if sheep drink from it, they immediately change their fleece to a black color. There are also the springs of the Laodiceans, near which any four-footed beast conceived is born with a yellow <term>giluo<gloss>a pale yellow or tawny color, similar to the color of honey or raw silk</gloss></term> color. In the territory of Gadara <note>original: "agro cadareno"; Gadara was a city in the Decapolis, modern Jordan.</note>, there is water which, if a beast tastes it, it loses its hair and hooves. Near the Hyrcanian Sea <note>The ancient name for the Caspian Sea.</note> there is a lake; anyone washed in it falls into the mange <note>original: "scabiem", referring to a skin irritation or itch</note>, and is cured only by oil. In Susa <note>An ancient city in Persia.</note> there is water that causes teeth to fall out. At the Zelonian pool <note>Possibly a reference to Zeleia in the Troad, mentioned by classical authors for its springs.</note> there is a spring from which people become sterile, and soon another nearby from which they are rendered fertile. And in Chios, one that makes people foolish. And elsewhere, water that—not just when drunk, but even when tasted—dissolves a person into death through laughter. There is even one that kills if you merely wash in it. And in Arcadia at Nonacris <note>Nonacris was the site of the legendary River Styx, which ancient writers claimed could dissolve any vessel except one made of a horse's hoof.</note>, there is a kind of water that is otherwise very pure, but it possesses such a venomous power that it cannot be contained by any metal vessel. And on the contrary, there are waters that restore good health: those of Puteoli, Sena <note>original: "fenenses", likely referring to the waters of Siena (Sena Julia)</note>, Volterra, Bologna, and those celebrated throughout Italy. But even greater is what they report of Corsica—that there was water which could knit broken bones back together, and by which the worst poisons were cured. There are others elsewhere that inspire good character and a prophetic spirit. Likewise in Corsica, there is a spring useful for the eyes; but if any thief denies a theft under oath in its presence and washes his eyes, he is struck blind. So much for these things. Furthermore, in some places water is found that is neither entirely pure nor entirely impure. For this reason, throughout Apulia <note>A dry region in southeastern Italy.</note>, they are accustomed to catch and store rainwater in cisterns.

## ¶ Four things to be considered regarding water / And from where it is generated, or breaks forth, or to where it flows.

### Chapter III.

Therefore, there are four things regarding water that pertain to the work: how you find it, how you convey it, how you select it, and how you preserve it. We must speak of these. But some things must first be surveyed which pertain to the general use of waters. I believe that water cannot be held except in a vessel, and I agree with those who, moved by this fact, assert that the sea is a certain immense vessel; and by similar reasoning, they interpret a river also to be a very long vessel. But the difference is that in these, waters flow and move by their own nature without any external force being applied. Others would easily remain still, were they not agitated by the buffeting of the winds. I shall not pursue here those questions of the philosophers—whether waters seek the sea as if it were a place of rest...

# Book 10. On the Restoration of Works.

...lest it happen by the moon, as the sea increases and decreases by turns <note>Alberti is referring to the tidal influence of the moon, which he dismisses as irrelevant to his current mechanical point.</note>. For these will contribute nothing to our purpose. This must not be overlooked, which we perceive with our own eyes: that water by nature seeks the depths; nor does it allow air to be anywhere lower than itself; <margin>The nature of water</margin> and it hates the mixing of all bodies, whether lighter or heavier than itself; and the more you prevent it from using its strength, the more stubbornly it struggles against it and pushes forward; nor does it rest until it achieves, as much as it can, that which it seeks for its repose. Once it has gained the seats where it may rest, it is content with itself alone, and spurns all other mixtures. It balances its top surface to an equal level of height at the edge and extreme lips. And I remember from <margin>Note from Plutarch</margin> Plutarch <note>Plutarch (c. 46 – 119 AD) was a Greek philosopher and biographer; Alberti refers here to his "Natural Questions."</note> what also pertains to waters. For he asked whether, when the earth is dug into, water drips in like blood into a wound; or rather, whether it flows together like milk gradually generated in a nurse’s breasts. There are those who assert that waters which flow perennially are not poured out as if received from a vessel, but are generated at every moment in the places from which they flow, out of the air—not indeed from all air, but from that which is finally more ready to become vapor. For they say the earth, and especially mountains, is like a sponge filled with passages, through which the conceived air is thickened by cold and condensed. They think this is proven both by other signs and especially by this: ☞ that they see even the greatest rivers rise from the greatest mountains. Others do not entirely acquiesce to the authority of these men. For they say that while there are many others, the Pyramus <note>A major river in Anatolia (modern Ceyhan River in Turkey), which Alberti notes rises in a plain rather than a mountain.</note> is a river by no means small—it is indeed navigable—and yet it does not rise from mountains, but in the middle of a plain. Therefore, he who says the earth drinks in the moisture of rains—which indeed penetrate by their own weight and subtlety, and drip into empty places—will perhaps be least refuted. For one can indeed see regions where rains are very rare lack water entirely. They say Libya was called, as it were, "lipygius" <note>original: "lipygiā"; Alberti is using a fanciful etymology likely derived from the Greek "leipein" (to lack) and "ge" (earth/land).</note> because it rarely rains there; therefore it lacks water. And who will deny that the most abundant waters are found where it has rained the most? It also helps in considering the matter that we see a person digging a well is not provided with water until they have descended to the level <term>libramentū<gloss>the horizontal level or balance point, often used in Roman engineering to describe the water table or the slope of an aqueduct</gloss></term> of a river. ...nor would I deny that the moisture of the nocturnal air is drawn in by the light earth, or enters spontaneously through passages and can easily be turned into liquid. Nevertheless, I have nothing sufficiently established in my mind as to what I should affirm; I find such various accounts of these matters among writers, and so many and diverse observations offer themselves to one considering the subject. 

Indeed, it is well known that in many places, either by earthquake or spontaneously, springs have suddenly erupted and flowed for a long time, only to fail at various seasons, so that some vanished during the heat of summer and others during winter; yet after these springs had dried up, they again overflowed with an abundance of water. It is also known that spring waters have flowed sweet not only from the earth but even from the middle of the waves of the sea <note>Alberti refers here to submarine freshwater springs, a phenomenon noted by ancient mariners.</note>. They even affirm that water flows abundantly from plants themselves. 

In a certain island among those said to rise by chance <note>This likely refers to the "Fortunate Isles" or Canary Islands, known in antiquity for "raining trees" (the Til tree), which condensed water from mist.</note>, they say there are stalks the size of trees; from those which are black, you may press a bitter juice, but from the white ones, pure water drips out, most suitable for drinking. And marvelous is what Strabo <note>Strabo (c. 64 BC – 24 AD) was a Greek geographer whose works were rediscovered in the Renaissance.</note>, truly a grave author, writes: that in the mountains of Armenia, animals are found—worms born in the middle of the snow—which are full of the best drinking water. Near Fiesole, and even near Urbino, although they are mountain cities, water is immediately at hand for those who dig; this is because the ground is stony and the rocks are bound together with clay. There are also clods of earth that contain the purest water within the folds of their outer skin. Having learned these things, it is certainly not easy to know the ways of nature, and the matter is very obscure.

### ¶ Chapter IV. Signs for finding hidden water, and the double method of digging.

**R**eturning to the matter at hand: you shall find hidden waters by certain signs. These signs will be provided by the shape and appearance of the place, the type of earth where you seek the water, and certain methods discovered by human ingenuity. Nature is such that any place which is winding and shaped like a hollow seems to be a vessel prepared for holding water. 

Where the sun's rays are strongest—because the moisture there is dried up by the heat—waters will be found either meager or non-existent; or if any finally appear in the plains, they will be heavy, sluggish, and salty. To the North <note>original: "septentrio"</note> in the mountains, and where there is the deepest shade, water is found very readily. Mountains that remain covered in snow for a long time offer the richest waters. 

I have noticed that mountains which have a level meadow at their summit never fail to provide water. And you will find that almost all rivers arise from no other place than such locations. I have also noticed that springs do not gush forth anywhere except where they have beneath and around them a soil of the earth that is whole and solid; but above them, either a sinking plain lies, or they are covered by earth that is thin and loose. If you consider the matter, you will not deny that the water flows out like water collected in the side of a broken basin. Hence it is that denser earth is less...

Aemilius, when he had his army at Mount Olympus and they suffered from a lack of water, found it by being alerted by the greenness of the forests. <margin>Signs of hidden water.</margin>
There are also closer signs that water is beneath in places where things grow and thrive that desire water or are sustained by it: willow thickets, <term>camuscula</term> <note>A type of reed or water-loving shrub.</note>, rushes, ivy, and those things which cannot reach their full size except with much nourishment from moisture. Columella <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella, a Roman writer on agriculture.</note> says that the earth which nourishes leafy vines, or especially that which bears dwarf elder, trefoil, and wild plum, provides good soil and sweet veins of water. Then also an abundance of little frogs and worms, and gnats and swarms of tiny winged insects where they gather together in flight, indicate that water is hidden there.

<margin>By what signs water is sought.</margin>
These are the things which the sharp-sightedness of the mind has tracked down. For investigators have noticed that all the rest of the earth, and especially the mountains, are composed of <term>cutes</term> <note>Literally "skins"; Alberti uses this term to describe geological strata or layers of rock and soil.</note> like <term>paginas</term> <note>Literally "pages"; here referring to the flat, layered nature of sedimentary rock.</note>, some denser, others rarer, others thinner. And in the mountains they noticed that these layers were placed one upon the other and heaped up, so that externally the orders of the heaps and the lines of compaction are drawn from right to left according to a level; but inward toward the center of the mountain, the layers slope down in an oblique line, though the entire top surface is level, but their course and succession is not continued to the very bottom. For at about every hundred feet in a transverse descent, the broken layers sink down in steps. And subsequently, with an interruption of the orders of this kind, they run in a similar gradation all the way to the centers of the mountain from both sides of the mountain. Therefore, having observed these things, men of sharp intellect easily understood that waters—whether generated within or from rain—are caught between the "skins" and the joints of the "pages," from which they make the inner parts of the mountain wet. From this they took the argument to seek the hidden waters by digging into the mountain, especially from that place where the descent of the gradations and the lines of the layers meet one another. This place is most ready there where the <term>musculi</term> <note>Literally "muscles"; Alberti’s term for the undulating spurs or slopes of a mountain range.</note> of the mountains, clinging to one another, have formed some hollow. Furthermore, they discovered that the layers are of various and diverse nature among themselves for soaking up or discharging...

# Leon Battista Alberti: On the Art of Building

...to be drunk. Indeed, red rocks are almost never found without being watery, but they are accustomed to deceive because they crumble through the fissures with which that type of stone abounds. Every flint stone that is "juicy" and active <note>The term "juicy" (succosum) likely refers to stone that feels damp or fresh from the quarry, rather than dry and weathered.</note>, which is broken at the foot of a mountain and is quite rough, will easily yield water. Even thin earth yields a plenty of water, but it is of a bad flavor.

However, coarse gravel and the sand which is called <term>carbunculus</term> <note>original: "carbunculus"; a type of reddish, burnt-looking volcanic sand or grit highly prized by Roman builders for its drainage and health properties.</note> provide waters that are not at all uncertain, very healthy, and perennial. The opposite occurs in chalk, for since it is too dense, it does not yield water from its own substance, but it holds "adventitious" <note>Water that has come from elsewhere, such as rain or runoff, rather than a natural spring source.</note> water. In common sand, waters are found to be very meager and muddy, and they settle deep down. From clay, water flows thinly, but it is sweeter than the others. From <term>tufa</term> <note>A porous limestone common in Italy.</note>, it is colder. From black earth, it is clearer. 

In gravel, indeed, if it be looser, the hope of digging is not certain. But where it begins to be denser deeper down, it is not entirely uncertain. <margin>Note</margin> In both cases, where water is found, it is considered to have a good flavor. 

Skill having also been applied, they have handed down a refined method to recognize the very place where a vein lies beneath. For they advise searching in this way: When the sky is clear, in the morning at dawn, lie face down with your chin braced against the ground itself. From there, scan the surrounding area on all sides: if you see rising vapors anywhere rippling the air, like the breath of men in the cold of winter, believe that water is not lacking there.

But to be more certain, dig a pit in that place four cubits deep and wide. In it, around sunset, place either a pottery shard recently taken from the furnace, or a fleece of unwashed wool, or an unbaked clay pot, or a bare bronze vessel turned upside down and smeared with oil; then cover the pit with boards and spread earth over it. The next morning, if much weight has been added to the shard; if the wool is soaked; if the unbaked clay is damp; if drops hang clinging to the vessel; likewise, if a burning lamp shut in there has consumed less oil; or if a fire built there makes the earth smoke: without a doubt, waters will not be lacking. 

At what time these things are more conducive to being done, they have not sufficiently explained. But elsewhere among writers, I find this: <margin>On the nature of the Dog Days.</margin> during the rising of the Dog Star <note>The "canicula" or Sirius; the "Dog Days" (late July/August) were traditionally associated with heat and specific environmental changes.</note>, the earth and the bodies of living things become much more moist. From which it happens that during those days, trees become quite damp under their bark from an abundance of moisture. Also during that time, the bowels are loosened in men, and because of the excessive moistening of bodies, frequent fevers infest; waters also emerge more than usual during that time. 

Theophrastus <note>A Greek successor to Aristotle, famous for his works on botany and natural signs.</note> thinks the causes of this are the south winds that blow then, which are by their nature wet and misty. Aristotle asserted that the earth is forced to emit vapors by the innate fire that is mixed within its bowels. If these things are so, those times will surely be suitable in which these fires are either stronger, or...

# Book 10. On the Restoration of Works.

...will be compressed by a great deal of moisture; or where the earth itself has not been completely dried and scorched. And indeed, the times of year that are approved by me for this task are: spring in drier places, and autumn in more shaded ones. Therefore, once hope has been confirmed by these signs which we have mentioned, we shall proceed to dig. <margin>About digging.</margin> Digging will be of two kinds. For one is a well [sunk] into the depth; the other is a <term>tunnel</term> <note>original: "cuniculus"; a horizontal gallery or underground channel.</note> [extended] in length. Those digging a well are sometimes in danger. This happens either from a bad vapor rising, or from the sides of the excavation collapsing. Among the ancients, slaves condemned for some crime were sent to the metal mines, where they would be finished off in a short time by the pestilence of the air. We are advised thus against vapors: let us move the air by constant ventilation, and let us employ burning lamps. <margin>Pestilential vapor which must be avoided.</margin> By which, if by chance the vapor is light, the vapor is consumed by the flames. If it is heavier: then let the diggers have a means by which, being protected, they may flee the harmful evil in a timely manner. <margin>How the harmful evil in the well is avoided.</margin> For when a heavy vapor rushes in, the flame will be extinguished. But if the vapors should rush in or persist, they say to dig venting passages <note>original: "aestuaria"; here referring to air-shafts or side-vents to allow gas to escape.</note> on both sides, to the right and the left, through which the evil force of the vapor may most freely breathe out. Against the danger of collapse, let the work be conducted thus: First, on the ground where you intend to dig the well, lay down a marble ring or one made of very firm material, as large as you want the width of the well to be. That will be for you the base for raising the work. Upon this, therefore, build up the sides of the well three cubits high, and let it dry. When it has dried, dig out the interior of the well and remove what is inside. It will happen that by as much as one deepens the excavation, by so much the masonry work will press itself down and seek the bottom. Then, by additions to both the excavation and the masonry, you will safely reach whatever depth you wish. There are some who wish the wall of the well to be built without <term>mortar</term> <note>original: "harenato"; a sand-and-lime mixture used to bind stones.</note>, <margin>Structure of a well.</margin> so that the veins of water are not obstructed. Others order a triple wall to be built, so that the water might distill more clearly from the very bottom. But it is of the greatest importance in what place you dig. For since the earth has various layers one upon another, it happens that sometimes rainwater is contained under packed earth in the first denser layer found; we shall reject that as being impure. And on the contrary, it will sometimes happen that where water was found, as you proceed to excavate deeper, it vanishes and is lost from sight. This happens for the reason that you have pierced the bottom of the vessel in which it was contained. For which reason, those who finish a well with a structure of this sort are very pleasing: as if they were going to make a cask, they fortify the interior of the excavated well with a double casing of wooden rings and planks, so that there is a space of a cubit between the two; and into that gap which is between the casings themselves, they pour a slurry of larger gravel, or rather of flint or marble fragments...

### ¶ On the Qualities of Water: Which are Healthier, or Best, or the Opposite. Chapter 5.

<margin>Various notes on waters.</margin> **O**nce waters have been found, let them not be given over rashly to human use; for while a plenty of water is desired for cities not only for drinking, but also for bathing, for gardens, for tanners, for fullers <note>workers who clean and thicken cloth</note>, and for sewers—and especially so that it may be abundantly supplied in the sudden event of fires—the best water must certainly be selected for drinking. The rest may finally be assigned according to what suits each purpose. Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle, known for his work on plants.</note> used to say that the colder the water, the more beneficial it is for plants; and also it is well known that muddy and turbulent water—especially that which flows down from fertile soil—makes a field more productive. Horses are not delighted by the purest waters; they grow fat on mossy and lukewarm ones. For fullers, the <term>rawest</term> <note>original: "crudissimae"; likely referring to 'hard' water containing minerals that reacted with soaps or dyes.</note> waters are highly valued.

Among the <term>natural philosophers</term> <note>original: "physicos"</note>, I find this: the necessity of water for maintaining the life of mortals is twofold—one, to quench thirst; the other, to act as a vehicle to carry the nutrients consumed during eating into the veins, so that the purified and digested juice may then be driven into the limbs. And they say thirst is a certain craving for moisture, especially cold moisture. And they think that cold waters, especially after dinners, strengthen the stomach in those who are healthy. However, waters that are a little too icy can induce a numbness even in the strong, striking the diaphragm, shaking the nerves, and extinguishing the digestive power through <term>indigestion</term> <note>original: "cruditate"; a lack of "cooking" or processing of food in the stomach.</note>.

<margin>The Oxus River is most unhealthy for drinking.</margin> The River Oxus <note>The Amu Darya in Central Asia.</note>, because it is always turbulent, is for that reason most unhealthy for drinking. Severe fevers seize the inhabitants of Rome, stirred up partly by the inconsistency of the air, partly by the nocturnal vapors of the river, and partly also by the afternoon winds. For during the summer, at the <term>ninth hour</term> <note>Approximately 3:00 PM.</note> of the day, when bodies are most burning with heat, these winds blow cold and constrict the veins. But in my opinion, both the fevers and almost all bad diseases arise for the most part from the waters of the Tiber, which nearly everyone...

<margin>The tiered quality of waters.</margin>
I return to the matter. Let us investigate the best water. Of waters, the physician Celsus <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus, a famous Roman medical writer from the 1st century AD.</note> established the following: that rainwater is the lightest. In the second place, spring water. In the third, flowing water. In the fourth, well water. In the last place, that which is made from melted snow or ice. Heavier than these is water from a lake. But the worst of all is that from a swamp. Below Mount Argus, the city of Mazara <note>A city in Sicily, modern Mazara del Vallo.</note> abounds in waters that are otherwise good; but because in summer they have no place to flow, they are unhealthy and pestilential. Indeed, all experts are of the opinion that water by its nature is an unmixed and simple substance, in which coldness and moisture reside. Therefore, we shall call that water the best which is least foreign to its own nature and least corrupted. For unless it is perfectly pure and free from any mixture of sluggishness and from every defect of taste and smell, impure water will undoubtedly be most harmful to health, 
<margin>Defects from water</margin>
by obstructing the internal passages—as they say, the paths of underlying growths—by clogging the veins with mud, and by blocking and suffocating the spirits <note>In ancient medicine, "spirits" (spiritus) were vital substances or "breaths" that flowed through the body to sustain life and movement.</note> that serve life. 
<margin>Underlying results.</margin>
This is why they say that rain—which sometimes results from the most delicate vapors being gathered together—is rightly the best of all. Provided it does not have this defect: that when stored, it easily putrefies and becomes infected with a stench, and having become thicker, it induces hardness of the bowels <note>constipation</note>. Some have said this happens because waters are drawn up by the clouds from too many various and diverse sources mixed into one: for instance, from the sea, into which every kind of spring flows; and they say nothing can be more easily or readily prone to corruption than a confused mixture of dissimilar things. The confused juice of many different grapes mixed into one cannot endure age. 
<margin>The Law of the Hebrews concerning seeds.</margin>
Among the Hebrews, there had been a law <note>A reference to the Biblical prohibition against mixing different types of seeds, as found in Leviticus 19:19.</note> that they should not sow any seeds except those that were selected and simple, indicating that nature utterly abhors the mixing of dissimilar things. However, those who agree with Aristotle—and who believe that vapors drawn from the earth are first condensed into a sort of mist in the cold part of the air, and then rain down in drops—feel differently. Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle, known as the "father of botany."</note> used to say that cultivated trees fall into disease more quickly than wild ones. For the wild ones, stiff with an untamed hardness, resist external impressions more sharply. But these others, by their own tenderness, show themselves weak in resistance, since they have been tamed into obedience by discipline <note>that is, the "discipline" of agriculture and cultivation</note>. They are led to a similar conclusion regarding waters: that the more "tender" you make them—to use his words—the more "passible" <note>original: "passibiliores"; easily acted upon or susceptible to change.</note> they are. And from this they assert that boiled waters, made milder by fire, cool down very quickly and boil again very quickly. 
<margin>Spring, rain, and well water.</margin>
But enough about rainwater. Next to these, everyone approves of springs. But those who prefer rivers to springs say this: "For what else is a river..."

## Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

We say that the abundance and flow of many springs are joined into a single collection, matured indeed by the sun, motion, and the winds. They argue that a well is also a spring, but a deeper one. If we do not deny that the sun’s ray contributes something to waters, it is obvious which of these would be "rawer" <note>original: "crudior"; in ancient and Renaissance physics, "raw" water was considered cold and "undigested" by environmental heat, making it heavier or less healthy than "cooked" or refined water.</note>. Unless, perhaps, we agree that a fiery spirit dwells within the bowels of the earth, by which subterranean waters are "cooked." Aristotle says that well waters become lukewarm in summer after midday. There are those who assert that well waters are not actually cold in summer but only seem so in comparison to the scorching air. Furthermore, contrary to the long-standing opinion of many, it can be proven by experiment that water drawn very recently does not leave dew <note>The author is discussing condensation; he argues that if the glass is clean and not greasy, the "sweat" or dew won't form, challenging the idea that the water is inherently "cold" or exhaling moisture.</note> if the vessel into which it is received is sufficiently clean and not greasy. 

But among the first principles from which all things are composed—since two are said to be "masculine" according to the opinion of the Pythagoreans, namely heat and cold <margin>Heat and cold: two males.</margin>—it is the nature and power of heat to penetrate, dissolve, break apart, and draw moisture to itself to consume it. Cold, however, compresses, binds, forces into hardness, and shapes. Yet from both of these, a nearly equal effect flows in some part, especially in waters, if they are present immoderately or more than is sufficient. For both cause nearly equal consumption of the thinnest parts, from which the dryness of "burning" follows. It is from this that we say trees are scorched by heat and also scorched by cold. This is because, when the softer parts are consumed and worn away by frost or by the sun, we see the material left behind as rough and parched. Thus, by a similar reasoning, waters are rendered sluggish by the sun and more "ashy" <note>original: "cinereofiores"; likely referring to a cloudy, gray, or sediment-heavy quality.</note> by frost. 

But among approved waters, there is yet another difference. For with rainwater, it matters greatly at what time of year, at what hour of the day, during which rain, and with which wind blowing you collected it; also in what place you stored it and how long it has been kept. They believe that waters given from the sky after the winter solstice are heavier. They assert that what is collected during the winter is sweeter than what is gathered in summer. <margin>The first rains after the Dog Days are bitter and pestilential.</margin> The first rains after the Dog Days <note>original: "caniculam"; the "Dog Days" refer to the hottest period of summer associated with the rising of the star Sirius.</note> are bitter and pestilential. For they are infected by the scorched mixtures of the earth; and they say the earth tastes of bitterness for the reason that it has been parched by the sun. Hence it is that they prefer water collected from roofs over that from a courtyard; and they consider the water collected from roofs after the first rain has washed them to be not at all unhealthy. The physicists who wrote in the Punic <note>original: "punica"; refers to the Carthaginian language or authors, likely referencing ancient agricultural writers such as Mago.</note> tongue affirm this: <margin>Thunderstorm rain is impure with saltiness.</margin> Rain that falls during the summer, especially with thunder, is impure and harmful due to its saltiness. Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle, known for his works on natural history.</note> considers night rain to be superior to day rain. Of these, they think the healthiest is that which falls while the North Wind <note>original: "aquilone"; the North Wind was traditionally viewed as bringing dry, healthy, and purifying air.</note> is blowing. Columella <note>A Roman authority on agriculture.</note> says that rainwater will be pure.

<summary>Alberti explores the physical nature of water, citing classical authorities to explain how heat, cold, and seasonal timing affect its purity and healthfulness. He emphasizes that rainwater's quality depends on factors like wind direction, time of day, and whether it has been filtered by previous rainfall.</summary>

# Book 10. On the Restoration of Buildings. Folio 159.

...it is not worst if it is led through earthenware pipes into a covered cistern. For under the open sky and the sun, water easily spoils; even when kept in a wooden vessel, it is prone to defects. The waters of springs also differ among themselves: those indeed <margin>Spring waters</margin> which gush from the roots of hillsides were thought by **Hippocrates** <note>Hippocrates of Cos (c. 460 – c. 370 BC), the "Father of Medicine," who wrote extensively on the relationship between environment and health in "Airs, Waters, Places."</note> to be the best of all. Furthermore, the ancients decided this concerning springs: that in the first place they held the spring which faces the north, or which faces the sun rising at the equinox. In the last place they put the spring which faces the south. <margin>Which springs are best.</margin> They think those which face the winter sunrises are next to the best; and they do not always entirely reject those facing the west. In whatever place the dew is accustomed to be both most abundant and very light, that place will indeed provide the sweetest waters. For dew is not sprinkled except in quiet, pure places with temperate air.

**Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle, often called the "Father of Botany."</note> believes that water is tainted by the earth no differently than the juice in the fruits of vines and trees: for all these taste of the earth through which they have flowed and of those things to which their roots are joined. The ancients said that as many types of wine are to be had as there are types of soil where the vine is planted. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the "Natural History."</note> used to say that Paduan wines taste of willow, because the people there "marry" their vines to willow trees. **Cato** <note>Cato the Elder, Roman statesman and author of "De Agricultura."</note> teaches that vines can be medicated with the herb hellebore <note>original: "veratro"; a plant used in antiquity as a powerful purgative.</note> to move the bowels without danger, by throwing bundles of that herb to the roots after the soil has been cleared away.

From this comes the opinion that waters which erupt from living rock <note>original: "petra rediviva"; natural, unbroken stone as opposed to loose or processed stone.</note> are to be preferred over those which groan from the muddy depths. But he considers that water to surpass all others which has distilled from the kind of earth which, if you mix it into a basin of water so that it becomes muddy, will settle immediately once the motion has ceased. Such earth leaves the water entirely pure in color, taste, and smell. For the same reason, **Columella** <note>A prominent Roman writer on agriculture.</note> thought that waters which tumble headlong over rocks were the best, because they are not tainted by foreign mixtures. However, not all water that flows over rocks is of the kind that we should highly recommend. For if it runs in a hidden channel with very shady and deep banks, it becomes harsh. But if it flows in an open channel, then I easily agree with **Aristotle**. For indeed, by the heat of the sun, the lighter part being consumed, the water is rendered thicker.

Writers prefer the **Nile** to all other rivers for these reasons: <margin>The Nile is preferred over all rivers for its purity.</margin> First indeed because it descends through a long course; and because it cuts through the purest lands, tainted by no defects of rot or the contagion of harmful dryness; and because it seeks the north; and because it flows in a full and cleansed channel. It cannot be denied that waters which come by a longer and slower course are rendered less "raw" <note>original: "crudas"; in the medical theory of the time, "raw" water was considered heavy and undigested by the sun's heat, making it less healthy.</note> by the motion; and by the "weariness" of the distance traveled, they are more refined and thus rendered well-cleansed, having dropped their burden of filth during the flow. Furthermore, all the ancients agreed on this: that waters are not only such as the earth is—as we were just saying—where, as if in a parent...

...preserved in the bosom [of the earth]; but furthermore, that they are rendered such as the very soil through which they flow. Such too is the juice of the herbs they have washed; not specifically because it pleases them to flow down there, but especially because the water has mixed with the "sweats" <note>Alberti uses the term *sudores* (sweats) to describe the moisture or secretions of the earth that infuse water with mineral or organic properties.</note> of that earth in which pestilential herbs flourish. Hence they say that degenerate herbs surely provide unhealthful waters. You will sometimes perceive stinking rain, and perhaps even bitter rain. They say this happens from the pollution of the place where that "sweat" first evaporated. They also declare that the juices of the earth, where nature has digested and ripened them, make everything they mix with sweet; and conversely, where they are undigested, they make everything bitter. You might say those waters which seek the north are more beneficial for the reason that they are colder. For they flee the headlong rays of the sun, and are purified by the sun rather than scorched by it. In contrast are those which flow toward the south, for they throw themselves, as it were, into the flames of their own accord. **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose physical theories dominated medieval and Renaissance science.</note> used to say that the fiery spirit <term>fiery spirit (igneus spiritus): a concept in ancient physics where a vital, heat-bearing substance was thought to reside in all things</term> mixed by nature into bodies is beaten back by the north wind when it is cold, and is driven deep inside so that nothing escapes; from this, waters are rendered more "cooked" <note>original: *coctiores*. In ancient science, "cooking" or "concoction" referred to the ripening or perfecting of a substance through heat.</note>. It is well known that this same spirit is dissipated by the flame of the sun. **Servius** <note>Servius (late 4th century AD), a famous grammarian and commentator on the poet Virgil.</note> reported that, in the opinion of experts, wells and springs of water under roofs do not emit vapor. This happens because the thin breath <note>original: *anhelitus*</note> sent out cannot pierce, penetrate, or push aside the dense air that is trapped and made heavy by the walls and roof.

<margin>
They do not approve of a well covered by a building.
</margin>
But under a free and open sky, the water breathes out more clearly, and its "breath," as it were, is released and purged. This is why they approve of a well under the open sky, but do not approve of one covered by a building. In almost all other respects, those things required in wells are the same as those demanded in springs. For in their nature, a well and a spring are kin; they differ in nothing except the motion of their pouring. Nevertheless, you may find frequent wells whose veins move with a large flow. And they affirm that no perennial waters can exist that are entirely immune to movement. For in stagnant water, the power is unhealthful. But if much water is drawn from a well every hour, it will be just as if it were a spring given back from there, appearing like a lowered spring. Conversely, if a spring itself does not overflow but remains quiet, it will be a moderately deep well rather than a spring. There are those who think that no waters are given that are "ever-flowing" <note>original: *iuges*</note> and perennial (as they say) which are not moved by the flow of a nearby stream or torrent. This indeed is proven to me.

<margin>
Lakes.
</margin>
Among legal experts, this is the difference between a lake and a pond <term>pond (stagnum): in Roman law, a *stagnum* was temporary standing water, whereas a *lacus* was permanent</term>: a lake indeed has perennial waters, while a pond has seasonal waters collected in winter. The lake itself is of three types. One is "stationary"—if I may call it that—which is content with its own waters and contains itself, never overflowing. The second is that which pours out waters equal to a river. The third is that which receives waters flowing in from elsewhere, and again [pours them out] through...
