...returns it flowing. The first has the flavor of a pond's nature. The second is most similar to a spring. The third, if I am not mistaken, is a river widened in that place. Therefore, those things we said concerning the spring and the river need not be repeated. To this should be added that any covered waters are colder and clearer because of the shade, but are "cruder" <note>original: "crudiores"; in Renaissance science, water was thought to be "cooked" or "digested" by the sun’s heat to make it more healthful; "crude" water was considered raw and potentially heavy.</note> than those which the sun has purified. Conversely, waters thoroughly baked by the sun are rendered salty and slimy. In both cases, depth is beneficial: in the former, to remove the burning heat, and in the latter, to prevent freezing without disadvantage. Finally, they do not think that a pond itself should always and everywhere be loathed. For where eels <note>Eels were often seen as indicators of water quality in antiquity, as they were thought to avoid truly toxic or putrid environments.</note> abound, they think the waters are not entirely disadvantageous to have.

<margin>Which stagnant waters are the worst.</margin>
They say the worst of stagnant waters is that which nourishes leeches; that which, once a film is drawn over it, becomes sluggish; that which provokes nausea with its stench; that which has a black and flowing color; that which maintains a great thickness in a vessel; that which becomes slimy with a mucous heaviness; and that which, if you wash your hands in it, dries slowly. But to summarize what has been said about waters: the best water ought to be very light, limpid, thin, and transparent. To these should be added those things which we touched upon in the first book. Furthermore, it will be found useful in practice if you observe for several months a beast that has both drunk and washed from that water which we said excels all others, to see how it fares in its limbs and its whole bodily condition. From the condition of its liver <note>original: "iocinere"; inspecting the organs of local livestock was a traditional Roman method (noted by Vitruvius) for determining if a site’s water and air were healthy for human habitation.</note> you will learn whether it is well. For they say that everything which causes harm, causes harm over time; and certainly those things which are felt more slowly are able to cause more grievous harm.

### ¶ Chapter VI. On the conveyance of waters and their uses most beautifully and fittingly.

**F**inally, once water has been found and approved, provision must be made so that it is conveyed most beautifully and provided most fittingly for its uses. The method of conveying water is twofold. For it is either diverted by a water-trench <term>water-trench (aquario fulco): an open channel or furrow used to guide water along the surface of the ground.</term> or it is confined in pipes <term>pipes (fistulis): usually referring to lead or terracotta pipes used in pressurized or enclosed systems.</term>. In both cases, the water will not move unless the place to which it is led is lower than where it began its motion. But there is this difference: water diverted in a trench must descend continuously, whereas water confined [in pipes] is able to rise for a certain part of its journey. We must speak of these things. Therefore, first, some things which pertain to the matter must be reviewed. Those who have investigated these things say that the Earth is spherical, although in many parts it is rough with mountains, and in many parts covered by the sea. But in so great an orb, this roughness is scarcely felt; and it is just as in an egg: which, although it is rough, yet in the magnitude of its circumference those minute prominences are not considered. And it is established that the greatest circumference of the earth is two hundred and fifty-two thousand stadia <note>A "stadium" was an ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 185 meters. This figure comes from the famous calculation by Eratosthenes.</note>, according to the witness of **Eratosthenes** <note>Eratosthenes of Cyrene (c. 276–194 BC), the head of the Library of Alexandria who first accurately calculated the Earth's circumference.</note>. And no mountain is found so high, nor any water so deep, whose plumb-line exceeds [a few] miles...

...gives fifteen cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length based on the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, roughly 18 inches.</note>. <margin>
A joke told about the earth and the sea.
</margin>

There are those who say jokingly that the Architect of the world used the cavity of the sea as a seal when he first formed the mountains. To these, geometers add a point that serves the matter excellently: if a straight line touching the globe of the earth is extended for a thousand paces from the point of contact, the gap there between that line and the maximum circumference of the earth would not exceed ten fingers <note>A "finger" or digit was about 3/4 of an inch. Alberti is explaining that the earth's curvature is negligible over short distances but must be accounted for in long engineering projects.</note>. For this reason, water is not moved in a water-furrow, but stagnates, unless for every eight stadia traveled, the bed is made a full foot deeper than it was at the place where the bank was first cut.

The inlet [Incile].

This place the legal experts call an **Inlet** <note>original: "Incile"; a technical term for a trench or ditch cut into the bank of a river to divert water.</note>, named from the "incision" of rock or earth made for the sake of leading water. But if in that space of eight stadia the slope descends more than six feet, they think the flow of water is rendered inconvenient for ships due to its rapid speed. However, to discern whether the surface of the bed is lower from the **Inlet** to the excavation of the diversion trench, and by how much the slope descends, certain instruments and a very useful art have been invented. 

<margin>
The slope of the trench which must be known.
</margin>

Unskilled men know this matter by placing a ball into the excavation itself; if it rolls, they judge that the slope will be sufficient for the channel. The instruments of the skilled are the **level** [libella], the **square** [norma], and finally all similar things that are defined by a right angle. There is a slightly more "secret" <note>In this context, "secret" refers to specialized or advanced technical knowledge not known to the general public.</note> art to this, but we will explain it only as far as it serves for use. It is done by sight and observation, for those are the "points" we name. If there is an unobstructed plain through which the water is to be led, the method of directing the sight will be twofold. For certain signs and boundaries will be placed either at moderate intervals or at longer markers. The closer the end points of the interval are to each other, the less the direction of sight will deviate from the curved circumference of the earth. But the more extended those intervals are, the more the circumference of the earth and the ground will be found to slope away from the straight line of the level. In these matters, it should be observed that for every thousand paces, you should descend as much as ten fingers. But if it is not an unobstructed plain, and a hill rises in between, then in these cases there will also be a twofold method: one so that you may learn the height from here at the **Inlet** [incile] and from there, conversely, at the **Outlet** [emissarium]. I call the **Outlet** the place destined for use where you want the water to arrive, so that from there it may be discharged either freely or for specific uses. ...I call them: of which one is the line of the visual ray, extended from the eye of the observer to a height equal to that of the eye. This is achieved with a <term>level<note>original: "libella"; a Roman A-frame leveling tool used to determine horizontal planes.</note></term> and also with squares. The second line is that which falls perpendicularly from the very eye of the measuring observer to his feet. In steps of this kind, note from their perpendiculars which sum of lengths exceeds the other, so that you do not accidentally ascend toward the summit from the <term>Intake<note>original: "Incile"; the point where water is first diverted into a channel.</note></term> on this side, or conversely, from the <term>Outlet<note>original: "emissarium"; the point where the water is discharged or reaches its destination.</note></term> on that. 

Another method will be to draw lines from the Intake all the way up to the very summit of the rising hill, and from there also draw lines to the Outlet, noting the straight angles—determined by the principles of geometers—that meet each other. But this method is indeed somewhat difficult to understand and not sufficiently reliable in practice. For over a great distance, even a slight error in the angle caused at the observer's eye has a very great impact on the final result. 

But there are certain techniques consistent with this principle, as we shall soon explain, which we may use very effectively to maintain proper directions if by chance a mountain must be tunneled through to lead water into a town. It shall be done thus: at the very summit of the mountain, from a point where both the Intake on one side and the Outlet on the other are visible, you shall mark a circle ten feet wide on leveled ground. This circle is called the <term>horizon<note>original: "orizon"; here referring to a surveyor's horizon circle or sighting disc.</note></term>. In the center of the circle, you fix a rod so that it stands perfectly perpendicular. 

<margin>
Note the clever method of direction.
</margin>

Once these things are done, the master director will walk around the outside of the circle, searching for the spot where the line of sight, aimed at one end of the water-channel, strikes that very end and passes through the base of the rod fixed in the center. In that certain and noted spot on the horizon circle, the master will mark this very line of direction, cutting the circumference of the circle on both sides. This will surely be the diameter of the circle itself, since by being directed through the center, it cuts the ring of the circle on both sides. 

If this same line, extended long and straight in the opposite direction from the sight-line, reaches the Intake on one side and the Outlet on the other, that layout will provide a straight course for the water to be led. But if it does not reach them—if one diameter points toward the Intake and another toward the Outlet, following different directions—then from the mutual intersection of these lines made at the central rod, it will be clear how much those directions differ from one another. 

We use the aid of this circle most excellently for surveying and mapping cities and provinces, and also for extending underground tunnels. But of these, we shall speak elsewhere. Therefore, by whatever channel water is brought—whether in small amounts for drinking or in great quantities for the use of ships—we shall use these directions which we have reviewed so far. But the work of preparing a channel will not be the same for a large volume of water as for a smaller one. Here we shall follow through, as we began, with those things pertaining to drinking water; later, in its proper place, we will deal with navigable water. The work of the channel will be either...

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

<margin>How a channel is to be prepared</margin> A channel may be built from masonry or dug into the earth. A trench will be of two types: either one led through a field on a level plane, or one that penetrates the very depths of a mountain, which is called a <term>conduit<note>original: "cuniculum"; a subterranean tunnel or gallery often used for drainage or water supply.</note></term>. In all of these, where you find stone, or <term>tufa<note>original: "tofum"; a porous rock composed of volcanic ash, common in Italy.</note></term>, or very dense clay, or anything similar that does not soak up water, masonry work will not be necessary. But where the ground or the sides are not solid, then it must be made with masonry. If the same trench is led through the bowels of the earth, then it shall be cut according to the principles we described above. For every hundred feet of individual conduits, ventilation openings for the wells shall be opened; and the digging shall be reinforced with masonry as the firmness of the earth requires. We have seen wells built in the <term>Marsi region<note>original: "Marsis"; an area in central Italy near the modern Abruzzo, famous for Lake Fucino.</note></term> at the outlet of Lake Fucino, built with elegant fired brickwork to an incredible depth. In the city of Rome, for four hundred and forty-one years from its founding, there were no masonry aqueducts.

<margin>Suspended rivers</margin> Afterward, things reached such a state that even "suspended rivers" were introduced. And it is said that there were many masonry conduits in Rome at one time, with such an abundance that every house was supplied. But in the beginning, they started building subterranean ducts. This had advantages: for being hidden, the work was less exposed to injury. Furthermore, they provided water that was more readily available and cooler, as it was exposed neither to frost nor to the heat of the dog days of summer; nor was it easily intercepted by raiding enemies. Later, for the sake of luxury—

<margin>Various types of water conduits</margin> —so that they might have spurting water for garden fountains and baths, they set about leading it by means of arched work, with structures in some places over one hundred and twenty feet high, extending for sixty thousand paces. This also had advantages. For elsewhere, as well as across the Tiber, they ground grain using the aqueduct; when this was destroyed by enemies, they saw to it that mills were built on ships in the Tiber. Add to this that the city's appearance and its spirit were made purer and cleaner by the abundance of water. Architects even added things for civil use that would mark the hours and seasons with the great joy of things moving there; for little bronze figures would walk about in front of the outlets, representing games and triumphal processions. They also heard—

<margin>Musical organs sounding by the motion of water</margin> —musical organs, and very resonant and sweet harmonies of the voice, moved by the water. They covered the masonry channels with a slightly thicker <term>vault<note>original: "testudine"; literally a "tortoise shell," referring to an arched masonry ceiling.</note></term>, so that the water would not grow warm in the sun; and they lined the inside with the same <term>lining<note>original: "crusta"; a waterproof hydraulic cement or plaster.</note></term> we said floors should be paved with, no less than six fingers thick. 

<margin>Parts of a masonry channel</margin> Moreover, these are the parts of a masonry channel. At the <term>Intake<note>original: "incile"; the point where water is first diverted into a channel.</note></term>, a barrier is placed; then <term>distribution tanks<note>original: "castella"; literally "castles," these were water towers or chambers used to divide and distribute the flow.</note></term> are interspersed along the channel. Where the ground rises more prominently, a <term>tunnel<note>original: "specus"; the channel of an aqueduct, specifically the hollowed-out portion through a hill.</note></term> is dug; at the final location, a <term>nozzle<note>original: "calix"; literally a "cup," a bronze fitting used to regulate and measure the amount of water delivered to a consumer.</note></term> is joined to the outlet. These are defined by the legal expert as follows: A channel is a place hollowed out lengthwise. Barriers are those things placed at the intake for the diversion of water...

# Book 10. On the Restoration of Works.

...for the sake of convenience. <margin>A Reservoir in the stream</margin> <term>Reservoirs<note>original: "Castella"; literally "little castles," these were distribution tanks or towers used in Roman engineering to manage water pressure and divide the supply.</note></term> are the receptacles which receive the public water. A <term>lookout<note>original: "Specus"; while often meaning a channel, here Alberti defines it as an elevated inspection point.</note></term> is a place raised above the banks from which the water may be observed. <margin>What a Calix is</margin> The <term>calix<note>original: "Calix"; literally a "cup" or "chalice," used here to describe the bronze delivery nozzle or regulator that connects a private pipe to the public main.</note></term> is the final part of the conduit where the water is poured out. <margin>Also a Calix</margin> All of these must be constructed with firm walls, a very stable floor, and an intact, non-leaking lining, and they must be <term>waterproofed<note>original: "psiciant"; likely referring to the application of a hydraulic cement or "opus signinum" lining.</note></term>. At the mouth of the enclosure, a gate should be placed as a barrier, so that you may exclude the flow of turbid water by closing the valves. This also allows one to repair any part of the work that has collapsed, according to one's judgment, without the water interfering. A bronze <term>sieve<note>original: "cribrum"; a filter or screen.</note></term> shall be attached so that the water flows in more clearly, leaving behind leaves, twigs, and the impurities of fallen debris.

After the enclosure, every hundred <term>cubits<note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note></term> thereafter, a reservoir should be built; and again, at another hundred cubits, either a reservoir or a tank should be constructed, twenty feet wide, thirty feet long, and fifteen feet deep below the level of the conduit. This is done so that the earthy mixtures of the falling water, which are seized and carried along by its momentum, may settle immediately upon finding a place to rest, thus allowing a clearer wave into the channel.

The <term>calix</term> will vary the amount of water to be poured out according to the impact of the flowing stream and the condition of the pipe from which it discharges. For the more the water is received from a large and rapid stream, or the more the same path is conducted more freely, the pressure and accumulation will increase the measure of the flow. Sluggishness in the conduit loses the rate of pouring. A pipe kept level and in a straight line will preserve the measure. They have a pipe ready to discharge the water—to use such a term—at the <term>outflow<note>original: "micturitu"; a rare term likely derived from "micturire" (to urinate), used here by Alberti to describe the pressurized jet or discharge of water.</note></term> of the water to be measured; and no kind of metal resists more densely than gold. <margin>Pipes.</margin> ☜

Thus far we have discussed how water is diverted by means of both digging and masonry. Furthermore, water is also compelled through lead pipes, or rather, through <term>terracotta tiles<note>original: "tabulis"; likely referring to ceramic or clay piping, which Alberti preferred over lead.</note></term>. For <term>natural philosophers<note>original: "physici"; the scientists or physicians of the ancient and medieval world.</note></term> attest that lead pipes cause abrasions of the intestines. Bronze will cause the same vice. Experts affirm that things to be drunk or eaten are more flavorful when coming from an earthenware vessel. For they claim that the natural home for both water and the things the earth produces is, of course, the earth itself. Wooden pipes, for a certain time, infect the water with an unpleasant color and taste.

Pipes must be very firm; bronze vessels induce <term>epilepsy<note>original: "epilentia".</note></term>, cancer, and pain in the liver and spleen. In a pipe, the diameter of the hollow space shall have the thickness of the solid side, at no less than four <term>joint-boxes<note>original: "pyxidatis commissuris"; likely referring to the reinforced sleeve joints used to connect pipe sections.</note></term>. One small tube shall enter into another; they shall be smoothed with <term>quicklime<note>original: "calce viva"; a caustic, highly alkaline substance used in making mortar.</note></term> and oil, and secured with a very strong structure, and they shall be strengthened by a heavy accumulation of weight. This is especially necessary where you lead the water in a curved track, or where it descends into a depression and rises up again, or where it is restricted in a turning bend. For indeed, from the weight of the pressing water, and from the mass and momentum of its falling, the tubes would easily be lifted and burst. To avoid that danger, experts especially in...

...joints, they used salvaged stone, especially red stone, perforated for the work. We have seen marble pieces more than twelve feet long, pierced from top to bottom with a hole a palm wide; we understood from the best conjectures and signs on the stone itself that this was achieved with a rotating bronze tube and sand <note>The use of sand with a metal drill was a standard Roman technique for cutting hard stone.</note>. To avoid the fault of a pipe bursting, you should slow the speed of the water with bends that are not sharply angled <note>original: "minime geniculatis"; literally "not like knees," meaning avoiding hard 90-degree elbows</note>, but moderately curved, so that they turn now to the right, now to the left; sometimes they should descend, and sometimes ascend, in repeated turns. Add to these things that there should be a place for a wall and a <term>reservoir<note>original: "castelli"; a distribution tank used to manage pressure.</note></term>, both for the sake of purifying the water and so that if any defect appears, it may more easily be revealed which place needs repair. 

But the reservoir should not be placed at the very bottom of a valley, nor where the water is forced to climb too steeply, but it should be placed where it maintains a constant evenness of flow. If by chance a conduit must be led across a pond or lake, it may be done with very little expense in this manner: Take beams of <term>holm-oak<note>original: "ilicea"; a species of evergreen oak known for its durability and resistance to rot.</note></term>; in these, carve a wide and deep groove along the length of the beam in the manner of a pipe. Fit the pipes into this groove, smooth it with lime, and secure them with very strong bronze fastenings. After this, with rafts laid out across the lake in a straight line, join and bind together these beams, end to end, in this manner. Have lead pipes of comparable thickness; let them be as many feet long as can be most easily bent where necessary. These pipes—if I may speak thus—you will <term>encase<note>original: "impixidabis"; likely meaning to box the lead pipe within the wooden beam-groove.</note></term> within the tubes, and you will smear the joints with lime tempered with oil, and secure them with bronze ties. In this way, assemble and extend the work of beams, suspended from the rafts, until it reaches from one bank to the other, with both ends of the work resting on dry land. 

Afterward, where the lake is deepest, first allow this same structure of beams which you prepared for the pipes to sink gradually and evenly into the depths; with the rest of the mass following along, it will descend to the bottom. By means of supports, the lead pipes will be bent as much as the situation requires, and the woodwork will settle itself most aptly on the bottom of the lake. Therefore, when the conduits are prepared, at the first admission of water, let in some ash at the same time, so that if there are any joints not sufficiently sealed, they may be coated <note>The ash acts as a temporary sealant, being drawn into small leaks by the escaping water.</note>. You should also admit the water gradually, lest by being poured in too greedily, <term>air<note>original: "spiritus"; in this context, it refers to air or pressurized vapor trapped in the pipes which can cause "water hammer" or bursts.</note></term> be introduced through the pipes. It is incredible to say how great the force of nature is when such air is confined and constricted in a narrow space. I find among the <term>natural philosophers<note>original: "physicos"; referring to ancient scientists or medical writers.</note></term> that the shinbones in a man have been known to crack from the eruption of trapped vapor. <term>Hydraulic engineers<note>original: "Ydraulici"</note></term> force water to leap upward from a vessel by means of air compressed between two bodies of water.

# Book X. On the Restoration of Works.
### Page 163.

<margin>Cisterns.</margin>
**I** come now to cisterns. A cistern is a somewhat large vessel for water, not unlike a distribution tank <note>original: "castello"; a reservoir used to manage water pressure in Roman engineering.</note>. It is necessary, therefore, that it be well-compacted, solid, and stable in its floor and all its sides. Furthermore, there will be two types: one for drinking water, and another to serve other uses, such as for fighting fires. Following ancient custom—just as they called silver intended for the table "dining-ware" <note>original: "escarium"; from "esca" meaning food or a meal.</note>—we shall call the former "drinking cistern." The other, prepared solely for holding any kind of water, we shall call "the container" <note>original: "capaquiam"; a term Alberti likely coined from the words for "capacity" and "water" to denote a bulk storage vessel.</note> because of its capacity.

<margin>Drinking cistern.</margin>
Regarding the drinking cistern, it makes a great difference whether it provides pure or impure water. In both cases, care must be taken that the water is correctly admitted, correctly preserved, and correctly distributed for use.

<margin>The container.</margin>
It is easy to send water into a cistern via conduits from a river or spring; likewise, people everywhere are accustomed to collecting rainwater from roofs or courtyards. But I was very pleased by an architect's invention: at the summit of a hill, he cut a deep trench ten feet wide around a vast, bare, protruding rock, which, like a crown, would catch all the rain falling from that bare mountain peak. Then, in a lower place on the flat ground at the foot of the hill, he built a "container" building accessible from all sides, made of brick and lime, thirty feet high, forty wide, and forty long. Into this, he led the rain caught in the upper trench through an underground conduit using pipes. For that trench was positioned much higher than the roof of the container structure. 

If you pave the cistern—or rather fill it to a certain height—with angular gravel or rather large, well-washed river sand to a depth of about three feet, it will provide pure, clean, and cold water. The thicker this layer is, the clearer the water it will provide. Sometimes water leaks from cisterns through the gaps of a poorly built and leaky container. Sometimes the water itself is spoiled by filth. Indeed, it is very difficult to keep water within the "prison" of the walls unless the structure is extremely firm and made especially of <term>squared stone<note>original: "lapide... ordinario"; referring to ashlar or regular masonry blocks as opposed to rubble.</note></term>. Above all, the work itself must be completely dry before you let in the water. For the water presses with its weight and seeps through any damp spots; finding pores, it clears them by dripping through, until it flows out quite freely as if through larger pipes. To provide against this inconvenience, the ancients—especially at the corners of the walls—applied multiple coats of <term>sanded plaster<note>original: "harenationum"; a base coat of plaster made with sand and lime.</note></term> and covered the work with a very careful "skin" of <term>marble-dust plaster<note>original: "marmorato"; a fine, waterproof, and polished plaster finish.</note></term>.

<margin>Remedy to prevent water from rotting in the cistern</margin>
But the outbreaks of water will be restrained by nothing more conveniently than by <term>clay<note>original: "creta"; in this hydraulic context, it refers to waterproof packing clay.</note></term> poured between the cistern wall and the side of the trench and very tightly packed by vigorous pounding. I have ordered that very dry clay, crushed into a powder, be used for this kind of work.

# Leon Battista Alberti: On the Art of Building

Some think that if you take a glass vessel full of salt, seal it well with lime mixed with oil so that no water can penetrate the vessel, and lower it so that it hangs in the middle of the cistern water, the water there will never spoil <note>original: "putrefcant"; literally "rot" or "decay," referring to stagnant water becoming foul.</note> over time. Some also add quicksilver <note>mercury</note>. Others believe that if you lower a new clay vessel full of sharp vinegar, well-sealed as we have described, the slimy water will be restored more quickly. They say that a cistern or a well is made cleaner by throwing in small fish. For they believe the fish are nourished by and feed upon the slime of the water and the ooze of the earth. 

<margin>The opinion of Epigenes.</margin> There is an ancient opinion of Epigenes <note>an ancient Greek astronomer and writer mentioned by Pliny the Elder</note> that water which has once become foul will be purified over time and restored; after this, it will no longer spoil. Water that has begun to spoil will lose its stench if it is vigorously agitated and repeatedly moved and stirred. It is well known that this same thing happens to slimy wine and likewise to oil. 

When Moses (says Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian</note>) had come into a dry place where there was no water except a well of bitter and filthy water, he ordered it to be drawn out. When the soldiers had done this with such shaking and agitation, it was rendered drinkable. It is certain that waters are purified by boiling and by distillation. He also says that nitrous and bitter waters are softened by adding barley meal <note>original: "polenta"; a mush or meal made from toasted barley</note>, so that you may drink it within two hours. 

But for drinking cisterns, to provide cleaner water, a "well-let" <note>original: "puteolus"; a small secondary well or filter chamber</note> should also be added, enclosed by its own wall, placed in a suitable spot, with its floor slightly lower than that of the cistern. This small well will have little windows in its side plugged with either sponge or pumice, so that no water from the cistern enters this well unless it has left behind its thicker impurities and has been well-strained. 

<margin>Pumice from Tarraco.</margin> Near Tarraco <note>modern Tarragona, Spain</note> in Spain, a white pumice is found filled with tiny pores through which water immediately drips out most clear. 

The water will also be strained if you block the inlet where it arrives with a vessel pierced everywhere with many holes and then fill it with river sand, so that the water penetrates through the very fine sand. 

<margin>Water which is strained in this way.</margin> At Bologna they have a yellowish sandy stone <note>original: "tofus"; tufa or porous limestone</note> through which water drips drop by drop, becoming very light. 

There are those who make bread with seawater, than which nothing is more prone to causing disease. The methods of filtration <note>original: "instillationes"; literally "drippings"</note> we have reviewed have such great power that they make even this water healthy. Seawater (says Solinus <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a Roman geographer</note>) becomes sweet if it is strained through clay; and it has been discovered that the salt is removed when it is strained again and again through fine river sand. If you submerge a well-sealed clay vessel in the sea, it will be filled with fresh water <note>original: "dulci"; literally "sweet," the standard term for non-salty water</note>. And this is not without reason: when they have set down the turbid water of the Nile river, if you rub an almond against the rim and edge of the water, it will immediately become clear. 

This is enough on these matters. If, however, the conduit pipes ever begin to be blocked by mud, throw in...

# Concerning the food and clothing that must be provided by agriculture: the manner of cultivating the field, and of assisting a less fertile region. Chapter VIII.

**N**ow let us come to the remaining matters. We said that food and clothing are owed to the inhabitants. Agriculture will provide these things; following these arts in detail does not belong to our present purpose. Nevertheless, there are some things from the architect that may benefit the plowman. Indeed, where a field is useless for cultivation, either due to dryness or due to an excess and nuisance of water, it will be helpful to have briefly considered some of these points.

<margin>On vines in a meadow.</margin>
You shall make a vineyard in a meadow or damp ground in this way: dig pits from east to west in straight lines at equal distances, as deep as possible, nine feet wide, and fifteen feet apart from each other. The earth you have removed from the ditch you shall pile up in the intervening area, so that by its slope it catches the midday sun. When little hills of this sort are made, the vine will be safer and more productive by hand. Conversely, on a dry hill, you shall make a meadow thus: you shall make a long ditch, not for drainage but for standing water, in the higher part, with the margin leveled and evened out. Into this you shall divert water from nearby springs; the overflowing water from the side will irrigate the field placed below with continuous uniformity. In the Veronese countryside, which is filled with rounded stones and otherwise bare and deeply infertile, they have brought it about in some places through frequent irrigation that a layer of turf is formed, and a most lush meadow has grown up.

<margin>So that a forest may grow.</margin>
So that a forest may grow in a marshy place, you shall turn the field with a plow and root out all the turf entirely; after that, scatter acorns from the oak <note>original: "robore"; refers to the *Quercus robur* or "hard oak," prized for its strength</note> at the time of their sprouting. By this method, the place will be filled with a bounty of plants, by which the overflowing moisture may be largely exhausted. Then, through both the growth of roots and the accumulation of fallen leaves and twigs, the soil will be rendered slightly more elevated day by day. If you also allow turbulent floodwaters to enter so that they may settle, you will overlay a crust upon the muddy areas. But of these things elsewhere. 

¶ But if a region is troubled by the nuisance of waters—such as we have seen in Gaul near the Po <note>the Po Valley in Northern Italy, which was historically prone to flooding</note>, or in Venice and such places—there are things that ought to be considered. For they will be troubled either by an excess or by the movement of water, or by both. We shall pass over these very briefly. 

<margin>Lakes drained by tunneling through mountains.</margin>
At Lake Fucinus, Claudius <note>The Roman Emperor Claudius, who famously attempted to drain the lake by digging a 3.5-mile tunnel through Mount Salviano</note> dug through a mountain and, because of the excess of water, led it out into a riverbank. And Lake Velinus <note>modern Lago di Piediluco; the ancient drainage created the Cascata delle Marmore</note> [was drained] by channels led out...

# Book 10. On the restoration of works. Folio CLXV.

...unless the flow of the river is contained, it will break forth. And by wasting the fields, it will flow far and wide and be scattered, so that even the use of overland routes is disrupted. Furthermore, if the bottom is slanted, who can doubt that the rushing water will drive back a ship moving against it? Add also that if there is anything rising from the bottom—rough or ridged—it will cause an obstruction. When the obelisk <note>This likely refers to the Vatican Obelisk, brought from Egypt to Rome in 37 AD by Caligula; transporting such massive weights required highly specialized ships and deep, reliable waterways.</note> was brought to Rome from Egypt, they realized that the Tiber was more convenient for navigation than the Nile. Indeed, the latter [Nile] lies open with an expansive breadth, but the former [Tiber] is more powerful due to its depth. For we do not require a large volume of water for the use of ships as much as we require depth. Although breadth also contributes to the matter, for near the banks the waters are made slower. 

When the bed of a river is not stable, its sides will also be very weak. Almost every bottom is unstable except for that which we have said is approved for structural works: that is, the kind of soil that rejects iron <note>original: "ferrum asperner"; meaning soil so hard or rocky that tools cannot easily penetrate it</note> by its own solidity. The ground will be entirely shifting where the bank is composed of chalk, or on a flat plain, or laid upon a ground of rounded and rolling pebbles. A river with weak sides will also have its channel obstructed by rough debris from collapses and by crosswise trunks or soft stones. Banks created by alluvium <term>alluvium</term> <note>sediment, such as sand or silt, deposited by flowing water</note> will be entirely weak and subject to change at any moment. 

From this instability of the banks follow the accounts told of the Meander <note>A river in modern-day Turkey, famous in antiquity for its many loops and bends, which gave us the word "meander."</note> and the Euphrates. For the former, because it cuts through weak soil, creates many new bends daily. The Euphrates, however, very often obstructs the canals into which it is led through the collapse of its banks. Our ancestors provided against such defects of the banks primarily by building an embankment.

<margin>On making an embankment for a river.</margin>

Now, the method of the embankment itself relates to other building principles. For it matters indeed along what line it is led, or by what work it is constructed and strengthened. An embankment led in a straight line along the river will not be worn away by the waves. But an embankment that the river strikes crosswise will be thrown down if it is weak. Or if it is low, the water will flow over it. An embankment that is not thrown down in such a place will increase daily from the bottom up. For the materials carried there will strike it, and piling up as if to climb over, the debris will raise itself in the channel; and having deposited there the things it can no longer carry or push further, the water will turn elsewhere. If the water throws down the embankment by its own force and mass, it will then act according to the laws of nature we have described: it will fill empty spaces, expel air, and sweep away whatever opposes it. But heavy things and those moved with difficulty will be gradually deposited along with the passing current. This is why at the mouths of floods, the inundation that spills onto a field leaves behind very deep, coarse sand. Further on, however, a lighter and more silty accretion of earth is found. If, however, the silt...

# Leon Battista Alberti: On the Art of Building.

...it will pour over the embankment: then, by the impact of the rushing waves, the loose soil will be stirred; and once stirred by the flow, it will be carried away until the work, undermined by the erosion, collapses. But indeed, if the flowing wave strikes the embankment not directly nor transversely, but at a bend, it will press and wear down both banks—not only the one where it is received but also the other where it is deflected—according to its own curve and the width of the river. 

A curve partakes in the nature of a transverse force. Therefore, it will endure the same assaults that are hostile to transverse structures, and it will be worn away by harsh abrasions. These will be all the more sharp and troublesome the more the whirlpools there boil—if I may put it that way—more rapidly and turbulently. For a whirlpool and a vortex of waters is like a drill <note>original: "terebra"; Alberti uses this mechanical metaphor to describe how rotating water "bores" into the riverbed or foundations.</note> to the flow; no hardness can resist it for long. One may see this from stone bridges, which are hollowed out and made deep in the lower part of the channel, as well as from those places in the flow which are constricted by banks: where they burst forth from narrower throats into wider spaces, they certainly swirl around and consume whatever banks or bottom they strike by falling and turning inward.

<margin>The Bridge of Hadrian.</margin>
I dare say that the Bridge of Hadrian <note>Known today as the Ponte Sant'Angelo in Rome; it was built by Emperor Hadrian in 134 AD to lead to his mausoleum.</note> in Rome is the strongest of all works men have made; yet floods have brought it to the point where I doubt it can resist much longer. For with the trunks and branches that the floods have snatched from the fields, they burden the piers with annual troubles, and they leave the openings of the arches largely blocked. Because of this, the waters swell; and then, from on high, steep and harmful vortices rush down and scour the base. Thus they undermine the piers and disturb the mass of the work. So much for the sides.

<margin>
Concerning the riverbed.
Nitocris.
</margin>
Now concerning the riverbed. Herodotus writes that Nitocris <note>A legendary queen of Babylon. Herodotus describes her engineering projects, including diverting the Euphrates to protect the city from the Medes.</note> among the Mesopotamians slowed the excessively rapid course of the Euphrates by a curved and winding path. It comes closest to being preserved for a long time where it flows out more slowly. And this is somewhat similar to someone descending a steep mountain not by a headlong path, but now to the right and now to the left of the slope. 

It is well established whether the excessive velocity of a river occurs in a suitable channel. A flow that is too fast and, conversely, one that is too sluggish are both harmful to use. The former undermines the banks; the latter easily grows weeds and easily turns to ice. A river that is narrowed will perhaps make the waters higher; and one that is excavated will have a deeper channel. The method and purpose for excavating, removing obstacles, and cleaning are almost the same as those we shall speak of shortly. But excavation there will be in vain unless the bottom toward the sea...

# Book 10. On the Restoration of Works. Folio 166.

### ¶ Chapter IX. On canals: ensuring a sufficient supply of water and preventing its use from being hindered.

**I** come now to the subject of canals. It is to be hoped that there is never a lack of water supply, and that the purposes for which the canal was established are not obstructed. To ensure the supply does not fail, two methods must be employed. The first is that water diverted from elsewhere should flow in abundantly; the second is that once the water is collected, it should be preserved for a long time. The diversion of the canal will be carried out according to the principles I have stated above. We shall ensure that the use of the water, once brought down, is not hindered through carefulness and diligence; for the canal must be cleaned often and any sediment brought in must be cleared out. <margin>A canal is a sleeping river</margin> Indeed, some say a water canal is a <term>sleeping river</term> <note>original: "fluuium esse consopitum"; Alberti uses this poetic phrase to describe the controlled, slower flow of a canal compared to a natural river.</note>; and it requires almost all the same things as a riverbed, especially the solidity and firmness of the bottom and sides, so that nothing absorbs the water let in or lets it leak away through gaps. 

Furthermore, a canal ought to be deeper than it is wide; this is not only for the sake of carrying a ship, but also so that it is less evaporated by the sun and grows fewer weeds. Many canals were led from the Euphrates into the Tigris, because the former sits higher in its bed. That part of Italy called <term>Gaul</term> <note>Alberti refers to Cisalpine Gaul, the region of Northern Italy encompassing the Po Valley.</note>, which lies around the mouths of the Po and the Adige, is entirely navigable by canals; the flat terrain there made this easy to achieve. <margin>/</margin> According to Diodorus <note>The Greek historian Diodorus Siculus, who wrote the "Bibliotheca historica."</note>, Ptolemy used to open a canal when he sailed from the Nile, and close it again once he had finished his voyage. The remedies for defects in these works will be: restraint, cleaning, and closures. Rivers are restrained by an embankment. The line of the embankment should be drawn so that it does not squeeze the sides suddenly, but rather presses and constricts them gradually. Where you intend to release water from narrower "throats" into wider shallows, do not let it in abruptly, but allow it through an extended channel so that the waves may widen gradually and the river may return to its original breadth. This prevents the water from causing damage through wanton eddies and whirlpools born from the license of sudden freedom. 

<margin>/</margin> The river Melas used to flow into the Euphrates. Perhaps led by a desire for fame, King <term>Artanatrix</term> <note>original: "Artanatrix"; this is likely a corruption of Ariarathes (Ariarathes V of Cappadocia), who famously dammed the Melas.</note> blocked the exit of the river and flooded the region far and wide. <margin>Artanatrix.</margin> Not long after, the mass of the dammed water broke through with such great whirlpools and force that it dragged many fields with it and devastated much of Galatia and Phrygia. <margin>Iphicrates blocked the exit of the river Melas.</margin> The Senate fined the man thirty talents for his insolence. It is also relevant to the matter to mention what we read of Iphicrates: when he was besieging Stymphalus <note>An ancient city in the Peloponnese, famous for its lake and the "Stymphalian Birds" of Hercules.</note>, he attempted to block the water of the Erasinus—a river which goes underground and rises again in the Argive territory—by throwing in countless sponges. But, warned by a sign from Jupiter, he desisted. Since these things are so, let it be helpful to advise thus: make the construction of the embankment extremely strong. This strength will be provided by the solidity of the material, the method of the work, and its sheer size. On the side where the wave falls over by overflowing, do not make that outer side perpendicular...

...with it, but let it be released with moderate restraint, so that it flows down very gently and without any turbulence. But if, by falling, the water begins to create scoured pits, fill them immediately—not with small rubble, but with large, whole, stable, and angular stone. It will also be useful to throw in bundles of brushwood so that the falling water reaches the bottom only when broken and weakened. In Rome, we see the Tiber narrowed in many parts by masonry work.

<margin>Semiramis</margin>
Semiramis, not content with brickwork, even applied a layer of asphalt four cubits thick over the embankment. Indeed, she also raised walls many <term>stades</term> <note>original: "stadia"; an ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 185 meters.</note> high to match the city's defenses. These are royal works.

<margin>Nitocris</margin>
We shall be content with an earthen embankment, such as Nitocris used among the Assyrians, made of mud; or such as we see in Gaul, where the largest rivers are as if suspended, until in some places they occasionally exceed the level of the rooftops of the <term>huts</term> <note>original: "mappalium"; referring to the simple, portable dwellings of nomadic peoples or rural laborers.</note>. It will be sufficient if the bridges are reinforced with masonry.

<margin>What river embankments should be constructed from.</margin>
For building embankments, there are those who provide grassy sod cut from meadows. This I also approve of. For they are welded together by the embrace of the small roots, provided they are made solid by vigorous tamping. The whole mass of the embankment, and especially that part which the waves lick against, must harden into an impenetrable and indissoluble thickness. There are those who interweave wicker rods into the embankment. This work is certainly firm, but by its nature temporary. For since the rods are easily rotted, it happens that the "rays" <note>small streams or trickles</note> of water occupy the spaces left by the decayed material. And from there, penetrating through, larger streams follow as the channels and pipes of the leaks enlarge. However, we will fear this less if we use green rods. Others plant willow, alder, poplar, and trees that love water in frequent rows along the bank. This indeed has its convenience, but there is a drawback, the same as what we said about the rods. For sometimes when the trunks of dead trees are consumed by decay, holes and tunnels flow through them. Others—which I especially like—plant shrubs and an abundance of all herbs that thrive in water, which are prolific in roots rather than branches, along the bank. In this category, the foremost are wild nard, rushes, reeds, and especially the <term>vitrex</term> <note>original: "vitrex"; likely referring to the *Salix vitellina* or basket willow, prized for its flexible branches and water-loving roots.</note>. For it grows with a large and populous root, spreading itself deep with very long and reviving fibers; by contrast, it rises with low and flexible branches, which play with the waves and provoke them very little. And what helps wonderfully is that this plant, through its greed for water, continuously advances itself through the submerged river. Moreover, in the place where the embankment is directed according to the force of the river, the bank ought to be completely bare and smooth, so that nothing creates an obstacle by which the gentleness of the flow might be provoked. ...where the embankment presents a bend to the river, so that it may resist more robustly there, it shall be strengthened with <term>screens</term> <note>original: "pluteis"; defensive boards or panels used to reinforce a structure against the force of the current.</note>. If, however, the entire mass of the river must be repelled or held back by a transverse barrier: then, in the place where the water is shallower in the open channel, construct a <term>hurdle</term> <note>original: "cratem"; a framework of woven branches or timber used as a foundation in water or marshy ground.</note> of very long oaken posts joined together. Secure the hurdle well with clasps and chains, and place the posts straight along the channel so that their ends receive the downstream current. Drive sharpened stakes into the channel as deep as the ground allows, inserted through holes made for that purpose. Once this is secured, lay down alternating transverse beams; and on such a hurdle, pile a mass of stones. Bind them together with lime; or, where the expense does not allow, bind them with bundles of juniper interspersed between. It will then follow that the immense weight and the strength of the hurdle will make them impossible to move. But if whirlpools attempt to undermine the foundation, it will actually help the matter. For it is better that the weight itself, by pressing down and embedding itself into the depths, should seek a very firm seat there. If, however, the river is of such a constant depth that these rafts cannot be placed, then we shall use those methods which we described in their proper place for raising <term>piers</term> <note>original: "pilas"; the heavy masonry supports for bridges.</note> of bridges.

### Concerning embankments and reinforcement on the seashore, and the protection of harbors and the blocking of river water. Chapter X.

The seashore will also be reinforced with embankments, but not the same kind as those used for flowing water. For the injuries caused by flowing waters do not damage in the same way as the waves of the sea. Indeed, they say the sea is by its own nature quiet and tranquil, but is agitated and driven by the pressure of the winds. From this, it happens that rising ranks of waves seek the shore. At that place, if something transverse and especially rough or jagged presents itself to them, they strike it there with their whole "chests" <note>original: "pectoribus"; Alberti poeticizes the waves, describing the front of a wave as a chest striking a solid object.</note>; they are then broken and spring back shattered. Thus, rushing in from the deep, they disturb the ground and, with persistent annoyance, hollow out and demolish whatever stands in their way. Evidence that this happens is found in the depths of the seabed which you find near maritime rocks. If, however, the shore presents itself with a gentle and low incline worn down by the waves, the sea—not being so agitated as to fight with a more boiling tide—loses its impetus and lingers, receding in softer waves. And if it has seized and carried any sand from the commotions, it drops it in the meantime and leaves it in a quieter place. From this, we perceive that shores extending in this manner from a low plain have grown daily into the sea. But where the sea hits a headland, and then flows into a bay or curve of the shore in a crooked line, there it runs swiftly and is turned back along the shore. From which it happens that the place...

...in this manner, <term>per</term><note>through/along</note> the shore, canals are excavated and <term>productique</term><note>extended</note> everywhere. Others <term>praedicant</term><note>proclaim</note> that the sea itself breathes in and out; and they have noted that a man <term>nunquam</term><note>never</note> breathes his last breath except when the <term>aestu</term><note>tide</note> is receding, as if the sea provides this evidence of itself: since our human life has something akin and in harmony with the soul and <term>motumque</term><note>movement</note> of the sea itself. <term>Sed</term><note>But</note> enough of these matters. Furthermore, it is manifest that the rising and falling of the sea indeed changes in different places. In the <term>reciprocatio</term><note>the ebbing and flowing; the prefix "reci-" appears in the margin</note> of the Chalcidican sea <note>The Euripus Strait between Euboea and mainland Greece, famous in antiquity for its erratic currents.</note>, the waves alternate six times every day. At Byzantium <note>modern-day Istanbul</note>, it does <term>non</term><note>not</note> change except by the outflow into the Black Sea. In the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara</note>, the sea by its own nature continuously rejects whatever has been carried in by the rivers, casting it back to the shores. For those things which are stirred up by agitations remain where a seat is given to rest. But since we see the force of sand or stones cast up on almost all shores, it is useful to recount <term>quod</term><note>what</note> I find among the philosophers.

<margin>Sand is made from mud.</margin>
We have said elsewhere that sand is made from mud: which the sun has thickened, after the <term>aestus</term><note>tide/heat</note> has divided it into minute particles.

<margin>Stones are born from sea water.</margin>
They claim that stones are born from the water of the sea. For they say that the water grows warm through the sun and motion, is dried out, and consequently thickened once the lighter parts are exhausted: and it is drawn to such a thickness that if <term>quando</term><note>at any time</note> the sea rests a little, it gradually covers itself with a mucous and very bituminous skin. They say this skin is soon <term>rumpiq3</term><note>broken</note> and scattered by the latest movements and collisions until it becomes spherical; and it becomes something very similar to sponges, and these globes are carried to the shore. At that place, it glues the stirred-up sands to itself and takes them into its mass. Once gripped, however, they are dried out by the force of the sun and salt and gathered more densely: and in time they harden until they become stone. This is their view. We, <term>tamen</term><note>however</note>, see shores growing everywhere at the mouths of rivers: especially if those are indeed rivers <term>quae</term><note>which</note> flow through loose soil, into which many torrents flow. For these <term>quidem</term><note>indeed</note> <term>per</term><note>through</note> their mouths heap up a great deal of sand and pebbles on this side and that at the seashore, and <term>producunt</term><note>extend</note> the coastline. The Danube and the Phasis of the Colchians <note>A river in modern Georgia, east of the Black Sea.</note> and others, and most greatly the Nile, demonstrate that this is so. The ancients called Egypt the home of the Nile, and they assert that it was once covered by the sea as far as the Pelusian marshes. They also report that a great part of the land of Cilicia <note>A region on the southern coast of modern Turkey.</note> was added by the river. Aristotle argues that the motion <term>rerum</term><note>of things</note> is continuous: and that in the space of time it will happen that the sea and mountains shall change places. Hence he says: "Whatever is under the earth, age <term>proferet</term><note>will bring</note> into the open. It will bury and hide things now hidden." <term>Praeterea</term><note>Furthermore</note>, I return to the matter. The waves have this quality in themselves: that they strike against a wall placed in their way and rise up; but as they fall back from on high, the driven waters excavate the sands by <term>quam</term><note>as much as</note> they fall. You may see there <term>quam</term><note>how</note> much deeper the sea stays near the rocks and crags; much more so there...

# Book 10. On the Restoration of Works. Folio CLXVIII.

...[so that the wave] might strike where it finds no obstructions except a soft and gentle shore. Since this is so, there will certainly be a need for great diligence and skillful ingenuity to restrain the force and spirit of the sea. For the sea will, in large part, frustrate both art and the hand; and it is not easily overcome by human strength. Indeed, the same kind of embankment <note>Alberti uses the term *exaggeratio*, referring to a raised mound or rampart of earth and stone.</note> we said was necessary for bridges elsewhere will be useful here. <margin>How to build ports</margin> ¶ But if the situation requires that a breakwater <note>original: *moles*</note> be extended into the sea for the sake of protecting a port, we shall begin the work from the mainland and dry ground; then, with subsequent additions, we shall extend the work into the sea. 

We must ensure above all that it is placed on a very stable bottom; and wherever you place it, it must be built up with a poured accumulation of the largest stones, so that the wall stands against the waves along a gradually sloping line. In this way, the mass and—so to speak—the "menacing nature" of the arriving waves may subsequently be extinguished; and not finding anything to clash with head-on, the receding wave will not dig it out, but will glide away most gently. For in this manner, the receding wave will receive and slow down the latest incoming waves following behind it. 

River mouths <note>original: *hostia*, a common Renaissance spelling of *ostia*</note> also seem to belong to the logic of the port, since ships take refuge from storms in those places. I would wish for mouths especially to be fortified and narrowed against the waves of the sea. Propertius used to say: *You are conquered or you conquer: this is the wheel in love.* <note>original: "Vinceris aut vincis haec in amore rota est." From Propertius, Elegies 2.8.8. Alberti compares the shifting fortunes of the tide to the fickle nature of love.</note> So it happens there. For indeed, the mouths are either eternally overcome by the sea's relentless defiance and blocked by sand, or conversely, they prevail through the persistence of their flow and the stubbornness of their victory. 

Therefore, it will be very pleasing if you discharge the river into the sea by two different branches, provided the water supplies are sufficient. This is not only so that easier entries are open for ships when winds change, but also so that if the force of storms stands in the way, or if one exit happens to be blocked by the blowing south wind <note>The *Auster*, a wind known for bringing storms and surges that could block estuaries with silt.</note>, the swollen alluvial deposits driven back do not overflow into the fields. Instead, they should have an opening through which they are received by the open sea. So much for these matters. <margin>Cleaning</margin> ¶ Next comes cleaning. Caesar took the greatest care in cleaning the Tiber. For it was filled with debris thrown into the river. 

There still exist immense mounds made from the materials carried out and removed from the river, located not far from the Tiber, both inside and outside the city. By what methods he extracted such great material from such a vigorous river, I do not remember reading. But I believe they certainly used <term>cofferdams</term><note>Latin: *septa*. Temporary enclosures built within a body of water to allow the enclosed area to be pumped out for construction or excavation.</note>, by which they blocked off the river and, having drained the water, dug out the obstructions. 

The dams shall be made thus. You will prepare beams hewn to a straight line; and from the top <margin>How to prepare a water-barrier</margin> to the bottom of their head, along the width of the side, you will cut grooves on both sides <margin>to be prepared</margin>, four fingers deep at the bottom, and wide enough for the thickness of the plank which will be used for the work prepared by art. And you will prepare planks of equal length and also equal thickness. Once these are ready, fix the beams we mentioned so that they stand...

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

...small posts <note>The Latin *pediculus* literally means "little foot," here referring to a vertical supporting post.</note> at moderate intervals from each other, according to the prepared length of the boards. Once the beams are set and properly secured, insert the boards by their ends so that they descend deep through the grooves of the beams. People commonly call a similar work sluice gates <note>original: *cataractas*</note>. You, however, shall join one board upon another and press them together so they cohere well. Then, arrange in suitable and convenient places Archimedes' screws <note>original: *cocleas aquarias*; these are spiral pumps used for lifting water.</note>, and siphons, and tubes, and pipes, and every instrument for draining; and employ a very numerous workforce: and immediately, with restless effort and without any intermission, drain the water enclosed by the barrier. If any water leaks in, block it with stuffed rags <note>original: *centonibus*; thick fabric or felt used for caulking.</note>. The work will succeed according to your wish. 

There is this difference between a water-barrier <note>Alberti uses the word *septum*, meaning a fence, enclosure, or cofferdam.</note> of this kind and the other we used for building bridges: for that one needed to be stable and long-lasting until the piers were not only finished but also solidified. This one is temporary; and the next day, once the mud is cleared, it must be removed and moved elsewhere. I advise this: whether you are cleaning with that barrier or diverting a river, take care not to struggle against the whole volume of water in one and the same place; but carry out the work in parts and additions. 

Works built against the mass and impetus of waters will resist more strongly if they are curved into an arch, with the "back" <note>The convex or outer side of the curve.</note> placed against the weight of the pressing water. You will deepen a torrent if you place an obstruction across it so that the water rises high and is forced to swell up greatly. For you will achieve this: the overflowing wave will deepen the ditch by its own fall; and likewise, the deeper you dig the lower part of the stream, the more the channel will be hollowed out all the way to the source. For flowing water moves forward continuously, disturbs the ground, and carries it away. 

You shall also clean a stream or water-ditch by sending in cattle <note>original: *bubulis*</note> like this: block the flow so the waters rise; then force the livestock to make the water muddy with frequent and rapid movements; immediately open the gate so it pours down headlong and washes the mud away. But if by chance something submerged or fixed in the river causes an obstruction, besides the other machines that the craftsmen know, <margin>👉</margin> this is the most suitable: bring in a loaded ship and tie it very firmly to the object itself—whether it be a pile or whatever you want to pull out. Then, lighten the ship of its cargo; it will happen that the lightened ship, rising up as it floats higher, will pull out the tied object by its roots. It will help if you twist the pile like a key while the ship is rising. 

In the territory of Praeneste <note>Modern Palestrina, Italy.</note>, we saw wet clay in which, if you fixed a staff or a sword no more than a cubit deep, you could not pull it out by any force of the hand. But if you twisted it slightly while pulling, it followed easily, just like a drill. # Book X. On the Restoration of Works.

...the man is found in our times, endowed with marvelous skill and nature, who has diminished the difficulty and opened approaches far and wide. It is rumored that he is accustomed to remaining under the waters, and for a great hour does not emerge for the sake of breathing. <note>Alberti is likely referring to a contemporary diver or "fish-man"; such individuals were often employed in the 15th century for salvage or underwater repairs.</note>

<margin>Mud</margin>
You shall haul up the mud from the deep with an oyster-net <note>original: *rete ostrecteo*</note> fitted with a sack; for by dragging, it will be filled. You shall also haul it where the sea is shallow, just as you would from marshes in a foamy place. It shall be done thus: Have <margin>For dredging</margin> two light vessels <note>original: *mioparones*; small, swift ships used here for their maneuverability in narrow channels.</note>; in one of these, you will fix an axle at the stern, upon which a very long yardarm <note>original: *antenna*</note> may play, not unlike a balance scale. At the head of this yardarm, which remains outside the ship, let a shovel <note>original: *pala*</note> be attached, three feet wide and six feet long. By immersing this, the workers will take up the mud and deposit it into the other light vessel prepared for that purpose. From these principles, many very similar and more useful things will be made, which would be long to pursue here. Thus far concerning these things.

<margin>Where the water flow is restricted</margin>
The closure follows. The flow of water shall be closed by sluice gates <note>original: *cataractis*</note> and it shall also be closed by barriers. In both, very firm stone lips should be made with the help of piers. Lift the weight of the sluice gate by a most skillful method <margin>For closing</margin> without danger to men, by employing toothed wheels <note>original: *rotis dentatis*</note> on the windlass <note>original: *tractatorium*</note>, which we may move as if in a clock, with the teeth of another spindle driven for that work and motion. But <margin>Swinging gate</margin> the most convenient of all will be the swinging gate <note>original: *valua*</note>, which has a spindle fixed at its center to a vertical pivot. To the spindle <margin>Sluices</margin> rectangular barriers shall be fixed; as it stands open, it is just like a square sail unfurled on a merchant ship, which can be swung by this or that arm toward the prow or the stern. But the arms of this gate shall not be equal; for one shall be a little shorter, by about three fingers. For it will then happen that it can be moved by a single boy, and yet close again of its own accord as the longer side is overcome by the weight of the water. Make double closures <note>Alberti here provides one of the earliest technical descriptions of a pound lock, essential for navigating rivers with varying elevations.</note> by cutting the river in two places, with a space left between that may contain the length of a ship; so that if a ship is about to ascend, when it has arrived there, the lower closure is shut and the upper is opened; but if it is to descend, let the upper be shut and the lower opened. In that manner, the ship will be carried by the following river with that released portion of the flow. The upper closure, however, will preserve the rest of the water. I shall not overlook what pertains to roads, lest we repeat such things: do not build up a road through a town by heaping up rubble—which is done by a wicked custom—but rather by taking it away; and by clearing and carrying it away far around, make it well-cleansed and well-sloped, lest the city blocks <note>original: *insule*</note> and the surfaces of the streets be submerged by the accumulation of pavement.

<margin>👉</margin>
Now I shall pursue as briefly as I can the other smaller matters that may allow for correction. In some places where water has been brought in, the region has been made warmer; and conversely, in some it has been made colder. At Larissa in Thessaly, the field was made stagnant and sluggish...

## Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

...it was covered with water, for which reason they had thick and stifling air. Afterward, when the water was drawn off and the field dried, the region became colder; so much so that thereafter, none of the olive trees, which previously grew in abundance all around, survived. On the contrary, among the Philippians: there, as Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC) was a Greek philosopher and the successor to Aristotle; he is often called the father of botany.</note> recalls, when the water was drawn off and the lake dried, the result was that they suffered less from the cold. The cause of these things is interpreted as being the purity or impurity of the air breathing there. For they declare that thick air indeed moves more slowly, but preserves longer those things which are impressed upon it by frost or heat. Thin air, however, is considered susceptible to freezing and is quickly affected by the changes of the sun's rays. And they say that uncultivated and neglected land produces thick and harsh air. Where dense vegetation has also grown up, so that neither the sun nor the winds penetrate there, the air will certainly be more raw. 

<margin>Lake Avernus</margin>
At Lake Avernus, the caves were so surrounded by the density of the woods that the exhaling sulfur killed birds flying above through the narrow passes. Caesar, by clearing the woods, rendered it pleasant instead of pestilential. 

<margin>Liburnum</margin>
At Liburnum <note>Likely modern Livorno, a port city in Tuscany.</note>, a maritime town of Etruria, they were vexed by very severe fevers during every dog-day period; by placing a wall against the sea, the inhabitants fared well. But afterward, when water was brought in through ditches for the sake of fortification, they were once again in danger. Varro writes that when he had an army at Corcyra and they were falling everywhere from the plague, he closed all the windows that opened to the south winds, and in that way saved the army. 

<margin>Murano</margin>
In Murano, a famous town of the Venetians, they rarely fall into the plague, even though the nearby metropolitan city [Venice] is both crowded and heavily infested. 

<margin>Fire purges poisons</margin>
They think this happens because of the abundance of glassmakers. For it is indeed certain that the air is purified in a greater measure by fires. And evidence that fire hates poisons is that they have noted that the poisonous carcasses of animals do not produce worms like those of others; because the nature of poison is to kill and immediately extinguish all force of life. But if these same carcasses are touched by lightning, they then indeed produce worms, because their poison has been extinguished by the fire. Moreover, worms are produced in the carcasses of animals from no other source than from a certain fiery force of nature moving that moisture there which is suited to fires; it is the property of poison to extinguish these fires where it prevails; but where it is overcome by fire, it can do nothing. 

If you uproot poisonous herbs, and especially the <term>squilla (sea-onion/squill)</term> <note>original: *squilla*; a plant used in antiquity for medicine, though Alberti here warns of its effect on the soil's health.</note>, it will result in the plants drawing that evil nourishment of the earth into themselves, and thus the foodstuffs will be infected. It will be helpful to set a forest, especially an orchard, against harmful winds. For the breeze which you receive through the shade of leaves matters greatly. 

<margin>Remedy for the consumptive</margin>
They say a pine forest is most beneficial for the <term>ptisici (consumptives)</term> <note>original: *ptisicis*; those suffering from phthisis or tuberculosis, characterized by a wasting away of the body.</note> and for those who do not recover their strength after a long illness. On the contrary, however, are trees which have bitter leaves, for these indeed provide unhealthy breezes; if the place is sweaty and marshy...

...or a marshy place: it will be helpful to make it wide open and well-lit. For the stenches and harmful small creatures that arise will quickly be finished off by dryness and the winds. At Alexandria, there is a public place where, more than anywhere else, the city’s waste and the debris of ruins are deposited. And they have already raised a mountain so high that it provides a great advantage to sailors seeking the harbor entrances. How much more conveniently might low and concave places be filled by such a practice. Venice—which I strongly approve of—has in my time enlarged its areas within the marshes using the city's refuse. Those who cultivate the fields near the Egyptian marshes, says Herodotus <note>Herodotus (c. 484 – c. 425 BC), the Greek historian known as the "Father of History."</note>, spend the night in very tall towers to avoid the force of gnats and flies. In Ferrara, on the Po, few gnats appear inside the city; outside the city, they are cursed by those unaccustomed to them. It is believed they are driven from the city by the abundance of fires and smoke. The fly does not stay in a shady, cold, and windy place, especially where it has windows placed high up. <note>A manicule in the right margin points to the following sentence.</note> There are those who say flies do not enter where a wolf's tail has been buried, and that venomous creatures are driven away by a suspended sea-onion <term>squilla<note>The 'squilla' or sea-onion (Drimia maritima) was often hung in doorways in antiquity as a charm or repellent against evil or pests.</note></term>. Our ancestors used many remedies against the heat. Among these, the <term>cryptoporticus<note>original: "criptoportticus"; an underground or vaulted corridor used in Roman architecture for cooling and shade.</note></term> and vaulted rooms were pleasing; these indeed would receive light only from the very top. Halls with wide windows facing away from the south were also pleasing, especially since they received shady breezes from sheltered areas. <margin>Metellus</margin> Metellus <note>Alberti likely refers here to Marcus Claudius Marcellus, the son of Octavia (sister of Augustus), though he names him Metellus.</note>, born of Octavia, the sister of Augustus, shaded the forum with awnings so that litigants might conduct their business more healthily. But you will realize that a breeze is more effective for cooling than shade if an awning is spread out in such a way that breezes reach it less. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of Natural History.</note> mentions that "receptacles of shade" used to be made in houses. They did not describe what these were like. But whatever they may be, nature must be imitated in them. You may observe that when you gape with an open mouth, you emit warm breath. But when you blow with tightened lips, then the air sent forth strikes as somewhat cold. In the same way, in a building where a breeze comes through a wide space—especially one lit by the sun—it is warm; but where it flows through a narrower and shady passage, there it is faster and colder. If hot water is led through a pipe through other cold water, it is cooled. The same principle will apply to the air. They ask why it is that those walking in the sun do not darken, while those sitting still do; the answer is ready. For breezes are stirred by movement, by which the force of the sun's rays is frustrated. Again, for shade to be cold of itself, it will be helpful to place roof over roof and wall over wall. And indeed, the more these are distant from one another, the more effective the shade will be against the heat. So long as a place thus covered and enclosed does not grow hot. For this gap between both walls has almost the same effect as a wall of equal thickness would have. But it is even better in this regard: because a wall having absorbed heat from the sun...
