...slowly loses heat; and also holds onto imported cold longer. Between these double walls we have mentioned, the air temperature remains steady; in places where the sun's heat is troublesome, a wall constructed from <term>pumice<note>A light, porous volcanic rock known for its insulating properties.</note></term> will absorb less heat and retain less of it. If the doors to the chambers are doubled—that is, if they are closed by outer leaves and likewise by another set of inner leaves, so that a cubit’s worth of air is trapped between the first and second leaves—they will ensure that what is spoken inside cannot be overheard by those outside.

### ¶ Some minor points concerning the use of fire. Chapter XI.

Now, if one must build in an excessively cold place, we shall use fire. The use of fire is varied. But the most convenient of all will be that which is held in an open and bright place. For if it is provided with the smoke excluded or in vaulted spaces, it will give off foul air, which causes watering in the eyes and dulls the vision. Add to this that the very sight of the flames and light from a living hearth is a most cheerful companion—as they say—to fathers conversing by the fireside. But in the middle of the chimney <term>throat<note>original: "gula"; the flue or chimney passage.</note></term> there ought to be an iron transverse valve above; which you should indeed turn and close when all the smoke has cleared and the glowing coal begins to warm itself, so that no external blast of air can be brought in through that opening. A flint or marble wall is both cold and damp. For it congeals the air with its cold and turns it into "sweat" <note>Condensation forming on cold, non-porous surfaces.</note>. Tufa and likewise brick is more <margin>Pay attention: it is more suitable when thoroughly dry. Do not inhabit the internal parts of new and wet walls.</margin> suitable when it has thoroughly dried. Anyone who stays overnight within new and damp walls—especially vaulted ones—will suffer severe illnesses of pain, fevers, and phlegm. Some have been found who lost their sight for that reason, their nerves became numb, their minds and spirits failed, and they became senseless. To make them dry more quickly, thorough openings must be left for the winds to pass through. The wall most favorable to health will be one made of raw brick dried for two years beforehand. A coating applied from <term>gypsum<note>A soft sulfate mineral used for plaster (plaster of Paris).</note></term> makes the air unhealthily thick and is harmful to the lungs and brain. If you line the wall with timber, especially fir or poplar, the place will be healthier and sufficiently warm in winter and not very hot in summer; but it will perhaps become infested with moths and bedbugs. This will be avoided if you fill the empty spaces with reeds, or block all the hiding places and refuges for pests. They will be most correctly blocked with clay, small pebbles, and <term>olive oil dregs<note>original: "amurca"; the bitter, watery sediment from olive oil production, used historically as a pesticide.</note></term> kneaded together. For every kind of creature that arises from putrefaction utterly loathes oil.

<margin>How to expel snakes.</margin>
**S**ince we have happened upon these matters, it is helpful to recount here some things we have read in the works of venerable authors. It is desirable that a building should be free from every annoyance. The Oetans <note>An ancient tribe of central Greece.</note> performed a sacrifice to Hercules because he had freed them from gnats. And at Meliunte, the Aeolians would sacrifice to Apollo to drive away caterpillars from the vineyards and to provide a "multitude of mice" <note>This likely refers to Apollo Smintheus, the "Mouse-God," who could both bring and avert plague and crop-destroying rodents.</note>. This was indeed a great benefit, but they did not hand down the exact method by which they achieved these things. However, I find the following among some writers: the Assyrians say that by burning the lung of a <term>latus<note>original: "lato"; a large fish of the Nile (Lates niloticus), often mentioned in ancient natural histories.</note></term> fish, or by hanging an onion or a <term>squill<note>original: "squilla"; the sea-onion (Urginea maritima), used since antiquity as a rodent repellent.</note></term> from the lintel of the doorway, all venomous animals are put to flight. Aristotle says that you will drive snakes out of houses with the scent of <term>rue<note>original: "rutae"; a bitter herb (Ruta graveolens) traditionally used to repel insects and serpents.</note></term>. And if you throw meat into a jar, you will trap a great number of wasps that enter it. And by placing sulfur and

Pliny says they are most effectively treated with the <term>heliotrope<note>A plant whose flowers turn toward the sun, believed in ancient medicine to have various neutralizing properties.</note></term> herb. Among the ancients, it is testified that there are sharp, innate enmities between certain things and living creatures from nature, to the point that one brings plague and destruction upon the other. And they say that on the head of a leech, when it clings stubbornly to human limbs, if you apply a bedbug, it will immediately let go and fall off languidly. ...the asp <note>original: "aspidem"; referring to various venomous snakes.</note> will flee. <margin>Remedy against caterpillars.</margin> Against caterpillars, they command that the skull bones of a female horse be placed on a stake in the gardens. <margin>Against bats and flies.</margin> Plane trees are offensive to bats. If you sprinkle a decoction made from elderberry flowers, you will kill all the flies. This is done even more quickly with hellebore; indeed, both the fly and the decoction of black hellebore will be lethal. Hound’s-tongue <note>original: "dens caninus"; likely the plant *Cynoglossum officinale*, though literally "dog's tooth," it was widely used in folk medicine to repel pests.</note>, when placed in a hall along with its tail or feet (as they say), drives away the nuisance of flies. <margin>Remedy against lizards.</margin> Lizards <note>original: "stelliones"; specifically spotted geckos or newts.</note> cannot endure the scent of saffron. <margin>Against gnats.</margin> The smoke of burnt lupins kills gnats. <margin>Against mice.</margin> Mice are killed by the scent of aconite <note>original: "aconiti"; also known as wolfsbane.</note>, even from a great distance. <margin>Against bedbugs.</margin> Mice and bedbugs alike are killed by the smoky scent of <term>ink<note>original: "atramenti"; likely referring to a pungent black vitriol or shoe-blacking used as a fumigant.</note></term>. <margin>Against fleas.</margin> If you sprinkle a place with a decoction of <term>colocynth<note>original: "coloquintida"; a bitter, desert-growing vine used as a powerful purgative and pesticide.</note></term> or likewise with sea-caltrop, all fleas will vanish. If, however, you sprinkle the area with goat’s blood, they will all run toward it in swarms <note>This was a method of baiting pests to a single spot to destroy them.</note>; they are put to flight by the scent of cabbage, and even more so by oleander. Fleas, jumping about aimlessly, are easily trapped by wide vessels full of water arranged across the floor. <margin>Against moths.</margin> Moths will be put to flight by the scent of wormwood, anise seed, and savin <note>A species of juniper used to protect textiles.</note>. They claim that a garment will not be touched by moths if it has been kept on a hempen rope. But let this be enough of these matters, which were perhaps more than a most serious reader might have required. Yet you will grant me pardon, as these things are not foreign to the correction of a site's defects—even if nothing seems to be entirely sufficient to combat the annoyance and hateful persistence of such most troublesome pests.

## ¶ On covering walls with tapestries, heating rooms, and reforming and correcting the faults of those walls. Chapter XIII.

**I** return to the matter at hand. It is a marvel why this should be so: if you clothe the wall of an atrium with tapestries woven of wool, you will have a warm place; if they are made of linen, it will become colder. If a location is excessively damp, dig sewers and well-like pits, and fill them with pumice or gravel so that no water becomes stagnant and rotten. Afterward, spread a layer of charcoal on the ground one foot deep. Upon this, spread coarse sand, or—more effectively and conveniently—small pipes <note>Small ceramic conduits used for drainage or air circulation under floors.</note>; then lay the pavement on top. It is entirely beneficial if air can circulate beneath the pavement. <margin>Against the heat of the sun and the severity of winter.</margin> But it will work most beautifully against the heat of the sun and the severity of winter if, otherwise, the ground is not moist but dry. Dig the area of the dining room to a depth of twelve feet and floor this with bare timber; with a floor covering laid over it, the air inside provides a surface above which you would believe to be most cold—so much so that even with shoes on, the feet grow cold from that material, even with no pavement laid except for the boards. If you make the roof of this dining room vaulted high above the head, you will marvel at how cool it is in summer and how warm in winter. But if by chance that occurs which the poet complains of in his satire <note>Alberti quotes Juvenal, Satire III, lines 236–238, regarding the noise of Rome.</note>: "The passage of carriages in the narrow turnings of the streets, and the abuse of the standing cattle-drivers, would snatch away sleep." From which noise the sick man, tormented by the labor...

# Book X. On the Restoration of Works. Folio 172.

...blunted <note>original: "ret."; completing "retundunt" from the previous page, meaning to blunt or dull sound.</note>. We learn how this inconvenience is most beautifully addressed from a letter of Pliny the Younger in these words: "Attached to it is a bedroom for night and sleep; into this, neither the voices of the servant boys <note>original: "suulorū"; likely a transcription error for "vernarum," meaning home-born slaves or servants.</note>, nor the murmur of the sea, nor the motion of storms, nor the light of lightning reaches; indeed, you do not even perceive the daylight unless the windows are open, so deep and hidden is its retreat. The reason is that an intervening space separates the wall of the bedroom and the garden; and so, it consumes all sound in the void between."

<margin>On defects in walls.</margin>
I come to walls. These are the faults of walls: for they either develop a crack, or they disintegrate, or they compress the framework <note>original: "ossa"; literally "bones," referring to the structural stones or "skeleton" of the masonry</note>, or they depart from the vertical alignment of the plumb-line. The causes of these evils are various, as are the remedies. Some causes are manifest; others are more hidden, and it is not sufficiently clear what would be of help until after the damage has been received. There are others, moreover, that are not at all obscure, but perhaps human laziness has persuaded itself that they do not have as much power to destroy works as they actually do. The cause in a wall will be obvious: for example, where it is more slender than is sufficient, where its joints are not suitable, where it is filled with harmful fittings, or finally where its framework is not sufficiently protected against the injuries of the weather. Those things which are hidden and happen contrary to expectation are these: earthquakes, lightning, and all the inconstancy of the soil and of nature. But above all, what harms all parts of works the most is human negligence and lack of care. <margin>The wild fig is a deaf ram.</margin> A "deaf ram" to walls, he says, is the wild fig tree <note>original: "caprificus"; the wild fig is notorious in classical literature for its invasive roots that can split stone.</note>; nor is it credible to say what immense stones I have seen moved and thrust apart by the force and wedge of a little root born between the fissures; which, if someone had wiped it away when it was first tender, the work would have remained free from the plague. 

->The ram.<-

I strongly approve of the ancients who established households from the public purse so that they might care for and protect public works. There were those whom Agrippa left, assigned to this number: two hundred and fifty. Those whom Caesar [assigned]: four hundred and sixty. They dedicated fifteen feet nearby to the work so that there would be a clear path around the aqueducts, lest the vaulting or the sides be loosened by the rising roots of trees. Private individuals also seem to have looked to this in those works which they wished to be eternal. For on their own tomb monuments, they would inscribe how many feet into the field were dedicated to religion <note>i.e., set aside as sacred and protected from agricultural use or encroachment.</note>. Some [dedicated] fifteen feet; others twenty.

<margin>How trees may be killed.</margin>
But lest I repeat myself: they believe that adult trees are killed and destroyed if they are cut back by one foot during the days when the sun enters the Dog Star <note>The "Dog Days" of mid-to-late summer, when the star Sirius rises with the sun.</note>; and after a hole is made through the pith, the oil called <term>petroleum<note>original: "petroleum"; literally "rock oil," referring to naturally occurring bitumen or naphtha used here as a herbicide.</note></term> is poured in, mixed with flour of sulfur; or if a decoction of burnt bean pods is sprinkled abundantly. You will extirpate a forest, says Columella, if the flower of lupin is soaked for one day in the juice of hemlock and sprinkled on the roots. A tree touched by menstrual blood loses its foliage, says Solinus. Others also assert that trees are killed by the root of a sea-parsnip.

# Leon Battista Alberti. On the Art of Building.

<margin>He teaches how to join a wall to a wall.</margin>
...effectively kill [the noise], says Pliny <note>original: "necant inqt Plini⁹"; referring back to the previous page's quote from Pliny the Younger regarding sound insulation.</note>. Now I return to the previous matters. If a wall is more slender than is sufficient, we will then either apply a second, new wall to the old one so they become one; or, for the sake of avoiding great expense, we will build only the **bones** <note>Alberti uses "bones" (*ossa*) to describe the structural skeleton of a building, such as pillars or framing.</note> between them: that is, pillars, columns, or beams. A wall is joined to another wall in this way: in the old wall, strong stone "teeth" <note>original: "capitibus lapideis"; literally stone heads or projecting blocks.</note> made of recycled stone <term>recycled stone (lapide redivivio)<gloss>Building stone salvaged from older ruins or structures to be reused in new masonry.</gloss></term> will be fixed at several points; they shall be secured so they protrude to enter the new wall you are raising, so they are like a suture between two skins; and this new wall should only be built with regular stone. You shall raise a pillar through a wall thus: mark its future width on the old wall with red chalk <note>original: "rubrica"; a red earth or chalk used by architects and builders for marking lines.</note>. After that, beginning from the foundation itself, you will dig a "window" into the wall whose width is slightly larger than the mark you made on the wall with the red chalk. The height of this window should not be great. Soon, it should be filled with square stone in level rows with the greatest care. It is done in this way: so that the part of the wall left within the red chalk marks is held by the thickness of the pillar, and the wall is made stable. By the same method by which you built the first part of this pillar, you shall then introduce the remaining parts until the work is finished at the top. So much regarding slenderness.

<margin>Bonding in a wall.</margin>
Where **bondings** <note>original: "nexure"; the structural joints or connections between wall sections.</note> are lacking, we will use iron or rather bronze ties. But care must be taken that the "bones" are not weakened by these "wounds" <note>He warns that cutting deep holes to insert metal ties can compromise the very pillars they are meant to support.</note>. But if by chance the weight of shifting earth presses against the side, or if it is damaged by moisture: dig a trench along the wall as wide as the situation requires, and build semicircles <note>buttressing arches</note> which will take the weight of the leaning earth; and add "nostrils" <note>original: "nares"; drainage holes or weep holes to prevent water pressure.</note> in several places, through which the seeping moisture may flow and be cleared away. Or, lay down timbers that hold the wall back from the encroaching earth with their ends, and fasten these timbers with cross-bars and then load them with rubble. This will be beneficial because the heaped pile will settle before the strength of the material fails.
¶ On those things which cannot be foreseen but can be corrected once they are done, such as fissures, foundations, columns, the structural framework of small shrines, leans, walls, and pavements.
->Chapter XIIII.<-

<margin>Cracks in walls.</margin>
**I** come to those things which cannot be foreseen, but can be corrected after they have happened. A **fissure** in a wall and the leaning of its lines sometimes happen because the vaults <note>original: "testudine"; literally "tortoise shell," a common architectural term for an arched or vaulted ceiling.</note> push out the walls, or they cannot tolerate the unequal weight placed upon them; but the most serious defects of this kind come only from the foundations. However, we can understand whether they come from the foundations or elsewhere by the signs. For a crack in the wall—to begin with that—will indicate the cause of the defect in the direction it leaned as it rose. But if the crack does not lean in any direction...

<summary>Alberti provides practical engineering solutions for reinforcing thin walls using "stone teeth" and pillars, as well as methods for protecting foundations from earth pressure and moisture, before discussing how to diagnose the causes of wall fissures.</summary>

# Book X. On the Restoration of Works. Folio CLXXIII.

...[the crack] had proceeded straight upwards, it falls apart at the top. We will consider the rows of stones on this side and that. For those that indeed descend from the level line will demonstrate that a weak foundation lies beneath them. But if the wall is undamaged at the top, and several cracks gape at the bottom with their "lips" touching where they rise toward their heads, then this indicates the corners of the walls are firm, but the fault lies in the middle of the foundation's length. If there is only one such crack, the wider it is at the top, the more it indicates a disturbance has occurred in the corners. 

Therefore, where it is necessary to provide for foundations, depending on the size of the work and the firmness of the soil, dig a narrow but deep pit next to the wall until you find solid and firm ground. Once the lowest part of the wall there has been undermined, immediately stuff it with **regular stone** <term>regular stone (ordinario lapide)<gloss>Stone cut into uniform, rectangular shapes (ashlar) to ensure even distribution of weight in masonry.</gloss></term> and let it harden when finished. When it has hardened, dig another similar pit elsewhere and build up in the same way, letting it dry when finished. By this method of staggered excavations, you will substitute a firm support for the wall. 

But if, according to your judgment, the soil does not provide a steady base, then in certain places a little distance from the corners, on both sides at the base of the wall—that is, in the area under the roof and the area outside directly opposite—pits should be made where piles will be driven very closely into the ground. These shall be equipped with very strong timbers on every side along the length of the wall. After that, thicker and by far the strongest beams will be passed across through the base of the wall so they sit upon the height of the timbers, supporting the wall with their "backs" like bridges or yokes. 

In all such restorations we have reviewed, care must be taken that this new work you are adding is not in any part weaker than what is required to carry the load well and for a long time. For the entire mass of the wall would immediately collapse into this weaker part by relying on it. But if the foundations have shifted toward the middle of the wall, and the upper parts remain undamaged, then you will mark a wide arch on the face of the wall with **red chalk** <note>original: "rubrica"; a red earth or chalk used by architects and builders for marking lines.</note> as the situation requires—that is, so it encompasses everything that has moved beneath it. Then, starting from either end of this arch, bore through the wall with a hole no larger than what can receive a single stone of the arch—which stone we have elsewhere called a **wedge** <note>original: "cuneum"; the wedge-shaped stone or voussoir used to construct an arch.</note>. Set this wedge itself to its lines just as a radius drawn from the center of that circle would direct. After that, open another contiguous hole and fill it with a similar wedge, and so 

<margin>Regarding the columns.</margin>
on, completing the arch with successive work. The undertaking will succeed with no fear and without any danger. ¶ If columns and **bones** <note>Alberti uses "bones" (*ossa*) to describe the structural skeleton of a building, such as pillars or framing.</note> are weakened anywhere, you will restore them thus: build a strong arch of tile and gypsum under the beam of the work...

->## Leon Battista Alberti: On the Art of Building.<-

...also of gypsum with masses suited for this purpose: so that the arch there, which will most recently be drawn up, might well fill the old openings. This construction should be done with the greatest haste and with no interruption of the work. For it is the nature of gypsum that it expands while drying <note>Alberti identifies a key chemical property of gypsum—its expansion—as an engineering advantage to ensure a tight fit when underpinning old masonry.</note>. Therefore, this newest construction will support the burden of the old wall or vault on its own shoulders as much as it has taken upon itself. Once these things are prepared, you shall remove the damaged column from there and substitute an intact one in its place. 

But if it pleases you to support it with timber and to strive with under-props: place levers <term>levers (stateras)<gloss>The Latin term 'statera' usually refers to a balance scale, but Alberti uses it here to describe a mechanical lever system for lifting masonry.</gloss></term> of beams underneath, and load the extension of these with baskets of sand. They will lift the weight gradually, without any shaking, and in a balanced manner. And if the wall has departed from the perpendicular: set up timbers so that they remain fixed against the wall. To each of these, add individual supports of very strong wood, with their lower feet spread out from the wall. Then, tighten them gradually with bars or small wedges, so that they push against the wall. Thus, by joining these distributed efforts together, the wall will be restored to its perpendicular. 

If that is not permitted: you shall steady the support of the beams on firm ground, and you shall pitch the beams well with pitch and oil, so that they are not corrupted by contact with the lime. Presently, build up buttresses <term>buttresses (anterides)<gloss>From the Greek 'anterides,' these are external supports built against a wall to strengthen it or resist outward thrust.</gloss></term> of squared stone, so that the pitched support is enclosed.

<margin>How we may lift a colossus or a small building from a leaning position.</margin>

It may perhaps happen that a colossus <note>A very large statue or monument.</note> or a small building is leaning entirely to one side along with its base. Then you shall lift the side where they are sinking, or you shall lower the side where they are rising. Both works are daring. Therefore, first join and bind together both the base and those parts which could be loosened by movement, using timbers and all that framing. The convenient method of binding is this: we shall lift the structures tightened with wedges by placing a beam underneath in the manner of a lever, which we have called a balance. 

You shall lower it by a trench gradually extended. It shall be done thus: for you will begin from the middle of the side under the roots of the lowest foundation, and there you will cut away to the depth an opening not very wide, but high enough so that you may lay underneath, at your discretion, the firmest **regular stones** substituted there. In building this substructure, you shall not render the opening completely filled to the very top, but you shall leave a few inches <note>original: "palmos"</note> empty, which you will fill with strong wedges placed quite close together. In the same way, you shall subsequently support the whole side of that shrine which you wish to settle more deeply from there. When these have taken up the weight, you should remove the wedges themselves very neatly and carefully, and by degrees you will restore the wall to the correct straightness of the perpendicular. Presently, where the empty spaces remain between the wedges, you shall reinforce them with wedges made of the firmest stone.

At Rome, at the greatest Basilica of Peter <note>This refers to the Old St. Peter's Basilica, which in Alberti's time was famously suffering from structural instability before its eventual demolition and reconstruction.</note>, where the walls of the aisles leaning on columns away from the perpendicular threatened the roofs with ruin, I had thought of it thus: to decide to cut away each leaning part of the wall that any column supports, and to move it out of the way. And that part of the wall which had been removed...

# Book 10. On the Restoration of Works.

...restore the work by the ordinary method, leaving <term>stone teeth (dentibus lapideis)<gloss>Protruding stones left in a wall to provide a mechanical bond for new masonry being joined to it.</gloss></term> and very strong clamps on either side, to which the new part of the structure may be annexed. Finally, for the roof, I would have commended the beam—from which the leaning part of the wall was to be removed—to be supported by <term>A-frame machines (capreis)<gloss>Called a 'capra' (goat) in Latin, this is a tripod-shaped hoisting machine.</gloss></term> erected above the roof, with the feet of the machines stabilized on both sides on the firmer part of the roof and wall. I would have carried this out successively on one column after another, as much as the situation required. <margin>The A-frame is a nautical instrument.</margin> **The A-frame** is a nautical instrument made of three timbers, the top ends of which are joined together with a pin and shackled; the feet, however, are placed in a triangle. We use this machine most conveniently with pulleys and screws for lifting heavy loads.

<margin>On the veneer of the wall.</margin>
When you are about to apply a <term>veneer (crustam)<gloss>A decorative or protective surface layer, such as plaster, stucco, or stone facing.</gloss></term> to an old wall or floor for the first time, first wash it with pure water and the clear liquid of lime mixed with marble dust, whitened with a brush; in this way, it will hold the sand-plaster. In a small crack in a floor or an outdoor pavement, it will become watertight if you work in and pour in ashes purified in a sieve and mixed with oil, especially linseed oil. Most suitable for this work will be chalk well-worked with quicklime and baked in a furnace, and immediately applied with oil after the crack has first been cleared of all dust. This shall be done by wiping with brushes and blowing away debris with many leaves <note>Alberti suggests using large leaves or perhaps a bellows-like action with foliage to clear fine dust from cracks before sealing them.</note>; and we shall not neglect the elegance of the work. If walls happen to be of an unappealing height, you should lead the eye with either attached moldings or <term>cornices (coronas)<gloss>Horizontal decorative projections that crown a wall or architectural feature.</gloss></term>, or by painted sections, which divide that height at appropriate places. But if the wall is excessively long, apply columns from top to bottom, not too frequently, but spaced out. For the gaze will be halted and delayed as if by resting places where the traveler may pause and be less offended by the vastness. This also serves the purpose. Indeed, many things situated in a lower place, or surrounded by walls lower than reason requires, will seem smaller and narrower than they actually are. It is well known that after many things were made higher, having been increased by floor or wall, they were seen from afar to be larger than they appeared before. And by providing suitable openings, or placing a doorway in a better spot, or opening windows in a higher part of the wall, it is established that dining rooms and chambers are rendered more dignified and far more elegant.

->**The most elegant and extremely useful work "On the Art of Building" by Leon Battista Alberti of Florence, a most distinguished man, was most accurately printed in Paris at the Golden Sun in the Street of Saint Jacques: by the labor of the masters Berthold Rembolt and Ludwig Hornken, residing in the same street at the sign of the Three Crowns across from Saint Benedict. In the year of our Lord 1512. On the 23rd day of August.**<-
